16025-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
For September 30, 1897, the children's newspaper The Great Round World led with news from the Ottoman Empire. The Sultan of Turkey, it reported, had at last ordered a commission to visit Armenian villages hurt by massacres, noting destroyed schools, churches, and monasteries. Two Muslims, three Armenians, and one Greek sat on the commission, which was also to plan orphan asylums.

The paper's promise was news made readable for children, without long speeches or hard words. Each number mixed foreign affairs with home news and short features, so a school reader could follow the world week by week. This issue captures a moment of late Victorian concern for Armenia and for the victims of mass violence.
23572-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number three hundred seventy nine for May eighteen forty seven, opens with a long essay on M. de Tocqueville, hailed as one of the greatest political thinkers of the day, fit to stand beside Machiavelli and Bacon. Less caustic than Tacitus and less eloquent than Burke, Tocqueville earns praise for calm judgment, a keen eye, and just reflection.

Born amid French party strife, placed between feudal ruins and modern rebuilding, he surveyed both worlds with rare balance, the essay argues. Other pieces in the number keep Blackwood's mix of politics, literature, and review. Readers of Victorian journals will enjoy the essay as a contemporary verdict on Democracy in America, written while its author still lived and Europe still argued over his ideas.
23690-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for April 1847 opens with a long review essay on Cromwell, taking Thomas Carlyle's edition of Cromwell's letters and speeches as its text. The reviewer praises Carlyle as an editor while sharply disputing him as a commentator, calling his hero-worship of the Puritan leader extravagant and his view of English Puritanism paradoxical.

As a monthly miscellany, the issue goes on to other articles, tales, and reviews in Blackwood's Tory voice. The Cromwell essay sets its tone: learned, combative, and sure of its judgments. For modern readers it is a window onto how Victorian Britain argued about its revolutionary past, in the very pages where such arguments were fought.
25633-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 384 for October 1847, volume sixty-two, gathers essays, tales, and reviews in the monthly's usual mix. Transcribers note that vowels with macron and breve marks are rendered with special signs in this text.

Contents list Hans Christian Andersen and the Emperor's New Clothes, the Vision of Cagliostro, pieces on Tiberius, Agrippa, Milton, Mirabeau, and Beethoven, Maga in America, and the times of George II. Art in early Christian ages, the Portrait, hounds and horses at Rome, and a song follow, with a note on Andersen's Improvisatore opening the reading.
26484-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for June 1847 leads with an essay on North America, Siberia, and Russia, following Sir George Simpson's overland circuit of the globe. The Hudson's Bay governor galloped from the Atlantic to the Pacific, then on to the British Channel, glancing at the Wall of China and the Arctic Circle. He pressed through polar regions, past tribes whose names alone survive, to the Russian court.

The essay wonders at the journey's purpose, which a governor dedicating his volumes to his company's directors does not reveal. Elsewhere the number turns classical, tracing a passage of Catullus to a freer rendering of Euripides' Hippolytus, where a garland is offered to Artemis from an untouched meadow. Travel, empire, and letters share the issue.
27020-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for August 1847, number 382, opens with a long review of Grote's History of Greece, praised as equal to the demands of a critical age. The reviewer sets Grote above earlier historians like Mitford for his judgment of evidence and his feel for past times.

The rest of the number ranges widely: Ben Nevis and Ben Muich Dhui, a letter on truths in popular superstitions, and a history of Napoleon's captivity at St. Helena. Fiction and essay follow, with Juancho the bull-fighter, The Emerald Studs, and a piece on Reid and the philosophy of common sense.
31859-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 377, March 1847, volume sixty-one, opens with an essay on pauperism and its treatment. It is introduced by Wordsworth's lines on turning elsewhere to see ill sights of maddening passions mutually inflamed. Its argument insists that to deal with pauperism, one must know the causes that impoverish individuals and masses.

The essay follows displaced workers, coachmen, guards, ostlers, horse-keepers, harness-makers, and farriers, into the back streets and alleys of London, the records of benevolent institutions, and conversations with administrators of parochial relief. Readers get a Victorian magazine issue that treats poverty as a practical problem, not a natural law.
32539-eight-days-in-new-orleans-in-febru:
Albert J. Pickett's Eight Days in New-Orleans in February, 1847 gathers sketches first printed in the Alabama Journal of Montgomery. Written from a few days' sojourn in the Crescent City, the book opens with De Soto's discovery of the Mississippi and the fate of his expedition.

Pickett describes New Orleans as a magnificent emporium of commerce, setting its present trade against its early history. He warns readers that his time for collecting facts was short and that he was trying descriptive and historic writing for the first time, asking charitable friends to forgive imperfections.
50322-orville-southerland-cox-pioneer-of:
Orville Southerland Cox, Pioneer of 1847 is a biographical sketch of a Utah pioneer. Part of it comes from a sketch by Adelia B Cox Sidwell, written for the Daughters of the Pioneers at Manti, Utah, in 1913. A poem by Clarence Hawkes on the pioneer spirit opens the pamphlet.

Cox was born in Plymouth, New York, on November 25, 1814. He was one of twelve children, ten of whom reached maturity. His father died when the boy was about fifteen. Cox was then bound out as apprentice to a blacksmith, under a deacon Jones. The deacon was a pillar of the church and counted an excellent man. The agreement bound the boy to obedient work until twenty one. Such family sketches, gathered by pioneers' daughters, preserved the plain record of the 1847 migration generation.
56537-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxx-no-2-feb:
Graham's Magazine, volume thirty, number two, for February 1847, is a monthly number of the famed Philadelphia magazine of literature and fashion. The issue carries a table of its stories, essays, poems, and fashion plates.

The number opens with Tribulation Trepid, a man without a hope, a phrenological tale by Joseph C Neal. Other fiction includes The Oath of Marion, a story of the Revolution, and The Executioner. Articles treat the game birds of America, the islets of the gulf, and the present romantic school of French literature, with a piece on Dumas and Hamlet. Poems include verses by Leigh Hunt on receiving a crown of ivy from John Keats. A print of herds of bisons and elks on the Upper Missouri, after Bodmer, and a Paris fashion plate fill out the number.
58888-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxi-no-4-oc:
Graham's Magazine for October 1847 forms this number, the fourth of its thirty-first year. The list of parts splits the sheet in two halves, as the sheet splits its fare. The first half is prose: tales, lore, and prose pieces. A tale of a town's sawbones stands at the head. A court of old days and a tale of a firkin of butter, a tale of a flirt, and a tale of the red men come in its train.

More prose runs on: the isles of the gulf in a long tale cut in parts, a ruse, a man with a big box, and the hunt. A look at new books closes that half. The next half gives verse, tune, and dress. Names like Le Follet, Brain Work and Hand Work, and Midnight and Daybreak show its spread.
andersen-improvisatore-howitt-1847:
Hans Christian Andersen published The Improvisatore in Denmark in 1835, and Mary Howitt Englished it in 1847. The novel made Andersen famous across Europe a decade before his fairy tales ruled nurseries. Antonio, a poor Roman boy with a gift for improvised song, tells his own story from childhood onward.

Antonio rises from street singer to admired performer, through love, loss, and patronage. Rome, Naples, and Venice glow in the background of his fortunes. Andersen drew on his own Italian travels and his hunger for recognition. Howitt, a tireless carrier of Scandinavian writing into English, gave the book its English life. It stands apart from the tales, as his great novel of the artist.
arxiv-2412-00747:
Marco Laudato and co-authors test whether a learning based operator can mimic how a platelet bends in blood flow, in a 2024 paper. Platelets are small cell fragments that help blood clot. Modeling each one in fine detail is costly, so faster stand-ins are needed for large clot models.

The team trained the operator on particle simulations of a platelet skin under shear stress. Given a start shape and the stress, the model predicts the bent shape. Its error stayed near half a percent across modes. The authors present the method as a building block that can plug fine platelet detail into broad models of clot growth.
arxiv-2412-00947:
Ryo Kamoi and co-authors test whether vision-language models truly see shapes, in work from 2024. Their test set, VisOnlyQA, asks direct questions on shape, angle, and size in figures, charts, chemical drawings, and 3D forms. Humans ace the set with ease. The team ran twenty-three top models through its twelve tasks.

Even the strongest models did poorly on these basic reads. Extra training on the set's own drills did not fix the flaw, even for like tasks. Models with stronger text cores saw shapes better, which hints the snag sits in how visual data is handed over. All data and code are shared.
arxiv-2412-01547:
Erick Galinkin and Martin Sablotny propose in 2024 a better way to catch jailbreak prompts aimed at large language models. Such prompts try to trick a model into giving answers that break safety, privacy, or content rules. Blocking the prompt early can stop the harmful reply before it starts.

Their method turns each prompt into a numerical embedding using models pre-trained for search-like tasks. Classic machine learning classifiers then judge whether the embedding looks like a jailbreak attempt. The authors report that this pairing beats every public method from open source security tools for language models. The work sits in a growing line of defenses that owners of these models add on top of training-time safeguards. It treats prompt detection as a sorting task rather than a reading task, which keeps the check fast and simple.
arxiv-2412-01647: Agrawal, Charalambous, and Donnay study in this 2025 paper the hidden symmetry algebra of Einstein-Yang-Mills theory. Working from the subleading part of the theory's equations far from sources, they build charges conserved up to second order in empty, non-radiating regions. Those higher-spin charges, they show, obey the celestial sw algebra, a symmetry first spotted in soft gluons and gravitons. The short paper ties a charge-based route to that symmetry.
arxiv-2412-01747:
Ziyun Wang and four co-authors estimate a continuous time human motion field directly from event camera streams. Frame based human mesh recovery suffers aliasing and motion blur from limited temporal resolution. Earlier event methods optimize over fixed pose sets at high frame rates, which grows prohibitively expensive as resolution rises.

A recurrent feed forward network predicts motion in the latent space of possible human motions. The motion field is a time implicit function, so poses can be queried in parallel at arbitrary temporal resolutions. A new hardware synchronized high speed dataset, built with a beam splitter, fills a benchmark gap. On it, joint errors drop by 23.8 percent against prior event methods while compute time falls by 69 percent.
arxiv-2412-02347: Emanuele Maggio derives in this 2024 paper an exact formula for electron states in crystals that doubles as a detector of topological materials. If the wave function expands in Gaussian-type orbitals, Bloch states in three dimensions can be written with theta functions and their slopes. Group rules act on those functions in closed form. Mixing group theory with smoothness demands, he builds a method that spots band inversions, the marks of a topological band layout, and tests it on two toy models.
arxiv-2412-03547:
Bihag Dave and Gaurav Goswami trained neural networks in 2024 to read dark matter properties from galaxy rotation curves. A curve shows how fast a galaxy spins at each radius, which reflects its dark matter halo and stars. Inferring halo values normally takes slow statistical fitting.

Networks learned from simulated curves, then read real curves of dwarf galaxies from a standard catalogue. They returned halo values such as particle mass and scale radii, plus the stellar mass-to-light ratio, with uncertainty estimates. Two uncertainty methods were compared with Bayesian results. Noise in training data was also studied, since real curves carry errors. The networks recovered values that describe the studied galaxies well.
arxiv-2412-03947: Parfenov and co-authors study how well a planned detector can measure sideways flow in fixed-target tests. The work dates to 2024 and comes from a large atom smasher project in Russia. A key goal of that project is to learn how dense nuclear matter acts when it is packed with extra matter charge. The team checks the planned setup for this flow task.
arxiv-2412-04047:
Alessandro De Gregorio and Francesco Iafrate speed up a family of sparse statistical estimators, in a 2024 paper. Bridge-type estimators fit models while shrinking many coefficients to zero, which selects the variables that matter. Pathwise methods compute the whole solution curve as the penalty strength varies, instead of refitting at each value. The catch is that bridge penalties with powers at or below one make the target bumpy and nonconvex, so standard solvers struggle.

The authors apply algorithms from nonconvex optimization theory to walk the path anyway. For some losses, these estimators gain oracle-like traits, finding the true variables as reliably as if they were known in advance. Fast full paths matter in genomics and finance, where analysts scan many penalty levels before choosing a model.
arxiv-2412-04247:
Marco Garosi, Riccardo Tedoldi, Davide Boscaini, Massimiliano Mancini, Nicu Sebe, and Fabio Poiesi wrote a 2024 computer vision paper on splitting 3D objects into their parts without training on those objects. Supervised models only know the fixed part lists they were trained on. Vision language models offer an open ended alternative, but they demand fiddly prompts and ignore 3D shape.

Their system, COPS, renders a point cloud from many viewpoints and pulls features from the images. It then projects those features back onto the 3D points and merges them with a geometry aware procedure that keeps neighbors consistent. Points are clustered into parts and labeled. Across five datasets, COPS set the state of the art for zero shot part segmentation while staying efficient enough to scale.
arxiv-2412-04347:
Alexandre Chénier and co-authors demonstrate quantized sideways drift in a photonic system built from frequencies in a 2024 paper. Topological materials conduct along protected one-way channels that shrug off defects, prized for metrology and quantum devices. Light is harder to steer this way than electrons, since photons carry no charge.

Their Chern insulator is encoded in the frequency modes of light rather than in real space, a synthetic dimension. They measure a Hall drift that lands on quantized values, proving the topology survives the encoding. Synthetic dimensions let tabletop optics mimic exotic matter cheaply. The result supports photonic circuits that route light with the same stubborn reliability electrons show in quantum Hall devices.
arxiv-2412-04547:
Pierre Pantaleón and co-authors design flat energy bands in a semiconductor in a 2024 physics paper. They study a thin sheet of electrons in gallium arsenide, fenced by a patterned gate. The pattern lays a repeating voltage landscape over the sheet.

Exact math solutions let the team map when narrow bands and fake Landau levels appear. A wave-based method tracks how bands shift as the pattern strengthens. Breaking the pattern's mirror symmetry yields a curved quantum geometry measure. A self-consistent step adds the push and pull between electrons. The map shows a contest between pattern strength and electron interplay. Such control could help build new quantum states on demand in chip labs.
arxiv-2412-04947:
The authors present C2LEVA in a 2024 paper on comprehensive, contamination free evaluation of language models. Benchmark scores can be inflated when test data leak into training data, and builders rarely reveal their training sets. Trustworthy testing needs tasks that renew themselves and stay protected.

Their bilingual benchmark covers twenty two tasks, each aimed at a specific ability or application. A systematic strategy automates test data renewal and enforces protection during release. Fifteen open and proprietary models were evaluated at scale. The authors argue the design gives a fuller and more honest picture of model ability.
arxiv-2412-05047:
Turchi and co-authors present a machine learning method that reads basic facts about stars from plain survey photos of the sky. Big photo surveys such as SDSS and SkyMapper cover millions of stars but give only brightness in a few colors. Richer detail normally comes from spectra, which are far slower to collect. Their work, published in 2024, aims to bridge that gap.

First the team merged spectra from several large surveys into one cleaned catalog with a single scale. A neural network trained on that catalog then infers a star's temperature, surface gravity, and metal content from photo data alone. Errors run near 100 degrees in temperature and a tenth of a unit in the other two measures. The method still works for metal-poor stars, where such estimates usually fail.
arxiv-2412-05247:
Vicenç Méndez, Rosa Flaquer-Galmés, and Arnab Pal study how long random walkers linger in a region in a 2024 paper. Their walkers have memory: step timing follows a broad wait law rather than fixed ticks, which can slow spread. The team also adds random resets that snap the walker back to a set point.

They solve a backward equation to get the full spread of linger times in a bounded stretch and in a half line. The half line case revisits the famed arcsine law, which the team tests across rest regimes. Shapes, means, and long run limits are worked out for both normal and anomalous spread. Computer runs matched the math well. The results feed fields from physics to search theory.
arxiv-2412-05747:
Daskalakis and five co-authors chart shapes of stories with game theory, modeling Romeo and Juliet as a game, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Stories record human experience, and mathematical tools can extract their structure. Prior tools were limited to one-dimensional charts and social networks. Modern AI can identify plot structure, incentives, and counterfactual branches.

Characters become players with incentives in the game model. Decision making can then be interrogated quantitatively scene by scene. The author's conception of the characters' world becomes partially visible. Shakespeare's tragedy demonstrates the technique in depth. Broader replication to other stories and real-life scenarios is discussed.
arxiv-2412-05947:
Akhil Nair, Lucas Foppa, and Matthias Scheffler build a materials search workflow guided by symbolic regression in a 2024 paper. Active learning finds good materials faster when a few key parameters describe the target trait. For acid stable oxides used in water splitting, those parameters were unknown because many atomic processes interact.

Their workflow uses a regression method that writes compact formulas from many candidate features. Ensembles of such models, trained on resampled data with random feature dropout, give both predictions and honest uncertainty. Guided by those formulas, the search checked a pool of 1,470 materials with high quality quantum calculations. It found twelve acid stable candidates in just thirty rounds. The maps also guard against missing whole regions of the search space.
arxiv-2412-06047:
Term rewriting is a formal way of simplifying expressions step by step, and Franz Baader and Jürgen Giesl ask a sizing question about it. Given a rewriting system, a starting term, and a bound n, can the start be rewritten into some term of size at most n? They call this the small term reachability problem, motivated by shrinking proofs in logic-based reasoning.

The answer depends on how the system's termination is proven. For length-reducing systems the problem is NP-complete. With polynomial termination orders it jumps to doubly or singly exponential time classes, and for a restricted order family it sits in polynomial space. Making the system confluent drops the length-reducing case to polynomial time. A large-term variant behaves differently again, sometimes depending on how n is encoded.
arxiv-2412-06447:
Ulaş Özdem calculates magnetic moments of exotic vector particles made of four quarks, to probe their inner structure, published in 2024. The full picture of how hadrons are built is a key open topic in the study of the strong force. Electromagnetic traits can help tell apart states whose structure is complex and not yet settled.

Özdem treats these hidden-charm tetraquark states as a diquark paired with an antidiquark. Using QCD light-cone sum rules, he works through four distinct currents that could couple to the states. The magnetic moments that come out differ a good deal between those structures. He reads this as a sign that more than one tetraquark may share the same quantum numbers and similar quarks, yet differ in this measurable trait.
arxiv-2412-06547:
Sören Bieler and Kerstin Weinberg compare, in twenty twenty-four, how well green lattice structures soak up impact energy. Lattice structures are light frames of repeating struts, now easy to print in three dimensions. Some soak up energy by bending their diagonal struts without breaking. That makes them useful where parts must survive repeated loads. The team tested five lattice types, each at several densities, printed from a rubber-like resin.

An impact bar test slammed the samples to measure strain pulses. From those pulses, the team worked out how much energy each structure absorbed. Traits such as lattice type, density, material, print method, and finish all shaped the result. The paper sets the types side by side.
arxiv-2412-06747:
Beka Modrekiladze, Ira Rothstein, and Jordan Wilson-Gerow build a theory for dense objects moving through sticky fluids at near-light speed, in this 2024 paper. Black holes and neutron stars can plow through gas in space, and drag from that gas shapes their paths. Solving the full fluid flow around each object is heavy work.

Their worldline effective theory sidesteps the hard boundary problem. It treats the object as a line through space-time and folds all fluid interaction into a source term in the action, the quantity physics varies to get motion. The approach holds when velocity changes stay gentle compared with the object's size. From it they derive the relativistic equations of motion for an object in a viscous fluid on a curved background. The authors offer the frame for gravity-wave astronomy, where such drag may leave marks.
arxiv-2412-07247:
Jiahan Li, Zhiqi Li, and Tong Lu report a winning self-driving system in a 2024 technical paper. Their entry topped the Driving with Language track of a major 2024 autonomous driving challenge. The task joins camera views of the road with language questions about the scene.

The team fine-tuned InternVL, a strong open model that handles images and text together, on the contest data set. Camera views from several angles were stitched in a fixed layout so the model could use its image skills well. A simple trick turned object centre points in the data into full boxes, adding useful training labels. Their single model scored at the top of the final leaderboard, the report states.
arxiv-2412-07447:
Jayita Dutta, Rui Chen, Virat Tara, and Arka Majumdar present a 2024 device study on tuning small ring-shaped light channels on a chip. Programmable photonic circuits could serve fast data links and new kinds of computing, and phase-change materials can hold a setting with no power draw. Their drawbacks are high switching voltage and few stable levels. The team clad a silicon ring in a wide-bandgap phase-change material and drove it with a tiny silicon heater.

The device switched at under three volts, within normal chip limits, and survived more than 2,000 switching cycles. Mixing a temporary heat effect with the lasting phase change gave 127 distinct levels, a seven-bit range, with strong repeatability. Switching cost little energy. The authors present the hybrid approach as a step toward large programmable photonic chips.
arxiv-2412-07547:
Mattia Coccolo and Miguel Sanjuan study a 2024 physics setup where a Duffing oscillator is pushed by two forces at once. One force repeats in a steady cycle. The other is non-linear and arrives with a time delay, as if sent by a coupled driver system.

Working together, the two pushes can spark a resonance that swells the swings of the oscillator. That resonance may sit near two other known resonances from coupled systems. The authors map when each one rules the response, so a rise in swing size can be tied to the right cause or to a mix of causes.
arxiv-2412-07647:
Laura Rogers and co-authors catch dust and gas flaring together around a dead star in a 2024 paper. The star is a white dwarf polluted by shredded planetary debris. Such dwarfs often carry dust disks and gas, but whether the two arise together was debated. The team watched one dwarf with spectra and infrared photometry nearly at once.

Gas lines from calcium and magnesium swung up and down over weeks, while oxygen and iron lines held steady. Dust glow in one infrared band shifted by up to two tenths of a magnitude on the same span, the fastest such change yet seen. The two strongest epochs matched: brighter dust came with stronger gas lines. The authors say dust and gas must be born together, most likely in collisions. The work ties the two debris signs to one source event stream.
arxiv-2412-07847:
Group field theory is an approach to quantum gravity that starts from a field theory on a group. That group is a mathematical stage holding the data of a single atom of geometry, not spacetime itself. Steffen Gielen reviews recent attempts to rebuild the theory on a Hilbert space with operators, the standard language of quantum mechanics. The theory is usually written as a path integral whose expansion sums over discrete geometries, like a foam of tiny building blocks.

The newer operator based versions are often developed with cosmology in mind, but Gielen aims to separate the constructions from those applications. He walks through the main ideas of each formulation and how they differ. The review places the work in the wider quantum gravity landscape, next to related matrix and tensor models. It is meant as a map for researchers entering this corner of the field.
arxiv-2412-08147:
Hugo Monzón Maldonado and co-authors propose in this 2024 paper a Bayesian way to preview good task mixes for multitask finetuning. Tracing the full Pareto front of trade-offs is costly, so others train cheap stand-in models by merging existing ones. No one, though, had designed merging to provably sharpen the front itself.

Their method, Variational Model Merging, recasts older mergers as special cases of blending probability beliefs about weights. The main theorem says richer belief shapes must yield better front estimates. Tests on vision and language transformers bear it out. Fuller Gaussian beliefs matched or beat simpler ones across the board. Task cooks gain a cheaper menu of mixes.
arxiv-2412-08347:
Sultan Alrashed reports how training ratios shape the reasoning of small language models in this 2024 paper. The work adapts a known post-training recipe to a 1.7-billion-parameter base model. Experiments with a smaller test model explored how learning rate and batch size interact.

A clear split emerged: reasoning tasks improved with higher learning-rate-to-batch ratios, while pattern tasks preferred lower ones. Guided by that split, the tuned model reached top scores among small models on instruction following. It also posted strong gains on grade-school math and science questions. The author releases the model, recipes, and ablation studies. He argues careful tuning of training dynamics can narrow the gap between small and large models.
arxiv-2412-08547:
Véronique Bruyère, Jean-François Raskin, Alexis Reynouard, and Marie Van Den Bogaard wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It studies how to build a system that holds its own when rational foes reply with subgame perfect play.

In these graph games one player, the system, states its plan first. The rest, the environment, then answer with strategies in subgame perfect equilibrium. Goals are ω-regular, given as parity conditions. The authors encode the task as a three-player game with hidden facts, which puts the cost in double-exponential time. With the foe count fixed, the cost drops a class, though the task stays hard both ways. For reach goals with fixed players, a fast method exists.
arxiv-2412-08847:
Zheyuan Zhang and co-authors build a health aware food recommendation system that explains itself, in a 2024 paper. The catalog title adds conference metadata, so the head title governs. Big platforms rank food by taste alone, though poor eating habits worry the United States. Past health aware systems rarely tuned advice to a person's own conditions, and few explained their picks.

The team first built two large benchmarks for personal, health aware food advice. Their system then weighs three goals at once: taste, personal health fit, and nutrient variety. A large language model adds plain reasons for each pick, drawn from healthy eating knowledge. The aim is advice people can judge and trust, not just obey.
arxiv-2412-09047:
Shohei Yuasa and co-authors propose a new probe for quantum critical points based on turning a magnetic field in 2024, using team framing for a long author list. Heat based ratios are classic tools for phase change study. Their new ratio swaps field strength for field angle as the control. Two strongly directional compounds were measured over wide heat and field ranges.

Data from both compounds fell on one scaling curve. The same exponents and a fixed critical angle fit both. The scaling shape reveals sharp directional quantum criticality. It grows from a critical line as the easy axis field part changes. The authors offer the method as a heat based way to find such points. It suits magnets where direction rules behavior.
arxiv-2412-09147:
Meng Li and seven co-authors take stock of dark patterns in a 2024 study. Dark patterns are design tricks in apps and websites that push users toward choices that serve the provider, often at the user's cost. The field has suffered from clashing definitions, weak detection tools, and patchy data sets.

The authors build a framework that sorts dark patterns into sixty-eight types, each described with its harm, likely settings, and real examples, checked against industry surveys. They then test the tools meant to catch such tricks. Of eight tools, the best coverage found only thirty-one types, under half of the list. Four data sets did no better, covering thirty types in over five thousand cases. The study gives regulators and designers a fuller map of the problem and shows how far detection still has to go.
arxiv-2412-09347:
Rhodes and co-authors track the flickering light of a neutron star binary across its 2018 to 2020 outburst in a 2024 paper. The system, Swift J1858.6-0814, pairs a neutron star with a low-mass companion it feeds on. Radio and optical telescopes watched the feast and the quiet after.

The optical light stayed strongly variable while its average held steady, mostly blue like a hot accretion disc, with occasional red flares from a jet. Optical and radio wobble sizes matched, hinting that changes born near the disc travel outward into the jet. Brightness also rose and fell with orbit phase in all colors alike, pointing to reprocessed light off the disc, the companion, and stripped material. Such ablation evidence helps explain how these binaries evolve toward lone millisecond pulsars.
arxiv-2412-09847:
Keiko Nagao studies how to detect dark matter that has been sped up by other dark matter in a 2024 particle physics study. The model holds two dark matter components, one heavy and one light, linked by a hidden force. Heavy particles annihilating near the center of the Galaxy can kick light ones to high speeds, making them easier to spot in a detector.

Directional detectors, which record which way a recoil points, suit this search because the boosted particles stream from the Galactic center. Nagao estimates event rates reaching the order of ten per year in a modest mass of detector material. Such rates put the scenario within reach of planned experiments.
arxiv-2412-10247:
Basilio, Kupriyanov, and Kurkov study a charged particle in a noncommutative electrodynamics in twenty twenty-four. The theory is the semi classical limit of a noncommutative gauge theory. Space coordinates in it fail to commute in a Lie algebra pattern. The authors focus on one charged point particle in a fixed gauge background.

They derive explicit formulas for gauge invariant variables that give the particle position. They then write the classical action and the equations of motion in full. In the limit where noncommutativity vanishes, standard relativistic dynamics return. As an example, they solve the Kepler problem under angular noncommutativity exactly. Other examples illustrate the framework. The work clarifies how noncommutative effects alter particle motion.
arxiv-2412-10547:
Juan Herrera and six co-authors model the heat inside an ultra-hot induction furnace in a 2024 paper. The furnace reaches twenty-five hundred degrees, a range where parts react, change phase, and shift how they carry heat, so reading the true inner temperature from surface points is tricky. Their model couples the heating field with heat flow through layered materials.

The setup places graphite crucibles inside a larger graphite body wrapped in zirconia grit. A finite element simulation produced the full temperature map, and tests at key surface spots on the real rig matched it within about three percent. The authors present the model as a guide for processing materials that demand such heat.
arxiv-2412-10747:
Aaron Pim, Tristan Pryer, and Alex Trenam solve a control problem governed by a kinetic equation, a model of many particles moving and colliding, in a 2024 paper. Steering such a system to a goal while spending little effort is hard, because the equation mixes free flow with diffusion-like spreading. The authors lean on a framework called hypocoercivity, which explains how such systems settle down even though damping acts only indirectly.

Within that frame, they prove the control problem is well-posed and that its best solutions inherit the settling behaviour, giving stability and robustness. They then build a finite element method, a grid-based solver, that keeps those good properties rather than breaking them. Numerical tests back the theory. The work matters for plasma and gas problems where controllers must respect delicate decay behaviour.
arxiv-2412-10847:
Florian Millo and co-authors study the symmetry of sound wave loss in a thin magnetic film, in a 2024 paper. Surface acoustic waves pass through the film, and magnetic resonance drains their energy. The team turned the applied field to many angles against the wave's travel direction and watched the loss change.

The loss showed an unexpected two fold symmetry. The authors test whether the stretch torque of the wave plus the film's resonance response can explain it. One source, they find, is a weak one axis preference inside the film itself. That source should persist even in ultrathin films, where a second known source fades away. The result refines how such coupled devices get modeled.
arxiv-2412-11047:
Peng Zhou and Dylan Muir lay out a 2024 pipeline for putting spiking neural networks onto a low-power chip for edge devices. Spiking networks send brief pulses rather than steady values, which suits chips that work event by event. The chip here is Xylo, a neuromorphic processor, and the software frame is Rockpool, which trains and prepares the networks.

The paper walks through each step of the move from a trained network in Rockpool to a running network on Xylo. It then grades the result on energy use and accuracy. The chip's digital spiking design and event-driven style fit tasks that must run in real time on a tight power budget, such as sensors that always listen. The pipeline gives other teams a tested route onto this hardware.
arxiv-2412-11147:
Kâzım Büyükboduk and Manisha Ganguly prove a functional equation for algebraic versions of Rankin-Selberg L-functions. Their paper appeared in 2024. These functions encode deep facts about number systems, and the p-adic versions vary over families of forms. The algebraic side is built from Selmer complexes, chain-like objects whose cohomology gives groups tied to the L-function.

The authors show the relevant size of the Selmer group, its characteristic ideal, can be read off as a determinant of the whole complex. To do so, they prove the complex is perfect in a narrow range and that its cohomology sits in a single degree. That step needs a careful study of Tamagawa factors in families. The result feeds the Iwasawa theory of Rankin-Selberg products.
arxiv-2412-11347:
Dial and ten co-authors report a detailed study of a single fast radio burst caught by an Australian array in two thousand twenty-three. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes from deep space whose sources stay unknown. A few show a near-regular pulse pattern inside the flash, which can hint at what made them.

This burst stood out for its rich shape in both time and polarization. The team fit its profile to test for rhythm, scattering, and twinkling. They found a possible beat of a few milliseconds, but the signal was weak. Its strong circular polarization did not come from a known conversion effect. Most traits fit a magnetar whose beamed emission carries fine structure. Other sources, the authors note, are not yet ruled out.
arxiv-2412-11647:
Tianyi Chen, Atsushi Miyauchi, and Charalampos Tsourakakis hunt for tight-knit, like-minded groups in social networks in a 2024 paper. Each person in the network carries a vector of opinions across several topics. The goal is to find clusters that are both densely linked and in positive agreement on many topics at once.

The authors anchor their method in the classic densest subgraph problem, then show their version is NP-hard with no good approximation in reach. They design two heuristic algorithms, one from a relaxed optimization and one that peels nodes away step by step. Tests on Twitter data about the Ukraine conflict and COVID-19 vaccines showed the methods extract meaningful groups.
arxiv-2412-12047:
Eduardo Flández, Alejandro Zamorano, and Víctor Muñoz wrote this 2024 astronomy paper on networks built from solar flares. Active regions on the Sun emit flares in sequence over each solar cycle. The team turned those sequences into networks, with regions as nodes and flare order as links.

They built networks for solar cycles 21 through 24, following a model first used for earthquake networks. In each cycle, the spread of links per node followed a power law, a sign that flares cluster in linked active zones. The key exponent was higher in even cycles than in odd ones. When the team slid 11-year windows year by year, the exponent traced a rhythm of about 22 years. That span matches the Hale magnetic cycle of the Sun.
arxiv-2412-12147:
Seongwoong Cho, Donggyun Kim, Jinwoo Lee, and Seunghoon Hong present Meta-Controller, a framework for robot imitation learning, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. A useful robot policy should transfer to new robot bodies and new tasks. Modular methods adapt to bodies but not tasks, while imitation methods usually assume one body.

Their few-shot behavior cloning needs only a handful of reward-free demonstrations. A joint-level representation unifies state and action spaces across different robots. A structure-motion encoder captures both shared knowledge and body-specific knowledge. A matching-based policy network then predicts actions for the new setting. Tests in the DeepMind Control suite showed the adaptive policy resisted overfitting while generalizing broadly.
arxiv-2412-12347:
Saaketh Desai and six colleagues wrote a paper in twenty twenty-four about AutoSciLab, a system that lets a robot lab run on its own. Robot labs can run tests fast and in large numbers. Yet picking what test to run next, in a space with many options, still rests on human hunches.

AutoSciLab plays the part of a stand-in researcher and works in four steps. It puts forward ideas, picks and runs tests, reads the results, and then starts again. Machine learning guides each pick, and the system shows its reasons in plain form rather than hiding them. It found anew the laws of projectile motion and of phase shifts in the Ising model. It also found a new way to steer loose light that beat the best known method.
arxiv-2412-13047:
Luca Savant Aira, Gabriele Facciolo, and Thibaud Ehret adapt in a 2024 paper Gaussian splatting for satellite image photogrammetry. Splatting builds 3D scenes fast, far faster than the neural field methods before it. Earth observation versions of those older methods can take a day to fit.

Their frame keeps splatting's speed while adding remote sensing fixes from prior work. Light calibration and shadow modeling carry over from a leading neural baseline. New parts add sparsity, view consistency, and opacity controls tuned for orbit views. The result hits top accuracy in minutes rather than a day of fitting. That speed opens rapid mapping from fresh satellite passes for users.
arxiv-2412-13847:
Yuchong Geng and Ao Tang propose a concept-centric framework for learning across modalities, in a two thousand twenty-four machine learning paper. Humans learn once and reuse knowledge across senses through a shared understanding of the world.

The framework centers on a modality-agnostic concept space holding structured, abstract knowledge. Separate projection models map each kind of raw input into that space and are trained independently, so new modalities plug in without retraining the core. Experiments show faster convergence than baseline models. On two downstream tasks the framework matches standard results with a smaller training footprint, no task-specific fine-tuning, and the interpretability of reasoning inside a shared concept space.
arxiv-2412-13947:
Ethan Baron, Idan Tankel, Peter Tu, and Guy Ben-Yosef wrote a 2024 paper on a hard test for vision-language models. The test is to classify an object from a written description of its parts alone. The name of the object itself is kept out of the description. Models that pair images with text can name an object at a glance. The fine traits of its parts are a far sterner test.

The team built description data for six fine-grained benchmark sets, with the names stripped out. They then trained CLIP on a vast and varied set of object categories. The written descriptions were generated by large language models. A modification lets the model view an image at more than one resolution. That sharpens its eye for small parts. Scores rose on all six sets and on a part-attribute benchmark. The code is available.
arxiv-2412-14147:
Ioannis Georgakilas and nine co-authors steer pairs of quantum fluid condensates by geometry, in a 2024 paper. The fluids form from exciton-polaritons, half-light half-matter particles. They sit in a photonic crystal waveguide with saddle-shaped dispersion. Two coupling styles link such condensates. Proximity coupling splits energies strongly, while flow coupling needs phase matching.

Rotating the pair relative to the crystal grating tunes between the styles. The all-optical setup needs no wires or gates. Spectra and mass flow showed the saddle dispersion at work. The dimer behaved partly like coupled oscillators with delay. It also echoed tight-binding physics from solid state models. The authors present photonic crystals as flexible test beds. Coupled quantum fluids can probe collective behavior there with fine control, they argue.
arxiv-2412-14247:
Cristian Baldenegro, Alba Soto-Ontoso, and Gregory Soyez propose a way to gather a clean sample of gluon jets at the Large Hadron Collider, in a paper from 2024. Jets are sprays of particles made when a quark or a gluon flies out of a crash. Telling the two kinds apart is hard, yet the split matters for many studies. Their trick uses pairs of jets that fly close together.

In such a pair, the weaker jet acts like a side jet born from the stronger one. The team charts the spray pattern inside that weaker jet. Both hand calculations and full event simulations say the sample is about ninety percent gluon jets. The purity holds up across event types and input settings. The method uses plain cuts that the collider teams can test at once.
arxiv-2412-14347:
Matias Bundgaard-Nielsen and co-authors propose a simple model of quantum noise in nanolasers in a 2024 paper. Tiny lasers run at low power, so quantum noise strongly shakes both their brightness and their coherence. Exact quantum equations handle the smallest devices, and classic noise equations handle large ones. Neither fits the middle range well. The team start from standard rate equations and add a simple guess for the phase of the laser field.

Their random model matches the exact quantum results for small lasers and the classic results for large ones, in numbers. That makes it fit for the middle range that the other tools miss. They use it to track laser linewidth across the turn on point. Below threshold, linewidth is set by the particle side of light. Above it, the wave side and index wobbles take over and broaden the line.
arxiv-2412-14747:
Giovanni Montani and co-authors wrote this 2024 cosmology paper that reworks Einstein's gravity for an expanding universe. In their version, the Einstein constant is not fixed but changes with the energy density of the universe. Near a vacuum state, they expand the theory and extend it to cover all cases.

The change yields an effective dark energy term and an extra pressure piece that acts like Chaplygin gas in the late universe. It also reframes the old puzzle of why vacuum energy looks so small. Comparing the model with data on the late universe, the team find the present vacuum energy fits zero within the error bars. They also discuss what the model means for the Hubble tension.
arxiv-2412-15047:
On sites like Reddit, people share hard parts of their lives with strangers, but a post can reveal more than they intend. Isadora Krsek and co-authors studied that risk in 2024 with 21 Reddit users. Each user ran a language model that flags risky disclosures on two of their own posts, then spoke about what the tool got right and wrong.

Users liked the tool despite its flaws, saying it caught mistakes and raised risks they had missed. Still, the team found that such tools must weigh post context, site norms, and each user's own threat model. Tools should explain a risk and inform choice, not simply tell users to stay silent.
arxiv-2412-15147:
Kunal Marwaha, Adrian She, and James Sud analyze how well quantum variational algorithms do on random networks, in a 2024 paper. The algorithms, cousins of the popular QAOA method, aim to find low-energy states of two-body Hamiltonians defined on graphs. The team derives formulas for the energy reached, averaged over random regular graphs of endless size.

Evaluating the formulas grows costly with depth, so tests stay shallow. A symmetry inside the method blocks progress on the Quantum MaxCut problem in general, yet the algorithms beat known rivals on a related Hamiltonian and on bipartite graphs. Five layers already land within 1.62 percent of the best energy on a ring.
arxiv-2412-15547:
Zheyuan Zhang and co-authors build a benchmark for diet advice that fits a person's own health profile, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Diet shapes health, yet tailoring advice to one person's conditions is hard. Their questions sit on a graph that links foods, nutrients, and survey health data.

Each item asks whether a food is healthy for a given user, with reasons tied to key nutrients. Three levels of question difficulty and three task types are included. Tests with large language models showed the set is a tough challenge. The authors offer it as a step toward personal nutrition reasoning.
arxiv-2412-16047:
The Majorana Demonstrator team reports a search for rare decays in which several core particles vanish at once. The experiment sat deep underground in South Dakota and used very pure germanium detectors kept in shielded cold chambers. It was built mainly to hunt a rare nuclear decay, and it gathered the full data set over years of quiet running.

No signal for the multi particle decays appeared. The team instead set new lower bounds on how long such decays would take, reaching beyond ten to the twenty-sixth years for one mode in a germanium isotope. Other modes were also updated. Null results still guide theory by ruling out fast versions of these exotic processes.
arxiv-2412-16147:
Four researchers in Denmark built a deep learning tool that finds eelgrass in underwater video, in a 2024 paper. Eelgrass meadows store carbon, clean water, and shelter sea life, so tracking them matters for coastal care. Today, people judge such video by hand, which is slow and varies from person to person. The team wanted a faster and steadier way to map where the grass grows.

The team first built a data set of more than eighty-three hundred labeled underwater photos. They then trained several image models and compared how well each spotted eelgrass. The best models scored very high on test photos, and cleaning up the images first helped them do even better. A new method also guessed how much of a scene the grass covered, matching expert labels well. The authors say such tools could scale up coastal surveys.
arxiv-2412-16347:
Riccardo Morandin and Dorothea Hinsen present a 2024 mathematics paper on energy storage functions for control systems. A dissipative system loses or stores energy in a controlled way, and a storage function tracks that balance. Such functions, cousins of Lyapunov functions, are powerful tools but are usually hard to find.

The authors study passive linear systems whose rules change over time, under very mild assumptions. They prove every such system has at least one storage function of a simple quadratic form that can vary with time. That narrows the search a great deal. They also show the rank of these functions can only shrink over time. A matching decomposition of the state space and a kernel condition narrow the hunt further.
arxiv-2412-16647:
Jiazhen Liu, Kunal Tamang, Dashun Wang, and Chaoming Song wrote a 2024 paper on how causal networks grow. A causal network maps which things cause which others, in fields from biology to innovation. Real causal networks show patterns in how their nodes link up: busy nodes tend to connect in telling ways. Where those patterns come from was poorly understood.

The authors propose a general way such networks grow, with two kinds of correlation built in. One ties a new link to the causes already present. The other ties it to how the system changes over time. From these rules, they show on paper that the observed link patterns must follow. Their formulas match data from four large networks of innovation, where ideas build on each other. The theory gives a shared frame for studying growth in causal systems of many kinds.
arxiv-2412-16847:
Kourosh Kakhi and co-authors wrote a review from 2024 on tracking fatigue with wearable sensors and artificial intelligence. Fatigue endangers people who work long shifts or heavy-demand jobs, and catching it early can prevent accidents. Watches and trackers now stream body signals all day, from heart traces to muscle and brain activity. The review gathered studies that feed those signals to learning models.

Following a standard review protocol, the team sorted studies by how they cleaned the signals, pulled features from them, and classified weariness. Blending several signal sources at once made the readings more accurate and more stable. Deep learning methods pushed signal analysis further, with less need to touch the wearer. The team sees wearable, AI-driven monitors as a strong option for live fatigue watching at work. Gaps remain in standard measures and long-term proof, which they flag for future work.
arxiv-2412-17147:
Sourav Chatterjee, Michael Tonks, William Gardner, and Marina Sessim model a failure mode in solid-state batteries, in a research paper from 2024. As a metal electrode gives up and regains ions during use, empty pockets, called voids, can grow where it meets the solid electrolyte. Those voids weaken the cell.

Their model follows the electrode surface and the voids at the same time. They test it on a sodium cell with a ceramic separator, in cases with a clean contact, one void, and many voids. Void growth rose in step with how fast sodium atoms left the void edge. Grain boundaries in the ceramic changed growth only locally.
arxiv-2412-17547:
Shuyang Liu and co-authors put probability density at the center of semi supervised learning in a 2024 paper. Such learning leans on two beliefs: neighbors share a label, and points in separate clusters differ. Most methods chase neighbors by similarity and neglect the cluster belief. The team first build a theoretical case for why density matters to the cluster assumption.

They then define a density aware similarity measure for finding true neighbors. A new label propagation algorithm built on it spreads labels through the data with clusters in mind. They also prove that classic pseudo labeling is a special case of their method. Across experiments, their approach beat recent rivals. The authors present density awareness as the missing ingredient in using unlabeled data well.
arxiv-2412-17747:
Luyang Liu, Jonas Pfeiffer, Jiaxing Wu, Jun Xie, and Arthur Szlam give a language model extra thinking power without changing the model at all. Standard ways of letting models think longer make them spell out reasoning steps as text first, which is slow and hard to train. Their approach bolts on a separate coprocessor that works directly on the model's key-value cache, the stored record of what it has read so far.

The coprocessor inserts extra latent embeddings into that cache, sharpening what the frozen model produces next. It is trained with the ordinary language modeling objective on standard text, end to end, while the main model stays untouched. Because it runs offline and asynchronously, the model still works normally when the coprocessor is absent. In experiments, augmented caches lowered perplexity on following text and improved results across reasoning-heavy tasks, with no task-specific training.
arxiv-2412-18047:
Lo Pang-Yun Ting and five colleagues design a control system, in a 2024 preprint, for charging electric cars at workplaces. New chargers can also discharge cars back into the building, which adds options and risk. Prices change through the day, and drivers leave at uncertain times. The goal is to cut the building's power bill while giving each car the charge it needs. A single controller would face too many shifting parts at once.

Their design splits the job into two levels. A top agent watches prices and decides which cars charge or discharge. Lower agents set the exact power for each car. A special critic tweak helps the lower agents judge choices when departure times are unsure. Tests on real power data showed clear savings. The system still met charging needs under both fixed and uncertain leaving times. A case study shows it shifting energy in real time.
arxiv-2412-18447: Georges Derache and co-authors study two attack scenarios against a long-range wireless network used in military settings. Their 2024 paper deals with LoRaWAN, a low-power wide-area protocol whose use in defense work is growing. The two attacks are replay attacks and sniffing attacks on the network. The authors aim to flag cyber threats that must be weighed before such tech is trusted in critical contexts.
arxiv-2412-18747:
X Tong and co-authors study exotic atoms in which a muon orbits an argon nucleus in this 2024 paper. A muon is a heavier cousin of the electron, so its orbits sit far closer in. The team found that the muon's orbit collapses at a set value of angular momentum. That value caps the states a muon can land in when captured by argon. Three kinds of calculation were used to check the picture. Two dynamic methods agreed once a mapping between them was fixed.

The authors also give a simple way to guess the collapse point for other noble gases. Their guesses matched the detailed values well. Capture states matter for experiments that use muons to probe matter. Knowing the cap helps predict what those experiments will see. The work blends quantum chemistry methods with atomic collision theory. It targets a niche but testable corner of atomic physics.
arxiv-2412-19647:
Some algebras in math encode both symmetry and braiding, and their representations can be hard to picture directly. Junkang Huang and co-authors use string-theory branes to picture one such algebra in a 2024 paper. They study the spherical double affine Hecke algebra of a type tied to a four-punctured sphere.

The team shows that compact Lagrangian branes match, one to one, the finite representations of the algebra. That match supports a deeper equivalence between the brane category and the representation category. A root system of type D4 runs through both sides and reveals a hidden braid group action. As a side gain, the geometry describes low-energy dynamics of a known gauge theory.
arxiv-2412-19747:
Attackers can fool image networks with changes too small for a person to see, sending a photo to the wrong class. Longwei Wang, Navid Nayyem, and Abdullah Rakin present a training method meant to harden such networks in this 2024 paper. Their recipe mixes two ideas about how the network's inner features should be arranged.

The first idea, supervised contrastive learning, pulls features of same-class images together and pushes other classes apart. The second adds a margin rule, borrowed from a classic classifier, that forces a clear gap at decision borders. Tests used the CIFAR-100 image set with a ResNet-18 network and a standard fast attack. Accuracy under attack improved with the combined method. The authors present the work as a step toward feature spaces that stay orderly even when inputs are tampered with.
arxiv-2412-20047:
Phi Vu Tran presented a simple recipe in 2024 for finding rare objects in images. Real datasets are long-tailed: a few common classes have many examples, while most classes have barely any, and detectors starve on the rare ones. Earlier fixes leaned on huge labeled databases from outside, which many real projects cannot use, or added complex meta-learning machinery.

SimLTD works in three plain steps: train on the abundant classes, transfer to the scarce ones, then fine-tune on a balanced sample of both. Optional unlabeled images, cheap to gather, can join through semi-supervised learning. On the hard LVIS benchmark the framework set new records in both modes. Simplicity is the point: no outside labels, no distillation tricks.
arxiv-2501-00147:
Michael Reh, writing for the T2K Collaboration, explains how the experiment prices in the flaws of its giant far detector. The report appeared in twenty twenty-four. T2K fires neutrinos from Tokai to the Super-Kamiokande tank and measures how they change flavor, but detector quirks rank among the biggest error sources.

The fix fits simulated atmospheric neutrino data to real readings with a Markov chain sampler. Errors are split by the true shape of each event, so each signal and background sample inherits the right share. The newest version adds samples rich in electron neutrinos and neutral pions. The fit now spans five hundred forty dimensions. Reh walks through how the results feed the main oscillation analysis.
arxiv-2501-00647:
Abdesselam Ferdi, writing solo, builds a lean detector for broken bones in children's wrist X-rays. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five, with a late two thousand twenty-four posting. Computer-aided diagnosis helps doctors read images faster. Existing fracture detectors are heavy and hungry for compute. Clinics with modest hardware cannot run them well. A lighter design is the goal.

His G-YOLOv11 builds on the newest YOLO detector family. Ghost convolutions cut the arithmetic while keeping feature counts. Fewer operations mean cheaper, faster scans. Tests use a public dataset of pediatric wrist images. Detection quality stays respectable at the smaller size. Point-of-care tools for children's injuries gain a candidate.
arxiv-2501-00747:
Yiwei Qin, Yixiu Liu, and Pengfei Liu present in this 2025 paper a fix for a dullness that creeps into self-improving language models. When a model trains again and again on its own answers, its range of replies narrows, a real loss on math tasks where varied attack routes matter. Their framework, DIVE, widens the sample pool and curates training pairs to balance variety with quality.

On two standard math sets, DIVE raised output diversity by ten to forty-five percent over plain self-improvement while holding scores steady. Knocking out either part hurt the result, confirming both earn their place, the authors report. Code for the method ships in public.
arxiv-2501-01147:
Gopi Chand Ananthu and Riadul Islam wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It designs a bridge chip block that lets a fast system bus talk to slow add-on gear, built and tested on an FPGA with a Raspberry Pi in the loop.

The high-speed AHB bus links cores and memory, while the lean APB bus serves slow parts. The bridge turns burst AHB trades into single APB steps, and handles clock gaps and flow pace so the two sides stay in step. Written in Verilog and run in Xilinx Vivado, the design is checked by test benches across many cases. The project shows a sound way to mix fast and slow parts on one chip.
arxiv-2501-01347:
Jaehun Kim and co-authors present in 2025 AdaptVC, a voice swap tool that turns one speaker's speech into a target voice. The words must stay the same while the voice traits change. The hard part is to split word sense from voice style in a clean way, even for new voices.

Small adapter parts tune rich self taught speech traits to pull the two apart. A flow based maker then fuses them with a cross focus on the target voice. In zero shot tests with new speakers, the tool beat past models on sound quality and voice match. Both ear marks and score marks back the claim.
arxiv-2501-01647:
Xuanloc Leu, Xuan-Hoai Thi Nguyen, and Jinhyoung Lee propose moving delicate quantum states between light cavities using a vibrating intermediary, in a 2025 paper. The states in view are superpositions of many photons, including Schrödinger cat states that sit in two conditions at once. Such states are prized for quantum computing and sensing, but they are fragile in transit.

A mechanical oscillator between the cavities switches the link on and off as it swings, a trick called phonon-induced dynamic resonance. Working in a nonlinear, weak-coupling regime with slow changes, the math shows transfer with fidelity near 0.99 using today's lab hardware. Faithful movers for cat states would let quantum devices share their strangest cargo.
arxiv-2501-01747:
Simulating a detonation across thousands of processors stalls when every processor must wait for its neighbors at each step. Aswin Kumar Arumugam and Konduri Aditya extend an asynchronous simulation method in 2025 that lets processors proceed with slightly stale boundary data, cutting that communication drag.

The discontinuous Galerkin method handles shocks sharply but syncs heavily. The asynchronous variant relaxes the sync, and the team derived new limiters that stay accurate when boundary data arrive late. A test of fuel-lean mixture ignition with detailed chemistry showed the flame front in the right place and boundary errors too small to matter. The work points toward combustion codes that scale to extreme machine sizes.
arxiv-2501-02447:
Avni Mittal and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on outlining skin lesions in photos with far smaller models. Diffusion models segment medical images well, but their usual U-net backbone is heavy, above all at high resolution. Clinics with weak hardware feel that cost.

The team swaps the backbone for neural cellular automata, tiny rules that grow a segmentation by local steps. Three designs are offered: a multilevel version that refines rough drafts, an attention version that weighs channels and space, and a combined version with a color-based guide loss. The combined model matched the U-net's accuracy on lesion data while using sixty to a hundred times fewer parameters. The authors aim at low-resource medical settings.
arxiv-2501-02547:
Yuan Cao and co-authors prove that a transformer model can act out the rules of a Bayesian network as it writes, in a paper from 2025. A Bayesian network maps how random events sway each other. Generating fresh samples from such a network is a core skill for a sequence model. The team ask whether a transformer can learn the odds from context alone.

They show a plain transformer can do two things at once. First, it can read a set of sample sequences and infer the network's odds. Second, it can then write a new sequence that obeys those odds. The proof rests on in-context estimation by maximum likelihood. Tests show a trained model does in fact behave this way. The result frames large language models as flexible samplers of learned chance structures.
arxiv-2501-02947:
Magnets whose spins point in mismatched directions, rather than lining up, can still show orderly patterns in how their spins vary with momentum. Paolo Radaelli and Gautam Gurung built a formal method in 2025 for reading those patterns, based on a tool called colour symmetry. Among all the textures a magnet's symmetry allows, their method picks out one special part.

That part stays unchanged under any rotation in spin space and can exist even without spin-orbit coupling, just as in a newly noticed class called altermagnets. The pair demonstrate the approach on three complex magnets, and for one of them their predictions match heavy computer calculations with and without the coupling switched on.
arxiv-2501-03047:
Arpan Das, Hriditi Howlader, and Alekha Nayak study in 2025 how light rays bend in a version of electromagnetism that breaks the symmetry between directions. The added term links the light field to a fixed outside arrow, so the laws differ along that arrow while charge rules stay intact. Ray optics is the limit where light travels as thin lines from source to eye.

The authors argue that both curved spacetime and the new term reshape the equation that rules the field. Yet in the ray limit, neither changes how the light's vibration direction is carried along the ray. That null result is itself a finding: some tests for the symmetry break must look beyond ray optics. The work sorts which observations could ever reveal the effect.
arxiv-2501-03347:
Syamantak Das and Tanmoy Paul study a fine point in the geometry of Banach spaces, in a 2025 paper. Banach spaces are complete spaces where distance and size behave in clean ways, and much of modern analysis rests on them. The pair look at how well points in such a space can be matched to centers of sets, a theme first studied by Veselý in 1997.

They set up a new property that links a space, a closed subset, and a family of bounded sets with a set of functions. Then they show how that property ties to reflexivity and to the Kadec-Klee property, which governs how limits behave. The work also probes smooth spaces and when a center-finding map stays continuous. Results of this kind sharpen the basic maps that pure math relies on.
arxiv-2501-03547:
Akanksha Singal and five co-authors present KIMetrix, a system that picks the small set of measurements a cloud software service actually needs for reliable monitoring. Their paper came out in 2025. Modern services split into many small parts, each emitting multitudes of metrics, and engineers drown in choices.

KIMetrix scores metrics using information theory, weighing how much each one reveals about the system's state and about the others. It works only from lightweight metrics and traces, needing no costly log processing and no hand-labeled training data. On standard benchmark services it found compact metric sets that cover the system well. Automating this choice promises fewer false alarms and fewer missed failures for the engineers on call.
arxiv-2501-03847:
Zekai Gu and co-authors use three-dimensional tracking videos as control signals for video generation, published in 2025. Diffusion models generate high-quality video from text or images, but precise control, such as moving the camera or editing content, remains hard. Prior control methods usually handle only one kind of control at a time.

Their insight is that videos are renderings of dynamic three-dimensional scenes, so 3D signals are the natural control input. Their system, Diffusion as Shader, takes 3D tracking videos and lets users reshape a generation by editing those tracks. The tracking links frames together, which also improves how consistent the video is over time. With a short fine-tuning run on a small video set, the system showed strong control across tasks such as mesh-to-video generation.
arxiv-2501-03947:
Ariel Scolnic, Ealeal Bear, and Noam Soker wrote a 2025 paper on how massive stars can gulp matter at very high rates without ballooning. Their sims use a one dimensional stellar code for stars of 30, 60, and 80 solar masses. The trick is a disk that launches jets, which strip the outer envelope as fast as accretion puffs it up.

The cycle adds mass and energy until the star swells by a few tens of percent, then removes mass until the star shrinks back. With that rhythm, stars took in up to a tenth of their mass with little growth. Disk density beats the puffed envelope density, so jets can fire from inside the envelope. The scheme fits eruptive systems that need a deep gravity well.
arxiv-2501-04347:
Andrea Calì, Davide Martinenghi, and Riccardo Torlone build a framework for keyword search over the deep web, in a 2025 paper. Much of the web's data hides behind forms, returned only in dynamic pages that search engines cannot index. The authors model such sources as relational tables with access limits, rules about which inputs a query must supply before the source will answer.

They define what an optimal answer means under those limits and sort out which queries can be answered at all. A query processor then builds a plan that reaches the answer with as few source accesses as possible. The work gives deep web search a formal footing.
arxiv-2501-04747:
Mohamed Sakhri and co-authors grow new local search rules with the help of neural nets bred by evolution. The work dates to 2025. Local search rules pick their next step from a set of kin spots. That pick drives how well the rule solves hard tasks.

A neural net takes the same facts as a stock rule and makes the pick. The team tests ways to cast those facts so the rule stays strong when the task's scale warps. Test beds use hill-form tasks whose size and rough grade can be set at will. The bred rules show fresh search forms can rise this way.
arxiv-2501-05347:
Karim Said and co-authors published a 2025 paper on reducing interference between users in machine-type communications. Fleets of sensors and meters share modern cellular networks with phones. Each user gets blocks of time and frequency. Sharp filtering keeps those blocks cleanly separated without wasting guard bands, but sharp filters stretch each signal in time, smearing symbols into each other.

The authors study precoding, pre-shaping the transmitted signal, over the standard multicarrier format used in 4G and 5G. The aim is to cancel the cross-talk between users that the stretched responses create, especially in dense machine deployments. Their analysis works at the level of transport blocks, the units networks actually schedule. The stakes are capacity: billions of small devices must share spectrum without shouting over one another. Better precoding squeezes more quiet conversations into the same airwaves.
arxiv-2501-05447: Piotr Pokora studied plane curves in twenty twenty-five through two polynomial invariants that encode their topology. The Betti and Poincare polynomials summarize a curve's homology in compact algebraic form. Computing them for complex curves is often done in bits. Small parts are added one at a time. Pokora uses this addition technique in a set way. The work gives polynomial identities. They link the invariants of reduced plane curves to those of their parts. Such formulas let researchers build global topological facts from local pieces.
arxiv-2501-06447:
Souvik Roy and Santanu Maiti study an electric current that flows in circles inside a tiny ring. The ring is threaded by a magnetic flux, the Aharonov-Bohm setup, and its atoms alternate between two kinds of links. On every other site the authors add gain or loss, an imaginary energy that stands for the ring exchanging energy with its surroundings, a trick from non-Hermitian physics.

Tuning the gain-loss strength, they track the current in both the real and imaginary parts of the spectrum. At special values called exceptional points, where states merge, the current jumps sharply. At other settings the imaginary part of the current vanishes, leaving a purely real flow. The pattern depends on how the alternating links correlate with the gain-loss setting and on the ring's size. The authors suggest such loop devices could show unusual, tunable behavior worth chasing in the lab.
arxiv-2501-06547:
Three authors, Chazottes, Gallo, and Takahashi, built a way to guess time series values path by path. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with category and count series whose symbol set has no bound. The task: from a finite sample, learn a rule that guesses a held out chunk from the rest with near best odds. Old stats paths first guess the chance laws in full. Their path skips that step and learns the guess rule direct.

Its learn speed does not rest on the size of the symbol set. The proof spans a wide class: finite Markov chains, some hidden ones, count models, and Gibbs forms. A margin term sets the pace. Readers in time series get a guess tool for wild symbol worlds.
arxiv-2501-07047:
Jianming Tong and ten co-authors run homomorphic encryption on AI chips to close the efficiency gap with custom hardware. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tackles encryption that lets clouds compute on sealed data. The privacy is strong; the cost is brutal. Graphics cards help but trail bespoke chips on energy by a wide factor. AI accelerators like TPUs promise ASIC-grade thrift at commodity scale.

Two mismatches block the port. Encryption math wants wide integers, while the chip's fast engine eats small ones. Its coarse memory also hates fine data shuffles. Their CROSS compiler fixes both. One transform recasts wide modular math as dense small-integer matrix work. Another bakes reordering into the kernels ahead of time. On a current TPU, throughput per watt beats the listed GPU and ASIC rivals.
arxiv-2501-07147:
Panu Lahti and Khanh Nguyen prove an approximation result in 2025 for rough functions in abstract spaces. The functions, of bounded variation, can jump and wiggle too much for smooth tools. A classic idea, tied to Lusin, says such a function can be matched by a nicer one except on a tiny set.

Working in measured spaces with a doubling rule and a key inequality, the pair build the nicer match for any chosen small error. The match agrees with the rough function outside a set of tiny capacity, and its upper and lower versions gain one-sided smoothness. On plain Euclidean space, one more niceness holds for a related maximal function.
arxiv-2501-07847:
Sukjung Hwang, Kyungkeun Kang, Hwa Kil Kim, and Jung-Tae Park prove solution existence for drift-diffusion equations in a 2025 paper. Such equations model how particles spread while being carried by a flow. Their data can be as rough as a measure, which strains standard theory.

The authors show nonnegative weak solutions exist with controlled gradient bounds. The drift term may sit in a class matched to the data's roughness. When the drift has no net source, the allowed class widens further and more diffusion rates qualify. A new energy estimate handles both rough features at once. Counterexamples prove the ranges are sharp. The method also builds solutions for a diffusion flow coupled to fluid motion.
arxiv-2501-08247:
Zachary Miksis and Gillian Queisser rebuild a classic shortcut for diffusion in tubes so that it stays accurate when tube radius changes fast. The one dimensional Fick-Jacobs model cuts a 3D problem down, but a 1992 critique showed it breaks for steep radial slopes, and later patches kept the flaw. Their 2025 paper finds the root in the original derivation's truncation.

Treating the old derivation as a local expansion yields a model whose error no longer depends on geometry. Its numerical scheme is provably stable and convergent, and the authors show the standard corrections can never reach the same answer, however fine the grid. Schemes for branched networks cost no more than the old ones. A nerve cell example matches full 3D results that the standard model misses.
arxiv-2501-08347:
Bhavin Jawade and eight co-authors present SCOT in 2025, a way to train image search that follows edits. In compositional retrieval, a user gives a photo plus a text tweak, such as a color change, and wants the edited match. Training such systems normally needs costly hand-built triplets of photos.

SCOT skips the triplets. It trains on plain photo-caption pairs, using a big language model to help and a vision model's text vector as a stand-in for the target photo. In zero-shot tests, it beat prior zero-shot methods and many fully trained ones on two standard benchmarks. The trick widens the task to new objects and domains.
arxiv-2501-08447:
