Henry Talbott studies a growth-rate value on curved surfaces with long borders, in a math paper from two thousand twenty-five. The surfaces live in a space of all such shapes, weighted by a standard measure. A graph built from the surface's spine offers a simpler stand-in space.

Talbott compares the growth value on the true space with its twin on the graph space. As border length grows, the two values meet on average. The shape measure on one space lines up with the graph measure, with uniform error bounds. The result bridges surface geometry and graph models in the long-border limit.
arxiv-2501-08947:
Leen Lambers, Lucas Sakizloglou, Taisiya Khakharova, and Fernando Orejas present the first systematic taint analysis for graph APIs, aimed at broken access control. Their paper from twenty twenty-five taints any graph node holding data that needs privileges to touch. Source and sink calls are modeled as graph transformation rules. Critical pair analysis then hunts dependencies that betray a tainted flow.

Direct and indirect flows get separate treatment, with conditions for when the static pass catches each. Flagged flows guide the design of dynamic security tests that confirm real risks. A slice of GitHub's GraphQL API serves as the testbed. Both failure directions surface: users wrongly locked out, and users wrongly let in. API security gains a systematic audit method.
arxiv-2501-09147:
Galaxy clusters carry clues about the cosmos in the way their mass thins out into the space around them. Charlie Mpetha and co-authors measure that outer fall-off in this 2025 paper by watching how cluster gravity bends the light of background galaxies.

Using an early shape catalog from a northern sky survey and three cluster lists, they stack the bending profiles and compare them with simulations. The most complete sample pins the matter share and lumpiness of the universe within a few percent. The team also measures where infalling matter splashes back for each sample, and expects far tighter answers from the final survey data.
arxiv-2501-09247:
Einstein's gravity can be stretched by letting the theory depend not only on spacetime curvature but also on the matter content itself. The authors of this study build universe models inside such a stretched theory, where gravity responds to curvature, matter, and the trace of the energy-momentum tensor together. They set up four models, each filled with a different cosmic fluid, from stiff matter to dust.

Each model is fitted against real data: thirty-one cosmic chronometer readings and more than seventeen hundred supernova distances. All four models show the universe switching from slowing to speeding expansion at late times, as observations demand. The team also checks that sound speeds stay within causal limits. Their fitted values land close to the standard picture while leaving room for the new coupling.
arxiv-2501-09347:
Shiu-hong Kao and co-authors present UVRM in a 2025 paper on rebuilding 3D objects from video. Classic training for such models needs the camera pose for each frame, a slow step prone to error. That need has kept training to fake data or small sets with poses marked by hand.

UVRM learns from plain single camera video with no pose data at all. A transformer folds the frames into a code that ignores pose, then decodes a three plane form of the object. Training leans on a guide method plus fake new views made by a diffusion model. Tests on two data sets show strong rebuilds across many object types. The model works fast as well as well, the team reports.
arxiv-2501-09547:
Mathieu Perron-Cormier and Nathan Deg lead a large team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It compares how lopsided the hydrogen gas in real galaxies looks, in the WALLABY pilot survey, against the same trait in the SIMBA simulation of galaxy growth.

The team built a scanline method to make fake survey data cubes with less noise than older particle-based ways. They then measured one- and three-dimensional lopsidedness for the real finds. The most lopsided cases were merging systems or ones with bridges and tails. Fake survey draws from SIMBA showed fewer high cases, but the gap was not firm. Bigger survey and simulation runs should sharpen the test.
arxiv-2501-09647:
Yu-Hang Su, Chengfeng Cai, and Hong-Hao Zhang published this dark matter study in 2025. They propose a model where dark matter is a charged scalar particle in a hidden sector. A dark photon mediates between that sector and ordinary matter through a faint mixing link. In this setup, dark matter can annihilate in two styles: secluded, mostly among its own kind, or catalyzed, sped up by the mediator. The team checked both styles against real observations.

Two datasets set the limits: gamma rays seen by the Fermi satellite, and the cosmic microwave background recorded by Planck. Earlier studies treated only the simplest annihilation channel and drew tight conclusions. Counting the full chain, where dark matter first makes mediators that later decay into ordinary particles, loosens those limits. A variant model tied to muon-related forces ends up least constrained of all.
arxiv-2501-09747:
Karl Pertsch and co-authors present a better way to encode robot actions in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Robot policies that predict action symbols need a scheme turning smooth movements into discrete tokens. Simple binning per joint and time step fails for fast, dexterous skills learned from high-rate data.

Their scheme, called FAST, compresses action sequences using a classic frequency transform. It lets autoregressive models learn skills that standard methods cannot capture at all. They also release a universal tokenizer trained on one million real robot trajectories. Paired with a vision-language model, the method trained on ten thousand hours of robot data much faster than a rival approach, with matching performance.
arxiv-2501-10147:
Mayu Hiraishi, Kensuke Tanioka, and Hiroshi Yadohisa propose a clustering method in a twenty twenty-five paper. Clustering groups data points so that alike points sit together. Their base method uses a scoring matrix from discriminant analysis, kept sparse so the groups stay readable.

The new version adds a penalty drawn from convex clustering. The penalty pulls points in one cluster closer and pushes apart points from distinct clusters, which sharpens the picture when plotted. The scoring matrix must stay orthogonal while it learns this shape, a hard pair of demands. The team builds an update rule with a majorizing function and tests it on simulations and real data.
arxiv-2501-10947:
Cunyuan Jiang derives the odd vibration spectrum of glassy solids from one simple demand. Amorphous materials lack the tidy lattice of crystals, and their low-frequency vibrations are famously more numerous than Debye's law predicts, following a fourth-power curve instead. Particle-level studies show the effect without settling its origin.

The argument starts from a quasi-equilibrium condition: over long observation, elastic energy must spread itself evenly through the material, however uneven its structure. Imposing that condition on an uneven elastic body yields exactly the fourth-power law at low frequency. Above a crossover set by the scale of the unevenness, the spectrum returns to the square law of crystals. The result suggests the anomaly is a fingerprint of thorough thermal mixing.
arxiv-2501-11047: Yuta Takahashi classifies weak Fano bundles of rank two over higher dimensional quadrics in this 2025 mathematics paper. A vector bundle earns the name when the variety built from it, its projectivization, is a weak Fano variety. The base spaces here are quadrics of dimension at least five. Takahashi presents classification results that list which rank two bundles on these quadrics qualify. Such lists pin down the possible shapes of these geometric objects and feed into the wider program of sorting Fano type varieties by their building blocks.
arxiv-2501-11647:
Olalla A Castro-Alvaredo, Stefano Negro, and Fabio Sailis extend a physics theory in a 2025 paper. The work concerns quantum field theories that can be solved exactly, and a known change that adds a length scale to them. That change reshapes high energy behavior in deep ways, even though it looks small on paper.

Most past work treated such theories with no edge. The authors ask how the change acts when the theory lives on a half line with a boundary. They propose a way to build the boundary scattering data under the change. The goal is a full form factor program for these edge cases, matching the bulk case.
arxiv-2501-12047:
Jiepeng Fang and Yixin Lan connect two deep structures in a 2025 mathematics paper. On one side sit canonical bases, special well-behaved bases for the representations of quantum groups. On the other side sit quiver varieties, geometric spaces built by Nakajima that realize those same representations.

Using characteristic cycles, a tool that reads the shape of sheaves, the authors build a map from the bases to the top homology of those spaces. They compare the basis elements with the spaces' basic classes. As a payoff, they show the whole realization can be defined over whole numbers, and they give a fresh proof of a known isomorphism claim.
arxiv-2501-13147:
Helena Treiber and co-authors chart twenty years of light changes in massive X-ray binary systems in a nearby galaxy. Their 2025 study uses survey data on 111 systems in the Small Magellanic Cloud. Each system pairs a heavy normal star with a compact partner that pulls gas from it.

Most systems vary on many time scales, in light and in color. That varying dance governs how much gas flows to the compact partner, which in turn stirs the donor star. The team builds a new sorting scheme for the long-cycle changes. The scheme links color shifts, orbit periods, and X-ray behavior in one frame. Most cases trace to the balance between disk glow and star glow. New candidate orbit periods also emerge.
arxiv-2501-13347:
Qingyue Long, Can Rong, Huandong Wang, and Yong Li build one model for many mobility trajectory tasks. Their twenty twenty-five paper proposes the GenMove framework. Trajectory data support network planning and city services alike. Past models were trained for single tasks like prediction or recovery.

Different tasks share common movement patterns, the authors argue. Masks unify the varied input and output formats. Past trajectories supply context about place, time, and user habits. A conditional diffusion model then handles generation, recovery, or prediction. One system replaces several separate task-specific models. The design aims to transfer learning across tasks instead of starting over each time.
arxiv-2501-13447:
Tillmann Buhler, Daniel Hug, and Christoph Thale study random covered regions in hyperbolic space in a 2025 paper. Their model scatters particles at random and looks at the set they cover, much like classic models in flat space.

Two ideas from the flat case are carried over: how often covered parts overlap, and how much volume stays visible from a point. The authors focus on the mean visible volume for such a model in curved space. They give a clear test for when that mean is finite. The test rests on the strength of the particle process and the mean surface area of a typical grain.
arxiv-2501-13747:
Yongyue Xiao and Yunnan Li present a 2025 mathematics paper classifying paired actions on a small, famous algebra. The Kac-Paljutkin algebra, with eight dimensions, is the smallest Hopf algebra that is neither group-like nor a dual. Matched pairs of actions on such algebras efficiently produce Yang-Baxter operators, key tools in quantum algebra.

The authors compute all matched pairs for this algebra and find exactly six. Four of them arise from known coquasitriangular structures on the algebra. The other two do not, and their Yang-Baxter operators turn out to be involutive, meaning applying them twice restores the input. The classification closes a case that tests how far the general construction reaches. It also hands algebraists two genuinely new operators.
arxiv-2501-14147:
Javier Yu, Timothy Chen, and Mac Schwager built in 2025 a system that lets teams of different robots jointly build one shared three-dimensional map with meaning attached. Robots stream images and rough positions from their own navigation systems. The devices differ, their clocks and formats differ, and nobody knows their starting positions relative to each other. A central server handles the merging.

One module aligns each robot's local map into a global frame. Another trains a semantic scene model online from the streaming data. Language labels distilled from a vision model let users query the map in words, such as asking it to go to the couch. In real-world tests the maps were twice as faithful as rival systems.
arxiv-2501-14447:
Hochang Lee, Kyung Chul Jeong, and Panjin Kim link two hard problems in a short 2025 paper. The first is shortening quantum circuits, whose depth drives errors on real hardware. The second is coloring the points of a graph so that linked points never share a color.

The authors show that for circuits built from gates that can swap order, finding the shallowest layout is exactly a coloring task. Gates become graph points, and edges join gates that cannot run side by side. Any good coloring tool can then serve as the circuit optimizer. Tests on known circuits, including arithmetic blocks used in quantum algorithms, confirm the approach. The trick lets quantum engineers borrow decades of graph research.
arxiv-2501-15347:
Farah Baracat, Luca Manneschi, and Elisa Donati study muscle signals for machine control in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Reading steady movement from skin sensors could drive prosthetic limbs and other interfaces. The team tests a brain-inspired way to encode those signals using groups of simple spiking units.

They vary the size of these groups and the settings of each unit, such as how fast it leaks and when it fires. A simple linear readout then turns the spikes into joint movement values. Mixed groups proved more robust and carried better to new cases than a single unit. The authors say tuning this variety matters for low-power, reliable interfaces.
arxiv-2501-15447: The BESIII Collaboration reports new decay paths of a charmonium state in a 2025 paper. The state, called h_c, can shed its energy as light and split into light hadrons, and one path ends in a known tensor state, f2(1270), among the debris. The paper announces the first sighting of these radiative decays to multiple light hadrons. Such decays test how heavy quark pairs turn into ordinary matter, and the tensor path gives a clean handle on the decay's inner shape.
arxiv-2501-15547:
Nathan Isong wrote this 2025 paper on building small neural networks for image sorting that still score well. Large networks sort images with high accuracy, but they need much memory and computing power. That makes them hard to run on small devices with tight limits.

Isong's method joins two training stages. One stage trains on both plain and altered copies of the images, which builds toughness to change. The other stage fine tunes a trained model by freeing its layers step by step. On three standard test sets, the small model reached 99 percent on handwritten digits and 89 percent on fashion images, with fewer than fifteen thousand settings.
arxiv-2501-16447:
Charles Lada and co-authors revisit, in a 2025 paper, what holds giant molecular clouds together in the Andromeda galaxy. These cold gas clouds are the birthplaces of stars, and a recent census found that, left to gravity alone, most of Andromeda's clouds would fly apart. Something must press on them from outside. The authors re-examine the cloud measurements with that pressure in mind.

When clouds are traced to their true outer edges, the outside pressure they need matches the estimated mid-plane pressure of the galaxy's disk. For the best-resolved clouds, the team measures internal pressure layer by layer: it climbs steeply with surface density, roughly as its square, and bends upward at the densest parts. Both habits match the theory of clouds in layered balance. The authors conclude that external pressure is a real, measurable partner to gravity in these clouds.
arxiv-2501-16947:
Sania Waheed and co-authors test whether big vision-language models can pin a photo to its place on Earth, in a 2025 paper. The task, called geo-localization, asks for the coordinates of a place from an image alone. For robots, the skill matters when a machine wakes up lost and must find itself with no prior map. The strongest models are often black boxes reached through an API, with no access to their training data or inner workings.

The team run the first systematic test of such models as stand-alone, zero-shot locators at planet scale, using a single text prompt. They vary the prompt wording and the query images, and they add a consistency score to track how steady the answers are. Their findings show both real skill and clear limits under these tight, realistic rules.
arxiv-2501-17147:
Baptiste Jego and three co-authors ask whether the cosmic web's faint threads can bend light measurably, in a 2025 paper. Dark matter mostly gathers in halos, but filaments and walls hold the rest, and their share grows in warm dark matter models.

Using fragmentation-free simulations with two particle masses, the team built mock lensing systems based on real galaxy lenses. They added the non-halo structures and refit with standard models. The extra mass shifted inferred lens parameters and the reconstructed source position. Yet ordinary lens models absorbed most of the effect, hiding it in plain sight. The shifts stay subtle, the authors conclude. Separating web pull from lens shape will be hard.
arxiv-2501-18047:
Oumeng Zhang and Changhuei Yang build a microscope that reads five dimensions at once in a 2025 paper. Fast single-shot imaging spares slow scans of living samples. Their scope joins a polarization camera to a light-field design.

One snap yields depth, brightness, and two polarization axes together. A test target with a star pattern confirmed sharp reads across polarization states and a wide depth range. Plant roots then showed split patterns in how their cellulose fibers align by section. The gains suit biology and environmental samples that shift fast. The design marks a step up for single-shot fluorescence work.
arxiv-2501-18147:
Youka Kaku, Akira Matsumura, and Tomohiro Fujita proposed a new test of gravity in a 2025 physics paper. Their idea asks whether gravity alone can link two objects in a quantum way. They set a trapped particle near a small oscillator that can sit in two states at once, each with its own rate of shaking.

Only one of those states can stir the particle by matching its motion. If the particle is then found stirred, the state of the oscillator must have collapsed at that same moment. That sudden loss, the authors argue, would be clear proof that gravity made the link. They also sketch how the test could be built with light and small moving parts.
arxiv-2501-18247:
Yang Hu, Aleksandr Druzhinin, Claudia Cancellieri, and Vladyslav Turlo sharpen a stress measure for stacked nano films in this 2025 paper. Nanomultilayers alternate two materials in films only atoms thick, and the stress at their interfaces shapes how coatings behave.

Standard measuring methods assume flat layers and smooth interfaces. The team adds corrections for wavy layers and rough interfaces and tests them on copper and tungsten stacks. Ignoring those features can inflate the measured interface stress by up to 0.4 joules per square meter. Even so, roughness alone cannot explain the extreme stresses on record, so atom scale effects like intermixing likely dominate. The paper gives practical rules for trustworthy measurement.
arxiv-2501-18347:
Dennis Perepelitsa describes di-hadron saturation signals with a universal nuclear parton approach in two thousand twenty-five. Paired hadron yields drop in proton nucleus hits at forward angles. That drop is often read as a sign of QCD saturation. The width of their angle spread stays put, which clashes with that tale.

Modern nuclear parton sets may explain the whole pattern instead. Shadowing of low momentum gluons does the work in his checks. Sets tuned by fresh precision data fit most of the drop. No extra dynamics that warp event links are needed. The width puzzle gets a natural answer that way.
arxiv-2501-18447:
Dave Dice and Alex Kogan sped up semaphores in a 2025 systems paper. A semaphore is a basic counter that threads use to take turns and guard shared data. Most other sync tools can be built from semaphores, and the Linux kernel leans on them hard, so their speed matters widely.

The pair first build a ticket-semaphore from a classic ticket lock idea. It is small and neat but fades as thread counts grow. They then add a waiting array that lets threads sleep in an orderly line instead of spinning. The result scales to many cores while staying compact. Kernel and app code both stand to gain.
arxiv-2501-18647: Atta, Singh, and Basu model, in a 2025 paper, how the magnetic fields of isolated neutron stars fade over time. Two clocks can read the decay: the second change in spin rate, and extra heat beyond standard cooling. For X-ray emitting stars, they find the spin-based rate matches the rate at which the main field sheds energy, if much of that energy escapes as X-rays. The field decay time comes out far shorter than the typical age of radio pulsars.
arxiv-2501-18847:
Jonathan Johnson and Khanh Le classify order-preserving symmetries in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. Free groups and surface groups can carry bi-orders, total orders respected by multiplication on both sides. The question is which finite groups of outer automorphisms keep such an order intact.

The authors give a complete answer for non-abelian free groups and for bi-orderable surface groups. They add a fresh criterion for automorphisms coming from braid actions. With it, they build examples whose underlying permutation is a full cycle. That settles a question posed by Kin and Rolfsen, in the affirmative. The work ties group orderability to braid dynamics in a precise way.
arxiv-2501-19147:
Pablo Pelaez and Araceli Reyes study algebraic cycles and a hoped-for filtration in a 2025 math paper. Algebraic cycles are formal sums of subvarieties, sorted into classes by how alike they are. One class gathers cycles that vanish under incidence equivalence, a fine notion tied to a classic kernel in the theory.

Their main result computes that class using a modern category of motives: it equals the second step of an orthogonal filtration defined by the first author. That filtration is finite and shares several traits with the still-unproven Bloch-Beilinson filtration. They also show that products of cycles that vanish in a coarser sense land in the same second step. Over finite fields and their closures, the result holds in every codimension.
arxiv-2501-19247:
Vladimir Jacimovic and Aladin Crnkic lay the math ground for clustering data in curved space, in this 2025 paper. Hyperbolic spaces, which curve outward, suit data with tree-like shape. Learning methods there are new, and basic tools were missing.

The pair define a center point for data inside a hyperbolic ball, then build the classic k-means grouping method on it. They also give a step-by-step fitting method for mixtures of new probability laws in the same space. The work is formal and proof-based. The authors present it as a base for unsupervised learning in hyperbolic geometry, much as classic tools serve flat space.
arxiv-2502-00247:
Abdullah Rasheed and Nidhi Dubagunta ask how close scattered computers can land when they must merge ranked choices, in a study from 2025. The classic task, lattice agreement, has each node pitch a value from a ranked grid; all must land on values that chain in rank. Close lands ease next steps, but the classic ask does not press for it.

The pair add a tightness rule with a gap gauge on the grid, an epsilon bound on how far apart land spots may sit. For step-locked nets they give rules that shrink the gap while they keep the classic deeds. For free-run nets they prove sharp bars: some tight earns are barred. A chance rule still lands tight most of the time, and tests show few rounds serve.
arxiv-2502-00447:
Physicists often sum series that diverge, using Borel-type methods tuned by control parameters, but the tuning equations can return several answers and no rule for choosing. Vyacheslav Yukalov and Simon Gluzman propose a tie-breaker in this 2025 paper: pick the parameters that minimize a cost function. They build new cost functions borrowed from lasso and ridge selection ideas.

The paper also introduces two fresh transforms based on fractional calculus, alongside the classic Borel-Leroy and Mittag-Leffler routes. Tested across a battery of model problems, the cost-guided choices gave good accuracy. The authors present the method as a general fix for a long-standing annoyance in resummation practice.
arxiv-2502-00847:
Jiawen Zhang, Kejia Chen, and five colleagues pursue privacy and robustness for language model services at the same time, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The two goals are usually chased separately: encryption schemes guard user data, while prompt ensembling blurs attacks by averaging several prompted answers.

Their system, SecPE, fuses the two lines of work. Private inference encrypts the data sent to and processed by the model. Prompt ensembling asks the model several rephrased versions of a request and aggregates the replies, which dilutes adversarial tricks. Simply bolting the two together is inefficient, the authors show, so they design the combination from scratch. The result aims at inference that is both confidential and hard to fool. Services facing the public need both traits at once. The paper is among the first attempts to deliver them jointly.
arxiv-2502-01247:
Ismail Khalfaoui-Hassani and Stefan Kesselheim ask which curves may serve as the activation functions inside deep networks. The usual choices are a small fixed menu, yet nothing sacred picks them. Their 2025 study builds activations from orderly bases instead: Hermite polynomials, Fourier waves, and a tropical cousin of the polynomial family, all set up so signal sizes stay tame from the start.

With plain variance-preserving starts and no clamping tricks, these activations trained deep models well, including a GPT-2 style model on web text and a ConvNeXt image classifier on ImageNet. The work tames the exploding and vanishing signals that plague polynomial choices. A side benefit is clarity: a network with polynomial activations is itself one big polynomial map. The team also shows the new curves can mimic classic activations closely enough to fine-tune old models, and ships them in a public library.
arxiv-2502-01347:
Simone Bombari and Marco Mondelli dissect why learning models latch onto misleading clues, in a 2025 paper. A model may lean on a feature that predicts the label in training yet means nothing in the world, which hurts robustness and fairness. The pair study high-dimensional regression with one true feature and one spurious one. They measure exactly how much spurious weight the fitted model carries, in terms of the data's spread and the strength of ridge regularization.

The spurious feature's simplicity is read off its covariance spectrum, and its link to the true feature off a matrix complement. They prove a trade-off: the regularization that minimizes test error sits where spurious reliance is still rising. Over-parameterized random feature models behave like the regularized linear case. Tests on synthetic and image data back the theory.
arxiv-2502-02047:
Nebiyou Daniel Hailemariam, Blessed Guda, and Tsegazeab Tefferi built a question-answering test set for Amharic, a language with few digital resources, and report it in 2025. They translated the well-known SQuAD 2.0 set into Amharic, a task that often breaks the link between a question and its answer span. To fix shifted answers, they matched text with word vectors from an Amharic-tuned model plus a longest-match method.

Training a large multilingual model on the new set lifted its scores on the Amharic test data. Scores also rose a little on a separate set of questions checked by people. The data set is public, so other teams can now build and test Amharic question-answering tools against the same yardstick.
arxiv-2502-02147:
Javier Fresán, Yeuk Hay Joshua Lam, and Yichen Qin settle two linked questions on a class of special functions, in a 2025 math paper. The functions, called G-functions, arise from power series with arithmetic roots. A problem posed by Siegel asked whether each can be built from pulled-back hypergeometric pieces. A kin guess by Dwork pointed the same way.

The authors prove the answer is no. Their counterexamples meet equations of the smallest order where a counterexample can live. In fact, they build endless many unlike systems of geometric origin that escape that form. Tools span Lie algebra tricks, classic monodromy counts, and trace field facts for surface groups.
arxiv-2502-03147:
Large language models can learn to reason over tables from examples shown in the prompt. But plain-text tables eat tokens fast, so only a few rows ever fit. Xumeng Wen and co-authors widen the window by adding retrieval: a custom module fetches the rows a task needs. The model is also tuned with retrieval-guided training so it learns to use those rows well.

Tested across sixty-nine well-known datasets, the approach improves results and scales to tables of any size. It still trails finely tuned numeric models overall. Yet it finds strong solutions in tight settings, adds variety to model teams, and shines on certain datasets. That hints at language as a flexible interface for table learning.
arxiv-2502-03447:
Yancheng Cao and a large team designed a 2025 virtual space to help autistic children read social cues near traffic. Knowing what a street scene asks of them is hard for many such children, and poor reads can put them at risk. Their space uses large language models to act out drivers, so children can train in a safe, staged street world.

The team first drew 17 design points from past work, grouped in four sets. They then built a system called AIroad that fills a room-sized screen world with drivers of varied moods. Readers see how the space was built and how it may coach safer street sense.
arxiv-2502-03547:
Lorenz Zwick and Johan Samsing show how motion across the sky could be measured for a special kind of gravitational wave event, in a 2025 paper. When a galaxy bends waves from a merging neutron star pair, two copies of the signal arrive. Comparing their phases can reveal how fast the source drifts sideways.

For planned detector upgrades, a strongly magnified event could show a faint phase shift if the source moves fast enough. The speeds needed match the spread seen in large galaxy clusters. For the most likely source setup, the sharper future detectors should almost always catch the shift above a set speed. The authors say a first measure of sideways motion this way may come within a few years.
arxiv-2502-04747:
Mengwei Xu, a solo author, argues that tomorrow's software agents should work inside programs, not at their surface, in a 2025 paper. Today's agents poke at apps through public buttons or screen pixels, and both routes are clumsy and error-prone. Xu's blueprint instead gives a large language model the program's source code and live runtime state, plus permission to write and run fresh code inside the app on the spot.

Two case studies on popular web-based desktop applications show the pattern at work. With internals visible, the model can check what the software is really doing rather than guessing from the screen. The paper also maps the hard parts: safety, permissions, and trust. Xu casts the shift as deep, a move toward software that understands, acts, and even reasons with its user. The piece is a position paper with prototypes, not a finished product.
arxiv-2502-04847:
Qijun Gan and eight co-workers wrote a 2025 paper on a pose-guided transformer that generates long videos of human motion. Makers struggle with hands and faces, above all in long or tricky sequences. Fixed resolution and drifting looks add to the problem. Their model trained on a wild set of many thousands of video hours.

The design accepts varied resolutions and clip lengths, aiding long takes. A prefix reference trick keeps a person's traits steady across a sequence. At run time, a keypoint module drafts future poses for continuation. An adapter also moves poses from one clip to another. Tests showed top results for long, pose-true videos.
arxiv-2502-04947:
Hélène Barucq and co-authors joined two ways of solving physics equations in 2025: the finite element method and neural networks. Finite elements are accurate and come with known error bounds but can be slow. Neural methods are fast, above all for hard cases, but their accuracy can be poor.

Their plan enriches the finite element space with a first guess taken from a neural network. The enriched method keeps proof of its error bounds and beats the classic method by a factor tied to how good the guess is. Tests in one, two, and three dimensions showed the same accuracy could be reached with a coarser mesh, saving time on problems with many settings.
arxiv-2502-05247:
Gamberale and Modanese study the excited states of coherent harmonic qubits coupled over long range through a shared photon mode. Ensembles of interacting oscillators or qubits can show quantum synchronization. In their system, identical two state units with a harmonic kinetic term couple to one dissipative photon mode. Strong coupling condenses the ensemble into a negative energy ground state. Its energy gap grows with system size.

A weak external oscillator probe scans for coherent transitions, revealed by changes in its occupation. A second external oscillator then tests energy transfer between the two probes through the qubit excited states. Above threshold, resonant transfer occurs at frequencies that sit higher and grow with the number of qubits.
arxiv-2502-05447:
Xinke Xie, Yang Lu, and Zhiguo Ding design wireless transmitters whose antennas can slide along a guide in a 2025 study. Pinching antennas place small dielectric pieces on a waveguide so signals radiate close to users, cutting the loss that grows with distance. Placing those pieces well, and setting their power, is a joint design problem.

The authors model the link between antennas and users as a bipartite graph. A graph neural network then learns placement and power choices together. Learning replaces repeated hard optimization for each new layout. Flexible antennas that follow users could raise data rates in crowded indoor and urban networks.
arxiv-2502-05847:
Zheng-Wei Zuo, Wanwan Shi, and Haisheng Li study in 2025 the edge states of bound pairs of particles in a chain where the pull between neighbors varies in a pattern. A doublon is two particles bound as one unit. The team asks what forms of protection these pairs gain when the varying pull has a set period.

They work through two model systems, one of bosons and one of fermions with no spin. In the strong pull limit, the pair's energy bands form a butterfly like pattern as the period changes. Math markers decode the pattern's protected traits, and bound states appear at the edges. When hopping grows strong, the pair bands can cross the bands of free pairs, which gives new phases. Results like these guide the design of lab systems that mimic protected quantum states.
arxiv-2502-05947:
Zhendong Zhang speeds up text generation with a flexible guessing tree in a 2025 paper. One trick lets a language model draft several words ahead with extra heads, then checks them in parallel, but the check tree's fixed shape wastes effort.

The new method grows the tree to fit the moment, using a simple, cheap rule to pick candidate paths. Early tests show faster decoding at the same output quality as the fixed tree version. The gain comes from spending checks where guesses are likeliest to hold. The work points to wider tuning room in multi head decoding.
arxiv-2502-06047:
Yesom Park and co-authors present a neural method for rebuilding surfaces from point clouds in a 2025 paper. Scanners yield clouds of points on an object's surface, and software must infer the smooth surface itself. Many methods learn a distance function that says how far each point in space sits from the surface, but they can miss its gradient, which guides the rebuild.

Their method learns the exact shortest path from any point to its nearest surface point, split into length and direction. Each part is trained to match the distance and its gradient, and a new loss enforces the path property. Tests on varied data sets gave high-quality surfaces that held up under noise and sparse sampling, beating leading methods.
arxiv-2502-06147:
Eri Onami, Taiki Miyanishi, Koki Maeda, and Shuhei Kurita built LegalViz in twenty twenty-five, a data set pairing legal documents with diagrams that explain them. Judgments and court orders demand expert knowledge; a simple diagram of parties, transactions, and legal sources can open them to lay readers. Their collection spans twenty-three languages and over seven thousand cases, with diagrams written in the DOT graph language.

The authors add evaluation metrics that judge a generated diagram by its graph structure, text similarity, and legal content. Few-shot and fine-tuned language models were tested across the languages. Models trained on LegalViz beat existing systems, including GPT-class models. The work treats legal visualization as a translation problem with its own quality measures.
arxiv-2502-06247:
Mamoru Shibata wrote this 2025 paper on quantum secret sharing, a way to split a quantum secret among a group so that only set subgroups can rebuild it. In schemes built on stabilizer codes, some shares can be handed out before the dealer even holds the secret. This early handout is called advance sharing.

It was known that a set of shares can be shared early only if the set is forbidden, meaning it is barred from learning the secret. Whether every forbidden set can in fact be shared early was open. Shibata gives a case of a forbidden set that the old scheme cannot share early. He then builds a new scheme, for quantum secrets, in which every forbidden set can be shared in advance.
arxiv-2502-06547:
Oskar Nordenfors and Axel Flinth write in 2025 on teaching a learning model to respect known symmetries of its task. A model is group equivariant when a symmetry applied to the input shifts the output in the matching way, and such built-in respect can sharpen performance. Their route uses training data alone: augment the data with symmetry-transformed copies.

Summarizing their earlier work and extending it, they show that augmented training paired with a regularization term yields an equivariant model. The result gives a practical recipe for baking symmetry into models without special architectures, for tasks where the symmetry group is known in advance.
arxiv-2502-06747:
Giulia D'Angelo and five co-authors build a vision system that copies how animals spot moving objects. Normal computer vision leans on huge data sets and heavy compute. Their 2025 system uses an event camera, which reports only changes in a scene, and a spiking neural network on low-power hardware. Small eye-like movements help the system tell moving objects apart from its own motion. It then turns to center the object of interest.

Tests on lab patterns and public video sets gave strong scores for finding moving objects. Detection stayed accurate in office scenes and in low light. A live demo answered scene changes in about a tenth of a second. The design needs no training, which the authors say makes it sturdy for robots.
arxiv-2502-07047:
Yuga Iguchi and Alexandros Beskos give a closed form expansion for the transition density of stochastic differential equations. They are central to inference for diffusion models, yet exact formulas for them are rare. Past work covers the elliptic case, but the hypo-elliptic class lacked a like result. In that class, noise acts on only part of the system.

The expansion runs in powers of the time step and can be run with symbolic software. Much of the work bounds the remainder for a fixed time step, which pins down the error size. The same method treats both cases in a uniform way. Tests show the method works well for parameter inference, even past the stated sufficient conditions.
arxiv-2502-07147:
Muhammad Zubair and co-authors present a 2025 study of antimony arsenide alloys that may act as Weyl semimetals. Such materials host points where electron bands cross, which gives them odd and useful traits. The team used density-based math to scan alloy mixes from pure antimony to pure arsenic.

All mixes with broken symmetry showed the Weyl phase, unlike a kin alloy family where only two mixes did. The half mix holds twelve crossing points near the energy level that matters, plus a strong spin-Hall response. It also nearly matches a common chip base, which eases growth and testing.
arxiv-2502-07547:
Yuan and co-authors propose stopping training early for each example on its own, rather than for a whole dataset at once. Standard early stopping watches a validation set and halts everything together, wasting effort on examples the model already knows. Their 2025 method judges mastery per example: when an example's loss stops changing in a steady way, it drops out of further training.

A second order check on the loss gives a consistent mastery signal, so one threshold serves all examples. Dropping mastered examples raises gradient sizes and speeds the fall of training loss, the team shows. Across benchmarks, the method cut backpropagation work by ten to fifty percent. Test accuracy and transfer performance held steady or slightly improved.
arxiv-2502-07647:
Simon Grad and Sandi Klavžar count matched edge sets in graphs built by gluing. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, studies matchings, sets of edges that share no endpoints. A k-matching holds exactly k such edges. Counts of these sets matter in chemistry, where graphs stand for molecules.

Their method uses a transfer matrix built on a matching vector. It works for any graph assembled by joins over two-point sets. That reach goes far past past methods for chains of rings found in fuels and dyes. Two worked cases show the steps, one of them a full chemical example. The tool turns a hard count into routine matrix work.
arxiv-2502-07747:
Kshitij Gupta, writing alone in 2025, builds a test that asks language models to solve whodunits. The data set, WhoDunIt, is drawn from open mystery novels and short stories, and the model must name the culprit after reading the tale. That task checks deduction inside a story, a skill apart from plain fact recall.

To probe robustness, Gupta scrambles character names in three ways: keeping the originals, swapping names among characters, and swapping in famous real or fictional names. Several prompting styles are tried as well. Three leading models were each tested many times, with the majority answer kept. Scores held up on untouched stories but fell under some name swaps, above all when the swapped-in names were widely known. The author reads this as models leaning on name fame instead of the story's clues, and releases the data set openly.
arxiv-2502-08047:
Zhao and co-authors introduce WorldGUI in 2025, a benchmark that tests computer-using agents from messy starting points. Most tests start apps in a clean default state. Real users ask for help mid-task, with settings changed and steps half done.

The benchmark covers ten common desktop and web applications. Each task comes in systematically varied initial states that mimic real work in progress. Even top agents lost much of their performance under these non-default starts, showing fragile planning. The authors also give a simple agent framework that critiques its own plan at three stages, which improved reliability. They release the code and data for other teams.
arxiv-2502-08147:
The authors refine a key number in particle physics in a 2025 paper built only from measured data. The number is the strong coupling, which sets how strongly quarks bind. They build it from records of tau particle decays into lighter particles, gathered by past collider teams, plus data from electron-driven production of the same particles.

New in this round is a large, high-quality data set from the Belle experiment for one main decay mode. Since Belle has no matching data for two other modes, the team reworked its analysis plan. From the rebuilt combined spectrum, they apply finite-energy sum rules, a math tool they honed earlier, to extract a fresh value of the coupling. The data-only base makes the result a clean check on theory.
arxiv-2502-08547:
Doudou Zhou leads a large team from the United States and France on a data problem in hospital research. Their two thousand twenty-five paper deals with electronic health records. Records are rich, but each hospital codes facts in its own way. Privacy rules also block sharing patient-level data across sites. Joint studies stall when the same idea wears many codes.

The team treats harmonizing the codes as a learning task on a graph. Their framework learns shared forms for clinical ideas across sites. It does so without moving raw patient data. The goal is studies that span many hospitals in both countries. Cleaner shared forms should make such joint work faster and more sound. The paper aims at research that no single site could run alone.
arxiv-2502-08747:
The highest-energy cosmic rays might be all iron, and a research team traced what that extreme mix would mean, in work from twenty twenty-five. Shower depth data from a giant Argentine observatory set the test. Two shower models were each shifted to fit the heavy picture.

A four-kind mix model was then fit across energies. Consequences fan out: per-kind spectra bend, shower physics studies shift, and the galaxy's magnetic field steers the heavy arrivals more. The scenario is a stress test, not a claim. It shows how much rides on what these rare rays are made of.
arxiv-2502-09647:
Long documents strain transformer models, yet only some of their attention heads truly need the far context. Konstantin Donhauser, Charles Arnal, Mohammad Pezeshki, Vivien Cabannes, David Lopez-Paz, and Kartik Ahuja find a way to spot those heads in a 2025 paper. Some heads stick to nearby words, while others swing between near and far as the query demands. The team predicts the far-needing heads from local keys alone.

A simple second-moment model of the long-range scores does the predicting. Spotting the hungry heads early could save heavy computing on long texts. The results expose plain structure inside attention that was easy to miss. Efficiency gains are the promised payoff.
arxiv-2502-09947:
Jin Cui and co-authors read dementia patients' daily movement patterns with a two-stage learning model in a 2025 paper. Home sensors record activities at fine time grain, and hidden habits may guide care. Their data follow people living with dementia at home. Stage one turns each activity series into a text string, then encodes it with a fine-tuned language model.

Stage two spreads those encodings into a two-dimensional map and runs a PageRank-style analysis over it. That reveals latent states and how patients move between them, exposing activity biases. Combined with diagnosis records, the patterns aim to support personal care plans. The authors frame self-supervised encoding as a way to squeeze meaning from unlabeled monitoring data. Routine, in this view, is a signal worth measuring precisely.
arxiv-2502-10447:
Sungnyun Kim and co-authors build a speech reader that watches lips as well as listens in a 2025 paper. In noisy rooms, adding sight of the speaker's mouth helps a machine catch words. Such audio-visual systems, though, are hard to grow without heavy compute costs. Their system, MoHAVE, uses a mixture of expert sub-networks to scale up at low cost.

Only the expert groups that fit the input switch on for each clip. A layered gate picks which groups to use based on context. That design adapts to shifts in sound and sight while keeping the bill low. On standard tests for lip-reading data sets, the system set a new bar. It handled both writing down speech and translating it.
arxiv-2502-10647: Jonathan Barron presents a new power transform and shows it unifies many tools across statistics and machine learning, in a research paper from 2025. Power transforms raise data values to a chosen power, which can tame skew and standardize a data set. Barron's version serves as a single framework behind a wide family of loss functions, kernel functions, probability distributions, bump functions, and neural network activation functions.
arxiv-2502-10747: David Lee tackles an extension problem for operators of higher order and of logarithmic type in a 2025 mathematics paper. The extension trick, first shaped by Caffarelli and Silvestre, turns a nonlocal problem into a local one in one added dimension. Lee builds the higher-order version with ideas borrowed from renormalization, a method for handling scale in physics. He also offers a fresh view of a recent extension result for the logarithmic Laplacian, published by Chen, Hauer, and Weth in 2023. The paper is aimed at specialists in analysis.
arxiv-2502-10847:
Michał Marczenko examines when the matter inside neutron stars turns nearly conformal, a state where sound speed follows a simple pattern. Neutron stars pack more than a sun's mass into a city-sized ball, and no lab can copy those conditions. Physicists instead test ideas about the matter's equation of state, the rule linking its pressure and density.

The study focuses on the speed of sound inside the star and its average over depth. Several theory tests claim to flag the onset of conformal matter, where the sound speed settles near one third of light speed squared. Marczenko checks whether these rival tests agree with each other. He finds that their agreement is not automatic: it holds only when the toughest current theory and telescope constraints are applied together.
arxiv-2502-11747:
Md Zarif Ul Alam and Hamed Zamani study video questions that need facts from beyond the screen. Their 2025 work deals with open-ended asks, not just choice tasks. Models do well on what can be seen, but they often fail when a question needs wider context.

The pair test ways to add retrieved facts to video models. They vary the source of facts, the mix of text and image input, and the form of the query. Both off-the-shelf and tuned setups get trials. Added facts help, but gains hinge on the source and the search method used. Careful query design and search depth prove key, and one setup lifts choice-task scores by a wide margin.
arxiv-2502-11847:
Chi Li and Zhengyi Zhou prove a bound on a number that measures how singular a point of a geometric space can be. The quantity, minimal log discrepancy, is a central gauge in the classification of algebraic varieties. The spaces here are Fano cone singularities, cone-shaped varieties with favorable curvature that sit isolated at their tip.

The authors show the discrepancy never exceeds the dimension of the variety. The proof runs through the geometry of orbifold rational curves, whose moduli spaces encode the singularity's hidden structure. They also propose a conjectured test that would single out weighted projective spaces among Fano orbifolds using those same curves. If true, the bound would be sharp only at smooth points, a tidy endpoint for the theory.
arxiv-2502-11947:
Frank, Milius, Rot, and Urbat develop ways to teach machines that handle data words in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their automata read streams where symbols come from an endless supply of names, like the fresh codes used in security protocols.

The team focuses on bar automata, which mark name binding directly in the input, and shows that any standard learning method for ordinary automata can be lifted to this richer setting. The key step is handling when two data words count as the same up to renaming. Their framework also extends to infinite words and trees, giving the first active learning methods for those data languages. The work matters for verifying systems that juggle fresh identifiers.
arxiv-2502-12047:
Minglai Cai and Christian Deppe study a channel where one sender may cheat, in this 2025 paper. Most work on noisy channels assumes attacks hit the channel itself, while senders follow the rules. Here two senders share one receiver, and one of them may break the protocol on purpose.

The pair define a mixed classical-quantum version of this cheating-sender channel. They then derive a data rate that can be reached safely in spite of the dishonest sender. The note is short and sets up the problem rather than closing it. It opens a path for later work on secure links where the threat sits inside the group, not outside it.
arxiv-2502-12147:
Xiang Fu and colleagues judged atomistic AI models by whether their simulations conserve energy in a 2025 paper. Machine learning potentials mimic quantum calculations at a sliver of the cost, yet low test error often fails to predict success on real properties like stability or heat flow. The authors propose a practical gate: run molecular dynamics and check that total energy stays constant, as physics demands.

Models that fail the gate show telltale design choices, which the team used to fix a highly expressive architecture. The resulting model, eSEN, topped benchmarks across materials stability, thermal conductivity, and lattice vibration tasks. A physics sanity check, they argue, predicts downstream usefulness better than leaderboard error alone.
arxiv-2502-12447:
Anjali Singh, Karan Taneja, Zhitong Guan, and Avijit Ghosh write in 2025 about guarding human thought as AI tools spread. Their paper, tied to a workshop on tools for thought, reviews what is known about how generative AI shapes the way people take in facts, think, reason, and learn.

The authors use two classic frames: a revised ladder of learning goals, and an account of reflective thought. With those frames they trace how the tools can help or harm the growth of mental skills. They focus on beginners such as students, who may lack both subject knowledge and skill in working with AI. The paper ends with ideas for reshaping school work so that it builds critical thought and deeper engagement rather than letting the tools do the thinking.
arxiv-2502-12847:
Marjieh, Anglada-Tort, Griffiths, and Jacoby wrote in twenty twenty-five about how songs change as people pass them along in groups. Culture can shift through what is on offer, what people pick, and how well they copy it. Past work rarely tested all three forces at once. The team placed two thousand four hundred four people in networks. Each person chose a tune from neighbors and sang it back.

Tunes in these networks grew more complex and more pleasant than in simple chains. The shape of the network mattered for what emerged. When the team removed choice bias or copying bias, those network gaps shrank. That pattern shows the forces work together, not alone. The study gives a clear test bed for how shared culture forms.
arxiv-2502-12947:
Gyeongman Kim, Gyouk Chu, and Eunho Yang shrink mixture-of-experts language models, whose size keeps them off smaller machines. These models hold many specialist subnetworks but use only a few for any given input. The usual way of compressing a big model into a small one overlooks the specialists left idle.

The authors show the idle experts still carry knowledge a student model can use. They propose two fixes. One samples the experts extra times to harvest more of their knowledge. The other trains the router, the part that picks experts, so all of them teach the student in good proportion. Across their tests, both methods beat standard compression for these models. The work is the first to tailor knowledge transfer to this model family.
arxiv-2502-13247:
Language models answer fluently but their reasoning is hard to check. Alfonso Amayuelas and co-authors ground each reasoning step in a knowledge graph in a 2025 paper, turning private chain-of-thought into an auditable trail.

Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities, a structure that suits verification. The framework works with three reasoning styles: linear chains, branching trees, and graph-shaped thought. On a benchmark of domain graph questions, the grounded approach beat plain chain reasoning by a wide margin and set a new best mark. The team also varies step depth, branching, and model size to learn when grounding helps most. The goal is answers that are both more accurate and easier to trust.
arxiv-2502-13847:
Feiyuan Zhang and co-authors present DH-RAG, a retrieval method that uses a chat's own history to fetch helpful background text, in a research paper from 2025. Standard retrieval systems lean on fixed knowledge bases and ignore what was said moments ago. Long chats drift, and good answers need the thread's context.

One module rebuilds each search query from the current turn plus past turns. Another keeps a history database refreshed as the talk proceeds. Clustering, layered matching, and thought tracking refine the queries. Tests show the dynamic approach beats static retrieval in multi-turn dialogue. The design mirrors how people lean on memory while conversing.
arxiv-2502-13947:
Armin Abdollahi, Mehdi Kamal, and Massoud Pedram wrote a 2025 computing paper on solving very large binary optimization problems by splitting them between quantum style and classical hardware. Such problems, known as QUBO, cover scheduling, routing, and chip design, but Ising machines that attack them have limited size.

Their method, IC-D2S, slices a big problem into sub problems sized for the Ising machine, then stitches the answers together. A set of control parameters steers how the slices are made, and a cosine shaped annealing schedule plus a mutation step keep the search from getting stuck. On three large problem sets, the method matched or beat a software solver and a commercial quantum hybrid service. The work targets problems too big for any single machine.
arxiv-2502-14147:
Maricela Best McKay, Bhushan Gopaluni, and Brian Wetton replace a heavy battery model with a fast learned stand-in, in a 2025 paper. Lithium-ion batteries need management systems that predict how they will perform and age. The trusted physics model, called P2D, tracks chemistry in fine detail but runs slowly at high currents.

The team trained a convolutional neural network on data simulated from the physics model across random driving cycles. The network learned to reproduce lithium concentration profiles across the battery with high accuracy. They also show the stand-in can be adjusted to match a battery's state of health as it wears. A fast, faithful copy of the physics model could let control systems plan charging in real time. The approach keeps physics accuracy while shedding physics cost.
arxiv-2502-14247:
Jiayu Yang and co-authors present a 2025 report on generating three-dimensional content with AI. Designers want full objects with surface detail from a photo, several views, or a line of text. The framework, Pandora3D, splits the job into shape building and texture painting, each with its own pipeline.

Shape comes from a model that encodes solid forms into a compact code and grows new codes by diffusion. A mesh-based route is also tried for simpler forms. Texture work starts with a front view, expands to many views, and converts color into surface material maps. A scheduler keeps the views pixel-consistent as they form. Code and trained weights are released in public for others to build on.
arxiv-2502-14547:
Ali Saadat and Jacques Fellay built a tool that predicts how strongly a cell will destroy faulty gene messages. The cleanup system, nonsense-mediated decay, removes transcripts carrying early stop signals, and its strength shapes how mutations show up as disease. Simple rule-based guesses capture part of the pattern, while models fed only on sequence embeddings did worse than the rules in their tests.

Their predictor, NMDEP, blends tuned rules, sequence embeddings, and hand-picked biological features, and it reached the best accuracy they measured. An explanation analysis confirmed known drivers such as where the stop signal sits, and surfaced new ones, including how heavily ribosomes load onto the message. They then ran the tool over more than 2.9 million simulated stop-gain variants, giving researchers a ready map of likely decay strength for interpreting variants in cancer and inherited disease.
arxiv-2502-14747:
Five researchers build an AI ideation partner for entertainment concept designers in a paper from 2025. The catalog title carries a preprint note, but the head title is clean, and the description follows the head. Concept designers invent detailed worlds for film, games, and television. Their early phase mixes research, brainstorming, and image play. Existing AI tools mainly generate images from fixed briefs, missing that exploratory workflow.

The team studied twelve professionals, then built AIdeation for flexible search and recombination of references. Sixteen designers tested it against their usual tools. Creativity, speed, and satisfaction all rose clearly. Two studios kept using it on commercial projects after a week-long field study. The authors argue ideation support beats pure generation.
arxiv-2502-14847:
Pengfei He, Yupin Lin, Shen Dong, Han Xu, Yue Xing, and Hui Liu expose a security hole, in a 2025 preprint, in systems where several AI agents work as a team. Such teams solve hard problems by passing messages between agents. That message channel is also a weak point no one had tested. The authors act as attackers and ask whether the whole team can be corrupted without touching any single agent. They may only intercept and rewrite messages in transit.

Their attack, called Agent-in-the-Middle, uses an AI-powered adversary to edit those messages. A reflection step helps it craft edits that fit the flow and each agent's role. Tests across frameworks, team shapes, and real applications showed the attack works. Teams followed the poisoned messages and failed or misbehaved. The authors warn these systems need defenses built around their communication layer, not just each agent.
arxiv-2502-15147:
Zhouhang Xie and co-authors combine language models with classical statistics to discover hidden factors in document piles, guided by a stated goal, in a 2025 paper. Pure language model reasoning finds concepts unreliably when data is noisy or vast.

Their system, Instruct-LF, asks the model to propose fine-grained, goal-related properties of documents, then estimates each property's presence across the whole set. Optimization then groups co-occurring properties into interpretable factors. On movie recommendation, game navigation, and legal document tasks, the factors beat the best baselines by wide margins on downstream performance. Human judges also preferred them nearly twice as often. The authors stress interpretability as the payoff.
arxiv-2502-15347:
Jan Grebik and Zoltan Vidnyansky survey links between two fields in this 2025 paper. One field is descriptive set theory, which studies definable sets and graphs. The other is distributed computing, where many processors solve a shared problem. Recent work has shown that ideas move in both directions between them.

The survey focuses on vertex and edge colorings of graphs. It explains how a games method from set theory was adapted to the LOCAL model of computing. It also covers a chain method that led to new algorithms for edge coloring. A list of open problems closes the survey. Readers also get a fast algorithm for a coloring problem on slow growing graphs.
arxiv-2502-15547: Hsueh and Hsu present a paper from twenty twenty-five on a scoring method for a dice board game. Their method builds the board score from data, with no hand tuning. It records how far each piece sits from the target corner, a list they say captures the core of the game. Their scorer beat many classic hand-made scorers and won first place in a twenty twenty-three contest for the game.
arxiv-2502-16447:
Lauren Henderson, Evan Kirby, and their co-authors published this astronomy paper in 2025. It reports chemical measurements for 491 stars in five small galaxies that orbit the Milky Way: Sculptor, Fornax, Draco, Sextans, and Ursa Minor. The team used medium-resolution spectra from the DEIMOS spectrograph, a choice that let them study far more stars than earlier high-resolution work could reach.

The authors measured strontium, yttrium, barium, and europium, elements built up when stars capture neutrons. Barium patterns in Sculptor hint that fast-spinning massive stars added material early in that galaxy's life. Europium patterns point to a source that enriched stars quickly, so neutron star mergers alone cannot explain the record. The sample is the largest uniform set of its kind for these dwarf galaxies.
arxiv-2502-16747:
Nguyen and co-authors present SQLong, a training data method that makes language models better at turning questions into database queries when schemas are huge. Open weight models do well on this task, but skill fades as the schema, and with it the context, grows. Their 2025 framework stretches existing schemas with synthetic extra tables and rows drawn from many real schemas.

Finetuning on the stretched data mimics long context work during training. On two standard benchmarks, Spider and BIRD, models trained this way clearly beat models trained on plain datasets. The gains held at test time on long schemas too. The authors argue the approach is practical for real systems where databases come with complex schemas and long prompts.
arxiv-2502-18147:
Lucy Farnik and co-authors push sparse autoencoders from reading a model's thoughts to tracing its arithmetic, in a 2025 paper. These tools find tidy, human-readable features in a language model's activations. But activations are not computations. Their Jacobian variant forces sparsity in the mapping itself, the derivative linking input to output features, so the computation between them also breaks into few parts.

Computing such giant matrices cheaply is the technical core. The new tools kept downstream performance about as well as classic ones while exposing real computational sparsity. Trained models showed more of it than randomized twins. Sparsity of computation, it seems, is something networks learn.
arxiv-2502-18347:
Victor Geadah and four co-authors model the joint activity of many neurons with a system that stays linear once context is known. Brain circuits behave in nonlinear ways that shift with task and behavior, which makes their activity hard to summarize. The team's models let smooth statistical priors learn how the circuit's rules bend with outside variables. With those variables fixed, the dynamics are plain linear motion, easy to read and to fit with sound Bayesian tools.

The models hold up even when data are scarce, down to a single trial per condition, because nearby conditions share strength through the prior. The authors show two uses: thalamic neurons that encode heading direction in a curved way, and motor cortex neurons during a cued reaching task. They offer the method as a general lens on population recordings.
arxiv-2502-18447:
Will Schwarzer and co-authors simplify the problem of inferring what a person wants from how they act, in work from 2025. People's behavior is messy: some actions are clumsy, and some are meant to communicate rather than to succeed.

Earlier methods assume tidy behavior models or work only in small table-like settings. The proposed approach, Supervised Reward Inference, instead learns directly from examples of behavior paired with known rewards. The authors prove it is asymptotically optimal under standard assumptions. It nearly tops a prior benchmark for learning from suboptimal behavior, and on robot tasks it reads rewards from even badly flawed demonstrations about as well as those demonstrations allow.
arxiv-2502-18547:
Ching-Chun Chang and Isao Echizen present a 2025 paper on hiding messages in video and sound. The field is called steganography, or covert writing. New AI tools can make fake media that looks real. Such fakes can wipe out the faint changes used to hide a message in space or time, so the authors ask what stays stable.

Their plan hides the message in words, beyond space and time. A chain of AI tools turns media into text, hides the message there, then rebuilds the media. Word choice carries the code, and word odds let a reader pull it back out. Tests check how well identity, meaning, and secrecy hold up. Attacks such as face swaps were also tried.
arxiv-2502-18947:
Viktoria Freingruber, Tommaso Lorenzi, Kevin Painter, and Mariya Ptashnyk build, in 2025 work, a drift model where a cell's trait is how full its sense docks are. Cells chase a scent by those docks; the fuller the dock, the stronger the chase — yet a fixed fuel purse means keen chasers breed less, and keen breeders chase less.

A bent-walk birth gives two linked laws for cell and scent counts. A log twist then lays bare the trait spread inside the band waves the counts form, and its one-way drift. Sims play the trade across scenes. Trait spread, not one cell kind, drives the band.
arxiv-2502-19047:
Truong and Le built this two-way tool in twenty twenty-five for guarding image generators. Diffusion models can be backdoored: a hidden trigger makes them output a set harmful image. Owners need to spot such traps, yet the search method itself is powerful. Their framework, PureDiffusion, works on both sides of that line.

Two new loss functions guide a search that reconstructs the hidden trigger. One uses shifts the trigger causes across the model's time steps. The other uses a consistency quirk that fires when the backdoor wakes. Recovered triggers then flag attacks with near-perfect accuracy in tests. Turned around, the same search can sharpen a planted trigger. The authors report far faster, stronger attacks that way.
arxiv-2502-19147:
Kiyoshi Igusa redraws an old, unpublished paper on a deep algebra invariant in this 2025 work. The generalized Grassmann invariant is pictured through diagrams, also called Peiffer diagrams, that stand for elements of a group's third homology. Igusa shows an algebraic K-group of a group ring matches the deformation classes of these pictures for a special Steinberg group.

He builds a picture for an element of order sixteen in a famous small K-group. In this updated version only the pictures change; the text stands nearly as written. A new appendix explains the pictures through quiver representations and root systems. Where roots go missing in the drawings, he offers two repairs, one using ghost handle slides and one building relative pictures with ghost modules.
arxiv-2502-20247:
Jonathan Colen and co-authors built in 2025 a reinforcement learning controller for particle accelerators that can show its physics homework. Operators distrust black-box agents on costly machines. Their framework learns a stand-in formula for a physical quantity, such as beam energy, and bends the agent's choices to respect it.

The stand-in can be a neural net or a sparse, readable dictionary model. Tested on simulated halls modeled on a real facility, the agents converged reliably even in high-dimensional control tasks where plain learners struggle. Reading the learned formula confirmed the agent had picked up the established physics of each hall. The authors say explainable constraints buy both performance and trust. The method suits any control room wary of opaque automation.
arxiv-2502-20347:
Ozkan, Chrstos, Canova, and Stockar modeled driver behavior in speed advisory systems in twenty twenty-five. Such systems show drivers a suggested speed, and the car works better when it can predict how the human will respond. Driver responses are nonlinear and change over time, which makes them hard to model.

Their approach uses the Koopman operator, a tool that recasts nonlinear dynamics into a linear form suited to fast prediction. A recursive least squares update keeps the model adapting as a driver's behavior drifts. They validated it on data from a human-in-the-loop driving simulator covering varied driver styles. The offline model already predicted behavior closely, and online updates improved accuracy further.
arxiv-2502-20647:
Colleen Gilhuly and Haleh Shahzad grade the faithfulness of machine written news summaries in a 2025 paper. Fluent summaries can still invent facts. The pair ran four generators, from a classic ranking method to two chat models. They scored the output three ways: two classic overlap scores and a model based check against the source text.

They also add a meta score for the grader itself, since the judge needs judging too. On a large multilingual news set, every generator's summaries proved more consistent with their sources than the human written reference summaries. The authors frame consistency checking as still an open problem.
arxiv-2502-20847:
A popular way to fine-tune language models on human taste, direct preference optimization, keeps underperforming its older rival in practice. Qinwei Ma and five co-authors dig into its training dynamics in a 2025 paper and name a culprit: gradient imbalance. The pull of winning and losing answers is uneven, and that skew bends the whole learning path.

The team shows the effect in theory and in runs: imbalance perturbs the trajectory, rattles stability, and lands the model at worse endpoints. Their fix, Balanced-DPO, reweights the gradient cheaply inside the standard objective. Experiments confirm the diagnosis, since the balanced version learns better across their tests. The authors offer the result as both a patch and a pointer: preference training still holds low-hanging gains for whoever balances its forces.
arxiv-2502-21147:
Eli Verwimp, Guy Hacohen, and Tinne Tuytelaars show in 2025 that updating a trained vision model on old plus new data can match retraining from scratch at half the cost. Retraining is the safe default when both data sets are on hand, yet it burns compute. Smarter reuse of the old model could save a great deal.

Their test frame scores savings while holding accuracy at or above scratch level. Four levers matter: starting point, regularization, data choice, and hyperparameters. Simple first-step methods on each lever already save much compute. Combined, they cut training time up to 2.7-fold across vision tasks. The authors urge the field to treat reuse as the baseline to beat.
arxiv-2503-00547:
Graph neural networks learn from data shaped as networks, such as molecules, and they power tasks in drug discovery. Yet two similar graphs can see wildly different results from the same model. Lukas Fesser and Melanie Weber investigate that unevenness in a 2025 paper, asking what drives it and what to do about it.

Studying both message-passing and transformer-style models, they find large performance gaps between individual graphs. The graph's shape alone does not explain the gaps. A distance measure that weighs shape and node features together links the gaps to how far apart classes sit. The authors propose fixing only the graphs that benefit from rewiring, and they show the best network depth depends on a graph's spectrum. Their lesson is to adapt the recipe to each graph, not the dataset as a whole.
arxiv-2503-01247:
Samson Abramsky, Thomas Laure, and Luca Reggio write a 2025 logic paper on games used to compare structures. Such games test whether two setups match on statements that use only a bounded set of resources. Past work recast these games in a uniform algebra-like frame, where the saved setups encode what each logic fragment can preserve.

The authors extend that frame to two weaker fragments: one that drops all-purpose claims, and one that drops denial. For the first, they show saved setups amount to a notion called pathwise embedding. For the second, they coin a new matching notion. Both results are shown in concrete form and in a broad axiomatic setting. As a payoff, they give a fresh proof of a known positivity theorem for modal logic.
arxiv-2503-01547:
A smart kitchen robot must notice when someone moves the mug. Arash Nasr Esfahani and four co-authors build a system that watches a kitchen and tracks where objects have been relocated. Their detector starts from a pretrained image model, fine-tuned on a custom kitchen dataset, and a new scoring method judges each frame for each object.

The score combines an object's position and appearance across frames to pick its best-matching view in each scene, and comparing scenes exposes what moved. The design sidesteps troubles that dog older approaches, such as lighting changes and objects partly hidden in some frames. In experiments the algorithm reached accuracy near ninety-eight percent, with precision and recall both around ninety-six percent. The authors present it as a simple, effective step toward homes that understand themselves.
arxiv-2503-02147:
Chia-Wei Hsu and four co-authors introduce a new training algorithm for neural networks, named Frankenstein after the way it stitches together parts of older methods, in this 2025 paper. Fast adaptive methods converge quickly but often land on sharp solutions that generalize worse than plain stochastic gradient descent. The new method borrows the strengths of several adaptive schemes.

Frankenstein adjusts its two momentum terms on the fly, based on the state of training, so it reacts at once to sudden changes in the gradient. Tests across image tasks, language tasks, few shot learning, and science simulations show it beating both adaptive rivals and plain descent on speed and final quality. The authors also probe why it works, using tools that compare learned features and map the loss surface.
arxiv-2503-02447:
Shalabh Anand simulates a chain of self-propelled, circling particles and watches it tie itself into spirals, in this 2025 paper. The particles are chiral active Brownian particles: each swims and turns with a built-in handedness. Linked into a flexible polymer in two dimensions, their collective behavior is far from a passive chain's.

Under the chiral drive the chain shrinks markedly, its radius of gyration falling. Correlation analysis reveals the shape: a pair of spirals winds up at the two ends, turning in opposite senses. The total turn count grows with turning rate and activity, then weakens again at extreme activity, a pattern Anand maps into a phase diagram. The chain's end-to-end line rotates steadily, its frequency following a power law with exponent three halves. Scaling between size and chain length shifts under the drive. The work speaks to designed active materials.
arxiv-2503-02847:
Brandon Hardy and co-authors weigh methods for estimating blood pressure fields from advanced MRI scans, in this 2025 paper. The scans, called 4D flow MRI, capture how blood moves through vessels in three dimensions over time. From that motion, software can infer relative pressure, richer than the single drop a catheter gives. The paper studies tears of the aorta, where pressure maps could guide care.
