Three leading estimators are put through a full analysis on the same footing. The team checks how close each comes to true pressure fields, not just single values. Errors that look small on a single number can grow across a full map. A fair ranking helps hospitals and researchers pick the estimator that deserves trust in the clinic.
arxiv-2503-02947:
Reshma Anna-Thomas and co-authors use fast radio bursts to prove a hot halo round a near galaxy in a 2025 paper on deep space. Bursts are tick-long radio flashes that probe charged gas on their path to Earth. Two bursts that pierce the near galaxy were caught and placed by a US rig in the work.

Host homes of the bursts sit far past the near galaxy in deep space at great range. Path bends from our own galaxy and the hosts are first peeled off with care. What is left charts the near galaxy's spread of loose charge in its halo.
arxiv-2503-03847:
Liu and co-authors simulate how foam structure shapes squeezing strength in this 2025 paper. Many closed-cell foams grow with cells stretched along the rise direction, which makes them stronger one way than another. The fine mechanics behind that difference were not fully mapped, above all for light foams with thick cell faces.

The team built digital blocks of foam with varied cell shapes and random layouts, and squeezed them in simulation. Flat cell walls carried the load by stretching at first; bending mattered only after walls buckled. Shape effects reach strength through three paths: load-bearing area share, wall buckling strength, and wall tilt. Simple formulas linking cell shape to strength were derived from the findings.
arxiv-2503-03947:
Aurelio Noca and co-authors present COARSE, a way to teach off-road driving perception when detailed labels are rare. Self-driving vehicles in wild terrain must label mud, rock, brush, and track in every image, yet hand-labeling such scenes densely is scarce and costly. Simulation data help but look different from real trails.

Their method mixes sparse, rough real labels with dense labels from out-of-domain data. Two decoders, working at pixel and patch level, teach each other through shared pseudo-labels on unlabeled images. On two public off-road sets the scores jumped by roughly ten and eight points. Coarse human hints, used well, can substitute for expensive annotation campaigns.
arxiv-2503-04347:
Izzy Newsham and co-authors published this computational biology paper in 2025. It tests whether large language models can infer causal links in biology, such as which gene affects which other gene, without any task-specific training. Causal networks in cells are hard to map because effects run through hidden variables and change with context. The team built a framework to check model claims against real experimental data where genes were deliberately perturbed.

The tests covered more than a hundred variables and thousands of causal hypotheses. The authors also tried several ways of prompting the models and of feeding them scientific articles, including large and conflicting sets. With the right setup, even fairly small models captured meaningful parts of the true causal structure. The authors suggest such models could serve as organizers of existing knowledge for later analysis.
arxiv-2503-04547:
Charles Dunkl reads set values of a group song for hook shaped youth charts, in a paper from 2025. Youth groups of a swap clan spring from sets of like steps in a power word. Their worlds split into pure swap worlds, and each pure world has a song made by mean over the youth group.

Dunkl reads the song at a loop that takes at most one step from each step set. Hook charts, with one long arm and one long leg, get full values here. The values feed work on a set of spin like tools in a linked work with a mate. The read is pure math, built by hand from the chart shape.
arxiv-2503-04747:
Jianlong Zhou and Fang Chen borrow the safety case method from aviation to give AI ethics a proof structure in this 2025 paper. Ethical principles for AI are everywhere, but checking a real system against them stays vague. Safety engineering solved a similar problem long ago with assurance cases that tie claims to evidence.

Their approach rests on three pillars: what users actually require, the evidence gathered, and validation that the evidence suffices. Hazard analysis methods from safety work shape the case. They built a platform that walks a team through building such a case. It was tried on an AI system that shortlists job candidates, a setting where unfairness has real victims. The case study showed the method working end to end. The authors offer it as a route from principles to auditable practice.
arxiv-2503-04847:
Santosh Bhupathi surveys the role of databases in apps that write and answer with smart models, in a paper from 2025. Such apps stand or fall on how well they store, fetch, and add context to data. Bhupathi sorts database jobs into three kinds, each tied to a kind of context the model needs to answer well.

Chat history fits fast key based stores and document stores. Facts about the world fit row based stores and pooled data lakes. Sense based search fits vector stores that find near matches by meaning. Fast live queries and vector search lift speed and hit rate, the paper argues. A mix of stores, picked with care, gives apps sharper, more tailored answers at scale.
arxiv-2503-05247:
Phones that unlock with a finger photo can be fooled by fake images, so the phone needs a way to spot such attacks. Anudeep Vurity, Emanuela Marasco, Raghavendra Ramachandra, and Jongwoo Park tackle that problem in a 2025 paper on finger photo attack detection.

The team first tested how well current systems hold up when photos come from a phone model they were not trained on, and found that performance drops. They then built a new network that pays close attention to color channels in small windows of the image. Tests on three public data sets, using phones such as the iPhone 13 Pro and Google Pixel 3, showed the new design stayed reliable across devices.
arxiv-2503-05447:
Weigao Sun, Disen Lan, Tong Zhu, Xiaoye Qu, and Yu Cheng introduce Linear-MoE, a system that joins two fast design trends for large language models, in work from 2025. Linear sequence models handle long inputs at low cost. Mixture of experts layers switch on only a few parts per input, which also saves cost.

Their system has two parts. A modeling part gives one frame that supports all forms of linear sequence model. A training part adds parallel methods, with a sequence parallel scheme built for these models. The team also tests hybrid models that mix their layers with standard transformer expert layers.
arxiv-2503-05547:
Hati and nine co-authors describe a way to make a very steady radio signal from light signals. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, reaches doubt levels below one part in a huge count.

Two chains each start with a laser held steady by a cold or glass space. Comb tools turn the light first to a fast wave signal, then down to a slower radio one. The team built a new, low-noise digital tool to check each step. They match its results with a known check method. The work aids clocks and tests that need radio tones of the utmost steadiness.
arxiv-2503-05947:
Beltz-Mohrmann and co-authors present a matched pair of giant universe simulations built to probe dark energy. Recent results from the DESI survey hint that dark energy may not match the standard constant picture. The team ran two simulations from identical starting conditions, changing only the cosmology. Each run follows an enormous particle count in a box 1.5 billion parsecs across.

The paper shows how the altered cosmology changes the clustering of matter, the numbers of dark matter halos, and how fast those halos gather mass. A new forward model also paints galaxies onto the halos, letting the team trace how star formation histories shift between the two worlds. Halo catalogs are public. For cosmologists, the pair offers a test bed for squeezing more dark energy signal out of nonlinear data than standard distance measures give.
arxiv-2503-06347:
Vikas Dwivedi, Bruno Sixou, and Monica Sigovan present a 2025 arXiv paper on fast physics-informed solvers for fluid flow. Their base method, an extreme learning machine with physics built in, beats deep networks on speed and accuracy for simpler equations, but nonlinear problems resist it. The team adds a curriculum plan that rewrites a hard equation as a ladder of easier ones.

Network starting values also gain a physical meaning through radial basis functions. Tests cover the viscous Burgers equation, with its shock solution, and lid-driven cavity flow up to a Reynolds number of 100. A final test predicts blood flow in a narrowed vessel.
arxiv-2503-06547:
Rasul Dent, Pedro Ortiz Suarez, and co-authors frame tongue spotting as a mine task to build pools for rare writ tongues, in a 2025 paper. Class sort wastes time on the vast dull share of web text. Rare tongue pools need the few gems found fast, not all text sorted in full.

A mine lens spends its work on finds, not on full class calls. A new pipe and fresh pools for French born creole tongues show the way. Pool growth runs fast with wide reach past old pipes in tests. Less writ tongues gain a build path that fits their odds. The frame may serve more rare tongues next.
arxiv-2503-07047:
Yongle Zhang and co-authors tackled image repair in 2025 for objects that are only partly damaged. Text-guided diffusion editors can repaint a masked region from a written prompt. But a prompt cannot say exactly where surviving edges and textures should continue, so repairs often clash with the intact part of the object. Sketch guidance helps, yet earlier sketch methods let information flow only one way, from the sketch into the hole.

Their method, built on a pre-taught diffusion model, makes the contact run in both directions. Context from the uncorrupted area first informs the sketch traits, and the enriched sketch then guides the inpainting, a pairing the authors call context-to-sketch and sketch-to-inpainting contact. The two-way exchange keeps the filled region steady with the surviving form, reducing the mismatches that betray a repair.
arxiv-2503-07147:
Shoham Letzter, Abhishek Methuku, and Benny Sudakov build long cycles inside sparse networks that still spread out well. Their target structures are sublinear expanders, graphs that expand modestly yet appear inside many larger graphs. The authors develop new ways to thread a cycle through nearly every vertex of such a graph, keeping good control of the leftover structure. They also develop new ways to find these expanders inside arbitrary graphs.

With those tools they advance a conjecture of Verstraëte that has stood for twenty years. The claim says that in any regular graph, almost all vertices can be covered by separate copies of a subdivided pattern graph. Earlier teams had settled special cases; this work extends the reach considerably. The authors add two further applications, arguing their expander methods should serve other embedding problems in sparse graphs as well.
arxiv-2503-07347:
Johan Edstedt and co-authors teach image keypoint detectors without any descriptor crutch. Their 2025 paper serves structure-from-motion systems, which rebuild scenes from thousands of photos. Keypoints anchor those rebuilds, but training detectors is awkward since the pipeline cannot be differentiated. Old methods lean on a paired descriptor, which ties the two parts together.

Their fix uses reinforcement learning with a self-made reward, plus balanced sampling to keep training sane. Oddly, two detector breeds emerged: one sees only bright points, the other only dark ones. A third model, DaD, merges both by matching their combined output. It beat prior leaders across many benchmarks. Code and weights are public.
arxiv-2503-07447:
Jeong Han Kim and BaoLinh Tran set a new threshold in a 2025 math paper on how opinions settle to one view on a random network. Each node starts red or blue and, day by day, copies the majority color among its neighbors, keeping its own color on ties. The question is when the whole network ends up one color.

Earlier work found conditions on link density and the starting gap between camps that make unanimity nearly certain. Those conditions were fairly demanding. Kim and Tran push the density limit lower, widening the range where a clear starting lead still sweeps the network. Their result tightens the math of social and sensor networks that update by local majority rule.
arxiv-2503-07547:
Nina Moorman and co-authors help robots and people fix mismatched mental models in a 2025 paper. Teammates each carry an inner picture of the task, the setting, and each other. When those pictures diverge, teamwork degrades. Older fixes assumed one side's picture was correct and aligned the other to it.

Their framework drops that assumption. A large language model hosts a semi-structured dialogue in which both sides can speak. Human and robot each name missing context that matters for the task. Round by round, the two pictures converge toward a shared one. The method treats misunderstanding as a two-way problem, not a one-way correction. It aims at smoother work for mixed human-robot teams on real tasks.
arxiv-2503-08247:
Linda Mauron and Giuseppe Carleo challenge claims of quantum advantage in annealing, in a 2025 paper. A quantum device had set new benchmarks for simulating spin glasses, a hard physics problem. The line between what classical and quantum machines can do was still open.

Their classical method uses a time-based variational approach with a wave function chosen for physical reasons. It matched the accuracy of quantum hardware on systems up to one hundred twenty-eight spins, with errors below seven percent. Its cost grew only at a polynomial rate, unlike some rival methods. The results push the claimed quantum frontier further out.
arxiv-2503-08647:
When a star is shredded by a black hole, dust around the hole glows in infrared light long after the flare. Megan Masterson and co-authors present the first James Webb telescope views of four such events in a 2025 paper.

All four events were picked out by their infrared glow rather than visible light or X-rays. The Webb spectra show lines from highly charged gas near the center, proof that the disruption's own energy lit the nucleus. Strong silicate features, far stronger than in active galaxies, point to thin dust clouds re-radiating the flare. Two events had no flare seen in other bands at all. The work opens a window on hidden disruptions in dusty galactic centers.
arxiv-2503-08747:
Del Campo and Malaina examine how far an AI system can go in doing cancer imaging research on its own. Their 2025 study, written in Spanish, uses breast scans that track contrast flow, a rich source for tumor analysis. A leading AI model was set to clean the data, propose hypotheses, and run clustering, prediction, and network analyses, building on an earlier human study.

Results were compared with hand-computed outcomes. The AI showed limits in the openness of its process and in the accuracy of some calculations. The authors use the case to open a wider debate on method and ethics. They ask whether automation could one day replace the human role in science.
arxiv-2503-09247:
Shreecheta Chowdhury, Amit Chakraborty, and Saunak Dutta propose an unsupervised hunting tool in 2025 for rare events at the Large Hadron Collider. One quarry is a rare top quark decay that swaps flavor, yielding a Higgs particle. Such signals hide in huge background data, and a method that needs no model of new physics is prized.

Their tool, a self-organizing map, sorts events onto a grid where signal and background settle in separate clusters. That separation highlights regions where the signal stands out most strongly. Tests show the map stays robust when aimed at other new-physics searches, both model-free and model-guided. The authors present it as a flexible anomaly finder for collider data.
arxiv-2503-09347:
Hongyu Chen and Seraphina Goldfarb-Tarrant show that language models judging content safety can be swayed by surface tricks, not substance. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tests eleven judge models across key safety domains. Three checks structure the study: consistency across repeat judgments, agreement with humans, and sensitivity to artifacts like apologetic or wordy phrasing. Verdicts wobble on all three.

Apologetic language alone can swing preferences by up to ninety-eight percent. Bigger models are not reliably tougher; some small ones resist specific artifacts better. Jury voting across models helps both robustness and human alignment, yet artifact sensitivity survives the best juries. The authors warn that comparative safety claims built on such judges rest on sand until artifact-proof methods arrive.
arxiv-2503-09447:
Saimouli Katragadda and co-authors build a system that maps language onto a live three-dimensional scene as a robot or camera moves. For an AI agent to follow spoken instructions in a real space, it must tie words to places in that space. Earlier methods baked language features into 3D maps offline, a slow step that blocks use in new settings.

Their framework, Online Language Splatting, runs inside a live mapping system based on 3D Gaussian splatting. A fast module produces detailed language features for each camera frame in milliseconds. A two-stage compressor squeezes those features down to a compact size without losing open-vocabulary search, and a split optimization keeps images crisp. The online method beat offline rivals on accuracy while running more than forty times faster.
arxiv-2503-09547:
Pirogov and co-authors study collapsing cores where massive stars form in a 2025 paper. Five dense cores, each tied to a massive star region, were mapped in two molecular lines from a sky survey. The cores sit at varied life stages and all show signs of shrinking.

Fitting a round model to the maps gave density fall-off rates and slow, nearly even inward speeds, unlike free fall. Two cores hint at rotation. Surrounding gas also drifts toward three of the cores. Readers get evidence that these cores collapse as whole systems while trading matter with their clouds.
arxiv-2503-09647:
Ryan Quek Wei Heng, Edoardo Vittori, Keane Ong, Rui Mao, Erik Cambria, and Gianmarco Mengaldo wrote a 2025 paper on using large language models for top down sector allocation in automated trading. Instead of picking single stocks, the system decides how much to hold in each market sector. That choice rides on macroeconomic conditions and market mood.

Their framework feeds the model several streams at once: policy documents, economic indicators, and sentiment patterns. The model reasons over them systematically and sets sector weights. In backtests, the approach beat traditional cross momentum strategies by a wide margin on both return and risk adjusted return. The authors present language models as viable macro analysts for systematic allocation, while the test remains historical rather than live.
arxiv-2503-09747:
Timo Eichhorn and co-authors fuse two simulation tricks to keep lattice field theory moving near the continuum limit, in a 2025 paper. When space becomes a fine grid, update algorithms stall between topological sectors, trapped behind high action barriers, a slowing seen across methods. Their remedy marries metadynamics, which flattens those barriers, with parallel tempering, which swaps configurations between temperatures.

The combination cut autocorrelation times sharply and needs no reweighting corrections afterward. The authors discuss how to carry the scheme into full QCD with dynamical fermions, and they report first results for two-flavor simulations at unphysical pion masses. The work aims at trustworthy strong-force physics from finite grids.
arxiv-2503-09847:
Koray Aydogan, Anthony Schlimgen, and Kade Head-Marsden offer a 2025 method for steadying the end state of open quantum systems. Real quantum systems leak to their surroundings, which is often seen as harm.

Weak contact with the surroundings can also help hold rich, mixed states in place. The hard part is picking the best settings for both system and surroundings. The authors give a way to tune those settings to reach a desired steady state that is out of balance. They test the method on three known models, across several quantum phases, and predict states that are both highly linked and highly mixed.
arxiv-2503-10047:
Wenjie Li and four co-authors sharpen blurry images with a network that works in two domains at once. Lightweight super-resolution must rebuild fine detail on a tight compute budget. Past methods that used frequency data tended to favor either broad structure or fine edges, and handled the frequency side slowly. Their 2025 network mixes wavelet and Fourier views of the image, so both global shape and sharp detail get attention. Modulation steps blend the two streams cheaply.

The design keeps the model small enough for phones and cameras. Better detail at low cost suits live uses, from video calls to drone feeds. The authors present the dual-domain idea as the fix for the old either-or trade. Tests on standard image sets check the claim.
arxiv-2503-10147:
Wenrui Yu and three co-authors secure distributed consensus in twenty twenty-five. Multi-agent systems often agree on a median value, which resists outliers and bad sensors. The data behind that median can be sensitive. Privacy-preserving median consensus had barely been studied.

The authors give the first rigorous analysis of privacy for this problem. Working in an L1-norm minimization frame, they find exact conditions for a double win. Consensus can be exact while privacy is perfect, meaning zero information leakage. Guarantees hold against passive and eavesdropping adversaries. Numerical experiments confirm the theory's practical feasibility. Readers in distributed systems get a rare case where accuracy and secrecy need not trade off.
arxiv-2503-10247:
Zhijie Zhu, Lei Fan, Maurice Pagnucco, and Yang Song wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It classifies images by object parts the model can point to, so each call comes with a reason a person can check.

Part prototype networks mimic how people judge: this looks like that beak, that wing. Past builds lean on dull, repeated parts, which thin the story they tell. Here the parts are learned by clustering deep traits from foundation vision models, with no set shape imposed. The parts come out distinct and varied for each class. Two new scores grade how distinct and how full the account is. On bird, car, and dog sets the method matches past scores while reading far better.
arxiv-2503-10347:
A spinning black hole can feed energy to light particles, growing a dense cloud around itself. Ning Xie and Fa Peng Huang study what changes when those particles push on each other, in a 2025 paper. Such particles, called axions, are also dark matter candidates, and they naturally self-interact.

With computer runs in full curved space-time, the pair find a new lower mass limit for cloud growth. Past that limit, cloud growth slows to near zero, so the drain on the hole ends early. The cloud's hum and its gravity wave tone also shift. Those shifts could show up in wave data. Past limits on axions may loosen once this effect is counted.
arxiv-2503-10547:
Vision models that grade images are powerful, yet their reasons stay hidden inside the network. Chuqin Geng and co-authors present a framework called VisionLogic in a 2025 paper that turns those reasons into plain logic rules. Earlier explanation tools leaned on correlation, pointing at image cues without checking that the cues truly drive the model's choice.

VisionLogic first finds small sets of internal features whose action reproduces the model's prediction. It states each feature's state as a predicate with a class-specific threshold. Then it grounds those predicates in real image regions by ablation: cover a region, and the linked predicate should switch off. Trials on standard image networks and a human study with 465 people showed the rules improved users' grasp of model behavior over two known explanation methods.
arxiv-2503-10647:
Krishna Subedi stress-tests two leading language models on medical diagnosis reliability, in a 2025 paper. Fifty-two clinical scenarios were reworded and modified under controlled rules. Some edits kept the diagnosis fixed while changing surface details. Others planted irrelevant but plausible story elements. A third set added context meant to shift the answer.

Both models were perfectly consistent across equivalent rewordings. Irrelevant details still swayed them often. One changed its diagnosis in forty percent of such cases, the other in thirty. Added context moved answers at different rates. Many context-driven shifts were judged clinically wrong by physician reviewers. Consistency alone did not protect against manipulation. The author demands clinician oversight for diagnostic use. Models must learn to flag weak evidence before deployment, the paper concludes.
arxiv-2503-10747:
Naixin Liang and Siang Peng Oh present a 2025 astrophysics paper on how cosmic rays wander through the galaxy in fits and starts. In the classic picture, each step a particle takes is small and bell-shaped in size. In real turbulent fields, rare very long jumps, called Lévy flights, can dominate the motion, while long waits between scatters can slow it below normal spread.

Their simulations face a catch: a galaxy is finite, so jumps cannot grow without bound before particles escape. With that cap in place, the motion settles back to classic behaviour over time, as limit theorems predict. The paper maps when the odd phase holds and when the classic picture returns.
arxiv-2503-11147:
Junhyuk Jo and co-authors present in 2025 AsyncSAM, a fast form of a sharpness aware training method for deep nets. That method lifts how well nets cope with new data, yet its cost kept it from wide use. Past cuts still ran its two steps in strict turn.

Their form lets the shake step and the update step run at once on split gear. Batch size for the shake is tuned to the rig, so even plain chips can help at no time cost. Proof shows the same meet pace class as the base form. Tests gave top marks and the best train speed of the kin set.
arxiv-2503-11347:
Zhenyi Zhang, Yuhao Sun, Qiangwei Peng, Tiejun Li, and Peijie Zhou review how to read motion out of single-cell snapshots taken across time and space, in a 2025 paper. Gene sequencing of single cells once froze one instant per cell. Newer methods stamp cells with time, place, or both. The review tours the math that sews those stamps into trajectories: Markov chains, stochastic equations, and transport-based generative models.

Together they reconstruct how cells travel between states and choose their fates. The authors argue the dynamical systems view unifies a fragmented toolkit. Development and disease progression, both journeys rather than states, are the prizes. They map where each method earns its keep.
arxiv-2503-11547:
Organic crystals that hover between metal and insulator can be pushed across the border by a squeeze. Jesse Liebman and co-authors stretched two such Mott insulators, built from flat carbon-rich molecules with mercury salts, along chosen crystal axes. A mere four tenths of a percent stretch switched the first material from a quantum dipole liquid into a charge-ordered state at thirty-three kelvin, where electrons settle into a fixed pattern.

The second material moved the other way: a stronger stretch suppressed its charge order down to ten kelvin. Light-scattering spectra watched the electrons' arrangement through molecular vibrations and a telltale collective hum near the border. The results confirm a predicted phase diagram and show strain as a two-way dial for electron order in these materials.
arxiv-2503-12147:
Ricardo Fraiman, Leonardo Moreno, and Thomas Ransford take up two problems about mixture distributions in this 2025 statistics paper. The first is estimating mixtures of multivariate normal distributions, and of t-distributions, from one dimensional projections of the data. The second is measuring how far apart two clusterings are by comparing the mixture distributions fitted to each.

Their approach rests on earlier work with a neat trick. Such mixtures can be told apart by projecting them onto a fixed finite set of lines. The number of lines depends only on how many components are involved and on the dimension. The authors give algorithms for both tasks, compare them with robust versions of the expectation maximization method, and test the methods in simulations.
arxiv-2503-12447:
Yicong Li wrote this 2025 thesis on teaching machines to grasp cause and effect in videos. Video models learn well from huge data sets, but their skill often breaks when the data shifts, as with rare events or skewed mixes. Li argues that models need the causal patterns behind what they see, not just surface links. The thesis takes up two test tasks: finding relations between objects in video, and answering questions about video clips.

Across both tasks, Li builds causal models that hold up better when test data differs from training data. The work weighs where causal methods help most and where they still fall short. It gives later researchers a base for video tools that fail less often in the wild.
arxiv-2503-12847:
Chen Liu and co-authors present a method to outline the object making a sound in a video, in work from 2025. Linking sound to the right region is hard when like objects sit nearby. Objects also start and stop sounding as scenes change.

Their system splits cues into groups and merges only the groups that answer to the sound. That focus stops the outline from spilling onto silent look-alikes. A teaching signal also trains the system to split sounding from silent zones. A second part grades how sure each outline is, which flags weak spots. The design aims for stable outlines across clips with shifting speakers, tools, and street noise.
arxiv-2503-13147:
Jiayi Fu and co-authors present IPC-Dehaze, a method for clearing haze from real-world photos, in a 2025 paper. Haze varies with depth and density across a scene, so one-pass fixes often fail on the thickest patches. Clear areas, though, hold clues for restoring the murky ones.

The method works in steps, using a pretrained image codebook. Codes decoded in one round guide the next round's guesses, which steadily sharpens the result. A critic module judges which codes fit together and flags the least trustworthy ones for resampling. That keeps good codes and reworks the doubtful ones. In tests, the method beat leading rivals on real hazy images. The authors frame the loop as a general trick for image repair.
arxiv-2503-13447:
Qin Liu and co-authors let a language model shop for its own thinking strategy before it answers. Models tend to reuse reasoning patterns from training rather than pick the tactic a task really needs, and fixed strategy add-ons help one task while failing others. Their 2025 framework, MetaScale, keeps a pool of meta-thoughts, short plans for how to think, and tunes the pool while the model works.

A bandit rule picks which strategy to try next, guided by a reward model, while a genetic step breeds the best strategies into new ones. On a hard arena benchmark the method lifted the win rate for a leading model by eleven points, edging past a strong reasoning model under style control. Gains grew as the sampling budget rose, and answers came out more structured and expert in tone. The authors pitch test-time strategy search as a general upgrade path.
arxiv-2503-13747:
Tung Nguyen and co-authors study how adding links changes population dynamics in stream networks in a 2025 paper. Habitats are modeled as patches on a graph, with streams connecting them. The authors add either a two way or one way link between two patches and track effects on growth rate and total biomass. The paper is dedicated to the memory of a professor named in its heading.

Adding a two way link often lowered both growth and biomass, a counterintuitive result. One way links had more intricate effects that depend on model parameters. Complete analytic results are proven for three patch networks, with generalizations and conjectures for larger networks backed by simulations. Readers learn that more connection can hurt a stream population.
arxiv-2503-13947:
Sayak Nag and five co-authors add honest error bars to scene graph generation in this 2025 paper. A scene graph lists the objects in an image and the relations between each pair, giving a structured summary of the picture. Skewed class frequencies and shaky predictions, though, mean users need to know how much to trust a generated graph.

Their framework wraps any existing scene graph method in conformal prediction, a statistical technique that returns a set of candidate graphs with a rigorous coverage guarantee. To keep the sets useful, a multimodal language model then picks out the graphs that look most plausible, visually and in meaning. The method can show several possible readings of one image, rate how reliable a generator is, and even lift its overall accuracy. The authors present it as a practical layer for making scene understanding systems accountable.
arxiv-2503-14147:
Felegary and co-authors examine a model of inflation, the burst of rapid expansion thought to have shaped the very early universe. Their model belongs to the K-essence family and adds a coupling between the field's standard energy term and its potential, a small change that ripples through many predictions.

By solving the equations both numerically and on paper, the team shows the coupling lowers key quantities such as the tensor-to-scalar ratio, which compares gravitational waves to density ripples. The adjusted values agree better with measurements from the Planck satellite and the BICEP and Keck experiments. The authors argue the model is a promising alternative picture of the universe's first moments.
arxiv-2503-14347:
Zishun Liu, Sam Power, and Yongxin Chen give a new proof of a core concentration inequality for sub-Gaussian random variables. The inequality bounds how sharply the norm of a random vector, or the operator norm of a random matrix, concentrates around its expectation. Standard proofs use epsilon-nets and union bounds.

Their method instead works with an averaged version of the moment generating function. Avoiding the union bound promises tighter concentration estimates. The argument covers both the vector and matrix cases in a unified way. Such inequalities underpin high-dimensional statistics and random matrix theory, so a cleaner proof with better constants has broad technical value.
arxiv-2503-14547:
Shuheng Li and five co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on recognizing human activities across different sensor types. Activity labels are often stored as simple one-hot codes, which carry no meaning. Newer work uses text labels instead, but text misses the physical core of an action. The authors argue that motion data should anchor the field.

Their framework, SKELAR, learns activity representations from skeleton data, the joint positions of a moving body. A self-supervised task rebuilds joint angles in a way that ignores who the user is and how sensors are placed. A matching module then weighs which body parts matter for each new signal type. The team also built a dataset with motion sensors, WiFi signals, and skeletons from 20 people doing 27 activities. All three streams are time-synced, a first for such breadth.
arxiv-2503-14647:
Hanchen Li, Yuhan Liu, Yihua Cheng, and two colleagues ask a money question about language model caches, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Many apps now reuse stored key-value caches. The model can then skip re-reading repeated input, cutting the wait for a first reply.

The open question is cost. Keeping those caches on cloud services means paying for storage, network transfer, and compute. The savings depend on how often text repeats, how long replies run, and how big the model is. The authors build a tested analytical model of those cloud costs. Their early results map when reuse pays for itself and when it quietly loses money. The work gives developers a way to price a popular speed trick before adopting it. It treats the cache not as free memory but as rented shelf space.
arxiv-2503-15247:
A large collaboration wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on sorting neutrino events with graph neural networks. The setting is a planned European experiment that will fire neutrinos from a particle source toward a huge water detector in Sweden. The near detector watches the particles flash in water, and each flash pattern must be read.

The task is to tell electron neutrino events from muon neutrino events, a split the physics goals depend on. The authors treat each event as a graph, a web of linked points, and let a graph neural network classify it. The paper reports how well that approach works for the water Cherenkov near detector.
arxiv-2503-15547:
Juhee Kim, Woohyuk Choi, and Byoungyoung Lee proposed in 2025 a security system for AI agents that use tools. Such agents take orders in plain language from users or from tool data at run time. That freedom opens a path for attackers to gain powers they should not have.

Their system, called Prompt Flow Integrity, uses three defenses. Agents are isolated from each other, untrusted data are handled in a safe way, and guardrails watch for power escalation. Tests showed the system blocked such attacks while keeping the agents useful. The authors frame the work in classic system security terms, rather than as a prompt trick.
arxiv-2503-15747:
Sylwia Cichacz and Claire Hilaire lead a team characterizing graphs where some path passes near every vertex, and exactly which forbidden patterns force that to happen. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Path eccentricity measures the worst distance from a chosen spine path. A classic result guarantees a fully spanning path when two small patterns are excluded.

Generalizing, they show that excluding two specific graphs caps eccentricity below any chosen bound. Conversely, a single excluded pattern works exactly when it hides inside two named families. Their proof leans on structural domination theory from earlier work. A polynomial-time algorithm finds the witnessing path robustly. The result also closes an open question from a recent paper. Such characterizations turn vague intuition about graph shape into checkable conditions. Algorithmic payoffs ride along with the theory.
arxiv-2503-15847:
Solvers for hard planning problems cut away weak options to shrink the search, and picking the right cuts matters. Shuli Zeng and co-authors argue in 2025 that cuts should be picked with the whole search in view. Older methods use fixed rules, and newer learning methods look at one node at a time. Both miss the wider context of the search tree.

Their method, called Global Cut Selection, draws the search tree as a two-sided graph. A graph network joined with trial-and-error learning then builds a picking strategy. Cuts are applied across all nodes, not just one. Tests on fake and large real problems beat both rule-based and learning-based rivals. The work targets mixed-integer programming, a core tool in logistics and planning.
arxiv-2503-15947:
Tianyi Hu and co-authors built Unreal-MAP in 2025, a playground for training teams of learning agents. Multi-agent learning needs rich test worlds, but building them is slow and costly. A game engine offers vast visual and physical resources ready for use.

Their platform runs on Unreal Engine and lets users craft custom team tasks with ease. It supports setup, editing, and viewing, and all parts are open source. A test framework works with both rule-based and learning-based methods from other toolkits. The team ran several leading algorithms on sample tasks and reported how each performed. They hope the tool speeds progress in team learning research.
arxiv-2503-16047:
Bisola Faith Kayode and a team of co-authors set out a new network defense model, called TSAN, to spot denial-of-service attacks in network traffic. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such attacks flood a service to knock it out, and they cost firms a great deal. Old rule-based and count-based tools adapt poorly as attack forms change. The new model watches both when traffic moves and how it spreads, so it can catch odd shapes that old tools miss. It joins a transformer-style encoder for time with a shaped filter for space. The aim is a guard that keeps pace with fast-changing attacks.
arxiv-2503-16247:
Max Gutbrod, David Rauber, Danilo Weber Nunes, and Christoph Palm build a benchmark suite for a safety problem in medical AI in this 2025 paper. Models trained on scans from one setting can fail when the input shifts to something unlike their training data. The suite tests how well methods can flag out-of-distribution inputs before they cause harm.

The suite, called OpenMIBOOD, holds three benchmarks from fourteen datasets across medical domains. Cases are sorted into shifted but valid inputs, near outliers, and far outliers. The team ran twenty-four detection methods through the same tests. A key lesson was that rankings from photo-based benchmarks did not carry over to medical images. The authors offer the suite as a yardstick so that detection methods for health care can be compared. This version of the paper also carries a corrigendum fixing reported results for two methods.
arxiv-2503-16447:
André Groß, Birte Richter, and Britta Wrede present a framework in 2025 that helps robots explain things to people in a way that fits each person's state of mind. Good explanations must guide attention and build understanding, not just recite facts. Their framework, called SHIFT, is built to work across domains.

The method folds research from fields outside computer science into a scoring system that a robot can run. The human partner is modeled in six states that can be observed, from lost to fully on track. The robot picks its next move to lift the partner toward understanding. A learning layer on top adapts the preset scores to each person. The team sets out the steps for building such cross field models, which other robot teams can reuse.
arxiv-2503-16947:
Henning Samtleben reviews, in a 2025 paper, exceptional field theories, a reformulation of the deepest known theories of gravity that makes their hidden symmetries visible. The theories in question, maximal supergravities in ten and eleven dimensions, come in many versions that were long treated separately. Exceptional field theory rewrites them in a language where a family of large symmetry groups acts openly, unifying the versions.

The review explains the framework's structure and its structural role in that unification. It then turns practical. The same language supplies efficient techniques for hard computations in the subject, the paper's second selling point. Samtleben writes for researchers entering the field as much as for veterans, and the piece doubles as a map of where the formalism has proved its worth.
arxiv-2503-17247:
Michael Bommarito, Daniel Martin Katz, and Jillian Bommarito build tokenizers, the text-chopping front end of language models, tuned for professional documents. General tokenizers waste capacity on legal and financial language, splitting formal terms awkwardly and inflating the cost of long documents. The team's KL3M family trains byte-pair tokenizers on legal, financial, and government text.

Their flagship cased tokenizer needs 9 to 17 percent fewer tokens than GPT-4o's or Llama 3's on domain documents, despite a smaller vocabulary. For specialised terms the saving is dramatic: up to 83 percent fewer tokens for legal terms and 39 percent for financial ones. A second branch of the family works at character level, in three sizes, to fix garbled text from scanners while keeping error and correction aligned. All tokenizers and code are released openly.
arxiv-2503-17547:
Bart Bussmann, Noa Nabeshima, Adam Karvonen, and Neel Nanda redesign sparse autoencoders, a tool for reading the concepts inside a neural network, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. These tools learn a dictionary of features from a network's activity, but the dictionary's size forces an awkward trade-off.

Make the dictionary bigger and the pressure for sparsity splits broad features into narrow ones, warping or erasing the high-level ideas. The team's Matryoshka variant trains several nested dictionaries at once, from small to large. Each smaller dictionary must rebuild the input on its own, without leaning on the bigger ones. That pressure sorts features into levels: small dictionaries hold general concepts, larger ones add specifics. High-level features survive instead of being absorbed. The design borrows its name from nesting dolls, and it aims to give interpreters a cleaner map of what a network knows.
arxiv-2503-17647:
Phil Pollett writes a short note on how long a random process spends in each of its states. His 2025 paper treats Markov chains, systems that jump between states with set odds and no memory of the past. A recent paper had worked out the time spread for a chain with just two states by counting paths one by one.

Pollett takes the general case of chains with countably many states in discrete time. His tool is the generating function, a compact formula that encodes a whole distribution at once. The route yields simpler formulas even for the two-state chain that started the question. The note offers probabilists a cleaner path to occupancy results.
arxiv-2503-17847:
Yicheng Zhang and co-authors show that the fast links between graphics processors in big computing clusters can leak secrets. Multi-GPU machines use NVIDIA's NVLink to move data quickly, and the team reverse engineered how that link behaves. They found two leak sources: timing shifts when traffic collides, and built-in counters that reveal communication patterns.

From those leaks they built hidden channels between two processors carrying over 70 kilobits per second with under five percent errors. They also ran spying attacks that identified which program was running, across eighteen test applications, and read characters from a 3D rendering program. The leaks even crossed between separate cloud accounts on Google's platform. The paper closes by weighing defenses.
arxiv-2503-18047:
Sergey Avvakumov and Alfredo Hubard tile spheres with cubes in a way that breaks a long-standing guess, in a 2025 paper. A cubical sphere is a sphere built from cube-like blocks. Kalai had conjectured that the most faces any such sphere can have is set by a family called neighborly cubical polytopes.

For spheres of dimension three and up, the pair build examples whose facet counts grow faster than that family's rate. The three-dimensional case with few vertices was already known to fail. Their method now settles all higher dimensions for large sizes, and even the growth order in the guess proves wrong. Polytope theory must look elsewhere for the true ceiling on cubical sphere faces.
arxiv-2503-18247:
Tadesse Destaw Belay and co-authors adapted a multilingual language model to African social media, a domain far from the religious and formal texts that dominate training data for many African languages. They built AfriSocial, a large corpus of social media and news text across the languages. They then continued pre-training the AfroXLMR model on it in two ways: adapting to the domain generally, and adapting to one task's unlabeled data before training another.

Domain adaptation improved scores by one to thirty points across sentiment, emotion, and hate speech tasks in nineteen languages. Task adaptation also transferred, with sentiment data lifting fine-grained emotion classification by up to fifteen points. Combining both gave the best results. The team releases the corpus and models openly.
arxiv-2503-18447:
Bouchenaki and co-authors compute, from first principles, whether a cerium filled cage crystal could turn heat into electricity. The compound, CeIr4P12, belongs to the skutterudite family prized for thermoelectric work, but its traits were unmeasured. Their 2025 study applies density functional theory with transport simulations to predict structure, elasticity, and heat behavior.

Calculations say the crystal is stable in structure, mechanics, and vibration, with a healthy binding energy. The team tracks how expansion and heat conduction shift with temperature, then derives the electric side: conductivity of heat by electrons and the figure of merit that grades such materials. The numbers encourage them to flag the compound as a candidate for energy conversion devices, pending lab checks.
arxiv-2503-18947:
Jae Joong Lee, Bedrich Benes, and Raymond Yeh present a 2025 method for amodal segmentation, labeling the full shape of objects even where they are hidden. Most methods learn this from hand-labeled masks or synthetic data, which limits variety. The new approach needs no training at all. It borrows image inpainting models, which tend to paint objects whole and unoccluded when filling gaps.

The pipeline inpaints the hidden parts of an object, then segments the completed picture. Across five data sets, the masks beat the best prior methods by about 5 percent on average. The authors stress the method's generality: any pretrained inpainting model can drive it, with no fine-tuning. The trick turns a quirk of generative models into a perception tool.
arxiv-2503-19047:
Quiñones and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-five, how a change in one trait of salt water shapes the heat and force side of salts in water. The trait is relative permittivity. It shows how well water screens electric charge. It falls as salt strength rises. Formulas fit from tests catch that fall for two salts, magnesium chloride and nickel chloride. The team worked out osmotic and activity coefficients. These show how far the mix strays from ideal behavior. They worked across a range of salt strengths. Their model treats ions as charged spheres in one smooth medium.

They matched four ways of working: two Poisson-Boltzmann theories, a mean spherical approximation, and Monte Carlo simulation. Two ways matched the simulation benchmark well up to fairly high salt strengths. One theory strayed early. All ways drifted from test results at high salt strength.
arxiv-2503-19147:
Van-Giang Trinh and four co-authors bound the number of stable end states in certain logic networks in a 2025 paper. Boolean networks model systems like gene circuits as nodes switching on and off by logic rules. Their attractors are the long-run patterns the system settles into.

Random-timing updates suit noisy biology better than lockstep updates. The paper studies a simple rule family built only from AND and NOT operations. Two new upper bounds on attractor counts come from the network's structure. Such bounds tell modelers how much behavioral variety a gene circuit can even show. The results connect wiring diagrams to possible fates of the system. They also guide searches that would otherwise drown in possible states.
arxiv-2503-19647:
Avogaro and co-authors ask whether big vision-language models are better prompted for image segmentation by showing them pictures or by telling them in words. Such models are often treated as all-purpose tools that can be steered by prompts alone, with no task training. Segmentation, cutting an image into labeled regions, is a demanding test of that claim.

The team tested several recent models with text prompts and with visual example prompts, on a set of unusual image collections. They add a scheme that gives the model a few example segmentations to copy. Even so, the general models trail specialist systems by about thirty percent on the standard overlap score. Careful prompting narrows the gap but does not close it.
arxiv-2503-20147:
Li Zhou, Kaijun Li, Aigen Li, and Zheng Zhou model the infrared glow of carbon ring molecules in the air of Titan, in work from 2025. Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, and its haze is rich in organic material. Ring molecules called PAHs are thought to seed that haze.

A past mission saw a glow band that proves such molecules float high in Titan's air. Their exact identity, size, and amount stay unknown. The new Webb telescope has the sharpness to settle those questions. The authors focus on one family with nitrogen added, the cyanonaphthalenes. Their modeled spectra can guide what Webb should look for.
arxiv-2503-20847:
Jim Achterberg and co-authors describe a paradox blocking synthetic health data, in a 2025 article. Fake data sets that mimic real patients promise a safe way to share information for research. They are built for sharing, yet they often stay locked away. The sticking point is the check for reidentification risk: the metrics used give unclear answers, so holders dare not release the data.

The authors argue the metrics clash with what rules and practice actually require. Because the scores do not line up with real sharing needs, caution wins by default. They discuss how the field could fix the mismatch, with clearer risk standards tied to regulation. The goal is a path where data made to be shared can finally circulate.
arxiv-2503-21047:
Game-like worlds with rare rewards are hard for learning agents, since good moves may pay off only after long chains. Jeremias Ferrao and Rafael Cunha adapt a curiosity method called CBET for world-model agents in a 2025 paper. The method rewards an agent for change it has not seen, and it can carry prior learning into a new task.

The pair tested the DreamerV3 agent, with and without the added drive, in two sparse-reward worlds. In the richer world, Crafter, the drive raised scores. In the simpler Minigrid world, scores fell, and prior training did not lead to a good final policy. The authors warn that a curiosity drive helps only when the change it seeks matches the task at hand.
arxiv-2503-21147: Jianping Jiang and Sike Lang prove a percolation result for a three dimensional Ising model in a 2025 paper. The model sits on a lattice built from a triangular sheet times a line, above its critical temperature. With a small external field, can endless clusters of both spin signs exist at once? The authors show a positive field threshold below which a unique infinite plus cluster and a unique infinite minus cluster coexist. The same result holds on the three dimensional triangular lattice.
arxiv-2503-21447:
Andreas Fring, Takano Taira, and Bethan Turner solve a quantum system with a reputation for ghosts, in a 2025 physics paper. Some theories with higher time derivatives seem to produce particles with negative energy, the so-called ghosts. The authors take a two-dimensional coupled system that can be reshaped into exactly such a theory while keeping its underlying structure intact. They map it onto the classic Pais-Uhlenbeck model, a textbook case of the ghostly kind.

They then quantise the system twice: by solving its wave equation directly through coupled recurrence relations, and by building states in a Fock space. The two routes agree exactly, giving the energy levels and well-behaved wave patterns. With exact answers in hand, they examine how the system's states spread or localise. The results give a rare firm grip on theories that are usually handled with unease.
arxiv-2503-21547:
Clean rings are an algebra topic where each element splits into well-behaved parts, a tidy unit plus a nilpotent scrap. Peter Danchev, Mina Doostalizadeh, Omid Hasanzadeh, Arash Javan, and Ahmad Moussavi study in 2025 the rings where only the non-units need be strongly weakly nil-clean, a looser demand.

They prove this class is strongly pi-regular, a strong structural property, and give a full characterization using the Jacobson radical and pieces of the two-by-two matrix ring. The results extend to Morita context rings and group rings. The paper builds on a definition from 2016 work by Kosan and Zhou and its follow-up by Chen and Sheibani, sharpening what the relaxed condition forces a ring to look like.
arxiv-2503-21747:
Aniket Didolkar and co-authors present CTRL-O in a 2025 paper on object-based learning from images. Such models split a scene into fixed slots, with one slot for each object. The catch is that users cannot tell the model which objects to track, since the model uses its own fixed view of what counts as an object.

CTRL-O lets a user guide the slots with plain language. The model binds words to the right objects in complex real scenes, with no mask labels needed for training. The team then uses the slots for two tasks, making images from text and answering questions about images, with strong results.
arxiv-2503-21947:
Arpit Thool and Chris Brown report, in a 2025 case study, how one software firm wove live security tests into its fast work flow. The firm builds web apps with Kanban boards and a pipe that builds and ships code on its own. Attacks on web apps keep rising, so checks must run in the flow, not at the end. The test in view, DAST, probes a running app for flaws as a hacker would. Its step-by-step form can clash with the loop pace of agile work.

The team used an action research path, with talks among the firm's own staff. They log where the fit stuck, what eased it, and what worked best in the end. Their aim is pace with safety kept: ships stay fast, and flaws are caught while the code is still fresh.
arxiv-2503-22047:
Open quantum systems leak energy and information to their surroundings, which makes their math harder than that of closed systems. Caio B Naves and Jonas Larson propose a fresh way to picture that math in this 2025 paper. They recast the standard equation for such systems as a grid, called a Liouville Fock state lattice, where the state moves much like particles on a classical lattice.

On this grid, states drift, gather, and drain in ways that closed-system states never do, because the grid's rules are not even-handed. The authors also try a second picture that looks more like a spread of chance values. They show that endless sets of steady states can arise from a kind of frustration in the grid. The framework may help design simulators that mimic open quantum behavior.
arxiv-2503-22147:
Sohail Reddy develops methods to describe quantum systems whose behavior depends on their past, in this 2025 paper. Such memory effects, called non-Markovian dynamics, matter for the noisy quantum hardware now being built. Standard tools assume the past does not matter, which can mislead control and error fixes.

Reddy frames the dynamics with a master equation that keeps memory, in both simple and richer forms. Two fitting methods fill in its parameters: a compact basis expansion and a neural network. Tests used real data from a superconducting qubit at a national lab. The basis method predicted the qubit's behavior best, which favors structured models for this job.
arxiv-2503-22847:
Particle physics keeps finding exotic hadrons, quark combinations beyond the familiar pairs and triplets, and no single framework has organized them all. Abhishek Mohapatra argues in a 2025 paper that the Born-Oppenheimer effective theory, built straight from quantum chromodynamics, is that framework for any state with two heavy quarks.

The method exploits the gap between the heavy quarks' slow motion and the light quarks' and gluons' fast dance. Mohapatra solves the coupled equations, including mixing between channels, for hybrids, tetraquarks, pentaquarks, doubly heavy baryons, and quarkonia alike, at leading order. He also lists the spin-symmetry families the theory predicts and the exact quantities lattice simulations must compute to feed it, from static energies to exotic Wilson loops. It is a bid to rule all two-heavy-quark exotics with one theory.
arxiv-2503-23047:
Sagnik Chatterjee and four co-workers wrote a 2025 paper on signs in gravitational waves that reveal how matter changes phase inside merging neutron stars. Such mergers probe the densest matter known. The team built a family of matter models with one dial. The dial sweeps from sharp to smooth hadron-to-quark changeovers.

After the stars merge, the remnant's waves carry the phase story. Extra peaks show up in the wave spectrum only when a changeover occurs. The time-frequency map bears a doubled signature as well. The dial also ties to the mass threshold for instant collapse. One past event's long-lived remnant caps the dial at a small value.
arxiv-2503-23447:
Naming the action in a video takes both a sense of space and a sense of time, and most models lean too hard on one. Four authors build a transformer system with separate spatial and temporal experts that swap information at every layer through a bottleneck cross-attention step. Each side's judgment is thus informed by the other, while the exchange stays cheap.

A fuller version adds a third expert for sound, letting hearing inform seeing. Tested on standard action benchmarks, the vision-only system performed in a balanced way across datasets that stress different skills. The audio-visual version also did well on four benchmarks that include sound. The authors present the design as a route to video recognition that treats sight and sound as partners, and they show the cross-attention module is where the benefit is created.
arxiv-2503-24047:
Shuo Ren, Can Xie, Pu Jian, Zhenjiang Ren, Chunlin Leng, and Jiajun Zhang survey a fast-growing field in a 2025 paper: AI agents built for science. Large language models are moving past chat and into labs, where agent systems plan tests, run code, and sift data. These science agents differ from general ones because they carry deep subject knowledge and strict checks on their work.

The survey maps how such agents are built, how they are tested, and where they are used. It covers tasks from forming ideas and planning tests to running models and reading results. The authors also weigh the risks, such as wrong claims that look sound, and the need to repeat results. Readers get a clear map of a field that is changing how research gets done.
arxiv-2503-24147:
Charles St-Arnault and a large team report a record optical link for data center reaches, moving three point two trillion bits per second down two kilometers of fiber. The system uses intensity modulation with direct detection in the O-band, carrying eight lanes of two hundred twenty-five gigabaud four-level signals. Thin-film lithium niobate modulators do the encoding, driven by a three-nanometer chip. Two standard configurations, for longer and shorter reaches, are both demonstrated.

A faster variant reaches four point two trillion bits per second with eight-level signaling. Error rates stayed under the hard-decision forward error correction threshold. The authors claim the first demonstration at these rates with this component pairing. Data centers hungry for bandwidth between buildings are the audience. The result presses commodity-style optics toward rates once reserved for coherent systems.
arxiv-2504-00047:
Nils Friederich and co-authors automate the microscope for live single-cell experiments, in a 2025 paper. Microfluidic imaging watches microbial factories cell by cell, but continuous filming misses fleeting events and reacts too late. Their pipeline, EAP4EMSIG, adds three parts: a neural autofocus that predicts the focus offset, a shootout of real-time segmentation methods, and a live analysis dashboard.

The autofocus landed within about a tenth of a micrometer, answering in under a tenth of a second. Of eleven segmentation methods, Cellpose scored best on quality while a distance-based method ran fastest at similar quality. Smart microscopes, the authors argue, should decide what to watch while the experiment still lives.
arxiv-2504-00147:
Collin Zhang, John X. Morris, and Vitaly Shmatikov study how much text can be recovered from a numeric summary of that text, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such summaries, called embeddings, power search tools and data stores. If text can be rebuilt from them, private content may leak.

Older recovery methods need a fresh trained model for each kind of embedding, plus many queries. The new method needs no such training and works on any embedding. It builds guesses by steering a text generator against the target summary. Tests on several embeddings show it recovers the key meaning of the source texts. The work gives a cheaper way to audit this leak risk.
arxiv-2504-00247:
Brain atlases, the average anatomy of a group, anchor most imaging studies, yet building one traditionally takes days of computation. Mazdak Abulnaga and seven co-authors build them in one pass in 2025 with MultiMorph, a feedforward model that pools features across a whole image group at once. No retraining is needed for a new population or scanner style.

Synthetic practice data teaches the model to generalize to unfamiliar modalities and groups. On small and large collections it beat both optimization based and learned rivals while running about one hundred times faster. Atlases that once discouraged experiments now arrive on demand, the authors argue. They aim the tool at researchers with no machine learning staff.
arxiv-2504-00847:
Aaron Anderson and Michael Benedikt studied in 2025 how learning a base family of functions relates to learning averages of those functions over random data. For example, if a family indexed by one input can be learned, can the family of its expected values also be learned? They look at two settings: random examples and examples chosen by an opponent.

For the case where labels may be noisy, they give sharper bounds on how many examples are needed, stated through size measures of the base family. Links to a model theory trick for adding randomness are drawn. Counterexamples are also given for the clean-label case, in both settings, showing where the transfer fails.
arxiv-2504-01147:
Dana Avramescu and four co-authors studied in twenty twenty-five how the glasma — the dense color fields filling a heavy-ion collision's first instants — pushes heavy quarks around. Heavy quarks are born early and witness the whole collision; whether the pre-equilibrium glasma stage leaves fingerprints on them was unclear. The team evolved the fields with classical Yang-Mills equations and the quarks with Wong's equations.

They computed the momentum-broadening coefficient, finding it anisotropic and initially very large. The standard suppression observable for heavy quarks, R-AA, shifted only moderately under glasma effects, less than nuclear parton distribution effects. The striking impact was on pairs: charm and anticharm quarks created back-to-back had their azimuthal correlation strongly smeared by the glasma fields — a potential early-stage signature.
arxiv-2504-01447:
Basabendu Barman, Arindam Das, and Prantik Sarmah read, in a 2025 paper, what a ghost bit at vast force, caught by KM3NeT, may say of mass and dark stuff. In a broad U(1) frame, the bit could be the ash of a dark thing that falls apart: a right-hand neutrino of 440 PeV. Born by freeze-in, a slow drip from the hot young world, such a thing can match the dark count we see. The team maps where that match holds. The same ground sits in reach of more than one gravity wave ear, they show.

Two fields thus test one tale: sea-floor ears for ghost bits, and space ears for the waves such births would stir.
arxiv-2504-01547:
Luca Ciampi, Gabriele Lagani, Giuseppe Amato, and Fabrizio Falchi teach machines to outline organs and tissues in medical scans with few hand labels in a 2025 paper. Pixel-level labels are costly, so methods that learn from mostly unlabeled images are in demand. Their design pairs a teacher and a student model in a loop.

The teacher first learns by rebuilding images from corrupted versions, guided by its own draft outlines. It then trains alongside the student: both learn from the labeled scans, and each supplies draft labels for the unlabeled ones. Extra rounds of rebuilt images sharpen the teacher's drafts further. On three public two-dimensional sets and one three-dimensional heart set, the method matched or beat leading rivals, with the biggest gains when labels were scarcest.
arxiv-2504-01647:
Tobias Fischer and a large team teach a generative model to imagine the extra viewpoints that a sparse three-dimensional scan is missing. Gaussian splatting renders scenes beautifully in real time, but quality collapses away from the photographed angles, and dense photo shoots are slow and costly. Earlier fixes distilled two-dimensional generators or hallucinated extra views from a few references, producing inconsistent inventions that corrupted the reconstruction. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's flow matching model instead learns the direct path from a sparse reconstruction's renderings to the renderings a dense capture would give.

Trained on millions of paired images, the model processes dozens of views in one pass on a single high-end graphics card. Pipelines using it beat earlier works on standard view-synthesis benchmarks in both sparse and dense regimes, the authors report. Virtual reality capture is the motivating customer.
arxiv-2504-02147:
Zhen Zhang and co-authors present a data-driven way to bound where an unknown linear system can go, without flattening the shape of the bound set. Their 2025 paper uses a rich set form that stays closed under a key operation. Past forms often force boxy approximations that inflate the bound.

An exact multiplication method keeps the true non-convex shape of reachable sets as they propagate. No rounding step is needed at that stage. Tests show tighter over-bounds than standard methods give. The work serves safety checks for systems learned from data alone. Keeping shape fidelity, the authors argue, is the core gain for sound reachability work.
arxiv-2504-02447:
Chun-Ming Yip and co-authors propose measuring a key weak-force constant with neutrinos from a nearby supernova, in a 2025 paper. The constant, the weak mixing angle, shifts with the energy scale at which it is measured. Its low-energy value is still being pinned down. A precise low-energy measure tests the standard theory and could hint at new physics in the neutrino sector.

Their plan uses Argo, a future ton-scale liquid argon detector built to hunt dark matter. When a star collapses nearby, it pours out neutrinos that Argo could catch. The team work through a scattering channel where neutrinos bounce off whole nuclei. They find Argo could reach a few percent precision for a supernova within about three kiloparsecs. That would be a strong low-energy result.
arxiv-2504-02547:
Patricia Puchhammer, Ines Wilms, and Peter Filzmoser checked whether official data groups match statistical clusters in a 2025 paper. Experts often pre-label observations into groups, by diagnosis or design, yet the data themselves may cluster differently, and single bad cells in a spreadsheet can wreck the comparison. Their multi-group Gaussian mixture model is the first built to ask that question directly, using prior groups as a starting point while letting the data reassign members to better-fitting groups.

Each group's observations are modeled as a mixture over all group profiles, so evidence can pull a case across the border. A penalized estimation method flags outlying cells and keeps them from distorting the fit, with proven breakdown resistance and an efficient algorithm.
arxiv-2504-02747:
Pradyumn Goyal and co-authors teach a model to predict how 3D objects bend and move, in a 2025 paper. Many objects, from laptops to cabinets, have parts that swing or slide. Guessing those motions from a single still shape is hard, and hand-labeled training data is scarce.

Their system, called GEOPARD, first learns without labels. A geometry-driven search finds part motions that are physically valid, with no parts tearing off or crashing into each other. Those found motions serve as practice for a transformer model. On a standard test set of movable objects, the method reached top scores. The work shows that shape alone can teach plausible motion.
arxiv-2504-02947:
The authors revisit limits on superconducting cosmic strings in light of the faint 21-centimeter signal from the cosmic dark ages. These strings are hypothetical defects whose cores carry a charged field. Moving through magnetized regions, a string radiates across the spectrum. That energy heats and ionizes the gas between galaxies, leaving marks on the global 21-centimeter signal.

Earlier studies looked mainly at radio emission, which leaves the gas unchanged. This work adds ionizing radiation from decaying strings. The dark ages signal is prized because the early universe was smooth, free of the messy effects of the first stars. By capping how much the signal at redshift 89 may depart from the standard model, the authors bound the strings' decay efficiency. The limit ties the allowed loop current and string tension to a single combined ceiling.
arxiv-2504-03047:
Reef Alturki, Adrian Hilton, and Jean-Yves Guillemaut present a multi-camera system for tracking people on foot in this 2025 paper. Single cameras lose people behind obstacles, so busy scenes are often watched from several angles at once. A common trick merges all views onto one ground map, but that warping distorts how people look.

The authors keep the merged view for finding people, then add attention links that tie each person to themselves across frames. Those links carry a person's features forward in time, building a steadier identity for each track. On two public test sets the system set the best scores reported, reaching about ninety-six percent on one identity measure for the Wildtrack set and about eighty-six percent on MultiviewX. The results suggest attention across time can offset the distortion that merged views introduce.
arxiv-2504-03247:
Chen Wang and Shi-fan Qi entangle two light or microwave modes through a shared vibrating part, in work from 2025. Two-mode squeezed states are a workhorse of quantum tech, prized for sensing and data tasks. Their setup couples one mechanical resonator to two photon modes in a three-part cavity. Strong pulsed drives, tuned over time, build the squeeze link.

Math checks on the full system back the slim effective model. A full open-system solve then tracks how the squeeze grows. With the right read angle, steady squeeze tops what stability caps would suggest. The plan also shrugs off drive errors and warm noise well.
arxiv-2504-03447:
Irena Radisic and five co-authors weigh a missed link in heart models in a 2025 paper. Computer models of the heart join electric waves, calcium flow, and muscle squeeze to study the organ without surgery. To keep costs sane, models often skip the back-pull of stretch on calcium stores, though that pull is real.

The team built a fast frame that adds the back-pull at near no extra cost. They then joined it to full heart models in two known forms. Their runs show how much organ-level acts shift when the link is on. The work helps modelers pick which truths they can safely skip.
arxiv-2504-03647:
Temitayo Adefemi wrote this 2025 guide to parallel computing for computer scientists. Parallel work splits a task across many processors at once. The guide starts with history, from early models like PRAM and BSP to today's many-core chips. It aims to give every reader the core ideas behind fast modern software.

The guide covers theory, work-sharing styles, and ways to keep shared data in step. It explains processes, threads, and the actor model for structuring parallel code. It also shows how chips, caches, memory, and accelerators shape speed and balance. Case studies ground the ideas in real programs. Readers finish with tools to design, tune, and debug parallel applications.
arxiv-2504-03747:
Francesco Bernardini and four co-authors work out how a swarm of moving relays can link fixed terminals under radio restrictions, in a 2025 paper. Some zones are off limits for transmission, shown as disks on a map. Neither the terminals nor the relays may broadcast into them.

The goal is a two-way network connecting all terminals at the lowest total cost, where cost is the combined area of all transmission disks. The authors solve small networks exactly and carry those solutions into bigger ones. For complex layouts they build algorithms around minimum spanning trees to cut cost. They also describe a procedure that maps the possible route shapes around obstacles, used to seed the network's evolution. The result is a toolkit for deploying relay swarms where parts of the spectrum map are forbidden.
arxiv-2504-04047:
Fan studies who bears the cost when new technologies such as automation and AI reshape demand for labor. The framework rests on a simple idea: workers move most easily between jobs that sit close together in skill space, and mobility fades with distance. Fan maps 306 occupations onto cognitive, manual, and social skill dimensions and estimates a compact model that keeps the fine detail of how jobs substitute for one another.

The model shows that automation and AI cluster in skill-adjacent jobs, which constrains how workers adjust and pushes more of the shock onto wages. In the estimates, 20 to 50 percent of a labor demand shock passes into wages, while mobility repairs only about a fifth of the losses. Both figures differ from standard models, which assume smoother adjustment. For policy, the message is that the shape of the skill map decides how painful a technology shock will be.
arxiv-2504-04147:
Zhibin Li, Danning Li, and Mei Huang looked for fingerprints of a critical point in quark matter in a 2025 paper. Holographic models borrow gravity calculations to mimic the strong force at high heat and density, where a critical end point may mark where smooth change turns into a sharp phase transition. Jets of quarks plowing through the hot matter lose energy, and how much they lose could betray the nearby critical point.

Across systems with two or more quark flavors, the team tracked the jet quenching measure and the energy loss of light and heavy quarks near the transition. All rose rapidly close to the critical temperature. Heavy quark loss also scaled with speed differently than familiar charged-particle loss in electric matter, hinting at collisional drag.
arxiv-2504-04647:
Yujia Su, Xinjie Li, and Lionel Wang recast how distances between drug classes are computed for lopsided data in this 2025 paper. Rare classes usually lose in long-tailed datasets. Drug chemistry breaks that rule in an odd way. Some rare drug classes are easy to spot thanks to odd molecular shapes. Standard fixes, like resampling, worship sample counts alone. They can over-serve the tail and hurt the common classes.

The new method splits classes into sub-clusters before measuring distances. Identifiability, not headcount, then drives the learning balance. The setting is drug classification with skewed categories. Better tail handling could speed compound screening. The paper challenges a static counting habit in the field. It is a machine learning methods study.
arxiv-2504-04747:
Yoojin Jung and Byung Cheol Song defend small, compressed vision models against adversarial attacks by ensembling trimmed copies of one base model, in work from twenty twenty-five. Compression makes models fit phones and edge gear, but trimmed models break easily under crafted attacks. Safety and size seemed at odds.
