Their method prunes the same base model by different importance scores, so each copy keeps different strengths. Voting across copies hardens the whole. The system also picks how many copies to run at inference time, skipping needless work. On two standard image sets it beat prior adversarial pruning methods. Inference ran up to about twice as fast. The authors pitch it for tight hardware.
arxiv-2504-05047:
Letting several language models debate a question can sharpen their answers, but every round costs computing time, and needless debates can talk a model out of a right answer. Sugyeong Eo and co-authors propose a thriftier setup called Debate Only When Necessary, or DOWN. Each agent first answers alone and reports a confidence score; debate starts only for questions where that score says the answer needs more thought.

When debate does start, the agents refine their answers while seeing their peers' replies and confidence scores, so weak claims carry less weight. On benchmarks, DOWN ran up to six times more efficiently than always debating, while matching or beating the accuracy of earlier methods. Further checks showed it also cut the spread of errors that needless rounds can cause. The authors present selective debate as a way to keep the gains of teamwork without paying for it on every question.
arxiv-2504-05147:
Amrita Roy Chowdhury and co-authors present a system that sanitizes sensitive prompts before they reach a large language model, in a 2025 paper. When users send prompts to a proprietary model service, private tokens inside them can be exposed. The task is to protect those tokens formally while keeping the model's answers good. Their system is named with a stylized form of the word Prompt.

They define a prompt sanitizer in cryptographic terms. Sensitive tokens split into two kinds. For tokens where only the format matters, like card numbers, they use format-preserving encryption. For tokens whose value matters, like age or salary, they use a distance-based privacy method. Tests show the split approach protects data while holding answer quality.
arxiv-2504-05247:
Lucas Hataishi and Roberto Hernandez Palomares build inclusions of algebras from tensor categories, in a 2025 paper on math. Their build uses a coend-type recipe inside unitary tensor categories to make faithful inclusions of C-star algebras. Older theory leaned on irreducibility, a trait that many natural cases lack, so the old frame left those cases out.

The work sets out more than one notion of discreteness for such inclusions when that trait is gone, all in one shared frame. The frame also covers actions of compact quantum groups, so a wide set of cases sits under one roof. Cases come from semi-circular systems and from factorization homology. When the trait does hold, the authors pin down when two discreteness tests agree, which tidies a corner of operator algebra theory.
arxiv-2504-06147:
Johanna Knapp and Joseph McGovern explore a string-theory model whose phases may realize a rare kind of geometric repair. Their model is a gauged linear sigma model with three circle groups twisted by a threefold symmetry. Its roomy phase is a known smooth space, a quotient of a triple intersection inside a product of planes. A special point in the equations hints the other phase should also be geometric. On inspection it instead looks like a hybrid, with unbroken symmetry and a Coulomb branch.

Using mirror symmetry and topological string tools, the authors gather evidence that this phase matches a noncommutative resolution of a singular space with 63 pinch points. They compute curve-counting invariants through genus eleven, refined to track the threefold torsion. Two integral bases built from the mirror data support the match.
arxiv-2504-06247:
Clark and co-authors map in 2025 the layered edge of a gas cloud in a small nearby galaxy, where starlight breaks molecules apart. Such zones shape how galaxies recycle their gas. In metal poor gas, theory says the layer where carbon atoms give way to carbon compounds sits deeper than the hydrogen layer, leaving much gas dark to standard tracers.

The team resolved the front in a cloud in the Small Magellanic Cloud. Radio data traced carbon forms, and heat glow data traced hydrogen pairs. Seeing all three fronts at once tests the theory head on. The maps show how far each front sits from the hot young stars.
arxiv-2504-06447:
Marius Crainic, Rui Loja Fernandes, and David Martínez Torres develop a broad geometry theory in a 2025 mathematics paper, with an appendix by Joshua Mundinger. Their subject is Poisson manifolds of compact type, a class that widens the familiar world of compact Lie groups and algebras. The paper builds the basic theory of these spaces from the ground up.

Among the main results are standard local forms, a natural layering of the space, and a method to smooth out its singular points. From these tools, the leaf space of such a manifold turns out to carry a rigid geometric structure, watched over by a reflection group of the classic Coxeter kind. The authors also build a counting theory for the proper cases and end with a surprise: every manifold of compact type must be regular. A closing list names open problems for the field.
arxiv-2504-06947:
Natalia Loukachevitch and four co-authors report a shared task on extracting opinions from Russian news in a 2025 paper. The contest asked systems to pull structured opinion tuples from a sentence: who holds the opinion, its target, the expression used, and the sentiment direction. Over one hundred submissions arrived.

Most participants used large language models, either as is, with examples, or fine tuned. Fine tuning won on the test set. The organizers separately compared thirty prompts and eleven open models of varied sizes in one shot and ten shot settings, identifying which combinations work best. The task gives Russian language technology a benchmark for opinion mining in news text.
arxiv-2504-07347:
Researchers prove in 2025 a design rule for systems that serve large language models and AI agents: keep the system busy whenever work waits. Demand for such models is surging, and wasted capacity costs money. Past gains came mostly from engineering, not from math theory.

The team builds a queue-based theory for how requests flow through batched servers. A broad class of busy-keeping schedules hits the top possible throughput, for lone requests and for agent jobs alike. Agent jobs branch and join in graph shapes, and the rule still holds. Checks on real systems confirm two known servers meet the bar, while two others fall short and can stall. Batch caps and looped routes remain open puzzles.
arxiv-2504-07447:
Tzu-Wei Kuo and Hoi-Kwan Lau worked in 2025 on measuring entanglement in spin ensembles that cannot be resolved particle by particle. Such ensembles are inherently mixed states, and mixed-state entanglement is hard to quantify in many-body systems. Their states, though, have a symmetry that can be exploited.

Using permutation symmetry, the authors show bipartite entanglement can be calculated exactly for a wide range of these states. The method handles any particle count, effective spin, and split of the ensemble. They apply it to states with fixed magnetisation and to useful superpositions such as GHZ and spin-squeezed states. The work may aid spin-based quantum technologies.
arxiv-2504-07647:
Ignacio Santamaria, Jesús Gutiérrez, Mohammad Soleymani, and Eduard Jorswieck study rates in beyond diagonal RIS systems in two thousand twenty-five. A reconfigurable intelligent surface shapes radio waves to aid a link. Beyond diagonal forms couple the surface elements in richer ways. Their case has line of sight paths to and from the surface.

The direct link lacks a line of sight path in their setup. They derive a closed form for the rate that can be reached. From it they get the best surface matrix in closed form too. Tests show the fix stays strong under a more standard fading model. Gains hold when the direct link is weak.
arxiv-2504-07947:
Grant Brodnik and colleagues show how to build tiny optical devices that convert laser light to new colors at high power without extra noise. Inside a ring-shaped resonator, a pump laser can split into two new waves, but rival processes usually compete and spoil the output. Earlier designs used a patterned ring to open a band gap that allows only chosen interactions. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team adds careful shaping of the mode spacing so unwanted interactions are suppressed, while the band gap switches on just one desired conversion.

Their devices produced strong output waves with clean spectra and weak side modes. By changing only the patterning numbers, they built four oscillators that each selected different output colors, showing the design can be tuned on demand. The authors present patterned resonators as a flexible and nearly lossless toolkit for compact light sources.
arxiv-2504-08047:
Kosuke Jamie Kanehisa, Marcel Pawlowski, and Noam Libeskind show Andromeda's dwarf galaxies lean hard to one side in a 2025 paper. Standard cosmology expects satellite swarms to spread near evenly around a big galaxy. Andromeda's swarm instead points at the Milky Way, and the team measured just how odd that lean is against sims of like systems.

All but one of its thirty seven known dwarfs sit inside a one hundred seven degree wedge aimed our way. In standard sims, fewer than three in a thousand Andromeda likes lean that far, and none lean as one. Joined to its known flat satellite plane, the lean marks the system as an extreme outlier. The authors say small scale structure theory has a problem to answer.
arxiv-2504-08247:
Liu Xiao, Li Zhiyuan, and Lin Yueyu grow a state-based sequence model so it can scale like its transformer kin. State models run in a straight line with fixed memory, a cheap trick, but they lack a way for tokens and weights to talk. Their 2025 design, Meta-State, builds that talk into the state itself.

Part of the model's state doubles as change weights, with no new matrices and no softmax step. Token order stays strict, as live text needs. Growth then means widening the state and the weight tokens, reusing all old weights. No retraining starts the scale-up. The team frames it as a bridge: state speed, weight talk, and room to grow in one frame.
arxiv-2504-08547:
Vassili Korotkine, Mitchell Cohen, and James Richard Forbes locate a robot that cannot tell its landmarks apart. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. The robot measures relative positions to known landmarks. It does not know which landmark each reading came from. Guessing wrong can wreck the position estimate. Local solvers often settle into that wrong guess.

Their method casts the problem as a semidefinite relaxation. It solves for robot states and landmark matches together. The answer is globally optimal, not just a local best. For moderate noise, the relaxation is tight in most cases. Tests in simulation and experiment beat Gauss-Newton baselines started from dead reckoning. The team also shares software for the method. Certifiable localization gains a practical tool.
arxiv-2504-08647:
Lázaro Costa, Susana Barbosa, and Jácome Cunha studied gaps in tools that support user studies in software research in 2025. User studies drive science forward, yet researchers hit many barriers when they run them, even with tool support. The team asked how well current tools and their features cover known barriers.

For barriers with no cover, they proposed new features. A survey of one hundred two researchers backed all but one of the proposals with clear positive support. Their analysis shows a wide gap: several barriers have no tool that helps with them at all. The work maps tool features to barriers so builders can see exactly where support is missing.
arxiv-2504-09047:
Robot teams that must work while their sight is fooled are studied by Rayan Bahrami and Hamidreza Jafarnejadsani in a 2025 arXiv paper. Small flying robots often lean on learned sight tools to spot things and judge place. Attacks on those tools can fake what a robot sees or slow its view. Such faults matter where robot work guards safety.

The pair treat fake sight as stray, off-and-on bad data for place tasks. Their frame joins motion sensor data with sight data to hold place well despite the faults. It also scores how much harm a set attack rate does to the team. Tests on a real robot group back the frame.
arxiv-2504-09947:
Hannes Wallimann and Noah Balthasar predict how Swiss children get to school in a 2025 paper. Travel habits formed young shape health and mobility for life. Little was known about what drives school trip choices in Switzerland. The pair applied a random forest, a machine learning method, to the national mobility census.

Distance stood out as the top predictor in every model run. The models sorted active travel from passive travel with about eighty-seven percent accuracy. Sorting car trips from non-car trips reached about seventy-nine percent. The results give school planners measured evidence on where habits form. They also show that learning methods can pull clear behavior patterns from messy national survey data.
arxiv-2504-10047:
Leviatan, Garcia-Ramos, Gavrielov, and Van Isacker test vibrational symmetry in cadmium isotopes with a boson model, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Nuclei from cadmium one hundred ten to one hundred sixteen were long debated as vibrators or mixed shapes. The team checks low-lying normal states against data. Most states fit a clean vibrational pattern with good U five symmetry.

Deviations occur in selected non-yrast states and need symmetry breaking. Their Hamiltonian breaks the symmetry only there while mixing weakly with intruder states. The approach uses partial dynamical symmetry, where a subset of states keeps exact symmetry. Results vindicate that notion for this isotope chain. Empirical spectra are reproduced with notable fidelity.
arxiv-2504-10247:
Jue Xu and co-authors proved in 2025 a hopeful fact about simulating quantum systems on today's noisy machines. Deepen the circuit, and both the hardware error and the stepping error shrink exponentially per added depth. That runs against the usual dread that depth only accumulates noise. Their analysis covers the standard Trotter approach to simulation.

Simulations across several systems and noise types confirmed the decay. The team then derives the best step count and the noise ceiling that together guarantee a target precision. A phase diagram maps safe territory in depth and noise rate. For fault-tolerant designs, the improved bounds promise real resource savings. The authors frame the work as a systematic guide to practical quantum advantage through simulation.
arxiv-2504-10847:
Saikat Das, Bing Zhang, Soebur Razzaque, and Siyao Xu test what a single ultra-high-energy neutrino says about cosmic rays. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies an event caught by the KM3NeT telescope. The neutrino's huge energy points to a parent cosmic ray of even greater force. A light-based birth path for it needs extreme cosmic-ray power per particle.

Three source stories are weighed: a brief flare, a steady diffuse glow, and a line-of-sight hit. Fits draw on KM3NeT alone and on joint data with IceCube and Auger. A flare source would need a new, common, gamma-dark class of events. The diffuse story strains the KM3-only fit at far distances. The joint fit holds for sources not too far away. A point-source birth near bright galaxy cores also stays in line with known limits.
arxiv-2504-11047:
Axel Maas, Simon Plätzer, and Felix Pressler search computer simulations of quantum gravity for hints of a geon, in a research paper from 2025. A geon would be a knot of gravity bound by its own pull, long proposed but never seen. The team used causal dynamical triangulations, which build space-time from tiny blocks.

They measured how curvature at one spot relates to curvature at another, for several gravity operators. Across a certain distance range, the pattern matched a heavy particle-like state, whichever operator they used. The simulated universe's fast expansion phase seemed to sway the mass. If real, such objects could relate to dark matter or early black holes.
arxiv-2504-11747:
Cai-Hong Wang and co-authors present a 2025 quantum paper on telling apart entangled states when the partners sit far apart. Distant labs can act on their own shares and phone each other, a rule set called LOCC. Some state sets defy that rule set and cannot be told apart locally. Past work built checker sets, called detectors, that can settle the question for set families of paired states.

The team show how to find all detectors for a given state set. They also build sets with no detectors, most of which still defy local reads, proving detectors are not a must. For one key system size, detectors turn out to be near-musts, with a lone exception. The local tell-apart problem for that size closes here. Detector maps help labs plan what they can learn at a distance.
arxiv-2504-12347:
Finland's national matriculation exam is a stern test of school mathematics, and language models are now sitting it. Mika Setälä and co-authors assessed in 2025 how successive generations of models score on that exam.

Early models earned middling grades. Later models improved sharply, with some reaching near-perfect or perfect scores, matching top students and qualifying for university admission. The study tracks that rapid climb across model generations. The authors read the results as evidence that models can support learning and teaching, while noting that such proficiency also pressures how exams are designed.
arxiv-2504-13147:
Qing-Yang Wang and co-authors wrote this cosmology paper in 2025. Dark matter might be born from gravity alone, with no other link to known matter. The team set that birth inside warm inflation, a take on the early cosmos where a warm bath lasts through the fast stretch. They traced each path by which gravity could seed dark matter there.

One path, where the inflation field's parts clash and merge, works quite unlike the cold case and makes less light dark matter. For seeds born of the stretch's own ripples, they find a clean link between mass and final share. Warmth must pass a floor value for enough dark matter to form at all. Matching sky data then pins the allowed mass span for both plain and shape-shifting couplings of the dark stuff.
arxiv-2504-13747: Parisel presents a paper from twenty twenty-five on scoring privilege risk in Microsoft Azure cloud accounts. Two scores cover the control side and the data side of the cloud. The control score orders accounts by their power to change settings. It weights write, action, and read rights in rising order. The data score gauges the widest reach of data theft or forgery. It leans on the tree shape of Azure tenant grouping. Together the scores form one frame for permission analysis.
arxiv-2504-13947:
Shahan Ali Memon and co-authors probe image-generating AI by asking it to do something it cannot honestly do: draw a person's headshot from their CV alone. The exercise is a designed context void, a task where facts are missing on purpose. The team fed professional CVs to a system pairing a text model with an image model, then studied the portraits that came back.

With no physical description to go on, the system invented faces. The qualitative analysis shows it reading markers of identity and competence in the CVs and turning them into visual traits. Those inventions leaned on stereotypes and hallucinations. The authors frame the method as speculative design: forcing a system into radical uncertainty exposes the values it fills gaps with. They argue such probes belong in the study of generative AI, because users often hand these systems thin context and receive confident output.
arxiv-2504-14047:
Junlin Wang and co-authors probe the limits of giving language models more thinking time, in a 2025 paper. Extra test-time compute, through repeated sampling or revision, is widely touted as a substitute for bigger models. The team ran scaling methods on hard reasoning tasks for both plain and reasoning-tuned models. A floor appeared: plain models plateaued no matter how much compute they burned.

Even with ten times the compute, general models could not match reasoning-tuned ones. Among tuned models, simple majority voting beat fancier revision schemes. Correct answers also carried a linguistic signature: shorter, with less hedging. Those surface cues predicted quality at zero extra compute. The authors suggest future agents should read their own style to judge themselves.
arxiv-2504-14247:
Black hole entropy may come in fixed steps rather than any value, and Mirjam Cvetič and Malcolm Perry test that idea in a stripped-down setting in this 2025 paper. They study black holes living in subtracted geometry, a simplified backdrop that keeps the same horizon area and surface gravity as the true holes. Ringing tones of these holes, called quasinormal modes, can be computed exactly there.

From the exact tone spectrum, the authors trace links to the conformal theories that describe horizon physics. The upshot is a clean rule: horizon area comes in units of eight pi times the Planck length squared. The finding supports the view that gravity's entropy has a discrete grain at bottom.
arxiv-2504-14347:
Group theory sorts finite groups by the subgroups inside them, and one special family of subgroups is called the Chermak-Delgado lattice. Jiakuan Lu and three co-authors ask in 2025 how far a group can sit from that family. They count, for each group, the sets of subgroups that lie outside the lattice, grouped by sameness under the group's own symmetries.

The paper settles the cases where that count is one, two, or three. For each small count, the authors pin down exactly which finite groups occur. Results of this kind give a map of how group structure can vary near a well behaved core. They also give other researchers a checklist for testing new claims about subgroup patterns.
arxiv-2504-14447:
Jeonghwa Lee, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, finds the large-scale limit of a walk whose steps rest on a fresh kind of linked chance chain. The chain can hold long-range links between its terms.

The limit is a new class of spread paths with no fixed step memory. In it are paths whose links fade at a set rate, as a power, or as a power damped by a set rate. Their spread rules take a split-order form, in some cases damped in time. Two known laws come out as set cases. Lee also treats time-changed forms of the paths, and sets out their rules and link build.
arxiv-2504-14747:
Qinghao Li and co-authors present a 2025 paper on safe self-driving on curved roads. Real traffic mixes curved lanes, moving obstacles, and the need for a smooth ride. A classic method that treats hazards as fields often fails on such roads alone. The team blends that method with two other tools to plan paths.

One tool remaps the road into a frame where curves act straight. A second tool tunes the chosen path in real time. A risk field shifts with how nearby cars behave, which shapes lane-change choices. Path shapes are drawn to keep turns smooth and comfy. Tests in models and real scenes showed safe margins and workable paths.
arxiv-2504-15047:
Quy-Anh Dang, Chris Ngo, and Truong-Son Hy build a faster, broader generator of attack prompts for language models, in a 2025 paper. Red teaming hunts for prompts that trick models into unsafe or biased output, but older methods are slow or narrow. Their framework, RainbowPlus, borrows from evolution: it keeps an archive of varied, high-quality attack prompts and breeds new ones from them.

Unlike earlier quality-diversity methods, it stores many prompts per niche and scores several at once. Across six data sets and four open models, it produced up to a hundred times more distinct prompts than a rival method. On a standard harm benchmark it beat the best rival's success rate and ran about nine times faster.
arxiv-2504-15347:
Miguel Prado Reynoso and five co-authors study sharp state changes in Kerr parametric oscillators, small quantum systems driven from outside. These systems serve in quantum computing, sensing, and basic research, and are built in circuits and light based setups. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team looks at how spin like symmetry in the system's phase space shapes its state changes. They study drive rates at one, two, three, and four times the natural rate. With the classic form of the system math, they find the key points where states shift. They also track true and near crossings of energy levels and how those crossings affect tunneling between states.
arxiv-2504-16147:
Roberta Sparta and co-authors describe joint work by target labs in Europe for studies of stars and atoms, in a paper from 2025. The labs make thin solid targets that beams can strike, so teams can learn how atoms react. The project links labs across the region under one shared effort.

The paper reports new targets made from forms of carbon, oxygen, and fluorine. Each target was made, checked, and in some cases tested under a beam. A new group now works to share common steps, raise quality, and offer target checks to other teams. The goal is steadier supply for tests that need rare or hard targets.
arxiv-2504-16347:
Junwei Chen, Marco Raiola, and Stefano Discetti gave a method to place flow sensors well without costly trial runs in two thousand twenty-five. Estimating a flow field from a few probes works better when past probe readings are stacked in time. Probe position is the key to accuracy, but searching positions in a live experiment is expensive.

Their trick uses rows of vectors from standard flow images as stand-ins for probe time series downstream. That lets the search run offline after one preliminary experiment, with no probes in the flow. Once the best spots are found, probes are installed for the real time-resolved work. The method beat even spacing and greedy search methods from the literature.
arxiv-2504-16647:
Greg Jackson, Stéphane Peigné, and Kazuhiro Watanabe present in 2025 a sharpened formula for the soft gluon radiation that a nuclear target induces when fast particles scatter inside it. Collisions of protons with heavy nuclei reveal how cold nuclear matter alters particle yields. Repeated kicks from the target make the incoming particle shed many soft gluons, and the long forming ones drain energy in a fully coherent way.

The new spectrum formula holds beyond the usual rough accuracy and for general scattering motion. Its main traits are shown on a quark gluon scattering case. Better formulas mean cleaner reads of what the nucleus does to hard probes, a base step for hotter collision studies.
arxiv-2504-16847:
Demazure and co-authors study what happens when a quantum magnet is driven by short laser pulses rather than a steady tone. Shaking a magnet's lattice can retune its magnetic couplings, a trick called magnetophononics. Earlier theory used endless single-frequency driving and found hybrid waves where lattice and spin motions repel each other. Real experiments, though, fire ultrashort pulses packed with many frequencies.

The team computed the system's response moment by moment, tracking the lattice sway and the spin excitations together. A slow beat appeared between the two sectors, energy sloshing back and forth, born from the hybrid waves pushing apart. A simplified approximation captured the effect and its fingerprints at sum frequencies too. The authors then modeled a real spin-chain compound with overlapping spectra to set criteria for spotting these effects in the lab.
arxiv-2504-17247:
Antimicrobial peptides are short protein chains that kill germs, and finding new ones could refresh the fight against drug-resistant infections. Diogo Soares and co-authors present OmegAMP, a generative system that designs such peptides to order. Its diffusion model can be steered toward chosen physical traits and toward killing specific species.

A biology-aware way of encoding peptides sharpens the generator's aim. Synthetic data also trains filters that weed out duds before any lab work begins, cutting false alarms sharply. The team made twenty-five of the computer's designs in the lab. Twenty-four of them killed germs, including strains that resist standard drugs. That hit rate, the authors say, shows designed peptides can move from screen to bench with unusual reliability.
arxiv-2504-17747:
Cameron Cianci, Luchang Jin, and Joshua Swaim test a simulation speedup method in this 2025 paper. Fourier acceleration is used in Hybrid Monte Carlo simulations of field theories. It cuts the link between successive field samples, which speeds up the simulation. In simple theories it can remove critical slowing down near phase changes.

The team applied the method to a linear sigma model in its broken symmetry phase. That model serves as a simple chiral theory linked to quantum chromodynamics. Acceleration cut autocorrelation and sped thermalization in their tests. They also give a way to set the key masses from the data as the run proceeds. Future work will test the strongly interacting case.
arxiv-2504-18147:
Rob Romijnders, Stefanos Laskaridis, and colleagues transfer knowledge between model modules without leaking private data in a 2025 study. Big models are often trained on mixed sources, and even modular designs, where experts specialize, can leak information about those sources. Training each module in isolation protects privacy but blocks the generalization that shared learning brings.

Their framework joins differential privacy with a two-stage, parameter-efficient fine-tuning scheme. Knowledge moves between modules under a privacy budget that bounds what any output can reveal. Modular adaptation with guarantees suits hospitals and firms that must pool skill without pooling records.
arxiv-2504-18447:
Ryo Yamaki and co-authors propose in 2025 an iterative way to split event camera data by motion. Event cameras report only changes, so their streams mix background motion with independently moving objects. Sorting events into motions supports tasks like object detection and robot control, yet noisy real scenes make the sorting hard in practice.

Their method extends a contrast maximization framework, repeatedly separating a dominant background motion from leftover foreground motion. The process yields sharp, motion-compensated edge images. On public and self-recorded data it beat prior methods by over thirty percent on moving object detection. Code is public.
arxiv-2504-18947:
Sainik Karak, Akshay Kumar, and Tanmoy Paul study when extending a linear measurement is forced to be unique in a 2025 mathematics study. The Hahn-Banach theorem guarantees that a functional defined on a subspace can be extended to the whole space, but extensions need not be unique. In locally convex spaces, broader than Banach spaces, they ask which subspaces enjoy a uniqueness property modeled on a classical one.

Characterizations follow for the new property, along with a description of spaces where every subspace has it. A bridge result ties the classical property to the weak topology version, letting old theorems do new work.
arxiv-2504-19047:
David Almog wrote this economics paper, published in 2025. It uses an online experiment to show why people ignore good advice from AI: they worry about how taking the advice makes them look, even when looking bad costs them nothing.

Hopes for human and AI teamwork rest on each side playing to its strengths. In practice, people often underuse AI tips. Almog shows that image concerns, cares about others' perceptions with no money attached, push participants to set AI recommendations aside. Performance on the task drops as a result. The finding names a quiet social force behind a common puzzle in workplaces and products. It suggests that making AI use look normal, rather than just making AI better, may be needed for people to accept its help.
arxiv-2504-19147:
Junichi Komatsu, Kenichiro Koga, and Jonas Berx used computer models to watch single chains of a water-shy polymer fold and clump. A lone chain can coil loose or ball up tight, a shift called the coil-globule transition. In a crowd, chains can also stick to each other. The team asked how the two shifts play off each other as heat rises.

They tracked shape measures such as the spread of each chain and how much the chains clumped. A second lens sorted the web of contacts into motifs, a book-keeping of who touches whom. In a crowd, all chains balled up at once at one sharp heat point, and clumping came with the fold. A lone chain, by contrast, folded by slow degrees. Contact motifs swung from in-chain to cross-chain at the same point.
arxiv-2504-19447:
Li-Jun Du, Wan-Tong Li, and Ming-Zhen Xin settle questions about traveling wave fronts in this 2025 paper. Their setting is a class of spread systems with reaction, diffusion, and drift, laid over a repeating medium. The fronts in question pulse as they travel and connect a stable state to an unstable one. Earlier work proved such fronts exist and found their speeds.

The authors first work out exactly how the fronts behave as they near the unstable state. From that they prove each nonzero-speed front is the only one of its kind, apart from a shift in position. They then show the fronts pull in nearby solutions that start front-shaped, making them stable in a strong global sense. A two-species contest system serves as a test case for the results.
arxiv-2504-19547:
Michael Elberfeld, Frank Kammer, and Johannes Meintrup design a compact way to store a graph and still search it depth-first. Their 2025 paper works with separable graphs, a broad family that can be split by small cut sets. Many real graphs have this trait, among them flat maps and graphs of small width. The stored form uses far less space than a plain list of links.

From the stored form, a depth-first search runs fast and uses very little extra space. After a search, the search tree is folded into the stored form itself. Common questions about the tree, such as the lowest shared ancestor of two points, then take constant time. For flat graphs, the team also shows how to build the stored form fast and within a tight space bound.
arxiv-2504-19647:
Yvain Bruned and co-authors wrote a 2025 review of a new way to compute wave-like equations with rough data. Classic schemes often fail when the solution swings fast, which leads to blow-ups and loss of accuracy. Wave type equations are hard in part because they do not smooth rough starts.

The new approach studies the swings through resonance, a check of how waves interact. It pairs that check with a decorated tree scheme drawn from work on singular random equations. Trees keep track of each interaction step in a clean form. The review lays out the method and its roots for other scholars. The authors hope to see the scheme used for more wave equations and past them.
arxiv-2504-19747:
Sora Kobayashi and Kei-Ichi Kondo settle which three-qubit entangled states can serve as the channel for perfect quantum teleportation. Teleporting an unknown qubit state perfectly is well known to work with a GHZ state shared between sender and receiver. Whether the other famous three-qubit class, the W state, can do the same was the open question.

The authors give an impossibility proof: the W state cannot be used to realize perfect teleportation of an arbitrary qubit state. The contrast with the GHZ state is sharp. They then show how to modify the shared state into what they call a W-like state. With that state, and under a prescribed measurement basis, they give a procedure achieving perfect teleportation. The result maps the boundary between two fundamental entanglement classes by what they can actually do, a distinction that matters for designing quantum networks.
arxiv-2504-19847:
Juhan Park, Kyungjae Lee, Hyung Jin Chang, and Jungchan Cho present a framework that predicts how people interact with objects in images, in a 2025 paper. Standard systems output triplets: a person, an action, and an object. Their version adds a fourth element, a precise outline mask for the person-object pair.

The framework builds on large vision foundation models that can outline anything they are pointed at. A special decoder carries those prompt-based skills into the interaction task, even though training covered only the task itself. On two public benchmarks, results matched the best current methods, even in some cases with no examples shown. The system can also answer fresh written or visual prompts, producing interaction outlines for cases it never trained on.
arxiv-2504-20047:
Ahmad and eight co-authors build a benchmark for answering questions over the messy tables people actually make. Tables in PDFs and web pages pack dense facts into complex layouts that resist database queries. Their benchmark, HCT-QA, gathers thousands of such human-centric tables with questions and answers.

The set pairs 1,880 real tables with nearly ten thousand questions, plus synthetic tables carrying many more. Tests of 25 language models and 9 vision models show wide gaps in skill. Fine-tuning one model on the benchmark lifted its score by up to 25 points. The authors offer the set, with rich metadata, as a measuring stick for table understanding.
arxiv-2504-20247:
Nikhil Chellam and co-authors highlight a fast quantum method for studying light-driven effects in tiny metal structures, in this 2025 feature article. Full quantum treatment of such systems is costly because they hold many atoms and change in trillionths of a second. The tight-binding method they review trades some detail for speed.

Its time-based form can follow thousands of atoms over the needed spans. Uses covered include light uptake, harmonic light generation, and light-driven chemical change. The method captures how plasmon peaks shift with particle size and how particles couple in groups. It also models hot carrier creation and a hydrogen-splitting reaction, linking quantum and classic views.
arxiv-2504-20647:
Yafei Wang and co-authors model how electric stimulation speeds tissue healing and reshapes growth in this 2025 paper. Experiments show voltage can speed recovery compared with natural healing. The team built a theory of growth that responds to that stimulation. Tissue can grow unevenly, and uneven growth can buckle into folds. Their model asks when healing stays smooth and when shapes destabilize. Stronger coupling between electricity and tissue mechanics improved healing in the model.

Stimulation also steered growth toward even, direction-free patterns. Delaying the buckling point gives tissue time to repair first. The work points to clinical uses of controlled voltage in wound care. It blends mechanics, growth theory, and experiment at once. Such models can guide how strong and how long stimulation should run. The paper is theory led by experimental contrasts.
arxiv-2504-20947:
Norah Alghamdi and Shinkyu Park propose, in a 2025 paper, a way for robot teams to pass through narrow corridors without deadlock. When many robots meet in a narrow space, each may wait for the others, and the whole group can lock up. Their framework treats the passage as a game and lets each robot hold an opinion on who should go first.

Those opinions shift under a model of group decision-making called Nonlinear Opinion Dynamics, which the team pair with a path planning algorithm. As opinions settle, the robots sort themselves into an order and flow through. The framework cuts the likelihood of a full deadlock. A game reduction technique keeps the coordination efficient as team size grows, so larger fleets stay in reach. Extensive simulation studies back the claims.
arxiv-2504-21147:
Soumen Roy and four co-authors update a test of Einstein's gravity law that uses the wave kits called IMRPhenomX. The test bends dials in the wave form and sees if real merger chirps fit the bent or the plain law. Old runs bent just the main tone. This run bends the side tones too and lets the spin of the pair tilt and wobble in the fit.

The team show why the fuller kit counts. Leave the side tones or the wobble out, and the fit can cry a fake break of the law. With them in, lopsided and wobbling pairs can be tried clean. They ran the test on the back half of the third watch run of the big wave ears. Mixed with past runs, the reads show no sign that the law breaks.
arxiv-2504-21247:
Software that flags odd samples as novel often trips when the test data come from a new setting, even if the subject is the same. Yangyang Qu and co-authors tackle that snag in a 2025 paper on novelty detection under domain shift. A photo of the same machine part under new lighting, for instance, may be wrongly flagged as a fault.

Their method pulls the subject's own signal apart from the background variation that carries the domain. It pushes the two representations to share as little information as possible, and it models the background with a deep Gaussian mixture. Detection then runs on the subject signal alone, untouched by background change. In wide tests the method carried over to unseen domains and beat prior approaches by a clear margin, the authors report.
arxiv-2504-21347:
Seonghee Lee and six co-authors introduce the IRL Ditto in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The Ditto is an embodied AI agent that stands in for a remote colleague in a shared office. People who are present in the room can meet this digital stand-in as they walk by. It can start greetings, share updates, or make small talk, much like the real person might.

The team ran a four-day study in an office. They asked how the Ditto shapes contact and ties among colleagues. They found that gains in social ties rested on how well people already knew the person the Ditto stood for. Strong prior ties helped; weak ones did less. The study shows that a fake presence can support office ties, but it cannot build them from nothing.
arxiv-2504-21547:
Aleksei Dorkin and Kairit Sirts described a system to help librarians tag books by subject, in a 2025 shared-task paper. Tagging by hand is slow, and the list of tags is huge. Their team, TartuNLP, treated the job as a search problem: use a document's content to pull likely tags from the full list.

Their system works in two stages. A first model casts a wide net and gathers candidate tags quickly. A second model then reads each tag against the document in detail and reorders the list. Recall rose well past single-stage methods, and judges rated the output as competitive. The authors present tagging as retrieval as a workable frame for library work.
arxiv-2504-21747:
Maxime Bouthors, Josep Crego, and François Yvon improve retrieval-augmented machine translation using text in the target language alone, in a research paper from 2025. Such systems usually search a bilingual memory for helpful past translations. But in many settings, only target-language text is plentiful.

Their retriever searches that monolingual text directly, guided by the source sentence. They train it with both sentence-level and word-level matching goals. Across three system designs, the approach matched the quality of memory-based models in controlled tests. On a larger real-world setup, it beat both the plain baseline and general-purpose cross-language retrievers by a clear margin.
arxiv-2505-00047:
Peter West and Christopher Potts show in 2025 that base language models beat their aligned kin at tasks that call for randomness and creativity. Alignment, most often by learning from human feedback, makes models safer and better at following orders. It has become a default step, yet the authors argue it should not be applied to every model by rote.

They test tasks that need outputs no one can predict: random number picks, mixed-strategy games like rock-paper-scissors, and creative writing. Aligned models lean to narrow habits in each, such as picking seven far too often as a random digit. They also turn near fully predictable in some game states and favour pleasant prose over fresh ideas. Across models, better scores on common benchmarks went with worse scores on these tasks, a clear trade-off.
arxiv-2505-00647:
Sirui Chen and co-authors present a robot hand control frame in a 2025 paper called GeoDEx. Touch sensors let robots feel contact and force, which helps with fragile objects and tool use. In practice, the force readings from touch sensors are noisy and hard to calibrate, so their value for control has stayed limited.

GeoDEx handles sensing, planning, and control in one frame built on simple shapes such as planes, cones, and rounded forms. Those shapes let the robot reason about contact even when force values are unsure. The frame covers both direct hand work and tasks where the robot pushes objects with other surfaces.
arxiv-2505-01147:
Frédéric Sabot, Pierre-Etienne Labeau, and Pierre Henneaux set out a risk-based way to judge and improve the safety of large power grids, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Load and supply swing with weather, and gear can fail in chains when guards misbehave. Likely grid states are built from weather data, a market model, and operator steps.

Sampled states are stressed with double faults to gauge risk, with rules for how many samples give a trusted error. A screen can cut the load of cases to run. Learning tools then point to root causes of the worst risks. A test on a seventy-three-bus grid shows the flow, with scaling notes for huge grids.
arxiv-2505-01247:
Black hole entropy puzzles often place a quantum system beside a bath and watch how shared information grows. Harvendra Singh, the sole author, studies two conformal field theory systems in contact, one wrapped around the other, with total size held fixed. He tracks how the bath's entanglement entropy changes as the size split shifts.

For strip-shaped systems, the bath entropy peaks when the two sizes follow a Fibonacci-style critical ratio. Past that point it falls, as island and iceberg contributions take over. Singh shows the iceberg part can be summed exactly for higher-dimensional cases, giving an exact island picture. A tidy identity links the entropy gap between the systems to those island terms. The work sharpens how island corrections control large-bath entropy.
arxiv-2505-01347:
Paulo Piva and two co-authors show how scattered sound traps can be tuned to block chosen tones, in a 2025 physics study. Neat, repeating materials can open band gaps where sound of some pitches cannot pass. Wide or stacked gaps are hard to build that way, since each gap wants its own repeat scale. The team instead scatters tiny Helmholtz resonators, bottle-like traps that ring at one pitch, at random in a host medium.

By picking the mix of trap sizes, they tailor which gaps open. They derive simple formulas for the mixed material's traits that hold across a broad pitch range. Heavy computer trials on random layouts back the formulas. The authors offer the recipe as a fast design path for sound-blocking materials. Disorder, they show, can be a feature, not a flaw.
arxiv-2505-02047:
Gómez-Bueno, Castro Díaz, and Parés presented this numerical methods paper in twenty twenty-five. It deals with balance laws, equations that track flows with sources, such as water depth or gas motion. Good numerical schemes should keep steady states exact rather than letting errors creep in. Earlier schemes did this by solving a hard problem in each grid cell at each step.

Those cell problems worked only when steady states were known in closed form. The authors recast each problem as a control task on a related equation system. A gradient from a companion problem then drives a Newton solver. They test the method on systems from a simple wave equation to shallow water and gas flow with gravity. Results confirm accuracy and exact steady states.
arxiv-2505-02147:
Prajwal Thapa and three co-authors build a phone app that names local herbs of Nepal from a photo, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Nepal's rich plant life holds many herbs of folk use, yet naming them takes a trained eye. A pocket tool could keep that lore alive and guide safe use.

The team hand built a set of twelve thousand herb photos over sixty species. They trained six deep nets by transfer learning, where a pre taught net is tuned to the new task. One dense net won out over the rest. Tricks that warp photos and curb overfit helped the nets hold up on fresh shots. The work aims at a field app for students, healers, and plant fans.
arxiv-2505-02447:
Anisha Banerjee and co-authors price the error protection nanopore DNA reading demands, in a 2025 paper. Nanopore sequencers read long strands fast but noisily, tangled by interference between neighboring bases. In their simplified model, a read vector of length n may carry up to t letter swaps. The question: how many spare bits must a code carry to fix them all?

Graph theory gives the floor: at least t times log n spare bits, a jump from the mere log log n that one swap needs. Matching codes that are optimal up to a constant drop out of the read vectors' own structure. DNA data storage gets its budget lines.
arxiv-2505-02847:
Zhang and a large team (2025) built SAGE, a framework that judges how socially perceptive a language model is by letting a simulated person talk with it. The simulated agent tracks its own shifting emotions and inner thoughts turn by turn: how its feelings change, what it feels, and how it should reply. That produces an emotion trajectory and readable reasoning, not just a score.

Across 100 supportive-dialogue scenarios, the final emotion score lined up strongly with established relationship and empathy measures from human psychology. The team also published a leaderboard of 18 commercial and open models. Frontier systems beat older baselines by up to four times on this test, gaps that ordinary leaderboards do not show. The authors offer SAGE as a principled, scalable way to track progress toward language agents that are genuinely empathetic and socially adept.
arxiv-2505-02947:
Arco, Heinemeyer, and Muhlleitner study how loop level effects change Higgs pair production in a 2025 physics paper. Measuring how the Higgs boson couples to itself is a key test of how mass arises and of physics beyond the standard model. The team work in a model with two Higgs doublets and focus on a future electron positron collider process that makes a Z boson plus two Higgs bosons.

They add one loop corrections to the triple Higgs couplings. The self coupling can grow to nearly six times its standard value, which lifts the pair rate a great deal. Corrections to a coupling with a heavier Higgs can also sharpen its resonance peak, easing detection.
arxiv-2505-03447:
Fumi Ogihara stretches a sum law for prime-plus-rare-square counts to thin spans once past reach. The count weighs each split of a count into a prime and a square-full part, where each prime rides a squared or higher block. Past work with a co-author set the law for spans past the square-root bar. Her 2025 study proves the same law for spans that dip far short of that bar, to a set low roof built from a square-root term.

The gain widens where the law can be run: short spans are the hard yard in count craft, where sums turn wild. Prime split laws feed ciphers and pure count lore both. Each span shaved off the floor is a step in a long craft push.
arxiv-2505-03547:
Eric Zhou and four co-authors build a system that grows a full text adventure game from a story seed. Language models write the tale first, then stock its world with places and things. Code for each act in the tale is then built to run in a game engine. Fixed act lists can cramp a tale, so their acts grow from the tale itself: each act need and effect is read off the story text.

Players can also try acts the tale never named. The system then breeds a fresh act on the fly and may rework past acts to fit. Play-through tests grade how much of each tale a player can finish by its own acts. Rates per tale type sit in the report. The work pushes game making toward full auto builds.
arxiv-2505-03747:
Viktor Marek, Ewa Orlowska, and Ivo Duntsch trace the birth of rough set theory in a 2025 note. Rough sets sort data by what can and cannot be told apart, a tool now used in learning systems. The note goes back to work by Zdzislaw Pawlak and his partners through the 1970s and into 1981.

The authors recall the key papers of that span and hunt the sparks that lit them. Old talks on data tables and vague bounds show up as roots of the theory. They close by sketching how the field grew from 1981 on data systems and rough sets alike.
arxiv-2505-03947:
Xiang Li, Yiyang Hao, and Doug Fulop present a 2025 paper on game-playing agents for Frogger. Reinforcement learning agents master many Atari games but train slowly per game. The field wants agents that adapt to new tasks fast. The team shows that recent reasoning language models can play Frogger with no task training at all. Their post-training came from other domains entirely.

In-context learning and reasoning effort are then varied to see what lifts scores. Last, language model demonstrations bootstrap a classic RL agent. The seeded agent learns faster and scores higher than one starting cold. Code for the work is shared in public. Agent researchers get a recipe that joins two camps: language models supply instant skill and teaching traces, while RL polishes them cheaply. Frogger's traffic timing makes it a sharp test of quick adaptation.
arxiv-2505-04147:
Lixing Niu and eight co-authors build a video data set that tests whether AI models can read a room the way people do. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Reading a room means guessing what others believe, want, and feel from faint social cues. Past data sets used scenes too simple to match real social life.

Their set holds rich clips of tangled social scenes, marked in fine detail. Notes cover events plus beliefs, intents, desires, and feelings, and the causal chains that link them. Questions come from both human writers and models. Tasks span grasping events, gauging minds, and tracing social causes. Top vision-language models fell well short of human-level steadiness. A prompting trick based on theory of mind helped them do better. The set gives the field a harder, fairer yardstick.
arxiv-2505-04447:
Dibya Chakraborty and Rudnei O Ramos warm a fibre growth model of the young sky in a 2025 paper. The model grows from string flux packs and fits sky reads at fit dial sets. Past work set it in the cold growth frame, where drive heat is nil at play.

Warm growth keeps a heat bath that saps the drive field as it rolls in the sky. Strong and weak sap bands are both tried for the fibre forms at hand. Fit to sky reads is the test of each band's worth.
arxiv-2505-04647:
Md Rahat-uz-Zaman, Bei Wang, and Paul Rosen build a visual tool for neural networks in a 2025 paper. Deep networks excel at vision tasks but hide their reasoning. Class separation inside the layers is a key hidden behavior.

ChannelExplorer shows activations across layers in linked views. A scatterplot view exposes confusion between and within classes. A similarity view measures overlap in activation patterns. A heatmap view lets users inspect single channels in detail. The tool favors data-driven reading over architecture reading. Readers in machine learning get a way to ask where a model confuses two classes, and why.
arxiv-2505-04947:
Hongliang Zhang and five co-authors propose DFPL, a way to run federated learning without a central server. In ordinary federated learning, many clients train a shared model and a server combines their updates, which leaves the whole system exposed if that server fails. DFPL removes the server and uses a blockchain so that training and mining run locally on each client. It adds prototype learning to cope with the fact that different clients hold very different data.

The design also cuts the number of parameters clients must exchange. The team analyzed how the method converges, modeling the computing resources that training and mining require. On four benchmark datasets with uneven data splits, DFPL beat the decentralized methods it was compared with on both model performance and communication efficiency.
arxiv-2505-05247:
Ozan Semin computes a quantum correction to axion-like particle coupling in a 2025 paper. These particles, if they exist, convert to photons in magnetic fields. That change lies at the base of telescope and lab searches for them. To know its rate well needs quantum corrections in the count.

A complete one-loop fermionic correction is worked out here. The background field is constant, uniform, and strong to any degree. Dressed fermion propagators handle the field exactly. A classic proper-time method derives those tools. Tensor splitting in a special basis sets out the algebra. The triangle loop diagram is worked out with no shortcut. Results are set against field-strength shortcuts used in other work. The things taken for granted behind those shortcuts become clear. Helioscopes and haloscopes both rely on this coupling. Astrophysical rate estimates sharpen with exact results. The paper serves those who search for dark matter.
arxiv-2505-05347:
Fabrizio Boninsegna presents InfTDA in 2025, a simple top-down method for private counting over grouped data. Differential privacy lets analysts publish counts while mathematically limiting what can be learned about any one person. Many real queries are hierarchical: counts by country, then region, then city, each level splitting the one above.

The mechanism builds a synthetic data set from the top down that answers all such hierarchical queries with bounded error. It extends an earlier version made for trip data to any set of categorical features. Simplicity is the selling point: complex private mechanisms are hard to implement correctly. Census and mobility analysts get a tool they can deploy with confidence.
arxiv-2505-05847:
Filters that answer set membership questions fast and small sit inside databases and networks everywhere. Johanna Elena Schmitz, Jens Zentgraf, and Sven Rahmann shrink one such filter in a 2025 paper. Cuckoo filters store short key prints in a hash table and can err on the yes side only.

Two changes drive the gain. The table no longer needs a size that is a power of two. Slots also overlap in sliding windows, so each print has fewer hiding spots to check. The new layout beat rival filters on size in real tests, with like query speed. Inserts ran slower, a fair trade for the saved space.
arxiv-2505-05947:
Bianca Steffes and co-authors teach a model to sum up German court rulings in a 2025 paper. A sharp sum can save a law hand hours, but a sum that drops or bends a fact is worse than none.

The team tuned a big word model on rulings dressed first with marks for the law's own things: people, courts, and rules in the text. Those marks helped the model find the meat of each case. To grade the sums they set classes for tongue, fit, fullness, and truth. Scores showed the help was real but thin. The sums are not yet fit for daily use, the authors say. The work maps what a law sum must pass before a firm can trust it.
arxiv-2505-06047:
Francesco Spinnato and Cristiano Landi present a shared frame for data that arrives at uneven times in two thousand twenty-five. Such data, with mixed rates, mixed lengths, and gaps, shows up in health, travel, and climate work. Each field has built its own tools, which leaves the area split into parts that do not talk to each other.

Their frame, called PYRREGULAR, sets a common array form for such series and a shared store of data sets. The store holds thirty-four sets for the task of sorting series into classes. They test twelve sorting models from distinct groups on that shared base. The aim is fair comparison and less repeated work across fields.
arxiv-2505-06347:
Qing-Hong Cao and co-authors use a large language model to design quantum circuits in a 2025 paper. Preparing a chosen quantum state is a core step in simulating nature, but the space of states is huge and grows without bound in field theories.

The model searched on its own and found a compact circuit with just four settings for a spin chain. Its energy landed within a percent of the target, and a real quantum processor confirmed the design. Guided by that win, the team extended the search to a field theory in more dimensions. The new circuit stayed shallow and its settings settled to fixed values as lattices grew.
arxiv-2505-07247:
Peichao Lai and co-authors build a benchmark for grading short answers in a 2025 paper. Short answer scoring matters in education and testing, but past tools give coarse scores with little reasoning. Large language models may grade with no training examples, yet they can be biased and hard to audit. A finer test set is needed.

SAS-Bench gives step-wise scores, expert error labels, and varied question types from real subject exams. The open data set holds over a thousand questions and more than four thousand student answers, each marked by experts. Tests across models show science questions are hardest, and a few examples in the prompt help a lot.
arxiv-2505-07347:
Jiewen Yang and co-authors present in 2025 an AI system that tracks high blood pressure in the lung arteries without an invasive test. Ultrasound scans of the heart can spot the disease, but judging how far it has advanced is hard. The standard check threads a tube into the heart, which is accurate but too invasive for routine use.

The team paired ultrasound videos and images with the invasive readings for 1,237 patients from twelve centers, and trained a model that reads many views at once. The model cut errors in estimating lung pressure and resistance by roughly half compared with doctors using ultrasound alone. It also sorted mild from severe disease better than the doctors did. In a forward-looking study it predicted how well treatment would work, pointing to earlier and more personal care.
arxiv-2505-08347:
Han Gao, Marianna Girlando, and Nicola Olivetti build, in a 2025 logic paper, a new proof system for intuitionistic modal logic. That system joins constructive reasoning with talk of necessity and possibility. This logic, known as IK, is a basic one in its family, matching a fragment of constructive first-order logic.

Their calculus nests proof steps in two ways, mirroring the two relations in the logic's models, and needs no labels. A defined search strategy turns it into a decision procedure: any claim can be settled as provable or not. When a proof fails, a concrete countermodel can be read straight off the attempt. That is a first for a label-free system for this logic.
arxiv-2505-08447:
Testing 5G antennas over the air needs fading channels that are dialed in and repeated. The five authors combine a reverberation chamber with an antenna test range to make Rician statistics in the lower FR2 bands, from twenty-four point two five to twenty-nine point five gigahertz. They test 39 setups with a fixed horn antenna, varying absorbers and polarization to see how well the K-factor can be steered.

The K-factor adjusted in every setup, with margins above the noise floor and at least 600 independent samples each. Goodness-of-fit tests confirmed Rician or Rayleigh behavior. Frequency-averaged K-factors spanned minus nine point two to forty point eight decibels, with steps of one point three decibels. Co-polarized signals gave large K-factors, lower losses, and better stability. The authors present the chamber as a cost-efficient, repeatable tool for millimeter-wave testing.
arxiv-2505-08647:
Zhenbin Yang, Yuzhen Zhang, and Wenwen Zheng wrote a short physics paper in 2025 on a shape called the de Sitter double cone. The shape was first put forth by Saad, Shenker, and Stanford. The authors ask what changes when watchers in fixed patches of space are added.

With those watchers in place, the team finds a steady linear rise that fits the pattern seen in random matrix work. They trace the rise to a shift in time between two clocks set in patches on opposed sides. The note adds a clear case to ongoing work on how space, time, and chance may link.
arxiv-2505-08847:
Fatima Ezzeddine and co-authors weigh a three-way trade-off in cloud machine learning in two thousand twenty-five. Firms rent ready models as a service, which saves cost but opens a theft risk: rivals can copy the model by probing it. Added explanations, meant to build trust, can leak clues that ease the theft, above all counterfactual ones.

The team tests differential privacy, a noise-adding shield, as a counter. Two spots for the noise are compared: inside model training, and at the explainer when it crafts the counterfactuals. Scores track how prediction quality, privacy, and clarity of the explanations fare under each choice. The paper maps where the shield helps most.
arxiv-2505-09047:
Parth Arora and co-authors advise where to place a small display inside smart glasses in a 2025 paper. Waveguide lenses now make everyday glasses with a see through screen feasible, but the image can sit center gaze, where it interrupts, or off to the side.

Pooling recent studies on one eye displays, the team weigh interruption, comfort, task speed, and how odd wearers look to others. For text tasks they suggest a modest field of view in the right lens, level in height but shifted earward. Glanceable bits can sit farther out for short checks. The guide balances use against social ease.
arxiv-2505-09147:
Takashi Ito and Ryosuke Kadono introduce an extended relaxation function for muon spin studies of ion motion in this 2025 paper. The standard tool assumes field changes at a muon come only from ions moving around it, and that muons stay fixed to oxygen atoms. Both assumptions can fail in real materials.

Their extended function handles cases where only some nearby ions take part in each field change. It behaves in clearly different ways from the standard function. It can also tell whether the muon or the ions are the ones moving. Applying it to older data on a sodium cobalt oxide flips the earlier reading: the field changes there come mainly from muons diffusing themselves. The paper offers a firmer basis for reading such experiments.
arxiv-2505-09347:
Andrii Kuibarov and co-authors measure the superconducting gap on the surface of a crystal called t-PtBi2, in a 2025 physics paper. They use ARPES, a technique that knocks electrons out with light to map their energies. It is the leading tool for reading the order parameter of superconductors, but this crystal demands unusually strict conditions.

Earlier laser-based work found record-narrow signals and a gap on the surface Fermi arc. Here, synchrotron light measurements detect the same gap under looser conditions. A simple model of the spectra sets the minimum needs for spotting the gap. The authors also mark cases where the gap cannot be resolved at all.
arxiv-2505-10247:
Futoshi Minato, Yifei Niu, and Kenichi Yoshida hunt in 2025 for the nuclear traits that best predict beta decay energy, a value that sets how fast unstable nuclei decay. A sound theory of the nuclear glue must reproduce those energies across the chart of nuclei. The team asked which bulk traits track the decay energy most tightly.

Using forty-two versions of a standard nuclear model, they scored links between decay energy and many traits. The symmetry energy at low density stood out, above all for models whose effective mass sits near one. From the pattern they name the symmetry energy and mass values most likely to match measured decay energies.
arxiv-2505-10347:
Gabriel Gama and Valdir Grassi compare training schemes for multi-task learning in this two thousand twenty-five paper. When one model learns several tasks at once, the tasks can fight each other. Their gradients may clash or differ in size. Specialized optimizers were built to balance this fight. Recent critics claim plain equal weighting does just as well, if tuned with care. The authors set out to settle the dispute with broad tests.

They ran the latest specialized methods on harder multi-task problems than past studies used. The specialists did perform well against plain uniform loss. Yet fixed well-chosen weights also stayed competitive. The paper explains when uniform loss keeps pace and when it falls behind. Code is shared for others to check the claims.
arxiv-2505-10447:
Iván Angiono, César Galindo, and Giovanny Mora carry a twisting construction from category theory into the world of Hopf algebras in this 2025 mathematics paper. The construction, called zesting, deforms a structured category in a controlled way. Hopf algebras matter because their comodule categories are a main example of the categories in question.

The authors show that zesting the comodule category of a Hopf algebra yields a slightly loosened algebra, a coquasi-Hopf algebra, whose comodules are exactly the zested category. They write out the changed multiplication and the associator in full, including the braided case. For pointed Hopf algebras they give concrete formulas, and for gradings by cyclic groups a full parameterization of the zesting data. The work turns an abstract categorical recipe into algebra that can be computed with directly.
arxiv-2505-10547:
Milan Ganai and co-authors present, in 2025, a safety framework that lets robots plan their own fallbacks when the world surprises them. Foundation models hold broad knowledge, but turning it into fast, physically valid escape plans is hard. Their system reasons ahead of trouble rather than during it.

During calm operation, the system imagines failure modes and marks safe fallback zones using multimodal models. If a monitor spots danger, it quickly builds a plan to a fallback goal while steering around newly unsafe areas. Tests on synthetic scenes, a real quadruped robot's data, and a flying drone beat slow on-the-fly prompting in both safety and planning success.
arxiv-2505-10747:
Ziang Niu and Zhimei Ren build in 2025 statistical theory for two-stage adaptive experiments, where later sampling depends on early results. Such designs boost welfare and efficiency, but valid inference after adaptation lacked firm foundations. They derive weak limits for mean outcomes and their differences under far lighter assumptions than earlier work required for these designs.

The results cover a broad family of weighted estimators. Sharp phase transitions appear across signal regimes. They also give convergence rates that expose a trade-off between exploiting data and keeping inference stable. A simulation method supplies valid critical values when limits are not normal.
arxiv-2505-11047:
Arghya Mallick and co-authors design smart charging in 2025 for electric cars that sell power back to the grid. Selling power earns money but wears the battery, and drivers differ in how they weigh the two. The hard part is a battery wear model that is both accurate and easy to optimize with.

They train a special neural network, shaped to stay convex in charging rate, on large lab data sets. The model captures how heat and time age a battery while keeping the math of the second stage fast. That stage computes a charging plan per car along a trade-off curve set by the driver's preference. Simulations show accurate wear forecasts and sensible plans.
arxiv-2505-11447:
Gianmarco Del Sarto and Marta Lenzi prove that a three-dimensional model of heat and fluid flow, shaken by random noise at its boundary, has exactly one solution when it starts small. Their 2025 paper studies a Boussinesq-type system, where temperature drives motion through buoyancy. Noise enters through the walls as a fixed-temperature condition with a random twist.

The boundary forcing is rough, living in spaces too weak for classical tools. The pair work in a carefully chosen rough space that fits both the flow and the temperature. For small starting data they prove a single mild solution exists up to a stopping time. Better, the chance that the solution lasts the whole interval climbs toward one as the noise shrinks. The result steadies a model class used for heated, stirred fluids.
arxiv-2505-11647:
Zhen Han and co-authors present in 2025 the design of a beam source that makes very cold, slow molecules for a precision physics search. The experiment it serves hunts for a tiny electric property of the electron, using thorium monoxide molecules. In the source, a laser blasts material off a solid target inside a cold gas cell.

Targets wear out, and swapping them normally means warming the whole device and breaking its vacuum, which costs days. The new design adds a load lock so targets can be changed while the source stays cold and sealed. Its output matches older sources: about 130 billion molecules per pulse at a slow forward speed. Changing targets every two weeks through the lock raised the long-term yield by about forty percent.
arxiv-2505-11947:
Evolution sometimes braids lineages together instead of splitting them, and the family diagrams that result are networks, not trees. Takatora Suzuki and Momoko Hayamizu ask, in a 2025 paper, which of those networks are just a standard class with extra arcs added. The question extends a line of work that began with trees hidden inside networks.

The authors generalize a structure theorem so it covers support networks, not only support trees. That yields direct descriptions of all support networks, and of the minimal and smallest ones. Each description spawns best-possible algorithms to count and list them. One runs in linear time and finds the support network with the fewest braids, a number biologists read as the tier of the network.
arxiv-2505-12247:
Yinqiu Liu and co-authors tune networks that host AI agents to what users truly mean, not just what runs fast. Users state wishes in plain words, and old tuning methods miss that sense. Their 2025 system, LAMeTA, works in two stages with a large AI model at its core.

Stage one pours the big model's grasp of wishes into light models at the network edge. Stage two pairs those light models with a learning tuner. User wishes become score guides that shape both state and reward for the tuner. Tests on a net of eighty-one agents cut wish-reading error by up to a fifth. The paired tuner beat plain learning by a like margin on user-rated quality. The team sees intent as a first-class dial.
arxiv-2505-12347:
Chon-Fai Kam proposed in 2025 an optical way to realize a subtle geometric phase that appears at quantum phase transitions in interacting systems. Such non-integrable phases are hard to study directly in their original settings. His scheme uses the polarization of light traveling through a special low-birefringence fiber.

An exotic term in the governing equation, tied to the fiber's symmetry, drives the effect. By slowly tuning the fiber's nonlinear properties, the light's polarization vector accumulates a Hannay angle, a classical cousin of the quantum phase with the same geometric structure. He suggests building it by depositing nano-crystals along the fibers in a graded way. The setup is presented as experimentally feasible.
arxiv-2505-12647:
Jung Hoon Lee and Sujith Vijayan published a computing paper in 2025 on using spiking neural networks to authenticate wireless devices cheaply. Radio transmitters carry hardware fingerprints in their signals, and deep learning can read them. Standard networks, though, burn too much power for edge devices. Spiking networks sip energy by firing sparsely, making them a candidate platform.

Tests show these networks can indeed learn transmitter fingerprints and name devices correctly. They are not immune to attack: crafted perturbations fool them too. An autoencoder filter scrubbed the perturbations and hardened the system. The authors present spiking networks as a low-power route to physical layer security, with defenses built in.
arxiv-2505-12747:
Zepeng Liu and three co-authors study a temporal SU(1,1) interferometer fed with broadband squeezed light. Temporal optics can stretch ultrafast pulses without loss, while SU(1,1) interferometers sense phase changes with high sensitivity in space. Moving that design into the time domain opens control of non classical light in time and frequency.

The device rests on a temporal Fourier transform system with two temporal lenses. Output spectra depend on the ratio of the lens dispersion values, called the scaling factor, and on the phase derivative applied. The phase derivative shifts frequency linearly. Squeezing concentrates at the center frequency and at shifted positions, with more weight at the center as the scaling factor grows.
arxiv-2505-13147:
Aswathy Velutharambath, Kai Sassenberg, and Roman Klinger ask whether lies can be spotted from writing alone in a 2025 paper. Earlier studies claimed good success at catching deception in text. The authors suspect those results came from quirks in how the test data was gathered, not from real clues in the words.

They define deception as a gap between what a writer claims and what the writer truly believes. Using that frame, they built three new text sets in German and English under varied conditions. Across all three sets, the word cues praised in past work showed almost no link to lying. Other English data sets showed mixed results at best. The authors conclude that text alone gives weak ground for catching lies. Tools sold for that job should be read with strong caution.
arxiv-2505-13447:
Zhengyang Geng and co-authors present a 2025 paper on image generation in a single step. Most image makers refine a picture over many steps, which is slow. Their method rests on a fresh notion: the average speed of the flow that turns noise into an image, rather than its speed at each instant.

A clean identity links average and instant speeds, and that identity guides training. The model needs no pre-training, no teacher model, and no staged lessons. Trained from scratch on a standard image set, it scored well with just one evaluation step. The work narrows the gap between one-step and multi-step image makers.
arxiv-2505-13647:
Taherifar studies special ideals in rings in a 2025 algebra paper. For each element of a ring, one can form the overlap of all minimal prime ideals containing it. An ideal earns the name in the title when it contains that overlap for every one of its elements, a closure-like fairness condition.

The paper first develops these ideals for non-commutative rings, where multiplication order matters. It characterizes them in several matrix ring families and in semiprime rings. It then explores new properties of the lattice of annihilator ideals, which record what kills a given set. The results organize a corner of ring theory used to probe how ideals reflect a ring's prime structure.
arxiv-2505-13747:
Lei Zhu and three co-authors found in 2025 a way to run two-photon microscopy through scattering layers that normally blur it away. The method leans on the optical memory effect, a quirk where speckle patterns shift predictably with angle. By reading the grainy pattern's self-similarity and running a phase retrieval routine, they rebuilt pictures of glowing objects hidden behind scatterers. No wavefront shaping hardware was needed.

Two-photon imaging is prized for deep tissue work, so peering through scatter matters for biology. The authors report clear reconstructions where standard imaging fails. Their approach trades heavy optics for computation after capture. They see it extending the depth reach of a workhorse microscope. The study appears in an optics journal as a research article.
