Further tests in living tissue will show how far the trick carries.
arxiv-2505-13947:
When language models train on their own output, quality can spiral down, a failure called model collapse. Shirong Xu, Hengzhi He, and Guang Cheng study that process in 2025 through probability theory. They picture repeated training as a random walk: each round moves the model estimate by a step whose size depends on sample size and whose direction depends on the fitting method.

Under mild conditions, they prove the sample size must grow at each round to avoid collapse, faster than in direct proportion when the fitting is unbiased. Bias demands still faster growth. They also ask when training on synthetic data can beat real data alone, and test the theory in simulations and on a real dataset.
arxiv-2505-14047:
Jihye Hwang and a large team of co-authors map magnetic fields where stars form in twenty twenty-five. The target is a massive clump called P2 inside a dark filamentary cloud. Magnetic fields shape star formation from core to clump scales. The team measured field orientations and strengths across parsec and sub-parsec scales.

Observations came from a polarization camera on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope. The survey is BISTRO-3, the third round of a long-running program. Dust grains align with the local field, so their polarized light traces field direction. Comparing orientations across scales shows how the field twists as gas gathers. Readers get a field map of a region where massive stars are being born.
arxiv-2505-14147:
Xiong Jun Wu and co-authors forge hard quiz tasks to train smart text tools in a 2025 paper. Such tools learn by prize and blame, but the well of hard, fair, checkable tasks runs dry fast.

Their forge sets three rules: tasks at grad and games grade, logic that holds tight, and one clear mark that can be checked. A three-step build then breeds tasks by theme and depth. A top tool of the day drafts and vets the tasks. The trained tool then loops on the prize marks its tasks earn. On a hard test set the forge-trained tool beat the old ways by a clear span. The authors say good tasks, made on rule, lift smart tools near the grade of adepts.
arxiv-2505-14347:
Neelabh Sinha proposes a simple trick to make language models summarize long texts better: answer questions first. Models often miss key facts buried in the middle of long inputs because of positional bias. Fine-tuning or multi-step pipelines can help but add cost and complexity. QA-prompting instead asks the model targeted questions about the text, then writes the summary enriched by those answers, all in one call per task.

Across several data sets and ten leading pre-trained models, the method beat plain baselines and prior approaches, lifting standard summary scores by up to twenty-nine percent. The questions must fit the domain: choosing them well was part of the method's success. Sinha presents the technique as a cheap, scalable fix that needs no retraining. It suggests that part of summarization failure is a retrieval failure, which a few good questions can cure.
arxiv-2505-14547:
Krever and three co-authors built a framework for making realistic games to test game theory algorithms in twenty twenty-five. Algorithms for equilibria are usually tested on toy games, economic classics, or random matrices. Security games model patrols and protection. They are realistic, but their underlying data, most of all target values, are rarely public.

Their framework, GUARD, builds matrix and security games from open datasets. Animal movement data model anti-poaching patrols. Demographic and infrastructure data model facility protection. Users can tune payoffs and parameters. Ready-made instances are included. The authors prove limits of random-game benchmarking. They also compare their generated games with random ones across standard equilibrium solvers. These include linear programming and no-regret self-play. They argue realistic instances expose weaknesses that random benchmarks hide.
arxiv-2505-14747:
Fatemeh Chajaei and Hossein Bagheri test how well laser scans can build simple three-dimensional city models in a 2025 paper. Such models, called LOD1, show buildings as blocks with flat roofs. They serve urban planning, environmental studies, and transport design. The quality of the blocks rests on how well the building outlines are first picked out of the scan data.

The team trained four deep segmentation models, all variants of the U-Net family plus one rival, to extract building footprints from LiDAR data using transfer learning. Two models led the pack on overlap scores. Heights were then estimated from the scan points with several summary statistics, from the median to a high percentile, and blocks were built from each. The study shows how much the first segmentation step governs the final model and the shape measures drawn from it.
arxiv-2505-14947: Tianhong Zhao derives a trace formula for finite matrix families in a 2025 math paper. Starting from von Neumann's ergodic theorem, which describes long-run averages of a system's states, Zhao takes its trace. The outcome extends the classic Poisson summation formula to higher dimensions. The paper also builds a family of crystalline measures with complex weights, objects that sit at the meeting point of harmony analysis and number theory.
arxiv-2505-15447:
Ziqiang Xu and seven co-authors present ViaRL, a frame that teaches video models to pick the frames that matter. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that human viewing is goal-led: we scan for what our task needs. Video chain-of-thought systems lack a direct signal for that pick. Heuristic rules and fake labels fill the gap at high cost and low reach.

ViaRL trains a frame picker by rule-based reinforcement learning. The reward is the final answer's accuracy from a partner model. No hand labels are needed. An iterated loop refines picker and answerer in turns. Tests on VideoMME, LVBench, and MLVU show steady gains in time grounding. One needle-in-haystack task jumped by a wide margin. The method scales across tasks with no costly annotation.
arxiv-2505-15647:
Youming Tao and co-authors present a 2025 method for training models on private data while still finding good low points. The task is to reach a flat low point of a rough loss curve, not just a steep slope point, while keeping each person's data private. Past methods had loose error bounds and needed extra private steps to pick a final model.

The new frame adds small random shakes to a standard descent method and tracks how far the model drifts. That drift tells the method when it has left a saddle point, with no need for curve shape data or extra checks. A sharp guess tool for slopes gives fixed error rates. The team also gives the first such proof for split learning with mixed data.
arxiv-2505-16047:
Peter Norwood and co-authors design a new adaptive randomization scheme for a long-running breast cancer trial, published in 2025. The I-SPY2 trial tests new drugs given before surgery for locally advanced disease. It was recently reshaped as a sequential trial with up to three stages of therapy, matched to tumor subtype.

In this design, a patient who does not respond moves to a second therapy, then to a rescue therapy if needed. So the trial judges whole treatment regimes, not single drugs. The new scheme updates assignment odds at each stage, based on the chance that a treatment belongs to the best regime. Test studies show it raises complete response rates within the trial, while picking the best regimes at rates like plain random assignment.
arxiv-2505-16647:
Sushant Gautam, Michael Riegler, and Pål Halvorsen fine-tune a vision-language model to point at, detect, and count findings in medical images, in a 2025 paper. Clinicians do all three at once when they read a scan, but models are usually trained for one task at a time. The team recast each task as written instructions for the model.

Training used a dataset spanning endoscopy images of polyps and tools, plus microscope images of sperm cells. Mixing tasks during tuning made the model steadier and cut counting errors, the team reports. Some edge cases got worse, with more missed points on empty images. The authors argue instruction-tuned general models can learn combined clinical reading patterns, while noting those weak spots need care.
arxiv-2505-16947:
Dékány and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on training chat models to resist trick prompts. Attackers can still force top models to produce harmful text. Training against attacks helps, but real attack prompts are costly to build at scale. Faster training uses smooth fake attacks, yet those miss some real weak spots. Their method mixes strong real attacks with fast smooth ones in one training run. They also coin a score for worst-case weakness across attacks.

Their mixed training cut worst-case attack success to under one in five. Prior defenses left success above one in two in their tests. Run time stayed close to the fast smooth methods. They also probe how chat formats and size cuts shift the results. The authors offer a safer path for model builders.
arxiv-2505-17547:
Chuhan Lei and Xiaoqin Zhan classify symmetric designs whose blocks can be shuffled by a highly transitive group. The objects are 2-(v,5,lambda) designs, arrangements where each pair of points sits in exactly lambda blocks of five. The question is which such designs admit a block-transitive automorphism group, split by how the group acts on points.

When the group is point-imprimitive, the count v must be sixteen, twenty-one, or eighty-one, and the authors classify every design for the first two values completely. When the group is point-primitive, it must be of affine, almost simple, or product type. The product case gets its own full classification of design and group pairs. Their 2025 paper continues the long program of using group theory to fence in which symmetric designs can exist.
arxiv-2505-18147:
Wojciech Stark, Connor Box, Matthias Sachs, Nils Hertl, and Reinhard Maurer simulate hydrogen molecules striking copper surfaces, facet by facet, to settle how much electrons matter in the chemistry. When hydrogen splits on a metal, some energy can leak into the metal's electrons, and whether that leak changes the outcome has been hard to test.

The team trained learning models to reproduce both the energy landscape and the electronic drag across four copper faces, then ran quantum-resolved scattering simulations. The predicted sticking and survival rates matched experiments closely. Turning the electronic drag on or off barely moved the results: the shape of the energy landscape and the molecule's starting vibration ruled instead. The models are released as the most accurate public set for this benchmark system.
arxiv-2505-18347:
Mohamed Mohamed and colleagues turn a browser game about growing cells into a testbed for agents that must keep learning forever. Continual reinforcement learning studies agents whose world keeps changing, so no fixed policy stays good. Existing setups mostly fake the change by swapping tasks between episodes, or offer worlds too small to be interesting. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team adapts the game Agar.io, where a cell eats, grows, and risks being eaten in an endless, partly hidden, ever-shifting arena. Their platform supports both one long open-ended challenge and smaller tasks that isolate single skills.

Standard algorithms were benchmarked on the main challenge and the side tasks, and three continual learning methods were evaluated as well. The suite separates which ingredients of the game, such as partial sight or sudden threats, break which learners. The platform is offered as shared infrastructure for the field.
arxiv-2505-18447:
Chi Zhang, Ziying Jia, George Atia, Sihong He, and Yue Wang built a transfer learning framework for reinforcement learning in two thousand twenty-five. Transfer aims to solve a new task with little data by borrowing from related tasks. Transferred policies can act badly, and poor sources can hurt rather than help.

Their framework rests on pessimism: it builds and optimizes a conservative estimate of performance in the target setting. That gives an optimized lower bound, which supports safe decisions. Performance also improves steadily as source quality rises, avoiding negative transfer. They build two kinds of conservative estimates, prove their value, and give distributed algorithms with convergence guarantees.
arxiv-2505-18547:
Image generators are often fine-tuned to please one reward, like beauty or text match. Real users juggle several wishes at once, and each person weights them differently. Min Cheng and co-authors tackle that problem at generation time, with no extra training per user. Their method, Diffusion Blend, mixes the generation paths of models tuned for single goals.

By blending those paths, the system can serve any weighted mix of rewards a user names. A second variant lets users dial how far outputs may drift from the base model. Across experiments in 2025, the blends beat rival methods and nearly matched models trained for one exact mix each.
arxiv-2505-18647:
Kiet Bennema ten Brinke, Koen Minartz, and Vlado Menkovski present STFlow, a generative model for simulating trajectories, in a 2025 paper. The head title is fuller than the catalog title. Paths of many body systems are sensitive to small nudges and hold patterns at many scales, which makes them hard to simulate from data.

The model joins graph networks with layered convolutions inside a flow matching frame. Instead of starting from plain noise, it starts from data coupled random walks, which lowers the work to reach real paths. That informed start speeds training and sampling. On many body, molecular, and human path tests it gave the lowest errors with fewer steps and better scaling.
arxiv-2505-18747:
Xiaolu Chen and co-authors solve a metering puzzle created by rooftop solar panels. A household meter sees only the net flow, generation minus use, so utilities cannot tell how much solar power a home actually produced. Splitting the two matters for planning and billing. Earlier methods struggled to extract clean patterns from the net signal and to connect them with the weather that drives sunshine.

The proposed method attacks both problems. A hierarchical interpolation technique pulls features out of the net load at several time scales, while a multi-head attention mechanism learns how weather factors relate to each other and to the signal. The design aims to work in any season, not just the one it trained on. Tests on real-world data show accurate recovery of the hidden solar generation, which the authors offer as support for smarter monitoring of distributed energy.
arxiv-2505-18947:
Zhenhao Zhang and co-authors generate hand and object scenes in a 2025 computer vision paper. Realistic hand action matters for virtual worlds and dexterous robots. Older methods cope with known objects and set tasks but fail on new objects or free form commands. Their system, OpenHOI, claims a first for open world synthesis, building long manipulation runs for novel objects from plain language.

A three dimensional multimodal model, tuned for the job, finds where on an object a hand should act, like handles and buttons. It also breaks a command into steps. Joining grounding and planning in one model may let virtual hands handle the long tail of daily objects, not just a training set.
arxiv-2505-19047:
Selcuk Topal builds a classification of security flaws in a new kind of smart contract in a 2025 paper. The contracts are written in the Move language but run on Ethereum style machines. Move was designed to block common flaws through strict ownership rules. Mixing it with the older machine, though, creates hybrid flaws that existing registries do not cover.

The new system lists dozens of categorized weakness types across six frames. Examples include hybrid gas metering, misuse of capability tokens, spoofed meta transactions, and flaws in AI linked logic. Checks of real contracts on two networks showed that current verification tools often miss these hybrid risks. The author also sketches how formal methods and language model audit agents could apply the classification. The goal is safer, more checkable contracts for next generation blockchains.
arxiv-2505-19247:
Tao Wang, Ruipeng Zhang, and Sicun Gao question a common belief about how to train AI by trial and reward, in a 2025 paper. Prize methods like PPO beat the plain policy gradient method on many tasks, and credit is usually given to their trust regions, guardrails that keep each update small. The team suspect the real edge lies elsewhere.

PPO-style methods also update their value estimates, their guesses of future reward, many more times per round. When the authors give the plain method the same extra value updates, it matches or beats PPO on all standard control test tasks. The boosted plain method also shrugs off knob settings that break the fancier methods. The lesson is plain: better value guesses, not guardrails, may drive most of the gain.
arxiv-2505-19347:
Yongmin Yoo, Qiongkai Xu, and Longbing Cao build PatentMind, a frame that judges how alike two patents are, by a graph of thought across many sides. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Patent likeness is key to work on who owns what. Past ways miss the rich build of a patent, which joins tech traits, legal bounds, and use fields. PatentMind splits each patent into those three sides and scores each side on its graph. The scores are then weighed by a step that reads the case's cues, in the way an expert would. The team built a test set of five hundred pairs, marked by people. Their scores tracked expert marks with high accord.
arxiv-2505-19647:
Xiaochuan Liu, Ruihua Song, Xiting Wang, and Xu Chen present a 2025 system that drafts the related work section of a research paper using three cooperating AI agents. Older tools read only abstracts or short parts of the cited papers, so their summaries stay shallow and treat each paper alone. The new system works from full texts. One agent picks which section to read next, a second reads it and updates a shared memory, and a third writes the section from that memory.

Two added strategies use the citation graph to plan the reading order, so links among papers shape the draft. Tests across three base models and several input setups showed steady gains. The graph-guided versions beat other selection methods and set the best scores reported for the task.
arxiv-2505-19747:
Ligong Bian and a large team of colleagues reviewed gravitational wave cosmology in a 2025 paper, surveying their research program's recent advances. Ripples from the early universe carry direct news about primordial physics, the nature of gravity, and cosmic expansion, unfiltered by the electromagnetic fog that limits telescopes. The review organizes that promise around the stochastic backgrounds, the faint hums left by ancient processes.

Inflation, phase transitions, and topological defects each leave a characteristic background, and the authors summarize what pulsar timing arrays and planned space detectors can already say, and may soon say, about each. Primordial black holes as wave sources and possible dark matter follow, then the imprint of large-scale structure on passing waves.
arxiv-2505-19847:
Wenqing Zhou, Yuxuan Yan, and Qianqian Yang spread question answering across edge devices and the cloud without pooling raw data, in work from twenty twenty-five. Standard retrieval systems gather all documents in one place, which risks privacy and adds delay and cost. Their frame keeps each edge device's data local.

Each device turns its documents into a knowledge graph and sends only summaries to the cloud for indexing. A query is first answered on the device itself. A gate checks trust and agreement across local answers to decide if the cloud must step in. For hard queries, the cloud matches summaries, pulls proof from the right devices, and writes the final answer. Tests beat spread out baselines with less cloud load.
arxiv-2505-20047:
Ganguly and co-authors ask when to trust chat tools in proof-based task work. Chat tools can draft proof specs and open such work to more hands. Yet tools run on odds, while proof needs firm vows of truth. That clash is the core strain the work probes in full. Five top chat tools took a set test of proof drafts. SMT-based drafts swayed truth by field in the test runs.

Logic tasks gained 34.8 percent, while fact tasks lost 44.5 percent. Stock doubt marks, like word odds spread, missed those flaws. A chance grammar frame, PCFG, models tool outs in the work. That frame gives a more fine doubt sort for the outs. Doubt marks prove task-tied: grammar spread fits logic best. A light fuse of marks lets pick checks cut flaws a lot.
arxiv-2505-20647:
Ian Langmore, writing alone in 2025, expands the energy distance into moments. The energy distance tests whether two distributions are equal and serves as a loss function in machine learning. It is zero only when the distributions match, but how strongly it reacts to different kinds of mismatch matters in practice.

For distributions that are close, Langmore shows the distance reacts more to differences in means than in covariances, for structural reasons independent of dimension. He also examines how sensitivity splits between diagonal and off-diagonal covariance parts near isotropy. The expansion tells practitioners which discrepancies their test will catch and which it may miss.
arxiv-2505-20847:
Robots and other moving machines need a hard promise that they will not collide, and control barrier functions supply that promise in math form. Zeming Wu and Lu Liu extend the method to ellipsoid-shaped bodies in a 2025 paper. Ellipsoids, stretched spheres, fit many real objects better than plain spheres do, but the safety conditions were missing for them.

The authors derive collision-free conditions for general ellipsoids using a tool called dual cones. They fold those conditions into the barrier framework by letting a separating plane between two bodies move as part of the system state. Proofs back the construction. Because the method needs only one level of optimization, it runs faster than leading rivals. Simulations and real-world experiments show the avoidance working in practice.
arxiv-2505-21247:
Konstantin Karandashev makes kernel ridge learning on molecule shape ensembles fast and cheap, in a paper from 2025. Molecules flex into many shapes, and sound learning should weigh the full warm ensemble, not one frozen pose.

His rewrite uses structured random features to turn the kernel sums into trig style nets with a physics bent. Cheap force field poses fed the training. On battery linked test sets, error fell in a steady way as training grew, and a few hundred molecules reached lab grade truth. Fresh loss forms eased tuning of the method.
arxiv-2505-21547:
Wang and six co-authors trace why vision-language models sometimes name objects that are not in the picture. Their hunch blames training habits: certain image tokens often appear together, so the model expects the whole group. They built a co-occurrence graph of image tokens from a labeled dataset to test the idea.

The tests supported the hunch. Made-up objects matched token clusters that dominated an image, and absent tokens in those clusters matched the false objects closely. Their fix edits the model's inner image representation during writing to mute absent tokens. Hallucinations dropped while the models kept their descriptive range. Code is available online.
arxiv-2505-22047:
Claus Metzner, Achim Schilling, Andreas Maier, and Patrick Krauss ask how biology-style wiring changes artificial neural networks in this two thousand twenty-five paper. A recurrent network can oscillate, run chaotic, or settle to fixed points, known to rest on the stats of its link weights. Brains have weights with order, though how such order steers dynamics was not clear. The team built weight matrices where three orders can be dialed up gradually.

The kinds are Dale's principle, where each neuron's outputs share one sign, and reciprocal symmetry, as in Hopfield networks. A third is modular structure: blocks with strong links in a weak background. Tuning each while they watched dynamical signs and reservoir marks gave verdicts. Dale monopolarity and modularity made marks better. Hopfield reciprocity hurt, driving early saturation and capping how the reservoir can bend. The upshots hint which biology design rules are to copy.
arxiv-2505-22347: Gleb Koshevoy and Vadim Schechtman, with an appendix by Daria Poliakova, present a short 2025 paper on joining rules built from a family of ranked orders. The orders rank the ways items can be sorted, step by step. Joining rules, called operads, say how small acts combine into larger ones. The pair describe some flat joining rules made from the higher forms of those orders, and show the rules carry a way to multiply their parts. The abstract is one line, so no cases or proofs are set out.
arxiv-2505-22547:
The T2K Collaboration reports a 2025 physics measurement on how neutrinos interact with oxygen. When a neutrino strikes a nucleus and knocks out nucleons without making a pion, stray neutrons can fly out. Counting those neutrons, through their later capture, tests the physics of the interaction.

Earlier work had not measured this neutron capture multiplicity for neutral-current, quasi-elastic-like events on oxygen. T2K used its accelerator-made neutrino beam and near detectors to do it for the first time. The result pins down how often one, two, or more neutrons follow such an event. That matters for experiments that hunt neutrinos from supernovae and for background estimates in proton decay searches. The paper adds a calibration point for nuclear models of neutrino scattering.
arxiv-2505-22647:
Zhe Kong and co-authors tackle in a 2025 framework the making of videos where several people talk, each driven by their own voice track. Older tools animate one person well but tangle who says what when voices mix. Their system, called MultiTalk, binds each voice to the right face.

A new position code, tuned by labels, solves the binding. Careful training choices kept the base model's skill at following prompts. Across head, body, and group test sets the system beat rivals. Such tools could ease dubbing, virtual hosts, and group scenes made from sound alone.
arxiv-2505-22747:
Shweta Sharma, Abhishek Sharma, and Abhinendra Singh study why thick particle suspensions suddenly resist flow. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Cornstarch in water is the classic case: stir it gently and it flows, push hard and it locks up. The lock-up is tied to grains touching and forming a network of force chains.

The team simulated networks built from sliding friction alone, then added resistance to rolling between grains. With sliding alone, chains needed side support from other chains to stay stable. With rolling resistance, chains grew longer and straighter and stood on their own. That also lowered the grain share at which the mix jams. The picture matters for real suspensions with rough or faceted grains, from cement to food pastes.
arxiv-2505-23047:
John Ball leads a team measuring fusion output from a spinning mirror plasma device for the first time. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. The Centrifugal Mirror Fusion Experiment sits at the University of Maryland. A central cathode sets up a radial electric field. Plasma then shears in a fast circular flow. That shear should improve confinement and calm instability.

Fusion yield is read from neutron emission. Two liquid scintillator detectors give the total count, calibrated by simulation. A larger detector tracks how the fusion rate changes over time. A helium gas tube detector, fixed in place, adds an independent check. Runs under varied conditions show how yield responds. The measurements ground hopes for this compact fusion concept.
arxiv-2505-23147:
Anke Fischer-Janzen, Thomas Wendt, Daniel Görlich, and Kristof Van Laerhoven explore eye control for robot arms, in a 2025 paper. For people with limited movement, gaze offers a natural way to steer a helper arm. Their design shares control between the user and the machine, so the arm helps finish tasks. Judging such designs early is hard, since full systems take long to build.

The team faked the automation with a hidden human operator, a Wizard of Oz setup. This let users try the design before any real build existed. One study surveyed people with disabilities, and a second ran the setup in person. Together they show what users expect, where the design strains, and how to make it easier to use.
arxiv-2505-23547:
Samsonov and co-authors study how X-rays scatter off films of smectic liquid crystals, layered materials that float freely as thin sheets. Such films act like organic Bragg mirrors with almost perfectly smooth layers, yet their diffraction peaks lack the shape that strong scattering theory predicts. Instead the simpler weak scattering picture fits, which is odd for a mirror thousands of layers thick. Their 2025 paper asks where the crossover between the two regimes lies.

Using synchrotron light on a real sample, the team analyzes the same reflections with both theories side by side. From that comparison they derive a concrete test for when scattering stops being weak and turns dynamical. The test explains why even very thick smectic films behave as if scattering were weak. The result gives makers of layered optical materials a rule for predicting which theory to trust.
arxiv-2505-23847:
Ronny Ko and colleagues map the security agenda for language model agents that cooperate across organizational borders. Joint disaster response and supply chains tempt firms to link their agents without surrendering data ownership. Cross-domain teamwork shatters the single trust zone that alignment techniques assume. A well-behaved agent can leak secrets or break policy purely from an untrusted peer's messages.

The position paper names seven categories of novel security challenge. Each comes with plausible attacks, candidate evaluation metrics, and research guidelines. The risks spring from emergent multi-agent dynamics, not classic software bugs. Containment built for one model in one house does not transfer. The authors aim to set the field's agenda before deployment outruns defense. Their taxonomy gives security teams a shared map of where cross-domain agents can be turned.
arxiv-2505-23947:
Müller and four co-authors argue in twenty twenty-five that a new kind of pre-trained net is the future of forecast work. These nets learn by training on huge sets of fake data made from a prior hunch. Once trained, they can act like a full Bayes model on fresh, small data sets.

The authors say this fits a world where compute power grows fast but fresh real data grows slow. Work that once fit tiny tasks now fits larger and harder ones. They map where the method could go and what holds it back now. They urge more work on these nets and kin tools.
arxiv-2505-24047:
Tanish Baranwal, Srihari Varada, Santanu Das, and Mohammad Haider designed a fault-tolerant sensor network in 2025 that leans on software copies of its own devices. High-reliability systems cannot go blind when one sensor dies. Their design triples the internet-of-things devices and fuses their readings at a central block.

Each physical sensor also gets a digital twin, a software model that duplicates its function. When a device faults, its twin stands in for a while inside the triple structure, until the hardware is repaired or replaced. The stand-in keeps the redundancy honest without buying a fourth device. Cost rises only slightly, the team argues, since the spare is code. Readers get a redundancy scheme where software watches the watchers, aimed at systems that must not fail quietly.
arxiv-2505-24147:
Chiwei Zhu and six co-authors test whether taught reasoning trails truly help a language model, or can harm it. Many past works say such trails lift scores, and the claim is now stock. Their 2025 study grades trails on two axes at once: end score, and reliability, how sound the acts of the model stay. The pair view gives a fresh split from past readings.

At times trails cut the score they were meant to lift. At times they raised reliability past even the raw model with no trails. Score shift and reliability shift moved in line, and both were driven by how hard the task is. Easy tasks and hard tasks pulled the pair in split ways. The team draws rules for when to use trails, and flags care in how human thought is baked into models.
arxiv-2505-24847:
Yiming Wang and five co-authors analyze a tug-of-war between two electronic orders in iron-based superconductors, in a 2025 paper. One order, called nematic, breaks the crystal's fourfold symmetry by picking a direction. The other keeps the symmetry while ordering charge. Where the two meet, theory expects surprises.

The authors study how fluctuations of one order behave inside the other. At the sharp border between the phases, a hidden continuous symmetry emerges, linking the two orders like components of one arrow. That symmetry forces a soft, wave-like excitation and softens others nearby. The picture mirrors a classic spin model, and the team cites experimental signs in its favor. Emergent symmetry may be a general trick of competing quantum orders.
arxiv-2506-00047:
Jan Göpfert, Jann Weinand, Patrick Kuckertz, Noah Pflugradt, and Jochen Linßen wrote this perspective piece in two thousand twenty-five. It warns of the risks that come as AI agents take over more of product development, and sketches ways to blunt them.

Machine-made design promises faster, better goods, but trust in non-human hands brings fresh hazards. The authors set out principles for safer work, stressing human oversight, clear accountability, and designs that can be explained. They sort risks into technical ones, which hurt the product, and social ones, which hurt the wider world. The field is young, they note, so the time to set norms and rules is now, without stalling the gains.
arxiv-2506-00447:
Mehedi Ahamed and co-authors test few shot learning for Bangla handwriting in a 2025 study. Few shot methods learn to read new classes from just a handful of examples. Bangla script is intricate, and labeled data for it is scarce. The team reasoned that a method that masters Bangla should transfer well to simpler scripts. They also built a new model for the task.

Their model, SynergiProtoNet, blends strong clustering with a rich feature extractor inside a prototype based learner. It reads features at both fine and broad levels. The team benchmarked it against five known few shot methods. Tests covered single data sets, transfers across data sets, transfers across languages, and digit only splits. Their model won across the board, the authors report, setting a new mark for this task.
arxiv-2506-00547:
Jonathan Hill proves a symmetrization result for high-dimensional dependent data in a 2025 paper. Symmetrization is a classic trick in statistics: it swaps a hard average for a signed version that is easier to bound. The classic form needs independent data and a ghost copy of the sample. Modern data often breaks both comforts, with far more variables than observations and strong links across time.

Hill's version works for dependent series in that harsh regime. Random sign flips are applied block by block, which respects the time structure, and a remainder term rests on Gaussian approximations that he then verifies under standard dependence conditions. Classic symmetrization falls out as a special case. As a payoff, he derives a maximal moment bound of the kind used to control the largest average across many variables at once.
arxiv-2506-00747:
When one particle in a scattering event goes soft, carrying almost no energy, the whole amplitude simplifies in predictable ways, called soft theorems. Kang Zhou derives those rules for three classic theories using a new tool: the 2-split, a special way amplitudes factorize on chosen slices of the kinematic space. The method leans only on how amplitudes break apart, both at ordinary poles and at these new split points.

Zhou recovers the known leading and next-to-leading soft rules for a scalar theory and for Yang-Mills theory, plus double-soft rules for the nonlinear sigma model. Higher-order rules take a universal form in reduced kinematic spaces. Two bonuses appear: the Yang-Mills and sigma model rules swap into each other by a simple replacement of variables, and the split currents obey their own tidy soft theorems. All results respect momentum conservation in physical content.
arxiv-2506-01147:
Prerak Srivastava, Giulio Corallo, and Sergey Rybalko build a compact parser that turns raw machine logs into clean templates, in a paper from 2025. Software logs pile up by the billion, and analysts first compress them into patterns that separate fixed text from changing values. Parsers that miss fine detail blur those patterns and weaken every later diagnosis.

Their parser reads logs one character at a time with a small neural network. It predicts a sequence of compact binary coded numbers that mark the template structure with high precision. On a revised public benchmark and a hand labeled industry data set, it matched the accuracy of parsers built on large language models. It beat meaning based parsers on speed and cost, which matters at log scale.
arxiv-2506-01247:
The authors study whether sparse features can steer vision language models in a 2025 paper. Sparse autoencoders are often used to interpret such models after the fact. The team ask whether the same features can actively improve image classification without labels, by nudging a frozen model at test time.

Their method trains a sparse autoencoder on unlabeled image features, then boosts each input active features to build a steering shift. A reliability gate falls back to the base model when reconstruction is poor. Across nine data sets, zero shot accuracy rose by up to several points with tiny extra compute.
arxiv-2506-01347:
Zhu and co-authors report a counterintuitive training result: teaching language models only by penalizing wrong answers can beat standard reinforcement learning, in a 2025 paper. They split the learning signal for math reasoning into reward for correct answers and punishment for incorrect ones, then trained several models with each part alone.

Punishment-only training improved accuracy across the whole range of sampling budgets, often matching or beating the full methods. Reward-only training raised first-try accuracy but narrowed the model's diversity and hurt later attempts. Analysis shows punishment works by suppressing wrong paths and shifting probability toward other plausible ones the model already favors. A reweighted objective improves results further.
arxiv-2506-01647:
Fürst presents a 2025 mathematics paper on trace formulas for Callias-type operators, a Dirac-style family over odd-dimensional space. Classic results need the potential to settle outside a core region, making the operator Fredholm. Fürst drops that demand, letting the potential take values in unbounded operators and misbehave at infinity. The operator then escapes the Fredholm world entirely.

A trace formula still survives, now written with higher order spectral shift functions. A tidy functional equation ties the pieces together, widening one found earlier by Pushnitski. Under a mild pointwise condition, a regularized index exists even here. The work claims the first multi-dimensional non-Fredholm extension of the Callias index story.
arxiv-2506-02047:
Goods such as livestock move through trade webs across the globe, but records of those moves are sparse and patchy. Farokhnejad and co-authors borrow tools from the study of human travel to fill the gaps. Their 2025 work notes that the standard chart for moves, a table of starts and ends, says nothing about places that never show up in the data.

Their fix treats flow as a field of arrows spread over the map, so each place gets a sense of which way goods lean and how strongly. That view can span scales, from local to global, where the table view leaves blank zones. Full logs of each load are costly and can clash with data rules, so a model that infers flow from thin data has clear worth. The study sets out the frame and its tests.
arxiv-2506-02147:
Joshua Rozner, Leonie Weissweiler, and Cory Shain test if small language models trained on child-scale data learn grammatical constructions. Construction grammar holds that learners gain form-meaning pairs from the stats of their world. Past work showed trained models are sensitive to constructions. But those models used amounts of data no child could meet. That cast doubt on their link to human learning.

The team uses causal probing on masked language models from the 2024 BabyLM Challenge. That challenge limits training data to amounts a child might meet. Even so, the models learn varied constructions. They include hard cases that look much alike on the surface. The team also finds linked proof that knowledge of constructions matters in use. Models that depict constructions better score better on the BabyLM benchmarks.
arxiv-2506-02647:
Niklas Baumgarten and David Schneiderhan wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It finds the best control for systems ruled by partial differential equations when the inputs are not known for sure, with a multilevel gradient method.

The twist is the gradient source: a parallel multilevel Monte Carlo scheme stands in for the true gradient. That gives tight rein over both the bias from coarse grids and the noise from sampling. Resources go where they pay most. The method homes in at a linear rate, yet never pays for the full gradient at top fidelity. On a two-dimensional case of flow through soil with wild coefficients, it beats plain batched descent on speed and accuracy both. Step rules and budget plans are weighed too.
arxiv-2506-02947:
Tarek Emmrich and Stefan Kunis extend a classic theorem in their 2025 paper. Chebotarëv's theorem says that every minor of a Fourier matrix of prime size is nonzero. A minor is the determinant of a square chunk of the matrix, and the claim has been found and proved anew several times over the years.

Following one known proof, the authors build two new versions. One works over the real numbers, and one over finite fields, where arithmetic wraps around a prime count. For the finite case they drop a side condition and lower the needed bound from earlier work. The results apply to a phase retrieval problem and to building wave-like bases.
arxiv-2506-03047: Zhiyi Chi works out how hard it is to simulate exactly the moment a stable random climber first crosses a falling barrier, in a 2025 paper. He reduces the sampling task to drawing from a two-variable distribution set by the climber's index and one barrier-free number. Three acceptance-rejection algorithms then cover the parameter plane, none needing numerical inversion or integration. Together they sample exactly, with cost growing only mildly as the index nears one. The paper gives the simulation a firm complexity footing.
arxiv-2506-03347:
Paul Zivich and Haidong Lu adapt a causal method to tricky selection bias in a 2025 paper. G-computation estimates effects by modeling outcomes, and it can be reshaped for many biases. Two hard cases anchor the paper: selection caused by the treatment itself, and paired biases that share no single adjustment set.

For each case the authors build the estimator, show how to code it, and test it in simulations. Writing the estimators as stacked equations keeps theory and practice tidy. Readers get a worked guide from causal diagrams to working code.
arxiv-2506-03447:
An isolated quantum system never truly settles, yet its measurable quantities often look settled after a while. Marcos Alpino and co-authors asked in 2025 whether a measure of complexity can track that drift toward balance.

They built a measure from the spread of a chosen quantity and its distance from the balanced value. In simulations of a spin chain, the measure rose and fell with the drift toward balance. It also flagged tame, repeating motion in states that explore only a small corner of their space. The authors suggest complexity can help explain how steady behavior, and even classical-like order, grows out of quantum rules.
arxiv-2506-03547:
Giulia Macario and a team of co-authors measured how cleanly a prototype radio telescope station separates the two polarizations of radio waves, in this 2025 paper. The station belongs to the test program for SKA-Low, the low-frequency half of the Square Kilometre Array rising in Western Australia. The telescope will scan the sky at low frequencies with extreme sensitivity, which demands that signals of one polarization not leak into the other.

Using a figure of merit called the intrinsic cross-polarization ratio, the team mapped leakage across the whole sky from real observations with the prototype station. They produced maps at three frequencies inside the telescope's band and compared them with simulations. The measured patterns matched the simulated ones well, and the radial profiles met the project's specification overall. The study is an early, evidence-based check that the giant array's polarization performance is on track.
arxiv-2506-03647:
Weiwei Luo and co-authors reported edge waves in 2025 at boundaries inside a correlated oxide film. Such oxides are usually poor metals whose losses kill the light-confining effects seen in noble metals or graphene. Yet boundaries between their metal and insulator regions may behave differently.

Using infrared near-field microscopy on a nickelate film, the team found strongly confined, long-travelling edge waves of mixed sound-like and charge character. Simulations showed the wave's nature depends on edge sharpness: sharp edges host a one-dimensional edge state, while broad boundaries act through a near-zero permittivity absorption. The findings stress nonlocal effects in imaging such split-phase materials and open an infrared route for this material family.
arxiv-2506-03747:
Yingjie Shi and twelve co-authors present a 2025 optics paper on imaging objects hidden around a corner. The method, called non-line-of-sight imaging, rebuilds the shape and depth of hidden things from light signals timed to trillionths of a second. Real tests need costly gear and careful setup, which slows the field down.

The team offers a faster way to fake the data. Their tool models how light intensity moves through a scene instead of tracing each ray, and every part of the scene can be set by the user. Images rebuilt from the fake data matched the hidden shapes well. The paper also shares an open benchmark data set for other groups.
arxiv-2506-03847:
Hugo Alcaraz-Herrera and co-authors evolve the shapes and controllers of soft medical actuators together, in work from 2025. Soft robots bend and squeeze through tight spaces better than rigid ones, which suits drug delivery devices. Their materials behave nonlinearly, so human design is hard and may be biased.

Their method encodes shapes and controllers as pattern-producing networks and evolves them with a cooperative scheme. Subpopulations evolve separately and are tested in collaborations, under four partner-selection rules. A standard optimisation method served as the baseline. Judging used upward bending reach and robustness of each shape across many controllers. The cooperative approach produced more suitable device shapes than the baseline. The authors argue evolved designs can beat human intuition for soft devices.
arxiv-2506-03947:
Tabeart, Gürol, Pearson, and Weaver wrote a numerical methods paper in twenty twenty-five on faster ways to solve the huge linear systems inside weather data assimilation. Those systems lean on covariance matrices, which describe how errors in one place relate to errors elsewhere.

A newer all-at-once layout spreads the work across many processors, but it needs a strong preconditioner, a helper that makes the solver converge in fewer steps. The best-known helper only works when a key matrix can be split by a Fourier transform, which often fails in practice. The authors give two workarounds. One uses a classic polynomial iteration with new error bounds; the other rewrites the problem in a real-valued saddle point form. Tests show both can match the best case when computing power is ample. A tuned version also holds up on a tight budget.
arxiv-2506-04147:
Robots with arms on moving bases have many joints to control, and learning that control directly in the real world is slow and risky. Jiaheng Hu and co-authors present SLAC in this 2025 paper, which first practices in a cheap simulator to learn a compact set of reusable moves.

That move set then becomes the control interface for learning real tasks through trial and error. The practice phase is tuned to favor moves that are safe, distinct, and stretched over time. On two-armed mobile manipulation tasks, the method beat rivals and learned contact-heavy whole-body skills in under an hour of real practice, with no demonstrations.
arxiv-2506-04347:
Chloe Taylor, Daniel Wilkins, and Steven Allen locate the source of a rhythmic X-ray flicker in a distant galaxy's core, in a 2025 paper. The galaxy hosts one of the few known quasi-periodic oscillations, a near-hourly pulse in its X-ray glow. Candidates for the metronome were the hot corona of gas above the black hole and the cooler disk below.

Seven long telescope observations were split into soft and hard X-ray bands, roughly disk light and corona light. The pulse appeared strongly in the hard band in five observations, and modeling showed the soft-band signal was entirely the corona's echo, with no disk contribution. The energy-dependent delays fit a picture where the disk merely responds, lagging the corona by about two thousand seconds. The flicker is the corona's own heartbeat.
arxiv-2506-04647:
Two companies may want the overlap of their customer lists without revealing the lists themselves. Private set intersection does that, but a cheating party can poison its data to extract more than the overlap or to mislead the other side. Zixian Gong and co-authors defined what data integrity should mean for this task in 2025 and built two protocols that enforce it.

Their schemes bolt Merkle tree proofs onto leading two-party and multi-party protocols, so every element a party claims can be checked. Costs stay close to the best unprotected schemes, with the tree proofs adding some overhead. Working code accompanies the paper, along with ideas for cheaper checks.
arxiv-2506-04747:
Hedge and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about finding a young galaxy cluster around a powerful radio galaxy. Radio galaxies can mark dense regions in the early universe. The team scanned a bright radio source with a large telescope array in Chile. Gas line signals fixed its distance at a redshift near three point nine. That places it when the universe was quite young. Its host galaxy is very faint in near-infrared light.

Gas around the host fell in two moving parts, hinting at a recent merger. Nearby sources with matching gas signals revealed five more cluster members. Photometry uncovered a rare, optically dark and very massive galaxy nearby. Simulations suggest the cluster will grow into a giant present-day cluster. The find shows radio beacons can locate hidden early clusters.
arxiv-2506-04847:
Mandar Thatte, Shreya Banerjee, and Prasanta Panigrahi design a two-way quantum communication protocol that reads a shared entangled state without destroying it. Quantum dialogue lets both parties send messages over one quantum channel. Reusing the state, rather than consuming it, saves scarce entanglement.

Their scheme discriminates a five-qubit cluster state non-destructively using ancilla measurements, so the entanglement survives for further rounds. The chosen form of the state needs only four components instead of thirty-two, and Pauli operations encode the messages while preserving its stabilizer structure. Security against common quantum attacks is argued, and scaling to longer messages is outlined. A run on IBM's Torino backend served as proof of concept, with a built-in error correction bonus.
arxiv-2506-05047:
Viet Nguyen and co-authors tackled a hard problem for deployed machine learning in 2025: knowing when a model has started to fail. Data shift over time, and some shifts hurt a model while others do not. Without true labels, staff cannot simply check accuracy.

Their method, called D3M, watches for disagreement between predictive models. Under shifts that do not harm the main model, false alarms stay low. Under harmful shifts, the method gives sample bounds for a high rate of true detection. Tests on a standard benchmark and on a large internal medicine data set showed the approach worked well. The authors offer it as an alert tool for high-stakes systems.
arxiv-2506-05147:
Zeidan Zeidan and co-authors show how a row of atoms can turn a weak light beam into clumps of photons, in a 2025 paper. The setup threads identical two-level atoms along a one-dimensional waveguide, spaced exactly one wavelength apart, bathed in a faint coherent drive. As atoms are added, less light passes straight through, yet the light that does pass bunches ever harder.

At the extreme, transmission becomes a joint act of the whole row: all atoms must excite together, spitting out multi-photon packets. The team calls this superbunching. Because the packets arrive heralded by the process, they could serve long-distance entanglement links and precision measurement. A traffic jam of light becomes a resource.
arxiv-2506-05247:
Takato Yoshimura and Ziga Krajnik, two authors writing in 2025, study charge fluctuations in a family of random cellular automata. These grid systems carry charge while also showing random drift. Away from a strict single-file limit, the charge spread takes an unusual form.

The systems mix two kinds of diffusion at once, a rare trait called linear degeneracy. Using a theory of large-scale fluctuations, the authors derive the full spread of charge values. Their formulas match both exact micro-level results and computer simulations. They expect the same frame to fit other systems with this mixed diffusion trait.
arxiv-2506-05347:
Anagh Malik and co-authors presented a system in 2025 that rebuilds scenes from videos of light itself in flight. Their tool works from many viewpoints of a light pulse spreading through a room, caught by a flash lidar device. Normal rendering tools cannot easily run that movie backward to recover the scene.

The system speeds the math with a neural store of light that has bounced any number of times, stretched to track time. It separates direct light from bounced light on its own. In tests, it rebuilt three-dimensional scenes well even where bounced light was strong. It can also replay the pulse from new angles and relight the scene as if the flash had moved. The authors call it a first for this kind of capture.
arxiv-2506-06047:
Feihao Pan and co-authors find field-induced magnetic order in a triangular-lattice crystal in a 2025 paper. Frustrated magnets, where spins cannot all agree, may hide exotic states like quantum spin liquids. The compound studied here arranges dysprosium spins on a perfect two-dimensional triangular grid.

Cooling to a tenth of a degree above absolute zero brought no order on its own. A small magnetic field, about a tenth of a tesla, switched on an ordered state holding a third of full magnetization, with an up-up-down spin pattern. Calculations based on dipole forces between the spins reproduced the ordering temperature and the field-temperature map. The authors present the crystal as a rare clean stage for dipolar physics on a frustrated lattice.
arxiv-2506-06147:
Vasileios Papastergios and Anastasios Gounaris monitor data quality in streams in a 2025 paper. Modern pipelines feed on data that never stops flowing. Static quality tools ignore timing and context entirely. Batch-flavored streaming extensions miss the point as well.

Their model treats streams as first-class citizens from the start. Configurable windows slice the flow for assessment. Constraints adapt dynamically as conditions change. Quality results themselves stream out for live awareness. An open-source Python framework implements the model. Over thirty checks from scattered tools were unified. Compositional rules let users build sophisticated constraints. Benchmarks beat a production-grade rival on speed and throughput. Native streaming features exceed the alternatives' offerings. Python-native design slots into data science workflows. Continuous monitoring becomes practical for ordinary teams. The paper argues quality is a stream, not a snapshot.
arxiv-2506-06247:
Sedick Baker Effendi and three co-authors present in 2025 a language-agnostic system for taint tracking, a way to follow untrusted data through a program to find security flaws. Their approach builds whole-program data-dependence graphs, which are powerful but face two walls: library behavior needs hand-written notes, and the graphs grow huge.

The new design over-approximates flows through libraries whose notes are missing, so notes can be added later without redoing the analysis. Because the representation ignores language quirks, one engine serves many languages. The system joins the open-source Joern platform for public use. Faster, scalable taint analysis fits the quick cycles of modern development pipelines, where security checks often get squeezed out.
arxiv-2506-06347:
Zachary Yang, Domenico Tullo, and Reihaneh Rabbany present a single system for spotting toxic chat across many games. Their 2025 paper builds on an earlier tool that worked in real time. Game chat is hard to police because each game and each language would seem to need its own model.

Their first fix adds game context tokens to one model, so the same model handles many games at once. The second fix uses a large language model to move labels into seven more languages. Tests on real chat in four languages gave mixed but useful scores, with German ahead of the English mark. In daily use at Ubisoft, the system flags players each day for staff to review, at far lower cost than split models.
arxiv-2506-06547: Daniel Cabarcas, Giulia Gaggero, and Elisa Gorla wrote a short 2025 note on the cost of a modeling method for a hard algebra problem. The problem, called MinRank, asks for a matrix of low rank hidden in a set of matrices, and it backs the security of some proposed codes. One attack models the problem with extra variables for small matrix blocks. The note supplies proven estimates for how costly that modeling runs, mostly confirming the rough guesses given in the paper that first proposed it.
arxiv-2506-06847:
Pavla Procházková, writing alone in 2025, built skew monoidal structures on actegories in category theory. An actegory is a category with an action by a monoidal category. A skew monoidal structure is a looser form of the usual tensor product, where some unit laws hold in only one direction.

Her construction starts from strong actions. When a certain adjoint exists, the actegory gains a skew monoidal structure, and the adjunction itself becomes monoidal. The frame unifies several known examples of skew monoidal categories under one account. Braidings on the acting category pass to braidings on the new structure. Conditions for the structure to be closed, with an internal hom, are also given.
arxiv-2506-07047:
Xuejun Yu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a system called Mathesis. Formal theorem proving with language models usually needs the problem already written in formal code. Real problems arrive as plain words, which blocks most users. Mathesis is an end-to-end pipeline from natural language to finished proof. Its first part, the Autoformalizer, translates word problems into formal statements. Reinforcement learning trains that translator, graded by a scoring framework called LeanScorer.

The second part, the Prover, generates the formal proof itself. Together they remove the expert middleman from the pipeline's front end. AI researchers get a full-stack answer to a known bottleneck. Autoformalization quality is the hinge: a wrong formal statement makes any proof worthless. A nuanced scorer for translations is thus as important as the prover. The work targets the Lean ecosystem, where verified proofs carry lasting value.
arxiv-2506-07147:
Wanting Sun, Shunan Wei, and Donglei Yang prove a packing result for weighted graphs in a 2025 paper. The question asks when a complete graph with weighted edges must contain many disjoint four-point groups. Each group should carry a healthy total weight to count toward the packing.

A minimum weighted degree condition drives the theorem. Once the graph is large and the degree clears a stated bound, a full packing exists. Every vertex lands in some four-group with weight above the target. The result confirms a conjecture for the tetrahedron case posed by four other researchers. Such packing theorems sit at the heart of extremal graph theory. They also model grouping tasks where pairwise links carry strengths.
arxiv-2506-07247:
Ngoc-Quan Pham, Tuan Truong, Quyen Tran, Tan Nguyen, Dinh Phung, and Trung Le fine-tune foundation models with ensembles whose members are pushed to disagree usefully, in a 2025 paper. An ensemble of models beats a single one when its members err differently; sameness wastes the trick. Standard Bayesian fine-tuning lets its sampled models huddle together.

Their framework, IBDR, adds interactions between the sampled models — the particles — so diversity is rewarded during training, while a robustness term guards against data shift. On a thousand-example adaptation benchmark and a reasoning task, IBDR beat the rival methods tested. Diverse ensembles that stay robust could make small-data fine-tuning of giant models safer for medicine and law.
arxiv-2506-07547:
Chiaki Miura and Ichiro Sakata compare fame gaps between early draft papers and journal papers in a 2025 study. Drafts, called preprints, spread new work fast and now often stand alone, not just as steps to a journal. Past checks found drafts and journal papers much alike in authors and quality. The team asked a new question: how evenly are citations, the nods from later work, spread in each world?

Draft citations proved far more skewed than journal ones in each field checked. The gap held after checks for paper age and field size. It was not driven by a few star papers or by the mass of ignored ones alone. Being in a journal later did not change the draft skew. Author fame, more than rich-get-richer growth, drove much of the gap. The elite thus gains more in the draft world.
arxiv-2506-07847:
Hengzhi Chen and co-authors split satellite images by frequency to map land cover at extreme detail. Their 2025 paper tackles ultra-high-resolution scans, where shrinking loses fine lines and tiling loses the broad scene. Two-branch nets try both, but cost much and fight during training.

Their net sends fine detail down one branch at full size, and broad layout down another at small size with short- and long-range arms. A fusion block joins the reads, steered by two new losses: one aligns meaning across branches, one balances their training pull. On two known sets the method tops the field. City and land planners gain crisper maps.
arxiv-2506-07947:
Paulius Rauba, Qiyao Wei, and Mihaela van der Schaar wrote a 2025 paper on how to test whether a language model's answers truly change after some intervention. A change might be a tweak to the input or a switch of model version. Single answers cannot settle the question, since the model answers with some randomness each time.

Their framework treats the task as a classic hypothesis test. Repeated sampling builds two clouds of answers, mapped into a small space based on meaning similarity. From those clouds, the method yields clear p-values and effect sizes, with error control when many changes are tested at once. It works on any black-box model. Case studies show it can measure real changes and false alarm rates. The work gives auditors a firm tool for robustness checks.
arxiv-2506-08047:
Forecasting which students will struggle is a classic task for machine learning, and Sandeepa and Mohottala compare standard models on school data mixing behavior, grades, and background details. A multi-layer perceptron, a small neural network, came out on top, reaching about eighty-six percent accuracy on held-out students. Averaged over ten validation rounds it scored near eighty percent, while memorizing the training set almost perfectly.

Careful feature selection did much of the work, and explainable methods were used to open the black box and check that the chosen features made sense. The authors argue that compact neural networks are data-efficient candidates for early-warning systems in schools.
arxiv-2506-08347:
Yinan Huang, Haoteng Yin, Eli Chien, Rongzhe Wei, and Pan Li set out to learn from networked data while formally protecting each entity in it, in a 2025 paper. Relational data — friendships, transactions, citations — power sensitive applications, yet each entity shows up in many links. That sharing breaks standard private training, since one person's data can sway the model through every relation they touch.

Differential privacy adds calibrated noise with a proof attached, but counting sensitivity across tangled relations is hard, and multi-stage sampling muddies the usual guarantees. The team deliver a full framework with a careful sensitivity analysis and entity-level protection. Private learning on graphs could then serve medicine and finance without exposing the people inside.
arxiv-2506-08547:
Wenxuan Tao and Fen Zuo sharpen an algorithm for a quantum toy model with a famous name, in a 2025 paper. The EPR model was proposed two years earlier by King. It is a cousin of a classic magnetism model, equivalent to the quantum maximum-cut problem. In it, neighboring qubits prefer symmetric Bell pairings over the antisymmetric one, because that choice maximizes the energy. Two groups had independently reached the same accuracy guarantee using fractional matchings. The authors refine one of those methods.

Their twist uses uniform or near-uniform fractional matchings to spread entanglement as evenly as possible. On regular graphs the guarantee improves at once. On irregular graphs it holds when the matchings are chosen with care. Better guarantees for toy models often seed methods for the real optimization problems quantum computers may one day tackle.
arxiv-2506-08647:
Oumaima El Khettari, Solen Quiniou, and Samuel Chaffron test whether summarizing a text first helps machines pull relations from it, in a research paper from 2025. Their field is the gut microbiome, where interactions among microbes matter and labeled data are scarce. Relation extraction names the links between entities in a passage.

Their pipeline uses a large language model to summarize the passage, which trims noise before a second model extracts the relations. Early results on a dedicated corpus show the summary step lifts the generative method's scores. Classic BERT-based extractors still beat the generative route for now. The authors frame the work as ongoing proof that generative tools can serve niche, low-resource fields.
arxiv-2506-08747:
Boyang Sun and six co-authors proposed a sample-efficient conditional independence test in twenty twenty-five for data that arrive discretized. Many real variables are recorded in bins because of measurement limits, and running standard independence tests on the bins can mislead. Earlier fixes binarize the data to reason about the latent continuous variables, but binarization throws away information and weakens the test.

The new test skips binarization. The authors show the latent independence question can be recast as an over-identifying restrictions problem solvable by the generalized method of moments. They derive a test statistic with the correct asymptotic distribution using nodewise regression. Theory and experiments across data sets show the test beats binarization-based competitors, especially when samples are scarce.
arxiv-2506-09247:
Karl Löwenmark and co-authors build an AI assistant for industrial condition monitoring, in work from 2025. Monitoring systems spot machine faults, but judging severity and choosing maintenance still falls on human analysts, while automatic alarms are often wrong.

Their framework, MindRAG, combines language-model agents with a retrieval system shaped for monitoring data such as sensor records and maintenance orders. Past annotations and work orders stand in for labels, letting the system learn from noisy real-world data. The agents answer analyst questions, help dismiss false alarms, and explain their reasoning. An experienced analyst judged early results as meaningful support for managing alarms, suggesting the approach can cut workload in process plants.
arxiv-2506-09347:
Xuemei Cao and co-authors present ErrorEraser, a plug-in that helps learning systems forget biased lessons, in a paper from 2025. Systems that learn task after task must hold old skills while gaining new ones. Real data carry biases, though, and models can pick up false links from them. Those false links then spread to later tasks and grow.

The tool works in two steps. First it learns the shape of each task's data and flags samples that look biased. Then it shifts the decision edge for those odd samples, so only the wrong lesson is wiped. A light update rule keeps the flagging cheap on new tasks. Tests across three styles of steady learning show higher accuracy and less forgetting. The code is shared in public.
arxiv-2506-09947:
Rudy Alexandro Garrido Veliz and co-authors present an AI platform that tracks and counters anti democratic talk online in Germany, in a paper from 2025. Social media help extremist views spread fast, most of all from the far right. Tools for monitoring must work without curbing free expression.

The platform applies learning models to a large set of German online data gathered daily. It gives journalists, researchers, and policy makers a broad view of trends in the digital sphere. Early analysis shows both the tangled nature of organized extremist behavior and the promise of the joined approach, most of all around major events. The authors frame the system as support for democratic discourse.
arxiv-2506-10447:
Igor Tominec and co-authors study the math of very thick flows with a free top surface, in a paper from 2025. Flows of this kind show up in ice sheets, lava, and slow rock deep in the Earth. The flow and the height of its surface affect each other, which makes stable computer models hard to build.

The authors prove stability and volume saving results for the linked system, for both simple and more complex fluids. They check the claims for models that step forward in time in two ways, one direct and one indirect. Guided by the proofs, they add a fix term that makes the direct method stable for any step size. Computer tests then back up the theory.
arxiv-2506-10547:
Hana Heidarian and co-authors test a model of the early universe against new sky data, in a 2025 paper. The model belongs to a family called alpha-attractor inflation, which describes a burst of fast growth just after the Big Bang. The team adds a twist from quantum gravity thinking: a smallest length that can ever be measured.

With that twist in place, they rework the growth equations and check the model's forecasts against data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. The plain model sits near the edge of what the data allow. Adding the smallest-length effect moves the forecasts into the range the data favor most, at a strength that matches bounds set by other studies.
arxiv-2506-11047:
Chirudeep Tupakula and Rittika Shamsuddin propose in 2025 spotting bias in machine learning by asking crowds to judge simple pictures of data. Classic bias checks need sensitive labels or rigid fairness scores, which real settings often lack. Their web tool shows stripped down charts, such as pay spread across groups, and collects yes or no calls on whether groups look alike.

Votes pile up to flag suspect segments, which then face statistical tests and model cross checks. The crowd's gut calls matched known bias cases well, the authors report. Layout and wording sway the eye, they note, so the design treats those as signals too.
arxiv-2506-11347:
Wenqian Ye, Guangtao Zheng, and Aidong Zhang present Evidential Alignment, in a 2025 preprint, a way to stop networks from leaning on spurious clues. A camel classifier that keys on desert sand fails in a zoo. Most fixes need group labels marking which examples carry the fake clue. Such labels are costly, and helper models may miss the full bias. This method needs neither. It measures how much evidence backs each prediction, using uncertainty math. Second-order risk training plus a calibration step expose where the model leans on the shortcut.

Once exposed, those leanings are suppressed while the core features stay. The authors back the method with theory: it can learn a biased model's patterns and debias it blind. Across architectures and data types, group robustness rose markedly in tests. The authors offer the method as a scalable, principled answer to shortcut learning.
arxiv-2506-11447: H Kaur and M Rana present a 2025 math paper on a new kind of integer partition. In their partitions, the largest part appears exactly once. The remaining parts themselves form a partition of that largest part. The authors derive the generating function that counts these partitions. They then explore several variations of the rule. Each variant gets its own generating function. The paper is short and formal, aimed at readers in combinatorics who work with partition identities.
arxiv-2506-11547:
Yinlong Liu and co-authors recast a core vision task, finding how an object has rotated, as a straight-line fitting problem, in a 2025 paper. Rotation estimates guide cameras and robots, and safety-critical uses need methods that shrug off bad data. Standard methods treat the task as a curved search that needs careful tuning.

The new view drops no rules and adds no singular points. Rotation is also shown as a great circle on a sphere of number sets, which leads to a simple voting method. The method runs in parallel on graphics chips and solved million-point cases with almost all data corrupt in under half a second. Tests on controlled and real data back its strength.
arxiv-2506-11847:
Mikhail Shaposhnikov reviews progress in Einstein-Cartan gravity, a version of Einstein's theory built by gauging the Lorentz group, the same trick that underlies the Standard Model's forces. Putting gravity on that footing gives the theory several advantages, including room for spacetime torsion. The review concentrates on a Weyl-invariant form of the theory, which respects a local scaling symmetry.

From that construction, Shaposhnikov turns to what the theory can do for particle physics and cosmology. Two applications headline the discussion: cosmic inflation in the early universe, and the strong CP problem. That puzzle asks why the strong nuclear force so precisely respects a symmetry it is allowed to break. The piece is an overview, gathering the theory's construction and its promised payoffs in one place.
arxiv-2506-12347:
AI coding agents ace tidy benchmark tasks but stumble on messy real-world work, so they are often built to collaborate with the developer. Aayush Kumar and co-authors watch nineteen developers use such an agent inside their editor in this 2025 study, tackling thirty-three real issues in projects they knew.

About half the issues got solved. Developers who worked in small steps and actively steered, questioned, and reworked the agent's output fared best, while one-shot users struggled. Trust and joint debugging were friction points. The authors urge agents that argue back and engage, rather than flatter and conclude, across the whole task.
arxiv-2506-12647:
Three researchers tackle blood supply in poor regions in a 2025 paper. Matching donors to patients and picking the right blood bank are hard when stock is thin and roads are long. Shortages can turn deadly if banks cannot see them coming.

Their system pairs matching rules with forecasts of shortage. The rules weigh distance, blood type fit, expiry order, and rarity of each unit. Moving from blind matching to the full rule set lifted accepted requests by near half. On 170 days of records, a simple linear model forecast shortages best of the three tried. A database built for scale holds the whole system.
arxiv-2506-12847:
Videos of digital humans look wrong when hands meet objects in stiff or blurred ways. Zhelun Shen and co-authors present iDiT-HOI, a 2025 system that reenacts hand and object contact in a more natural way.

The system first builds a key frame that places the chosen object into the hand region of a scene. A second stage then extends that frame into a smooth, coherent video. The design reuses what a large pre-trained video model already knows, without adding new parts. That helps it handle people and objects it has never seen, and it supports long clips. Tests show clearer, more seamless contact than prior methods, even in messy real-world scenes.
arxiv-2506-12947:
Ismail Emir Yuksel and eight colleagues present a 2025 hardware study on a security flaw hiding inside a promising computing trick. Processing-using-DRAM computes inside memory chips by firing several rows at once, easing the data movement bottleneck. But hammering rows is also how the RowHammer attack flips bits in neighboring rows. Nobody had checked whether multi-row activation disturbs memory worse.

Testing three hundred sixteen real DDR4 chips from four makers, the team found it does, dramatically. The hits needed for the first bitflip fell by up to about one hundred fifty-nine times versus classic RowHammer. The attack even slipped past a built-in defense. Three countermeasures and an adapted industry mitigation are evaluated, though the strongest fix costs heavy performance. The authors warn PuD systems must be designed around this.
arxiv-2506-13047:
James Cline and Varun Muralidharan published a 2025 cosmology paper testing simple models of dark energy against new sky survey data. Dark energy is the force thought to speed up the expansion of the universe. Recent results from the DESI survey hint that this energy may be fading over time instead of staying constant.

Most tests assume a formula for how dark energy behaves. These authors instead used quintessence models, where a simple field with a rising or curved energy profile drives the expansion. With one supernova dataset, the models clearly favoured changing dark energy, though the fit strained another cosmic measurement. With two other datasets, the preference shrank to mild. The paper shows how much the conclusion depends on which data are trusted.
arxiv-2506-13447:
Ning Li and Qizhou Wang share first credit on this paper from two thousand twenty-five, with He, Burguete-Lopez, Xiang, and Fratalocchi. It reports a camera-based sensor that spots dopamine at trace levels, in real time, with no added chemicals.
