Catching brain chemicals this faint is a long goal for the study of brain disease. The platform uses crafted light-scattering films and optical boosters built into trade vision cameras. It reads dopamine live at video rates, even with uric and ascorbic acid in the mix, at levels far below past best tools. The setup swaps a bulky bench station for a small camera box. The booster can be retrained for other targets, the team notes.
arxiv-2506-13647:
Bertrand Even, Christophe Giraud, and Nicolas Verzelen map where fast algorithms must fall short in grouping tasks, in a 2025 paper. In many high-dimensional problems, the best quick methods cannot reach the accuracy that slow, unlimited methods provably achieve. This suspected gap between what statistics allows and what computing allows needs firm bounds.

The team builds a sharper way to bound what low-degree polynomial methods, a stand-in for fast algorithms, can do in models with hidden structure. Using the hidden structure more fully, they get stronger bounds with simpler proofs. They apply the scheme to clustering, sparse clustering, and grouping rows and columns together, and prove matching fast methods where possible, giving a full picture of the gaps in all three tasks.
arxiv-2506-13747:
Jan Miśkiewicz, Maciej Konieczka, and Wojciech Satuła report a 2025 nuclear physics calculation. They study a rare decay in which a calcium-48 nucleus turns into titanium-48. Two neutrinos are emitted in the process. The rate of the decay hinges on a value called the nuclear matrix element. Getting that value right matters for a related, even rarer decay that could reveal deep facts about neutrinos.

The team used a model that starts from a self consistent field picture. It then restores broken symmetry and mixes many shapes of the nucleus. Their result for the matrix element lands close to values from shell model studies. It also sits near the best estimate drawn from experiment. The authors say this match raises trust in their model for the rarer decay that physicists hope to find.
arxiv-2506-13947:
Kazuto Fukuchi tackles fair prediction in a 2025 math paper. The fairness rule in view is demographic parity, which asks that a model's outputs not split by group. Past work found best-possible fair methods for guessing a number, but each proof was tied to one data setup.

Fukuchi proves broad meta-results that can be checked across many setups at once. They show when a method counts as the best fair method under the rule. Fair best results can be reached by post-processing, the paper also shows: fix the output of a normal method after training. That frees builders to improve plain methods first, then adapt them for fairness with a light final step. The frame may save each new study from proving the same point from scratch.
arxiv-2506-14147:
Emma Dodoo, Tamara Nelson-Fromm, and Mark Guzdial ask how school coding teachers pick tools for students who are still learning English. Programming languages use English words, and most class materials are in English too, which loads these students twice. Teachers must ease that load while they hew to state course rules and train students on professional-grade tools. Their 2025 study sits with such teachers and logs their calls.

Each pick trades ease now for skill later: a kind tool may not match the test, and a pro tool may shut new language learners out. Care for the students, rule books, and job aims all pull on the pick. The team maps what tips the scale in real classrooms, case by case. Their aim is class craft that keeps both doors open.
arxiv-2506-14347:
Yoav Ravid and six co-authors study how curved parts in a cell's skin steer the shape of the whole sac. Their work, from two thousand twenty-five, is a theory study.

The parts come in two forms: bow-shaped and saddle-shaped. They sense curve, line up like a liquid crystal, and meet at flaw points, all under a fixed bulk. For sacs fully clad in bow parts, the shape shifts from a string of beads to a tube as the lined-up acts grow strong. For part-clad sacs, saddle parts hold the necks between bare, round zones. The team maps the calm shapes and finds flaw points sit at set spots.
arxiv-2506-14447:
Mikko Partanen and Jukka Tulkki derive the slow swivel of planetary orbits, the perihelion precession, from quantum field theory rather than from Einstein's geometry. Their 2025 paper extends the Standard Model of particles to include gravity. The orbit effect is a classic test that general relativity passes with high precision.

The authors model a bound electron with a Dirac equation built for their unified gravity view. They then take the limit where that quantum state behaves like a classical planet. The orbit that falls out swivels at the same rate general relativity predicts. The pair present this as proof that core relativistic orbit effects can grow straight out of quantum theory, with no curved-space framing invoked.
arxiv-2506-15847:
SafeMimic is a 2025 research paper by Arpit Bahety, Arnav Balaji, Ben Abbatematteo, and Roberto Martín-Martín. It tackles a home robotics problem. A mobile robot must learn a new task by watching one video of a person doing it, with no one standing by to keep it safe.

The method first breaks the video into steps and works out what changed and what moves the person made. It then shifts those moves into the robot's own view and body shape. Before it acts, the robot tests each move for safety with tools trained in a computer model, and it steps back and tries a new path when no safe move exists. Tests on seven tasks show gains over older methods.
arxiv-2506-16347:
Carbon claims that can be checked without spilling secrets are designed by Jessica Man and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Data centers owe much of tech's carbon bill. Firms like to flatter their counts and hide their books. Hired checkers for each chain link would cost too much. The team's fix uses zero-knowledge proofs, math that proves a claim while the inputs stay shut.

Claims can then ride the whole supply chain, from power firms to cloud users. Users get counts they can trust for their own reports. Providers stay on the hook for true data.
arxiv-2506-16547:
Peter Giblin and Alexander Wettig extend a classic drawing trick that traces glowing curves from chords of a circle, in a paper from 2025. Joining points at angles in a fixed ratio traces an envelope with cusps, the stuff of string art. The old version used whole-number ratios on one circle.

Ratios can now be any fraction, even negative. Formulas count the cusps, far-flung points, and self-crossings of the new envelopes. A second build uses two rings, chords spanning between them. That opens richer spike shapes that hide their inner form. Shifting one ring's center breaks the symmetry and unfolds the shapes fully, swallowtails and butterflies included.
arxiv-2506-16847:
Netzer Moriya builds a theory of messy optical surfaces in a 2025 paper on wavefront reconstruction. A wavefront describes how light waves line up after passing through or reflecting off a surface. Chaotic surfaces bend light in tangled ways that classic aberration theory, built for orderly flaws, handles poorly.

Moriya joins two toolkits: Zernike terms, the standard language for optical flaws, and Lyapunov measures, which track how fast paths in a chaotic system spread apart. The hybrid framework links surface chaos to standard measures of optical performance and sets rules for when its expansions settle down. Possible uses include smoothing beams, cutting speckle, and shaping wavefronts on purpose. The paper aims to give controlled chaos a firm design base.
arxiv-2506-16947:
Zhao Jing Chen and Bao Yuan Sun examine in 2025 how a part of the nuclear force shapes clusters of four particles inside a neon nucleus. Clustering, where protons and neutrons group into helium like units, acts like a phase shift in the nucleus and is very sensitive to the force details. The team asks how the nucleus's stretched shape and one force component affect the clusters.

They use a deformed model that joins two standard methods for heavy computation. It gives binding energies and single particle levels at each degree of stretch. The tensor force, carried in one part of the model, is switched in view so its role can be read. They study both the ground state and a highly stretched excited state. The results show how that force helps or hinders cluster formation.
arxiv-2506-17047:
Haolin Liu and five co-authors deepen attacks that steal neural network secrets. Their 2025 paper improves end-to-end extraction, where queries alone reveal a model's inner numbers. A landmark method splits the theft into signature and sign steps. In practice it stalled on shallow networks, and the sign step could blow up in time.

The team reworks the signature step, fixing rank gaps and noise that grows with depth. Their fixes let extraction reach much deeper networks than before. Fresh tricks also sharpen the numbers' precision. For signs, they marry two polynomial methods to dodge slow searches on unsure neurons. The work warns defenders that black-box access leaks more than once thought.
arxiv-2506-17147:
Adam Smith, Wenjun Ding, Yogesh Vohra, and Cheng-Chien Chen explain in 2025 why some mixed-metal alloys keep superconducting under crushing pressure that kills the state in simpler metals. Experiments show niobium-based high-entropy alloys holding their critical temperature nearly steady past a hundred gigapascals.

The team ran first-principles calculations of electron-phonon coupling for pure niobium, a niobium-titanium crystal, and two disordered alloy structures. Comparing the orderly and messy cases reveals what stabilizes the pairing of electrons in the alloys. Robust superconductors that shrug off pressure could serve in extreme magnets and deep-space hardware.
arxiv-2506-17347:
Jennifer Wang, Andrew Selbst, Solon Barocas, and Suresh Venkatasubramanian argued in twenty twenty-five that AI regulation must split task-specific systems from general-purpose ones. Over the past decade, policy tools were built for narrow AI that does one job. General-purpose AI, which adapts to many jobs, breaks several assumptions baked into those tools.

The authors name four gaps. General systems make a poor single target for rules; their evals are hard to design; they raise fresh legal questions with new stakeholders; and their supply chain is spread across many firms. They urge policymakers to sort which older tools still fit and where new ones are needed. Three recommendations close the paper, on picking targets and using pressure points across the wider ecosystem.
arxiv-2506-17447:
Akash Halder and co-authors solve a deformed version of the basic quantum equation and mine it for information measures in a 2025 paper. The Dunkl framework bends the standard derivatives with reflection operators, modeling particles with special symmetry. The authors solve that equation for a molecule-like potential, the Deng-Fan form, in spherical coordinates.

They report the ro-vibrational energies of four metal hydrides, scandium through chromium compounds, under a fresh approximation for the spin term. The wave functions come out in classic special functions, Jacobi polynomials for the angles and hypergeometric forms for the radius. From those solutions they compute a shelf of information measures: Shannon and Renyi entropies, uncertainty, and disequilibrium. The numbers show how the Dunkl deformation spreads or squeezes a molecule's quantum state.
arxiv-2506-17847:
Cristian Del Gobbo wrote a solo study in two thousand twenty-five comparing two open-source toolkits that make fake data tables. Fake, or synthetic, data copy the patterns of real data without exposing it. Good training data are hard to get, above all for small firms, so such tools have clear appeal.

The study tests six generators, three from each toolkit, on a real data set about energy use and weather in Belgium. Each tool was trained on just one thousand rows, a low-data test. It then had to make sets of the same size and ten times larger. Scores covered how close the fake data stayed to the real patterns.
arxiv-2506-18347:
José Fernando and Riccardo Ghiloni settle a question left open since 1957 in a 2025 paper. Cartan proved that well-behaved curved sets, called coherent analytic sets, let every smooth function on them extend to the space around. Whether only such sets have that gift stayed unproven for decades.

The authors prove the converse: if a real analytic set has the extension gift, it must be coherent. For every misbehaving set they produce many functions that refuse to extend, almost cataloguing the failures. The same test then passes to Nash sets, a stricter algebraic cousin where the tools fight back harder. The result closes a long chapter in the geometry of real curved sets.
arxiv-2506-18547:
Asma Mouhoub and four co-authors present a 2025 paper on how spin waves split in layered magnetic materials. A spin wave is a ripple of magnetic alignment that runs through a material. One known effect lets a fast wave split into two slower waves, which matters for wave based computing.

The team studied this split in channels made of stacked magnetic layers that point in opposed ways. They drove waves in, read them out, and imaged them with scattered laser light. Slow waves of one kind split into pairs of a second kind, which stand still across the channel yet travel along it. Several split paths can run at once, and the paper maps the rules.
arxiv-2506-18747:
Lorenzo Simone, Davide Bacciu, and Shuangge Ma present a way to make generative models forget selected parts of what they learned, in a 2025 paper. Erasing data from a trained model, for privacy or safety, usually means costly retraining, and the data to erase may no longer be at hand. Their framework works within flow matching, a modern way of building generators.

A reweighting loss, guided by energy-based stand-ins for the unwanted data, softly subtracts those regions from the model's output distribution. The authors prove this steers the model exactly as if it were trained toward the subtracted target. Tests in flat toy worlds and on images, with clear visuals and scores, support the method. Targeted unlearning without the original samples is the prize.
arxiv-2506-18847:
Anthony Kobanda and co-authors teach agents to reach distant goals from past trajectories alone, in this 2025 paper. Goal-conditioned learning trains on recorded runs without fresh interaction. Long journeys break it, because small value errors pile up over many steps.

Their method, ProQ, learns an asymmetric distance that suits directed travel. The distance spreads a sparse set of key points evenly across the learned space, pushing them apart like a repulsive force. The same geometry then prices short hops toward chosen sub-goals. A detector flags points that drift out of reach. On navigation tests, the plan drove long goal runs more robustly than before.
arxiv-2506-19247:
Theodosios Papazoglou and Guosheng Yin propose a supervised version of a classic data method in a 2025 paper. Principal component analysis compresses data into a few strong patterns, but it ignores any outcome the user cares about, so the patterns may miss what matters. Supervised versions add the outcome in, yet older ones are hard to read or need touchy optimization.

Their covariance-supervised method balances two goals: patterns should track the outcome and still capture much of the data's spread, with one dial setting the trade. The solution comes in closed form from a standard eigenvalue calculation, and a sampling shortcut speeds it for huge data. Simulations and real applications show strong scores across many measures.
arxiv-2506-19347:
Manpreet Kaur and six co-authors study how a small particle called the kaon changes inside dense strange matter. Their 2025 paper deals with matter made of nucleons and hyperons, packed tight and rich in strange quarks. Such matter may sit deep inside some dead stars.

Working in a light-cone quark model, the team tracks how the kaon's quarks spread out in that dense setting. They weigh those spreads against the same traits for a free kaon. Mass shifts for the quarks, drawn from a second model, feed into the sums. In dense matter, the charge form of the kaon is pressed down. Its charge also spreads in a new pattern.
arxiv-2506-19547:
Soumik Bhattacharyya and co-authors study what slows a star that spirals inside the loose outer layer of a giant companion star. This shared-envelope phase is ruled by drag on the two inner bodies as they plow through the gas. Older single-body models of that drag can be far off.

The team ran a full 3-D fluid model with two equal-mass points to keep things symmetric. They found that almost all the drag comes from gas within about one gap-width of the pair. That gas roughly turns with the pair. A simple stretched-ball model of the gas, tilted at a fixed lag angle, tracked the drag well over time. The work points to better drag rules that respect the pair.
arxiv-2506-19647:
Smolyakov and co-authors analyze how plasma speeds up inside a magnetic nozzle, in a 2025 physics paper. A magnetic nozzle guides plasma through a field that first narrows, then spreads, converting heat into thrust. Such nozzles serve electric spacecraft propulsion and open fusion devices. The team focuses on two drivers often left aside: electromagnetic effects and the push from plasma rotation.

Spinning plasma and its ring-shaped magnetic field feed each other, and their combined energy adds extra acceleration. At wide expansion, flow can reach and pass the Alfvén speed, a key signal speed in plasma. The authors find steady solutions that pass smoothly through all critical points where flow matches signal speeds. Time-based simulations show those steady flows are stable and attract unsteady ones toward them.
arxiv-2506-20147:
Xi Geng, Sheng Wang, and Weijun Xu find the exact long-time growth of a random heat equation on curved space in a 2025 probability study. The parabolic Anderson model describes a quantity spreading while multiplied by a frozen random landscape, a picture used for populations in patchy environments and for disordered materials. Their space is hyperbolic, where volume grows far faster than in flat space.

With a steady Gaussian random potential, the solution starting from constant data grows, with probability one, at a precise exponential rate in time. Both the power of time in the exponent and the constant differ from the flat-space values. An explicit optimization produces the constant.
arxiv-2506-20347:
Malik Shahid Sultan, Hernando Ombao, and Maurizio Filippone asked in 2025 whether a neural network can learn cause-like links in time data on its own. Granger causality marks a link when past values of one series help guess the next values of another. Classic tools for it are straight-line models that miss curved links. Past network work treated the task as picking which inputs to keep.

Their tack is to train one network on all series at once, then drop one series' past and watch how the errors shift. A well-tuned network can find the true link web with no special loss terms, they show. Tests set the single joint model against sparse methods and three network types. It held up as a strong, low-fuss base line.
arxiv-2506-20447:
James Fant-Male and Roel Pieters review personalisation in work shared by humans and robots, in a 2025 paper. Industry is shifting toward a human-centered model where well-being sits at the center of new technology. Robots that adapt to each user are a core part of that shift.

The review tracks recent work on robots that adjust their actions and interaction style to the person. It covers which personal factors are used, how work cells are designed, and how tasks are adapted. The field is growing but lacks a shared approach. The authors discuss ethics and rules for such systems in detail, as key issues for future work.
arxiv-2506-20947:
Reading a stream of signing into words is held back by thin data: few long videos carry exact gloss labels. Dejie Yang and three co-authors enrich the text side in 2025. Each gloss is grown into a tree of sub-actions, fleshed out with facts drawn from a large language model.

The tree lets the learner match sight to text step by step, coarse first, fine later, and the tree shape trims the cost of that match. A contrast push pulls the sight and text views closer still. The frame is tested on the standard sets for the task. The bet is that gloss words hold more than a label: they hold a script of the hands' act, and a learner should read it.
arxiv-2506-21047:
Tianyu Wang and seven co-authors show that fast electron diffraction can film electrons and hydrogen atoms moving together. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tackles a core wish of ultrafast science. Watching coupled electron and nucleus motion in real space and time has been out of reach. Their test case is ammonia breaking apart under light.

Mega-electron-volt electron pulses scatter off the excited molecule. A charge-pair distribution function is drawn from the scatter. Fine time resolution lets that map split the intertwined paths of valence electrons and hydrogens. The linked dance during the split becomes visible. The authors stress method reach over the single molecule. Many quantum dynamics studies could adopt the charge-pair lens. It opens a route to movies of charge and matter in joint motion.
arxiv-2506-21247:
Xianghang Zhang builds an action for open superstring field theory in a 2025 paper. The theory covers strings with extended supersymmetry labeled N equals two. Zhang starts from a ghost sector cohomology with a fixed zero mode rule. Interaction terms are then built step by step.

All vertices arise by recursion with no singular terms. The algebra behind the action carries an A infinity structure. Checks show the theory returns the correct scattering matrix order by order. Clean vertices matter because singular terms can wreck calculations. The result gives researchers a firmer base for superstring field work.
arxiv-2506-21647:
Guha Majumdar sets a working threshold for when spatial entanglement survives ionizing hits in twenty twenty-five. Entanglement is fragile when one partner sheds energy through ionization or scattering. A full quantum electrodynamics model tracks the decay here. The fall off proves exponential, driven by recoil spreading the momentum.

A sharp line splits the quantum coherent side from the classical side. Cross it when total recoil blur tops the state's own momentum width. The rule reaches past weak coupling and Gaussian toy models. It gives numbers to design hardier quantum sensors and imagers. Radiation rich settings are the target use.
arxiv-2506-21947:
Baruah and Phukon reclassify the phase changes of black holes using fractional calculus, a math that allows orders between whole numbers. In the holographic picture, a black hole in a curved space mirrors a hot quantum system on its border, and its changes of state echo there. Classic schemes label changes as first or second order, which blurs real differences.

Their 2025 study applies a fractional version of the classic classification to three black hole families, including charged ones and one built on modified statistics. Points where heat capacity blows up split into two kinds, carrying fractional orders of three halves and four thirds. The split depends on whether the point caps or bends the temperature curve. The authors say the finer labels reveal structure the old scheme hides.
arxiv-2506-22047:
Paul Gallot and Sebastian Maneth settle, in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper, a decision problem about programs that transform trees. A tree transducer is shape preserving when its output tree always has exactly the same shape as its input tree, differing only in labels.

The authors prove this property can always be decided for top-down and bottom-up transducers, and for compositions of total deterministic macro tree transducers. More than a yes-or-no answer, any shape-preserving transducer can be rewritten into a clean normal form. In that form, every input node creates exactly one output node, making the transformation transparent and easy to reason about.
arxiv-2506-22647:
Nadia Padhan and Axel Voigt simulated three-way fluid mixtures to see when their patterns turn hyperuniform in a 2025 paper. Hyperuniform matter hides large-scale density swings while staying disordered up close. Flow and diffusion equations for mixtures let the team vary surface wetting and water-like flow.

Flow weakened the effect, as in two-fluid systems. Wetting mattered just as much: when all three fluids meet on equal terms, each shows a like degree of hyperuniformity. When one fluid coats the other two, that coating fluid loses much of its hyperuniform character. The authors name wetting balance as a dial for spatial order in soft materials. Such control could matter for coatings and cell-like assemblies.
arxiv-2506-22947:
Lauren Conger, Franca Hoffmann, Eric Mazumdar, and Lillian J Ratliff define a new kind of monotonicity for systems of many interacting species. Their 2025 paper works with flow equations that preserve total mass. Distance is measured by the Wasserstein-2 metric, the cost of moving one pile of mass into another. Monotonicity in that setting turns out to be a powerful organizing property.

When the property holds, the system has exactly one steady state and every solution settles into it. Velocity fields and second moments converge too, and distances shrink at rates set by the strength of the monotonicity. In the special case where each species descends its own energy landscape, the steady state is the Nash equilibrium of those energies, extending known zero-sum results to general games. Examples run from cross-diffusion to mean-field games, and a market model shows the theory working in simulation.
arxiv-2506-23147:
Jonathan Schuster and Fabian Transchel release a Python package that sorts driving maneuvers from vehicle sensor streams. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in vehicle telematics. Naming maneuvers helps score driving for insurance, safety, and fuel use. The task needs steady time series classification on data that is awkward to move, clean, and store.

Past work dwelt on data gathering and model craft. A ready toolkit was the gap. Their package covers preprocessing, modeling, and scoring in one place. A built-in LSTM network can be reshaped to fit new tasks. The demo uses phone sensor data from three drivers on real roads. The authors pitch the package as a fast on-ramp for telematics teams. It turns raw streams into maneuver labels with set tooling.
arxiv-2507-00447:
Restoring a damaged face photo forces a trade: sharpen it and the likeness drifts, stay faithful and it looks fake. Xin Luo and six co-authors work that trade in 2025 by moving a recent flow-based restoration method into the compressed latent space of an autoencoder.

Working in latent space aligns the repair with how humans judge pictures, rather than raw pixels. The best achievable faithfulness is then capped by the autoencoder's own rebuilding error, so the team designed a stronger autoencoder for the job. On blind face restoration tests their method beat rivals on the perception-faithfulness balance and converged nearly six times faster than the pixel-space version. Code is promised as open source.
arxiv-2507-00747:
Diemen Delgado-Cano, Erick Kracht, and colleagues learn simple equations for systems with fast and slow parts in a 2025 study. A popular data-driven method finds sparse, readable dynamics, but high-dimensional slow-fast systems make its regression huge and ill-conditioned. Restricting attention to the slow manifold, where long-term behavior lives, should shrink the problem.

The catch is that dropped fast variables must be repaid with higher-order terms, which explode the candidate list again. The authors develop ways to manage that growth while staying on the manifold. Compact learned models help engineers predict systems from turbines to climate components without simulating every fast detail.
arxiv-2507-00847:
Keiichiro Kimura and co-authors expose a Bluetooth security flaw in a 2025 paper. Bluetooth links billions of devices over short range. Safety rests on pairing, where two devices set up shared secret keys. Many audio devices pair on their own for ease of use. The team found that this convenience hides a serious weakness, which they call Stealtooth.

Some devices slip into pairing mode under set conditions without telling the user. An attacker nearby can hijack that moment and silently replace the stored link key. A stronger version adds a power saving trick to enable a man in the middle attack. The team tested ten devices from major makers and found the flaw across the board. Only basic hardware and free software were needed. They suggest fixes at device and protocol level, and shared their findings with vendors, some of whom have issued patches.
arxiv-2507-01447:
Masuda Akter and Mohammed Mustafa Rizvi plan curved drone paths that catch a moving target while dodging obstacles, in work from 2025. A chasing drone flies at fixed speed on a path with bounded turn. The target also holds speed, so timing the catch is part of the puzzle.

The authors cast the chase as a constrained control problem. Geometry tools yield the conditions any best path must meet. Cases grow from one obstacle to a finite field of them. Simulations test the model's speed and success on sample chases. A final case study uses real map data, with placed obstacles and a set target route. The work targets patrol and intercept planning.
arxiv-2507-01847:
Arlinskii and Schmüdgen chart all full forms of flip-fair math tools in this twenty twenty-five paper. A flip law on a smooth space sets when a tool counts as fair. Loose tools may wear the trait in part; full tools wear it whole.

Inside, the pair names each full form a part-fair tool can grow to. A test from near-whole wave paths tells when a tool is full-fair. The split of a tool in pole parts also marks the trait. Their marks serve tools with no bound, the hard case in the field. The work rounds out flip-fair tool lore for smooth spaces.
arxiv-2507-02247:
Jinlu Li, Xing Wu, and Yanghai Yu prove negative results for fluid equations in twenty twenty-five. They study the basic equations of fluid dynamics on a torus. The Euler equations describe inviscid flow, while Navier-Stokes adds viscosity. Solutions are sought in Besov spaces, a scale of function spaces used for rough data.

The authors construct new initial data and give a simple proof of ill-posedness. That means solutions in the chosen space fail to depend well on their starting values. Their result covers earlier work on both Euler and surface quasi-geostrophic equations. They also prove that the inviscid limit fails to converge in the same space. Both Navier-Stokes and quasi-geostrophic flows are covered. Readers get sharper limits on where fluid theory can hold.
arxiv-2507-02347: Marco Mackaay, Vanessa Miemietz, and Pedro Vaz took early steps in 2025 toward categorifying the Zelevinsky tensor product for extended affine type A Hecke algebras. They worked with Soergel bimodules induced from a maximal parabolic subalgebra. Categorification lifts algebra-based forms into richer categorical ones, and the Zelevinsky product is a key construction on representations of these algebras. The paper begins that program for the extended affine setting.
arxiv-2507-02647:
Luis Garza-Soto and Nathan Hagen show how rotation phase, the twist a wave picks up by a rotation path, grows from plain wave additions. Past work built the story on straight wave kinds. Their 2025 work runs it on round wave kinds too, and on a rotated rotator: a spin tool that is itself spun. In each case, two part waves of split direction and size add, and the direction of the sum leans to the bigger part.

That lean is the phase. Two classic cases prove the way: a three-mirror set, and a coil of glass fiber. In both, the shift falls out of the wave direction counts with no deep shape math and no solid-angle sums.
arxiv-2507-02747:
Ten researchers present DexVLG, a large model that tells a many-fingered robot hand how to grasp objects in line with spoken or written instructions. Robots with simple grippers have advanced quickly, but dexterous hands are harder, mostly because training data is scarce. The team works from a single color-and-depth view of a tabletop scene.

To train the model, they built DexGraspNet 3.0 in simulation: 170 million grasp poses spread over 174,000 objects. Each pose was matched to a named part of the object and a detailed written caption. A vision-language model reads the scene and the instruction, and a pose generator then shapes the hand's approach. In physics simulations the system reached over 76 percent success on objects it had never seen, with leading accuracy for grasping the requested part. Trials on a real robot hand confirmed that the grasps work on physical objects too.
arxiv-2507-03247:
Ruining Zhao and six co-authors report spectra of the comet 12P/Pons-Brooks in two thousand twenty-five. The comet is of Halley type and prone to outbursts. Spectra were taken in visible and near infrared light during two outbursts. Big telescopes on the ground did the work.

The infrared spectra show dips that match water ice. Fine crystals of ice at cold heat fit the bands well. Tiny hard grains, like amorphous carbon, add the red dust glow. Visible light shows gas bands from carbon and nitrogen groups. Gas ratios mark the comet as typical in one trait and low in another. Ice change likely drove the outburst.
arxiv-2507-03347:
Sachith Gunasekara and Yasiru Ratnayake compare structured and free form reasoning in language models in 2025. Many systems force models to output neat structured plans. That aids trust and control, but may cost skill. The pair adapt a self discovery method to work case by case. Models build their own plan for each task in one of two forms.

Tests span many benchmarks with top open models. Free form plans won in a steady way. On a hard math test, the gain reached near a fifth over structured plans. Free form with no examples even beat structured plans with five examples. The best plan grain, case or task, depended on context. The authors urge a rethink of forced formats.
arxiv-2507-03447:
Michal Wlodarczyk speeds up a classic graph task: finding the widest gap between any two points in a network. Exact answers take too long on big graphs, and even rough answers hit a hard wall in general. Past fast methods worked only for flat or near-flat graphs. The 2025 paper pushes past that limit.

Two new methods give answers within a hair of exact, in near-linear time, for two wider graph families. One covers graphs that avoid a fixed peak-like pattern; the other covers graphs built from a flat base plus a few extra hubs. A stepping stone is a fast distance lookup tool for the first family, the first of its kind beyond flat graphs. All the methods are fixed, with no random steps.
arxiv-2507-03747:
Sudhakantha Girmohanta, Yuichiro Nakai, and Zhihao Zhang propose a dark-sector origin story for matter's edge over antimatter in a 2025 paper. The universe holds far more matter than antimatter, and dark matter outweighs both. Their scenario brews both facts in one event after the early hot era.

A supercooled phase change in a dark sector drives the process out of balance. A mother particle, born through resonance during the change, decays unevenly between matter and antimatter forms. That dark imbalance is then reprocessed into the visible world. The numbers work out for a transition near one GeV in energy. The same event could explain a faint gravitational wave hum reported by pulsar timing teams. Neutron-antineutron tests may probe the idea.
arxiv-2507-03847:
Reilly Haskins and Benjamin Adams present a system that not only catches language model hallucinations but explains them, in this 2025 paper. Their framework builds a knowledge graph from the model's answer and compares it with trusted graphs from Wikidata or supplied documents. Graph kernels measure how the structures differ, and semantic clustering groups the mismatches into readable reasons.

Detection accuracy held up on both open and closed question sets. More importantly, the output is contrastive: it shows what the answer claims against what the record supports. That makes the flag useful to a human checker rather than a bare score. The authors aim the work at high-stakes uses where a wrong sentence costs real harm, and sketch multi-source checks as the next step.
arxiv-2507-04247:
Qiang Heng and Caixing Wang stake out a middle path in optimization: cheaper than second-order methods, faster than first-order ones, in a 2025 paper. First-order steps are cheap but crawl; second-order steps fly but demand expensive matrix inversions each round. Their trick is to minimize a fixed-curvature quadratic cap over the true objective at every step.

Because the cap's curvature never changes, its matrix factorization is computed once and reused across iterations and even across regularization settings. The framework, QMME, adds momentum-style extrapolation and comes with convergence guarantees under standard assumptions, analyzed through the cap's induced norm. Applied to large kernel learning problems, including a new equation-based model for multinomial regression, it beat established rivals in reproducible Julia experiments. It also paired well with sketching approximations. The authors pitch the reuse idea as the real export.
arxiv-2507-04347:
Mikaelian gives, in a solo 2025 paper, an explicit algorithm for the Higman Embedding Theorem, a classic result in group theory. The theorem states that a finitely generated group can be embedded in a finitely presented group if and only if the group is recursive. The original proof shows that such a host group exists, but gives no clear recipe for building it.

The new algorithm takes any recursive group, given by its effectively enumerable generators and recursively enumerable relations, and writes out the finitely presented host group in full. The host can even be chosen to have just two generators. The method has been applied to the additive group of rational numbers, a case mentioned as open by earlier authors. It rests on standard constructions such as free products with amalgamation and HNN extensions, plus new modifications. The paper also analyzes which steps of the original proof remain non-explicit.
arxiv-2507-04747:
Aliev, Guliyev, and Jabiyev solve a best approximation problem for functions of three variables in twenty twenty-five. The question asks how well such a function can be matched by a sum of three single variable functions. Each term depends on just one coordinate. The error is measured by the largest gap over the unit cube.

They prove a formula that computes this smallest possible error. The formula holds under certain conditions on the function. The infimum runs over all triples of continuous one variable functions. Results of this kind are rare in multivariable approximation theory. Exact error formulas help judge when separable approximations suffice. The work is a theoretical contribution to approximation theory.
arxiv-2507-04847:
Jinsheng Li and co-authors rebuild in a 2025 study a sensing task — recovering many signals that are sparse in frequency — as filling in a partly blank tensor. Stacking the signals into a Hankel tensor exposes a low-rank shape the recovery can exploit. Their algorithm, ScalHT, descends with scaling while respecting both the low-rank and Hankel structures.

Fast formulas wring up to an order-of-magnitude saving in memory and time from the interplay of the two structures. Proofs of recovery and steady convergence, the first of their kind here, back the speed. Simulations beat prior methods on cost and accuracy alike.
arxiv-2507-05047:
Philipp Kessler and co-authors report in a 2025 paper a pattern imprinted charge order on ultrathin ruthenium oxide films. The compound draws fame as a candidate for a novel magnetic order. Bulk proof of that order stays shaky, so thin films and surfaces draw the focus.

Films one layer thick on a ruthenium base were probed by tunneling scans and two theory methods. A nonmagnetic charge order follows the moire pattern of the film stack. Scattering inside a flat surface band sharpens that order, the team find. A second, switchable surface pattern arises from soft surface vibrations in the films. Polarized scans find no trace of magnetic order on the surface at all.
arxiv-2507-05247:
Farooq and co-authors rethink how deep learning should scan the genome for disease links. Standard genome-wide studies miss tangled, nonlinear gene interactions, and earlier learning methods either restricted the search to known pathways or leaked information through careless feature selection. The team instead tunes network architecture to work honestly on the full data.

Their framework then stretches to five diseases at once, exploiting the genetic overlap between them. Run on five million variants across 37,000 samples, it reaches solid predictive scores without leakage. The authors present it as a scalable, biologically meaningful route to multi-disease genome analysis, with covariates prevented from inflating the results.
arxiv-2507-05347:
Rodolfo Capdevilla proposes catching gravity waves by watching light twist. This 2025 letter rests on a known effect: a passing background of gravitational waves shifts the polarization of photons. The setup fires a vertical-polarized laser pulse through the wave field, then through a crystal that splits light by polarization. Photons that come out horizontal count as the signal.

A space rig spanning a million kilometers, on the scale of the LISA mission, could do the job with a millisecond pulse. It might even catch the hidden pulsars blamed for extra gamma rays at the galaxy's center. Changing the pulse length tunes the hunt to other wave backgrounds from the early universe. The letter sketches a fresh observational path.
arxiv-2507-06447:
Arkady Krasheninnikov, Yung-Chang Lin, and Kazu Suenaga review a way to make new flat materials inside a double sheet of graphene, in work from 2025. Graphene is a one-atom-thick sheet of carbon, strong and calm in most settings. Slipping atoms or small units between two such sheets is called intercalation.

The sheets shield what sits between them, so even shaky flat materials can be held steady there. Some sheets made this way are wholly new and have no bulk form. Sharp microscopes can watch their structure through the graphene. The review weighs lab results against theory, notes where they clash, and maps open problems. It also looks at using other layered hosts for the same trick.
arxiv-2507-06547:
Yonghyun Park and co-authors ask which training images taught a picture generator a specific concept in this 2025 paper. Whole-image credit is too blunt when disputes concern a style or an object inside an image. Their method, Concept-TRAK, reshapes influence analysis to score contributions concept by concept.

Special training and scoring losses isolate the chosen concept rather than overall image likeness. On new concept benchmarks and an established one, the method beat earlier attribution tools by wide margins. It also handled real text-to-image prompts mixing several concepts. The authors pitch concept-level credit as firmer ground for copyright questions and model transparency.
arxiv-2507-07247:
Zhengyu Tian and co-authors published a 2025 study measuring what eight ways of paying attention actually cost to train. Attention is the core mechanism of language and vision models, and also their bottleneck: it eats memory and time. Many leaner variants exist, but papers usually report theory, not meter readings. The team trained the same mid-size language model with each variant and measured everything.

Their meters tracked training time, graphics memory, raw operations, processor load, and electric power. Variants with well-optimized low-level code, such as Flash Attention, led the pack. The rankings by energy and memory did not always match the rankings by theoretical cost. That gap is the paper's lesson: big-O notation does not pay the power bill. For labs planning training runs, the study offers rare like-for-like numbers on hardware, turning a design choice into an informed budget decision.
arxiv-2507-07347:
Zhenyang Xiao and David Burghoff present a cleaner way to filter signals in a 2025 paper. Bandpass filtering is a staple of spectroscopy, the study of matter through light. The usual trick of padding a signal's edges with mirrored data bends the ends of the result.

Their rubber band filter pads the signal in an optimal way during filtering, so the edges stay clean. The method runs in loops but needs only a few extra transforms over standard practice. They show it on three real cases: time-domain, Fourier-transform, and dual-comb spectroscopy. In each, the new filter beat the standard one, which makes it a handy tool for labs.
arxiv-2507-07447:
Ying-Lin Li, Po-Hao Chou, and Chung-Yu Mou map the topological character of magnetic phases in a model of electrons that hop, repel, and feel spin-orbit coupling. The model has several orbitals per site, and allowed magnetic orders go beyond the up-down pattern. Two spin-orbit coupling forms are compared, named Dresselhaus and Rashba after their discoverers. The team reshapes it into a simpler t-J form and computes spin patterns at half filling.

Under one coupling, spins settle into the classic alternating pattern. Under the other, spins lie in a plane, slightly tilted, mixing alternating and aligned behavior along different axes. Each carries its own topological index and protection. The authors also check surfaces: states there stay open or gapped depending on how the surface faces the pattern's aligned part. They offer it as a guide to real magnetic materials.
arxiv-2507-07847:
Youngjoon Jang and five co-authors show that cleaning up pronouns and names in retrieved documents makes retrieval-augmented chatbots answer better, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such systems fetch documents to ground their answers, but tangled references, a bare 'he' or 'the company', blur what the text means. The team measured the damage and the repair across the pipeline.

Resolving who each pronoun points to improved both the fetching step and the final answers. One pooling choice, averaging, captured the cleaned context best. Smaller models gained the most, since they struggle hardest with ambiguity on their own. The authors offer the fix as cheap guidance for knowledge-heavy AI tools.
arxiv-2507-07947:
Researchers warn in 2025 that plain, harmless-looking prompts can trick image models into rebuilding memorized training pictures. Past rebuild attacks needed heavy compute, partial access to training data, or crafted prompts. A low-cost route would widen the privacy and copyright risk a great deal.

Their attack hunts for benign prompts tied to templated shop photos, where layouts repeat with pattern-like text. One bland prompt for a blue unisex T-shirt yields the face of a real person from one model. Blending the weak spots with real user prompt logs finds more prompts that echo memorized visuals. The flaw, they argue, grows from scraped shop data itself, not from attacker skill alone.
arxiv-2507-08847:
Gabriel Silva ties steering power, steering cost, information, and entropy in one frame for linear flows. His test bed is the damped spring oscillator, a plain case with rich behavior. His 2025 work works out the steering Gramian set and its spread for each damping kind. That spread reads as least steering cost: how cheap a push can drive the system to a set state.

Damping grade and sway rate shift the cost in set ways. Information forms face the Gramian set and line up: keen readings and cheap steering prove two faces of one coin. Entropy stories join too: ease of steering tracks how much information the system holds and sheds. One frame thus binds cost and information for flow craft.
arxiv-2507-08947:
Lorenzo Miretti, Slawomir Stańczak, and Giuseppe Caire prove that two jobs radio staff now do apart can stay apart at no cost. The jobs are to gauge the channel and to form beams. In nets with lots of users and antennas, send-side beam work and read-side blends could tangle with the gauge work. Their split rule says no. MMSE gauge first, then MMSE beams, is as good as any joint plan.

Two stock net types fall in the rule's reach. One is cell-based and leans on the two-way trait of air paths. The next is cell-free and huge. Hub-based and spread-out builds are in scope. Plain cases and test runs show the uses. Build the gauge block and the beam block apart. Each can be best at its own task.
arxiv-2507-09247:
Mihailo Stojnic presents in 2025 an algorithm that nearly reaches the best known ground state energy for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass model. Finding that state is a hard binary optimization problem in the worst case, yet the model's randomness lets fast methods get close in typical cases. A gap between those fast results and the optimum had remained.

His method builds on a controlled loosening approach first used in planted models. Analysis through a lifted theory matches the runs well. For sizes in the few thousands, the method reached about the level expected in the limit for very large systems. The author argues that, for practical use, the gap is nearly closed.
arxiv-2507-09447:
Konghao Sun and Haiping Hu build a band theory for messy systems in a 2025 physics paper. A newer theory explains odd effects in materials that gain or lose energy, such as modes that pile up at edges. That theory needs a perfect repeating lattice, so it fails once disorder enters.

Their version works in real space, using growth rates called Lyapunov exponents. It links the spread of energy levels and how states localize to those rates, under different edge rules. A sharp test also emerges: edge piled modes carry a nonzero winding count, while plain trapped modes carry zero. The test exposes the deep nature of the shift between the two.
arxiv-2507-09947:
Eric Herrison Gyamfi builds a mathematical model of cholera that breathes with the seasons and includes vaccination as the main control. The model follows susceptible, vaccinated, sick, and recovered people, plus the level of cholera bacteria in the environment. Transmission rises and falls across the year, and the vaccine is imperfect, with protection that fades over time.

His threshold measure is the reproduction number: when conditions hold it down, the disease-free state can be reached, and when it stays high, the disease persists. Testing the model's sensitivity, he finds that raising the vaccination rate and slowing the loss of immunity both push the threshold measure down strongly. Seasonal swings complicate timing, so campaigns land best before high-transmission periods. Gyamfi offers the model as a planning tool for poor regions with seasonal outbreaks, best combined with sanitation and education.
arxiv-2507-10447:
Tomasz Sroka and co-authors test how well a fake-music detector holds up when the audio is altered, in a 2025 paper. As AI music generators improve, telling machine-made tracks from human ones grows harder, and detectors have been built to do it. Real audio, though, rarely stays pristine: it gets compressed, filtered, and re-recorded.

The team built a dataset of real tracks and synthetic ones from several generators. They then ran a range of audio tweaks over the set and measured how a recent top detector scored each version. Accuracy fell sharply even under light tweaks. The authors warn that lab scores overstate how these detectors will fare in the wild, and they frame robustness testing as a must for the field.
arxiv-2507-10747:
Kaustubh Tangsali and colleagues set out a test frame for AI models that predict airflow for cars. The frame sits inside the open-source NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo-CFD toolkit. It is meant to check accuracy, speed, scale, and how well models cope with new cases. It does so in a set, shared way.

The frame supports a wide set of scores that matter for car design work. Users can add more models and more data sets. To show it in use, the team tests surface and volume flow results from three AI models. The models are DoMINO, X-MeshGraphNet, and FIGConvNet, and the data set is DrivAerML. They also give rules for adding scores that fit the physics. Clear tests should help teams pick and improve AI tools for car design.
arxiv-2507-10847:
The smallest stars, late-M dwarfs, spin in ways that differ from the steady slow-down of hotter stars. Measuring their rotation can reveal how spin evolves near the boundary between stars and brown dwarfs. Samantha Lambier and co-authors used light curves from the TESS space telescope to study 399 candidate single late-M dwarfs in 2025.

The team first estimated spin periods with a standard period-finding method, then refined them with a flexible curve-fitting approach, requiring confirmation across observing sectors where possible. They secured 133 periods, from two hours to six days, and found that the share of stars showing spot-driven variation climbs with more data toward about half. Their results grew the known sub-day periods by about three quarters. Across spectral types, the fastest allowed spin quickens from five hours for early M dwarfs to one hour for the coolest dwarfs.
arxiv-2507-11247:
Veronika Shilova and co-authors propose a way to group people by a continuous trait, such as skin tone, so that hidden discrimination in face analysis can surface, in a paper from 2025. Fairness checks usually split people into fixed groups first. For a graded trait, preset bins can bury the very subgroups that suffer most.

Their method lets the data choose the split: it searches for the grouping that maximizes the spread of measured discrimination between groups. Tests on synthetic data showed the split stays sound when the population shifts. Applied to two large face datasets with machine-read skin tone, the method found finer patterns of bias than fixed bins had shown. A special case where fairness should change smoothly with tone is also treated.
arxiv-2507-12047:
Michal Dvořák and co-authors study route-finding in graphs that delete their own edges as you walk in a 2025 paper. Each stop on the walk can erase a set of edges, so the map shifts under your feet. The task is to reach a set end point, or to find the shortest such path, without crossing an erased edge.

Even on very tame graphs, the plain reach task is as hard as the hardest check-type problems. The shortest form is hard in a layered sense when graded by path length. For some shape grades, though, the team finds fast schemes, and shows no small core summary exists for others.
arxiv-2507-12147:
The Dirac system is a pair of linked differential equations that sits under relativistic quantum models. Much of the theory built on it depends on how its solutions behave when the spectral parameter grows very large. Alexander Gomilko and Łukasz Rzepnicki derive detailed asymptotic formulas in 2025 for the system's basic solutions. They work on a finite interval, and they allow the coefficients to be rough rather than smooth. Their formulas hold across a whole half-plane of the complex parameter, not just along the real line.

The payoff reaches beyond the Dirac system itself. The results give new half-plane asymptotics for the classic Sturm–Liouville equation in the hard case where its potential is singular. Formulas of this kind matter wherever eigenvalues and scattering data are computed from such systems, so the paper serves both the Dirac theory and its older cousin.
arxiv-2507-12547:
Lionel Wong and co-authors model open world cognition as on demand synthesis of probabilistic models, in a 2025 paper. People facing a novel case can pull in relevant background knowledge from many fields and reason over it in a coherent way. How the mind does that so flexibly is the puzzle at the heart of the work.

Their architecture uses language models to fetch what is relevant and draft a bespoke model, while probabilistic programs keep the reasoning sound. A test set built around sports vignettes asks for judgments on novel causal setups with new variables. The hybrid matched human judgments better than language only baselines. The result hints at how people build fresh mental models on the fly.
arxiv-2507-12947:
Pechonkin, Klen, and Semenov present a circular-beam approximation for quantum channels in turbulent air, in a research paper from 2025. Free-space quantum links suffer as air turbulence makes transmittance flicker at random. A standard elliptic-beam model fits data well in a narrow range, but it is complex and can bias results outside that range.

The circular-beam version simplifies the model while keeping fair accuracy. Its parameters come from the first two moments of transmittance, a direct route that avoids the old bias. The range of channel settings where the model holds grows wider. The tool gives labs a practical way to characterize air channels for quantum use.
arxiv-2507-13347:
Yifan Wang and co-authors rebuild 3D scenes from photos without crowning any one photo as the reference. Earlier feed-forward reconstructors anchor everything to a chosen viewpoint, and a bad anchor wobbles the whole result. Their 2025 network, named pi-cubed, is permutation-equivariant: shuffle the input images and the answer shuffles to match, nothing privileged.

From the image set it predicts each camera's pose in a form indifferent to the scene's overall placement, plus per-view point maps that ignore global scale. Across camera pose estimation, depth estimation from one or many frames, and dense point mapping, the design reached state-of-the-art results. The authors credit the symmetry itself: removing the reference bias removed a failure mode. Code and models are public, an invitation to build on the bias-free recipe.
arxiv-2507-13447:
Barry Dillon and Michael Spannowsky link physics theory with machine learning in this 2025 paper. Their task is to match particles seen in collider events back to the base particles that made them. That matching task grows fast as events get more complex. Most tools learn it from labeled data and act like black boxes.

Their method turns matching into a step-by-step game. A network earns a score at each step based on how much a physics formula changes. Since the score comes from theory alone, no labels are needed. The tool held up on top quark events of rising complexity. They also build a classifier and an anomaly search tool from the same base.
arxiv-2507-13547:
Some heat equations spread unevenly, flowing freely in one direction while barely moving in another, and the Grushin operator is a classic tool for that kind of spread. Ahmad Fino and Arlucio Viana study a heat equation driven by this operator and disturbed by two nonlinear reaction terms. One term carries memory, so today's flow depends on the whole past, adding effects that reach across time. The authors first prove that solutions exist for a short time and behave well, in spaces that measure size and in spaces of smooth functions fading at distance.

They then build comparison rules, which bound a hard solution between easier ones, to find when solutions last forever. Whether a solution exists for all time depends on the strength and character of the two reaction terms. The memory term shifts that balance in visible ways. The results extend the theory of such uneven heat flow.
arxiv-2507-13847:
Katsumi Inoue and Daniil Kozhemiachenko present a 2025 paper on the cost of finding explanations in a logic where truth comes in degrees. Everyday claims like "the lift is loaded" are partly true rather than simply true or false. The logic they use gives every statement a value on a scale.

Abduction means proposing causes that would explain what is seen. The authors define such problems for this fuzzy logic, enriched with statements that bound a variable's value. They then grade the core tasks: checking a candidate answer, deciding whether one exists, and judging whether a guess is needed. In the clause only fragment, the tasks prove cheaper than in the full language, unlike the classic case.
arxiv-2507-14147:
Insomnia is common, and standard treatments often bring side effects such as headaches and dizziness. Kevin Monteiro and three co-authors ask whether brain modeling, already used in other brain disorders, can help explain the sleepless brain. They record long stretches of brain-wave data and build networks from how strongly the recording sites connect and how far apart they sit.

A graph-based neural network then learns to tell insomnia patterns from healthy ones. The best setup used 50-second windows of data and reached 70 percent accuracy per window and 68 percent per person. Removing three particular electrode pairs hurt performance most, and those sites sit near regions known to connect oddly in insomnia. The work is an early step toward model-guided treatment.
arxiv-2507-14247:
Shiruo Wang charts how the bend count grows in a tower of bent lines in a 2025 paper. The tower climbs line on line, each bent path a wrap of the last, and its whole crew of turns is a round ring of counts.

Such towers serve the lore of sums on finite fields. Wang asks when the bend count, the genus, grows as a clean square law in the tower's height. For tall towers she finds all the crews for which that clean law holds. The proof sorts the towers by how their wraps branch. The work gives a full list for this crew kind, a list past lore had in part. Wang casts the square law as a stamp a tower can be known by.
arxiv-2507-14347:
Ole Hans and Benedikt Walter wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about choosing remote support for self-driving vehicles. Highly automated cars still meet situations they cannot handle. With no driver aboard, help must come from afar, either as remote driving, where a human steers directly, or remote assistance, where a human advises while the car drives itself.

Developers often pick by system design or by which option is simpler to build. The authors argue the real test is the match with the vehicle's defined operating domain and its use cases. They apply a known framework to describe that domain in a structured way. Their method weighs how well each support style complements the automated system in each scenario.
arxiv-2507-14547:
Noman Ahmad and co-authors map what is known about software architecture decay in a 2025 paper. Systems slowly drift from their intended design as fixes and features pile up, a process called architectural degradation. The harm lands on quality, upkeep cost, and the ease of future change. Yet the research on it is scattered, with clashing definitions and tools.

The team reviewed 108 studies from journals and gray sources alike. They sorted definitions, causes, measures, and repair routes into one taxonomy spanning design debt, code debt, and process debt. Old views framed decay as a code-level fault; newer ones treat it as a social and technical problem. Detection is well covered, with dozens of metrics and tools. Ongoing repair is not, and the authors urge joined-up prevention.
arxiv-2507-14647:
Go Nishikawa and five co-authors built a system that predicts how natural a synthetic voice sounds, whatever sampling rate it arrives in. Human opinion scores guide speech synthesis, but collecting them is slow, and recordings at different sampling rates expose different detail, tripping up automatic judges. Their entry to a 2025 prediction challenge adds a sampling-frequency-independent layer to a self-supervised speech model, so features are extracted on an even footing.

Two training tricks improved the judge: distilling knowledge from a strong pretrained model, and pretraining on a large opinion-score dataset before fine-tuning. The submission placed first on one official metric and fourth overall. Ablation tests showed which parts of the recipe mattered most. The authors present the work as a step toward automatic voice-quality checks that treat a cheap phone-rate clip and a studio-rate file by the same standard.
arxiv-2507-15147:
Yiqi Zhao and co-authors present a 2025 paper on writing precise rules for groups of cooperating machines. Fleets of robots, smart city sensors, and similar systems must meet mission, safety, and reliability goals. Those goals depend on how agents sense each other, share messages, and depend on each other's tasks.

The authors model agent links as several directed graphs, one per kind of tie. They then define a logic, called STL-GO, with graph operators built in. These operators can state rules such as requiring an agent to sense at least two neighbors able to work with it. They also give ways for each agent to check the rules using only local information, and they compare how much the new logic can express.
arxiv-2507-15747:
Sabrina Caputo and Giusi Vaira wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five about a critical Choquard equation. Such equations describe a field that interacts with itself across distance, through a convolution term. The authors study a version with a symmetric potential that depends only on distance from the origin.

Using a finite dimensional reduction method, they prove a strong existence result. If a certain scaled form of the potential has a local peak or dip at some positive radius, the equation admits infinitely many solutions that are not radial. Those solutions can have arbitrarily large energies. The result adds to knowledge of how nonlocal terms and symmetry shape the solution set of such equations.
arxiv-2507-15847: Maciej Borodzik and Weronika Buczynska study in a 2025 paper one parameter families of Morse functions on manifolds with boundary. Morse functions read a shape through their critical points. Letting one parameter slide shows how those points can merge, split, or vanish. The pair list every degeneracy that can arise in a generic such family. Boundary cases get full treatment alongside the interior ones in the catalog. The list serves as a map for tracking shape change in families.
arxiv-2507-16147:
Jian-Qi Liu, Yan-Hong Yao, Yan Su, and Jia-Wei Wu test a cosmos where dark matter flows like a fluid with pressure. Cold, pressureless dark matter rules the standard model but strains at small scales. Their variant gives dark matter one fixed pressure trait. Dark energy, meanwhile, emerges from the cosmos itself rather than sitting as a constant.

The team checked the model against four major data sets. Sky maps of the early universe, galaxy distance markers, and exploding stars all fed the test. The combined data hint that the dark matter trait sits above zero. Its sound speed shares the same value in their setup. Yet when models were scored head to head, the standard model won by a wide margin. The authors report both the hint and the verdict plainly.
arxiv-2507-16347:
Yumeng Wang and co-authors teach graph networks to cope when neighbours carry unlike labels. Their 2025 paper notes that most graph methods assume linked nodes match, yet many real graphs break that rule. Older fixes lean on direct links alone and miss wider structure.

Their model, HPGNN, blends a PageRank-style spread with higher-order patterns in the graph. A fast approximation captures long-range ties at several scales while cutting cost. The added structure also damps noise from clashing labels nearby. On standard test graphs the model beat most rivals on unlike-label data. It stayed competitive where labels do match. Code is public.
arxiv-2507-16447:
Masaharu Nagayama, Koya Sakakibara, and Keisuke Takasao study a model of a self-propelled deformable object in this 2025 paper. Their phase-field model separates the body from the surrounding fluid with one equation. A second equation tracks the surfactant that drives motion through surface tension effects.

The authors ask what happens as the interface thickness shrinks toward zero. They prove the fuzzy model converges to a sharp-interface limit, still coupled to the surfactant equation. In that limit, the surface moves with a speed set by its mean curvature, the surface tension, and a volume-preserving effect. The result puts earlier modeling of such swimmers on firmer mathematical ground. It also clarifies which terms survive the idealization.
arxiv-2507-16547:
Edoardo Ballico and Changho Keem study Hilbert schemes of smooth curves of low degree in five-dimensional projective space. A Hilbert scheme parametrizes all curves of a given degree and genus in that space. The authors focus on the Hilbert function of a general member of each component, especially for degrees up to fifteen.

They determine the irreducibility of these Hilbert schemes for degrees up to fourteen. They also study in detail the natural map from the Hilbert scheme to the moduli space of curves. For a general curve, they describe the fiber of that map over the curve's moduli point, and they determine when the curve is projectively normal or arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay. The results map out how low-degree curves sit inside projective space and how their equations behave. Such classification work underpins algebraic geometers' understanding of curves and the spaces that collect them.
arxiv-2507-16747:
James Hughes and Jiajie Ma settle, in a 2025 math paper, when a class of knotted curves can be filled in by a special surface. The curves come from closing a three strand braid, in a setting where curves carry a contact structure. A filling is a surface that ends on the curve and meets a set of exactness rules, and it may or may not have a handle like orientation.

Their main result supports a published conjecture about the orientable case. A three braid closure has such a filling exactly when it is quasipositive, a notion of being built from positive twists, and when a known bound from a knot polynomial is sharp. As a side contribution, they build explicit representatives with the largest possible value of a classic knot measure. The work ties braid algebra to surface geometry in a complete answer for this case.
arxiv-2507-16947:
Robert Korom and co-authors report a real-world test of an AI helper for front-line clinics, in this 2025 study. The clinics belong to a network in Nairobi, Kenya. Their tool, AI Consult, uses a large language model to act as a safety net. It scans visit notes and flags likely errors in records or care choices, speaking up only when needed. Clinicians stay in charge throughout.

The study compared visits where clinicians had the helper against visits where they did not. It covered close to forty thousand patient visits in live care. The team tracked how often errors were caught and whether care quality changed. Their work offers rare field evidence on whether such AI support helps or hinders daily practice in busy clinics.
arxiv-2507-18647:
Rayyan Ridwan made a pneumonia sensor for children's chest X-rays that explains itself in a 2025 paper. Pneumonia kills many children worldwide, and fast, trustworthy reading of scans could help clinics with few specialists. Deep models can be exact yet opaque, which slows adoption where a wrong call is dangerous. The study pairs a residual network with an explainability method that also reports its own doubt.

The network reached high accuracy and discrimination scores on a large pediatric data set. Its visual explanations highlighted regions health staff found meaningful for the diagnosis. Pairing a strong score with an honest map of evidence, plus doubt where the map is unsure, is the combination health rollout demands.
arxiv-2507-19047:
Guru Sharan and Armin Straub count special shapes hidden inside number partitions, in a 2025 paper. A partition splits a whole number into a sum of smaller parts, often drawn as rows of boxes. Inside such a drawing, the largest triangle with rows of length one, two, three, and so on is called its Durfee triangle, a cousin of the better-known Durfee square.

The pair work out the counting formulas for partitions whose Durfee triangle has a fixed size. The formulas come out as neat rational functions, much like the classic square case. They also pin down how fast the count grows as the number itself grows large. Counts like these help mathematicians see the hidden order inside simple sums.
arxiv-2507-19147:
Ignacio Sardinero and co-authors study current flow between superconductors in 2025. The pair they model are quasicrystals ordered by the Fibonacci sequence, a pattern that never quite repeats. Such layers can host edge states with energies above the normal gap.

Those edge states gain pairing traits of their own and carry part of the flow between the layers. The authors name these states after the Fibonacci pattern and the classic bound states they extend. Their share of the flow can be tuned by shifting the sequence pattern. In short junctions, they can outweigh the usual states entirely.
arxiv-2507-19447:
Daniil Klyuev and Joseph Vulakh wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It sorts the positive traces on two families of algebras known as Coulomb branches, which arise from gauge theories in three and four dimensions.

A positive trace is a map on the algebra with a sign-like trait tied to a flip of the algebra. In the first case the algebra is a quantized Kleinian singularity of type D, with a bound on the parameter. In the second it is a larger algebra built from a loop group, holding the branches for two related gauge groups. Sorting these traces can sharpen what is known about the theories at hand. The paper is a work of pure theory.
arxiv-2507-19547:
Atrial fibrillation is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder, and burning away faulty tissue cures it only when doctors find the true trouble spots. Pablo Peiro-Corbacho and co-authors teach a computer to read the heart's own electrical traces, recorded from inside the heart during procedures. Their data cover more than eleven thousand recordings from 291 patients.

An autoencoder network first compresses each trace into a compact code, without being told what to look for. Those codes kept the traces' shape while shrinking them greatly. Simple classifiers working on the codes could then spot spinning or focal activity fairly well. They were strikingly good at flagging tangled signals, a marker of problem regions. The authors say the method runs fast enough to guide doctors during live procedures.
arxiv-2507-20047:
MohammadHossein Bateni and co-workers give fast parallel algorithms for hierarchical clustering with tricky distance rules, in a 2025 paper. The clustering method repeatedly merges the closest pair of groups. Near-optimal parallel algorithms existed only for distance rules that never decrease after a merge.

Popular rules such as centroid and Ward's distance can decrease, and no parallel method was known for them. The authors prove the merge tree stays shallow for a broad class of such rules in low dimensions, which yields efficient parallel algorithms. A hardness result suggests the low-dimension limit is real: in full dimension the problem resists parallel solution. The structural finding may interest clustering researchers broadly.
arxiv-2507-20347:
Deepshikha and Aniruddha Samanta wrote a 2025 math paper on backup representations that survive losing several pieces of data. A frame is a redundant set of vectors for encoding signals, and a dual frame does the decoding. When some coefficients are erased, a good dual keeps the error small. The authors study duals that are spectrally optimal, minimizing the worst case error, for frames built from graphs.

Extending earlier work on one and two erasures, they treat any number of erasures. For frames from a connected graph, the standard canonical dual is the unique best choice. For disconnected graphs, the canonical dual is still optimal but shares the crown with others. Unitary copies of a frame share the same error behavior with their canonical duals.
arxiv-2507-20747:
Akhil Panicker and Sasidevan study how people changing their behavior can blunt an epidemic, in a 2025 paper. During an outbreak, many pull back: they travel less and meet fewer people, guided by news of how widespread the disease is. The pair model this response in space, where a share of the population shrinks its range of contact as case counts rise.

They test three ways the responding share can grow with case counts: steady, as a power curve, and as an S-shaped curve. In a well-mixed population they compute the response level needed to stop an outbreak, and in a fixed spatial layout they bound it. A simple proportional response adds nothing over a steady share, they find, while the S-shaped response can make case counts swing up and down.
arxiv-2507-20847:
Chaithra P and co-authors introduce marked versions of coloring counts for hypergraphs in this 2025 paper. A hypergraph lets edges join many vertices at once, widening the classic graph setting. The authors define marked multi-colorings, their counting polynomials, and a related independence series.

They show the coefficients of a power of the series match the marked coloring counts, extending a graph result from earlier work. The notions carry over to subspace arrangements, where the count of marked colorings is again a polynomial. For hyperplane arrangements, a signed power of the series has all non-negative coefficients. For hypergraphs, that niceness forces every edge to have even size, though the authors show evenness alone is not enough.
arxiv-2507-20947:
Ryota Matsuda and Zongping Gong give a plain sums line for a knot score in free charge crowds and draw wide caps from it. The score, entanglement negativity, counts how tied a mixed set stands. Their 2025 line runs through a bent shape sum of the set's own marks. Caps on the score and on its shift pace in play fall out of the line.

One cap ties the score straight to how fast ties fade with span, the root of the area law for tied size. Best terms for that law in long-tie mixed crowds are pinned. A like cap binds tie growth in open sets. Charge-set tie craft gains a set of hard walls.
arxiv-2507-21047:
Michelle Brann, Karin Öberg, and Mahesh Rajappan show in 2025 that reactive oxygen atoms can build a complex molecule inside icy grains like those in cold space clouds. Ultraviolet light frees excited oxygen from ozone in the ice. With radicals barely able to move at such low temperatures, direct oxygen insertion offers another route to chemical complexity on grains.

In vacuum chamber tests from ten to forty kelvin, oxygen inserted into methyl cyanide to form mainly methyl isocyanate. Rates showed no temperature dependence. In water or carbon dioxide ices the product still formed, though yields fell and side products appeared.
arxiv-2507-21247:
Ankit Singh and three co-authors teach video models to find actions when only some training clips are labeled. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Labeling where and when an action happens in video is costly, so methods that learn from few labels matter.

Their network uses two guides at once to pick better guessed boxes for unlabeled clips. One guide checks the action class for the whole frame. The other predicts the box itself, and the two must agree across frames and boxes. On three standard action data sets, the method beat adapted image-based rivals by a clear margin. The authors show that the double check is what lifts accuracy when labels are scarce.
arxiv-2507-21447:
