Zachariah Sollenberger, Rahul Patel, Saieda Ali Zada, and Sunita Chandrasekaran test whether large language models can write and grade compiler tests, in a two thousand twenty-five software engineering paper. The target is directive-based parallel programming models such as OpenMP.

Their dual system pairs a generative model that makes tests with a discriminative model that judges them, aiming at fully autonomous verification. Hallucination and unverifiable thinking are the central worries. Several models of varied sizes are compared across ten carefully defined metrics. The findings suggest language models can indeed generate quality compiler tests and check them automatically, a hopeful route to cheaper test development for high-performance computing.
arxiv-2507-21647:
Muhammad Anjum and co-authors present a 2025 study of blazars, galaxies whose jets point almost straight at Earth. The team modeled the full spread of light from bright blazars, using a picture where jet electrons are cooled and randomly sped up. A single-zone model with a curved electron energy spread fit the high-energy light well. The work then tracked how the peak of the light output shifts across objects.

One class of blazar followed a known trend in which brighter peaks sit at lower pitch. The team argues that this trend is real, not a trick of jet aiming. It seems driven by a balance between the jet's magnetic field and its particles. A second class of blazar broke from that balance, with jet traits varying more freely. A link between peak pitch and curve shape backed random speeding of particles in the jets.
arxiv-2507-22047:
Xiuwen Zheng and co-authors report on a 2025 challenge to improve speech recognition for people with speech disabilities. Automatic speech systems have advanced fast, yet they still serve disabled speakers poorly, partly because public training data is scarce. The challenge used a project data set of more than 400 hours of speech from over 500 people.

Teams were scored on word error rate and on a meaning-based score. Of 22 valid teams, 12 beat a strong standard system on errors, and 17 beat it on meaning. The top team led on both scores at once. The results set new benchmarks for recognizing impaired speech. The challenge was hosted on an open evaluation platform.
arxiv-2507-22147:
Alexander Zuyev and Julia Kalosha modeled a flexible beam with attached masses in 2025, working in the frequency domain. The beam rests on simple supports and carries a spring-loaded control device, with some local damping. Such setups matter for control systems that must handle bending and vibration.

Using a classic energy method, they derived the equations of motion in state form, with care for the points where parts join. They then worked out transfer functions for two beam models, one simpler and one that also counts shear effects. Charts compare the two models for different sensor choices and damping levels, showing where the models agree and where they part.
arxiv-2507-22647:
Lorenzo Volpi, Alejandro Moreo, and Fabrizio Sebastiani wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It deals with transductive learning, where the unlabeled data a model must label are known ahead of time, during training.

The paper tackles model selection, the step of tuning a model's settings, when the class balance in the data has shifted. Standard tuning relies on cross-checks within the labeled training data, which can mislead under such a shift. The authors propose tuning the settings directly on the unlabeled target data instead. Tests show this targeted approach beats the standard route. The work matters for tasks like sorting documents or screening cases, where the mix of classes in new data rarely matches the training mix.
arxiv-2507-22847:
Han Jiang and co-authors published a study in 2025 on how work on large language models draws on psychology. Their team looked at papers from leading venues on artificial intelligence from 2023 to 2025, and at the psychology papers those works cited. The aim was to map where the two fields meet and where they still miss each other.

Inside, the authors count which areas of psychology are cited most often and which are left out. They also check how theories from psychology are put to use, and where those theories are used in the wrong way. Readers get a clear map of the link, plus plain advice for using ideas about the mind with more care.
arxiv-2507-22947:
Shou'ang Wei and co-authors introduce a tool to test large language models in school settings, in a 2025 paper. School uses for these models are growing fast, but tests vary by scene and many new scenes have no fit test at all. Most current tests check general skill, not teaching skill.

Their open tool, ELMES, lets users build multi agent talks from simple setup files, with no deep coding needed. A mixed engine scores teaching traits that are hard to judge, using a model as judge. Tests in four school scenes, from explaining ideas to making lesson plans, showed unlike strengths across models. The tool gives schools a shared way to compare models.
arxiv-2507-23147:
Md Meftahul Ferdaus and co-authors review foundation models for clean energy forecasting in this 2025 paper. Grids need sharp forecasts of wind and solar output and of demand as clean power grows. Foundation models are large AI systems that can handle complex time data fast. The review covers how such models are built for this task. It also covers how they are pre-trained and then tuned for a site or task. Data types used in energy forecasting get their own survey.

Wind and solar are the twin focus areas of the piece. Designs that track space and time patterns together get special attention. The authors note how domain knowledge can be baked into the models. Gaps and open problems for the field are mapped as well. The review aims to guide both energy planners and AI builders. It appeared in a leading journal for renewable energy research.
arxiv-2507-23347:
Georgios Konstantinou, a solo author, reworks the theory of slow change in quantum systems, in two thousand twenty-five. The theory uses geometric structures that arise as a system's settings shift. Those structures, tied to the Berry phase, shape how quantum states gain extra phase beyond plain dynamics.

Konstantinou defines gauge fields from the full, time-based wave function, not a frozen snapshot. A Berry electric field then appears naturally, which standard treatments miss. He builds Maxwell-like equations for the Berry fields and checks them directly. The form exposes charges and currents hidden in the setting space. It also unifies still and changing cases in one frame.
arxiv-2508-00247:
Sergei Gleyzer and co-authors propose a new variant of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in work from 2025. These networks build complex functions from sums of single-variable functions, using learnable curves instead of fixed activation rules.

Their variant replaces both inner and outer functions with weighted sine waves whose frequencies can be learned. Phases are fixed at evenly spaced values, and the authors prove the design is valid in theory. In tests on multi-variable functions, the method beat fixed-frequency Fourier methods and matched standard perceptron networks. The work extends the search for better activation forms in this network family.
arxiv-2508-00747: Alexander Lytchak and Stephan Huckemann settle a question about averages on curved spaces in a 2025 math paper. A Frechet mean is the point that best stands in for random data on a curved surface, and its cut locus is the set where distance paths split. The authors prove that set carries zero probability for the mean, a claim known only in special cases before. They rule out a sticky effect, give rough examples, and discuss wider settings.
arxiv-2508-01147: Alexander Dukhovny offers a short foundations paper from 2025 on why probabilities multiply for independent events. The rule, that the chance of two independent events both occurring equals the product of their separate chances, is usually taken as a definition. Dukhovny instead derives it from a broader principle of fair judgment when no reason favors one outcome. He frames that principle as a maximum relative divergence rule applied to grading functions on an ordered set.
arxiv-2508-01747:
Traianou and co-authors image the jet of the blazar OJ 287 at record sharpness with a space radio telescope, in work from twenty twenty-five. OJ 287 is a galaxy core that fires a near light speed jet toward Earth. Fine jet shape tests ideas about the giant black hole pair thought to sit at its center.

A space antenna plus twenty-seven ground dishes formed baselines up to about five Earth widths. The innermost jet resolved into sharp bends, a ribbon like strip running down to tiny scales. Some spots shone at extreme brightness, a sign of strong beaming. Polarization pointed to a field running along the jet near the core. Older forty-three gigahertz data showed the jet angle swinging, like a rotating helix.
arxiv-2508-01947:
Yuly Wu, Jiamou Liu, and Libo Zhang tackle in 2025 how to learn the hidden rule machines behind agents that act with partial views of the world. Such agents' rewards and shifts can depend on history, not just the present, which breaks plain learning. Past rule machines covered reward history alone, forcing awkward problem setups.

The authors add transition machines for shift history and merge both into one dual machine. Their learning method reads past traces and infers the machine without costly conversions. Speed gains reach a thousandfold in tests, they report. Conditions for finding the smallest true machine are also given.
arxiv-2508-02447:
A wireless link can hide its message by jamming eavesdroppers, but jamming burns power that both ends must harvest from the air. Shalini Tripathi and co-authors tune that bargain in a 2025 paper, splitting power between the sender's signal and the receiver's noise. Batteries are small, so choices made now shape what is possible later.

Their method plans over a fixed stretch of time using learning from trial and error. It beat both a simple greedy rule and a version that pretends time never ends. The greedy rule nearly matched it when the sender's battery was full, and the endless version caught up as the time window grew.
arxiv-2508-02647:
Merging p-values from many tests is a basic statistical move, but discrete p-values break the usual recipes. Gonzalo Contador and Zheyang Wu extended in 2025 a transport-based fix that reshapes discrete values into a smooth stand-in distribution.

Their framework unifies five classic merging rules under one approach. Theory and simulations show error control holds when the adjusted spread matches the smooth case. When the best possible test is a monotone function of a merging rule, their approximation nearly matches its power. They demonstrate the method on a study of rare genetic variants and ship it in a free R package.
arxiv-2508-02747:
Moffat and Thompson set out a unified theory that aims to give the masses of all known particles in a 2025 paper. Their framework, called the Holomorphic Unified Field Theory, starts from a single action written on a complex version of spacetime. Built-in smoothing factors keep the loop calculations finite without breaking the theory's symmetries.

After the known force symmetries break, the theory yields formulas for the mass patterns of electrons, quarks, and neutrinos. Two free inputs fix the rest through a small flavor sector. Running the values across energy scales then predicts particle masses, mixing angles, and the Higgs boson's mass and self-interactions. The authors argue that force unification, three particle families, and the shape of the Higgs potential also fall out of the framework rather than being put in by hand.
arxiv-2508-03047:
Malek Itani, Tuochao Chen, and Shyamnath Gollakota shrink speech-splitting AI to fit inside an earpiece, in a 2025 paper. Splitting one voice from a noisy room helps hearing aids and earbuds, but top models are too heavy for tiny, low-power chips. Their new network works on the sound's time-and-pitch map. Flat layers sweep the map by channel and by pitch, while small filters handle time at each pitch band.

The trained model chews sound in six-millisecond bites, fast enough for live use on a named low-power chip. It beats older live models at both blind splitting and pulling out one target voice. It also runs three to four times faster than prior speech splitters. The work points to earpieces that can clear up speech on their own, without a phone or cloud doing the lifting.
arxiv-2508-03147:
Shang, Zedini, Kammoun, and Alouini design a relay chain that carries signals through the sky to indoor and outdoor users, in a 2025 paper. Their non-terrestrial system starts at an optical ground station. The beam bounces off a reflecting surface on a high-altitude platform. An earth station then relays it onward. Finally it passes through a smart building surface that both transmits and reflects.

The authors model both the optical and radio legs. For the radio link they introduce a sharper approximation than the standard approach. They derive exact formulas for outage chance, capacity, and error rate. Simpler high-power limits reveal the system's diversity behavior.
arxiv-2508-03247:
Shintaro Sakai and co-authors test cultural patterns in model answers in a 2025 paper. Clinical research says Western patients voice depression in mind based terms, while Eastern patients stress body complaints. As language models enter mental health work, the team asked whether models copy that split. They prompted models with Western or Eastern personas and read the symptoms the models produced.

In English, the models mostly failed to mirror the clinical pattern. Prompting in Chinese, Japanese, or Hindi improved the match in several setups. Two causes stood out: models barely heed persona cues, and a fixed symptom ranking overrides culture. The results warn that a model can sound fluent in mental health talk while missing how real patients in each culture present their pain.
arxiv-2508-03547:
Following written steps for a hands on task can be slow when the work is in front of you and the guide is on paper. Ada Yi Zhao and three co-authors present Guided Reality in 2025, a system that writes the steps and paints visual cues right onto the real scene through augmented reality glasses. Large language models draft the steps, and vision models find where each cue belongs.

The team sorted visual cues into five kinds drawn from user manuals, and the system picks a kind based on the step at hand. Sixteen users tried the system on real tasks and in open use. Four instructors also weighed in on how it could fit their training work.
arxiv-2508-03947:
Vishnu Murali, Mohammed Adib Oumer, and Majid Zamani introduce, in a 2025 paper, control closure certificates for building controllers with formal guarantees. The targets are endless-horizon rules, such as visiting a zone again and again forever. Standard proofs mix invariants with ranking arguments that show progress must end.

Closure certificates replace single rankings with disjunctive ones: several partial progress proofs that jointly force the goal. The authors show how to build such certificates for visiting a region endlessly, or only finitely often. Combining the two handles parity rules, the general form of such specs. A sum-of-squares search can then synthesize the certificate, and with it a controller that provably enforces the rule. Tests show the method designing working controllers.
arxiv-2508-05047:
Priya and co-authors build a particle theory model in a 2025 paper that tries to explain two puzzles at once: neutrino masses and why the universe holds more matter than antimatter. Their Type-III seesaw setup uses a modular symmetry with a fresh non-holomorphic twist to shape the couplings.

Fitting the model to current neutrino data gave a normal ordering of masses and tight limits on key phases. Heavy triplet decays in the hot early universe then create a matter-antimatter gap of the right size. Strong washout forces the process to a very high energy scale. Readers get a single frame linking lab neutrino data to cosmic origins.
arxiv-2508-05347:
Giedrius Alkauskas published this paper in 2025. It studies a jumping game with three fleas on a plane. At each move, two fleas leap to complete a square built on the segment between them. Starting from three set points, the question is which areas the flea triangle can ever span. Every positive half-integer area turns up. Integer areas hit every remainder class for every modulus.

Yet one family is missing entirely: no perfect square area ever occurs. The author explains the ban with quadratic reciprocity, a classic number theory law. Digging deeper, he ties the flea moves to integral Apollonian circle packings, a fractal circle geometry. A computer search up to a trillion found only five other missing non-square areas. The paper blends play, proof, and computation in a small, neat package.
arxiv-2508-05747:
Wahid and five colleagues propose using Composer packages to speed student Laravel projects in twenty twenty-five. Laravel is a web framework widely taught at universities. Students often struggle to finish projects within tight academic timelines. Composer is the standard dependency manager for the PHP language.

The paper curates packages that cut development effort for typical student systems. It frames their use in both practical and pedagogical terms. Good packages also teach professional workflows and code quality habits. Risks include package conflicts and over reliance on ready made tools. The authors give best practices to mitigate those risks. They stress that teachers must explain when and why to use a package, not just how.
arxiv-2508-05947:
Richard Lieu wrote this 2025 paper proposing that some fast radio bursts come from star winds bending radio waves. These bursts are millisecond flashes of radio energy from deep space. Their origin is still debated, and any new channel must match how evenly they spread across the sky.

Lieu models the wind of a star like the sun's, where plasma thins with distance squared. Just outside the star, the plasma pushes a passing signal outward about five times more than gravity pulls it in. The combined lens can focus a faint steady source into a millisecond flash. His count gives roughly eighty bursts a day across the sky, and binary stars could make some repeat.
arxiv-2508-06047:
Language models can write chip code, but the test sets used to grade them are stuck on toy circuits. Suresh Purini and five co-authors built ArchXBench in 2025, a six-step ladder of real digital designs. Its tasks span hard math circuits and parts drawn from code-breaking, image work, learning chips, and signal gear. Each task ships with a spec and a test rig, so scores can be checked by machine.

Four top models took the ladder with plain prompts, five tries each. The best solved sixteen of thirty tasks, all on the lower three steps. From step four up, every model failed every task. The gap marks where today's chip-writing aids stop being of use. The catalog record pastes address text into the title field, so the draft follows the clean head title.
arxiv-2508-06247:
Zichun Ye, Runqi Wang, Xutong Liu, and Shuai Li design a learning algorithm for repeated group choices in a 2025 paper. The setting is a bandit problem, where a learner picks a set of options each round and sees rewards for the picked set only. Good methods exist, but some pay an extra penalty that grows with time, while others cost heavy computing.

Their method, CMOSS, removes that time penalty while staying cheap to run. Its regret, the loss versus the best fixed choice, nearly matches the known lower limits. The analysis covers two cases based on how large the picked set can be. The method also extends to settings where rewards arrive in a cascade. Tests on made-up and real data back the theory.
arxiv-2508-06447:
Lingkun Long and co-authors present SlimInfer in 2025, a method that speeds up language models working on very long inputs. Long prompts are costly because most systems still process every token at every layer.

The key insight is that information from key tokens spreads across the whole sequence as layers pass. After that spread, extra tokens can be dropped mid-network without losing meaning. SlimInfer prunes tokens layer by layer, guided by fine-grained importance. Its cache manager fetches needed blocks ahead of time without predictors. On a standard model it more than doubled the speed to first output, with no loss on a long-context benchmark.
arxiv-2508-06747:
Maria Alejandra Valdez Cabrera and Amy Willis build a new math space for family trees of species, in a 2025 paper. Such trees show how species relate through evolution. A well-known space for comparing them has strong math traits. It fails, though, when the trees cover different sets of species.

Their new space, called Towering space, extends the old one. It links many copies of the old space through steps that cut or rejoin branches. The authors study the shape of paths in the new space. They also give a method to compute distances between trees there. Modern data sets, such as gene trees that span many groups of life, need this wider reach. The work opens those sets to the tools of the older space.
arxiv-2508-06847:
Lam Ngo, Huong Ha, Jeffrey Chan, and Hongyu Zhang widen a search tool for hard design tasks. The work came out in 2025. The tool is Bayesian search, used to tune costly black-box systems. Most forms of it need smooth knobs that turn by small steps. Many real tasks do not fit that mold at all.

Some picks come from a fixed list, like which stuff to use or which build to pick. High counts of knobs make the search worse. Their tool, MOCA-HESP, cuts the space into curved zones. It tries more than one way to turn list picks into numbers. A bandit rule learns on the fly which code works best. The frame is a meta tool, so other search tools can plug in. The team built three such tools on top of it.
arxiv-2508-07347:
Mark Spivack shares 2025 notes on derivations, a type of map on operator algebras, for the largest triangular algebras on a Hilbert space. When the fixed lattice of the algebra is smooth at one point, he builds one operator that carries out any bounded derivation in full. The build is stated step by step.

For a broader class of such algebras, the same build works if and only if the derivation also meets an added three-term product rule. The notes draw on parts of his thesis that were not published, and they give a variant proof of a known wider result.
arxiv-2508-07747:
Junhyuk So and three co-authors speed up image-making models in a paper from 2025. These models build an image one token at a time, in sequence, which makes them slow. A known speedup drafts tokens ahead and checks them, but it accepts only the single most likely token. Image tokens, the authors show, often allow many valid choices at once.

Their method checks whole clusters of valid tokens instead of one token, and rebuilds the clusters on the fly. In tests it sped up image models by about 3.7 times on average with no loss of image quality. No extra training is needed, and the code is public.
arxiv-2508-08447:
Grant Moles and Talha Khan study when orders in real quadratic number fields are locally associated, a notion introduced in twenty twenty-five to tackle factorization problems. An order is a subring of a number field, and properties like being associated, ideal-preserving, or locally associated govern how elements factor inside it. The paper restricts to fields obtained by adjoining the square root of a prime.

The authors develop strategies and results that make determining whether a given order in such a field is locally associated much easier. They also highlight the relatively few cases that defy simple characterization. Those stubborn cases lead to a conjecture about solutions of Pell-type equations. Factorization in non-maximal orders is famously unruly, with non-unique factorization the norm. Classifying which orders enjoy tamer local behavior gives number theorists a map of where the pathology lives. The work is pure number theory.
arxiv-2508-08647:
Nobu Kishimoto and Kiyeon Lee analyze a nonlinear Schrödinger equation from plasma physics, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The kinetic derivative version adds derivative nonlinearities and a nonlocal term from the Hilbert transform. Such features make long-term behavior hard to prove.

The authors establish global existence for small initial data in a weighted Sobolev space. They also prove optimal time decay for the solutions. Energy methods and a frequency-localized gauge transformation handle the nonlocal difficulties. Beyond decay, the solutions show modified scattering. A precise asymptotic profile, with a suitable phase correction, describes them at large times. The results give a rigorous picture of how these plasma waves settle down.
arxiv-2508-09247:
Francesca Acanfora and Felix Kahlhoefer study a hard-to-see dark sector process, in a 2025 preprint, and how the Belle II experiment could catch it. Dark photons are proposed particles that could link dark matter to normal matter. Most searches look for dark photons that decay fully into visible matter or fully out of sight. The authors focus on a middle case, where a dark Higgs boson is also produced.

In their setup, the dark Higgs lives a long time before decaying into normal particles. That gives a decay point away from the collision point, plus missing energy. The process can appear alone or with an extra photon. Both shapes carry clear peaks that help cut background noise. The authors argue Belle II could cover ground that past searches missed. Pairing the two shapes could also reveal facts about the dark sector itself.
arxiv-2508-09647: Hlib Husarov and a co-author present a 2025 algorithm for a classic number puzzle, in short form. The puzzle asks for all finite lists of positive whole numbers whose product equals their sum. Their recursive method starts from solutions of shorter length and extends them step by step toward valid longer ones. The search is efficient, with running time much like the quick sort algorithm's. The note gives the full method and its cost bound.
arxiv-2508-09747:
Nazira Dunbayeva and co-authors teach a model to estimate biological age, and show that change over time beats any single snapshot, in work from 2025. Biological age should capture how fast a body is truly aging. Models that read one round of biomarkers often fail when asked to predict years later.

The team used a cohort measured in two waves, 2019 to 2020 and 2021 to 2022. A model on static markers alone generalized poorly to the second wave. Adding each marker's rate of change as a feature changed that. The final gradient boosting model predicted later age well for both sexes. Aging, it turns out, is best read in motion.
arxiv-2508-10047:
Ziyang Xiao and co-authors survey in 2025 the fast-growing craft of letting language models build optimization models. Turning a word problem into math that a solver can chew takes scarce expert time. The survey covers the whole stack: data synthesis, fine-tuning, inference frameworks, benchmarks, and scoring.

One finding stings: the benchmark data sets carry a surprisingly high error rate. The team cleaned them, rebuilt a fair leaderboard, and opened a portal with the data, code, and papers. They close by marking where current methods fall short and where the field should push next.
arxiv-2508-10147:
Yuhan Xie and three colleagues propose a semi-supervised training method that shapes neural network representations toward a known geometric pattern, in a 2025 paper. Well-trained classifiers show neural collapse, where class representations settle into a symmetric frame. The team bakes that target into pretraining, using a fixed rotated frame classifier plus pseudo-labeling so few labeled examples are needed.

To respect time order in the data, they add generative practice tasks and a new augmentation scheme for sequences. Tested on recurrent, transformer, and state-space models across three multivariate time series data sets, the method beat earlier pretraining tasks by a clear margin. The authors argue that aligning pretraining with proven geometry pays off downstream.
arxiv-2508-11047:
Massaro, Shinn, Thudiyangal, and del Campo test a classic rule about swirling flow in a newborn superfluid. When a gas cools fast into a superfluid, whirlpools called vortices form, and a known mechanism predicts how many. Their 2025 study looks at the circulation around loops of different sizes in such a condensate, a Bose-Einstein condensate made of ultracold atoms.

For small loops, a rule from classical turbulence theory holds: the circulation pattern depends on loop area, not shape. For larger loops the rule breaks down in a universal way the team characterizes. The moments of the circulation follow power-law scaling with cooling time, as the formation mechanism suggests. The work extends vortex statistics beyond the standard picture.
arxiv-2508-11347:
Yifei Li and six co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on SAGE, a framework for keeping knowledge graph embeddings current as the graph grows. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities and relations. Their vector embeddings are usually trained on a frozen snapshot, yet real graphs gain new facts constantly. Retraining from scratch is wasteful, but naive updates forget old knowledge.

SAGE first sizes the embedding space to the scale of each update, expanding dimensions when growth is large. A dynamic distillation step then balances keeping learned knowledge against absorbing new facts. Across seven benchmarks, SAGE beat existing continual methods, improving a key ranking score by 1.38 percent. The authors also evaluate performance across the whole update process, not just at the end. The work targets real-world graphs that change at uneven rates.
arxiv-2508-11447:
Maximiliano Cristiá and Gianfranco Rossi show how to reason about arrays using set theory in a 2025 paper. They encode an array as a function, and a function as a set of ordered pairs. The size of that set matches the length of the array, so array questions become set questions.

The authors define a fragment of set theory rich enough to specify a real class of array programs. They give a decision procedure for that fragment and add it to an existing solver tool where sets and relations are basic types. Users can then reason about sets, functions, and arrays in one language with one solver. The procedure extends earlier ones that lacked array support.
arxiv-2508-11547:
Martin Jiroušek, Tomáš Báča, and Martin Saska build fully onboard state estimation and trajectory tracking for drones carrying suspended payloads. Tracking a cable hung load usually needs motion capture systems, extra cameras, or instrumented payloads. Real deployment favors minimal hardware on standard aircraft.

Their framework uses only real time kinematic satellite measurements and the onboard inertial unit. The full coupled dynamics of vehicle and payload are modeled. A linear Kalman filter estimates state, while model predictive contouring control plans and an incremental predictive controller tracks. Simulations match ground truth based control within six percent and tolerate payload parameter changes. Field experiments confirm reliable outdoor performance on off the shelf hardware.
arxiv-2508-11647:
Logan Nye builds in this 2025 paper a way to grow neural networks that cannot break logic. Networks ace pattern tasks but often violate basic reasoning rules mid-answer. Rather than police them in training, Nye encodes logic into the wiring itself, using category theory: logical theories become algebra-like structures that transform into networks inside a formal map system.

Logical slips then become mathematically impossible, not just unlikely. A worked case builds trainable networks for propositional logic that keep boolean reasoning intact. The main theorem pairs every finitary logic with its networks one-to-one. Nye pitches the frame as groundwork for AI that must reason provably, from theorem proving to safety checks.
arxiv-2508-12247:
Haolong Chen and three co-authors forecast long runs of data that move across a map in a 2025 paper. Traffic and weather nets give such data: many sites, long spans, patterns at many time scales tangled with each other. Past deep models strain to learn the long view cheaply.

Their model mixes experts by scale, each tuned to a rhythm band, over a fast sequence backbone. A graph that learns cause links between sites handles the map side. Steady routing rules and a contrast drill keep the scales apart and the learning calm. Math checks back the design's smooth routing claims.
arxiv-2508-12647:
Hengnian Gu and colleagues set out Cognitive Structure Generation, a frame to build a student's cognitive structure on its own. A cognitive structure is how a student sorts a body of knowledge. It holds concepts and the links between them, as the student has built them. To gauge such a structure has long been a hard task in student modeling.

The frame first trains a diffusion model to build such structures from prior facts about schooling. It then tunes the build steps as a policy. It uses reinforcement learning with layered reward signals. The aim is to match real growth levels in how students think. Tests on four real data sets from schools show the built structures depict students more fully. Scores rose a lot on knowledge tracing and on diagnosis tasks.
arxiv-2508-12747:
A storyplan shows a changing graph as a strip of frames, each a drawing of the parts active at that moment, with every vertex appearing in one unbroken run of frames. Dobler, Holzmüller, and Nöllenburg ask whether demanding straight-line drawings, not just tidy curved ones, changes which graphs qualify when every frame must stay planar.

They give a graph that admits a planar storyplan with curved edges but none with straight segments, so the two settings truly differ. Adapting the older hardness proof, they also show that testing for the straight-line version stays NP-hard. The work closes a question left open when planar storyplans were introduced.
arxiv-2508-12947:
Michael Mayer and Mario Wüthrich study Shapley values, a fair way to split credit among inputs. Their 2025 paper comes from game theory's tool kit, now widely used to explain machine learning forecasts. Each input feature gets credit for its share of a prediction. Exact credits are costly to compute, so practitioners sample instead.

Two sampling schemes dominate: one built on kernels and one on permutations. The authors prove both schemes' estimates settle into a bell-shaped spread as samples grow. They also test paired sampling, a tweak that draws samples in matched pairs. Paired sampling gives exact answers when features interact at most in pairs. The permutation version also recovers totals exactly, while the kernel version does not.
arxiv-2508-13047:
Joni Salminen, Danial Amin, and Bernard Jansen analyze, in 2025, how researchers prompt language models to create user personas. Personas are fictional user profiles used in design, and models can now generate them from a prompt. The team studied eighty-three prompts drawn from twenty-seven research articles.

Most prompts asked for a single persona, and many asked for short ones, a break from the rich profiles of tradition. Text was the most common output form, often mixed with numbers, and demographic traits appeared in nearly all personas. Few studies compared models, and most used only a few prompts. The authors discuss what this shift means for representing users.
arxiv-2508-13147:
Gautham Varma K, Azaz Ahmad, and Gargee Sharma study how strain can create heat flow effects in odd metals. Their 2025 paper looks at metals that lack a center of symmetry and have strong spin-orbit links. When such a metal is stretched, the stretch acts like a field on its moving charges.

The authors use a tight-binding model to show that strain makes the spin-orbit link uneven and creates an axial electric field. They then track charge and heat flow with a classic transport method. Strain plus a magnetic field can set up a temperature gap through the Nernst-Ettingshausen effect. The size and direction of that gap depend on the angle of strain and on several forces at once.
arxiv-2508-13247:
Nina Rajcic and Anders Søgaard argue that goal-directedness lies in the eye of the beholder. Their 2025 paper questions how we attribute goals to complex agents, a step our predictions of their behavior rest on. Two probing styles compete: watching behavior, and reading inner model states.

The authors work through the assumptions under each style. Formalizing goals in agent systems breeds technical and conceptual snags on both paths. Their surprising verdict: goal-directedness cannot be measured objectively. What looks like a goal depends on the observer frame. New directions follow, modeling the trait as an emergent property of dynamic multi-agent systems. The paper reframes a measurement debate as a modeling choice with real stakes for agent safety.
arxiv-2508-13347:
Susanne Albers, Waldo Gálvez, and Ömer Behic Özdemir study a two-dimensional twist on the classic bin packing problem, in a 2025 paper. In their version, each bin is a timeline, and each job is a rectangle with a set length and height. Think of appliances drawing power over time. Jobs must fit into as few timelines as possible without the stacked heights ever passing a fixed cap.

The authors prove that even simple versions are hard: no fast method can promise answers within a factor of two of the best, for short jobs or for square jobs alike. For those versions they give methods that reach the best promise allowed. For the general problem they offer a method within a factor of three. All the methods sort big jobs into a tidy frame first, then slot small jobs on top with a classic packing rule.
arxiv-2508-13447:
Morales-Salgado models a society as a gas of particles, each person's stance on an issue standing in for a particle's position. His 2025 paper builds the statistical mechanics of that picture. Individuals move through an abstract stance space, and each carries a response weight that varies with position, like a mass that changes from place to place.

Treating the crowd like a canonical ensemble yields a partition function and, from it, social analogs of pressure, volume, and temperature. For one family of weight functions the resulting equation of state takes the ideal gas form, a hint of shared pattern under unlike individuals. An extension lets groups trade members through a chemical potential, opening the model to open societies.
arxiv-2508-13647:
Jan Krejčí and four co-authors borrow radar tracking methods to follow pedestrians in video. Their 2025 paper treats each pedestrian as a point object, the standard model from radar work, and runs a filter that keeps a mixture of possible track sets. The input is two-dimensional boxes from a detector, tested on the public MOT-17 data set.

Model settings rooted in continuous time needed care: birth and survival chances for tracks among them. Some values came from first principles, others were fitted from the data. The resulting tracker performed promisingly. Still, the exercise exposed a gap between the point-object model and real pedestrian data. The authors argue that naming the parts of the model that clash with the data is the point: fixing exactly those parts should yield better model-based trackers in future work.
arxiv-2508-13747:
Noël Kury, Dmitry Kobak, and Sebastian Damrich blend two map-making philosophies for high-dimensional data, in a 2025 paper. Analysts flatten data into two-dimensional pictures to see structure. Favorite tools keep either the local neighborhoods honest or the global layout, never both. Their method, DREAMS, adds a simple pull toward the global PCA picture inside the local t-SNE picture, yielding a dial between the two extremes.

Eleven real data sets benchmark the blend. Across scales, the embeddings kept both neighborhood and continent structure better than predecessors. One tuning knob trades the microscope for the atlas. The authors offer it as a default first look at messy data.
arxiv-2508-13847:
Jordan Gué, Peter Wolf, and Aurélien Hees ask whether the future space observatory LISA could tell a dark matter hum from a gravitational wave, in a 2025 paper. Ultralight scalar dark matter would tug test masses rhythmically through its coupling to ordinary matter, printing a Doppler wiggle on the laser links between LISA's spacecraft. That wiggle could masquerade as a near-monochromatic gravitational wave from a distant binary.

Using a year of realistic LISA orbits and Bayesian inference, the team simulated both signals and tried to separate them. LISA will indeed be able to discriminate the two, they find. The distinction matters: mistaking dark matter for a binary would corrupt the gravitational wave catalog, and mistaking a binary for dark matter would waste a discovery. The study supports adding dark matter searches to LISA's science case with confidence about false alarms.
arxiv-2508-14247:
Saswata Jana, Subhajit Pramanick, Adri Bhattacharya, and Partha Sarathi Mandal send short-sighted robots onto a graph to occupy a vertex cover. The robots enter one by one through special door vertices and see only a limited distance. Working asynchronously with purely local knowledge, they must settle so every edge touches an occupied vertex, using as few vertices as possible.

The authors set lower bounds on the visibility range needed and on the running time. For trees they give two algorithms: a single-door version optimal in both time and memory, and a multi-door version optimal in memory. Their technique even finds the minimum cover on trees with one door, despite that problem being hard in general.
arxiv-2508-14547:
Molecular clouds are where stars are born, and Xin Zhou and co-authors mapped them across two great swaths of the Milky Way using a Chinese sky survey's carbon monoxide data. Their catalogue holds nearly twenty-five thousand clouds in inner and outer galaxy regions, traced in three variants of the molecule that reveal different densities.

Nearby, they found vast, slow, curtain-like sheets of gas. Farther out, clouds bunch along the spiral arms, yet a real population also fills the gap between two arms, where the gas disk runs thinner. Disk thickness tracks the galaxy's warp, hinting at a shared origin, and the inner disk measures about two hundred twenty parsecs thick. Cloud speeds scatter less at larger galactic radii, easing distance estimates there.
arxiv-2508-15747:
Shashank Shalgar and Mariam Gogilashvili study how neutrinos change flavor in dense matter in this 2025 paper. Neutrinos are tiny particles that can switch type as they travel, and stars hold huge numbers of them. The team solves a set of quantum kinetic equations that track this change, and asks whether bumps in matter density can upset the results.

The authors ran the equations at three grid sizes and found the answers nearly the same even on the coarse grid. They then added random bumps to the density, both steady and changing in time, and watched the flavor mix. The bumps caused no real instability and only small shifts in particle counts and energy spread. The finding suggests that density noise of this kind can be set aside in round, even models of neutrino flow.
arxiv-2508-15847:
Mohammed Abu Baker and Lakshmi Babu-Saheer probe how hidden backdoors change the inner workings of a large language model, in a paper from 2025. A backdoor can turn a model into a sleeper that acts badly only when it sees a secret trigger. The team compares a clean model with copies fed a one word trigger and copies fed a longer trigger phrase.

Using cuts, swaps, and gap scores on the attention heads, the team finds clear shifts in the late layers of the model. The short trigger left tight, local marks, while the long trigger spread its marks across many heads. The authors argue that these marks give a foothold for tools that spot and remove backdoors before a model is put to use.
arxiv-2508-15947:
Thomas Kite and five co-authors trained a neural network to read breathing rate from heart telemetry in hospitalized patients in a 2025 paper. Breathing rate is a key vital sign, yet counts by hand are slow and often wrong. Steady monitoring exists in intensive care but not on most wards.

Heart traces carry several faint traces of breathing, which the network learns to read. Its error stayed under two breaths per minute across test sets from the same and other sources. In past cases that ended in breathing failure, the steady trace tracked the slide toward a breathing tube. The authors see this as a step toward a hospital-wide early warning system built on gear already in place.
arxiv-2508-16447:
Álvaro Guglielmin Becker and Gabriel Bauer de Oliveira tested in 2025 whether large language models can write working board game software from written rules. Coding a board game by hand is slow, and language models have shown skill at code generation for narrow tasks. A framework that turns plain-language rules into playable games would speed up prototyping considerably.

The authors asked three leading models to implement a dozen popular and obscure games, both freely and inside Boardwalk, their proposed general game playing framework. Game names and parts were disguised so models could not lean on memorized knowledge. Programs were scored for playability and rule compliance. The approach proved viable: the best model produced over half the games with no errors at all, and the study catalogs success rates and the common mistakes each model made.
arxiv-2508-17347:
Shaban and Habash proposed a new score for Arabic dialects in twenty twenty-five. Arabic varies widely by region, yet computer models often treat each dialect as a fixed box. A recent measure grades how dialectal a text is, but it squeezes rich variation into one number.

Their Arabic Generality Score instead grades how widely a word is used across dialects. They built a pipeline that aligns words across texts, measures spelling distance with respect for word origins, and smooths the results. A model then learns to predict the score for words in context. It beat strong existing systems on a multi-dialect test set. The authors offer the score as a grounded way to enrich how models represent Arabic.
arxiv-2508-17547:
Weikang Wan, Jiawei Fu, Xiaodi Yuan, Yifeng Zhu, and Hao Su presented LodeStar in 2025, a system that teaches robots long, skilled tasks from a few human examples. Such tasks need both fine hand control and smooth linking of many steps. Gathering enough real examples to train a robot is slow and costly.

LodeStar first splits each human example into clear skills, using ready-made foundation models. It then creates many varied fake examples in simulation through trial-and-error learning. A single policy learns to chain the skills in order and adapt to changes in the scene. On three hard real-world tasks, it beat earlier methods in success and robustness, the authors report.
arxiv-2508-17647:
Tong Bao and co-authors build a data set and a quality-aware writer for scientific surveys in a 2025 paper. Writing a survey means sifting a field's papers into one synthesis. Language models can draft surveys, but no standard test bed exists to judge them against human work. Their SurveyGen collection holds over forty-two hundred human-written surveys with their quarter-million references, plus quality data on both.

On top of it, their QUAL-SG system upgrades retrieval-augmented writing. It scores source papers for quality before feeding them to the model. The team tested top language models at several levels of human help. Semi-automatic pipelines came partly close to human surveys. Fully automatic ones still suffered weak citation quality and shallow critique. The authors release the resource to anchor future assessment. They frame quality-aware retrieval as the lever that matters most.
arxiv-2508-18047:
Shruti Dubey, Nilanjana Kumar, Tanumoy Mandal, Subhadip Mitra, and Rachit Sharma probe a paired new-physics case in this two thousand twenty-five particle physics paper. Collider hunts have long sought leptoquarks and vectorlike leptons, each on its own. In views with enhanced gauge symmetries, both could be there at once. Acts through leptoquarks would then boost how many vectorlike tau leptons the Large Hadron Collider makes.

The team studies odd leptoquark acts. These make new marks in how the heavy tau partners are made and how they break down. They weigh the odds of a find in the high-luminosity phase of the collider. The end states hold one lepton or two. More paths that could count are also talked through. The work shows a risk in one-at-a-time thinking. Marks can show up just when two guessed kinds of particle act on each other.
arxiv-2508-18147:
Mathieu Garrigues and co-authors scale up in 2025 a quantum method for molecular docking, the task of predicting how a drug molecule fits a protein pocket. The problem maps onto a graph puzzle that neutral atom quantum machines can attack, but real molecules make graphs far bigger than today's devices hold. A divide and conquer trick splits one huge graph into small sub problems solved one by one on an emulator, at modest extra cost.

Tests on ten real protein drug pairs, with graphs up to nearly six hundred points, beat a greedy baseline and hit the proven best answer on one large case. Rebuilt poses were checked for how many true contacts they kept. The work lays out a workable path for quantum docking.
arxiv-2508-18247:
Carlos Arreche and Matthew Babbitt tackle a problem in the math of elliptic curves, in a paper from 2025. The problem asks when a function on the curve can be written as the gap between a second function and its shift. That shift moves points along the curve by a fixed step. Past work in 2018 defined residue values that can block such a form.

The pair add two new residue values of their own. With the older ones, the new values form a full set of blocks: if all are zero, the form exists. They build the theory from scratch in three settings for the curve, and in two of them for any number system. Worked examples show the values for functions that do and do not fit the form. The paper closes with fresh results drawn from the new tools.
arxiv-2508-18547:
Youssef Abdelsalam and co-authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five asking whether humans and language models stumble over the same confusing code. Programmers now work daily with AI assistants, so a mismatch in what confuses each side could cause bugs and wasted effort. The team set out to compare the two directly.

They measured model confusion by perplexity, the model's surprise at the code. Human confusion was read from brain signals tied to eye movements while programmers read clean and confusing code. The model's surprise spikes matched the human brain responses in both place and size. That likeness suggests both sides trip on the same spots. The authors then built a tool that flags code regions likely to confuse people.
arxiv-2508-18847:
Yibo Li, Miao Xiong, Jiaying Wu, and Bryan Hooi teach language models to say how sure they are in a 2025 paper. Models often state wrong answers with total confidence, which is dangerous in law, medicine, and science. Earlier fixes leaned on prompting tricks or rough training labels.

Their method, ConfTuner, fine-tunes with a new loss built from the Brier score, applied token by token. The authors prove the loss is a proper scoring rule, so honesty about uncertainty is the winning strategy. Calibration improved across reasoning tasks and even transferred to a black-box model. Better-stated confidence then helped models correct themselves and hand off hard questions.
arxiv-2508-19247:
Lin Li and colleagues present VoxHammer, a method with no training to edit three-dimensional objects with care in their native 3D space. Local 3D editing matters for games and for robot work. Past methods edit rendered multi-view images and then rebuild the model. But they fail to keep unedited regions exact. They also fail to keep the whole object coherent.

VoxHammer first predicts a model's inversion path. It captures its inverted latents and key-value tokens at each step. In denoising and editing, it swaps the traits of regions meant to stay untouched with those cached values. Kept areas are thus rebuilt in a steady way, while edited parts fit in well. To gauge this well, the team built Edit3D-Bench, a data set marked by humans. Tests show VoxHammer beats past methods by a lot.
arxiv-2508-19847:
Erdi Kara and Panos Stinis build a fast solver for flow through porous rock or soil. Their paper from twenty twenty-five treats two linked tasks. One is steady flow, set by the Darcy rule. The other is the spread of a dissolved substance over time. The substance starts from sharp, narrow sources, which make steep fronts that are hard to compute.

Their method pairs two tools. A finite element solver finds the flow field with high care. A neural operator network, trained with the physics built in, then learns how sources map to spread patterns. A smart choice of test points helps it track steep fronts. Tests match trusted solutions well. The method runs far faster than classic solvers, which suits real field use. Code is shared in public.
arxiv-2508-20147: Simone Calogero, writing alone, introduces a diffusion equation for gases moving near light speed, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The equation respects Lorentz symmetry and keeps the standard conservation laws for particle number, energy, and momentum. Its resting state is a twist: slowed to everyday speeds it becomes the familiar Maxwell profile, yet it is not the Jüttner distribution that textbooks usually pair with relativity. Written on a curved spacetime, the equation also fits the geometric identities behind Einstein's theory, so it can be coupled directly to general relativity.
arxiv-2508-20247:
Keith Taddei and co-authors test a claim about a crystal in a 2025 paper. The compound was put forward as a near-perfect case of a Weyl semimetal, with just one pair of special points. Such a clean case would let researchers watch the linked particles with no clutter.

The team grew small needle-like crystals and measured their traits in depth. Two shifts in magnetic order showed up at low heat levels, near eight and four degrees above absolute zero. The crystals were clear to light and showed a large energy gap. That gap undercuts the claim of semimetal behavior, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2508-20647:
Rabsan Ahmed, Adithi Udupa, and Giulia Ferrini design quantum error codes that span many light modes at once. Such codes store a quantum bit in the spin states of light, where turn symmetry guards it from phase noise. Past codes used one mode, which forced a trade: guard phase and lose guard on light loss. Their build grows codes from group math, set by which gates must stay simple in the lab.

Turn symmetry is kept across all modes in the new family, a first for this line. The full Pauli gate set runs by plain light tools in their scheme, with no exotic parts. Two-mode cases built and scored in the work beat both one-mode kin and past multi-mode codes on phase noise. Exact fixes for linked phase slips are also in reach.
arxiv-2508-20847:
Matthew Stover proves that certain symmetry groups keep a rich echo in every corner, in this 2025 paper. The groups come from ball quotients, spaces built by dividing a complex ball by a tidy arithmetic group. Stover studies their profinite completion, a vast object that bundles all finite snapshots of the group at once.

He shows that inside the completion sits an open subgroup whose every smaller open subgroup still carries nonzero cohomology classes in all degrees up to twice the dimension, for large enough primes. For dimension two or more the result is new beyond the first degree. It lifts the known floor for the group's virtual cohomological dimension from one to twice the dimension. The proof builds a profinite version of the space's fundamental class.
arxiv-2508-21047:
Seven researchers tackle service quality in low orbit satellite networks in a 2025 paper. Such networks can fill coverage gaps in the countryside and back up city networks. Traffic types differ a lot, from calls that hate delay to downloads that need bulk speed.

Their method, DSROQ, plans routes and bandwidth jointly and treats quality goals as soft limits. A search method modeled on game tree search picks the routes, while a math rule runs the queues. Tests on a model of the Starlink fleet show gains in user experience and fairness over a base scheme. As traffic shifts from delay driven to bandwidth driven, routing choices matter more than scheduling.
arxiv-2508-21247:
Jiaxun Song, Li He, and Bo Zhen work out why some light matter hybrids barely glow in a 2025 paper. The hybrids form when light binds tight to excitons, the paired states a material makes when it soaks up light. Long lived hybrids would boost quantum and nonlinear light tools, yet past simple models treat their glow as two plain parts added up.

Their frame tracks the shared, synced nature of the bound state. They show the glow from the exciton crowd can cancel itself, and cancel the glow from the light part too. That wipe out can trap light in states that in theory never fade. The work hands designers new rules for hybrids with tuned glow.
arxiv-2508-21347:
Sabbir Ahmed, Nursadul Mamun, and Md Azad Hossain build a voice ID system that holds up in noise. Naming a speaker from a short clip gets hard when rooms echo or sounds distort. Their 2025 system turns sound into a picture modeled on the inner ear, called a cochleagram.

A bank of one hundred twenty-eight filters splits sound across a wide pitch range. Clean and noisy pictures, down to very harsh noise levels, train a neural network to learn each speaker. The model is then tested on fresh noise types, echoes, and distorted clips. Scores beat an older ear-based system by a clear margin. The team offer the method for real-world voice checks where sound is rarely clean.
arxiv-2508-21647:
Rupert Yu studies orbit structure inside Lie algebras in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. His setting is a Borel subalgebra of a complex semisimple Lie algebra, a standard scaffold in the theory. Inside it sit nilpotent ideals, sets closed under the algebra's operations. The author looks at a special subset of nilpotent elements tied to one such ideal. This set stays fixed as a whole under the action of the matching Borel subgroup.

He proves the set contains exactly one closed orbit under that action. That orbit belongs to a nilpotent element whose support is the set of smallest roots for the ideal. Pinning down a unique closed orbit anchors the whole orbit picture. The result serves specialists in representation theory and algebraic groups.
arxiv-2509-00047:
Jina Kim, working alone, studies brain-inspired replay as a cure for forgetting in neural networks in 2025. When a network learns new tasks in sequence, it tends to lose old skills, a flaw called catastrophic forgetting. Brains ease this loss by reactivating past traces during rest, a process tied to memory consolidation, which firms up new memories.

Internal replay revives hidden codes for past cases while new learning proceeds. Kim tests it on the CIFAR-100 image set in a class-by-class setup, alone and with Synaptic Intelligence, a method that guards key weights. Replay cuts forgetting a lot, most when paired with that guard, but it lowers early accuracy on new tasks. The trade-off frames how brain tricks might steady lifelong learning.
arxiv-2509-00247:
Yong Zhao, working alone, reviews fresh steps in 2025 that sharpen how the inner traits of the proton are computed from lattice QCD. Partons are the quarks and gluons inside a proton. Their maps show how the proton's momentum is shared among them. Large Momentum Effective Theory, called LaMET, gets those maps from lattice sims of the strong force.

LaMET matches lattice values, called quasi-distributions, taken at large proton momentum to the true maps. New gains include a hybrid scheme that tames a known runaway term, plus matching terms worked out to more loops. A gauge-fixed route also eases the work and sharpens maps of side-wise momentum. Tighter error bars bring lattice results closer to what lab tests can check.
arxiv-2509-00447:
Rupendra Yadav and Aparna Mehra present a robust portfolio optimization framework in 2025 built around mixed conditional value at risk. Portfolio choice balances return against risk. Mixed conditional value at risk blends several tail-risk gauges into one objective, while a chance constraint guards expected returns and a cardinality limit caps how many assets are held.

The robust model assumes ellipsoidal support for random returns, with no fixed distribution. An uncertainty set built in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space handles the chance constraint, and the problem reduces to a second-order cone program, a tractable convex form. Tests on six financial markets show higher expected returns and better reward-risk ratios than nominal, market, and equal-weight portfolios.
arxiv-2509-00747:
Francesco Caravelli leads a team of six authors on physical learning systems. Their topic is self-organising memristive networks. Learning with physical systems uses a material's own dynamics to learn. It avoids running neural software on standard transistor hardware. These networks are built from nanoscale resistive memory parts. Their electrical circuitry reconfigures itself as they run.

The authors review experiments on such networks. They cover mean-field theory and graph theory as analysis tools. They also discuss links to criticality in disordered systems. Parallels with plasticity in biological neurons are drawn. Such networks could give brain-like continual learning at low energy cost. Uses include edge intelligence, sensing, and personal healthcare devices.
arxiv-2509-01647:
Interstellar comets carry material from around other stars, and 3I/ATLAS is a newly found visitor of that kind. Luis E. Salazar Manzano, with eight co-authors, reports a ten-night campaign of spectroscopy and photometry in August 2025, using two telescopes at the MDM Observatory. The comet was inbound, between about three point two and two point nine times Earth's distance from the Sun.

Nightly spectra caught the onset of gas activity: a weak CN emission feature, absent at first, grew steadily in the coma. The measured CN production rate sits toward the low end seen in solar system comets. Photometry also showed the coma's profile and dust measure rising slightly. The team derives a gas-to-dust production ratio and reads the pattern as evidence of strong carbon-chain depletion, a chemical trait that sets this visitor apart.
arxiv-2509-01947:
Mahdi Farzandway and Fatemeh Ghassemi automate repair of C programs by pairing fault localization with large language models. Their loop first flags suspect code regions from test pass and fail patterns. Runtime feedback and a chain of thought prompt, where the model reasons step by step, guide each patch try. Past patch outcomes feed the next round of reasoning.

That memory cuts repeated errors and clarifies why some bugs resist fixes. The loop edits code, reruns tests, and refines its plan each cycle. On a benchmark of thousands of bugs, their method fixes a higher share than strong baselines. The gain over a top model with the same prompting style is a few points. The work shows a practical route for AI assisted debugging.
arxiv-2509-02247:
Rasika Vijithasena leads three co-authors in a calm aware joint talk and steer plan for wireless control webs. Such webs close steer loops by air links with thin stores of power and range. Non straight, control non affine acts, where steer acts in tangled ways, make calm hard to vouch. Next gen nets are set to back these live self led loops at scale.

A deep Koopman model lifts non straight acts to a straight space where reads and plans come easy. A Lyapunov based plan deals talk slots by calm need and stock on hand. Steer acts come from a straight type rule in that lifted space. Tests in mixed terms beat base lines that take affine steer or same acts in both spaces. Calm holds with fewer sends than the base lines need.
arxiv-2509-02347:
Alessio Lapolla wrote a 2025 solo mathematics paper deriving recursive formulas for survival chances and first passage times in systems with many moving parts. The focus is the nth component of a jump-and-diffusion process that faces a killing barrier, an absorbing limit that ends the process.

Lapolla starts with two components, then extends the formulas to three or more. He admits the results are general but hard to implement. Two examples show their use. One is single file diffusion, where particles cannot pass each other. The other is financial: pricing an nth-to-default credit default swap, a contract that pays when the nth firm in a group defaults.
arxiv-2509-02447:
Xinrui Zhong and eight co-authors present a 2025 systems paper on finding watermarks hidden in generated images across huge collections. Accuracy under edits and attacks gets much attention, but raw detection speed at scale is often ignored.

Their QRMark system borrows error correction ideas from QR codes and splits images into tiles. A Reed-Solomon code repairs accuracy lost through tiling. On the system side, a resource-aware fusion policy gives more processing streams to heavy stages. Tile workloads are interleaved so data loading overlaps with computation, and kernels are scheduled across stages. End-to-end tests show detection running more than twice as fast as a sequential baseline, while keeping accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2509-02547:
Guibin Zhang and twenty-four co-authors wrote a 2025 survey of agentic reinforcement learning for large language models, where models act as autonomous agents in changing environments rather than answering in one step. The survey draws on more than five hundred recent works.

Older language model training fits a single-step decision model, while agentic settings stretch over time with partial information. The authors organise the field two ways: by core abilities such as planning, tool use, memory, reasoning, self-improvement, and perception; and by application domains. Their central claim is that reinforcement learning turns fixed heuristic modules into adaptive behaviour. A compendium of open environments, benchmarks, and frameworks supports future work. Open challenges for building general-purpose agents close the survey.
arxiv-2509-02847:
Arjen van der Wel and Sharon E. Meidt present a 2025 astronomy paper proposing EASE, a mechanism where short-lived spiral arms reshape galaxies early in cosmic history. Between redshifts one and three, many galaxies already show early-type shapes, and their formation needs explaining.

EASE stands for early, accelerated, secular evolution. Torques from stellar spirals, seen by the Webb telescope in young galaxies, slowly heat and compact the galaxy and build its bulge. The process is secular yet fast, because orbital times were much shorter then. A new wave calculation shows transient open spirals influence a wider region than steady spirals do. Using galaxy size as the test, EASE predicts an early-type size distribution matching observations. Spirals are common enough at those epochs to drive the transformation.
arxiv-2509-02947:
Ambuj and 6 co-authors wrote a 2025 paper that brings a classic idea from communication theory into game theory. Claude Shannon's zero-error idea asked when messages can cross a noisy channel with no mistakes at all. Here the players hold private information and must land together on a Nash equilibrium, a stable outcome no one gains by leaving alone.

The authors show some Bayesian games, where players act under uncertainty about each other, allow no sure classical coordination. Links known as Bell nonlocal correlations, a quantum effect tying distant particles, make it possible there. They also build games for three players, where true entanglement is required, and for two players under a stronger demand. The edge survived realistic noise in their checks.
arxiv-2509-03147:
Karl Dilcher and Larry Ericksen wrote a 2025 combinatorics paper sparked by a counting pattern that hides famous numbers. They study colored partitions in base three, ways of splitting a whole number into parts whose labels carry colors and place value. The counting function for one such family contains the even perfect numbers, numbers equal to the sum of their divisors, as a subsequence.

The authors define polynomials in four variables, arranged as a sequence, and explore their properties and counting meanings. Certain subsequences connect to the Chebyshev polynomials, a classic family with two kinds. Later sections turn to single-variable polynomial sequences with their own counting interpretations. Their zero distributions, the patterns of where these polynomials vanish, also get attention.
arxiv-2509-03447:
Aexandre Fernandes, Zbigniew Jelonek, and José Edson Sampaio proved a metric version of Arnold's corank problem in a 2025 mathematics paper. In 1975 Arnold asked whether the corank of a holomorphic function, a measure of its degeneracy, is unchanged by ambient topological changes of the surrounding space. The metric version asks the same for bi-Lipschitz changes, which may stretch distances but only within bounded factors.

The authors obtain a complete positive answer to that metric question. A consequence is that, for complex hypersurfaces, having multiplicity equal to two is also an ambient bi-Lipschitz invariant. They further prove the original Arnold problem for holomorphic functions of three variables. Other topological invariants are presented along the way. The work settles a fifty-year-old question in its metric form.
arxiv-2509-03647:
Self-preference bias in large language models used as judges is examined in a 2025 research paper by Dani Roytburg and five co-authors. When a model grades answers, it tends to favour its own outputs over other models' work. That favouritism threatens fairness in preference tuning and model routing, where judges steer real decisions.

The team asks whether small steering vectors, directions added inside the model's activations at answer time, can curb the bias without retraining. Their curated dataset separates justified self-preference, where the model's answer really is better, from unjustified cases. Two construction methods are tested: contrastive activation addition and an optimisation-based approach. Steering cuts unjustified self-preference by up to almost all of it, beating prompting and preference-training baselines. Yet the same vectors behave unstably on legitimate self-preference and on neutral agreement. Self-preference seems to span several, possibly nonlinear directions, limiting simple fixes.
arxiv-2509-03847: Graphs belonging to the Wp class, a family defined inside graph theory, are what Do Trong Hoang and two co-authors examine in a 2025 mathematics paper. They establish new characterisations of such graphs, meaning equivalent conditions that decide membership in the class. Within the same class, they also characterise locally triangle-free alpha-critical graphs, a special family where small changes alter a key independence property. As a consequence, their results give a partial answer to Plummer's 1993 question, for the case p equals two.
arxiv-2509-04347:
Johanna Brunar and two co-authors prove that certain puzzle-like languages are far less expressive than they appear in a 2025 mathematics paper. The setting is constraint satisfaction, where values must honor a set of rules, extended here to infinite domains. Temporal and phylogeny systems, tied to family trees of species, carry famous complexity classes. Systems failing to build everything turn out to be solvable quickly, a known result the authors deepen.

Such systems can only interpret very limited graphs and hypergraphs through a standard building method. Many algebraic results follow, including special four-ary polymorphisms, symmetry operations that keep solutions valid. Two unlike families share a common proof core. The work supports a major open conjecture in the field.
arxiv-2509-04447:
Bitan Roy, writing alone, extends two classic counting theorems to Dirac systems that leak energy in a 2025 physics paper. Dirac fermions are particles described by the Dirac equation, and textured mass patterns or magnetic fields can trap robust zero-energy states on them. Index theorems by Aharonov-Casher and Jackiw-Rebbi or Jackiw-Rossi count those trapped states exactly. Roy augments the Dirac Hamiltonian with a mass-like anti-Hermitian term, making the operator non-Hermitian, as suits open systems that exchange energy with surroundings.

Across a wide parameter range the energies stay fully real, governed by an effective Fermi velocity. Explicit zero-mode solutions show magnetic fields of any shape still bind such states when flux is finite. Mass textures bind them only when that velocity is real.
arxiv-2509-04547:
Alexandre Champagne-Ruel and two co-authors test whether spatial patterning alone can fake a signature of life in a 2025 research paper. Assembly theory holds that only living systems produce certain complex molecules in bulk, offering a life-detection tool. Controls so far used meteorite samples or well-mixed chemistry. Self-organization research warns that spatial patterns can foster complexity without life, risking false alarms. The team modeled a fake chemistry where molecules spread and react across layouts.

Transport factors like diffusion strongly shifted which species appeared where. Ordered lattices raised the bar for abiotic complexity a bit, though arbitrary complexity never emerged. Diffusion could also hide high-complexity molecules from detection. Life-hunting missions must mind geography, the results warn.
arxiv-2509-04647:
Games where each player's cost depends on the whole population's states and strategies are analysed by P. Jameson Graber, lead author with two co-authors, in a 2025 paper on mean field games of controls. The system uses a fractional Laplacian, an operator that captures long-range effects. Solutions are shown to exist for a range of its orders.

The authors assume the Lasry-Lions monotonicity condition on the coupling. They derive moment estimates, estimates for fractional parabolic equations, and new results on how the population distribution changes in time. Those estimates, with a fixed point theorem, establish existence of solutions.
arxiv-2509-04947:
Critical points in lattice models can be hard to find when systems are small. Anran Jin and one co-author apply an entropy-based strategy to that search in a 2025 note on strange correlators. The strategy uses an entropy function designed to detect criticality even at small system size, combined with transfer matrices built from a topological holographic principle.

The authors find the combination cost-effective for identifying critical boundary conditions. It also estimates central charges and maps entire phase diagrams in a multi-dimensional parameter space. Their note presents the method as an efficient route to critical lattice models.
arxiv-2509-05747:
Two people acting out everyday scenes together, faces and voices included, form a new motion dataset from Leo Ho and seven co-authors in a 2025 computer graphics paper. Earlier capture work covered one person, or two people talking with bodies nearly still, missing how partners move through space over longer interactions.

InterAct holds hundreds of motion sequences, each a minute or longer, where two actors with assigned roles and emotion labels complete a shared task. Audio, body motion, and facial expression are all recorded. The activities are diverse and the interaction patterns longer than in earlier sets. A diffusion-based method that estimates both people's motion and expressions from speech is demonstrated.
arxiv-2509-06447:
Electricity, gas, and heat networks in one mathematical picture is the framework of a 2025 paper by Marwan Mostafa and three co-authors. Sector coupling and decarbonization tangle the three systems together, and separate models miss their interactions. The authors build a multi-layer graph: one layer per energy carrier, with coupling technologies as edges between layers through a dedicated coupling layer.

A block-structured Newton-Raphson solver computes flows and state variables for all carriers jointly at steady state. On a realistic case study from a German distribution network, the solver converges accurately with consistent cross-domain behavior. The team offers the model as a base for system-wide analysis and future optimization of integrated energy systems.
arxiv-2509-06647:
Shining strong light on quasicrystals to probe how their electrons get trapped is proposed by H. K. Avetissian and three co-authors in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Quasicrystals sit between ordered and disordered matter, and they can show Anderson localization and mobility edges without any disorder. Optical probes that work without contact are therefore valuable.

Using general Aubry-André-Harper models and a smooth incommensurate potential, the authors show that high-harmonic output, light emitted at multiples of the driving frequency, tracks those trapping changes. They define a new quantity, dipole mobility, capturing how transitions within a band affect the signal. Harmonic output can differ by orders of magnitude between regimes, and the cutoff frequency shifts with the edge's position. That shift gives experimenters an accessible signature of the trapping in this matter.
arxiv-2509-06747:
Finding known planets in reflected starlight starts with knowing where to point, and Logan A. Pearce and two co-authors build a tool for that in a 2025 astronomy paper. Future telescopes will image cold, mature planets directly. Planets found by radial velocity or astrometry are prime targets, but many orbits are too imprecise to predict a planet's spot on the sky.

Their open-source Python package, projecc, turns published orbit solutions into probability maps for a planet's sky position. Two test cases show the range: one planet's location is well pinned down, while Proxima Centauri b remains highly uncertain. A web app lets observers explore these predictions for the known targets plus many more from the literature. Planned upgrades aim to support observing campaigns with the coming generation of large telescopes.
arxiv-2509-06847:
Escaping air on sixteen giant exoplanets is measured through a helium line by Jaume Orell-Miquel and seven co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The near-infrared helium triplet is a strong tracer of atmospheric escape on close-in planets. Observations came from the Habitable Zone Planet Finder spectrograph on the ten-meter Hobby-Eberly Telescope, at high resolution.

First constraints are reported for five planets, earlier detections are confirmed for five more, and several non-detections are recorded. One earlier narrow-band detection was not confirmed at high resolution. Combining the survey with published studies, patterns emerge: warm Jupiters with helium detections orbit K-type stars.
