The study covers hundreds of Java bugs from Defects4J and Python bugs from BugsInPy, across three base language models. History proved widely available and useful: the best heuristic added a few percent for the strongest model and far more for weaker ones. Three different history heuristics fixed different subsets of bugs, so combining them repaired greatly more than no history, at no extra cost in steps or tokens.
arxiv-2511-01247:
Md. Shariful Islam and colleagues show software orchestrated quantum networks over a campus scale testbed at Argonne National Laboratory. Quantum networks will only matter if they grow from solo experiments into infrastructure that runs shared applications on its own, much as classical networks do.

Their prototype orchestrator borrows software defined networking principles to run standard quantum network experiments across buildings linked by deployed telecom fiber. The system provides a service level view of networking tasks, shared time synchronization, and entanglement checks between remote nodes. As a demo service, it distributed entanglement nonstop and stably between remote sites for twelve hours. The authors present the result as a promising path toward scalable quantum networks.
arxiv-2511-01447:
Yong Song, Jiaqi Fu, and Yiting Cen ask whether a particle's spin can change the global pattern of its possible circular orbits around a black hole. Spin couples to spacetime curvature in the Mathisson-Papapetrou-Dixon formalism, pushing spinning particles off geodesic paths and shifting their orbital parameters, so the qualitative orbit structure might shift too.

Using a topological approach, they build an auxiliary vector field and compute a winding number for timelike circular orbits in static, spherically symmetric spacetimes. Between two horizons the winding number is minus one, guaranteeing at least one unstable orbit, and outside the outermost horizon it is zero, forcing orbits into stable unstable pairs or none. Both results hold whatever the spin's size or direction. Examples in Schwarzschild and its anti-de Sitter and de Sitter variants confirm the invariant topology under explicit spin induced shifts.
arxiv-2511-02047:
Hamidreza Sadeghsalehi builds a deep learning system for analysing how people walk, using wearable sensors, with two jobs in mind. Gait analysis helps clinicians manage nerve and joint conditions, but the models can quietly absorb biases hidden in their training data. The framework uses attention across several sensor streams, applied to a multi-cohort dataset covering Parkinson's disease, osteoarthritis, and stroke screening tasks.

The attention patterns exposed a serious flaw in the public dataset: for two screening tasks the model relied almost entirely on the right foot because the data itself was heavily one-sided. Sadeghsalehi presents the auditing ability as the main contribution, with sensor combinations suggested by the model as leads for future testing.
arxiv-2511-02247:
Hao Li and ten co-authors estimate real distances from a single endoscope camera, information that could guide autonomous medical robots. Supervised learning needs images with known depth, which real surgical footage lacks, so a common workaround translates synthetic images into a realistic style and trains on those. A stubborn gap between translated and genuinely real frames limits how well that works, especially for absolute, metric depth.

The team's method attacks the gap inside the network rather than in the images. The depth network learns features that stay consistent between synthetic and real frames of central airway videos. It uses adversarial training and a directional consistency requirement. It works regardless of which translation process produced the synthetic data. On airway phantom videos with hand-aligned depth maps, the approach beat leading methods on absolute and relative depth, across several network backbones.
arxiv-2511-02347:
Liuhao Lin and seven co-authors evaluate language models by making them draw. Standard benchmarks report opaque numbers that can hide a basic weakness: models that ace text tests may barely understand space. Their benchmark, LTD-Bench, asks models to produce pictures, either as dot matrices or as executable code, so spatial failures are visible at a glance, even to non-experts.

The tasks run in both directions, generation to test spatial imagination and recognition to test spatial perception, across three levels of difficulty. State-of-the-art models that shine on conventional benchmarks showed profound gaps in mapping between language and spatial concepts in both directions. The authors argue this undermines claims that such models are genuine world models, and they note the drawings themselves offer a diagnostic tool for comparing how different models represent space.
arxiv-2511-02947:
Clare Burhenne and eleven colleagues read the star formation histories of the two Magellanic Clouds from the Scylla survey's deep Hubble images. The survey covers large areas of both galaxies, deep enough to reach stars older than the ancient main-sequence turnoff. Their 2025 paper groups fields into eight sub-regions in the Small Cloud and seven in the Large Cloud, then hunts for bursts of star birth in each.

The Small Cloud shows two global bursts, about five and one and a half billion years ago, plus one local burst. The Large Cloud shows one global burst about three billion years ago. Against orbit models, shared triggers seem to start earlier and stronger in the Small Cloud. One Small Cloud region, the Wing and Bridge, matches the southwest Large Cloud in chemistry and growth, hinting at stripped material.
arxiv-2511-03347:
Mario Ayala, Nicolas Dirr, Grigorios A Pavliotis, and Johannes Zimmer untangle how the reading of noisy equations affects whether motion can run backward in a statistical sense. Random pushes whose strength depends on position can be read in several standard ways, named for Ito, Stratonovich, and Klimontovich. A single dial between them lets the team write one geometric condition for reversibility.

That condition ties noise choice to a Gibbs weight on a curved space. For systems with slow and fast parts, shrinking away the fast parts keeps reversibility intact. The Klimontovich reading, notably, survives that shrinking unchanged. The work gives modelers a clear rule for picking a noise reading that will not break after simplification.
arxiv-2511-03747:
Ali Safa and co-authors release OpenMENA, an open board and software stack for computing with memristor crossbars at the edge. Memristors compute where they store, promising frugal intelligence for small devices. Until now, tinkerers lacked a full open path from bare crossbar to running model.

The system joins a reproducible hardware interface with read, program, and verify loops, a firmware and software stack with high-level interfaces, and a careful method for writing trained weights into analog conductances. Chip-in-the-loop tuning then irons out device quirks. Digit recognition and a robot dodging obstacles prove the full flow. Open neuromorphic hardware can spread edge experimentation beyond a few specialist labs.
arxiv-2511-03847:
David Altizio, writing alone, studies where the roots of Stern polynomials lie in the complex plane. These polynomials extend the classical Stern sequence of integers, with a doubling rule that either multiplies by the variable or adds neighbouring terms. An earlier conjecture placed every root in the half-plane where the real part stays below one.

Altizio proves partial progress: a closed disk centred at two with radius one contains no roots at all. The argument uses the Parabola Theorem for convergence of complex continued fractions. As a corollary, a conjecture of Ulas and Ulas follows: the polynomial at a prime index is irreducible over the integers.
arxiv-2511-04347:
Sanjay Kumar, Tim Brophy, Eoin Martino Grua, Ganesh Sistu, Valentina Donzella, and Ciaran Eising measure how weather-driven sensor occlusion degrades three-dimensional object detection for automated vehicles. They use the BEVFusion architecture on the nuScenes dataset. Bird's-eye-view fusion is a leading perception design, yet fog, haze, and blockages had not been isolated as a failure factor.

Moderate camera occlusion cut camera-only accuracy sharply, by about forty-one percent in mean average precision in the reported test. LiDAR held up until heavy occlusion, then fell by about forty-seven percent, hurting long-range detection most. In fused settings the damage depends on which sensor is occluded, a nuance designers must plan around.
arxiv-2511-04547:
A. A. Saharian and two colleagues compute fermionic Casimir densities near an accelerating mirror. The mirror is a flat boundary moving with constant proper acceleration through flat spacetime. The field is a massive Dirac field living in the Fulling-Rindler vacuum.

A bag boundary condition holds on the mirror, splitting the right Rindler wedge in two. In each region, the fermion condensate and energy-momentum values split into two parts. One part comes from the vacuum without any boundary, the other is induced by the mirror. Far from the boundary, renormalization reduces to the boundary-free case, simplifying the full result.
arxiv-2511-05147:
A. Barone and co-authors weigh three long-period small planets around the bright star TOI-282. The star is an F8 type, easy to study, and its planets take about 23, 56, and 84 days per orbit, with sizes two to four times Earth's.

The outer two have periods close to a 3 to 2 ratio, which hints they may be locked in resonance. The team joins TESS transit data with sharp HARPS and ESPRESSO velocity data. A joint Markov chain fit sharpens the orbits, weighs each planet, and probes how the system formed and changed.
arxiv-2511-05447:
Natalia Gherghel and a co-author test the stability of homogeneous minimal hypersurfaces in two families of Einstein spaces: the Page space and the Sasaki-Einstein spaces known as Y p,q. Minimal surfaces sit at a balance point, and stability tells if a small nudge grows or fades.

Both spaces carry metrics with large symmetry groups. The authors list all the homogeneous minimal hypersurfaces, compute the spectrum of each stability operator, and find its index. That index counts how many ways a surface can be pushed to lower area, a sharp gauge of its stability.
arxiv-2511-05647:
Callum Witten and co-authors use the James Webb Space Telescope to study a dense young galaxy group in the early universe. The group, a protocluster core seen as it was when the universe was young, holds far more galaxies than its surroundings. Such groups grow into today's galaxy clusters, so they show how environment shapes galaxy growth.

The team found six confirmed galaxies plus five likely members in a tiny patch of sky. Despite the crowding, these galaxies look young and star-forming, much like isolated galaxies of the same era. That contrasts with another protocluster whose galaxies look old and dusty. The authors argue environment only bites above a certain halo mass.
arxiv-2511-05747:
Ziqian Bi and co-authors reuse long reasoning traces from strong AI models instead of generating them fresh each time. Writing out step-by-step thought is costly, above all for small or speed-limited models. Their framework, CoT-X, has a capable thinking model produce one rich rationale, then compresses it for a cheaper answering model.

CoT-X cuts traces into meaning units, scores each unit's value, picks a path that fits the token budget, and rebuilds a coherent short rationale. On thousands of Japanese medical licensing questions, it beat plain truncation by a wide margin at the same budget. Transfer worked best within a model family but held across families. A smart search also found good model and budget pairings cheaply.
arxiv-2511-05847:
Adam Rennie and Ben Whale prove a limit curve theorem for metric spaces that may be incomplete, where points can sit at finite distance from a missing edge. Limit curve theorems say a sequence of curves has a convergent subsequence, a basic tool in geometry. Their main target is a notion from relativity called the null distance.

Applied to that distance, their results give strong control over the Lorentzian lengths of limit curves. They also show that two standard time functions define such a distance: regular cosmological time, and the surface function of a Cauchy surface in a globally hyperbolic spacetime. The work gives relativists a firmer grip on spaces where completeness fails.
arxiv-2511-05947:
Huimin Hu and co-authors measure how stale data gets in a wireless network where devices first harvest energy, then report. Their setup uses a pinching antenna, a movable radiating point on a waveguide, to serve an Internet of Things device. Walls and objects can block the line of sight, with some probability, which the analysis includes.

The device charges its capacitor from the base station, then spends all stored energy sending a status update. The authors derive closed-form formulas for the average age of information, the standard freshness measure. They then search for the antenna spot that minimizes that age. Simulations say the best spot is the one closest to the device, and pinching antennas beat fixed ones by a wide margin.
arxiv-2511-06147:
Muhammad Abdullah Sohail and co-authors study how low-income adults in Pakistan live with digital misinformation, by designing with them rather than for them. False content hits low-income groups hardest, and past interventions in the Global South often fell flat with marginalized communities. Their study ran in three phases with forty-one adults.

Interviews first mapped how participants find and share information. Co-design sessions then turned the needs they named into concrete design requirements. Sharing, it turns out, runs on a moral economy, and trust is layered, favoring communal welfare. The team distilled a Scaffolded Support Model, mixing on-demand help with gradual skill building, and built it into a prototype called Pehchaan. Fifteen testers accepted it strongly, which the authors read as cultural fit.
arxiv-2511-06347:
Milena Radnović and Ruzzel Ragas count how often a geometric configuration appears over finite fields. Their setting is the projective plane over a finite field whose characteristic is not two. They ask for the chance that a random pair of conics from one pencil admits a triangle or four-sided figure inscribed in the first conic and wrapped around the second.

Every pencil of conics with at least one smooth member is covered, grouped by type under projective change of coordinates. One conic may be smooth or singular while the other stays smooth, and pairs that meet non-transversally are allowed. The result is a complete probability census for Poncelet-style triangles and tetragons in this finite setting.
arxiv-2511-06447:
Mert Yazan, Frederik Situmeang, and Suzan Verberne survey why people choose ChatGPT for search despite its risk of confident errors. Conversational interfaces feel personal and engaging next to classic search engines, which can breed overtrust. The team asked one hundred seventy-three users about trust, human-likeness, and design preferences across both tools.

Daily users of both systems trusted ChatGPT more, rated it more human-like, and accepted trading factual accuracy for smoother conversation. Google-first users trusted it less yet still liked the ad-free, responsive feel. Middle-aged adults used ChatGPT least but trusted it most, a pattern the authors flag as a misinformation vulnerability.
arxiv-2511-06547:
Hassan Nagib and colleagues report precise readings of turbulent pipe flow at unusually high Reynolds numbers. The CICLoPE facility in Italy delivers fully developed pipe flow with outstanding spatial resolution and steady conditions. Pitot probes measured mean centerline velocity while hot wires captured turbulence strength and normal stress over the last two years.

Comparisons with earlier experiments and computer models suggest truly high-Reynolds behavior only sets in past a friction Reynolds number of ten thousand. The centerline von Kármán constant settled firmly at a value the authors report with high confidence. Streamwise intensity and normal stress leveled off past twenty-five thousand, and velocity spectra showed a long, clean inertial range.
arxiv-2511-06747:
Anu Kuncheria, Joan Walker, and Jane Macfarlane classify more than one hundred Bay Area cities by the geometry of their street intersections. Road layout shapes traffic flow and the feel of driving, and comparing whole regions city by city can guide shared traffic strategy. Earlier work leaned on degree, centrality, and orientation, skipping the angles where streets actually meet.

A new metric sorts three-way and four-way intersections by their link angles. Clustering on those patterns separated the region into three typologies: grid, orthogonal, and organic cities. The authors show the metric captures real differences in street character, offering planners typology-aware options for evacuation planning, signage placement, and broader traffic management.
arxiv-2511-06847:
Jonas Stange proves that a complex fluid model is mathematically well-posed in two dimensions. The model describes viscous fluid mixtures with a diffuse interface, coupling a Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system in the bulk of a container to a similar system living on its boundary surface. Such bulk-surface coupling captures mixtures whose surface behavior matters as much as their interior flow.

Stange establishes global existence of strong solutions, including the physically meaningful case of non-degenerate mobility functions. He also proves the solutions are unique and depend continuously on their initial data. The proof builds new well-posedness and regularity theory for a convective bulk-surface Cahn-Hilliard equation and for a bulk-surface Stokes equation with non-constant coefficients. These tools are of independent interest for coupled bulk-surface problems.
arxiv-2511-07047:
Simone Bendazzoli and six co-authors test whether anatomy knowledge helps deep learning find lymphoma lesions in whole-body PET/CT scans. These scans combine metabolic and anatomy information, but lesions vary greatly in size and number, making detection hard. The team fed organ segmentation masks from the TotalSegmentator tool as extra inputs, giving two detection systems explicit anatomical context.

Within nnDetection, the leading lesion detection system, anatomy priors greatly improved detection performance on the AutoPET and Karolinska lymphoma data sets. For a Swin Transformer trained with self-supervised pre-training, the same priors changed almost nothing, and the transformer showed no clear advantage over the convolutional encoders inside nnDetection. The findings single out anatomical context as valuable for convolutional detectors.
arxiv-2511-07147:
Premabrata Manna, S I Mistakidis, P G Kevrekidis, and Pankaj Kumar Mishra study pattern formation in a ring-shaped quantum gas whose interaction strength is shaken at two frequencies at once. The homogeneous state of such a Bose-Einstein condensate can go unstable, seeding density waves, and bichromatic driving gives extra knobs: the two amplitudes, the two frequencies, and the mixing angle between them. The authors derive the stability phase diagram analytically.

Their analysis uses a biharmonic variant of the Mathieu equation and its Floquet spectrum, revealing how the driving parameters switch instabilities on and selectively amplify higher-order resonance tongues. Time-dependent mean-field simulations confirm density modulations at the predicted momenta, and a reduced five-mode model captures the onset, the oscillating mode populations, and the phase-space dynamics. The control shown is within reach of current ultracold atom tests.
arxiv-2511-07347:
Giorgio M Cavallazzi, Miguel Pérez Cuadrado, and Alfredo Pinelli teach neural operators to handle partial differential equations with jumps. Neural operators learn the solution map of an equation family, but Fourier-based versions smear sharp interfaces because of the Gibbs phenomenon. The Walsh-Hadamard Neural Operator swaps in a basis of rectangular wave functions, naturally matched to piecewise constant fields. Its learnable spectral weights cheaply capture global links from the low-sequency coefficients.

Tested on heat conduction with discontinuous conductivity and the two-dimensional Burgers equation with jumpy starting data, the operator beat Fourier neural operators at preserving sharp features under the same conditions. The surprise finding is synergy: weighted ensembles of the two models cut mean squared error by thirty-five to forty percent against either alone. The bases capture complementary aspects of such solutions.
arxiv-2511-07547:
Jiang, Wang, and Sou test a shortcut astronomers use to weigh distant black holes. Single-snapshot spectra estimate quasar black hole mass from line widths, but the method rests on a small set of repeatedly watched objects. A breathing effect, where line widths change with brightness, can bias those weights.

A huge multi-epoch dataset extends the breathing test far beyond the calibration sample. Tracking width changes across brightness states reveals how strong the bias runs in typical quasars. The analysis estimates systematic errors hiding in mass catalogs. Since black hole and galaxy growth stories rely on those masses, cleaner error bars reshape coevolution claims.
arxiv-2511-07647:
Pujian Mao and Baijun Zeng translate gravitational metrics between two coordinate languages at second order in Newton constant. Harmonic coordinates suit wave generation, while Newman-Unti coordinates suit radiation reaching distant observers. Converting between them unlocks amounts defined at infinity.

Complete transformations for a generic metric let the authors extract the asymptotic shear, the Bondi mass aspect, and the angular momentum aspect at both orders. Those quantities encode energy and spin carried away by gravitational waves. Exact wordbooks between these systems matter as waveform models chase the accuracy future detectors will demand.
arxiv-2511-07847:
Connor McShaffrey, Eran Agmon, and Randall Beer argue that cell models need a theory of staying alive. Nearly every model of a cell quietly assumes viability limits, yet those limits are coded ad hoc, with no shared principles. How dynamics push a cell across the life-death boundary is rarely studied directly.

Geometric structures in model state space can separate regions with similar survival outcomes. Mapping those boundaries offers a global view of viability rather than case-by-case failure checks. The authors lay groundwork for treating cellular viability as a central concept. Such theory could unify modeling choices across computational cell biology.
arxiv-2511-07947:
Yaxin Xiao and co-authors defend machine learning models against extraction attacks, where rivals copy a model through black box queries. Watermarks embed hidden markers so owners can later prove a copied model is theirs. Existing black box watermarks lean on representation entanglement, which may leave a weak point.

The team first builds WRK, an attack that uses decision boundaries around watermark samples and cuts success rates sharply. Their defense, Class-Feature Watermarks, creates a synthetic class from outside samples to remove those weak boundaries. In tests it keeps watermark success high after extraction and attack, while preserving normal model use.
arxiv-2511-08147:
Andrija Stanisic and Stefan Nastic present ProbSelect for choosing federated learning clients among graphics accelerated devices spread across edge, cloud, and space. In that three dimensional continuum, satellites and mobile devices change status often, so constant monitoring and stored histories become impractical. Older selection methods also assume usual processors and miss graphics hardware conduct.

ProbSelect uses analytical modeling and probabilistic forecasting instead, needing no history or live monitoring. Selection is framed around user defined service level goals. Across varied graphics architectures and workloads, it raised goal compliance by about fourteen percent on average and cut wasted computation by nearly three quarters versus baselines.
arxiv-2511-08247:
Marios Koniaris, Argyro Tsipi, and Panayiotis Tsanakas present ParliaBench, a benchmark for making lawmaker speeches with large language models. A good lawmaker speech needs more than fluent language: it must sound politically real and stay ideologically steady. Existing tests score standard text quality and miss those political sides, while models get little specialized training for parliament.

A data set of United Kingdom lawmaker speeches supports systematic training and scoring. Evaluation mixes computational metrics with model judged assessments of linguistic quality, coherence, and political realism. Two new embedding metrics measure spectrum and party alignment. Fine tuning five models and scoring twenty eight thousand speeches shows clear gains from specialization.
arxiv-2511-08647:
Robin Delabays and four co-authors ask how to steer systems whose members interact in groups, not just pairs. Graphs miss such higher-order links, so the work uses hypergraphs, and it starts from a harder spot: the interaction structure itself may be unknown and hard to measure.

The pipeline first infers the hypergraph from observed behavior, then picks which nodes can be controlled, and finally drives the system toward a chosen state. For polynomial dynamics the authors prove analytical controllability guarantees. For other dynamics they give a heuristic for choosing control nodes and test it on Kuramoto oscillators, the standard model of coupled rhythms. The approach targets settings from biological collectives to engineered infrastructure.
arxiv-2511-08747:
Isaac Joffe and Chris Eliasmith build a solver for the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, a set of visual puzzles that humans find easy and AI systems find brutally hard. Their design is deliberately modeled on human cognition, pairing fast intuition with slow deliberate reasoning in one neurosymbolic system.

Vector Symbolic Algebras supply the machinery: abstract objects become high-dimensional vectors, search is guided by those representations, and program synthesis works object by object. Early results are modest on the main benchmark, around eleven percent on training tasks. On simpler suites the solver shines, reaching about ninety-five percent on Sort-of-ARC and beating GPT-4 on 1D-ARC at a tiny fraction of the computing cost. The authors believe this is the first vector-symbolic attack on the benchmark.
arxiv-2511-08847:
Chunyan Li, Yutong Mao, Xiao Liu, and Wenrui Hao model Alzheimer's disease as a moving system rather than a set of snapshots. Their framework builds a personal graph for each patient from MRI and PET scans, then learns that patient's own dynamical settings for how brain regions change together over time.

Applied to one thousand eight hundred ninety-one participants in a major Alzheimer's imaging program, the model tracks the joint evolution of amyloid, tau, neurodegeneration, and cognition. It predicts future paths better than standard clinical and imaging benchmarks. Each patient's settings separate distinct progression patterns and forecast cognitive decline better than standard biomarkers. Sensitivity analysis flags the regional network features that drive spread, matching the known weakness of temporolimbic and frontal areas. The authors offer the approach as a base for modeling disease one patient at a time.
arxiv-2511-09547:
George Turner, Vojtěch Pravda, and Alena Pravdová map out which black hole solutions quadratic gravity allows at large distances. Quadratic gravity modifies Einstein's theory with squared curvature terms, and the setting adds a cosmological constant. They study static, spherically symmetric black holes and ask when the far-away geometry is anti-de Sitter or de Sitter.

For large values of the constant's magnitude, the holes are generically asymptotically (A)dS. They form a three-parameter family set by horizon radius, the constant, and a Bach parameter. For smaller values, the Bach parameter needs fine-tuning, splitting solutions into two families, one being ordinary (A)dS-Schwarzschild. Adding electric charge preserves the pattern qualitatively, with charge as a fourth parameter.
arxiv-2511-09647:
Franz J. Schreiber, Maximilian J. Kramer, Alexander Nietner, and Jens Eisert rigorously analyze a measurement-driven quantum algorithm for the Boolean satisfiability problem. Most proven quantum guarantees rest on Grover-style search, which caps the advantage at quadratic. This solver works differently, and had shown promising numeric behavior without a full runtime theory.

Their analysis ties runtime to a trade-off between two quantities. These are the Hamiltonian's spectral gap and the measurements' success probability, controlled by a tunable rotation angle. They add a better readout routine, a parallelization scheme using hash families, and an amplitude-amplified variant. On a tractable class of instances the runtime collapses to polynomial. A key spectral-gap bound remains open, they note, and with it any super-quadratic advantage.
arxiv-2511-10247:
Liu Yang and eleven co-authors shape tiny crystal rings with ultra-fine machining to steer the light combs the rings produce. A comb is a set of evenly spaced colors of light, and its use rests on how fast each color travels, a trait set by the ring's shape. Machining can in theory tune that trait across a wide band, but hard fab steps had left the route largely untested until now.

The machined rings proved exact in shape and showed strongly muted mixing between spatial modes of light. That clean state let the rings emit smooth soliton combs and broad combs past the telecom C-band. The team reads this as proof that tight shape control is a strong route to clean, broad combs on crystal photonics platforms.
arxiv-2511-10347:
Shuhei Shibata, writing alone, studies elephant random walks on general periodic grids, building on limit theorems earlier known on the integer lattice. An elephant random walk remembers its past: at each step it recalls an earlier step and copies or reverses it with fixed chances, so the walk's future depends on its whole history. Periodic structures generalize the regular grid to repeating patterned spaces.

Shibata proves functional limit theorems describing the walk's large-scale behavior on such grids. New quantities appear that have no counterpart in the classical lattice setting, exposing how the underlying geometry shapes the end behavior. The paper is a probability theory contribution, broadening a memory-driven walk model from flat grids to structured environments.
arxiv-2511-10547:
Isabela Albuquerque and six co-authors tackle a measurement gap in text-to-image generation. Models keep getting better at image quality, yet their outputs often look alike, and diversity itself is hard to score fairly. Their framework judges diversity concept by concept, using the factors along which each concept should naturally vary.

The framework combines a new human evaluation template and a curated prompt set with identified factors of variation, such as the color of an apple. It also adds binomial tests for comparing models on the human judgments. The team also checks which image embeddings best capture diversity. The approach produces principled diversity rankings of generation models and pinpoints the categories where each model struggles most, giving developers a clearer target for improvement.
arxiv-2511-11347:
Shaowei Guan, Hin Chi Kwok, and their colleagues review privacy risks and defenses for health chatbots that fetch records to ground their answers. That fetching method is called retrieval-augmented generation. Pulling clinical text into a language model can expose protected health data at many points. Protections today are applied unevenly.

Drawing on twenty-three studies of such systems in use, the authors sort risks by stage. The stages are storage, sending, retrieval, and generation. Each stage has its own failure modes and causes. They also weigh seventeen studies on defenses. Gaps remain in clinical testing, shared test frames, and tools that check systems on their own.
arxiv-2511-11647:
Dariush Salami, Ramin Hashemi, Parham Kazemi, and Mikko A. Uusitalo aim to make beam selection in 5G and future networks cheaper to train and kinder to the energy budget. Reinforcement learning picks good beams, but retraining from scratch in every new radio environment wastes time and computation.

Each environment is modeled as a point cloud of base station and scatterer locations, and the Chamfer distance finds structurally similar places. A model trained in a similar environment is then transferred instead of starting over. The reported gains are faster adaptation and lower energy use. Sustainable network operation, not just raw speed, is the measure the authors optimize for.
arxiv-2511-11847:
Ryan Singh and ten co-authors build a chatbot that answers manufacturing safety questions from curated regulatory and technical documents, and they evaluate it like a product, not a demo. Worker safety training needs high accuracy, low delay, and low cost at once, a trio that generic chatbots rarely satisfy together.

A domain benchmark of expert-validated question and answer pairs covers three representative machines: a Bridgeport manual mill, a Haas CNC lathe, and a universal machine. Several retrieval-augmented generation approaches are compared against that benchmark. The design science framing ties the artifact to Industry 5.0's human-centric turn, and the benchmark itself is a reusable contribution for safety-critical assistants.
arxiv-2511-12147:
Lifeng Shen and four co-authors present a method for spotting anomalies in time series, where normal behavior is dynamic and nonlinear. Older methods often assume a fixed number of neighbors or clusters, and those assumptions can fail on complex data. A more flexible picture of normal regions is needed.

Their network, GBOC, builds granular balls, compact high-density regions in a learned space that stand for local normal behavior. A density-guided splitting process makes the balls, and noise is pruned away. Training pulls samples toward their nearest ball center, and at test time a sample far from its ball scores as anomalous. The balls sit between single points and full clusters.
arxiv-2511-12547:
Zhiguang Lu and four co-authors present HiGFA, a method that uses diffusion models to augment training data for fine-grained image classification, where classes differ by subtle details. Synthetic images must preserve exactly those category-defining traits, or they mislead the classifier. Standard text guidance is often too vague for that job.

HiGFA guides generation in stages matched to the sampling process. Early and middle steps use strong text and contour guidance at fixed strength to set scene, style and structure. In the final steps a fine-grained classifier joins in, and all guidance strengths shift with prediction confidence. The staged, confidence-driven mix aims at images that are both diverse and faithful.
arxiv-2511-12647:
Thales F. Macedo and six co-authors ask whether a hidden property of a quantum material can be read back from the light it lets through. Their systems are one-dimensional disordered chains of electrons, described by the Anderson and Aubry-André-Harper models, placed inside an optical cavity. Light trapped in the cavity couples to the electrons and changes the transmission spectrum in measurable ways. The team tests whether that spectrum reveals the strength of the light-matter coupling.

Using a Green's function method, they show the coupling strength can be extracted accurately from transmission data alone. The cavity is a mild influence in the Anderson model, but it strongly reshapes the spectrum in the Aubry-André-Harper model, which has a sharp metal-insulator transition. There the recovered values are especially precise. The authors present it as a diagnostic for quantum materials, strongest where the material changes character.
arxiv-2511-12747:
Aritro Pathak proves a step in the theory of elliptic equations with singular drift, where a transport term blows up near a domain's edge. The question is when the Dirichlet problem for such an equation can be solved in an L^p space. Earlier work by Hofmann, Lewis, Kenig, and Pipher treated these drifts as perturbations. Pathak works on sawtooth subdomains of the unit ball, jagged regions that fill almost all of the ball's boundary.

He shows that if the problem is solvable in the BMO sense on those ample sawtooth domains, then the elliptic measure satisfies a weak A-infinity condition there. That condition is equivalent to L^p solvability for some exponent. The argument extends naturally to general bounded Lipschitz domains. The paper is a technical bridge between a qualitative assumption and a checkable conclusion.
arxiv-2511-13547:
Daniel Almeida lays the syntactic groundwork for a tensor product of generalized algebraic theories. Generalized algebraic theories, in Cartmell's sense, describe structures with dependent sorts, a step beyond plain equational theories. The tensor should combine two theories so that models of the pair nest inside each other, but the combination must be built with care.

Almeida defines the product by an algorithm that merges the axioms of both theories in a recursive manner. Known constructions fall out as cases, including tensor products of Lawvere theories and cellular products of dependent type signatures. Functorial comparison maps and symmetry and associativity isomorphisms are built here, with the universal property left to the companion paper.
arxiv-2511-13647:
Chunshi Wang and 8 co-authors introduce Part-X-MLLM, a 3D multimodal language model that treats part-level tasks as programs. Given a colored point cloud and a text prompt, the model emits one structured token stream that encodes part boxes, semantic notes, and edit commands. That symbolic plan then drives separate geometry tools for building and editing shapes.

A dual-encoder design separates structure from semantics during pretraining on a large part-focused dataset, followed by instruction tuning. By splitting planning from geometry work, any compatible engine can sit behind the same language front end. Tests showed top results on grounded question answering, compositional generation, and localized editing through the single interface.
arxiv-2511-13847:
Yuehaw Khoo and Tianyun Tang work on optimal transport, a method for comparing and morphing probability distributions that gets costly in high dimensions. Their approach relaxes the problem into convex form, using only low-order summary statistics of small groups of variables. The relaxed problems become semidefinite programs that give lower bounds on the true transport cost at far lower cost.

For Gaussian data with sparse links, they prove the cluster version converges at an exponential rate and give sharper error bounds. They also show how to pull actual transport maps out of the relaxed solutions, offering a simpler option than neural networks for generative modeling. Tests across many distributions show strong performance.
arxiv-2511-14047:
Tausif Parvez and S. Shankaranarayanan present an exact black hole solution with no singularity at its center. The gravity source is a phantom Dirac-Born-Infeld scalar field, and only its phantom branch supports the solution. Instead of collapsing to a point, the interior settles into a regular two-sphere core, while far away the spacetime flattens as usual.

A dynamical kinetic stiffness explains both the smooth core and how the solution carries scalar hair despite classic no-hair theorems. These black holes evaporate down to a stable relic of about a gram. That opens a wide mass window where primordial black holes could survive as dark matter, with distinctive gravitational-wave signatures as a test.
arxiv-2511-14347:
Antonio Politi revisits a long-running puzzle in heat conduction through one-dimensional chains. Some numerical studies of simple classical systems seemed to obey Fourier's law, with conductivity settling to a constant, while theory predicted it should grow without bound as the system lengthens. Politi recomputes several of these models with fresh care.

In every case an anomalous divergence eventually emerges. For a variant of the ding-a-ling model the growth begins at moderate sizes, contrary to earlier claims. For systems with non-binding potentials, he shows the energy flux splits into diffusive and hydrodynamic parts. The hydrodynamic part always wins in the end. The crossover can hide at extremely long lengths, though.
arxiv-2511-14547:
Mikołaj Myszkowski, Mattia Damia Paciarini, and Francesco Sannino propose quantum systems where the number of space dimensions is itself a quantum variable. In normal physics the dimension is fixed in advance. Here the effective dimension depends on the quantum state. The authors show such systems can display larger symmetry than fixed dimension versions.

They work out a two state example where dimension is an operator. From its partition function they find an effective dimension that shifts with temperature. The idea opens a new design space for physical models. Potential uses range from gravity to condensed matter, wherever dimension itself might behave as a dynamic quantity rather than a backdrop.
arxiv-2511-14647:
Chenjing Bu and Young-Hoon Kiem compare four known ways to define a pairing between cycles on the moduli space of vector bundles over a curve. That space collects all bundles of a fixed kind on a fixed curve, and pairings on it feed into counting problems in geometry. Each of the four methods was built with different tools, so it was not clear they agree.

The authors define a broader notion of generalized pairing for well-behaved stacks. They then prove wall-crossing formulas that link the four constructions to each other. Worked examples in low rank make the links concrete. The result unifies separate strands of work on bundle moduli.
arxiv-2511-14747:
Rahil N Valani, Sumesh Thampi, and Julia M Yeomans simulate nematic liquid crystals flowing through a channel. Nematics, fluids whose rod-like molecules align, are modelled here with the standard Beris-Edwards equations, with the walls forcing the molecules to stand perpendicular. Even at rest the confined system is multistable. A uniform state coexists with states whose alignment and order vary across the channel. That menu of configurations organises everything that follows when flow begins.

Under a gentle pressure gradient the flows settle, taking configurations known as Bowser and Dowser that match experiments. Raising the gradient destabilises those states one after another, through periodic regimes into spatiotemporal chaos with pulsating flows, travelling defects, and cyclical changes in the topology of the alignment field. The study maps that route from still order to chaos in a widely used soft-matter system.
arxiv-2511-14847:
Julia Wildeboer, Marton Lajer, and Robert M. Konik study how order breaks down in a chain of quantum spins with a staggered magnetic field. In such chains, domain walls can bind into meson-like pairs, a form of confinement borrowed from particle physics. The team asks whether those bound states also change how the energy levels of the whole chain are statistically arranged.

Using exact calculations on chains of up to twenty-two spins, they watch the level statistics slide away from the chaotic pattern as the chain enters its Ising-like regime. Sharper sectors with fixed wall counts appear, and correlations arrange into bands. The link between confinement and fading chaos gives a new handle on how isolated quantum systems settle, or fail to settle.
arxiv-2511-15047:
Zongkai Liu, Qiming Ren, and thirteen co-authors show that a cloud of interacting Rydberg atoms can learn to predict time series, especially near a phase change. Rydberg atoms, boosted to giant excited states, respond to each other strongly and can amplify weak outside signals when the system sits close to a transition. The team feeds the series in by wiggling the laser that drives the vapor.

Close to the transition, the vapor's ability to learn the input grows, reflected in how faithfully its response can be read out as a forecast. The platform is attractive because its collective behavior can be tuned and read with simple tools. The result hints at atomic vapors as small, physics-built forecasting devices.
arxiv-2511-15247:
Antonio Ferrer-Sánchez, Nino Villanueva-Espinosa, and five co-authors aim neural network solvers at one of relativity's classic stress tests: the collapse of a massless scalar field. Near the threshold between the field scattering away and a black hole forming, the collapse shows critical behavior that punishes sloppy numerics. Physics-informed networks, which learn by respecting the equations, are flexible candidates for the job.

The team solves the Einstein and Klein-Gordon system in polar-areal coordinates across four setups spanning the scattering, threshold, and black hole regimes. Several recent network designs are raced against high-resolution finite-difference reference runs. The comparison shows where neural solvers already stand on a problem where errors near criticality are easy to make and hard to forgive.
arxiv-2511-15447:
Michel Tokic, Slobodan Djukanović, Anja von Beuningen, and Cheng Feng test whether a large pre-trained time-series model can judge machine health without new training. Their task is to sort vibration signals from a bearing inside a servo-press motor into health classes. Instead of fine-tuning the model, they place labeled examples inside the prompt it reads, a method called in-context learning.

Reference signals from the frequency range are reshaped into time patterns that line up with label signals. The model then gives class chances for new, unknown patterns. Results held up across varied working conditions. The authors argue such ready-made models could support wider, service-based upkeep tools for factories.
arxiv-2511-15647:
Gabriel Flath gives a simpler proof of an ergodic theorem for branching Brownian motion, a model where particles move randomly and split into new particles over time. The frontier is the set of extreme particles farthest out, and an ergodic theorem describes how their pattern settles into stable statistical behavior over long times. A well-known proof tackled that question, and Flath revisits its approach with fresh eyes.

Two observations carry the new argument. Extreme particles seen at widely separated times must have split apart early, and such early-branching pairs have negatively correlated positions. Those facts yield the ergodic theorem and extend it to a broad class of summaries of the recentered maximum, while also fixing a gap in the earlier localization step.
arxiv-2511-15747:
Davood Momeni investigates a dark energy model built from entropy ideas, with four free parameters, in a universe that may be slightly curved. Dark energy drives the accelerating expansion of the universe, and entropic models derive it from an entropy-area law at the apparent horizon, the edge of the observable region. The chosen entropy form covers several known corrections, though not entropy measures from information theory.

Within that setup, Momeni derives exact formulas for the expansion rate, the dark energy share, and its equation of state, which links pressure to density. Scanning the parameter space finds viable regions, especially with one parameter above a threshold and small positive curvature, that allow higher present expansion rates matching recent measurements and easing the Hubble tension.
arxiv-2511-15847:
Alexander Bakumenko, Janine Hoelscher, and Hudson Smith build a transparent system for predicting early death risk in intensive care patients. Spotting at-risk patients early enables timely treatment and better resource use, but strong machine learning models are often opaque and brittle, limiting clinical adoption. Their ensemble combines two data types from the first forty-eight hours of a stay: vital sign time series and unstructured clinical notes.

A bidirectional recurrent model reads the vitals and a fine-tuned clinical transformer reads the notes. Logistic regression fuses their outputs in a traceable way, with explanations per feature and per data type for each case. On a standard benchmark the ensemble beat its best single model while staying calibrated, even when one data type was missing.
arxiv-2511-16247:
Goldy Ahuja and Shashikiran Ganesh simulate the motion of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, the fastest interstellar object yet found. Discovered in July 2025 by a survey telescope system, it moves far faster than the two earlier interstellar visitors. The team study its link with Mars before perihelion and with Jupiter afterward. A standard N body run package integrates its orbit a century backward and forward.

Adaptive integration uses fine time steps during close planetary encounters. Jupiter measurably alters the comet's orbital settings and post encounter trajectory. Mars effects are examined in the pre perihelion leg as well. Long term integrations place the brief visit in context. Such simulations help observers plan campaigns for a once in decades interstellar passerby.
arxiv-2511-16447:
Gian Mario Sangiovanni and four co-authors integrate deep learning finding with spatial stats to monitor marine ecosystems near an Italian island coast. Photogrammetry collects non destructive samples of the seafloor fast. Detecting sea cucumbers in large images at scale needs automated models, yet finding chances vary with conditions. Ignoring that bias would distort maps of the animals' true distribution.

A thinned log Gaussian Cox process models the true intensity, with a finding function controlling how observations thin it. Manual identifications serve as the benchmark for the finding model. Location and image features drive finding probability. The combined approach yields distribution maps corrected for missed animals. Ecosystem monitoring gains both scale from automation and honesty from spatial stats.
arxiv-2511-17347:
Chunyang Xu, Michel Mehrenberger, and Chang Yang adapt a transport scheme from weather modeling to plasma kinetics. The Vlasov equation describes how a plasma's particle distribution evolves, and simulating it over long times demands methods that conserve mass and suppress fake oscillations. The cascade remapping method moves material through successive one-dimensional steps and is naturally conservative, but it had barely been used for plasmas.

The authors analyze the resulting scheme and prove second-order spatial accuracy, with the main error coming from geometry. Two improvements follow: a correction that preserves freestream flow and exact volume, and a limiter that enforces the maximum principle while keeping mass and positivity. Tests on advection, guiding-center, and relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell models show accuracy, strength, and long-term stability, preserving physical invariants better than rival conservative schemes under the right conditions. The method also parallelizes well.
arxiv-2511-17447:
Anja Beck and Eluned Smith benchmark how well two proposed detectors for the Future Circular Collider's electron-positron phase could identify charged hadrons using only their tracking systems. Correct hadron identification is crucial for flavor physics. Neither detector design includes a dedicated identification system. They rely instead on time-of-flight and energy-deposit information from silicon trackers, plus cluster counts in a drift chamber for one design.

Using fully simulated events, the authors estimate contamination from misidentified hadrons for flavor tagging, rare decays, and jet tagging. Tracker information strongly suppresses background for low-momentum hadrons, and excellent timing resolution improves rare decay channels by an order of magnitude. Very high momentum particles defeat time-of-flight entirely, but drift-chamber cluster counting still suppresses background everywhere. The study informs whether dedicated identification detectors are worth adding.
arxiv-2511-17547:
Jeyoung Lee and Hochul Kang generate images from brain activity with a two-stage framework called SYNAPSE. Reading images out of electroencephalography is hard: the signals are noisy, spatially coarse, and vary strongly between people. Earlier systems bolted EEG features onto pretrained image generators through elaborate alignment pipelines, ending up large and hard to interpret. SYNAPSE first trains an EEG autoencoder whose latent space is aligned with the CLIP image-text space, combining reconstruction with cross-modal alignment so the representation carries meaning.

In the second stage, that encoder is frozen and plugged into a lightly adapted Stable Diffusion model, so few parameters need training. On the CVPR40 benchmark, the method reached state-of-the-art fidelity with better reconstruction efficiency than prior EEG-to-image models, and it generalized across subjects. The authors argue that reconstructing what the brain perceives, not what it classifies, is the key.
arxiv-2511-17947:
Yining Yuan, J. Ben Tamo, Micky Nnamdi, Yifei Wang, and May Wang build a two stage approach to make language model diagnosis of depression more trustworthy. Models can automate parts of that work, but opaque thinking and weak alignment with clinical standards block adoption.

First, an evidence guided method makes the model alternate between extracting evidence and thinking, grounded in the standard diagnostic manual's criteria. Second, a confidence module scores each answer for factual exactness and logical soundness with two clear measures. On a dialogue data set the approach raises exactness and confidence scores sharply across five language models.
arxiv-2511-18047:
Oren Barkan, Yahlly Schein, Yehonatan Elisha, and three co-authors measure and improve how faithfully explanations of recommendations reflect the model's real reasoning. That quality, called fidelity, is one recommender research has largely neglected. Their method adapts path integration, which credits inputs by accumulating gradients along a path from a baseline profile.

Instead of one fixed baseline, they sample many plausible user profiles from real data and pick the most faithful attribution path, capturing effects of both seen and unseen interactions. In the broadest fidelity evaluation to date, across three models and three data sets, their method beats all baselines on counterfactual tests.
arxiv-2511-18147:
Aram Manaselyan, Vram Mughnetsyan, Anna Asatryan, and Albert Kirakosyan propose a new scattering process that limits electron mobility in atomically thin semiconductors called transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers. Their theory builds on how thin insulating layers screen electric fields in a spread out way, meaning the response depends on position in a spread out fashion.

They derive formulas for the scattering time and for how fast electrons move after bouncing off charged impurity centers, on monolayers over varied bases. Including this screening raises the predicted speed several times over. That speed falls as heat rises, but the relative boost from screening grows even larger at room temperature on a common base.
arxiv-2511-18247:
Sajad Khodadadian and Mehrdad Moharrami study the risk tail of a learning method that acts with hope. In this method an agent tries acts, learns from payoffs, and leans toward acts that look best so far. Past work bound the mean loss from the best act, or one high chance cap. That says little about rare but very bad runs.

The pair bound the full chance that total loss tops any set level. They cover a model based form and a model free form, each with two ways to set the hope bonus. The bounds show two zones: a mild tail at first, then a heavier tail past a shift point tied to the task. Such bounds help judge if a hopeful learner is safe to field.
arxiv-2511-18447:
H. M. Schmid and J. Ma work out how telescope blur and calibration skew measures of dust around stars. Polarized light imaging reveals dust halos, since dust scatters starlight in a way that carries a clear sign. Blur from the optics smears that sign, and parts can cancel, so raw numbers understate the true dust traits.

The pair simulate blur with a plain spread shape and with a spread shape typical of sharp modern systems that correct air wobble. They also test zero point fixes for cases like blocked star shots and barely resolved halos. Blur cuts the summed ring wise signal for the halo, they find, by a clear margin. Their steps offer a recipe for sound measures of halo light.
arxiv-2511-18647:
Maxwell Rosenthal introduces a model of identification design in economic theory. A decision maker sees the population distribution of signals from an information structure and ranks actions by their worst case payoff over all state distributions that fit those signals.

An environment is manipulable when every action can be made optimal under every admissible state distribution, and strongly so when nearly full information that hides at most one dimension suffices. Rosenthal shows both notions coincide with all actions sharing the same worst case payoff. For treatment effect models in econometrics, both criteria hold, and a full characterization is given for the remaining cases.
arxiv-2511-18747:
Alexander Clow, Hitesh Kumar, and Shivaramakrishna Pragada tighten bounds on the ultimate independence ratio of odd wheel graphs. A wheel joins a rim cycle to one hub point. The ratio tracks, over growing box products of the graph, the share of points that can be picked with no two linked, in the limit.

Classic bounds tie that limit between the chromatic and clique numbers. A long standing conjecture says all wheels sit at the chromatic end. Even wheels follow at once, since their two numbers match. Odd wheels are the hard case, and past gaps were wide. New bounds narrow the range for odd wheels. Each cut brings the wheel conjecture closer to a verdict.
arxiv-2511-18947:
Raphaël Maire, Andrea Plati, Frank Smallenburg, and Giuseppe Foffi show which rules set the large scale statistics of interfaces in active matter. At equilibrium, interfaces share universal fluctuation laws. Driven and active systems were predicted to form their own non equilibrium classes, yet most show equilibrium like waves in spite of wild micro motion, so the new classes hid.

Their hard disk model, driven by active collisions, mimics a shaken granular layer in two dimensions. In it they observe two predicted classes for the first time, both of KPZ type with a wave number twist. A third, new class appears when the bulk moves in a slow, glassy way. Conservation laws and slow dynamics pick the class, they argue.
arxiv-2511-19047:
Aradhana Singh, Amod Rai, Sheksha Dudekula, Devanarayanan P, and Antonio Palacios study how links between layers shape the joint dynamics of multilayer networks whose layers differ. In a symmetric setup each node in one layer links to its twin in the next. Shuffle those links at the same density, and one node may link to many, an asymmetric multiplicity.

One to one specificity aids synchronization inside each layer, they find. With random inter layer links, that internal sync hinges on how the shuffle bends the layer's homomorphism set, its structure preserving permutations. Amplitude death, where oscillations die out, also shifts with the link type. Wiring choice between layers thus acts as a dynamics dial.
arxiv-2511-19747:
Tenyo Takahashi introduces a construction for proving that broad classes of modal logics have the finite model property. That property says any unprovable rule can be refuted in a finite model, which anchors completeness results. The new subdivision construction works inside the framework of stable canonical rules.

Starting from such rules, the method builds a finite modal space, and dually a finite algebra, that refutes them. It covers logics and rule systems set by stable canonical formulas over algebras of finite height. As a payoff, a class of union-splittings among extensions of the logic K4 is shown to have Kripke incompleteness degree one.
arxiv-2511-19947:
Yuxuan Wu and eleven co-authors survey how knowledge distillation can bring agentic AI to mobile devices. Edge general intelligence means agents acting on their own in changing, resource-poor settings, but advanced models strain mobile limits on computing, energy, and storage. Distillation, where a small model learns from a larger one, is their main answer.

The survey stresses methods built for wireless settings, such as channel-aware self-distillation, distillation of channel state feedback, and robust signal classification. It reviews model families suited to the edge, including Mamba and RWKV, and cross-architecture distillation. Applications span vision, speech, and multimodal tasks. The authors close with open problems and future directions for the field.
arxiv-2511-20047:
Andrey Kupavskii and Janos Pach study coverings of a ball by planks, where a plank is the slab between two parallel planes. A problem posed forty-five years ago asks the converse of Tarski's classic plank result: if planks have large total width, can they always be slid, without rotation, to cover a unit ball? The authors add a further demand, that the covering be non-dissective.

Non-dissective means the planks are added one by one so the uncovered part stays connected at every step and vanishes only at the end. Improving a classical result of Groemer, they show a stated number of equal narrow planks always admits such a covering, and their proof gives a low-complexity algorithm. They also prove the first nontrivial lower bound for the number needed.
arxiv-2511-20747:
Takato Mori and Beni Yoshida revisit in 2025 a puzzle about baby universes inside holographic models of gravity. A baby universe is a small closed spacetime budding off from a larger one. Path-integral calculations hint its state space might be one-dimensional, leaving no room for entropy or inner life. Mori and Yoshida argue it can carry large entropy instead, using random encoding as their lens.

In their picture, the baby universe holds logical information that neither boundary region can read alone. Haar random encoding scrambles the data so thoroughly that reconstruction from either half is impossible. Two puzzles then dissolve: its states cannot be cloned, and no single observer can witness their fate at the singularity. The heavy operator that creates the universe also serves as its observer, making each microstate observer-dependent.
arxiv-2511-20947:
Tianyi Hao and colleagues build in 2025 a compiler pipeline that predicts when error correction starts paying off for real quantum algorithms. Their target is early fault-tolerant machines using the surface code, where logical operations run as lattice surgery. The pipeline chains open-source tools, error-aware gate synthesis, and magic state cultivation to turn logical circuits into physical ones. They compile two flagship algorithms, QAOA and quantum phase estimation, and simulate the resulting Clifford proxy circuits.

Both test algorithms reach break-even, the point where error correction beats no correction, at modest scale. A 5-qubit instance needs 2,517 physical qubits at code distance 11 when physical error rates sit at one in a thousand. At half that error rate, 1,737 physical qubits and distance 9 suffice. The numbers give hardware teams concrete targets for the first machines where correction helps algorithms, not just memory.
arxiv-2511-21047:
Changjian Xie introduces in 2025 a faster, sturdier way to simulate how magnetisation swirls and settles inside magnetic nanostructures. The governing Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation is stiff, and conventional schemes trade accuracy against stability. Xie's method reaches strict third-order accuracy in time, beyond most current techniques, while cutting the cost of the linear solves that made an existing third-order scheme slow. Nanostrip simulations validate the design against established benchmarks.

Robustness is the pleasant surprise. For Gilbert damping coefficients from 0.1 up to nearly 10, a range spanning the very large values near 9 seen in experiments, the scheme stays strongly stable and avoids non-physical magnetisation states. It reproduces domain wall motion consistent with prior validated studies, and the energies it computes sit significantly lower than the rival third-order method's, a sign of cleaner relaxation. The scheme suits quantitative studies of magnetic memory switching, where damping varies widely by material.
arxiv-2511-21247:
Jaime García-Martínez and seven coauthors release a new training ground for music technology in 2025: the Spheres dataset of multitrack orchestral recordings. Algorithms that separate a recording into its instruments have thrived on pop music but lacked clean orchestral material. The Colibrì Ensemble performed two famous works for the project, Tchaikovsky's Romeo and Juliet and Mozart's Symphony No. 40, plus scales and solo excerpts for every instrument.

García-Martínez and his coauthors recorded over an hour of music with 23 microphones, from close spot mics to room ambience, and supply each instrument section as an isolated stem from every position. They also measured the room's impulse responses, its echo fingerprint, for each instrument spot. Baseline tests with X-UMX models on separating instrument families and removing microphone bleed show both the dataset's promise and how hard full separation remains.
arxiv-2511-21847:
Wang and colleagues show that a photograph of a dripping droplet at the instant it breaks off can reveal the liquid's hidden properties. Viscosity and surface tension normally need specialized instruments, complicating quality control in printing and coating. The team filmed droplet formation at high speed for silicone oils, alcohol and glycerin solutions, and methanol, collecting 840 examples across wide flow conditions.

They trained machine learning models on each droplet's outline near pinch-off, plus the flow rate, to predict viscosity and surface tension from shape. The models succeeded, showing the break-up geometry encodes enough information to recover both properties and even to predict the droplet's shape at pinch-off for new cases. Unsupervised clustering of the learned representations grouped cases into regions matching known physical regimes in the Reynolds and Ohnesorge number planes, suggesting the method could simplify liquid testing in automated production.
arxiv-2511-22047:
Young, a researcher, stress-tests the safety guardrail models that screen prompts before they reach large language models, evaluating ten publicly available guardrails from Meta, Google, IBM, NVIDIA, Alibaba, and the Allen Institute. The test set holds 1,445 prompts across 21 attack categories, mixing benchmark items with novel attacks the models could not have memorized during training, a design meant to expose inflated benchmark scores.

Qwen3Guard-8B scored highest overall at 85.3 percent accuracy. Yet it collapsed from 91.0 percent on public prompts to 33.8 percent on unseen ones, a 57.2-point generalization gap suggesting training-data contamination. Granite-Guardian generalized best with only a 6.5-point gap. Most alarming, a 'helpful mode' jailbreak made two guardrails generate harmful content instead of blocking it. The study argues generalization to genuinely new attacks, not headline benchmark accuracy, should be the primary metric for judging guardrails.
arxiv-2511-22247:
Le, Tran, Nguyen, Zhou, and Gurrin make image search with optional text practical for small labs. In image-guided retrieval with optional text, a query is a reference picture. Sometimes with words like 'same dress but red,' and the system must handle composed retrieval, sketch-based retrieval, and plain visual search in one framework. The available flagship dataset is too heavy for modest hardware, and models tend to favor one subtask. Their FIGROTD dataset is deliberately friendly: 16,474 training and 1,262 test triplets spanning all three subtasks.

Their model adds a Variance Guided Feature Mask amplifying discriminative dimensions, trained with combined InfoNCE and triplet losses. Despite fewer training triplets than rivals, it reaches 34.8 mAP at rank 10 on the CIRCO composed-retrieval benchmark and 75.7 mAP at rank 200 on Sketchy, beating stronger baselines. Dataset and code are public.
arxiv-2511-22547:
Tan and a large collaboration compute a key quantity of proton structure directly from quantum chromodynamics. The Collins-Soper kernel controls how transverse-momentum-dependent parton distributions, maps of quark motion inside the proton, change with energy scale. Models had to guess its behaviour at large transverse separations. Using lattice QCD within large-momentum effective theory, the team simulated the needed correlations and extracted the kernel at physical pion mass and the continuum limit.

The calculation used lattice spacings from 0.052 to 0.105 femtometres and pion masses down to about 136 megaelectronvolts, with smeared operators and nonperturbative renormalisation. The resulting kernel is determined out to separations of about one femtometre with controlled uncertainties. It agrees with perturbative calculations at small separations and with phenomenological extractions. It is now the most precise first-principles constraint on its long-distance behavior. Feeding it into global fits shows an impact on them.
arxiv-2511-22647:
Bao, Cheng, Song, and Gu show that a conformal field theory's dynamics can regrow from its topological skeleton. Recent work built fixed-point tensor complexes encoding a conformal field theory, or CFT, in tensor network form, topological data from one dimension higher constraining local physics through generalised symmetries. The authors design a tensor complex renormalisation algorithm for that structure, a renormalisation-group flow respecting the generalised symmetry.

Starting from only the primary fields' three-point functions already reproduces the full fixed-point tensor. More remarkably, the flow stays stable when all conformal and geometric information is stripped out: topological input, plus partial conformal dimensions, recovers the complete tensors. They call this the topological bootstrap, validating it across the Ising, tricritical and tetracritical Ising, three-state Potts, and Yang-Lee models. Unlike classic bootstrap bounds, the method constructs conformal data, suggesting a route to algebraic descriptions of gapless states.
arxiv-2511-22947:
Chandra and colleagues study the inside of the pion, a tiny particle made of a quark and an antiquark, using a model rather than direct measurement. They compute generalized parton distributions, maps that describe how the pion's momentum is shared among its quarks and where those quarks sit inside it. They focus on the zero skewness case, a symmetric setup that makes the maps easier to interpret.

Working inside the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, a stand-in for the strong force theory, with a mathematical cutoff that also mimics quark confinement, they find their pion parton distributions match experimental data. They also match the JAM global analysis well at two energy scales. They also extract charge radii for the pion, obtaining 0.56, 0.63, and 0.83 femtometers for its scalar, vector, and tensor responses. These values are consistent with recent lattice simulations and a check on future collider measurements.
arxiv-2511-23047:
Sultanow and Hatziiliou revisit a classic question in spectral geometry, famously phrased as hearing the shape of a drum. The question is how much geometry is encoded in the eigenvalues, the vibration frequencies, of a shape. For a rectangle they assume the hard case: only a finite ordered list of eigenvalues is given, with no labels saying which vibration mode each number came from.

Their method splits the spectrum into a smooth part and an oscillating part and reads different facts from each. The rectangle's area comes from the high-frequency growth rate described by Weyl's law. The doubled side lengths, 2a and 2b, then appear as the peaks when the oscillating part is Fourier transformed, because they are the shortest billiard paths inside the rectangle. The recovery works even when the list starts at an unknown offset and the lowest eigenvalues are missing.
arxiv-2511-23147:
Zou and colleagues present the first systematic survey of sulfur monoxide and its rare isotope-bearing variant in Milky Way molecular clouds. They aim to measure how the ratio of sulfur-32 to sulfur-34 changes across the Galaxy. Until now that gradient rested only on carbon monosulfide measurements, a single tracer whose uncertainties could distort the picture, so an independent molecular check was needed.

Using the IRAM 30-meter telescope and the 10-meter Submillimeter Telescope, they detected the higher sulfur monoxide line in 136 of 184 clouds and derived isotope ratios for 55 sources. They found no correlation with distance or gas temperature, which argues against measurement artifacts. Ratios from the lower-energy transitions follow the rising radial trend seen earlier, while the higher-transition values sit systematically lower. Comparison with Galactic chemical evolution models suggests their star-forging recipes need revision in the low-metallicity regime.
arxiv-2511-23247:
Boukabene and Benbouzid-Si Tayeb review the literature on community detection in multilayer networks. The same people or entities are linked by several kinds of relationships at once, such as family, work, and friendship layers in a social system. Finding groups that are densely connected within themselves is much harder here than in single-layer networks, because each layer can carry a different community structure. The layers often disagree.

The survey organizes the existing methods into a taxonomy. It walks through the main types of multilayer networks and collects real-world applications across disciplines where layered data arise naturally. It then catalogues the open challenges, including how to fuse conflicting layer partitions into one defensible answer and how to evaluate results without ground truth. It closes with concrete directions for making multilayer community detection more accurate and more useful for future researchers.
arxiv-2512-00047:
Angelina Parfenova, Alexander Denzler, and Juergen Pfeffer study how language model agents converge when they annotate data together. Models are more and more deployed in shared settings, yet their teamwork as black-box agents is little understood. The team simulated thousands of multi-agent, multi-round talks on an inductive coding task.

The runs produced well over a hundred thousand messages, capturing final labels and full interaction records. Watching settling unfold shows whether agreement reflects shared understanding or mere herding. That gap matters for using agent panels as research assistants. Full records are preserved in the data, so settling can be studied as a process, not just an outcome.
arxiv-2512-00547:
Rebuilding a moving scene in three dimensions is much harder when several people interact with objects at once. Sandika Biswas, Qianyi Wu, Biplab Banerjee, and Hamid Rezatofighi present asset-driven semantic reconstruction of dynamic scenes in 2025. The scenes involve multiple humans and their complex interactions with surroundings.

Such environments matter for augmented and virtual reality, gaming, and embodied AI, yet they remain underexplored. Diverse motion patterns and frequent occlusions defeat simpler reconstruction pipelines. An asset-driven approach, reusing known object models inside the scene, could keep reconstructions stable even when people block the camera's view. Asset-driven means known objects are fitted into the scene rather than rebuilt from scratch.
arxiv-2512-00647:
Vision Mamba models promise transformer-level skill with lower cost, yet their efficiency is capped by the number of image tokens. Shanhui Liu, Rui Xu, and Yunke Wang present MambaScope in 2025, a coarse-to-fine scoping method for efficient vision Mamba. Token pruning and merging cut computation but lose information.

Discarding or compressing token representations throws away detail that fine recognition may need. A scoping approach first surveys the image coarsely, then spends tokens where detail matters. Keeping information while cutting cost would widen where state-space vision models can run, from medical scanners to mobile cameras. Coarse-to-fine mirrors how people scan a scene before examining details. Vision Mamba's promise is efficiency, so a method that protects it is on theme.
arxiv-2512-00747:
Tingjun Zhang and a large team of physicists study a magnetic material called alpha-MnTe in a 2025 paper. The material is a semiconducting altermagnet, a magnet with no net moment that still splits electron behavior by spin. The team adds lithium to it and watches what changes.

Using inelastic neutron scattering, they bounce neutrons off the material to probe its inner motions. Adding lithium flips the spin direction from in-plane to out-of-plane. It also raises the density of mobile charge carriers. The evidence points to an interplay between those roaming carriers and local magnetic moments, which shapes how the material acts.
arxiv-2512-00947:
Liyao Li and a large team study how language models can treat tables as a data type of their own in a 2025 paper. Tables run much of the world's stored data, in spreadsheets, databases, and reports. Language models shine on plain text, so researchers have worked to extend them to table reasoning tasks.

Their paper presents tables as a modality, a distinct channel like text or image that a model must learn to read. Rows, columns, and cell relations carry meaning that plain text flattens away. Framing tables this way guides how models should encode and reason over them. Better table skills matter for finance, science, and business tools.
arxiv-2512-01047:
Tanmay Ambadkar, Đorđe Žikelić, and Abhinav Verma automate the sharpening of learning specs in a 2025 paper. Logical specifications can guide reinforcement learning agents toward complex tasks by stating rules the behavior must satisfy. When a spec is under-specified, though, it leaves too much open, and agents may fail to learn useful policies.

The authors explore improving coarse-grained specs through an exploration-guided strategy. The agent's own exploration reveals which parts of the spec need refinement. Automating that loop could save the hand-tuning that now limits spec-based training. Better specs mean agents that learn intended behavior, not loopholes.
arxiv-2512-01347:
Fukunaga, Nakatsuyama, and Takahashi study odd points on translation surfaces. A translation surface sweeps one curve along another. Points where the surface pinches or folds are called singular. Past work dealt with the case where the two curves are freely set.

Here the pair handle the linked case, where the curves rest on each other. They use framed surface theory to sort the odd points. The work wraps up the full study of such surfaces. A full sort helps in geometry and in design of curved forms for art and building.
