Luminous fast blue optical transients and some tidal disruption events, where a star is torn apart by a black hole, display puzzlingly featureless light. The authors map which combinations of source and gas properties should produce emission lines of hydrogen and helium instead.

One-dimensional radiative transfer calculations draw the landscape. Very luminous sources with compact ejecta run so hot and ionized that lines are suppressed entirely. Intermediate cases favor helium lines from doubly ionized gas, while dimmer, more extended atmospheres show conspicuous hydrogen and neutral helium emission. Expansion speed further reshapes the outcome, giving observers a key for reading these transients.
arxiv-2601-01047:
Pablo Berná and three colleagues study how building blocks can rebuild any object in a function space. They also ask how fast a greedy method can do it. A greedy method grabs the biggest useful piece at each step. The authors use the order structure of these spaces, where some functions sit above others, as their main tool.

They prove that greedy rebuilding settles down in the order sense exactly when a certain largest-value inequality holds. They also show that looser building-block systems, called absolute frames, may fail to rebuild under the usual order, but do work under a weaker order taken from a larger space. Last, they link these systems to the shape of the space itself. One result pins down when such a space can be placed inside a space of continuous functions.
arxiv-2601-01447: Platon Promyslov studies a ruin problem for an annuity model in which a fixed fraction of the capital is invested in a risky asset. Under weak assumptions on the jumps of that asset, he shows the ruin probability satisfies a second-order integro-differential equation. For large initial capital, the ruin probability decays like a power function.
arxiv-2601-01547:
Gu and 6 co-authors test whether vision-language models grasp how people move objects for a purpose. People read a scene by linking change over time to a goal, not just by naming things. Models that score well on fixed tests often miss that link in messy real settings.

The team built EscherVerse from more than eleven thousand real videos, with a test set and a larger training set. Twenty-seven models were tried against human answers. The best model reached about fifty-seven percent, while people averaged about ninety-one percent. Extra training on goal-aware real data helped open models, but a wide gap remained.
arxiv-2601-01947:
Layered magnets that can be peeled apart, called van der Waals magnets, promise new spintronic devices, and CrSBr is a favorite because its electronic bands and magnetism are tightly linked. Shalini Badola and six co-authors alloy CrSBr with chlorine, replacing some bromine, and track how the magnetic and optical properties shift with composition.

Using Raman scattering and magneto-optical measurements, they find the alloys stay direct band gap semiconductors with the same coupling between electrons and magnetism. Exciton energies move only slightly, while the magnetic fields needed to saturate the material change a lot, showing that halogen mixing retunes both interlayer magnetic exchange and electronic interactions. Composition thus becomes a knob for setting magnon energies in future devices.
arxiv-2601-02047:
People read news that agrees with them, and interactive systems could offer balance if only they could sense selective exposure as it happens. Thomas Krämer and four co-authors test brain and eye signals as that sensor. They record EEG and eye movements. Participants read online news during the tests.

Eye tracking identified which passages each person actually read, and EEG measured the response. Agreement with the news correlated positively with theta band power over the parietal region of the scalp. The integrated setup suggests a future path. Systems could detect a reader settling into a filter bubble. They could respond with a more balanced information diet. This is a body-based route into a problem usually studied only through clicks.
arxiv-2601-02447:
Bennet Kahrs and five co authors improve three dimensional analysis of retinal scans made by optical coherence tomography. In routine care the slices of such a scan are spaced far apart, so the volume is sparse and uneven. Most learning methods dodge the problem by treating each slice as a flat image, which can leave neighboring slices disagreeing and ties the model to the resolution it trained on.

Their approach stores the scan as an implicit neural representation, a continuous function of coordinates, which does not depend on any one resolution. Two frameworks built on that idea produce dense three dimensional results from sparse input, including layer surfaces that stay consistent through the volume. The method can also be applied to scans taken under a different imaging protocol.
arxiv-2601-02547:
Federico Ardila-Mantilla and five co authors, including June Huh, connect combinatorics, geometry, and economics through one equivalence. A set function has the gross substitutes property, a demand condition from economics, exactly when its homogeneous generating polynomial is Lorentzian for all positive values of a parameter up to one. That answers a question posed by Eur and Huh.

The proof refines a classical result of Graham and Pollak by giving a sharp rank bound for the distance matrix of an ultrametric tree. With the characterization in hand, the authors resolve open problems that strengthen Mason's log concavity conjectures about counting independent sets of a matroid. Those conjectures had been posed in forms for valuated matroids, and in original forms by Dowling in 1980 and Zhao in 1985.
arxiv-2601-02847:
Bangwei She, Tian Tian, and Karel Tuma analyze a numerical method for problems where a moving fluid pushes on a flexible shell. Their scheme is linear and partitioned, meaning the fluid and the structure are solved in separate steps, which keeps each step cheap. The work uses a moving-mesh framework that lets the grid follow the structure as it bends.

The authors prove the method stays stable and derive bounds on its error, without assuming the shell barely moves or ignoring the fluid's own motion. They use simple elements for fluid speed, pressure, and structure speed throughout. Numerical tests match the predicted rate of convergence, which supports using the scheme for realistic fluid and shell problems.
arxiv-2601-03147:
Andrey Chernyshev develops a new approach to normal form theory, the method for simplifying a system of differential equations near a singular point. In the classical Poincaré-Dulac theory, a change of variables strips away every term that can legally be removed. Chernyshev instead builds a normalization flow, produced by a continuous averaging method, that moves a vector field continuously toward its normal form.

In the algebra of formal power series, he proves the procedure achieves full normalization. When convergence is taken seriously, he bounds the radius of convergence of the normalizing change from below. Building on these methods and related approaches, he also gives a new proof of the Siegel-Brjuno theorem, a classic result on when the normalizing transformation actually converges.
arxiv-2601-03247:
Leonardo Bettini and three co-authors build a data-driven model for controlling soft robotic muscles, the hydraulically amplified electrostatic actuators known as HASEL actuators. These artificial muscles suit compliant robots but are hard to control because their dynamics mix nonlinear multiphysics with memory effects and hysteresis. The team's strategy rests on spectral submanifold theory, which describes how fast motions settle onto a slow, low-dimensional surface.

When inputs change slowly, trajectories quickly converge to that slow manifold, so the authors learn an explicit input-to-output map on it from forced-response data alone, skipping decay experiments that can trigger hysteresis. They deploy the model for real-time control of an antagonistic HASEL-clutch joint. Tracking error dropped substantially compared with feedback-only and feedforward-only control under identical conditions.
arxiv-2601-03347:
Matteo Tagliazucchi and three co-authors warn cosmologists using gravitational waves as standard sirens to mind the peaks in the black hole mass distribution. Spectral siren cosmology reads the expansion rate from the shape of that distribution, so missing a feature biases the answer. The team analyzes one hundred thirty-seven binary black hole events from the GWTC-4.0 catalog with a flexible, data-driven spline model that places its knots where the data are most informative.

The flexible model resolves three distinct peaks, near ten, eighteen, and thirty-three solar masses, and the data prefer it over standard parametric models with Bayes factors up to two hundred twenty-six. Because those features correlate with the Hubble constant, precision improves by roughly twelve to twenty-one percent. The message is that the mass distribution's full complexity is essential, not decoration.
arxiv-2601-03447:
Anna Zavei-Boroda and four co-authors test cheap radar sensors as a way to watch water levels in the field. Knowing water height matters for flood control, water supply choices, and ecology, but standard gauges cost a lot and cover few sites. Radar measures from above without touching the water, so it stands up well to rough conditions.

The team ran commercial radar units in real outdoor tests and applied statistical filtering to clean the readings. One sensor reached centimeter-level precision with little calibration. That makes radar a practical option for wide, low-cost monitoring networks. The sensors could also ride on drones and robots to check remote or flooded places that people cannot easily reach.
arxiv-2601-03847:
Ly Ly Trieu and Tran Cao Son review and build an explanation system for deep neural networks powered by answer set programming. Deep networks are black boxes, and explanation methods differ by scope and style: some summarize behavior across all classes, others explain a single prediction. Well-known statistical tools like SHAP rank feature importance, rule extraction rewrites network behavior as if-then rules, and counterfactuals show the smallest change that flips a decision.

Their system, xDNN(ASP), sits in that landscape with a logic-based approach to generating explanations. The paper surveys the alternatives to position its method, contrasting statistic-based and rule-based strategies. Logic-backed explanations have a special appeal in regulated settings: they can be checked, enumerated, and argued with, rather than merely visualized as heat maps over the input.
arxiv-2601-04147:
Stephen R. Sharpe, as sole author, reviews how lattice QCD now yields scattering results for three particles at once. Lattice methods compute particle energies inside a finite box. Turning those energies into real scattering behaviour, and into resonance traits, is the hard part that recent work has advanced.

The review explains how finite-volume spectra feed into integral equations whose solutions are scattering amplitudes. Those amplitudes can be continued into the complex plane to hunt for resonance poles, the signatures of short-lived states. Sharpe also maps where the programme can go next, in both new systems and sharper methods. Readers get a guided summary of a fast-moving bridge between raw lattice numbers and physical three-body scattering.
arxiv-2601-04247:
Zhixin Liu and five co-authors design a backdoor attack on time series forecasting that fires late and unevenly. A backdoor hides a trigger in training data so a model misbehaves on cue. Existing attacks force the trigger and its target pattern to line up in time and across variables, which real settings often cannot promise.

Their framework, TDBA, injects triggers that encode where the target pattern should appear later. Activation can then land at any forecast position and differ by variable. One module builds position-guided triggers from smoothed Gaussian priors, and another weights training by trigger completeness, pattern coverage, and time offset. On real data sets TDBA beats existing baselines on effect while staying stealthy, and removal studies confirm the design can be controlled and holds up well.
arxiv-2601-04847:
Ernesto Fuentes Noriega and John Christos Vassilicos examine how turbulence spreads and cascades at once in a 2026 paper. They study the decay region near the centreline of three quite different turbulent plane wakes, the disturbed flow behind a body. There the turbulence is non-homogeneous, varying from place to place, and two-point diffusion works against the energy cascade down to very small scales.

They find the combined transfer rates stay roughly proportional to the dissipation rate across the inertial range, with a constant that varies by wake and position. One exception appears at the near-field edge. The result refines basic turbulence theory, which often treats diffusion and cascade separately, and matters for predicting wakes behind vehicles and turbines.
arxiv-2601-04947:
Maria Gorizia Ammendola and 11 co-authors test liquid-crystal metagratings as tunable beam splitters for quantum light in a 2026 paper. Structured optical materials offer a route to photonic quantum information processing in free space, without waveguides. Beam splitters are a basic building block of photonic circuits, and geometric-phase elements have already mixed circularly polarized light modes, including modes carrying orbital angular momentum, in open space.

Liquid crystals add electrical tuning: voltage-controlled birefringence changes how the metagrating splits transverse-momentum modes. A splitter whose behaviour can be adjusted in place makes free-space photonic circuits more flexible. Tunable components matter for quantum communication and sensing setups that must be reconfigured without rebuilding the optical table.
arxiv-2601-05247:
Oskar Fiuk's 2026 paper gives a new proof, by a probabilistic method, of the finite model property for the Guarded Fragment of first-order logic. The Guarded Fragment restricts how variables may interact in logical formulas, keeping the logic decidable while still expressive. The finite model property says that any satisfiable sentence has a finite model, and Fiuk's proof builds on ideas of Gurevich and Shelah developed for the Gödel class.

The proof stays conceptually simple. It yields the best possible doubly exponential bound on minimal model size, analysed up to constant factors. Matching example sentences show the bound is tight, and the approach extends to the triguarded fragment. Such bounds set realistic expectations for automated reasoning tools built on guarded logics.
arxiv-2601-05447:
Ian A O MacMillan and Lee P McCuller address, in a 2026 paper, a low-frequency noise problem that limits the LIGO gravitational-wave detector. Noise from many suspended-optics control loops mixes together. In bilinear noise, two such noise streams multiply and can mask real gravitational waves, forcing trade-offs across frequencies.

The authors build benchmark cost functions and figures of merit for this noise. Standard optimal control reaches aggressive feedback that saturates those lower bounds. They then combine that approach with robust control methods to compute stable feedback directly, using LIGO's alignment system as the test case. The resulting bounds can guide current observatories and set control requirements for next-generation detectors.
arxiv-2601-05647:
Xinyue Wang and 2 co-authors argue, in a 2026 paper, that transformers trained to predict the future naturally learn causal structure from time series. A causal graph shows which past variables actually drive which future ones. Their claim is that no explicit causal training objective is needed for that structure to appear.

When a transformer predicts future values, the sensitivity of its outputs to past inputs recovers the underlying causal graph. The authors prove this link under standard identifiability conditions and build a practical extraction method from aggregated gradient scores. On nonlinear, long-dependency, and non-stationary tests, the approach reportedly beat leading discovery algorithms, improving further as data volume and diversity grew.
arxiv-2601-05747:
Hassaan Farooq and 2 co-authors present FlyPose, a 2026 system for estimating human poses from drone views in real time. Drones flying near people, for delivery, traffic monitoring, or disaster response, need to perceive poses and actions reliably. Aerial images are low resolution, steeply angled, and often occluded, which defeats ground-level methods.

FlyPose is a lightweight top-down pipeline trained across multiple datasets. Person detection improved on several aerial test sets, and pose estimation gained substantially on the challenging UAV-Human benchmark. The system runs onboard a quadrotor during flight experiments with roughly twenty-millisecond latency on an embedded developer kit. The authors also release a small, difficult aerial pose dataset with manual annotations to support further work.
arxiv-2601-06347:
Building one named entity recognition model for many languages involves dozens of design choices. Jonas Golde and 2 co-authors test those choices systematically in a 2026 paper. Named entity recognition finds names of people, places, and organizations in text. Prior work often evaluated components only in combination, hiding which choices actually help.

Their extensive study varies transformer backbones, architectures, training objectives, data composition, and threshold selection for zero-shot multilingual models. Building on the findings, they present Otter, a small encoder model that beat strong multilingual baselines by a clear margin. Otter stays close to models vastly larger than itself while running one to two orders of magnitude faster, a practical combination for broad deployment.
arxiv-2601-06447: Boris Ryabko proposes a new approach to error correction in communication channels in a 2026 paper. Instead of adding redundancy in the usual way, the sender first transforms the input sequence so that its symbols become strongly interdependent. After transmission over a noisy channel, the receiver exploits that interdependence to detect and correct errors, reducing the remaining error rate significantly. Both encoding and decoding run in linear time, so the method's cost grows only in proportion to the length of the sequence being sent.
arxiv-2601-06547:
A good call on the morrow must do more than be close on the mean. Marc Wildi builds a call frame that weighs three aims at once in a 2026 paper. The aims: call the sign right, keep the miss small, and cross zero at a sane pace. A call that flips each day is hard to act on, no matter how close it is.

His frame, Smooth Sign Accuracy, folds the three aims into one score. It grows out of the old mean-miss score, not in place of it. He stretches it to series that drift and climb, with a keen eye on one-way runs. A test on tools for the trade cycle shows the frame at work in a real shop. The point is a trade that can be tuned, not a blind chase of one score.
arxiv-2601-06647:
Krishna Vinod and co-authors present eSkiTB in 2026, a synthetic event-based dataset. Its purpose is tracking skiers, a hard vision problem. Tracking in RGB broadcast footage faces motion blur and clutter.

Static overlays also obscure the fast-moving athlete in broadcasts. Event cameras sense contrast changes asynchronously, avoiding many such artifacts. Yet a controlled benchmark for winter-sport tracking has been missing. Their synthetic dataset fills that gap for event-based tracking research. Synthetic data lets researchers vary conditions that broadcasts fix arbitrarily. Ski speed, lighting, and background can be controlled in generation. Vision readers get a new testbed for event cameras in sports. It may guide real broadcast analytics for winter events later.
arxiv-2601-06847:
Mengmeng Zhang and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on vision-language models in medicine. Such models can write smooth, clear text about a scan or a photo. Yet they often fail to point to the spot in the image that backs up their words.

The authors trace that flaw to a lack of good training pairs. Few sets link a phrase in text to the right spot in a medical image. To fill the gap, they built MedGround. MedGround is a tool chain that turns mask data into pairs of text and image spots. The pairs are checked, so teams can train models to ground their claims in what they see.
arxiv-2601-07147:
Ji He wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on hidden wireless links that must stay unseen. The setup uses a system called PASS. A set of wardens watch the air for signs of a link. The wardens are spread out, and each one makes a yes-or-no call on what it hears. The calls are then merged by a majority vote.

The link in view sends data down to a user. At the same time, it sends random noise to hide the link's trace. The design uses two waveguides at once. One path bears the data, and the other bears the noise. He tests three laws for how PASS spreads its power. The laws are named as general, proportional, and equal. The goal is a link that works while the wardens, as a group, fail to spot that it is there at all.
arxiv-2601-07547:
Wentu Song, Kui Cai, and Tony Q. S. Quek study how many damaged copies are needed to rebuild a sequence exactly. The setting is the Levenshtein sequence reconstruction problem. A sequence passes through a channel that deletes one symbol and substitutes two others. Several erroneous copies arrive at the receiver. The question is the minimum number of copies that guarantees correct reconstruction.

Answers to this question set the redundancy needed in storage and communication systems. DNA-based data storage faces exactly these deletion and substitution errors. Knowing the threshold tells engineers when reconstruction is possible in principle. The authors work on the single-deletion, two-substitution channel as a clean test case. The paper serves coding theorists and storage system designers. It adds one precise piece to the broader reconstruction theory.
arxiv-2601-07647:
Caspar Schauß and colleagues examine a blind spot in studies of pit thermal energy storage. A pit store is a large lined hole filled with hot water, used with district heating. It adds flexibility on both daily and seasonal scales. Most large energy system studies, the authors note, ignore temperature differences between the store and the network.

Their setting is a sector-coupled energy system with high-temperature district heating. Sector coupling links electricity, heat, and transport in one model. When network and storage temperatures differ, usable stored energy changes. Ignoring that gap can distort plans for storage size and operation. The paper speaks to energy modelers who design heating systems for renewable-heavy grids. It argues for temperature detail in models that guide real investment.
arxiv-2601-08247: Liu He builds reinforcement learning agents that carry human cognitive biases into financial trading. The 2026 arXiv paper notes that markets reflect behavior that deviates from full rationality. Standard reinforcement learning models assume rational agents and may miss psychological effects. He integrates cognitive biases into the learning framework for trading decisions. The hypothesis is that biased agents can show human-like trading behavior. A second hope is better risk-adjusted returns than standard agents achieve. The study serves readers at the join of behavioral finance and machine learning.
arxiv-2601-08747:
Rubing Chen and four co-authors ask when a smart system should look facts up, and when it should just think. Many systems now fetch text at each step to help them solve hard tasks. That habit costs time and power. It can also fill the work space with text that does not help, and scores can drop.

The team builds an agent that learns to choose. At each step it can fetch new text, or it can reason with what it has. The aim is to grow the work context in a wise way, not by force. A reader gets a plan for AI help that is both cheaper to run and less prone to noise from poor search hits.
arxiv-2601-08847:
JV Roig sets out a new way to grade AI tools that fetch facts. Old tests use fixed asks and fixed right replies. Such tests can leak into train sets, so scores rise with no real gain. Human made right replies also cost much and can hold bias. Roig flips the task on its head to dodge all three flaws.

His method is called RIKER. It first builds a fake world where all facts are known by design. It then makes texts from those facts, and asks drawn from them. Since the truth was set first, grading is cheap and firm. A reader who grades fetch tools gets a repeat plan. It can make fresh tests that no train set has seen.
arxiv-2601-09747:
Marcílio Ferreira dos Santos and Cleiton de Lima Ricardo map dengue in Recife, Brazil, with tools from physics. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers reported cases from 2015 to 2024. Cases are treated as point clouds in space, and their connectivity is tracked across scales.

The authors use Vietoris-Rips filtrations and zero-dimensional persistent homology. Those tools watch clusters of cases merge as the scale grows. The multi-scale view reveals in detail how the city's many cases organize and connect. Patterns of spread can guide where mosquito control teams and clinics will do the most good.
arxiv-2601-10147:
Mei-Qi Gao and co authors ask if noise can calm chaos in light based rigs. Past work on chaos in such rigs used a mean field view. That view takes the rig as smooth and free of noise. It is a clean but fake case.

Chaos is quick to grow from small shifts. Even tiny noise can blow up in time. That puts the clean view in doubt. The team adds real noise to the rig. They find that noise can quench the chaos. The rig then acts in a more tame way than the clean view would say.
arxiv-2601-10247:
S. Ghinescu and S. Stoica update key counts for double beta decay hunts. In this decay, a core sheds two electrons at once. Hunts for a rare form of it may prove new physics. To plan a hunt, labs need exact counts for how the electrons share energy.

Those counts are named phase space factors. The team also give the full energy hues and how the pair's paths link. Fresh counts help labs tune their gear for the best catch. They also help labs tell one decay form from the next. The work is a ref update for the field.
arxiv-2601-10647:
Guido De Philippis and Alessandro Pigati work on the Michael-Simon inequality, a tool from geometric analysis. The classic version deals with area, the isotropic energy of a surface. They study energies that depend on direction, called anisotropic. Such energies arise when a material's cost varies with how a surface is tilted.

Their functional adds up a direction-based weight over a surface's tangent planes. They prove bounds for energies close to plain area. The proof leans on multilinear Kakeya-type bounds, deep results about how tubes can overlap. The paper links two fields that rarely meet. Its methods may help analysts treat a wider class of surface energies.
arxiv-2601-10747:
Silke K. Kaiser evaluates how to place traffic sensors across a city's streets. Planners need traffic volumes for every street segment to guide urban policy and greener mobility. Sensors are pricey to install and keep up, so only some streets have them. The rest of the network's volumes must be filled in from those readings.

Kaiser's data-driven study asks which sensor layouts make that fill-in most trustworthy. Placement choices made early lock in years of data quality. A poor layout leaves blind spots where policy flies dark. The work speaks to city governments that must stretch a sensor budget across a whole street network.
arxiv-2601-10947:
Anders Høst-Madsen studies faithful simulation of broadcast measurements in a quantum setting. A central server, Charlie, holds a quantum system and measures it with a general POVM. Two others, Alice and Bob, each care only about a partial function of Charlie's outcome. The question is how Charlie's single measurement can be shared so both get what they need.

The setup captures a common pattern: one measurement, many partial readers. Faithful simulation asks when the partial results can be produced without loss. The answer bears on quantum networks where measurement data are precious. It also touches the theory of how quantum information can be split among parties with different interests.
arxiv-2601-11147:
Zixu Wang, Bingbing Xu, Yige Yuan, Huawei Shen, and Xueqi Cheng rethink agentic workflow generation for multi-agent systems. Such systems solve tasks by coordinating agents through workflows. Workflows can be generated per task or per query. Query-level generation tailors each run, but its costs and benefits against task-level design were unclear. The authors analyze both, with theory and experiments.

They find that query-level generation is not always needed. A small set of the best task-level workflows already covers as many or more queries. That finding can cut the cost of running agent systems sharply. It tells architects to spend on a few strong workflows rather than bespoke ones for every request.
arxiv-2601-11247:
Valerie Gillot and Philippe Langevin study APN functions, a topic in finite fields. Their 2026 preprint reports new checks on the known cases. APN maps are prized in cipher design for their strength. They resist a class of attacks based on differences.

The team gives new invariants for these rare functions. They also give a test for when a function can be extended. A backtracking search then checks known facts one by one. The checks back a standing conjecture on 6-bit APN maps. The claim is that just 14 CCZ classes hold them all. Finite fields work of this kind feeds secure code and ciphers.
arxiv-2601-11347:
Sebastian Arnold and Eugenio Clerico find best e-values for a mean test. Their 2026 preprint deals with bounded random variables in statistics. An e-value is a newer tool for testing claims with data. It can grow as evidence piles up against a null claim.

The test asks if a mean beats a set rival value. The rival side is composite, a range and not a point. The team derives the unique e-values with best growth. Growth is judged in the worst case, in relative terms. The quality bar comes from work by Grunwald and others. Their frame first asked for matching hypothesis setups. This work is the first use past that strict setup.
arxiv-2601-11447:
Wadid Foudhaili and six coauthors guard secure chips with a smart monitor. Their 2026 preprint names it IMS, an intelligent monitoring system. Modern systems-on-chip talk through the AXI protocol bus. That bus has security flaws that attackers can exploit.

Protocol-violation attacks can cause denial of service on the chip. Parts or all of the chip can be forced to stall. Recent defenses lack live semantic checks of the protocol. They also evade full compliance checks in practice. IMS adds a dedicated real-time watch on AXI traffic. It checks meaning, not just form, as data flows. The aim is to catch attacks while they unfold.
arxiv-2601-11847:
Alexander Clow studies small quasi-kernels in directed graphs. A quasi-kernel is a set of nodes with no links among them. Each node in the graph must sit at most two steps from that set. Chvátal and Lovász showed in 1974 that each such graph has one.

The open part is how small such a set can be made. Clow builds them with a greedy method, step by step. Small quasi-kernels act as tight hubs for reach in a network. The work adds bounds and a clear build route for this graph problem.
arxiv-2601-12047:
Ina V. Kalitukha, Victor F. Sapega, Dmitri R. Yakovlev, and their co-authors probe spin in a lead halide perovskite crystal, CsPbBr3. They use light scattering that depends on spin, in magnetic fields up to 10 tesla. The light is tuned to exciton-polariton states in the crystal.

Their spectra show rich traits from Zeeman splits of excitons. Splits of electrons and holes that act with the excitons add more traits. Spin data guide use of such crystals in light and quantum tools. The work maps those splits with care.  Such spin maps are rare for this class of crystal.
arxiv-2601-12747:
Jingkai Li and six co authors adapt a pretrained transformer for MRI scans. These models do very well on photos of the world at large. MRI scans are a harder fit for two clear reasons. The shapes inside a body follow rules that photos do not teach. Scans are also scarce, since they are private health data.

Their model learns from scans with no labels at all, a trick called self supervision. That route needs no hand labels, which are slow and dear to make. A strong base model for MRI could lift many clinic tasks at once. Cuts, spots, and scans could all start from the same base. The work aims at a base model for health imaging as a whole.
arxiv-2601-12947:
Eslam Ibrahim, Yury Lysogorskiy, Ralf Drautz, and Pablo M. Piaggi compute the phase diagram of water from a general purpose potential. The phase diagram of water remains one of the most intricate benchmarks in molecular modeling. Many ice forms and the odd behavior of liquid water make it a stern test. Their potential is an atomic cluster expansion, a flexible machine learned model.

The potential was trained on density functional theory calculations. Those calculations use a named exchange correlation functional with dispersion corrections. Computing a full phase diagram from such a potential tests its transferability hard. A general purpose model that passes would serve many simulation tasks at once. The work matters for climate, chemistry, and materials modeling.
arxiv-2601-13147:
Jaydeb Das, Saurabh Niyogi, and Tripurari Srivastava study a lean dark matter model with a scalar gate. Their model adds two new bits to the Standard Model. One is a real scalar with no group charge. The other is a lone Dirac fermion, which plays the role of dark matter.

One twist sets their set up apart. The scalar does not take a fixed mean value at zero heat, as in the plain case. That twist links two fields of study. One is Higgs traits seen at colliders. The other is a strong first order shift in the early universe, when the electroweak force split. The paper shows how one lean model can be probed from both sides.
arxiv-2601-13347:
Aryeh Keating and Mirjeta Pasha build a step wise frame for big dynamic inverse tasks by parameter fits. An inverse task works back from data to the hidden state that made it. Big such tasks are ill posed, since the state is huge and data is thin. Rules that add past facts help, but the full form can eat more memory than any machine holds.

Their frame runs in steps. Data and state move through in a stream, so no full store is kept. At each step the model parameters are fit anew. That lets large tasks run on line as data lands. For scan and sensor teams, the frame fits tasks too big to hold at once.
arxiv-2601-13447:
Elliott P. Horch and co-authors share first three scope work with the Southern Connecticut Stellar Interferometer. The rig sits on the campus of Southern Connecticut State University in New Haven. It joins light from three scopes to read star sizes at fine scale, a task one scope cannot do.

The team gives two kinds of reads. One is a three scope read of Vega, a bright test star. That read proves the three scope mode works. They also give a fresh size read for a second star, whose name is cut in the record. For a small campus rig, three scope work that yields star sizes is a firm step.
arxiv-2601-13547:
Yujia Hu and Roy Ka-Wei Lee grade the why of hate speech flags, not just the flag. Hate speech tools are a core part of content care. Most tests score if a flag is right. Few score if the stated cause for a flag is sound. A right flag with a poor cause can still harm trust and appeals.

Their suite is called HateXScore. It holds four parts, each a mark of cause grade. Such parts can split a clear cause from a vague or off mark one. For care teams, cause grade is what a user sees on appeal. A suite to score it fills a blind spot in how such tools are judged.
arxiv-2601-13947:
Mattia Mattei, David Soriano-Paños, and Alex Arenas study how bacteria can coexist by avoiding rivalry in 2026. Bacteria regulate motility, their self-driven motion, through quorum sensing and other signals. Quorum sensing lets cells gauge how crowded their group is. Nonlinear density-dependent motility is known to create spatial patterns in active matter.

Its effect on coexistence of growing, interacting species is less explored. The team shows nonlinear competition avoidance favors coexistence in microbial populations. Species that ease off when crowded may share space in a stable way. The finding speaks to ecology and to engineered microbial groups. The result is a clear hint for work on gut and soil microbes. It may also help teams grow mixed strains in tanks with less strife.
arxiv-2601-14647:
Yuchen Fang, Xinshou Zheng, and Javad Lavaei propose an optimization method in this 2026 paper. Their method, TRSVR, is a stochastic trust-region method for unconstrained nonconvex optimization. It incorporates stochastic variance-reduced gradients, SVRG, to accelerate convergence. Classical trust-region methods limit each step to a region where the model is trusted. They usually need function value evaluations.

The proposed algorithm relies solely on stochastic gradient information. It never requires function values. Its trust-region radius is adaptively adjusted, based on a radius-control parameter and the stochastic gradient estimate. The cost is low. Each step needs just one pass of the kind used in most deep nets. The steps are few. That keeps the cost low when the task is large and the funds are tight. Readers get a step-size scheme for hard nonconvex problems where only noisy gradients are cheap.
arxiv-2601-15247:
Rian Dolphin, Joe Dursun, and co-authors pull structured risk data out of corporate filings. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with 10-K reports, the yearly filings firms must make. Each filing lists risk factors in free text, which is hard to use at scale.

The authors build a three-stage pipeline for the task. A language model first extracts risks with supporting quotes. Embedding-based mapping then ties each risk to a fixed taxonomy. A second model, acting as judge, filters out false assignments. The pipeline also improves itself on its own over time.
arxiv-2601-16647:
Baradhwaj Coleppa, Benjamin Fuks, and Akshat Khanna hunt for rare decays of the top quark. The top quark is the most heavy known basic part. In the base theory, it should not swap its flavor with no charge shift. Some wider theories say such swaps can still occur. Their 2026 preprint tests one such wider theory.

That theory adds two more Higgs fields to the known one. The three fields share a neat three-way pattern. In this frame, rare top decays arise through loops. The authors work out how large those decays could be. Their rates can then face tests at big colliders. A clear miss or hit would trim the list of live theories.
arxiv-2601-16747:
Doan-An Trieu and a team of seven co-authors push a lab route to soft X-rays. Bright bursts of high notes of light can reach that range. Such tabletop sources would aid scans of atoms and films. A weak terahertz field may stretch the burst range. Yet how that help works at weak strength was murky. Their 2026 preprint digs into that gap.

The team runs time-based quantum sims of the burst. They pair the sims with old-style path checks. A quantum path view adds a third lens on the act. The work shows how the flat top of the range grows. That growth points to brighter soft X-ray tools on a bench.
arxiv-2601-17047:
Yuanjie Gu and a team of six co-authors teach AI to read noise as a sign, not a flaw. Each scan tool leaves its own noise print on shots. That print mixes with the true scene in hard ways. Past work fought noise as mere dirt to scrub. Their 2026 preprint builds a base model that reads noise prints across shot types.

The model learns by contrast, pair by pair. It sorts prints by tool and scene traits. No vast tagged sets are needed for its train. Noise prints could flag bad gear or fake shots. They may also help join shots from unlike tools.
arxiv-2601-17147:
Margaret Garcia and a team of eight co-authors sort city water plans by how fit they stay in change. City water works now face states they weren't built for. Drought, growth, and storms push past old plans. Their 2026 preprint names dynamic fitness as the aim. That aim joins foresight with fast response in plan form. The team sorts real plans in archetypes by that aim.

Archetypes show which plan shapes bend and which break. Each shape trades foresight and response in its own way. Towns can set their plan next to the map. Weak spots then show before a crisis hits. Water boards gain a plain guide for reform.
arxiv-2601-17247:
Julius Graf and Thibaut Mastrolia study market making across a full trading day. A trading session has two parts. First comes open trade on a limit order book. Then comes a closing auction that sets the end price. Most past models treat end-of-day risk with a flat penalty on stock held. That skips the real chance the auction gives to trade.

The authors build learning into that two-part day. Their market maker can plan for the auction, not just fear it. That change should give more true quotes and risk control. For exchanges and trading firms, the work shows why the close must sit inside the model. It is where much liquidity lives.
arxiv-2601-17447:
Jorge Torres Gómez and five co-authors argue for joining literacy skills with STEM training. Well-rounded graduates need technical and soft skills at once. Most agree on that goal. Few technical schools show how to teach both in core classes. The authors build a bridge between the two schools of thought. They seek a practical path, not just a plea.

Their plan puts literacy-based skills inside the STEM curriculum. Reading, writing, and argument become part of technical work. That fit can raise the quality of reports and teamwork. It can also help engineers reach public audiences. The work serves teachers who must merge both aims in real courses.
arxiv-2601-17647:
Akila Sampath, Vandana P. Janeja, and Jianwu Wang quantify causal links in Arctic sea ice change. Ice melt and freshwater spread interact in complex ways. Their effects show as regional shifts in sea surface height. The team uses that height as a proxy for ice dynamics. They apply time-varying causal treatment methods. Those methods track effects that change over time.

Causal proof is stronger than correlation for climate choices. It can show which feedbacks drive polar change. Polar change drives global sea-level rise. Sharper causal maps help planners weigh risks to coasts. The work brings modern causal tools to a hard climate case. Time-varying effects fit a system that never stands still.
arxiv-2601-17947:
Bora Yimenicioglu and Vishal Manikanden build a label-free way to read the stiffness of red blood cells. Their 2026 preprint presents FlowMorph. Cell mechanics can flag blood and body-wide disease, so labs test how cells bend as they flow. Microfluidic tests can push thousands to millions of cells through tiny channels. Old pipelines, though, lean on hand-marked training data or hand-built charts, and they rarely use the physics of the flow itself.

FlowMorph trains itself with supervision drawn from that physics. The flow in such channels is smooth and ruled by Stokes flow laws. Using those laws as the teacher removes the need for labels. Faster, label-free tests could bring cell mechanics into wider lab use.
arxiv-2601-18047:
Amanuel Anteneh, Kyungeun Kim, J. M. Schwarz, Israel Klich, and Olivier Pfister turn laser interferometry into a learning machine. Their 2026 preprint presents an optical neural network built only from linear tools. The tools are field displacement and interferometry applied to coherent states of light. A neural network needs a nonlinear step to learn, and optics is mostly linear. The team gets the needed nonlinearity from how the input is encoded into phase.

Encoding tricks let plain optics do a smart machine's work. Light-based learning promises speed and low energy use. It may also resist some flaws of electronic hardware. The work adds a robust platform to the race for physical machine learning.
arxiv-2601-18247:
Óscar Bou Marqués and co-authors report direct views of droplets of vortex liquid in a superconductor. Their 2026 preprint studies the iron pnictide CaKFe4As4, written in the title as CaKAs4Fe4. Type-II superconductors in a magnetic field stay free of resistance while vortices stay pinned. When vortices depin, dissipation begins. Heat can melt the vortex solid into a vortex liquid, a change akin to ice melting. The team observes droplets of that liquid at half the critical temperature, in a field of 0.5 tesla.

Droplets show the melt begins in patches, not all at once. Pinning and melting set the current a superconductor can carry. Direct views guide both theory and magnet design.
arxiv-2601-18847:
Zihan Wu and four colleagues build MulVul, a team of smart agents that hunt flaws in code. A lone model is a poor fit for the hunt. Flaw kinds are too many and too un-like: what marks one kind is noise for the next. To set a lone model for each kind by hand would take a huge store of prompt craft. The team split the hunt by kind, with one agent per group of kinds.

Each agent's prompt grows by a kind of paired growth: two models trade drafts till the prompt sharpens. A search step pulls past code that fits the kind at hand, to ground each call. A wide, sharp hunt could catch flaws that a lone tool drops. It could also scale to new flaw kinds with less hand work.
arxiv-2601-19147:
Pankaj K. Agarwal and four co-authors plan the best paths for two square robots in a right angled world. The setting is a polygon with straight, axis aligned walls, possibly with holes. Each robot is a unit square that slides without turning, and both must move inside the space without clashing.

The team seeks optimal motion plans, the provably best routes for the pair. Two body planning is a classic hard case: each robot is an obstacle that moves with intent. Exact plans for even this simple case sharpen the theory behind warehouse and factory robot fleets.
arxiv-2601-19247:
Jiarun Liu and five co-authors align text, images, and 3D shapes in one shared space. Vision language models have tied words to pictures with great success. Adding the 3D sense, through point clouds and 3D Gaussians, opens training for retrieval, zero shot sorting, and scene naming across all three.

Their method, TIGaussian, disentangles the Gaussians so the alignment stays spatially aware. Knowing where things are, not just what they are, is what 3D tasks demand. Aligned text, image, and 3D data would let a user search a scene with a sentence, a fresh power for design and robotics.
arxiv-2601-19347:
Yang Ouyang and six co-authors help readers of online comments judge more fairly. Comments sway what readers think, yet their order and framing are set by platform algorithms that can bias judgment. Anchoring effects, where the first views drag later ones, are one such pull.

Their tool, CommSense, supports bias aware, reflective browsing of comment streams. It aims to slow the snap judgments that ranked comments invite. The work was shared at the CHI conference. Tools that make readers pause could lift the quality of public debate without censoring a single word.
arxiv-2601-19547:
Hiroshi Fukuda and Hiroshi Ozaki study a famous dance of three bodies in gravity. In the figure-eight choreography, three equal bodies chase each other along a single eight-shaped path. New solutions branch off from this orbit at certain points, a process called bifurcation. The authors look closely at what happens near one of these branch points.

They find cases where a branching solution folds back on itself at one side of the branch point. At the fold, the action, a key quantity in mechanics, forms a cusp. They present three worked examples under a Lennard-Jones-type force law. One more example uses a simpler homogeneous force. Such folds show how rich the three-body problem stays, even in its most famous special case.
arxiv-2601-19747:
Jiale Liu, Taiyu Zhou, and Tianqi Jiang build a framework for designing computer chips with language models. Models can now write RTL code, the register-transfer level description of a chip. Getting that code silicon-grade correct is the bottleneck. Simulation-based checks miss cases, iterative debugging can introduce regressions, and repairs can hallucinate.

Their framework, Veri-Sure, attacks all three problems. It is contract-aware, tying generation to formal statements of intent. Multiple agents share the work, and a temporal tracing system tracks changes over time. Formal verification then checks the result with proof rather than tests alone. The aim is chip designs that stay correct through the whole repair loop. The work targets a costly pain point in electronic design automation.
arxiv-2601-20047:
Divit Rawal and Sriram Vishwanath prove that curved space learns hierarchies exponentially more efficiently than flat space. Hierarchical data, like trees of categories, are common in language and biology. Euclidean embeddings of deep trees suffer volumetric collapse: too many distant leaves are squeezed close together. Hyperbolic embeddings avoid this by expanding outward.

The authors prove an exponential separation in sample complexity between the two geometries. Their setting uses hierarchies of given depth and branching under standard Lipschitz regularity. For Euclidean models, bounded radius forces the collapse; hyperbolic models escape it. The theorem gives theory to a practice already popular in representation learning. It tells practitioners when geometry choice is not a detail but the whole game.
arxiv-2601-20147:
Saima Afrin and five colleagues study how to make code summarization cheaper by choosing which tokens matter. Instruction-tuned models now write summaries of code, but feeding them whole files costs time and compute. The authors take a data-centric view: not all tokens in a code sample carry equal value for a good summary.

Their work asks which parts of the input can be trimmed while keeping summary quality high. That question matters as code models grow and usage scales up. Cutting wasted tokens would lower cost and latency for tools that document code for developers every day.
arxiv-2601-20247:
Jens Palsberg and nine colleagues report on the computer science challenges of quantum computing as it enters the era of early fault tolerance. Their report argues that progress will now be shaped as much by computer science as by better hardware. System design, integration, and evaluation become the main bottlenecks.

The authors survey what must change: compilers, programming tools, testing, and benchmarks for machines that partly correct their own errors. The report is a roadmap for researchers and funders. It makes the case that the next gains in quantum computing will come from software and systems work as much as from physics.
arxiv-2601-20347:
Chengying She and six colleagues present MMSF, a framework that joins medical images with clinical data to classify tumors and predict patient survival. Whole slide images are gigapixel scans that capture tumor shape in detail. Clinical descriptors add patient-level context for prognosis, but the two data kinds have very different statistics and scales.

MMSF is a multitask, multimodal supervised framework built on a backbone with linear complexity. It decomposes and fuses the cross-modal signals explicitly. Joining both views could give pathologists sharper risk estimates than either source alone. The hope is plain to state. Two weak views, joined well, can beat one strong view on its own.
arxiv-2601-20747:
Elham Aghakhani and Rezvaneh Rezapour study how people use AI chatbots for emotional support. Their 2026 paper draws on Reddit posts about mental health. Large language models are now often used outside clinics for comfort and advice. Yet little is known about how users judge these systems in daily life. The title phrase, like a therapist but not, captures that tension.

The team analyzed more than five thousand Reddit posts. The posts came from forty-seven mental health communities. They describe hands-on or exploratory use of AI for support or therapy. The study reads these stories to learn how people relate to the tools. It shows what users value and what worries them. Such evidence helps shape safer support tools.
arxiv-2601-21147:
Kevin Han, Haolin Cong, Bowen Deng, and Amir Farimani smooth a hidden source of error in learned atom models. Their 2026 paper concerns machine learning interatomic potentials, or MLIPs. These models power countless drug and materials discovery applications. They simulate molecular dynamics far faster than quantum methods. Two bottlenecks block realistic scales, though. Inference time is one; memory consumption is the other.

The authors target the cutoff, where atomic interactions are switched off. A sharp cutoff can jolt energies and forces. Smooth dynamic cutoffs ease that transition as atoms move. Better cutoffs mean stabler, larger simulations. The work serves anyone running MLIP-driven discovery pipelines. Small numerical kindnesses compound over millions of time steps. The paper polishes a part of the stack that many users never see.
arxiv-2601-21447:
Demetrio Lacava and Edoardo Otranto study how trade policy uncertainty moves the link between stocks and bonds. The pair uses daily United States data across a recent decade. Major stock indexes are tracked against the benchmark long-term Treasury bond.

A two-step framework based on volatility models estimates how their correlation shifts over time. Several model types, from fixed to smoothly shifting correlation, are compared. When trade news turns shaky, investors often flee stocks for bonds, which changes the link. Knowing how that link moves helps investors balance portfolios when policy risk spikes.
arxiv-2601-21647:
Eden Avrahami and Eliya Nachmani steer masked diffusion language models while they generate, without any training. These models build text by filling in blanks in parallel, a real alternative to word-by-word writing. Controls for steering them at run time are still little explored.

Their method refines the model's inner representation step by step, guided by one reference sequence. The reference pulls the output toward a desired style or content. Because nothing is retrained, the steering can be swapped per request. Run-time control matters for products that must adapt tone or obey fresh constraints on the fly.
arxiv-2601-21747:
Vincent Lemaire, Nédra Mellouli, and Pierre Jaquet model sepsis over time in a way doctors can fully read. Sepsis is among the hardest syndromes in intensive care, with varied paths and varied responses to treatment. Deep learning predicts it early but hides its reasons and ignores hidden patient subtypes.

Their relational model stays fully interpretable while tracking the patient's course. It also respects the latent groups that make one patient's sepsis unlike another's. A model a clinician can read line by line is easier to trust at the bedside. It can also teach, by showing which relations drive the risk.
arxiv-2601-21847:
Zechuan Huang and co-authors automate a piece of algorithm design that humans usually handcraft: the reward function. In meta-black-box optimization, a reinforcement learning policy learns how to design optimization algorithms. Until now, the rewards guiding that learning were written by human experts.

Human-written rewards bring design bias and invite reward hacking, where the learner games the score instead of solving the problem. The team's 2026 preprint, READY, focuses on discovering rewards automatically for this meta-optimization setting. If rewards can be learned rather than guessed, automated algorithm design changes. It becomes less dependent on expert intuition. It also becomes less prone to hidden distortions.
arxiv-2601-22447:
Yiting Liu and Zhi-Hong Deng read sparse autoencoder features by their weights, not just their firing patterns. These tools split a model's inner states into parts a human can grasp. Their 2026 preprint notes that most readings watch when a feature fires, and skip what the feature does next.

A feature exists to rebuild a state that the model then uses. Reading its outgoing weights shows that role. The shift can give truer, more useful labels for features. Better labels mean better maps of how models think. The work refines a core safety and science tool.
arxiv-2601-22547:
Shilong Zhao and a large team built PersonaAct, a set of fake short-video users that act like real ones. Platforms fear filter bubbles, where picks narrow what a user ever sees. Their 2026 preprint notes that real user studies cost much and raise privacy flags. Past simulators, built on text alone, act in thin, fake ways.

PersonaAct gives each agent a personal profile and richer behavior. Teams can then test what would happen if the platform changed its picks. Such counterfactual audits can flag bubbles before they harm. The work makes a touchy test cheap and safe.
arxiv-2601-22647:
Jinwoo Jang, Minjong Yoo, Sihyung Yoon, and Honguk Woo give embodied agents a team of world models to swap between at test time. Such agents act in the real world through language-guided plans. Their 2026 preprint notes that a fast-changing world breaks any one fixed model of it.

Their mixture keeps several world models and picks among them as the scene shifts. The idea borrows from mixture-of-experts designs. Flexible world sense should lift planning in homes, streets, and wards. The work aims at agents that adapt, not just act. It is tested in dynamic settings.
arxiv-2601-22947:
Mengyu Ye, Ryosuke Takahashi, Keito Kudo, and Jun Suzuki study a new kind of language model that fills in masked words. Masked diffusion models are a rival to the standard left-to-right approach. They match rivals on many tasks, but lag on open-ended writing.

The authors blame strict position rules: shifting a token by one place can wreck the meaning. They show this with controlled tests, then relax the alignment demand. Looser position rules could help these models write more freely while keeping their speed edge. Controlled interventions support the claim: a one-position shift alone was enough to badly damage the model's output semantics.
arxiv-2602-00047: Laha Ale and colleagues cut the cost of training on edge devices by pruning the training set itself. On device learning guards privacy and cuts delay, but training on huge local data drains batteries and strains heat and memory limits. Their method ranks samples by loss stats from a short warm up run, then keeps only the most telling points. Tests on image tasks show time and energy fall near in step with the prune rate.
arxiv-2602-00247: Samyak Jha and Junho Kim propose CAPA, a contribution aware pruning method for large vision language models. Attention scores are a poor proxy for true contribution, the authors argue, while Attention Contribution, weighting attention by value vector size, tracks it better. Visual attention sinks split into Probability Dumps, low contribution and safe to prune, and Structural Anchors, high contribution and essential. Feed forward networks for visual tokens also show redundancy, mainly in middle layers where image tokens behave linearly.
arxiv-2602-00447: Youjie Chen and team study student engagement with a generative tutor across 200 classes at ten institutions, using interaction logs. Generative AI creates opportunities for individualized learning support, yet students may use these tools in ways that fail to support learning. Engagement may vary across class contexts, potentially leading to unequal experiences. The authors examined engagement from 11,406 students through two stages, first identifying four engagement types per session. In particular, 10.4% of sessions showed shallow engagement with prevalent copy-pasting. At the student level, they show how engagement patterns differ.
arxiv-2602-00647: Noorain Mukhtiar and colleagues address unfairness in federated learning, where uneven data and uneven participation leave some clients behind. They separate two harms: bias in representations from misaligned clients, and bias in joint work from inequitable weight when models are combined. Their CoRe-Fed framework tackles both together, aligning local and global embeddings to cut drift and adjusting each client weight by past participation and alignment. Tests across varied models and data sets show gains in both fairness and overall performance over leading baselines.
arxiv-2602-00947: Mohan Reddy argues chat tools degrade analysis performance for multi-step tasks, via the 1984 Keyhole Effect. Viewing large spaces through narrow viewports carries cognitive cost, stated as overload equals max of zero, task items minus visible items minus working memory limits. Mechanisms include displacement harming spatial memory, hidden state filling memory, verbalization dimming visual recognition, linear text blocking aids, and serialization costs growing with size. When overload exceeds zero, error probability rises and biases amplify. Eight hybrid patterns address these failures.
arxiv-2602-01047: Xinrong Chen and co-authors cut down made-up sights in vision-plus-text models with a no-train trick at decode time. Word habits can push these models to pen smooth text with no tie to the picture. Their Residual Decoding leans on past tokens, inner thought traces, and shifting token odds to rein in that word pull. Tests show it curbs word-led fakes, ties text to pictures, and cuts fake objects. It also held up well on broad vision-plus-text tests, hinting at wide use.
arxiv-2602-01247: Maryam Maghsoudi and Ayushi Mishra trace how brain-to-speech decoders carry info across spoken, mimed, and imagined speech. Such decoders score well in all three modes, yet the inner routes that let info travel across modes stayed murky. With cross-mode patch swaps, three-mode blends, and fine-to-coarse causal hunts, they find small but not scattered cell groups steering cross-mode transfer. Speech modes sit on one smooth causal sheet, with transfer run by tight, layer-bound subspaces in a ranked, direction-tied layout.
arxiv-2602-01747: Hongseok Choi and colleagues improve essay scoring, where scarcity of labeled data blocks robust systems in practice. They add three techniques to DualBERT: two stage fine tuning with low rank adaptations for essays. Score alignment matches score distributions, and uncertainty aware self training on unlabeled data adds pseudo labeled samples while limiting noise spread. Tests on ASAP++, TOEFL11 and ELLIPSE show all three techniques help with thirty two samples. Their integration reaches over ninety percent of full data performance, and score alignment helps in both limited and full data settings.
arxiv-2602-02247: Julian Koellermeier derives a new energy equation for the shallow water linearized moment rules, extending the shallow water rules for free-surface flows. Classic rules assume a depth-averaged vertical velocity profile, while moment rules allow vertical variation through a polynomial profile with extra rules for its coefficients. The derivation follows the standard shallow water energy derivation and uses the skew-symmetric formulation of the model. It should help extend the method to other moment variants and their numeric answer, giving an energy treatment where only the standard derivation existed.
arxiv-2602-02447:
Thomas M. Prinz and 2 co-authors sharpen the complexity of two classic questions for workflow nets, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Petri nets model processes as tokens moving through places and transitions. Reachability asks whether a given token pattern can occur, and covering asks whether a pattern containing at least those tokens can occur.

For sound, acyclic, free-choice workflow nets, the authors bring both problems down to a quadratic bound. They also explain answers, not just decide them. Three new concepts do the explaining: admissibility, requiring all marked places to be pairwise concurrent; maximum admissibility; and diverging transitions that originally produced the concurrent tokens. Algorithms borrow post-dominance frontiers from compiler construction. The result is a straightforward implementation that can say why a marking is or is not reachable.
arxiv-2602-02547:
Hankyeol Kim and 1 co-author make physics-informed neural networks survive corrupted measurements, in a 2026 arXiv paper. These networks solve inverse problems and recover governing equations by baking physical laws into training. Complex noise and gross outliers degrade them badly, and the noise distribution is usually unknown beforehand.

Their noise-adaptive network embeds an energy-based model inside the training loop to learn the distribution of prediction residuals. The learned energy landscape powers a trainable reliability gate that filters data points whose residuals look anomalous. A rejection cost prevents the trivial escape of discarding valid data wholesale. Benchmarks on partial differential equations with non-Gaussian noise and varying outlier rates followed. The method significantly beat existing robust baselines, isolating outliers while reconstructing the true dynamics under severe corruption.
arxiv-2602-02947:
How disaster graphics help or fail other audiences is examined by Anuradha Madugalla and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Hazard maps, evacuation diagrams, and pictorial guides must convey danger quickly. Yet many graphics are hard to interpret, and access for at-risk people remains uneven and little studied.

The authors interviewed disaster communication practitioners and scholars. Graphics are widely expected and heavily relied on across preparedness, warning, and response. Big access gaps persist for people with vision impairments, older adults, and culturally diverse communities. Adapting graphics during an unfolding emergency proved hard due to time pressure, limited guidance, and scarce resources. The paper offers advice for agencies and designers.
arxiv-2602-03047:
How particles settle under repulsion is characterized by Sung-Soo Byun and 3 co-authors in a 2026 mathematics paper. They study Riesz gases, systems whose pairs interact through a power-law kernel, in rotationally symmetric external fields. The equilibrium measure shows where the particles gather in the long run under those competing forces in higher dimensions.

For broad classes of confining potentials, the balance sits on the unit ball with a clear density. The main contribution reverses the problem. Starting from a prescribed density written as a power series, the authors determine the potential that produces it. A hypergeometric identity is a key proof ingredient. Uses include power-type potentials and a Coulomb gas confined to a half-space.
arxiv-2602-04247:
Emotion in Alzheimer's speech is measurable, and a new corpus makes it researchable. Cheonkam Jeong and colleagues release DementiaBank-Emotion in a 2026 paper, the first multi-rater emotion annotation of Alzheimer's speech. Nearly fifteen hundred utterances from over a hundred speakers were labeled for six basic emotions plus neutral.

Patients expressed non-neutral emotions far more often than healthy controls. Acoustic analysis hinted that pitch modulation for sadness nearly vanishes in patients while loudness still separates emotion categories. The authors release the corpus, guidelines, and training materials. Small samples temper the acoustic claims, and they flag the need for replication plainly.
arxiv-2602-04347:
Practice works best when each exercise lands at the edge of a learner's skill. Lukas De Kerpel and 2 co-authors build a recommender that picks those exercises using contextual Thompson sampling, a bandit method that learns from outcomes. Their 2026 paper targets digital practice in operations research and analytics courses.

At each step, the system selects the exercise most likely to raise the targeted skill, using learner features and past performance. Skill gain is measured as the change in estimated skill around each exercise. On data from an online mathematics tutoring platform, recommendations produced greater improvement and adapted across learners. Instructors also learn which exercises carry consistent teaching value.
arxiv-2602-04647:
Saak Gabriyelyan, Alexander V. Osipov, and Evgenii Reznichenko characterize a convergence property for topological groups in a 2026 mathematics paper. The property, named with the Greek letter kappa and the Fréchet-Urysohn names, concerns how sequences can approach points using only certain small families of open sets.

Their characterization yields several consequences. A hemicompact group has the property exactly when it is locally compact. Quotients and products behave well: the property lifts from a quotient and survives multiplication by a nicer space, within topological vector spaces. Under an extra set-theoretic assumption, the authors also build a countable Boolean example with the property that lacks a related stronger trait. The paper organizes a subtle corner of general topology.
arxiv-2602-04747:
Bijan Bagchi and Anindya Ghose-Choudhury connect a generalized quantum framework to classic nonlinear equations in a 2026 paper. They reduce a recently introduced scheme by Chodos and Cooper to the Levinson-Smith and Liénard families, which describe oscillators with position-based damping and restoring forces.

For Levinson-Smith equations, the authors find links to quantum systems whose mass depends on position. Soliton-like solutions, stable wave packets, emerge from a level surface rule in that setting. For Liénard equations with coefficients of fit symmetry, they convert the problem to a standard Abel form. Closed-form solutions then exist. The work widens the class of acceptable solutions open to this quantum framework and ties it to known oscillator models.
arxiv-2602-04947:
Mitchell Karmen and 3 co-authors wrote this 2026 astronomy paper, published in The Astrophysical Journal, about tidal disruption events. These flares occur when a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole and gets torn apart. Counting them across cosmic time could reveal how many black holes of each mass exist, especially small ones far away.

The team built a model that predicts event rates under several assumptions about the black hole population. They fold in changing galaxy densities, merger rates, dust, and possibly different star mixes in the early universe. Rates rise toward cosmic noon, then fall. Forecasts follow for the Rubin LSST survey, the Roman telescope's time-domain survey, and the JWST COSMOS-Web field, plus a method to turn LSST counts into direct limits on black hole numbers.
arxiv-2602-05047:
Rendering a 3D scene in real time often uses Gaussian splatting, which paints scenes from millions of soft blobs. Grzegorz Wilczyński and 4 co-authors add quantum circuits to that pipeline in this 2026 paper. The weak point they target is view-dependent color: sharp reflections and transparency, which the standard spherical harmonics describe poorly.

Their framework, QuantumGS, replaces the small classical networks that modulate color with variational quantum circuits. Viewing direction is mapped directly onto the Bloch sphere, the natural geometry of a qubit, which suits directional data well. A hypernetwork generates or conditions the circuits for each blob. The authors report better expressiveness and generalization than classical rivals when the parameter budget is small. Code is available in the supplementary material and on GitHub.
arxiv-2602-05147:
How does the inner ear sort sounds by frequency so sharply? Yasuki Murakami, writing alone, offers a compact answer in this 2026 biophysics paper. His claim is that frequency analysis in the mammalian cochlea is an active, energy-dissipating process, not a passive mechanical filter.

A minimal active beam model carries the argument. Inside it, a spatially varying viscous coupling generates forces that spread in a wave-like way, while local energy injection competes with spatial redistribution to govern the motion. That balance is enough to reproduce, quantitatively, four hallmarks of real hearing: sharp tuning, high gain, compression of loud sounds, and spontaneous otoacoustic emissions, the faint sounds healthy ears themselves emit. Murakami closes by placing hearing within a broad class of nonequilibrium pattern-forming systems, kin to other active matter rather than to a microphone.
arxiv-2602-05247:
PDS 70 is the one disk where two still-forming planets have been caught in the act, making it the prime laboratory for dust growth. Hauyu Baobab Liu and 6 co-authors present the first deep full-polarization observations of the disk at 873 micrometers in this 2026 astronomy paper, accepted by Astronomy and Astrophysics. Polarized light betrays grain sizes, because grains scatter most efficiently when their size matches the wavelength.

Across the disk's great ring, the team measured linear polarization of about one to two and a half percent, with angles preferentially aligned to the disk's projected minor axis. The standard reading is self-scattering by grains no larger than about a hundred micrometers. Radiative transfer simulations narrow that to about 87 micrometers in a slightly lopsided, marginally opaque ring. The cap on grain size suggests icy grains stop growing by fragmenting or bouncing off each other.
arxiv-2602-05547:
A model trained on many reasoning tasks at once can surge ahead on some while stalling on others, which makes average scores misleading. Shyam Sundhar Ramesh, Xiaotong Ji, and 6 co-authors tackle that imbalance in GRPO, a popular reinforcement learning method for language models. Tasks differ in how often their prompts give zero advantage, and hence no learning signal, which further skews what the model actually learns from.

Their method, Multi-Task GRPO, adjusts task weights on the fly to lift the worst-performing task, not just the average. A ratio-preserving sampler makes sure the adjusted weights are truly reflected in the gradient signal. In three-task and nine-task tests, the method beat baselines on worst-task accuracy by clear margins while keeping average accuracy competitive. The paper targets teams who need reliable performance across a task suite.
arxiv-2602-05647:
A fundamental solution is the basic building block for solving a differential equation, and Stefano Biagi and Marco Bramanti construct one for a new class of higher-order operators. These operators are built from Hörmander vector fields and are homogeneous under a family of dilations, but they are not tied to any Lie group structure. The authors call the lifted, well-behaved versions generalized Rockland operators.

They prove the operators are hypoelliptic, meaning their solutions gain smoothness in a strong sense, and, under a natural condition on the degree, that a global fundamental solution exists. That solution is jointly homogeneous in its two variables and obeys sharp estimates. The theory also covers some higher-order heat-type operators and their fundamental solutions. It extends tools that were developed for group-based settings to operators with no group behind them, widening the range of equations analysts can treat.
arxiv-2602-05847:
Video models that also hear sound still reason poorly across the two streams, and Zhangquan Chen and 12 co-authors propose OmniVideo-R1 to close that gap. The reinforced framework teaches models to think with omnimodal cues, in the authors phrase. Two strategies carry the design.

First, query intensive grounding, built on self supervised learning, ties reasoning to what the question actually asks. Second, modality attentive fusion, built on contrastive learning, weighs audio and visual evidence against each other. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show the model consistently beating strong baselines. The authors highlight robust generalization as a further strength. The work targets the growing class of omnivideo systems used in media understanding. Its lesson is that fusion should be guided by the query, not applied uniformly across a clip. The paper runs to nineteen pages with twelve figures.
arxiv-2602-05947:
A young pulsar in a tight orbit with another compact star is a laboratory for general relativity. Vleeschower and 11 co-authors present eighteen years of timing for the binary PSR J1906+0746. Six radio telescopes contributed data, from Arecibo and Green Bank to MeerKAT and FAST. The pulsar spins every fraction of a second and orbits its companion in just under four hours, on a mildly eccentric path.

A coherent timing solution across the full span sharpens three relativistic measures: the advance of periastron, the Einstein delay, and the shrinking of the orbital period. Assuming general relativity holds, the team derives precise masses for both stars, consistent with a double neutron star system. A fitted change in the projected orbit size shifts those masses somewhat, an effect expected from correlations in the fit. If confirmed, that drift matches spin orbit coupling seen in a sister system.
arxiv-2602-06147:
Some of the most symmetric algebraic structures in math grow out of a construction called a cubic norm pair. Tom De Medts and Torben Wiedemann build Lie algebras from such pairs over any commutative base ring. Lie algebras are spaces where a bracket operation encodes symmetry and motion.

The algebras they build carry a grading by the G2 root system, a labeling that sorts pieces by simple weights. When the starting pair is a cubic Jordan matrix algebra, the grading sharpens to the larger F4 system. From these algebras, the pair then construct matching groups. Many detailed structure results for both the algebras and groups fill out the work.
arxiv-2602-06347:
Before a flow solver can be trusted, it must prove itself on problems with known answers. Yujoo Kang and Sang Lee verify and validate their lab's high-order solver for compressible flow, built on a compact finite difference scheme. Such flows involve shocks, turbulence, and sharp layers that punish sloppy numerics.

Five classic cases make up the test suite: a one-dimensional shock tube, a shock meeting a shear layer, channel flow, a turbulent boundary layer, and a shock striking a turbulent boundary layer. Against exact answers and reference simulation data, the solver captured shocks cleanly, resolved swirling structures, and matched first and second order flow statistics well. The study documents the solver's readiness for harder work.
arxiv-2602-06447:
Steering two mixed fluids with a chemical source term is the control problem studied by Sheetal Dharmatti and Greeshma K. Their system couples the Cahn-Hilliard equation for phase separation with Navier-Stokes flow, modeling two immiscible, incompressible fluids. The cost is measured only at a finite set of sensor points over time, matching realistic setups.

Pointwise readings make the cost rough in a mathematical sense, which is the core difficulty. The authors prove strong solutions exist, that an optimal control exists, and that the control-to-state map can be differentiated.
