An adjoint system built by a transposition method then yields first-order necessary conditions for optimality. A variant adds a final-time pointwise term, and the analysis extends to singular potentials.
arxiv-2602-06547:
AI coding agents now run third-party skills, bundles of instructions and scripts that execute with the user's full privileges. Yi Liu and 6 co-authors scanned nearly a hundred thousand skills from two major registries and found real malicious behavior hiding inside. Static pattern matching plus dynamic behavior checks confirmed the findings.

In total, over a hundred and fifty skills carried confirmed malicious behavior, spanning hundreds of vulnerabilities across a dozen attack techniques. Threats looked deliberate: each bad skill averaged several vulnerabilities across attack phases. Two dominant strategies emerged: stealing credentials through remote code execution, and manipulating the agent through instructions planted in documentation. Over half the cases traced to one actor using templated brand impersonation at scale.
arxiv-2602-06847:
Kuan-Cheng Chen, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, Mahdi Chehimi, Felix Burt, and Kin K. Leung design scheduling for distributed quantum neural networks, where several quantum processors train together over a quantum internet. Entanglement, the resource that links the processors, is fragile and decays with time, while training demands tight sync. Their framework, CEAS, co-designs the consensus protocol with entanglement care.

Updates are weighted by quantum Fisher information so noisy parts count for less, and Bell pairs are scheduled as perishable goods that expire. The framework also includes quantum-authenticated Byzantine fault tolerance, so bad nodes cannot derail training. Theory guarantees convergence under varied noise. Simulations show CEAS holds 10 to 15 percentage points more accuracy than baselines that ignore entanglement under coordinated attacks, while using 90 percent of its Bell pairs.
arxiv-2602-07047:
Muhammad Rashid and three co-authors explain image model decisions at pixel level with a new method, ShapBPT. Pixel-level attributions help users see which image features sway a prediction. The Owen formula for hierarchical Shapley values is widely used for such explanations, yet old hierarchical methods ignore how image data nests across scales. That leads to slow convergence and weak fit to true morphological features, and no prior Shapley method had used data-aware hierarchies for vision.

ShapBPT ties Shapley coefficients to a binary partition tree built for images, so attributions track intrinsic image morphology. Relevant regions gain priority, and compute overhead falls. Tests show better fit to image structures and better efficiency than old explainable vision methods. A study with 20 human subjects found people preferred ShapBPT explanations, which links hierarchical Shapley theory to structured visual data in a more efficient, meaningful way.
arxiv-2602-07247:
Black hole coronae, the hot clouds that shape X-ray emission, change size during outbursts, but tracking that change across many systems is painstaking.  Yuexin Zhang and fourteen co-authors use NICER archival data on nine black hole X-ray binaries, selecting 171 observations with quasi-periodic oscillations.

Modeling spectra, oscillation amplitudes, and phase lags with a time-dependent Comptonization model, they constrain corona size and feedback fraction through outbursts.  Oscillation frequency climbs from about 0. 1 to 10 hertz in harder states and steadies near 4 to 5 hertz in the soft-intermediate state, while the corona starts huge and contracts.  Space experts get a thorough picture of corona evolution across the population.
arxiv-2602-07447:
Speakers of related languages partly understand each other, but measuring that intelligibility has relied on slow human testing.  Liviu P Dinu and four co-authors build a computational metric from lexical similarity, combining surface and meaning similarity of related words.

Applied to French, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, and Romanian in both written and spoken forms, across corpora and word-meaning models, the scores confirm known asymmetries in mutual intelligibility. They also correlate significantly with human cloze-test results.  Linguists and language tech teams get a fast, validated way to estimate who understands whom across the Romance family.
arxiv-2602-07547:
Bigger language models align better with brain activity, but is scale itself the driver, or could smaller models suffice?  Subba Reddy Oota and seven co-authors compare full-precision models, small models, and compressed quantized and pruned variants by predicting fMRI responses during natural language comprehension.

Across families up to 14 billion settings, 3-billion-size small models match larger models in brain predictivity. 1-billion models degrade, and linguistic properties and scale interact in shaping match.  The study asks what minimal capacity captures brain-relevant representations.  Brain experts and model builders get evidence that brain match does not require the largest models, just enough of the right capacity.
arxiv-2602-07747:
The bilayer ruthenate Sr3Ru2O7 sits near magnetic and electronic instabilities, so tiny structural changes can reshape its behavior. Sethulakshmi Sajeev and twelve co-authors grow thin films of the material on two other substrates and map their electronic structure with photoemission spectroscopy and density-functional calculations.

The substrate strain matters a great deal: films squeezed on LSAT show Fermi-surface traits with orthorhombic-like symmetry, while films stretched on STO look tetragonal-like. Both films also show weakly dispersing traits just below the Fermi level. The study shows strain as a powerful knob for tuning this quantum material, guiding future tests on its exotic phases.
arxiv-2602-08147:
Lyapunov rates measure how fast nearby paths split, but for set matrix products they are often hard to compute. Reza Rastegar studies thinly coupled linear cocycles, where set zero patterns, including block-triangle shape encoded in a directed sparsity graph, allow cut to an tame wider form of upper-triangular grids.

Mixing fixed triangular controls with a refined Furstenberg-Kifer lemma. He obtains plain bounds and, in good cases, rules for the top rate, valid for tamed fixed runs and steady ergodic random cocycles alike. Uses include nudge models and low-rank updates, where the cut shrinks the problem to lower-sized or scalar cocycles. Dynamics fans and control theorists gain doable rates for set systems.
arxiv-2602-08647:
Treatment effects vary across people, but much of that variation may survive even after accounting for measured covariates. Yuta Kawakami and Jin Tian introduce measures for heterogeneity unexplained by covariates, extending beyond the binary settings of prior work. Their arXiv paper defines positive and negative versions for binary treatment with continuous outcome, and again for continuous treatment via stochastic interventions.

Identification and bounding theorems support the new measures, which separate subjects helped from subjects harmed rather than averaging them away. An application to a real dataset demonstrates the approach. Readers get tools to ask not just whether effects vary, but for whom they run in each direction, even when covariates explain only part of the story.
arxiv-2602-08747:
Inference pipelines chain several neural models under tight latency limits, and timeouts cascade when requests pile up. Zhixin Zhao and ten co-authors argue that dropping requests only when forced, the reactive policy, drops too late and drops the wrong ones. Their arXiv paper proposes PARD, a system that drops proactively to raise goodput across the whole workload.

Dropping decisions use live pipeline state to choose timing, while an adaptive priority mechanism picks which requests to drop based on how much latency budget remains and how heavy the load is. Tests on a 64-GPU cluster over real workloads show goodput gains of 16 to 176 percent over leading systems, with drop rates and wasted compute cut severalfold. Readers get a counterintuitive lesson: timely, precise dropping serves more users.
arxiv-2602-08947:
Detecting a distant object with faint reflected light is a job for quantum illumination, and Sujai Matta and five co-authors demonstrate it over nearly a kilometer of lossy open air. Polarization-entangled photon pairs are made in a Sagnac interferometer, with a Bell-test score of 2.802, close to the quantum maximum. One photon stays home as a reference while its twin flies to the target and back.

Even when only a few dozen probe photons return, correlations stay strong, with Bell scores above 2.6. The result shows polarization entanglement survives kilometer-scale scattering off real objects. It lays groundwork for practical quantum-assisted detection and ranging in noisy, real-world channels.
arxiv-2602-09047:
Hugo José Ribeiro tests quantum computing on a real-world problem: balancing carbon, biodiversity, and social impact in an 88-variable portfolio for the Brazilian Cerrado. The study runs the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm with zero-noise extrapolation on IBM's Torino and Fez processors, across seven independent hardware runs, against a greedy baseline from old-style code.

The quantum workflow averages a score of 58.47, a 31.6 percent improvement over the standard 44.42, with strong statistical significance and a large effect size. A validation run thirteen days later confirms stability against calibration drift. The author presents this as empirical quantum utility in earth science, where current noisy devices plus error mitigation spot synergies that myopic standard methods miss.
arxiv-2602-09147:
Janek Bevendorff and eleven co-authors present PAN 2026, the latest round of a long-running workshop on computer-based style study and text forensics. Five tasks run this year: Voight-Kampff AI-made-text spotting in mixed and hidden writing, text watermarking, multi-author writing-style analysis, AI-made plagiarism spotting, and reasoning-trajectory spotting. The last two add new tasks beside returning ones.

As in past years, teams submit software as easy-to-repeat Docker containers, most through the TIRA testing platform. Since PAN 2012, more than 1,100 entries have arrived that way, making the workshop a durable benchmark for repeatable forensic methods. The overview lists tasks, data, and test design for the 2026 edition.
arxiv-2602-09347:
Artificial intelligence now rebuilds and enhances radiology images at speed, producing pictures that look sharper, smoother, and more detailed while letting clinicians review them faster. A 2026 communication led by Jana G. Delfino, with four co-authors, warns that this polish can mislead. Sharper does not always mean more informative, and AI reconstruction brings failure modes that older imaging did not.

The paper's concern is the growing gap between how good an image looks and how much trustworthy information it actually carries. Users may trust a clean-looking reconstruction that quietly invents or erases detail. By mapping where AI-enabled reconstruction and enhancement can go wrong, the authors aim to help readers gain the technology's benefits while keeping its risks in view. Safe use, they argue, starts with knowing what the picture may hide.
arxiv-2602-09547:
Benjamin Gess and Daniel Heydecker study a zero-range process with faster-than-linear jump rates that, under fluid-scale shrinking with shrinking bits, tends to the porous medium law. Their 2026 paper proves a large drift principle in any scaling regime of shrinking particle size. The result tells rare-event odds for the particle system as it nears its smooth limit.

The hard part is a tameness estimate for the curved term, in a setting where neither pathwise smoothness nor Dirichlet-form smoothness is at hand. The authors resolve it with a novel multi-scale trick that exploits pathwise smoothness showing across scales. The paper thus extends large-drift theory for the porous medium law to regimes where standard smoothness tools fail.
arxiv-2602-09747:
Supriyo Jana and Soumen Sarkar map all poly Kolmogorov vector fields for which the standard n-sphere is fixed in their 2026 paper. Fully solved Kolmogorov vector fields of degree m on the n-sphere are shown for any degree above two. The authors then show that no cubic energy Kolmogorov vector field can make an odd-dim sphere fixed.

Rules under which a cubic Kolmogorov vector field carries a Darboux first sum are studied, with many cases settled into needed and enough rules. Full solving of cubic Kolmogorov vector fields with a fixed n-sphere is also studied. The paper thus maps which Kolmogorov flows keep the sphere, which admit Darboux sums, and which achieve full solving.
arxiv-2602-09847:
Conditional Value-at-Risk is a central tail-risk measure in random structures. Yet exact evaluation under high-dim, space-linked matter doubt stays too costly for classic Monte Carlo. Alireza Tabarraei uses bounded-mean rewrites fitting quantum size guessing in his 2026 paper. He builds a quantum-boosted reading frame casting evaluation as a steady trust-bound maximum size guessing problem.

The method extends repeat quantum size guessing. Explicit maximum reading sits within a strictly held span design. Global truth under finite-shot noise and the non-one-to-one wavy Grover response is secured with a steadied scheme. Multi-guess tracking, timed clearing, and a bounded restart gear under a stated failure budget are used. Square oracle-cost edge is kept with finite-sample trust pledges and reduced spread. Benchmarks with space-linked log fields show far lower oracle cost than classic Monte Carlo at matching trust.
arxiv-2602-10047:
Holomorphic vector fields can harbor singular sets that are not isolated points but smooth, positive-dimensional pieces. A 2026 paper led by Maurício Corrêa, with two co-authors, studies fields whose singular locus contains such a local complete-intersection component. The authors derive a precise global formula for the component's Milnor-Poincaré-Hopf contribution.

They also prove a sharp local lower bound, stable under holomorphic perturbations, in terms of the component's embedded contribution. For gradient fields, the bound limits the total Milnor number of isolated critical points near the component, and for a morsification it bounds the Morse points converging there. Explicit families show the bounds are sharp and reveal singularities redistributing toward infinity.
arxiv-2602-10247:
Bayesian inverse problems gain real power from priors, yet their measure-based roots live in infinite-dimensional function spaces. A 2026 paper by Daniela Calvetti and Erkki Somersalo bridges that distribution-space theory for linear inverse problems to computing practice without discretizing the forward model. The key result is that discretizing the unknown is unnecessary for numerical treatment. Numerical quadratures free of any discrete representation are the only approximations required.

An X-ray tomography inverse problem shows the approach can work in the proposed framework. The paper also studies the link between the new approach and discretization-based methods, showing how distribution-space theory can reach computation directly. The work narrows the gap between infinite-dimensional theory and the inverse problems solvers actually face.
arxiv-2602-10347:
Massive early-type galaxies show total density profiles near isothermal, but how their slopes evolve over time remains debated. A 2026 paper led by Pritom Mozumdar, with three co-authors, investigates total mass density slope evolution over the last six and a half billion years. It analyzes about two hundred early-type galaxies at intermediate redshift in detail. Spatially resolved stellar kinematics come from MUSE-DEEP spectra, and surface brightness models come from HST imaging. Jeans Anisotropic Modeling coupled with Multi-Gaussian Expansion constrains mass distributions.

Combining the intermediate-redshift dataset with a local MaNGA sample under identical methodology ensures consistent comparison. Intermediate-redshift profiles show a median mass-weighted slope just under two point two, shallower than the local baseline just over two point two. That shift is a redshift gradient of about minus zero point two, detected at five-sigma significance. The trend proves robust against model assumptions.
arxiv-2602-10447:
X. Liu, D. Wu, and J. Zhang trace how cosmic magnetic fields get their start in a 2026 paper. Turbulent dynamos can amplify weak seed fields, but a gap remains between microscopic seed making and the large-scale dynamo. Electron-scale models saturate too early through magnetic trapping, leaving seeds too weak and small to feed the dynamo.

Using high-resolution kinetic simulations with a realistic mass ratio, the authors open up the ion-kinetic regime. Under steady shear driving that mimics large-scale cosmic flows, electron instability saturation turns out to be a prelude, not an endpoint. Massive ions then sustain a distinct evolution that builds stronger, larger fields, bridging the kinetic-fluid gap and giving dynamos seeds worth amplifying.
arxiv-2602-10647:
Michael G. Cowling and two co-authors study Brascamp-Lieb inequalities on Lie groups in a 2026 paper. These inequalities bound integrals of products of functions pulled back along homomorphisms, and their constants measure how sharp the bounds can be. The paper treats homogeneous and compact Lie groups in parallel.

For homogeneous groups, the constant equals the corresponding constant on the Lie algebra, reducing analysis to linear algebra. For Heisenberg-like groups, only multilinear Holder inequalities can occur. For compact groups, the authors find necessary and sufficient settings for finiteness of the constant. The results sort a spread landscape, showing which inequalities survive on which groups and why.
arxiv-2602-10847:
Fanpu Cao and three co-authors extend time series forecasting beyond its immediate past in a 2026 paper. Multivariate forecasting models lean on limited historical context, missing global cyclic patterns that span cycles far longer than the input horizon. Naively lengthening the window invites overfitting, heavy runs, and redundant processing.

Their global time retriever is a lightweight plug-and-play module that maintains an adaptive global time embedding of the entire cycle. It dynamically retrieves and fuses relevant long-range patterns into any forecasting model, extending time awareness without extending the input window. The design lets forecasters capture slow rhythms, like seasonal or operational cycles, that short horizons cannot see.
arxiv-2602-11147:
Block proposers who know they are next may stall for extra profit. Rasheed M and two co-authors study timing games in leader-based blockchains, where a fast proposer delays a block to capture rewards meant for the next block. That delay risks missed blocks and treats later proposers unfairly.

Their fix, called 2-Prop, picks two proposers per slot and confirms one block, with rewards shared by propagation speed. Under uniform network terms, prompt proposal is a Nash balance in the resulting Latency Game. Under varied terms, a faster proposer still prefers promptness unless its rival is extremely slow. The mechanism thus curbs timing games without heavy machinery.
arxiv-2602-11247:
Multi-turn attacks spread malice thinly across turns, dodging per-turn checks. J Alex Corll, writing alone, proposes a proxy-level scoring formula that needs no language model call. A plain weighted average fails here: it converges to the per-turn score regardless of turn count.

Peak-plus-accumulation scoring instead combines peak single-turn risk, persistence ratio, and category diversity, drawing on change-point finding and belief updating. On more than ten thousand multi-turn conversations, it reaches high recall at a low false-positive rate. Sensitivity analysis finds a sharp transition where recall jumps with little false-positive cost. Code, patterns, and harness are released as open source.
arxiv-2602-11347:
Astrochemical models rarely meet lab data head-on. Valeriia Sokolova and nine co-authors test whether rate-equation models built for the interstellar medium can reproduce cold-surface reactivity tests. Their case is low-heat hydrogenation of carbon monoxide, a path to methanol and other molecules.

Nine tests vary heat and dose, with careful focus to vocabulary and scales for fluxes and times. Three codes, NAUTILUS, pyRate, and MONACO, are run under lab terms. Fair agreement is achieved, with discrepancies between models and tests and among models themselves. The authors discuss whether chemical networks or physical descriptions explain the gaps, showing lab confrontation is feasible.
arxiv-2602-11447:
Open-source projects live or die by keeping helpers. Zixuan Feng and five co-authors study community managers' keeping challenges through interviews, literature review, and surveys, following a design science approach. Current dashboards look backward, giving backward views rather than early warnings of leaving.

Through repeat build-and-evaluate cycles, the team developed plans for diagnosing keeping risks and informing engagement, operationalized in a web prototype refined with feedback from over one hundred practitioners. In-situ tests across two communities tested the result. The study offers empirical insight into keeping work, actionable plans for managers, and a practical frame for future research on open-source sustainability.
arxiv-2602-11547:
Hidden messages can be tucked into the block structure of compressed video, and most detectors look elsewhere, at motion data, prediction choices, or transform values. Xiang Zhang and six co-authors build the first detector aimed squarely at coding-unit block structure in HEVC video. Their approach turns block-shape changes into a gradient map and pairs it with a block-level map of prediction modes.

Those two views feed a network called GradIPMFormer, which mixes local detail with long-range links across blocks to catch both small boundary shifts and wider structural patterns. Tests across varied quality settings and resolutions, and against several hiding methods, show it beating rival detectors throughout. The result is a new line of defense for spotting covert traffic inside ordinary video files.
arxiv-2602-11847:
Cosmic ray muons rain through the atmosphere daily, and their flux responds to upper-air heat and space magnetic field. Paul and nineteen co-authors study that response using 22 years of data from the GRAPES-3 muon telescope in Ooty, India, spanning three solar cycles. The large-area array detects about four billion muons daily with fine angular resolution, giving small errors on the hourly muon rate.

Once pressure shifts are removed, the team compares muon data with upper-air temperatures from NASA MERRA-2 data and field data from spacecraft at Lagrange point L1. A joint fitting method run in rounds using Fourier transforms and a narrow band-pass filter yields heat and field numbers, both negative and tightly measured. The results show the array can serve as a real-time monitor of upper-air heat and space magnetic field.
arxiv-2602-12047:
Learned dynamics models fail most dangerously outside their training data, exactly where safety guarantees matter. Anutam Srinivasan and two co-authors present a framework for robust off-distribution planning and control combining conformal prediction with system level synthesis. High-confidence model error bounds come from weighted CP with a learned, state-control-dependent spread model.

Those bounds feed a robust nonlinear model control setup that tightens constraints over the horizon via volume-tuned forward reachable sets. Theory assures coverage and robustness under data drift, with analysis of how data density and tube size affect hit rates. Tests on curved systems of growing complexity, including a four-dimensional car and a twelve-dimensional quadcopter, improve safety and robustness over fixed-bound and non-robust baselines, especially beyond training data.
arxiv-2602-12147:
Forecasting models that claim to work on new data are often tested on old, reused sets, so their scores can flatter them. Zhongzheng Qiao led this benchmark work with nine co-authors, building TIME from 50 fresh data sets and 98 forecasting tasks. The tasks are set up for strict zero-shot tests, with no leaked test data.

People and large language models worked together to check data quality and to shape tasks around real work needs and what can sensibly be predicted. Rather than rating whole data sets, the team scores models by time pattern, using the shape of each series. Twelve foundation models were tested, and the ranked results are shared online for closer study.
arxiv-2602-12247:
Language models now pull facts from PDFs into JSON, but judging that work is tricky when fields need different kinds of rightness. Nick Ferguson led this work with six co-authors, presenting ExtractBench, a benchmark and scoring frame for PDF-to-JSON extraction at enterprise scale. No prior test covered that full path, from broad schemas to nested fields.

The benchmark pairs 35 PDFs with schemas and hand-checked gold labels, giving 12,867 fields to score across valuable domains. Its frame treats each schema as a runnable spec, with exact match for IDs, tolerance for numbers, and semantic match for names, plus rules for arrays, gaps, and invented facts. Top models still fail badly as schemas widen, hitting zero valid output on a 369-field finance schema.
arxiv-2602-12747:
Published methods in computational social science are often hard to rerun, thanks to tangled workflows, shifting software, and patchy docs. Fakhri Momeni and two co-authors test what actually helps, comparing three setups: raw docs, tidied docs, and tidied docs plus a preset run environment. They ran 47 usability sessions, tracking success, time, and errors alongside surveys and interviews.

Tidied docs cut errors at the repository level and helped users read method outputs better. Adding a standard run environment helped more, giving the best success rate and fastest finish times. Across all setups, users often turned to AI tools to fix problems on their own. The authors conclude that barriers stack up across docs, environment, and clarity, so fixes must be coordinated rather than piecemeal.
arxiv-2602-12847:
Field-programmable gate arrays can run machine-learning inference fast, but picking the right accelerator settings on the fly is hard. Alexandros Patras and three co-authors present DPUConfig, a runtime framework built around a reinforcement-learning agent that chooses configurations for deep learning processor units on an FPGA. The agent watches live telemetry, system load, power draw, and application performance to guide each choice.

Tests on several convolutional networks on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ board show the agent reaching 95% of the best achievable energy efficiency on average. For latency-sensitive services like autonomous driving and augmented reality, that near-optimal efficiency without hand-tuning matters. The framework shows that learned runtime management can squeeze most of the available efficiency from flexible FPGA hardware.
arxiv-2602-12947:
Josephson junctions built from chiral superconductors may host Majorana modes, exotic states that could underpin new quantum devices. Daniel Gresta and five co-authors study heat flow and non-local electrical behaviour in four-terminal junctions where a normal region meets two chiral superconducting leads, with Chern numbers zero, one, and two. They ask when a single chiral Majorana mode yields a robust half-quantised thermal conductance.

The answer is conditional: quantisation appears near a phase difference of pi, but only at low doping in the central region and for intermediate to long junctions. Electrical conductance stays strongly suppressed by particle-hole symmetry. At finite Zeeman fields, the Chern-one phase tracks lead topology, while the Chern-two phase deviates depending on where Majorana modes sit in momentum space. The paper sets clear criteria for probing chiral Majorana modes thermally.
arxiv-2602-13047:
Speech can reveal early mind decline, but most screening research studies one-tongue speakers, leaving many-tongue groups untried. Madhurananda Pahar and six co-authors signed up 1,395 people in Sheffield and Bradford. The group mixed one-tongue English speakers and many-tongue speakers using Somali, Chinese, or South Asian tongues, taping over 263 hours of speech through the CognoMemory agent. They tested speech-to-text and downstream models for mind sorting and MMSE fit.

Speech-to-text closeness differed little across groups, yet downstream models misclassified many-tongue speakers as weakened in a pattern, most of all on memory, fluency, and reading tests. Wrong weakness labels ran 28% to 37% for many-tongue speakers versus 12% to 16% for one-tongue speakers, roughly 2.5 times higher. Training on DementiaBank deepened the bias. The first large-scale analysis of its kind for UK many-tongue minorities, the study warns that strong overall scores can hide bias.
arxiv-2602-13147:
The Haldane honeycomb model with non-reciprocal next-nearest-neighbour hopping hosts unusual spectral features. Aditi Prabhudesai and two co-authors study this variant: on a torus it supports time-reversal-protected exceptional rings, which act as flux tubes for Berry curvature, confining curvature inside the rings. On a cylinder with zig-zag edges, edge states have zero group velocity at transverse momentum pi, making them non-chiral.

Those edge states bifurcate at an exceptional point and leak into the bulk. As non-reciprocity grows, approaching bulk states convert into exceptional-point pairs, then proliferate in nested, Russian-doll fashion, an exceptional-point cascade occurring only at specific non-Hermiticity values, giving a step-like pair density. Wave-packet dynamics reveal a tunable regime where non-chiral edge states, though ephemeral through self-acceleration diffusion, stay localised late for wide packets at small non-Hermiticity.
arxiv-2602-13247:
Lean is a proof assistant that checks math with machine rigor, but its libraries still lack a full account of flows on curved spaces. This paper fills part of that gap by proving, inside Lean, that integral curves of vector fields exist and are unique on Banach manifolds, a broad class of infinite-dimensional curved spaces. It starts with differential equations on Banach spaces, covering the Picard-Lindelof theorem and the Gronwall inequality, then lifts those results to manifolds.

Built on the Mathlib libraries for calculus and manifolds, the work aims to give future libraries for dynamical systems and differential geometry a base that working mathematicians can trust and reuse. The proofs are checked by machine rather than by eye alone, which is the point of formal work. Weichen Winston Yin leads the paper with one co-author, Yury Kudryashov.
arxiv-2602-13347:
Warehouse robots stow millions of items into bins, and knowing how a bin will look after a planned stow could prevent bad placements before they happen. FOREST is a world model for that foresight. It represents bin states as item-aligned masks and uses a latent diffusion transformer, conditioned on stow intent, to predict the post-stow layout from sparse snapshots.

Predicted layouts matched true layouts far better than heuristic baselines on geometric agreement. Swapping real post-stow masks for FOREST predictions cost only modest performance in load-quality checks and multi-stow reasoning, suggesting the forecasts are good enough to guide planning. Lijun Zhang leads the work with ten co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13447:
Picking out which speaker a listener attends to from brain signals is hard when several voices compete, and most methods work on time windows, trading timing precision against accuracy. Hidden Markov smoothing can ease that trade, but only as a separate post-step. This paper folds decoding and smoothing into one probabilistic framework, a Markov switching model that links EEG signals to speech envelopes under each attention state while tracking how attention shifts over time.

The joint model decodes attention at the sample level, estimating parameters and attention states together via expectation-maximization. Tests show accuracy comparable to Markov post-processing, with faster detection of attention switches, a practical edge for hearing devices and brain-computer interfaces. Yuanyuan Yao leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13847:
Fabrizio Falasca and one co-author set out a 2026 arXiv paper on compact models of turbulent flow that obey physics. Such models must match long-run stats, predict how a system reacts to a push, and still work on real-world data. The authors build a discrete-time form with energy-saving nonlinear terms.

They parameterize that form with neural nets, then check forced responses with the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, using calm data alone. Tests on two ideal models of geophysical turbulence passed, and a tropical climate model matched key El Niño stats. Adding a memory-aware random term improved the match further, and the model helped trace long-term drivers of El Niño swings.
arxiv-2602-14147:
Shufan Li and eight co-authors present a 2026 arXiv model for reasoning with diffusion language models. Diffusion models offer an alternative to auto-regressive models, and recent work extended them to multimodal tasks. Yet reasoning versions were usually trained per task with reinforcement learning alone.

LaViDa-R1 instead unifies multimodal understanding and generation in one general-purpose reasoning model. Its post-training blends supervised fine-tuning with multi-task reinforcement learning, plus tricks such as answer-forcing, tree search, and complementary likelihood estimation. Tests span visual math reasoning, reason-heavy grounding, and image editing, where the model shows strong performance across the board.
arxiv-2602-14347:
J-B. Gerent and five co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv method to gauge atom-surface interactions via tunneling times. An ultra-cold gas of neutral atoms near a face is hard to probe straight.

So the team joins a light dipole trap bounced by the face, a magnet trap from wires below the face, and spin of the face itself. That setup moves a rubidium-87 Bose-Einstein cloud gently from a few micrometers to a few hundred nanometers from the face. At such close range, atom-face links reshape the trap and raise the leak rate toward the face. Weighing cloud life against a leak model yields the Casimir-Polder force factor in the retarded regime. With noise heat, calibration bias, and life gauge exactness in view, the guessed relative error is 10 percent. The method should work for other atom kinds too.
arxiv-2602-14647:
Open quantum systems leak memory into their surroundings, and one term in that memory is hard to handle. Andrew C. Hunt, with Stuart C. Althorpe as co-author, works on Matsubara-decay terms in hierarchical equations of motion. Those terms track how bath modes spread along imaginary-time paths.

The authors show a known Ishizaki-Tanimura correction splits smooth from Brownian parts of the path spread. Tweaking that split makes the method faster for fast baths. They also fit the spread with a pole sum via an adapted AAA algorithm. The result is a far more efficient low-temperature solver for open dynamics.
arxiv-2602-14747:
Saboura Zamani, Vincenzo Salzano, and Dario Bettoni ask whether a non-minimal coupling between dark matter and gravity can shape the inner dynamics of ultra-diffuse galaxies. In their framework an extra term, set by a length scale, modifies the gravitational potential where spacetime curvature meets dark matter. Spherical Jeans modelling then tests three galaxies spanning the extremes, from dark-matter deficient to dark-matter dominated: NGC 1052-DF2, NGC 1052-DF4, and Dragonfly 44.

Several halo profiles, two anisotropy models, and stellar-to-halo mass relations with and without that link are compared against kinematic data. The paper probes whether faint galaxies can reveal a coupling that brighter systems hide. Ultra-diffuse galaxies become quiet laboratories for gravity.
arxiv-2602-14847:
Florian Grundbacher and Tomasz Kobos stretch John splits to best affine nests of curved bodies. The classic case, most volume in a host body, is well known: John's split names, and in flat space fully pins, the best spots.

For most other nest tasks, no broad best-spot rules were known. Following O. B. Ader, the team gains a John-type split as a must for best affine chains, where bodies nest by scale and shift in high space. Curved-body nesting thus gains best-spot rules past its best-known case.
arxiv-2602-15047:
Chandak and colleagues test the standard cosmological model against its main rival using the Pantheon+ Type Ia supernova sample. Recent JWST and DESI findings have strained inflationary cold dark matter, with evidence suggesting the standard model breaks at least one energy condition from general relativity. Those conditions exist to ensure positive energy, attractive gravity, and flows no faster than light.

The team derives model-independent limits on the distance modulus from the energy conditions and compares them with Hubble diagrams from both models. Standard cold dark matter breaks the strong energy condition over the redshift range studied, while the rival meets all four conditions. The rival is favored by the data, and the model without inflation is strongly favored over the current standard model at both high and low redshifts.
arxiv-2602-15247:
Bian and Bull derive a closed-form sample size rule for testing the overall effect of a single nucleotide polymorphism in joint models of tracking and survival data. Tracking biomarkers are often collected in clinical work because they link strongly to time-to-event outcomes. While joint model methods have advanced, little attention has gone to design questions, above all sample size and power math in gene studies.

Yet right sample size estimates are vital for enough power and valid findings. Gene variants may shape event risk directly and via tracking biomarkers. Trials show the rule holds up well in finite samples. The team shows its real-world use with data from the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial.
arxiv-2602-15347:
Bezdek introduces the class of basic r-ball polyhedra in d-dimensional Euclidean space for d greater than 1 and r greater than 0. The paper investigates their face structure.

For given integer values i between 0 and d minus 1 and n at least d plus 1 at least 3, it determines the maximal number of i-dimensional faces. The count runs over all basic r-ball polyhedra in d-dimensional space with n facets. In addition, the paper establishes that for d greater than 2, every basic r-ball polyhedron is globally rigid with respect to its inner dihedral angles.
arxiv-2602-16147:
Megan Lee leads a team of six researchers improving brain-computer interfaces that must work for new users unseen in training. Cross-subject generalization in EEG-based interfaces remains hard. Neural signals vary from person to person. The team asks whether spectral representations give more stable features for transfer than temporal waveforms. Correlation analyses across three EEG paradigms, SSVEP, P300, and motor imagery, give a clear answer. Spectral features are consistently more similar across subjects than temporal signals.

That finding motivates ASPEN, a hybrid design that fuses spectral and temporal streams multiplicatively. Features propagate only when the two streams agree. Across six benchmark data sets, ASPEN dynamically finds the best spectral-temporal balance for each paradigm. It tops unseen-subject accuracy on three of six data sets and stays competitive on the rest. Multiplicative fusion thus supports effective cross-subject generalization.
arxiv-2602-16247:
Soren Raza and coauthors survey dielectric materials that break the Moss rule, an empirical link between refractive index and band gap energy. Photonic devices depend critically on dielectrics, with higher bending indices and lower absorption losses enabling new functions. The Moss rule states that index falls as band gap energy rises. Materials that surpass the rule, called super-Mossian dielectrics, combine large bending indices with wide optical transparency.

The review surveys the expanding landscape of high-index dielectric and semiconductor materials, focusing on rule-breaking cases. It discusses how electronic band structures with a large joint density of states near the band edge give rise to super-Mossian behavior. Finally, it shows how index sets performance limits for nanoresonators, waveguides, and metasurfaces.
arxiv-2602-16347:
Jon Vehovar leads three coauthors on parallel node generation for meshless methods. Meshless methods solve partial differential equations by approximating each node's operator as a weighted sum of neighbours. An n-dimensional Poisson disc sampling method generates suitable nodes, handles complex shapes, and supports variable node density.

The authors adapt that method for parallel execution with spatial indexing and work hypertrees. The work hypertree is prebuilt from node density, so each leaf stands for a balanced unit of work. Threads advance separate fronts and claim leaves as needed, avoiding leaves beside those claimed by other threads. Combining node placement constraints with the partly prebuilt hypertree removes the need to lock the tree while it changes. Handling collisions at leaf level sharply cuts the mutex acquisitions needed for point insertion checks. The paper tests the algorithm, compares it with earlier parallelization attempts, and weighs adapting it to distributed systems.
arxiv-2602-16547:
Onirban Islam and Lennart Ronge develop an equivariant index formula for a twisted Dirac operator. The setting is a compact globally hyperbolic spacetime with a timelike boundary. A group acts by isometries, and Atiyah-Patodi-Singer boundary conditions apply. The formula matches the familiar Riemannian shape. For each group element, the index is an integral over its fixed point set. Boundary terms are added.

The proof uses a simple reduction from the equivariant case to the non-equivariant one. It yields a Lorentzian version of the index-equals-spectral-flow formula. Readers in geometry and mathematical physics get a clean bridge to the better-known Riemannian theory. Boundary effects are handled in full.
arxiv-2602-16747:
Xidong Wang and co-authors introduce LiveClin, a live clinical benchmark designed to resist leakage and staleness in medical language model evaluation. Static benchmarks inflate scores through data contamination and outdated knowledge. LiveClin is built from contemporary, peer-reviewed case reports and updated twice a year, keeping clinical currency high and contamination low.

A verified AI-human workflow with hundreds of physicians turns authentic cases into complex, multimodal scenarios spanning the full clinical pathway. The benchmark holds over fourteen hundred case reports and over sixty-six hundred questions. Tests on twenty-six models show stark difficulty, with the top model reaching only about a third case accuracy, while chief and attending physicians beat most models. Medical AI builders get a continuously evolving, clinically grounded yardstick.
arxiv-2602-16847:
Richa Madhogaria and co-authors study electron flow and device-linked change in ultra-clean graphene transistors. Fast electrons in high-mobility graphene offer a solid-state analogue of a relativistic quantum fluid. Seeing viscous flow needs a long momentum-relaxation path. That path is capped mainly by impurity and phonon hits. Many knotty device shapes have been tried to curb momentum-relaxing hits.

Yet results stay sensitive to how devices are made and shaped. That raises doubts about hydrodynamic signs themselves. The team studies several ultra-clean graphene transistors in a plain rectangular four-terminal design. Transport measures gauge pristine device quality. They trace resistance in the doped zone versus carrier density and heat. Strong device-linked change appears even in this simplest design. It is tied to competing momentum-conserving and momentum-relaxing hits.
arxiv-2602-16947:
Chuqin Geng and co-authors propose SymGraph, a symbolic alternative to message passing for expressive and interpretable graph learning. Graph neural networks are essential in high-stakes domains such as drug discovery, yet their black-box nature blocks trust. Self-explainable graph networks attempt to bridge that gap, but they often rely on standard message-passing backbones with fundamental limits, including the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman expressivity barrier.

SymGraph replaces continuous message passing with discrete structural hashing and role-based aggregation. That theoretically surpasses the 1-WL barrier with better expressiveness and no differentiable optimization cost. Tests show state-of-the-art performance, beating existing readable graph nets, with ten to one hundred times faster training using only CPU execution. The gain is large. SymGraph also generates rules with better semantic granularity, offering great potential for scientific finding.
arxiv-2602-17147:
Yu Wu led a seven-author team explaining why some halide materials block heat so well, and how to hunt for more of them. In halide perovskites and related cage-like frameworks, low heat flow comes from two paired routes, the authors show. First, halogen-halogen links enable soft spinning modes that reshape the low end of the vibration spectrum and boost phonon scattering. Second, twists in the octahedral cages raise anharmonicity and cut phonon lifetimes.

First-principles math on cesium lead bromide shows bromine-bromine links driving the soft modes, while cage twists on their own cut particle-like heat flow and leave wave-like heat flow intact. The team then defines a shape-based distortion factor and screens for halogen-linked blocks plus strong twist, finding a new material with very low heat flow at room temperature. The two routes become portable design rules for heat-blocking halides.
arxiv-2602-17247:
Sehani Siriwardana led a five-author team on goal-oriented remote monitoring with energy-harvesting sensors and a moving receiver. Unlike systems that assume fixed base stations, the framework accounts for receiver motion, such as a satellite or drone, which makes channel quality vary over time as a finite-state Markov process. The monitoring problem becomes a partially observable Markov decision process, recast as a belief-state problem and solved by relative value iteration.

Two estimation strategies, Maximum Likelihood and Minimum Mean Distortion, are compared under optimal sampling and transmission policies. Numerical results show that folding receiver motion and channel state knowledge into the optimization cuts average distortion by between a tenth and two fifths against baselines and fixed-channel assumptions. The finding underlines how much base station motion knowledge matters for goal-oriented communication.
arxiv-2602-17847:
Bryce Christopherson and Farhad Jafari study Brockett openness profiles and gain-limited feedback stabilization. Brockett's condition says a continuously stabilizable nonlinear control system must have a vector field open at the equilibrium. The paper shows the numbers behind that openness condition constrain possible growth of stabilizing feedbacks.

The authors assign each vector field an openness profile: the largest ball around zero inside the image of a ball of given radius. Brockett's condition becomes positivity of that profile for all sufficiently small radii. If feedback obeys a growth bound, the closed-loop profile obeys a matching inequality in terms of the open-loop profile. Any prescribed lower openness rate for closed-loop motion thus forces a lower bound on feedback growth. For power-law openness profiles, linear-rate closed-loop openness forces a specific power-law feedback growth. That exponent is sharp in elementary polynomial examples.
arxiv-2602-18047:
Rong Fu presents CityGuard, a topology-aware transformer for privacy-safe identity search across city cameras. City-scale person re-matching must survive severe look changes from occlusion, viewpoint, and domain shift, while privacy rules bar raw images. It works from codes rather than images.

Three parts carry it. A spread-adaptive metric learner adjusts instance-level margins by feature spread, shrinking person clusters. Coarse geometry, such as GPS or site floor plans, steers graph-based self-attention for steady cross-view alignment from coarse priors without survey-grade tuning. DP embedding maps with compact approximate indexes support secure, low-cost use. They yield descriptors robust to viewpoint change, occlusion, and domain shift, balancing privacy and utility under strict DP accounting. Tests on public benchmarks and database-scale search studies show gains in match precision and query throughput over strong baselines.
arxiv-2602-18447:
Siran Liu and Cyril Y. He speed up step-by-step reasoning in large language models. Their 2026 paper notes that chain-of-thought reasoning boosts performance on complex tasks but adds high latency from long traces. Step-level speculative reasoning aims to cut that cost, yet existing approaches trade accuracy against speed and resources.

The team proposes ConfSpec, a confidence-gated cascaded verification framework resolving the trade-off. The key insight is an asymmetry. Generating a correct step needs large model capacity, while verifying a step is a constrained task where small draft models are well calibrated in their range. High-confidence draft decisions are accepted directly, and uncertain cases escalate to the large target model. Across diverse workloads, ConfSpec reaches over twice the end-to-end speed while matching target-model accuracy, needs no external judge models, and combines with token-level speculative decoding for further gains.
arxiv-2602-18647:
Gabriel Raya and eight co-authors tune diffusion noise. Their 2026 paper introduces InfoNoise, an online adaptive noise schedule that shifts effort to noise levels where denoising is most informative. With loss weighting, a noise schedule sets a split of effort across denoising problems, often fixed before informative levels are known.

InfoNoise makes this split data-adaptive by estimating a conditional-entropy profile from denoising loss, with no extra models or search. Through I-MMSE, the profile marks where noisy views quickly cut doubt about the clean sample and guides the mix. It changes only that mix, leaving goal, weighting, and model form fixed. On image tests, it matches or slightly beats baselines and reaches the same quality in fewer updates. On representation, sequence, and modality changes, including DNA work and language generation, it beats fixed and adaptive baselines and hits target quality with up to three times less compute.
arxiv-2602-18847:
Mars hides a layer of fairly pure water ice under a few centimetres of dry soil at mid-latitudes. E. Vos, with five co-authors, asks in 2026 where that ice came from. Earlier models failed to capture its spatial structure. New calculations with the Mars Planetary Climate Model offer an answer.

The buried ice may be the remnant of a surface ice sheet laid down when Mars tilted more than today. If that ice then sublimated and was buried under a lag layer, its present depth depends on when it was emplaced. Ice placed about six hundred thousand years ago matches observed depths and longitudinal variation. Ice placed over four million years ago does not. The mid-latitude ice is therefore younger than four million years.
arxiv-2602-19447:
Fireballs and how they break apart reveal meteoroid internal structure, but measuring them needs fast, wide-range light measurement. Dale Giancono and four co-authors built an all-sky camera system running at up to 500 frames each second, with its novel Detection Localised Auto-brightness Control. Its custom software handles high data volumes through transient spotting and region-of-interest saving plus real-time light curves.

Two field trips check accuracy against standard 30-frame-per-second cameras and capture a bright magnitude minus 15 fireball with little saturation. The system spans brightness levels minus 3 to minus 17, giving light curves with minimal saturation for most fireballs. A semi-empirical breakup analysis confirms the data can support detailed physical models of meteoroids.
arxiv-2602-19747:
Spin-boson models pair a small quantum spin with a bath of oscillators, and they serve as the standard test bed for quantum dissipation. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yifan Sun and Lian-Ao Wu lays out how symmetry is organized in general spin-boson Hamiltonians.

By exploiting those symmetries, the authors obtain the spectra of the models explicitly rather than by approximation alone. To show the general case at work, they demonstrate the exact solution numerically for a two-mode version. Readers get a symmetry-based route to exact results in a model family that underpins much of open quantum systems theory, with the two-mode example as a concrete illustration.
arxiv-2602-20747:
Phonon frequency combs are a rare and striking effect in quantum solids. Materials with special phonon band shapes are likely hosts. Tea Belojica and twelve co-authors study the layered Van der Waals compound indium silicon telluride. Polarized Raman scans reveal marked roughness in symmetry-set modes and a self-set frequency pattern near a local high-energy phonon mode.

That strong phonon-phonon coupling shows as an odd heat link around two hundred kelvin. It matches higher-order bursts within the phonon density of states gap. These findings position that compound as an unusual base where built-in highly structured phonon tone links and very strong rough effects coexist. That opens new avenues for exploring new shaking effects in thin solids.
arxiv-2602-20847: Perfectoid fields are a central object of modern arithmetic geometry, but their logical profile has stayed partly open. Franziska Jahnke and Ferreol Lavaud identify, in this 2026 arXiv paper, the elementary class generated by all perfectoid fields of a fixed residue characteristic, working in the language of rings. The result builds on earlier work by Jahnke and Kartas. Readers get a precise logical description of which fields belong to this class.
arxiv-2602-21047:
The rational torsion of an abelian variety over a number field embeds into its reduction at any large prime, so the torsion order divides a common divisor of point counts. Jessica Alessandri and Nirvana Coppola ask about the converse for abelian varieties of GL2 type in this 2026 arXiv paper. They draw inspiration from a 1981 paper by Katz.

The authors exhibit a conjectural list of possible torsion orders for modular abelian varieties over the rationals, in dimensions up to five. The list is conjectural, not proven, and it gives researchers a concrete target for testing. Readers get a precise guess about which torsion orders can occur, plus a converse direction worth probing.
arxiv-2602-21147:
Cosmic rays shape shocks, interstellar chemistry, galactic winds, and observable gamma rays and radio emission. Nimatou-Seydi Diallo, Yohan Dubois, Alexandre Marcowith, Joki Rosdahl, and Benoit Commercon model them spectrally in this 2026 arXiv paper via RAMSES-MCR, a multi-group method in momentum space inside the RAMSES code. A two-moment formalism evolves cosmic-ray energy and number density with their flux.

Processes covered include advection, diffusion, streaming instability, Coulomb and hadronic losses, adiabatic changes, and feedback onto gas. The method extends naturally to electrons and multiple species, passes standard multi-dimensional tests, and is applied to a supernova remnant expansion. There, cosmic-ray energy redistributes by momentum and alters gas momentum during the snowplough phase.
arxiv-2602-21247:
Graph indexes for nearest-neighbor search are fast to query but slow to build, bottlenecked by random-access beam searches. Tobias Rubel, Richard Wen, Laxman Dhulipala, Lars Gottesburen, Rajesh Jayaram, and Jakub Lacki remove that bottleneck in this 2026 arXiv paper with PiPNN, an ultra-scalable graph construction algorithm. Its HashPrune online pruning algorithm maintains sparse edge collections with bounded memory during construction.

Partitioning into overlapping sub-problems plus dense matrix multiplication for bulk distance comparisons yields major speedups. Builds run nearly twelve times faster than one leading method and nearly thirteen times faster than another, with higher query throughput. For the first time, high-quality billion-scale indexes build in under twenty minutes on a single multicore machine.
arxiv-2602-21547:
Yuchong Wu and seven co-authors propose RAC, Relation-Aware Cache replacement for large language model services. Scaling such services faces steep cost and latency challenges, making effective caching under tight capacity crucial. Existing policies, from heuristics to learning-based methods, lean on limited-window statistics like recency and frequency.

Those signals prove fragile for real-world language-model workloads, which show long reuse distances and sparse local recurrence. RAC instead uses semantic relations among requests to guide eviction. It synthesizes two relation-aware signals. Topical Prevalence aggregates access evidence at topic level to capture long-horizon reuse. Structural Importance uses local intra-topic dependency structure to rank entries by future reuse value. Extensive evaluations show RAC beating leading baselines by 20 to 30 percent in cache hit ratio across diverse workloads.
arxiv-2602-21747:
Anna Werkovits and two co-authors study lying-standing transitions in the first molecular layer at organic-inorganic interfaces, shaping interface dipoles and alignment. Collective rates are hard to predict, so the team links adsorbates to rates with first-principles Monte Carlo simulations and mean-field coarse-graining. For tetracyanoethylene on copper, no single step explains the collective rate: it emerges from coupled reorientation, adsorption, and diffusion.

A local two-step reorientation captures the slow-diffusion regime. Moving lying molecules speed the transition where diffusion helps by blocking reverse flips via vacancy-molecule decoupling. A regime factor bridges both rates. Size and footprint ratio show geometry itself controls the rate: the collective rate scales roughly with area, and larger footprint ratios yield huge speedups via extra vacancies and diffusion-aided settling. An analytic formula links temperature- and pressure-linked microscopic rates to geometry, reproduces the simulations and yields design rules.
arxiv-2602-21947:
Sohan Venkatesh and colleagues test whether leading language models can reason about how algorithms behave, using causal discovery as the test bed. They score eight frontier models against ground truth taken from actual algorithm runs. The motivation is practical: many users now lean on these models to pick and deploy algorithms.

The verdict is harsh. Predicted ranges run far wider than the true confidence intervals, yet still miss the true average in most cases, and most models score worse than random guessing. The best model's small edge looks more like memorized benchmark answers than sound reasoning. The authors name the failure algorithmic blindness: a gap between knowing about algorithms and predicting what they will do.
arxiv-2602-22047:
Many control problems run forever in an uncertain world, with side clues arriving over time about the hidden conditions. Johannes Milz and two co-authors study such infinite-horizon problems, where a Markov chain steers an unknown distribution of randomness. Because that distribution is unknown, they recast the problem in Bayesian terms, learning it from data as the system runs.

The recasting yields a Bayesian Bellman equation, and the authors prove the learned distribution settles on the truth under Markov sampling. When the model is correctly specified and identifiable, the Bayesian value function converges uniformly, and the data-driven value follows a normal limit law of Bernstein-von Mises type. The theory gives a principled footing for controllers that learn their world as they go.
arxiv-2602-22147:
This algebra paper studies symmetry groups of a refined kind: proper projective similitudes of an algebra with involution of the first kind. M. Archita and Karim Johannes Becher focus on base fields of characteristic other than two, where every nine-dimensional quadratic form has a nontrivial zero. That class includes function fields of p-adic curves and certain extensions of the complex numbers.

The main results extend earlier work by loosening the conditions on both the base field and the Clifford invariant for orthogonal involutions. The paper thus widens the territory where the structure of these similitude groups is understood. Specialists gain a broader base-field setting for results that previously needed stricter hypotheses.
arxiv-2602-22247:
Single-cell foundation models like scGPT learn rich gene vectors, but what biology those vectors encode has been murky. Ihor Kendiukhov decodes scGPT's inner geometry through dozens of rounds of automated hypothesis screening, testing nearly two hundred ideas. The model, he finds, sorts genes into a structured biological map rather than an opaque feature space.

The main axis separates genes by cell location, from secreted proteins at one pole to cytosolic proteins at the other. Middle layers briefly encode mitochondrial and endoplasmic-reticulum compartments in an order mirroring the secretory pathway. Other axes encode protein-interaction networks with graded fidelity. The study thus reads the model's geometry as biology, not black-box magic.
arxiv-2602-22447:
Long-range dipolar forces between ultracold polar molecules should drive exotic quantum phases, but direct many-body signs in cold Fermi gases have stayed elusive. Shrestha Biswas and eight co-authors report one: a controlled warp of the Fermi surface in a deeply quantum gas of sodium-potassium molecules. Double microwave shielding readies thousands of molecules at about a quarter of the Fermi temperature.

That shielding cuts inelastic losses threefold over single shielding while keeping strong elastic dipolar scattering. The team sees Fermi-surface warps up to seven percent, more than twice those seen in magnetic atoms despite far lower densities. Above all, they steadily tune the interaction potential from axial to biaxial symmetry, showing controlled symmetry breaking in action.
arxiv-2602-22647:
Zhengyang Su and twelve co-authors speed up constrained decoding for LLM-based recommendation on accelerators. Industrial systems often restrict outputs to a business-approved subset, such as fresh content or one category, but standard decoding cannot enforce that natively. Prefix-tree methods that can enforce it crawl on TPUs and GPUs.

Their technique, STATIC, flattens the prefix tree into a static compressed sparse row matrix, turning awkward tree walks into vectorized sparse matrix operations. Deployed on a large industrial video platform serving billions of users, it added only a tiny fraction of a millisecond per step and a quarter of one percent of inference time. Speedups reached nearly a thousandfold over a CPU trie and roughly fiftyfold to a thousandfold over a hardware binary-search baseline, enabling the first production-scale strictly constrained generative retrieval.
arxiv-2602-22747:
Kaizheng Wang and five co-authors settle a match-up many thought ruled out: set-based versus spread-based views of epistemic doubt in neural networks. One camp uses posterior value spreads, the other credal sets, convex sets of chance spreads. Split meanings, scoring habits, and ground rules had kept them apart.

The team builds both views from the same finite pool of forecast spreads from one shared network, cutting the view off from raw scores. Judged by three doubt tests across eight benchmarks, six base models, and ten runs per setup, the camps prove truly matched. The study covers choosy guessing and out-of-distribution spotting, showing how second-order view choices shape real-world doubt-aware results.
arxiv-2602-22847:
Kerrian Le Caillec and three co-authors bring ranking aggregation to decentralized networks. Finding a median ranking, a consensus order from many preference lists, is well understood centrally, where all data sits in one machine. Peer networks, internet-of-things systems, and multi-agent setups scatter preferences across communicating nodes instead.

The challenge is consensus with guarantees of convergence and resilience to corrupted nodes, plus scalability through lean communication. The team's approach leans on random gossip communication: autonomous agents swap rankings through local chats only, with no coordinator or central authority, and still converge on a global consensus ranking. New questions follow, especially robustness to bad nodes and communication cost.
arxiv-2602-22947:
Michele Rossi revisits Fujino-Sato results on complete non-projective toric varieties and their conjectural factorization by flips. Their main results gain short conceptual proofs from Cox rings and Mori Dream Spaces, with no restriction on dimension or Picard number. Small modifications are organized through the GKZ decomposition of the moving cone.

The viewpoint extends beyond toric varieties. For complete factorial weak Mori Dream Spaces, any non-projective variety admits a divisor and a flip to a projective Mori Dream Space. Chambers and wall-crossing in the secondary fan emerge as the unifying frame for these constructions, turning a technical factorization conjecture into a clean chamber story.
arxiv-2602-23447:
Yifan Li and four co-authors present SALIENT, a system for creating synthetic CT scans to help detect rare lesions. Rare lesions in whole-body CT are hard to spot because they are scarce and tiny relative to scan volume, so precision collapses even when overall scores look strong.

SALIENT runs diffusion over discrete wavelet coefficients rather than raw pixels, splitting low-frequency brightness from high-frequency detail. Learnable frequency-aware goals separate target traits from background traits, and a 3D VAE makes varied lesion masks with paired slice labels. Realism improves sharply: MS-SSIM rises from zero point six three to zero point eight three and FID falls from one hundred eighteen point four to forty-six point five. Training with SALIENT scans also lifts long-tail detection, with the largest AUPRC gains at low prevalence.
arxiv-2602-23547:
Sasha Boguraev and two co-authors give a neural account of lines that look like repeats yet sound fine. One example: 'She will go to France or Spain, or perhaps to Germany or France.' Such lines become fine when each mention carries distinct context information. Think of a philosophy program versus a mathematics program.

Prior studies used symbol-based formal forms. The authors instead present observed evidence from humans and large language models. It shows the apparent lack of repeats is solid across contexts. In language models, two linked parts stop the repeats. Models bind the right information by context to same words. Transformer induction heads attend only to those context-allowed forms. The neural account thus adds to symbol-based studies of meaning shaped by context.
arxiv-2602-23747:
Kristian Paolo David and three co-authors report a 2026 study of hand-tracked extended reality, where users move without hand-held controllers. The paper asks whether sight and sound cues shown on a virtual hand can stand in for touch, or whether they instead change how an interaction feels.

The team built a mixed-reality prototype that kept the touched surface plain to look at, while cues on the hand varied in motion, glow, and sound. In a small test, people rarely felt lasting touch or heat, yet their mood shifted in a steady pattern. Rough, warm cues felt less pleasant and more tense, while smooth, cool cues felt calm and pleasant. The result treats such cues as a channel for feeling, not as a direct copy of touch.
arxiv-2602-23947:
Oscar Hill and two co-authors introduce hierarchical concept embedding models, a family of interpretable neural models that organize concepts in layers. The 2026 paper notes that concept embedding models map inputs to human-readable concepts before predicting, yet they ignore relations between concepts and demand annotations at every granularity during training.

The new models, HiCEMs, explicitly represent concept hierarchies, so explanations can move between coarse and fine levels. A method called Concept Splitting discovers finer sub-concepts automatically from a pretrained model's embedding space, without new annotations, letting HiCEMs give detailed explanations from limited labels. Tests across datasets, including a user study and a new kitchen-render dataset, show that split sub-concepts are human-interpretable and train accurate models. They support test-time interventions at several granularities, aiding debugging and debiasing.
arxiv-2603-00247: Angel and colleagues propose searching for dark photons via inverse Compton scattering, where laser photons strike an accelerated electron beam to produce a dark photon. They study two complementary plans built on the missing-energy signature: a single-photon veto, and a recoil-electron spectrum measurement, with angular information as an extension. Assuming incident photon energy near 1 eV and electron beam energy of 3 GeV, they derive projected sensitivity. The setup could cover unexplored parameter space as a promising probe of dark sectors.
arxiv-2603-00347: Polson and Sokolov develop synthetic priors for generalized linear models from Good's device of imaginary observations, where a conjugate prior equals a likelihood on pseudodata. Experts reason about response probabilities at chosen values, so the prior elicits Beta priors on mean responses at expert-chosen points. With Pólya-Gamma augmentation, the posterior admits an exact Gibbs sampler with no tuning. Ridge regression, catalytic priors, and prediction-powered inference all fit the same pattern. On Challenger data, the prior is more moderate at the 31-degree Fahrenheit launch temperature.
arxiv-2603-00547: Liu and Lai explain the circumbinary planet desert, the absence of transiting planets around binaries tighter than about seven days, through resonance driven eccentricity growth. As an eccentric binary decays under tides, an outer planet can lock its apsidal precession to the binary, driving extreme eccentricity growth. Around a single planet the effect stays limited, but with several planets the excited orbit crosses neighbours and triggers scattering, collisions, or ejections. Mutual gravity thus turns a local instability into a system wide clear out of inner regions.
arxiv-2603-00847: Song and four colleagues use the South Korean God Saeng trend, strict group self growth, as a lens on daily life. In a 10 day probe with 24 young adults and small missions, people leaned on planning, check-ins, and tracking to stay steady, yet those habits raised self watching pressure. They juggled tensions between routine and freedom, realness and image, and output and ties, seeing daily tasks anew. The insights suggest design paths for user data tools beyond tracking, toward tools for handling tensions and making meaning.
arxiv-2603-01047: Niu, Wu, and Qian bridge value-based and policy-based training for Generative Flow Networks, which sample candidate sets along one-way acyclic graphs. They show flow balance over partial runs yields a sound policy evaluator for divergence, and propose a balance goal to learn it. The approach strengthens policy-based training's trust while adding freedom: tuned backward policies and offline data use both fit with ease, as synthetic and real tasks confirm.
arxiv-2603-01147: Guo and five colleagues track needles during continuous ultrasound-guided insertion, where poor and flickering visibility defeats many methods. ConVibNet builds on VibNet with temporal links across frames to estimate tip position and shaft angle continuously. A new loss exploiting motion links between consecutive frames strengthens this tracking. It beats VibNet and UNet-LSTM baselines with tip error under three millimetres and angle error under two degrees, improving tip accuracy by three quarters of a millimetre while staying real-time.
arxiv-2603-01347: Sponzilli and thirteen colleagues analyze 51 Class 0/I close-pair systems, 38 with seen outflows yielding 42 outflows, from ALMA views of 11 Perseus and 40 Orion. Pairs formed straight at small scales of about 500 au or less via disk splitting, or at larger scales over 1000 au via stormy splitting then inward drift. Disk-splitting pairs should show mostly aligned disks and outflows, while stormy-splitting pairs should show no favored lineup. The team checks pair angles against gas outflow angles to test which pathway wins.
arxiv-2603-01547:
Sorting childhood brain tumors is hard because tissue patterns are complex and labeled cases are few. Jian Yu, Joakim Nguyen, Jinrui Fang, and colleagues combine three kinds of data to help in this 2026 study. Slide images alone miss facts held in written reports and in maps of cell nuclei.

Their system, PathMoE, joins slide images, pathology reports, and cell graphs through a set of expert models. Each expert learns what one data type adds alone, what it shares, and what emerges only when types combine. A gating step weights those experts per case, so staff can see which mix drove each call. Scores rose on both an in-house child tumor set and on outside cancer sets, with clear gains over image-only tools.
arxiv-2603-01647:
Rundong Wang, Wei Ba, Ying Zhou, and colleagues draft pathology reports from whole-slide tissue images in this 2026 work. Current tools write a broad diagnosis for a slide but fail to tie fine claims to the exact spots that support them. They also give users no way to say which details a report must hold or to check them.

Their agent, QCAgent, mimics how pathologists scan many fields of view with a goal in mind. A user checklist states the required details and limits before drafting starts. A critique step scores the draft against that list and sends the agent back to key regions. Text-to-patch search then helps revise the report so claims match visual proof. Tests show reports with more of the wanted detail and stronger clinical value.
arxiv-2603-01747:
Jan Moser revisits a lemma from a famed 1921 paper by Hardy and Littlewood in this 2026 work. That old result bounds how zeros of the Riemann zeta function spread along its critical line. The zeta function sits at the heart of deep questions about prime numbers.

Moser proves that the century-old lemma can generate a vast family of new equivalent forms. Each form restates the Fermat-Wiles theorem, the settled claim about sums of like powers, in zeta terms. The family is as large as a continuum, so the supply of such restatements has no countable end. Work of this kind links two landmark results that seem far apart on the surface. It shows how one sharp estimate can echo through very different corners of number theory.
arxiv-2603-02047:
Manuel Serna-Aguilera, Raegan Anderes, Page Daniel Dobbs, and Khoa Luu build tools to fight the nicotine public health crisis. Their 2026 work notes that flavored pouches and similar products lure young users and undo anti-tobacco gains. Past research stays narrow and cannot connect facts across very large data collections.

Their NICO data set holds over two hundred thousand multimodal samples across dozens of tobacco and nicotine brands. Images and text descriptions sit side by side for public health researchers to mine. Their retrieval system, NICO-RAG, organizes extracted entities and relations into hypergraphs at build time. Queries can then match images by look or by the semantic content of their descriptions. Tests over many questions show performance comparable to a top image-adapted rival, without costly image token processing.
arxiv-2603-02147:
Kyu Hwan Choi, Jiyong Cheon, Joonwoo Jeong, and Sho Takatori measure how molecules spread in a special liquid in this 2026 study. The liquid forms ordered stacks that guide motion in one direction more than another. They use a light method that bleaches a spot, then watches color return as molecules move in. Two dyes let them compare weak and strong ties to the stacks.

In the ordered phase, both dyes moved faster along the stack direction than across it. A dye bound tight to the stacks slowed in all directions as stacks packed closer. The loose dye sped up along the stacks, hinting at tiny channels. The results show how inner structure steers flow in soft matter.
arxiv-2603-02247:
Always-on keyword spotting must adapt on the device itself, and this 2026 paper studies how. Phones and speakers listen for a wake word under tight speed and energy limits. Voices and rooms differ, so a fixed model fits poorly over time. The three authors pair on-device training with a shrinking of the model itself.

Their method, OnDA, prunes whole channels from the network while it learns in the field. They compare pruning rules that use live user data with rules that ignore it. On two public data sets, the model shrank to about a tenth of its size at equal accuracy. On a small embedded chip, training and listening both ran faster. Energy use fell as well, which matters for always-on devices.
arxiv-2603-02347:
Yoon-Joo Kim classifies singular fibers of abelian fibrations in this 2026 mathematics paper. A fibration maps a space onto a curve, with most fibers shaped like abelian varieties. Some fibers degenerate into singular forms that need sorting. Kodaira famously sorted such fibers for the one-dimensional case, elliptic fibrations.

Kim treats minimal fibrations of any relative dimension over a curve. The work covers fibers whose main part is one dimension below the fiber itself. Three families organize the options: semistable, unstable, and multiple fibers. Multiple fibers split further into semistable-like, mixed, and unstable-like types. The result unifies Kodaira's work with later results on Lagrangian fibrations. One framework now covers all of these settings.
arxiv-2603-02447:
Satish Chandran, Nícolas Roque dos Santos, Yunshu Wu, and colleagues regularize diffusion models in the frequency domain in this 2026 paper. Diffusion models learn to turn noise into images and audio. Standard training scores each point alone, ignoring frequency and scale structure. Natural signals, though, live across many scales at once.

Their losses add Fourier and wavelet terms to the usual training objective. The diffusion process, network design, and sampling all stay unchanged. Those terms act as soft biases toward balanced frequencies and coherent fine detail. The method fits several major diffusion variants with negligible extra cost. Image and audio tests show steady quality gains. High-resolution unconditional tasks, where fine structure is hardest, gained the most.
arxiv-2603-02547:
Junzhe Shen, Jieru Zhao, Ziwei He, and Zhouhan Lin diagnose why continuous diffusion language models lag in this 2026 paper.
