Hits in an iron scintillator calorimeter become graph nodes, and the network beats classical methods on the same tasks. A faster scintillator light simulation, twenty times quicker than the default, plus an automated tuning pipeline, lets them map design tradeoffs across energies.
arxiv-2604-08647: Zhichao Zeng and six colleagues test whether a past close passage between the Milky Way and Andromeda fits self interacting dark matter. Replaying Local Group analogues from IllustrisTNG under cold and self interacting models, they find the Milky Way's deep baryonic potential drives self interacting halos past core formation straight into core collapse. The compact disk and bulge survive close encounters, while the diffuse stellar halo breaks apart more easily.
arxiv-2604-08747: Liu, Bogdan, and Baudry trace how JavaScript developers reclassify dependencies over time, beyond version updates, by reading commit level package.json changes across 33,087 projects. Reclassification touches about 79 percent of projects and about 19 percent of maintenance commits, nearly all projects remove dependencies at some point, and 38 percent reassign roles across Core, Dev, and Peer. Removed dependencies return in about 33 percent of projects, with a median reclassification span of 408 days.
arxiv-2604-09247: Dermatis and colleagues present a time-domain method for loads on floating structures in fully nonlinear waves, with second-order consistency. It uses spectral potential flow solvers, applying transfer functions to the incoming wave field. A potential force formula extends the Pinkster approximation to such waves, while the quadratic force uses total motion and velocity. Radiation potential is treated in the time domain, and coupled to a motion solver, the model is tested on a moored container ship, improving markedly over standard theory.
arxiv-2604-09347: D'Eugenio and colleagues present a first carbon-II view of high-redshift quiescent galaxies from ALMA data on five massive quenched galaxies. Molecular gas fractions vary extremely, from a tenth of a percent to 25 percent, assuming a standard conversion factor. Calibration against dust continuum and CO data finds no strong deviation from the standard value. Dust data suggest higher temperatures than expected, reaching about 40 to 50 kelvin in two galaxies, and disturbed morphologies support a merger-driven origin.
arxiv-2604-09447: Dinelli and Muzzeddu unify a theory of motion-driven active matter. They cover systems from lone units to linked chains. In these systems, self-motion responds to outside cues or quorum sensing. Under broad rules for how headings change, they derive a closed set of flow laws for scalar active matter. At large scales, heading effects reduce to the autocorrelation tensor, yielding broad large-scale sameness and showing anti-MIPS, where dense phases show more motion.
arxiv-2604-09847: Sun and Borissov present a quantum method for n-bit integer products with log circuit depth and T-depth, using squared gate counts and spare qubits. The build makes partial products via flag copying, then sums them with a tree of two-way 3-to-2 adders plus one quantum carry-ahead adder. Building on Kim's carry-save adders, the team mixes full input fanout, workspace reuse, and phase-fixed gate builds to reduce T-depth. The paper gives exact circuit designs, proofs that they work, and closed-form resource bounds.
arxiv-2604-10347: Kage and Andreadis present Scale-ALiBi, a linear bias focus model with a spatial coding bias between image patches at varied ground sample distance scales. They build it over aligned high- and low-detail optical imagery plus low-detail SAR space imagery, using a triple-compare and rebuild design. It lifts results on the GEO-Bench benchmark, and the newly curated dataset is shared openly. The work tackles vision base models that must operate across multiple scales and modes.
arxiv-2604-10447: Bandara, Roberts, and Keller detail the SpinQuest microwave rig for polarized proton targets. A 140 GHz source drives dynamic nuclear polarization in solid ammonia under harsh radiation. Fine tuning comes from a motor driven cavity plus live NMR feedback and cold diagnostics. A Monte Carlo twin of the process backs self steering rules, learned controllers, and plain feedback. Remote running cuts radiation risk, and joint cavity plus voltage control steadies power across wide field spreads.
arxiv-2604-10747: Rani and three colleagues survey engineering students using GitHub Copilot on open-source project issues in a course setting. They examine how students use each feature, including chat, code generation, autocompletion, and repository-aware suggestions, and how useful they find them. Students used chat and code generation more than other features. Gender, programming proficiency, and familiarity with AI all shaped feature usage and perceptions, showing that background and experience drive how learners adopt coding assistants.
arxiv-2604-10847: Passos-Reis and colleagues model Seyfert II NGC 1068 with turbulence-driven magnetic reconnection to explain its light. Data show more neutrinos than GeV gamma rays and no TeV counterpart. Their model reconnects fields from a 20 million solar mass hole to corona lines, speeding protons by a Fermi process. It fits the spectrum at a field near 10,000 gauss and power near 10 to the 43rd ergs per second. Inside, protons reach about 10 to the 14th electronvolts. They strike coronal matter, making neutrinos by proton-proton hits while gamma rays fade.
arxiv-2604-11047: Gupta and four colleagues report traits of the Dirac semimetal PdTe2 in mosaic crystals. Using muon spin, magnetic response, and resistivity data, they probe the state. Response reveals two transition temperatures matching earlier reports. Against reports, the crystals prove to be type-II rather than type-I superconductors. The authors observe a flux line lattice through a diamagnetic shift and Gaussian spread of Fourier spectra, likely caused by disorder in the mosaic crystals. Study of the entry depth reveals a gapped state fitted by an s-wave model.
arxiv-2604-11247: Martinien and six colleagues examine 14 highly inclined protoplanetary disks with ALMA, Hubble, and SPHERE imaging. In 11 of 14 disks, gas extends furthest, then micron dust, then millimeter dust, while three disks look wider in millimeter continuum than in scattered light. Inclined disks appear fainter and less extended in gas than flatter disks, a pattern tightened by correcting fluxes for inclination, and millimeter dust sits settled in the midplane, decoupled from gas.
arxiv-2604-11447: Cai and three colleagues make human-to-humanoid motion imitation safe with control barrier functions. A single camera captures human skeletal keypoints, turned into joint angles for the humanoid. The robot must copy the person without bumping into itself or the person. A barrier-function layer set up as a quadratic program filters imitation commands to prevent both self-collisions and human-robot collisions. Simulations validate the framework for real-time collision-aware imitation.
arxiv-2604-11647: Martínez-Sykora and three colleagues investigate the inverse First Ionization Potential effect, a rare solar-atmosphere anomaly in chemical fractionation. Using simple 1D multi-fluid MHD models that solve the equations with multi-fluid and multi-species effects, they explore where the inverse effect could occur. For upward Alfvén waves, a negative ponderomotive force arises when field strength and flux-tube expansion with height offset dissipation and damping from multi-fluid interactions. The study clarifies what could drive this rare fractionation.
arxiv-2604-11947: Aboudib, Lopez, Brady, and Cruz propose ResBM, a Residual Bottleneck Model built for low-bandwidth pipeline training. Large multi-node training leans on data and pipeline parallelism, but splitting work this way still demands ultra-high-bandwidth links. ResBM places a residual encoder-decoder bottleneck across pipeline splits, trainable end to end with a low-rank identity path. It reaches 128-fold activation compression, a state-of-the-art figure, without notable loss in convergence speed or added memory and compute overhead.
arxiv-2604-12147: Liu and four colleagues measure how faithfully coding agents follow instructed plans, analyzing 21,120 trajectories from SWE-agent across four models and eight plan variants. Giving the standard plan improves issue resolution, and periodic reminders curb violations. But a poor plan hurts more than none at all. Extra early phases can degrade performance when they clash with a model's own strategy. They call for training that teaches plan following rather than memorized workflows.
arxiv-2604-12647: Tsai-Ning Wang and four colleagues route respiratory audio by difficulty at test time. Scarce labels limit screening. Zero-shot inference avoids task training but spends equal compute everywhere. Their TRIAGE framework routes samples through tiers of rising richness. Three tiers rise in richness, from fast scoring to descriptor matching to language model reasoning. A confidence router ends easy cases early, spending more on ambiguous ones. Nearly half of samples exit at the cheapest tier. Mean AUROC reaches 0.744 across nine tasks, beating prior zero-shot methods.
arxiv-2604-12747: Arshad Beg and two colleagues outline Learning-Infused Formal Reasoning, a vision joining learning and proof. AI systems excel at language and perception, yet stay opaque and hard to check. Formal methods give strict proof tools, but writing specs is laborious and hard to scale. The framework pursues three directions: contract synthesis from natural language, semantic reuse of proof artifacts, and foundations. Graph matching and embeddings power artifact reuse. Unifying Theories of Programming and the Theory of Institutions ground the foundations. Together, the threads turn proof into a cumulative process.
arxiv-2604-13247: Kowalski and Piotrowska study cross-platform domain adaptation for multi-modal MOOC satisfaction prediction when target-platform labels are scarce or absent. Their ADAPT-MS framework encodes review text with a frozen language-model encoder and behavioral traces with a canonical-vocabulary network. It aligns representations through domain-adversarial training and corrects rating bias with a latent-variable calibration layer. It reaches target-platform RMSE of 0.66 with zero labeled target samples and 0.60 with 1,000, beating pooling, uncalibrated alignment, and full fine-tuning baselines.
arxiv-2604-13647: Romeis moves past the dipole approximation for magnetically soft particle systems. Simple dipole models badly understate forces when particles draw close, while full-field methods cost too much compute. Starting from the exact two-body solution, he builds an analytic scheme for many-body interactions in a compact operator form that looks dipole-like. It captures cluster formation and dispersal in applied fields, and it is easy to implement.
arxiv-2604-13847: Xu and ten colleagues present SparseBalance for long-context training with dynamic sparse attention. Sparse attention eases long-context compute, but distributed training faces wild variation in sequence length and sparsity response, causing imbalance and weaker results. Their co-design tunes sparsity with two-way adjustment, removing stragglers and using idle bubbles for free gains. Sparsity-aware batching adds coarse balance. Results show up to a 1.33-fold end-to-end speedup while LongBench capability rises by 0.46 percent.
arxiv-2604-13947: Ouattara and colleagues detect weather from ordinary color images, predicting type plus 11 attributes across 53 classes. Style-inspired tools, including Gram matrices, a truncated ResNet-50, and PatchGAN variants, run in a multi-task setup with attention. Their released set holds 503,875 annotated images, and scores pass 96 percent on internal tests and pass 78 percent zero-shot elsewhere, with the compact PMG model running in real time.
arxiv-2604-14047: Jiang and colleagues convert Nature Communications review letters from 2017 through 2024 into structured reviewer-author exchanges, using a fixed-prompt language-model pipeline. Review pressure concentrates in round one and on core claims, not presentation. Stronger criticism, better comments, and heavier revision burden track higher later citations among accepted papers. That runs against the intuition that strong papers sail through smoothly.
arxiv-2604-14447: Spanodimos, Qian, and Cui present a hybrid switched-capacitor converter with a three-state modulation scheme for wide-range regulation in 48-volt car power systems. A three-state sequence beyond standard two-to-one resonant operation gives variable step-down ratios while keeping soft switching mostly, covering zero-current and zero-voltage modes. A closed-loop proportional-integral controller, tuned by reinforcement learning, handles the nonlinear, variable-frequency behavior with good transient response. A prototype holds zero-current switching across conversion ratios of 0.2 to 0.4, with peak efficiency above 92 percent.
arxiv-2604-15047: Jayasundara and Patel survey neural nets that store signals as smooth math functions rather than grids of samples. They trace how early nets favored slow, low-frequency patterns and how newer designs widen the range they can capture. The review links this growth to sampling theory, scale, and frequency behavior in signal work. It frames these models as one shared tool for images, sound, video, and 3D shapes.
arxiv-2604-15347: Tang builds SocialWise, a browser app that coaches conversation skills for people with autism spectrum disorder, a condition affecting more than 75 million people worldwide. Users pick everyday scenes such as ordering food or joining a group, chat by text or voice, and get instant structured feedback on tone, engagement, and phrasing. Built with Streamlit, LangChain, and ChromaDB, it runs on any internet-connected computer.
arxiv-2604-15447: Salami studies what happens to Zeckendorf-style splits when recurrence coefficients may be zero, focusing on the Lagonacci sequence. Although each integer loses its unique split, core statistics survive: greedy-split counts converge to a Gaussian curve and gaps between indices decay geometrically. An ensembles-equivalence case extends the results broadly, while legal splits grow exponentially at rate 2.
arxiv-2604-15647: Chen, Lau, and Frermann present Conversational Information Gain, a way to judge talk by how much new useful info it adds, not by tone or shape. A live store of claims drawn from what each speaker says rates each claim for newness, fit to the topic, and how much it implies. On 80 bits of debate and forum talk, this store's ups and downs match what people rate as gain far better than length or word-count tricks. The same scores can power tools that guess gain from text.
arxiv-2604-15747: Gong, Liu, Zhang, Zheng, and Xu build a nerve net where chloride balance sets the fire-calm mix via channel inflow and outflow. The calm-link inflow share steers seizures through pre-fit, tonic-fit, and clonic-fit. Cutting that share shortens fits and blocks starts, while a high share births tonic and clonic stages and spin waves. Mid shares skip the tonic stage to clonic fits; looped fire widens tonic-clonic fits, calm drags out pre-fits and blocks clonic fits.
arxiv-2604-15847: Li, Chen, and Ding introduce CiPO, a method for making large reasoning models forget facts without harming reasoning. Existing unlearning tools either leave traces in thought chains or damage reasoning itself. CiPO instead has the model write a logically valid counterfactual reasoning trace for the target answer. It then tunes preferences toward that trace, updating the tuning data in rounds to widen the gap from the original model. Tests show it removes target knowledge from both thought steps and final answers while preserving reasoning skill.
arxiv-2604-16347: Yanahama and Sannai present Lean Atlas, a joint proof tool for scalable human-AI formal work. AI autoformal work grows fast, but a proof tool's type checker ensures only logical rightness, not whether claims truly capture meant math content. AI proofs can therefore pass the checker while missing the meant math, a meaning hallucination. Lean Atlas lets human scientists and AI produce formal proofs jointly, with humans checking meaning content. It shows a Lean 4 project's link graph, and its Lean Compass method extracts nodes whose rightness can affect target theorems.
arxiv-2604-16547: Zhang and colleagues study how leak motion affects path tracking in looping networks. Inner motion across time spans is linked to regular spatial activity, but handling across time spans is unclear. Adding changing time spans through a leak term forms leaky networks from smooth loops. They show greatly stronger, highly regular hexagonal firing patterns. Versus vanilla networks, leaky networks give more exact position guesses and more steady grid-like patterns. Under the same noise they stay more stable, forming torus loops with a clear central hole.
arxiv-2604-16647: Chirolli and colleagues propose isolating Cooper quartets, four aggregates generalizing Cooper pairs, in a dot device. It couples to super and normal leads, and driving it off balance yields a resonance at high bias voltage. That resonance involves a two-Cooper-pair exchange process with finite quartet correlations. An Andreev current peak at high bias widens with quartet coupling, tuned by extra lead phases. Equal auto- and cross-correlations mark coherent two-Cooper-pair oscillations between dots and leads. The platform opens exploration of quartet correlations and states.
arxiv-2604-16747: Droby diagnoses overfitting in dynamic 3D Gaussian splatting, where training quality stays strong but generalization lags. On D-NeRF the train-test gap averages six point one eight decibels, rising to 11 on individual scenes. Splitting drives over 80 percent of the gap: disabling it collapses the cloud and the gap to one point one five. A local-smoothness penalty on the deformation field, Elastic Energy Regularization, cuts the gap by about 41 percent. With two further regularizers, gap reduction reaches 57 percent, and coherence generalizes to a second architecture.
arxiv-2604-16847: Morales-Durán and colleagues investigate remote band mixing effects on fractional Chern insulator stability. The asymmetry between one third and two thirds fillings reflects competition among an insulator, an electron crystal and a hole crystal. Without band mixing, the electron crystal leads at one third while the hole crystal competes at two thirds. Band mixing lowers electron crystal energy substantially but weakly affects the hole crystal, destabilizing the insulator more at one third. The mechanism also explains re-entrant integer quantum anomalous Hall states beyond filling one half.
arxiv-2604-17147: Gao and ten colleagues introduce ScenarioControl, the first vision-language control system for learned driving-scenario generation. From a text prompt or an input image, it synthesizes diverse realistic 3D scenario rollouts, including maps, reactive actors, pedestrians, infrastructure, and ego camera views. Scenes are generated in a vectorized latent space joining road structure and dynamic agents, with a cross-global control giving fine-grained control over layout and traffic while preserving realism.
arxiv-2604-17347: De Giacomo, Kampik, Kirchdorfer, Montali, and Weinhuber lay the mathematical groundwork for agentic business process management, where workflows are carried out by autonomous decision-makers rather than fixed scripts. Each agent pursues assigned goals under assumptions about the others, choosing strategies as best it can. The organization can then set guardrails at the strategy level instead of micromanaging every step. The paper formalizes three such settings and analyzes four foundational problems, giving the young field a rigorous footing.
arxiv-2604-17647: Girish, Akhtar, and Singh introduce a paralinguistic supervision approach for low-resource multilingual speech emotion recognition, using non-verbal vocalizations for prosody cues. Conventional systems lean on labeled verbal speech and transfer poorly across languages. The approach recasts the task as non-verbal-to-verbal transfer, adapting supervision from a non-verbal source to unlabeled speech. Their NOVA ARC framework models feeling structure in the Poincaré ball, discretizes patterns with a hyperbolic codebook, and captures intensity through a hyperbolic lens. Optimal-transport prototype alignment adapts it without labels.
arxiv-2604-17847: Goel studies S(q), residue classes modulo the Pisano period where q divides Euler's totient of each Fibonacci number in the class. For a Sophie Germain prime q meeting a stated divisibility condition, Goel proves S(q) is a nonempty arithmetic progression. Above 5, its size is odd and q is congruent to 8 modulo 15. Conversely, a prime p congruent to 1 modulo q meeting the condition must equal 2q+1. Goel conjectures that nonempty S(q) always forces such a prime.
arxiv-2604-18347: Baiamonte, Fano, Gabburo, Simonazzi, Rigutini, and Zugarini build multilingual training and evaluation resources for vision-language models. Such models lean heavily on English, lacking multilingual data and cross-language benchmarks. A regeneration-translation pipeline yields Multi-PixMo training data plus benchmarks in English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish. Tests on three models show multilingual training helps non-English benchmarks consistently, with positive transfer back to English.
arxiv-2604-18547: Lee and six colleagues introduce Fully Unsupervised Score Ensembling, improving verification quality by pooling verifiers without truth labels. Output checking is rising as a key tool for training and deploying large language models, yet ground truth is slow and costly, so flawed judges and reward models are used. FUSE manages links between checkers to improve spectral pooling. Despite needing zero truth labels, it usually matches or beats semi-guided rivals in scaling tests. Validation covers GPQA Diamond and frontier tests including Humanity's Last Exam and IMO Shortlist items.
arxiv-2604-18647: Singh and five colleagues build a phase-space route to quantum-deformed gravity, then boil it down to a four-dimensional spacetime model. A scalar field linked to momentum directions warps the gravity Hamiltonian, giving changed Einstein equations that the team uses to model cosmic inflation, slow roll, and ripples in the early universe. The main inflation changes trace to the warp itself and to how it shifts with time.
arxiv-2604-18747: Xie and six colleagues propose URoPE, a general form of rotary position embedding that works across camera views and across dimensions. For each image patch, the method samples 3D points along the camera ray at preset depth anchors and maps them onto the query image plane, where standard 2D rotary embedding then applies. It adds no new parameters, uses camera intrinsics, and works with existing rotary-optimized attention kernels. In tests on view synthesis, 3D detection, tracking, and depth estimation, it lifts transformer models across the board.
arxiv-2604-18847: Li and three colleagues formalize harm recovery for computer use agents. Recovery means bringing an agent back to safety from a harmful state, per human preferences, after prevention fails. A user study names valued recovery dimensions and yields a natural language rubric. Its 1,130 pairwise judgments show context dependent shifts in importance. The insights feed a reward model that reranks candidate plans, tested on BackBench, a benchmark of 50 tasks.
arxiv-2604-18947: Forbes, van Heumen, and Tang revisit the distance and globular cluster system of the galaxy UDG1 in the NGC 5846 group. Two earlier studies using the same imaging counted 54 and 33 clusters and disagreed on group membership. A new surface brightness fluctuation distance of 26.5 Mpc places the galaxy squarely inside the group. Counting only clusters brighter than the turnover magnitude reconciles the two studies. Both then imply about 50 clusters in total and a massive halo of over 100 billion solar masses.
arxiv-2604-19047: Cho and Lee present RARE, a retrieval benchmark framework for highly similar corpora like finance, legal, and patent documents. Standard benchmarks assume distinct documents, but real systems face redundant texts with overlapping evidence. This mismatch undervalues retrievers returning sufficient evidence and overrates benchmark stars. RARE splits documents into atomic facts to track redundancy, scoring criteria separately and fusing decisions by rank. On finance, legal, and patent corpora, it yields RedQA, where a retriever drops from 66.4 percent PerfRecall at 10 to between 5 and 28 percent at 4-hop depth.
arxiv-2604-19147: Zhao and six colleagues present Nexusformer, swapping linear query, key, and value projections for a nonlinear Nexus-Rank layer using dual signals in higher spaces. Linear projections trap features in fixed subspaces, curbing power and capacity. New capacity enters along two axes through zero-start blocks keeping knowledge. Nexusformer matches Tokenformer on perplexity using up to 41.5 percent less compute while scaling from 240 to 440 million weights. Zero initialization gives stable convergence and a scaling law predicting performance across scales.
arxiv-2604-19747: Chen and nine colleagues present AnyRecon, a scalable tool for 3D rebuilding from arbitrary, unordered sparse views that keeps direct geometric control. Earlier diffusion methods synthesize new views but use only one or two capture frames, which limits shape consistency and scale to large or diverse scenes. AnyRecon builds a persistent global scene memory from a prepended capture view cache and drops time-based compression, preserving frame-level correspondence.
arxiv-2604-19947: Li and four colleagues search for small Kochen-Specker sets in three dimensions, extending the 13-ray Yu-Oh set, the minimal witness of state-independent contextuality. Their SAT-based orderly search pairs recursive canonical labeling with the NAUTY graph tool, keeping checks at millisecond speed where older lexicographic methods blow up exponentially. An exhaustive search up to 33 rays, costing 1,641 CPU hours, finds Schütte's 33-ray set is the smallest containing the full 25-ray set. All non-existence claims carry checkable proof certificates.
arxiv-2604-20047: Liu and four colleagues present PASTA, a patch-agnostic backdoor attack on vision transformers that stays stealthy in both pixel and attention domains. They exploit the Trigger Radiating Effect, in which a patch trigger activates backdoors across neighboring patches through long-range self-attention. Multi-location trigger insertion during training strengthens the effect, and bi-level optimization balances stealth against strength. PASTA hits 99.13 percent attack success across arbitrary patches on average, while improving visual stealth over 144 times, attention stealth about 19 times, and robustness nearly three times.
arxiv-2604-20347: Zhang and four colleagues present a vision-language-action model for adaptive sound-guided needle insertion and tracking on a robot sound system. A cross-depth fusion tracking head blends shallow spot cues and deep meaning cues from the vision backbone. A tracking-conditioning log adapts the pretrained backbone for tracking with less tuning. A doubt-aware control rule plus a free-running pipeline then steer insertion in real time, beating top trackers and manual work on tracking hits, insertion wins, and procedure time.
arxiv-2604-20447: Maracani and four colleagues propose SpanDec, an efficient span-based framework for named-entity recognition built for strict latency and throughput demands. Span-based methods reach strong accuracy but often list huge numbers of spans and process each with marked inputs, raising inference cost. SpanDec computes span interactions at the final transformer stage through a light decoder handling spans alone, avoiding repeat work in earlier layers. A filtering step prunes unlikely spans before costly processing. Across benchmarks, SpanDec matches strong span baselines while raising throughput and cutting cost.
arxiv-2604-20747: Harmanec, Yang, Slechta, Grundstrom, Ribeiro, and Harmanec analyze radial velocities of two narrow components in the Mg II 4481 A line. They show that omicron Cas's secondary is a tight pair of two B7 stars circling each other every 11.6604 days. Orbit fits plus spectral disentangling agree on the system properties. The system matters greatly for Be star research. Coming interferometric observations with fine spatial detail could pin down a Be star's mass and perhaps even its radius mostly on dynamical grounds.
arxiv-2604-20947: Asai, Iyama, Mousavand, and Paquette extend two ideas from finite lattice theory to endless systems. The ideas are left modularity and extremality. The systems they treat are well-separated kappa-lattices and weakly atomic completely semidistributive lattices. Those systems agree on finite lattices but part ways for endless ones. For both systems, the two notions imply each other. The left modular elements themselves make up a complete distributive sublattice. Applied to torsion classes, the notions hold exactly when the algebra is brick-directed.
arxiv-2604-21347: Alberto Dayan, Adrián Llinares, and Miguel Monsalve-López study function spaces in the Dirichlet range, defined by an integral condition on holomorphic functions of the unit disc. They answer two definers' questions with no. For exponents away from 2 and above one-half, it need not be a vector space. Its norm need not grow with the exponent either. A matching account via Poisson integrals yields inner-outer factorizations. As a corollary, the exponent-1 space sits in the weak product of a Dirichlet-type space.
arxiv-2604-21547: Vinayak Kulkarni constructs an integrable model of many-body exceptional-point amplification in the Anderson impurity. Two spin-orbit branches fold into chiral components, with a pseudo-Hermitian matrix. A canonical change preserves the interaction, and a position version maps it to the Anderson Hamiltonian with a pseudospin charge and twist. The R-matrix yields Yang-Baxter, RLL, and twisted RTT rules. At a special match the twist is not trivial unipotent, and every pseudospin multiplet gives a single Jordan block, shifted, unsplit, by finite U.
arxiv-2604-21647: Murphy-Barltrop and colleagues use statistical deep learning to study how climate change alters simultaneous floods and droughts across neighboring catchments. Applying the deep SPAR framework to simulated discharge from four Upper Danube catchments, they capture joint extremes accurately. They project growing odds of joint flooding and drought-like states toward the end of the century under a high-emission scenario. Crucially, shifts in how extremes depend on each other drive much of the change, a pattern traditional methods would miss.
arxiv-2604-21847: Kocurek, Oveis Gharan, and Tjowasi design a sampling algorithm for the hardcore model on random regular bipartite graphs. It works while fugacity lambda is at most 1 over the square root of degree. Combined with Jenssen, Keevash, and Perkins, this gives a fully polynomial randomised approximation scheme for the partition function at any fugacity. The algorithm analyses two Markov chains working in complementary regimes. Its proof shows the simplicial complexes are top-link spectral expanders and appeals to the trickle-down theorem for fast mixing.
arxiv-2604-22247: Chiba and Houri study symmetry equations for a lifted version of a flat expanding-universe model. The model is driven by a scalar field. Reducing the prolonged conformal Killing equations leaves a nonlinear second-order equation. It governs the ratio of a potential's slope to the potential itself. Solving it locally gives two branches, but only the regular branch fits the full equations. The potential from their earlier work is thus the most general local potential of its kind in that sector.
arxiv-2604-22347: Bera and five colleagues catalogue winged radio galaxies, irregular galaxies with a pair of secondary lobes, or wings, beside their primary lobes. Using high-resolution data from the second release of the LOFAR Two-Metre Sky Survey, they identify 621 new winged galaxies and 403 further candidates. Of the confirmed sources, 382 are X-shaped and 239 are Z-shaped. Most show edge-brightened lobes and high radio power, matching the FR-II class. Their median size is 498 kpc, and about 16 percent exceed 0.7 Mpc, making them possible giant radio galaxies.
arxiv-2604-22547: Luo and 29 colleagues report electron spin resonance of a single electron in a planar silicon-MOS quantum dot near a valley level anti-crossing. Mixing of magnetic spin-flip and electric valley-flip transitions produces one- and two-photon resonances, letting the team rebuild the energy diagram of a four-state system. Near the anti-crossing, the Rabi frequency, the rate of driven oscillation between states, is enhanced. The boost traces to an electric-dipole transition from inter-valley spin coupling, strongest for out-of-plane fields.
arxiv-2604-22647: Lee and 29 colleagues test a lead-scintillating fiber prototype for the Barrel Imaging Calorimeter at the EIC with beams at CERN's PS T10 line in August 2024. It uses unit modules with a sampling structure of lead sheets and fibers, about 11 radiation lengths. Beam tests with momenta from half to 3 GeV/c gauge its energy and timing. The study covers it and informs future beam tests, calibration and readout tuning, and larger-scale prototype building.
arxiv-2604-23147: Li and four colleagues build a graph neural network surrogate predicting galaxy properties from dark matter merger trees plus semi-analytic model parameters. Trained on Uchuu trees with the Galacticus model, it predicts stellar mass, luminosity, angular momentum, gas metal mass, and star formation rate to redshift 5. Stellar mass predictions to redshift 3 carry scatter near one-quarter dex with determination scores close to one, showing strong agreement with truth. One graph model thus reproduces galaxy traits across many model runs, trees, and redshifts, opening wider parameter searches.
arxiv-2604-23747: Limozin and colleagues show that the standard supervised-then-reinforcement pipeline for language-model reasoning was judged unfairly because its baseline carried two bugs. A DeepSpeed optimiser bug silently dropped micro-batches during gradient accumulation, and an OpenRLHF loss bug misweighted mini-batch losses. Once fixed, the standard pipeline beats every published mixed-policy method tested, by about 4 points on one model and over twenty points on another.
arxiv-2604-23947: Agarwal and four colleagues present GamED.AI, a hierarchical multi-agent framework that turns teacher questions into playable, pedagogically grounded games checked by contracts. Built on LangGraph sub-graphs, quality gates, and Pydantic schemas, it covers two template families with fifteen interaction mechanics spanning procedural execution, higher-order Bloom's taxonomy objectives, and spatial reasoning. On 200 questions across five subject domains it reaches a 90 percent validation pass rate and 98.3 percent schema compliance, with 73 percent token reduction over ReAct agents, about 73,500 down to about 19,900 tokens per game, at 46 cents per game.
arxiv-2604-24247: Maggi and colleagues describe the data analysis pipeline for the Microchannel X-ray Telescope aboard the SVOM mission, launched in June 2024. SVOM, a Sino-French mission, hunts gamma-ray bursts and other high-energy transients, with MXT following up burst afterglows in X-rays. The ground pipeline ingests raw event lists automatically, calibrates, filters background and time, corrects instrumental effects, and delivers science-ready images, light curves, and spectra. Its modular design sits inside the wider SVOM ground segment, and real datasets show it meets mission performance needs.
arxiv-2604-24347: Li and four colleagues infer tissue segmentations from label proportions, without pixel labels. Many segmentations can satisfy the same proportions, so the task is unclear. Their Variational Segmentation from Label Proportions method runs a ready net with test-time boosts for scores. A second stage fuses scores through energy tuning with an earth-mover fidelity term and a smoother. Unlike end-to-end networks, it shows its fidelity-control energy. It beats weakly taught and untaught methods on two public datasets.
arxiv-2604-24447: Zhou and five colleagues analyze VLA models for robot deployment. GPUs hide edge trade-offs; the authors build a leaderboard scoring pairs on cost, energy, and time. Right-sized edge devices beat GPUs on cost and energy while meeting control rates. Profiling reveals two phases: a compute-bound backbone, then a memory-bound action expert, causing underuse and inefficiency. Guided by this, DP-Cache and V-AEFusion cut diffusion redundancy and enable pipeline parallelism. They reach up to 2.9 times speedup on GPUs and 6 times on NPUs with slight success loss.
arxiv-2604-24647: Dehghanighobadi and Fischer address the memory bottleneck of long-context language-model inference: the key-value cache grows linearly with sequence length. Existing pruning methods cut cached tokens by attention score but apply one pruning ratio to every layer. The authors show layers differ sharply in pruning sensitivity. Their DepthKV framework allocates a fixed global cache budget across layers by sensitivity. Across models and tasks it consistently beats uniform pruning at the same global ratio.
arxiv-2604-24747: Liu and Tripathi derive a determinant identity for the sum of two matrices built from contour integrals. The determinant equals a Fredholm determinant, built from a kernel tied to a function that solves a system of equations. When the defining functions are set to certain rational functions, that function becomes the characteristic function for inhomogeneous directed last passage percolation and totally asymmetric simple exclusion models. They also obtain a random-walk hitting expectation form. That link drives the paper.
arxiv-2604-25147: Zhang and Hou present an encoded net for high-dimensional backward stochastic differential equations and parabolic partial differential equations. Standard nets give each input dimension a single neuron. Their encoding instead turns input coordinates into multi-channel tensors, read as images by convolutional nets, so space and time features stay in balance. On the Black-Scholes-Barenblatt and Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman benchmarks, the encoded net does better, with less work and more accuracy, than the plain forward-backward net.
arxiv-2604-25747: Asaka combines quantum spatial distribution with gauge symmetry to strengthen quantum error correction, within Poulin's stabilizer formalism. Spatial distribution means a superposition of particle spin and position states. The study uses five particles on nested squares from a companion paper. Three encode Shor's nine-qubit code, while two detect errors via spin measurements. Gauge symmetry first gives resilience against three noise types on one particle. That spread then lets error-correcting systems stack vertically and horizontally, with gates built from nearby interactions only.
arxiv-2604-26247: Yang and six colleagues proposed TimeMM, a recommender that lets time reshape the user-item graph. How recent each link is sets a set of time kernels that reweight the graph edges, and a spectral filtering step blends those kernels by context to fit each guess. A routing step then tunes visual and textual signals to the same moment. On real test sets, it beat top multimodal rivals while keeping run time linear in scale.
arxiv-2604-26347: Tsai and seven colleagues put emotion-similarity scoring for speech generation to the test. The method scores a generated sample against a reference by comparing vectors from emotion encoders, trusting those vectors to carry feeling despite wording and speaker shifts. Yet even strong classifiers leave wording and speaker cues swamping feeling in those vectors, so zero-shot comparisons mislead. Adversarial probes and checks against human ears showed the score strays from what people hear. It thus rewards sound mimicry over true emotional synthesis.
arxiv-2604-26947: Benson and fourteen colleagues study singlet-triplet splittings in a double quantum dot built from Ge/SiGe layers, key parameters for hole spin qubits. Splittings are known to track lateral confinement, yet gate-voltage changes usually leave them nearly untouched. Using photon-assisted tunneling and pulsed-gate spectroscopy, the team finds a surprisingly strong gate-voltage dependence that distorts tunneling measurements. A model combining both measurements captures the linear gate-voltage trend, and retuned dots show similar trends at very different splitting ratios.
arxiv-2604-27047: Moreno and ten colleagues examine hydrogen starless halos nearby across three simulations: FIREbox, Recal-EAGLE, and NIVARIA-LG. All three produce such objects, with hydrogen masses up to 2 dex above Cloud-9, but densities varying by a factor near 30. The populations span mass spaces: NIVARIA-LG makes objects with high hydrogen and gas masses, while FIREbox confines them to narrow gas and mass ranges. Recal-EAGLE and NIVARIA-LG show a gas-mass correlation with different normalizations. The gaps argue for a sample of halos to tell predictions apart.
arxiv-2604-27147: Huang and four colleagues recast guidance of generative flow models as a deterministic optimal control problem. Guidance steers samples toward a user reward, such as beauty or human preference, but existing methods need costly multi-particle runs or rest on poorly understood approximations. Their hierarchy of algorithms subsumes older methods at its coarsest level. The flow map, prized for fast inference, emerges naturally in the optimal solution and drives their training-free Flow Map Reward Guidance method.
arxiv-2604-27247: Hoeser and four colleagues work toward a wide-use national product mapping hedges and linear woody features in Germany from Earth observation data. Hedges aid climate adaptation and varied life in intensively farmed landscapes, sheltering varied flora and feeding, resting, and nesting animals including pollinators. They need dedicated management and protection. Yet shared workflows remain a challenge, given diverse sensors, detail levels, acquisition conditions, and complex landscape variation across the country.
arxiv-2604-27547: Taghanaki and twelve colleagues present GoalCover, a tool that spots capability gaps in data meant for fine-tuning language models. It breaks a high-level goal into small, separately testable subgoals, scores each sample against every subgoal, and flags missing skills from low-scoring cases. In tests across medical, legal, and code tasks, target subgoals fell by about 26 percent against about 2 percent for others. On a finance summarization task, GoalCover-filtered data lifted the judge reward to 4.12 out of 5, and adding synthetic samples did best.
arxiv-2604-27647: Matsuda, Machida, and Lo propose NvRec, a tail-aware API recommendation method that runs several model versions and filters unreliable outputs. Code data sets often over-represent common APIs and under-represent rare ones, so tail APIs get unreliable recommendations. NvRec profiles each model's performance on individual APIs with their tail properties, then filters unreliable recommendations at inference time. The best three-model mix reaches 83.8 percent accepted with about 81 percent rejected, while the five-model mix reaches about 83 percent accepted with 69 percent rejected, a better balance.
arxiv-2604-27947: Kafantaris builds and tests an attractor FCM learning by gradient descent under physics limits, in Jacobian form not Hebbian, agentic, or hybrid. It keeps leftover memory, learns through time, and anchors on a fixed point refreshed step by step to update weights, keeping system memory. A Newton step first finds the fixed-point attractor, then descent reshapes the landscape, steering weights through attractor dynamics. Descent shifts with sigmoid saturation to dodge early local stalls. A causal mask filters updates by physics and expert views, driving error to target.
arxiv-2604-28147: Kiegeland and colleagues untangle how surprisal theory should treat units, a choice often left vague in studies of processing effort. Experiments split text into linguistic units such as words, while language models score fixed token alphabets that rarely match those units, conflating the unit definition with the choice of regions scored. Their unified framework separates the two choices and treats tokenization as an implementation detail, not a scientific primitive.
arxiv-2605-00047:
Eduardo Jiménez-Fernández, Jesús Rodríguez-López, Aurora Sánchez-Martín-Orozco, and Enrique A Sánchez-Pérez revisit an extension theorem for fuzzy Lipschitz maps. An earlier paper by three of the authors extended the classical McShane-Whitney result to real-valued fuzzy Lipschitz maps between fuzzy metric spaces, with a Euclidean fuzzy metric space as the codomain. That is, a Lipschitz map defined on part of a space can be extended to the whole space without breaking its constant.

The catch is that some results of the earlier paper quietly assume a certain function is invertible, though it was only required to be increasing. The authors now propose an alternative possibility that weakens the demand: the function need only also be left-continuous. The paper thus repairs and extends the earlier extension theorem on cleaner hypotheses.
arxiv-2605-00147:
Bala Prenith Reddy Gopu and six co-authors present Images2Mesh, a pipeline for rebuilding the three-dimensional surface of non-cooperative space objects from inspection photos. On-orbit imagery reveals the geometry and condition that debris removal and servicing missions need, but most neural surface methods were proven on synthetic data with known camera poses and controlled light. This pipeline is demonstrated on real footage.

The tests use publicly released space station inspection footage from the STS-119 mission and on-orbit footage of a Japanese rocket upper stage. Segmentation-based background removal proves vital: background variation between frames made direct camera pose work fail entirely. A photometric fix for per-frame exposure differences is also folded in. Its behavior in shadowed regions is checked across the datasets. The authors note the work is independent of the space agencies involved.
arxiv-2605-00447:
Cole Morgan and 3 co-authors revisit the linking of issue reports to the code commits that fix them, a backbone of software traceability. Many automated linkers have been proposed, from heuristics to deep learning. The authors rerun established techniques head to head, asking which are truly most effective and efficient at reranking candidate links.

The pipeline has two stages: retrieval narrows the commit pool, then a reranker orders it. Dense, meaning-based retrieval beat keyword retrieval at finding the right commits, and mixing the two improved recall further. In the reranking stage, traditional machine learning models outperformed large language model approaches, including well-known chat models. Their practical moral is unfashionable but useful: retrieval pipelines with modest models remain a strong, efficient answer, and costly language models should earn their place before being adopted.
arxiv-2605-00547:
L. A. S. Evangelista and 3 co-authors test an extended theory of gravity against a strange question: can a universe contain time loops? Their model lets the gravitational action depend on the Ricci scalar, the matter Lagrangian, a scalar field, and its kinetic term. Gödel and Gödel-type spacetimes, rotating universes famous for closed timelike curves, serve as the test beds.

They examine which geometries the model allows, with a perfect fluid and with scalar-field configurations as matter. The standard Gödel metric proves incompatible with the scalar sector unless the theory collapses back to general relativity. Gödel-type geometries admit wider solutions, whose causal character depends on parameters and matter. Fluid sources can go either way. Scalar-field sources pin the geometry to the causal limit, blocking time loops entirely.
arxiv-2605-00947:
Eike Neumann and Margret Tembo study whether linear and affine loops over the real numbers always terminate, in the bit-model of real computation. Termination is a basic correctness question for programs, but real-number loops raise special issues because values are not finite bit strings. The authors show both problems are as close to decidable as one can reasonably expect.

They prove sound partial algorithms exist that halt on every instance whose answer is robust, meaning it survives all sufficiently small perturbations of the problem. They also show the set of non-robust instances has Lebesgue measure zero, so almost every instance is covered. Readers get a precise boundary between what can and cannot be decided for such loops.
arxiv-2605-01047:
Joseph Spracklen and three co-authors present Adaptive Unlearning, a method to suppress package hallucinations in language models after release. Such errors invent non-existent software packages, complete with install commands. Attackers can register those names with malicious code, a supply-chain attack known as slopsquatting. Developers or autonomous agents may then install and run them.

Their method uses a hybrid token-level objective that reinforces valid outputs while suppressing hallucinated ones. A self-tuning loop also surfaces new error-inducing contexts without human supervision. Package hallucination rates fall sharply while standard coding results are kept. Changes focus on package-related generation, leaving general coding behavior largely unaffected. No human annotation is required.
arxiv-2605-01247:
Ethan Wang, Zubair Shafiq, and Yash Vekaria present FP-Agent, the first controlled measurement study of AI browsing agents and how they can be fingerprinted. Such agents navigate websites autonomously in real browsers and perform everyday tasks, making them hard to distinguish from humans or from each other. Using an instrumented honey website, the team collects browser and behavioral features while seven agents and human users complete flight booking, shopping, and forum tasks.

Browser fingerprints give limited power when several agents share them. Behavioral fingerprints, covering typing, scrolling, and mouse behavior, are distinctive and separate agents from humans and from one another. In a case study, their classifier detects all seven agents, whereas a commercial bot detection service detects only one.
arxiv-2605-01447:
Yuki Ishihara and sixteen co-authors settle the magnetic ground state of a kagome lattice crystal, a metal where atoms sit on a pattern of corner-sharing triangles. The compound, with neodymium, ruthenium, and aluminum, had been reported to order with two unequal moment sizes on its two neodymium sites.

Using single-crystal neutron diffraction, backed by polarized neutron tests, the team finds a simpler state. All moments line up in one direction with one shared length, a collinear ferromagnet with no repeating offset. The polarized beam's flipping ratio matches this uniform state and not the older two-size claim. The crystal orders near 41 kelvin, and the corrected ground state gives a firm base for reading its large Hall and Nernst responses, which grow from thermal fluctuations near that point.
arxiv-2605-01747:
Gaurav Bhatnagar and Amritanshu Prasad prove an identity that a counting problem over finite fields had left as a conjecture. The question grew out of enumerating subspaces, a basic census in finite geometry. It concerned a q-analogue of the binomial theorem, the decorated cousin of the schoolbook expansion where powers are weighted by q-combinatorial counts.

Their result is broader than the conjecture that prompted it. They establish a bibasic, double-sum identity: two bases instead of one, and two layers of summation, extending the terminating q-binomial theorem into that wider family. Identities of this kind are the load-bearing walls of q-series, the branch of mathematics behind partition counts, quantum groups, and much of modern combinatorics. A proof here does double duty, settling the subspace count that raised the question and adding a general tool that other counters can now cite.
arxiv-2605-01847:
Xiao Jia introduces NeuroState-Bench, a benchmark that tests whether a language model agent keeps its commitments across a long, multi-turn task. Success at the end alone does not show whether the agent held to what the task required. The benchmark uses fixed side questions, built into each task, rather than guesses about hidden model states.

The set holds 144 tasks and 306 side probes across eight failure types, with clean and distracting versions and three levels of difficulty. Human checks on sampled tasks showed strong agreement. Across 32 model profiles, the leader on task success was not the leader on commitment, and most profiles changed rank when the score switched to commitment.
arxiv-2605-01947:
Srinjana Routh and colleagues report a radio sign of poleward flow high in the Sun's atmosphere. Flows and magnetic fields together move angular momentum and magnetic flux on the Sun, but behaviour in the upper chromosphere, where magnetism dominates, was uncertain. The team used twenty-seven years of full-disk radio images at 17 gigahertz from the Nobeyama Radioheliograph.

They find a poleward pattern about three thousand kilometres up, with speeds that mirror the known surface circulation and vary with the solar cycle. Bright radio features track poleward magnetic flux closely. The authors read this as first evidence that flows seen at radio heights reflect deeper circulation, in line with a magnetic tree picture.
arxiv-2605-02147:
Vincent Pacelli, Akash Ratheesh, and Evangelos Theodorou improve sampling-based control for nonlinear robots by using optimal transport. Methods such as MPPI and cross-entropy sampling are vital where dynamics jump and gradients fail. But their information-based goals ignore the geometry of the cost landscape, which can cause mode averaging when good solutions split into separate clusters.

Their method, OT-MPC, couples candidate control sequences to low-cost proposals through an entropy-regularised transport plan. That refines candidates toward nearby good samples while keeping coverage of the solution space across the group. Updates are closed-form and gradient-free via the Sinkhorn algorithm, allowing real-time use. Tests cover navigation, manipulation, and locomotion tasks.
arxiv-2605-02347:
Lukas Rustler and Matej Hoffmann present ShapeGrasp, a robot grasping method that completes an object's shape while it grasps, as humans do with touch. People combine a first visual estimate with tactile and body feedback during contact. ShapeGrasp couples visuo-haptic shape completion, building a full 3D shape from partial data, with physics-based grasp planning in an iterative loop.

From one RGB-D view it infers a complete shape, generates candidate grasps by rigid-body simulation, and executes the best feasible grasp. Each attempt adds constraints from tactile contacts and gripper occupancy, which update the shape. Failures trigger pose re-estimation and regrasping with the refined shape. Real-world tests use two robots and grippers.
arxiv-2605-02447:
Maoheng Li and five co-authors build a system to detect sarcasm when words and nonverbal cues point in opposite ways. Sarcasm is hard for machines because the text may sound warm while a face or voice shows the reverse. Past systems often mixed the two streams late and in a uniform way, which can blur the clash that marks sarcasm.

Their model, PC-MNet, checks fit at two levels and lets a polarity signal steer attention. A routing step fuses only the most useful evidence, guided by a prior graph and by training that stresses contrast. On the MUStARD bench and on balanced versions built to cut false cues, the system beat the strongest prior multimodal baseline on a key score.
arxiv-2605-02647:
Mario Rodríguez Béjar and three co-authors present ContextualJailbreak, an automated red-teaming method that attacks language models through staged conversation. Single prompts can be blocked by safety training, but earlier turns can quietly prime a model toward compliance. Hand-built multi-turn setups beat single-turn tricks, yet automated search had mostly stayed single-turn.

Their method runs evolutionary search over a simulated primed dialogue, in black-box fashion. A graded harm score from a two-level judge guides the search, so partly harmful replies steer the next step instead of being discarded. Five meaning-based mutation moves reshape the dialogue, covering roleplay, scenario, expansion, troubleshooting, and mechanism angles. The work is defensive in aim: mapping which priming forms work helps builders close them.
arxiv-2605-02747:
Alexandros Eskenazis, Apostolos Giannopoulos, and Natalia Tziotziou tackle two geometric problems about log-concave measures, a broad class of probability laws with a convex log-density. One is a dimensional form of the Brunn-Minkowski inequality, which bounds the measure of a blend of two sets by the measures of the parts. The other asks how large the perimeter of such a measure can be in the isotropic, standardized case.

For symmetric convex sets and even measures, the authors prove the dimensional inequality with an explicit, if small, exponent, using diffusion operators and gradient bounds. For the perimeter problem, they show the maximum grows on the order of the dimension itself. A shared ingredient is a known gradient bound for isotropic log-concave laws. Further uses cover projections, moments, and surface measures.
arxiv-2605-03147:
Rasmus T. Aavang, Rasmus Tjalk-Bøggild, Alexandre Iolov, Giovanni Rizzi, Mike Zhang, and Johannes Bjerva study how to pull performance indicators from earnings calls. Unlike templated SEC filings, calls are unlabeled, unstructured, and conversational, so models trained on filings face a hard domain shift.

The team introduces three benchmarks, including an earnings call set and an expert-annotated subset, and finds encoder models struggle with that shift. They then propose a language-model system for open-ended extraction from call transcripts. Human checks gave strong precision, setting a baseline for tracking emerging indicators over time.
arxiv-2605-03247:
Wenshuo Wang and Fan Zhang propose posterior-first simulation for neural solvers of partial differential equations that see only one field at deployment. A single snapshot can hide which underlying problem state produced it, and a direct field-to-future model collapses that ambiguity into one guess, harming rollouts.

Their method first infers a probability distribution over the smallest sufficient hidden state, then predicts from that distribution. Theory ties the target, learning rule, and failure mode together, with scores that make the posterior learnable. On hidden-metadata PDEBench tasks, rollout error fell markedly, closing much of the gap to an oracle.
arxiv-2605-03547:
JuneHyoung Kwon, JungMin Yun, and YoungBin Kim introduce CoVUBench, a benchmark for copyright unlearning in vision-language models. It tests whether such models can truly forget protected visual content. Models trained on web data can memorize characters and logos. Unlearning promises removal after training, but multimodal erasure is hard to test robustly.

The benchmark uses legally safe synthetic data. Visual variations in composition and domain test whether forgetting generalizes. It scores both erasure strength, from the rights holder's view, and retained utility, from the deployer's view. That trade-off measurement gives a standard tool for responsible unlearning research.
arxiv-2605-04047:
Priyam Srivastava and eight co-authors compare two entanglement swapping disciplines for quantum repeater chains that distribute key material for quantum key distribution. Repeaters join short entangled links into long ones by swapping, but stored pairs lose fidelity while waiting, so swap timing affects the secret-key rate. Both schemes studied use the same reinforcement-learned link controllers, isolating the scheduling effect on a simulated four-hop chain.

The sequential scheme builds and stores partial chains, while the synchronized one waits until all links are ready before swapping. When stored pairs cannot keep enough fidelity for even one time step, the sequential scheme produced no key while synchronized retained a small rate. Once sequential becomes viable, it outperforms synchronized by up to about nineteen percent in homogeneous chains, with the advantage shrinking as memory lifetime grows.
arxiv-2605-04247:
Paula Pacheco, Pablo Granitto, and Juan B. Cabral work on spectral unmixing, the task of working out which materials are present in each pixel of an image taken from above. A simple linear model works well until light scatters more than once, which breaks its assumptions.

Their method decides, pixel by pixel and from physical cues in the data, whether the harder nonlinear treatment is truly needed there. It blends three nonlinear models through a learned weighting and produces maps that show which regime each pixel falls in. Tests on three standard scenes beat the baselines they compare against.
arxiv-2605-04747:
Leon Witt and four co-authors design a way to pay federated learning participants fairly for their contributions without any ground truth to check against. In federated learning, many clients train a shared model on their own data. Rewarding honest, useful work normally requires a public test set. It can also require knowledge of the data distribution.

Their knowledge-free correlated agreement mechanism is provably strictly truthful when an honest majority holds, fixing a label-flipping vulnerability in an earlier agreement scheme. They test it on federated tuning of language model adapters. They also test it on a real printed-circuit-board inspection task. Rewards can be computed efficiently in real time. That suits decentralised and blockchain-based incentive designs.
arxiv-2605-04847:
Soyoung Park, Hwanjun Song, and Sungsu Lim tackle uncertainty estimates for graph neural networks, which predict from data linked in a network. Honest error ranges matter in high-stakes uses, but graph message passing breaks assumptions that standard methods rely on. Fixes often need costly resampling or extra calibration after training.

Their framework, QpiGNN, gives predictions and uncertainty through two separate heads trained together with a new loss. It needs no quantile inputs and no post-processing, yet carries guarantees on coverage and near-best interval width. Across nineteen benchmarks it gave higher coverage with intervals about half as wide as baselines, while staying robust to noise.
arxiv-2605-04947:
Alexander Lauer and three co-authors shrink the structures used to analyse conflicts between graph transformation rules. Conflict analysis shows how rules can interfere, based on critical pairs in minimal contexts. The essential information about a conflict, though, sits in much smaller structures called essences, first developed for simpler rule conditions.

The authors extend disabling essences to rules with arbitrary nested application conditions, not just one normal form. From them they build symbolic conflict essences capturing how two rules interact. They prove a transformation pair is dependent exactly when such an essence embeds in it, and they relate essences to the established notion of initial conflicts.
arxiv-2605-05047:
Pablo Concha-Vega defines a local update rule for two-coloured graphs, inspired by adaptive networks and the pull toward similarity called homophily. Under the rule, each vertex takes the majority colour of its neighbours, then links to same-coloured neighbours and unlinks from opposite ones. The question is whether a given pair of vertices ends up connected after repeated updates.

Concha-Vega shows the rule can simulate Boolean circuits step by step. Using that simulation, he establishes that deciding whether a given pair becomes connected is P-complete under logspace reductions. The result places this simple social-style dynamics among the hardest problems solvable in polynomial time.
arxiv-2605-05547:
Brazil's Atlantic Forest is a biodiversity hotspot where only a small share of the original cover survives. Alice Heiman asks whether satellite-based AI embeddings can track how well cleared land is being restored. Ground reporting cannot scale to thousands of sites, and common vegetation indices saturate before young forest matures.

Heiman studied over seventeen hundred restoration sites in São Paulo using AlphaEarth embeddings. She defines success by similarity to mature secondary forest, a reference trajectory in embedding space. Sites clustered clearly by land use, and some showed clean change signals, though the embeddings still miss some site details.
arxiv-2605-05647:
The stationary Navier-Stokes equations describe fluid at rest under steady forcing, and Liouville theorems say when only the trivial flow can exist. Gastón Vergara-Hermosilla proves such a result using a condition on just one part of the velocity: its radial component. Classical results demand decay or integrability of the whole field.

He shows any finite-energy solution is trivial when the radial component lies in a certain Lebesgue space, with the exponent between three halves and three. A second result works in variable-exponent spaces, needing the condition only on a bounded region. Rigidity, it turns out, can be driven by localized information.
arxiv-2605-05947:
Motoi Endo and Takumu Yamanaka investigate how light dark matter could be made by kaons in the early universe. Their setting is freeze-in, where dark matter builds up slowly through rare interactions, inside a cosmos that reheated to a low temperature. The link runs through a flavor changing interaction between strange and down quarks and dark matter particles.

Below the QCD crossover, kaon decays and scatterings set the dark matter abundance the authors compute. The same interaction also drives rare kaon decays that experiments such as NA62 and KOTO can search for. Lower reheating temperatures demand larger couplings, they find. That makes this dark matter story testable at rare kaon decay experiments, including the planned KOTO II.
arxiv-2605-06047:
Duong Nguyen, Mohammed Jawhar, and Nicolas Chesneau adapt tabular foundation models to new tasks without touching their weights. These models predict well on tables with no training, through in-context learning, but their built in biases stay fixed. Full fine tuning is costly, and lighter weight tuning must be refitted to each model's inner design.

Their adapter, TFM-Retouche, learns a small correction in the input space instead, so it works with any frozen backbone. Training runs end to end through the frozen model, and a guard falls back to the plain model when adaptation does not help on held out data. On a 51 data set benchmark, the adapted model topped the leaderboard and gained 56 Elo points.
arxiv-2605-06147:
Matthew Debono, Jackson Levi Said, and Gabriel Farrugia explore a generalized Brans-Dicke theory as a route to dynamical dark energy. The standard cosmic model faces tensions with precision data, hinting that dark energy may change over time. Their version couples a scalar field to gravity in a non minimal way and gives that field a non canonical kinetic term.

They recast the field equations as an autonomous dynamical system and study its equilibrium states and their stability. Three widely used potentials, constant, power law, and exponential, each yield solutions that match the standard model at background level. The behavior still differs noticeably from other scalar tensor models, a direct effect of the coupling and the unusual kinetic term.
arxiv-2605-06347:
Xuening Wu and seven co-authors model humans and language models as one coupled dynamical system that can collapse epistemically. People increasingly lean on AI to generate, summarize, and reason, while models retrain on the resulting flood of AI shaped text. Past work studied human cognitive offloading and model collapse separately, and this paper joins them into a single feedback loop with three variables: human cognition, data quality, and model capability.

Analysis of the minimal model reveals three regimes. Systems can settle into co-evolutionary enhancement, a fragile equilibrium, or degenerative convergence toward a narrow, low diversity state. Simulations show heavier reliance on AI can tip the loop into that poor equilibrium. In information terms, the loop develops a bottleneck where falling entropy means lost diversity rather than useful compression.
arxiv-2605-06647:
Zeyu Yang, Xu Han, Qi Ma, Jason Chen, and Anshumali Shrivastava present SIRA, a retrieval agent designed to search like an expert instead of a newcomer. Retrieval-augmented agents usually issue exploratory queries, skim snippets, and reformulate for many rounds, wasting time and missing evidence. SIRA instead asks which terms separate wanted evidence from similar-looking confusers in the whole corpus.

Offline, a model enriches documents with missing search vocabulary; at query time it predicts evidence terms the query omits, then filters them with corpus statistics. One weighted BM25 search finishes the job. Across ten BEIR benchmarks SIRA leads the comparison without relevance labels, and a new hard Wikipedia benchmark shows it beating multi-round commercial agents.
arxiv-2605-06847:
BoRui Li, Bofan Yu, and Xing-Dong Yang study how people feel about privacy inside sensor-filled smart car cabins. As cabins gain cameras and other sensors, they become smart environments shared by owners and temporary users such as family, friends, or renters, whose privacy expectations may differ. Semi-structured interviews with eighteen participants surface the factors shaping each group's views.

Some factors influence owners and non-owners alike, while others weigh much more heavily on one group. From those patterns the authors draw design implications for balancing the needs of multiple stakeholders in one shared cabin. The study gives car interface designers an early map of a privacy problem that grows as sensing spreads.
arxiv-2605-06947:
Chenhui Xu and four co-authors tackle a hard problem in 3D generation: making brick structures that actually stand up. Earlier systems checked each brick with an outside physics simulator and rolled back bad placements. That checking made generation slow and clumsy.

Xu and colleagues instead train the model with reinforcement learning, using rewards at the level of the whole structure. The rewards favor avoiding collisions, keeping the build connected, interlocking bricks, and matching the target shape. The trained model then generates stable structures in one pass, with no rollback, and the authors report top quality at much faster speeds.
arxiv-2605-07147:
MathlibPR is a benchmark from Zixuan Xie, Xinyu Liu, and Shangtong Zhang for judging whether language models can review math library contributions. Mathlib, the shared Lean mathematics library, grows through pull requests that human reviewers must check against conventions. That review step has become a bottleneck for the whole ecosystem.

The benchmark is built from real pull request histories, with a staged protocol for judging merge readiness. Tested models and coding agents both struggled to tell truly merge-ready requests from ones that merely built successfully. The authors hope such data can train reviewer assistants and steer models toward contributions maintainers would actually accept.
arxiv-2605-07647:
Abigail Victoria Gurin Schleifer and four co-authors examine automated scoring of short student answers, now often done by large language models with a few examples rather than fine-tuned graders. The risk sits in the middle of the quality range: partly correct answers need nuanced judgment, and errors there could unfairly penalize students whose understanding is still developing.

They compared three few-shot language models, a fine-tuned encoder, and a human expert on hundreds of biology answers. All AI systems degraded sharply on mid-range responses, while handling clear right and wrong answers well. The degradation shrank as task-specific adaptation increased, with the fine-tuned encoder best. Human agreement stayed highest and stable across the whole quality spectrum.
arxiv-2605-07847:
Shuhaib Mehri and six co-authors measure how closely AI user simulators imitate real people. Simulators are used more and more to train and evaluate assistants, and they are trained to sound human. But whether they reproduce the broad, varied distribution of real user behavior was an open question.

Their method extracts behavior profiles from real and simulated conversations, clusters them into discrete distributions, and computes gaps between them, checked by a human study. Evaluating twenty-four simulators on coding and writing tasks revealed a large gap from real users that varied by model family, scale, and behavioral facet. Most simulators resembled each other; combining behaviorally matching ones matched real users better than either alone. A word analysis of the clusters exposed which behaviors they capture, miss, and invent.
arxiv-2605-08247:
Andrea Valenzuela Ramirez, Cristian Gutierrez-Gomez, Marta Barroso, Dario Garcia-Gasulla, and coauthors teach a language model to translate between compiler intermediate languages. GCC and LLVM dominate modern toolchains but use different internal representations, which blocks reuse of frontends, backends, and optimization passes across ecosystems. Rule-based translators exist but are costly to build and maintain.

The team fine-tunes a fourteen billion parameter transformer, IRIS-14B, to translate GCC's GIMPLE into the LLVM representation, learning the mapping from examples. A data-driven translator could lower the barrier between the two ecosystems and let tools and optimizations travel across languages and compilers more freely.
arxiv-2605-08547:
Mikhail Nesterenko and Joseph Oglio present QUANTAS 2, a tool for testing distributed algorithms and measuring their performance. The first version ran abstract round based trials that kept results free of one machine or network setup. The new version adds a concrete mode where the same code runs over real sockets on one or many computers.

A reusable fault interface lets researchers inject crash, lying, and selfish behavior without rewriting the algorithm under test. Trials cover blockchains, agreement methods, hash tables, and data links in both modes. Distributed systems researchers gain one compact platform for quick exploration, real checks, and hostile fault tests side by side.
arxiv-2605-08647:
Aritra Mazumder and twelve coauthors build AgentCollabBench, a diagnostic test for failures that hide inside multi agent teamwork. A final answer can look right while an agent quietly dropped a constraint upstream, and outcome only grading never sees the damage. Their nine hundred human checked tasks span software, operations, and data work, each isolating one of four risks.

The risks cover constraints fading under peer pressure, falsehoods spreading by consensus, information leaking between tasks, and marked data failing to reach the end. Four leading models show distinct weakness profiles, and network shape explains much of the loss, especially where branches merge. Multi agent design emerges as a structural reliability problem, not just a model quality one.
arxiv-2605-09147:
Matthias Schöffel and co-author Esteban Garces Arias compare ways to tag parts of speech in medieval Romance texts, a job made hard by shifting spelling, rich word forms, and scarce labeled data. Their 2026 study covers medieval Occitan, Catalan, and French, and pits older rule-based and statistical taggers against modern open language models. Settings include prompting with no examples, prompting with a few, single-language tuning, and transfer across languages.

Across historically grounded datasets, the language model approaches beat the older taggers, with fine-tuning and multilingual training giving the largest gains. Transfer across languages helps under-resourced varieties a lot, and focused two-language training can beat broader mixes for some targets. The authors stress that closeness between languages and dataset traits shape what works best. They release code, models, and processed datasets, giving digital humanities scholars a practical guide for tagging old texts.
arxiv-2605-09247:
Avalos and two colleagues test a shallow restricted Boltzmann machine on a one dimensional ℤ2 Bose-Hubbard chain at half filling under a hard core adiabatic limit. They use variational Monte Carlo with the machine as the ansatz, comparing the neural quantum state against the established adiabatic description. The study targets the chain's ground state and phase diagram as seen through magnetization observables.

The variational results recover the broad shape of the phase diagram, distinguishing polarized and Néel ordered regions. They also recover typical spin patterns and site fillings for staggered insulating setups chosen by a weak symmetry breaking field. Overall, the results show a shallow restricted Boltzmann machine recovers the main adiabatic phase structure and the chosen symmetry broken insulating patterns at half filling. The work supports shallow neural quantum states as a workable tool for one dimensional quantum chains in this hard core regime.
arxiv-2605-09447:
Liu addresses the controllability of a class of quasilinear parabolic equations with multiplicative mobile controls. To prove a control exists that forces the solution to rest at time T greater than 0, he first establishes how solutions decay for the uncontrolled system. Unlike the linear heat equation, the nonlinear leading term brings major challenges.

Those hurdles demand a novel approach, leading Liu to settle the controllability problem in the standard solutions setting. Through a neatly built smooth shift, he shows that a multiplicative control exists bringing the state exactly to rest by time t equals T.
arxiv-2605-09747:
Angelis and Bramoullé used network theory to open up the matching function, the black box linking job seekers and vacancies in labor economics. They traced matching properties to granular connections between applicants and vacancies, unifying scattered literature by recovering several functional forms, including the CES form, as special cases. A testable condition says when matching in a broad network class behaves as if CES, up to a first-order approximation.

Their theory of match efficacy puts inequality in search intensity at the center: dispersion of search effort on either side of the market hurts matching. Strikingly, a rise in mean search intensity can reduce efficacy when it comes with a higher Gini coefficient of intensities. More average effort, unevenly spread, can make matching worse.
arxiv-2605-09847:
