The team built a test based on the Folin Ciocalteu colour method. Roots were extracted in an acetone and water mix. Best settings used thirty minutes and a wavelength of 760 nanometres. The reference compound was pyrogallol. Checks showed the method was straight, precise, and repeatable. It also held up under small changes in conditions. The work gives makers a tool to prove each batch holds the same phenol content. That step is needed before any safe product can return.
europmc-pmc6297847:
Van Dyken and Lacoste review how metabolic syndrome harms the blood-brain barrier. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Metabolic syndrome groups obesity, diabetes, and related ills. It drives inflammation across the whole body. The blood-brain barrier guards the brain from toxins and germs. It also controls what reaches nerve cells.

The authors explain how obesity and diabetes loosen this guard wall. Leaks let immune cells and waste build up in the brain. Leptin and insulin resistance play a part in the damage. The review maps the signals and cell paths involved. It also links barrier failure to diseases like Alzheimer's. Gut microbes and brain inflammation get a closing look. The piece shows why body-wide ills reach the brain.
europmc-pmc6323947:
Kriventseva and co-authors present OrthoDB version 10, a catalogue of ortholog groups. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Orthologs are genes descended from one shared gene. They often keep that gene's function. This update greatly widens species coverage. It samples 1,271 eukaryote and 6,013 prokaryote species. Virus coverage reaches 6,488 genomes.

Groups are sorted by how close species are. Closer species get finer detail. Notes on gene roles come from many sources. Each group also gets computed notes on its past. Registered users can test gene set completeness online. Their own data can be mapped to the catalogue. Downloads and code access are offered too. The resource narrows guesses about gene roles.
europmc-pmc6362447:
Signer and co-authors present a software article in Ecology and Evolution. They introduce amt, an R package for working with animal tracking data. Tracking devices now produce huge location datasets, and researchers need shared tools to manage and analyze them.

The package centers on step-selection functions, which compare real animal steps with random ones. That approach links habitat features to movement choices. The package also handles data cleaning, exploratory plots, home-range estimates, and simulation from fitted models. A fisher dataset serves as the worked example, shown in four steps. The authors aim to give movement ecologists one open workflow instead of scattered scripts.
europmc-pmc6364647:
Marr and co-authors present an essay in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface. They weigh a dispute about damp air and flu. Some studies say one form of humidity, called absolute, drives flu patterns. Marr's team argues that the other form, relative humidity, plus heat explains the same data just as well.

They recheck past work on virus survival in fine droplets, spread in animals, and flu rates in people. Warm air can hold more water, so absolute humidity rises and falls with heat. That link can hide the true cause. They give a physical account based on how droplets dry out and change as they shrink. On their view, relative humidity is the more likely driver of virus survival and flu spread.
europmc-pmc6439147:
Miranda-Mendizabal and co-authors synthesize longitudinal studies on gender differences in suicidal behavior among people aged 12 to 26. Five databases were searched to January 2017, and 67 population-based studies met the criteria. Suicide is the second leading cause of death worldwide at ages 15 to 29, so the patterns matter for prevention.

Females attempted suicide more often (odds ratio 1.96), while males died by suicide far more (hazard ratio 2.50). Prior mental or substance disorders and exposure to interpersonal violence raised risk for both sexes. Female-specific factors included eating disorders and dating violence; male-specific ones included conduct problems, hopelessness, and access to means. Almost no evidence covered female suicide death.
europmc-pmc6446947:
Zhang and co-authors survey mRNA vaccines for infectious diseases. The platform moved from concept to human trials within two decades of RNA research. Early and clinical work shows these vaccines can raise safe, long-lasting immunity. They can also be made fast, since production does not depend on growing pathogens.

Design sections cover how the message is built, capped, and tweaked so cells read it strongly without too much innate alarm. Delivery systems that carry the message into cells get their own treatment. Trial results across diseases are weighed. The authors close on better stability, targeting, and scale, which would widen use, with future roles against cancer and allergens.
europmc-pmc6682547:
Swarbrick and co-authors systematically review microRNAs as biomarkers in Alzheimer's disease. Their review appears in Molecular Neurobiology. Small non-coding RNAs are deregulated in patients' blood. The reviewers extracted every significantly deregulated blood microRNA. They cross-referenced these against brain changes at Braak stage III. The overlap yielded a panel of ten microRNAs. Names include mir-107, mir-146a, and mir-125b. The panel may shift early in disease. That could be twenty years before symptoms.

Network analysis mapped the panel's associations. Immune function and cell cycle regulation featured. Stress responses and Wnt signalling also appeared. Cellular senescence and Rho GTPases completed the list. Early blood biomarkers remain an urgent need.
europmc-pmc6743147:
Crooke and co-authors review immunosenescence, the aging of the immune system, and what it means for vaccines. As immunity declines and falls out of tune with age, older adults catch infections more easily. Their vaccine responses also weaken. Yet direct links between cell changes and clinical outcomes remain scarce.

Known shifts in T and B lymphocyte numbers and function are well described. The review covers diseases that hit older adults hardest, including influenza and respiratory syncytial virus. It then surveys vaccines and boosters designed for older immune systems. Two vaccines draw notably strong responses, though why is poorly understood. Better designs aim to protect a growing elderly population.
europmc-pmc6827047:
Braicu and co-authors review the MAPK pathway as a cancer drug target, in Cancers. MAPK is a chain of proteins that carries signals from outside a cell to its core. It helps decide whether the cell grows, divides, or dies. Changes in this chain are common in cancer. Blocking it is already part of some treatments.

The review maps the pathway's branches and how each is switched on. It covers drugs aimed at links such as BRAF and ERK, and where they work. Tumours often escape by waking a side route, so the authors stress paired drugs. They close with open questions on resistance and patient selection.
europmc-pmc6835347:
Dabeek and Marra review two plant compounds in the journal Nutrients. Quercetin and kaempferol are polyphenols found across fruits and vegetables. Eating more produce is tied to lower heart disease risk. Whether these two compounds explain part of that benefit depends on how much the body actually absorbs. In plants they mostly ride attached to sugars.

The review compares food sources by absorbed dose rather than content alone. Onion forms joined to glucose seem to be absorbed best. Once taken up, both compounds are changed quickly in the liver. Human studies of heart outcomes are then weighed. The evidence, the authors find, is suggestive but still thin.
europmc-pmc6857047:
He and co-authors report a study in Theranostics on how ovarian cancer spreads. Spread needs new blood vessels, which feed the tumour and give it routes out. Cancer cells send messages in exosomes, tiny parcels shed into fluids. The parcels here carried a small RNA, miR-205. Levels of it ran high in ovarian tumours with dense vessel growth.

The team showed ovarian cancer exosomes deliver miR-205 into vessel-lining cells. Inside, it silenced PTEN, a gene that normally restrains growth signals. Freed from that brake, the vessel cells built new tubes faster. In animal models the parcels sped vessel formation and tumour spread. Blocking uptake blunted the effect. The authors propose this parcel traffic as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc6877647:
Mao and co-authors report a study in Nature Communications on a chemical mark inside gene messages. The mark, m6A, decorates messenger RNAs. About 35 percent of its sites sit in the coding region, the part that is read to build protein. It was thought to slow that reading down. The team found the opposite can hold.

Marked coding regions did make ribosomes pause at certain codons. Yet stripping the marks lowered protein output further. The marks, it turns out, loosen tangled folds in the message, easing the ribosome's path. A reader protein with a helicase motor, YTHDC2, helps carry out this effect. The result reframes coding-region marks as aids to translation.
europmc-pmc6943047:
Howe and co-authors present the 2020 update of Ensembl Genomes, a resource for species outside the vertebrates. Their article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The site gathers genome-scale data for bacteria, protists, fungi, plants, and invertebrate animals. It mirrors the main Ensembl platform, with updates four times a year.

Users get reference sequences, gene models, expression data, and variation records for each species. Comparative tools show which genes match across species, as orthologues or paralogues. Recent work has made those gene family sets more robust and repeatable. Plant pages gained richer views of gene expression and function. Deeper links with the main Ensembl project, the authors say, will help handle the flood of new genomes.
europmc-pmc6946647:
Li and co-authors review genome editing as a tool for treating human disease. Their review appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Editing tools can target and modify DNA directly in nearly all cell types. That power improved disease models and opened new routes to therapy.

Three main platforms lead the field. Zinc-finger nucleases and TALENs came first, followed by CRISPR-Cas systems. Each uses a programmable cutter to change a chosen stretch of DNA. The authors track how tools derived from them are used in cells and animal models of disease. They also survey clinical trials now applying editing to patients. Remaining challenges, from delivery to safety, get an honest closing look.
europmc-pmc6970947:
Ponti and co-authors review how imaging reveals body composition changes with age. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology. Aging brings total fat gain, loss of lean muscle and bone, and fat shifting toward the trunk. Fat also creeps into organs such as liver and muscle. Simple measures like body mass index miss that redistribution.

These shifts raise the risk of heart disease, diabetes, muscle wasting, and weak bones, and can lead to disability. The authors argue that detailed scans deserve a central role in care of older people. Computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, and ultrasound each measure fat, muscle, and bone with far greater accuracy. Tracking the balance among the three, they say, supports personalised prevention of age-related disease.
europmc-pmc6990847:
Mullin and co-authors test a cough medicine, ambroxol, as a possible brain-protective drug in Parkinson disease. Their trial report appeared in JAMA Neurology. Mutations in the glucocerebrosidase gene are the strongest genetic risk factor for Parkinson disease. The faulty enzyme lets the protein alpha-synuclein build up in the brain.

Ambroxol is known to boost that enzyme. In this open-label trial, 17 patients took the drug, with and without the gene mutations. Ambroxol crossed into the brain and spinal fluid, engaged its target enzyme, and raised enzyme levels. Spinal fluid alpha-synuclein levels also rose, a sign of changed handling of the protein. The treatment was tolerated. The authors argue the results justify larger trials of ambroxol as a protective therapy for both patient groups.
europmc-pmc7065247:
Yang and co-authors introduce medical databases and data mining in the Journal of Evidence-Based Medicine. Healthcare now generates data at explosive speed, and buried in it lies knowledge that could guide care. Data mining searches large datasets for valuable patterns. It runs through preparation, mining itself, then expression and analysis of results. Databases are the organised stores that make such searching possible.

The review explains database technology as the science of structuring, storing, designing, managing, and applying databases, then introduces several medical databases and mining techniques in turn. Its audience is clinical researchers who sense the potential of big data but lack the technical background to use it. Worked areas include critical care, where risk models and treatment records pile up fastest. The authors' goal is practical literacy: enough understanding of the tools for clinicians to collaborate with data specialists and mine their own records well.
europmc-pmc7145647:
Urban and co-authors update PHI-base, the database of pathogen and host interactions, in Nucleic Acids Research. The database curates genes proven to change the outcome when a pathogen meets a host, drawn from peer-reviewed papers. Genes whose alteration made no difference are included too, for fair comparison. Viruses are excluded, being covered elsewhere.

Version 4.8, released in September 2019, holds 3,454 curated references covering 6,780 genes from 268 pathogens tested on 210 hosts in 13,801 interactions. Plants make up about 60% of hosts, split evenly between cereals and other plants. Information on pathogen effector proteins grew by more than a third, and crop pathogen entries rose sharply.
europmc-pmc7150947:
Ahmed, Quadeer, and McKay hunt for vaccine targets against the new coronavirus by reusing immune data from the 2003 SARS virus, in Viruses. The two viruses are close genetic relatives. The team screened experimentally confirmed B cell and T cell epitopes, the protein fragments the immune system recognises, from SARS-CoV's spike and nucleocapsid proteins.

A set of those fragments matched SARS-CoV-2 exactly. None had mutated among the 120 virus sequences available on 21 February 2020, so vaccines aiming at them might protect against the new virus too. Coverage analysis estimated which fragment sets would suit most people's immune types worldwide and in China. The screened list was offered to guide laboratory vaccine work.
europmc-pmc7170847:
Jiang and co-authors report a hybrid nanoparticle built to treat cancer with heat and iron-driven cell death. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The particle combines a light-absorbing polymer with an iron-chelating catalyst. Under near-infrared light it heats up and guides imaging of the tumor. Heat also speeds the chemical reaction that makes the treatment work.

That reaction produces hydroxyl radicals, which push cancer cells toward two forms of death, ferroptosis and apoptosis. After reacting, the particle shrinks from about 42 nanometers into tiny fragments. Smaller pieces can move through tumor tissue more easily. The authors present the design as a way to make iron-based cancer therapy stronger. Their tests point to imaging and treatment in a single agent.
europmc-pmc7231147:
Lyons and co-authors review breast milk as a source of helpful microbes for infants. Their article appeared in Nutrients. Breast milk gives complete nutrition plus many protective factors. Breastfed infants show better immune development and fewer gut diseases. They also die at lower rates than formula-fed infants. Milk was once thought sterile, its bacteria dismissed as contamination.

It is now accepted that milk carries its own microbiome. Those bacteria seed the infant gut and block harmful germs from attaching. Where the milk microbes come from remains an active question. Methods matter: different gene targets give different pictures of the community. The review gathers what is known about this living food. It argues that milk microbes are part of its protective design.
europmc-pmc7233447:
Simpson and co-authors present expert consensus language for reporting chest CT findings linked to COVID-19. Their document appeared in Radiology: Cardiothoracic Imaging. Routine CT screening for the disease was not recommended. Yet scans of suspected patients kept rising in number. Radiologists also faced incidental findings that might be COVID pneumonia.

The guidance sorts findings by how typical they are for this disease. It offers ready-made wording for each category. Unique codes in brackets allow later data mining of reports. The language avoids claiming an exact likelihood for any single scan. Probability depends on local prevalence and the patient's story. Three major radiology bodies endorsed the document. It aims to make reports consistent across hospitals during the emergency.
europmc-pmc7237447:
Asnicar and co-authors present PhyloPhlAn 3.0, a tool for placing microbial genomes on the tree of life. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Genomes from cultures and from metagenomes now arrive at a huge pace. Placing them correctly, from strain to phylum level, demands speed and precision. The new version builds species-level bins from over 230,000 public genomes.

It judges each genome against 400 optimized marker genes. Automatic checks drop genomes missing too many markers. Tests covered tens of thousands of assembled genomes from human and environmental samples. The method stayed accurate even for close relatives. Large microbiome projects can now sort their finds consistently. The authors offer the tool as shared infrastructure for a fast-growing field.
europmc-pmc7285147:
Kaźmierczak-Barańska and co-authors review the double nature of vitamin C, which can protect cells or push them toward damage. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Vitamin C is a familiar antioxidant that scavenges free radicals. Yet under some conditions it acts as a pro-oxidant, generating the very stress it usually fights.

The authors ask whether that second face is a flaw or a useful trait. They cover vitamin C in cancer prevention, where pro-oxidant action may harm tumor cells, and its role in keeping redox balance in the central nervous system. Evidence on oxidative DNA damage markers is weighed, along with studies suggesting vitamin C can protect tissue from radiation. The review maps where supplementation helps and where caution is due.
europmc-pmc7333347:
Zhang and Zhang review the role of T cells in fibrosis for Frontiers in Immunology. Fibrosis is the buildup of stiff connective tissue, heavy in collagen, that can wreck organs such as the liver, lungs, kidneys, and heart. It helps heal wounds, but when it runs on, it drives high rates of illness and death.

Macrophages have long been studied in this process; the two authors focus instead on T cells, the adaptive immune cells that learn to recognize targets. They walk through the main T cell types, from killer cells to regulator cells, and how each can push or restrain scarring. The receptor that lets T cells sense targets shapes which cells join the fight. Readers get a guide to an understudied side of fibrotic disease.
europmc-pmc7334447:
Zhang and co-authors argue in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that airborne spread drove COVID-19. They compared case trends and control measures in three early epicenters, including Wuhan and northern Italy, plus the United States. The question was which route, air, surfaces, or contact, best explained the curves.

Their analysis points to tiny airborne particles as the dominant and highly efficient route. Mandated face covering, they find, marks the turning point in each trend, cutting infections sharply. Distancing alone, as used in the United States, did not protect the public enough by itself. The authors close by urging that sound science guide pandemic policy. Mario Molina, a Nobel-winning chemist, is among the authors.
europmc-pmc7349647:
Buonfrate and co-authors present a prevalence study in Pathogens on a worm infection. The parasite is Strongyloides stercoralis, a neglected tropical disease threat. Older global counts ranged widely and rested on weak tests. The team set out to give a firmer world estimate.

The authors reviewed prevalence studies from 1990 to 2016 across endemic countries. They adjusted each result for the test used and for age. A statistical model then filled gaps for countries with no data. They estimate a global prevalence of about 8 percent for 2017. That equals roughly 614 million people infected. South-East Asia, Africa, and the Western Pacific held most cases. Readers get country-level numbers to guide mass drug campaigns.
europmc-pmc7356147:
Tornesello and co-authors review antimicrobial peptides as cancer drugs in Molecules. These small molecules are part of the innate immune defense in many organisms, where they kill bacteria, viruses, and fungi. Many carry a positive charge that lets them latch onto negatively charged cell surfaces.

Cancer cells expose a negative fat, phosphatidylserine, on their outer surface, which healthy cells keep hidden. Charged peptides can therefore strike cancer membranes selectively. Some peptides, such as LTX-315, also wreck inner cell structures so tumor antigens spill out and alarm the immune system. The review covers how the peptides work and strategies to turn them into usable drugs, alone or in combination. A real medical need drives the search.
europmc-pmc7394547:
Lendner and co-authors hunt for a brain signal that tracks arousal across sleep and anesthesia, in eLife. Deep sleep and propofol anesthesia show slow synchronized brain waves, but REM sleep, also a low-arousal state, looks wake-like. Something other than wave synchrony must mark how aroused the brain is.

Across four independent datasets, with recordings from inside and on the scalp, one feature separated wakefulness from every low state: the slope of the spectrum's background, its 1/f fall-off. The slope alone could tell wakefulness from REM sleep. A common marker for reduced arousal, they conclude, hides in the brain's non-rhythmic activity. Such a marker could guide anesthesia depth and sleep science alike.
europmc-pmc7413047:
Tang and co-authors review the evidence for aerosol transmission of SARS-CoV-2 in Environment International. By August 2020 confirmed cases had passed 20 million worldwide. Most official guidance named droplets, contact, and surfaces as the routes, while China also listed the airborne route.

Growing evidence, the authors argue, makes aerosol spread plausible under favorable conditions: confined spaces, poor ventilation, and long exposure to concentrated aerosols. The World Health Organization had begun acknowledging that route, especially indoors. The review weighs laboratory, outbreak, and modeling evidence, then turns to prevention and control, from ventilation to masks. Readers get a careful mid-2020 brief on the pandemic's most contested transmission question.
europmc-pmc7419547:
Huang and co-authors review targeted drugs for hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer. For a decade sorafenib was the chief drug, and many new drugs failed to beat it. That changed when lenvatinib proved at least as good in trials.

The review then covers second-line drugs such as regorafenib, cabozantinib, and ramucirumab. Immune checkpoint drugs get close attention for their strong effect. The authors also weigh paired treatments, such as drugs that block blood vessel growth plus immune drugs. Other pairs join targeted drugs with surgery or local treatments. A final thread is drug resistance and the search for new agents. The piece gives a clear map of a fast-moving field.
europmc-pmc7426847:
Zhang and co-authors report a catalyst that speeds water oxidation, the slow step in splitting water for fuel. High-valence metal sites can drive the reaction fast, but they are hard to form. The team worked with a film of iron, cobalt, chromium, and nickel alloy.

On the film surface, a rebuilt oxyhydroxide layer forms during use. Iron helps nickel climb to the rare Ni4+ state in steps. That state pushes holes into oxygen atoms and wakes lattice oxygen for the reaction. Iron-nickel pairs then act as the true active sites. The catalyst reached high mass activity and turnover at an overpotential of 300 mV in alkaline solution. Spectroscopy and theory together explain how the sites form and work.
europmc-pmc7444947:
Futoma and co-authors argue that machine learning in health care is judged by the wrong standard. Teams often demand that a model work everywhere at once. The authors call that broad generalisability a myth that can block useful tools.

A model built for one hospital or one task may help at that bedside even if it fails elsewhere. Chasing universal performance can hide those local gains. The authors urge wider tests of value: does the tool help real care, in a real setting, for real patients? They set out paths beyond generalisability, such as local checks and clear limits of use. The piece reframes how clinical machine learning should be judged and adopted.
europmc-pmc7571347:
James and co-authors estimate the global burden of falls from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017. Falls can cause severe health loss and death. Past work showed they matter across all ages.

Estimates cover 195 countries and territories from 1990 to 2017. Age-standardised incidence was 2238 per 100,000 in 2017. That rate fell by 3.7% since 1990. Age-standardised mortality was 9.2 per 100,000 people. That equaled 695,771 deaths in that year. Falls caused 35,940,787 disability-adjusted life-years in total. Fractures of the lower leg or ankle were most common. The authors call for more prevention and care access.
europmc-pmc7582347:
Lee, Cha and Lee review antioxidant protection in the brain. The brain is prone to oxidative harm for several reasons. It is rich in lipids and uses much energy.

Its antioxidant capacity is weak compared with other tissues. Reactive oxygen species can damage neurons and impair function. Metals overload can also raise oxidative stress in the brain. The review covers enzyme and non-enzyme defenses in depth. It weighs benefits and method issues for candidate compounds. Trials in brain disorders are assessed for neuroprotection. Courses for future antioxidant treatment are suggested. Readers get a broad guide to redox defense in the nervous system.
europmc-pmc7699647:
Savastano and co-authors study a SARS-CoV-2 protein that gathers into droplets with viral RNA. The protein is the nucleocapsid protein, which wraps the viral genome. It is made in large amounts in infected cells and boosts viral copying. The team used lab tests and cell imaging.

They show that RNA triggers the protein to split into liquid-like droplets, rich in RNA. These droplets pull in the viral copying machinery, which may speed viral RNA making. In cells, the protein also joins stress granules, like droplets that viruses exploit. Blocking droplet forming could stall a key step in viral growth.
europmc-pmc7790747:
Dasari and co-authors present a white paper on circulating tumor DNA in colorectal cancer. The paper comes from expert panels of the US National Cancer Institute. Blood tests can catch tumor DNA shed into circulation. Study results in this area are growing fast.

The panel focused on four uses with practice-changing potential. These are finding leftover disease after treatment and guiding rectal cancer care. Watching response to therapy is a third use. Tracking how tumor clones shift under targeted drugs is the fourth. General guidance for ctDNA research is also given. The goal is fast, sound entry of this testing into routine care.
europmc-pmc7834447:
Crommelin and co-authors address the cold storage problem of mRNA vaccines. mRNA vaccines led the late-stage race against COVID-19. Their weakness is keeping them stable. Deep freezing was the early answer.

The authors first list company storage plans from public sources. They cover the full supply chain. Next they review the science on mRNA product stability. Ways to harden the products are surveyed. Tests that track decay are covered too. Rules for product checks and storage are included. The authors say a systematic hunt for decay routes is missing. Better formulas should hold at fridge or room heat. They urge solving this before the next pandemic.
europmc-pmc7994447:
Wang and co-authors present a software framework called scGNN for single-cell RNA sequencing analysis. Such data reveal how tissues and diseases vary cell by cell. Two flaws dog the data: many values drop out, and gene patterns are tangled. The team built a deep learning system that treats cells as a network, letting each cell borrow strength from its neighbours.

The framework stacks three autoencoders that refine each other in rounds. A special statistical model handles the messy gene patterns. On four standard datasets, the tool beat rivals at filling in missing values and at grouping cells. The team then ran it on 13,214 single nuclei from the brains of Alzheimer's patients. It drew out disease-linked paths in nerve development. The authors offer the tool for general single-cell work.
europmc-pmc8050947:
Toelzer and co-authors find a fatty acid pocket that locks the SARS-CoV-2 spike shut. The spike trimer opens and closes to grab its host receptor. Drugs that freeze it closed could block infection. The team made spike protein in insect cells. Cryo-electron microscopy then revealed its structure at fine detail.

The closed form dominated their dataset. A molecule of linoleic acid, an essential fatty acid, sat in a pocket on each spike unit. That binding steadied the locked shape. A similar pocket appears in earlier dangerous coronaviruses. Past work had hinted at links between infection and fat metabolism. The authors suggest aiming drugs straight at the pocket. A small molecule wedged there could hold the spike shut. The virus would lose its key before reaching the door.
europmc-pmc8067447:
Yadav and co-authors review the proteins of SARS-CoV-2 and the drug targets they offer. The virus carries a positive-sense RNA genome of 26 to 32 kilobases. Its spike binds the human ACE2 receptor with 10 to 20 times the grip of the older SARS virus. Entry proteases then cut the spike to open the cell. Inside, two large polyproteins are translated first.

Those polyproteins are chopped into the working machinery of the virus. Its replicase copies the genome and prints nested sets of messages. Structural proteins then build new virus particles around fresh genomes. The review walks through each protein's job in that cycle. It sorts the best points of attack for drug design. Convalescent plasma therapy gets a section as well. Candidate vaccines close the survey of defenses.
europmc-pmc8211847:
Deng and co-authors map fibroblast diversity in fibrotic skin disease with single-cell RNA sequencing. Fibrotic skin disease burdens health care worldwide. Fibroblasts drive it by multiplying and laying down excess matrix.

Keloid, a model fibrotic disease, held four fibroblast subpopulations. They ranged from secretory types to a mesenchymal type. The mesenchymal share was far higher in keloid than in normal scar. The team probed what that group does in the tissue. The map gives drug work a sharper target. It also explains why one-size treatment fails. Keloid offered a clear test case for the approach.
europmc-pmc8282847:
Sanchez-Garcia and co-authors present DeepEMhancer, a deep learning tool for cryo-EM map clean-up. Cryo-EM maps guide protein model building. They lose contrast at fine detail, so they need sharpening first.

Standard fixes apply one global correction and miss local quality swings. DeepEMhancer learned from pairs of raw and model-sharpened maps. It now post-processes new maps on its own. Local detail improves without hand tuning. The tool aims to make maps easier to read at once. It serves the many labs that lack sharpening experts. Cleaner maps should mean better models.
europmc-pmc8310547:
Koppula, Zhuang, and Gan examine the cystine transporter SLC7A11 in cancer and therapy. The transporter imports cystine to build glutathione. Many cancers switch it to high levels.

High levels shield tumours from ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. That shield helps tumours grow. It also carries a steep metabolic cost. Such cancer cells grow dependent on glucose and glutamine. Those cravings are weaknesses therapy can target. The review maps both sides of the trait. It shows how one transporter can be armour and Achilles heel at once. Nutrient dependency is the cost side of the shield.
europmc-pmc8330547:
Dolina and co-authors review CD8 T cell exhaustion in cancer and its new picture. Tired T cells were once seen as one fading mass. Single-cell work has redrawn that view.

Exhausted cells form several linked subpopulations. Stem-like cells still answer checkpoint blockade. Terminally set cells do not. Each group lives in its own niches, in blood and tumour. Gene programmes govern moves between states. The review gathers the key findings behind the shift. It matters for therapy: only some tired cells can be revived. Drug design now chases the stem-like pool.
europmc-pmc8528847:
Wang and co-authors map the global prevalence of depression after childbirth. Postpartum depression is the most common mental condition after delivery. It can harm the social and thinking health of partners, babies, and children. A full world overview of its scale was still needed.

The final analysis held 565 studies from 80 countries or regions. Rates varied widely around the world. Southern Africa showed the highest rates, per the authors. Developed and high-income areas showed clearly lower rates. Study size and country development drove much of the spread. Many life factors mattered too, from partner support to money strain and life stress.
europmc-pmc8589647:
Han and co-authors examine brain aging in major depressive disorder using a large shared dataset. Depression links to brain shrinkage, age-linked disease, and early death. The team asked if the brains of depressed adults look older than their years. Data came from sites around the world in the ENIGMA group.

The team built an age model from brain scans of healthy adults. They then used it on scans from depressed adults and controls. On average, the depressed group showed a brain age gap of 1.08 years above controls. The gap did not track with relapse, drug use, age at onset, or symptom level. Readers get a careful test of a small but real brain aging signal.
europmc-pmc8707347:
Kowalczyk and co-authors review mitochondrial oxidative stress as a cause of disease and a target for therapy. Excess reactive oxygen species, paired with weak antioxidant defense, create this stress. Mitochondria are the main source of these free radicals. The radicals can damage DNA and other cell parts.

Damage can disrupt mitochondrial work and kill cells. Over time, this process feeds many disease states. The review spans cases from Alzheimer disease to autoimmune type 1 diabetes. It gathers the strongest evidence for each link. It then reviews attempts to treat disease by curbing oxidative stress. Antioxidant therapy gets a careful, mixed appraisal.
europmc-pmc8906647:
Richardson and co-authors use genetics to preview how lipid drugs ripple through human metabolism. Eight drug targets shape blood lipids. Some lower LDL cholesterol, others HDL or triglycerides. The team built genetic scores that mimic each drug. Mendelian randomization then estimated each target's effects. Blood data came from up to 115,082 UK Biobank participants. A panel of 249 metabolic traits was measured. Heart disease risk served as a check.

Most target scores cut coronary risk as expected. Targets aimed at the same lipid trait gave matching metabolic signatures. HMGCR and PCSK9 scores agreed closely. Targets from different classes diverged sharply. Triglyceride drugs hit an inflammation marker hard. LDL drugs barely touched it. The authors say such signatures can guide drug development. They may also help measure treatment response.
europmc-pmc8928147:
Kers and Saccenti ask which diversity metrics give microbiome studies real statistical power. Sequencing keeps getting cheaper. Bigger samples are now within reach. But the metric chosen can quietly decide the result. The team ran retrospective power calculations. They used animal data, human data, and simulated data. Many alpha and beta diversity metrics were compared. Each metric's effect on needed sample size was measured.

Beta diversity metrics proved most sensitive to group differences. Among them, Bray-Curtis usually needed the smallest samples. Alpha metrics varied with the data's structure. The authors warn of a trap. Trying metrics until one turns significant is p-value hacking. Sensitive metrics can also create publication bias. Their advice is firm. Plan the analysis before the experiment. Report several metrics, not the winning one. Power calculations should be routine.
europmc-pmc9005347:
Bellenguez and co-authors run a vast genome study to find new genetic roots of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Genes shape much of the risk for these diseases. The two-stage study pooled 111,326 cases with 677,663 controls. Proxy cases filled out the case count. The scan found 75 risk loci in total. Of those, 42 were new at the time. Pathway tests confirmed amyloid and tau routes. They also flagged microglia, the brain's immune cells.

Gene ranking inside the new loci named 31 genes. One fresh route ran through tumor necrosis factor alpha signaling. The team built a new genetic risk score as well. It predicted who would develop dementia later. It also predicted decline from mild impairment. The top tenth of scorers carried far higher risk than the bottom tenth. Age and the APOE gene still counted separately. The work widens the target list for drug hunters.
europmc-pmc9047147:
Velazquez-Meza and co-authors review antimicrobial resistance through the One Health lens, which joins human, animal, and environmental health. Resistance grows where antimicrobials are overused in medicine, farming, and livestock. Poor infection control, farm waste, and pollution then spread resistant bacteria widely. Movement of infected people and animals carries the problem further.

The review sorts out the actors and duties inside the One Health approach. Because resistance touches all three domains at once, no single sector can solve it alone. The authors argue for joint action on drug use, waste, and infection control.
europmc-pmc9267347:
Jones and co-authors estimate infectiousness across the full course of SARS-CoV-2 infection. They link viral load in patient samples with the chance of growing virus in cells. The data come mainly from Berlin, where about 400,000 people were tested from February 2020 to March 2021. About 6% tested positive, and 25,381 positives were studied in depth.

People became infectious within two days of infection. In hospital cases, peak viral load came one to three days before symptoms began. About 8% of positives had very high viral loads. Loads were about tenfold higher in people infected with the variant first found in the UK. Children had slightly lower loads than adults. Findings apply even to people with few or no symptoms.
europmc-pmc9307547:
Salminen and co-authors argue that sun-driven skin aging and normal aging share one engine: immune remodeling. Heavy ultraviolet exposure triggers skin inflammation and cell aging. The body counters with suppressive cells such as regulatory T cells. That suppression weakens effector cells and harms nearby tissue as a side effect.

The review compares this photoaging path with slow chronological aging. Both show chronic low-grade inflammation, dubbed inflammaging in the aging case. Both also build up suppressive activity that dulls immunity. The triggers differ, but the immune pattern looks much the same. Over 30 years ago, ultraviolet light was already known to block skin allergy responses. The authors say this shared frame can guide research on both processes.
europmc-pmc9434547:
Li and co-authors review lactate metabolism in human health and disease. Lactate was long seen as a waste product of sugar breakdown. Work on the Warburg effect in tumors changed that view. Lactate now looks like a signal that links cells, organs, and tissues.

The review covers how the body makes and clears lactate. It explains the lactate shuttle idea and energy roles. A newer thread is lactylation, a protein change first reported in 2019. That change bears on tumor growth, nerve activity, and inflammation. Later chapters trace lactate in wound healing and ischemic injury. Tumor spread, blood vessel growth, and tumor immunity get full sections. The authors aim to give future work a clear base map.
europmc-pmc9782747:
Arruda and co-authors compare two free tools that map the shape of a research field. Literature on any topic now grows too fast to grasp raw. Maps of citations show how papers, authors, and themes connect. Such maps guide reviews, hiring, and research plans.

VOSviewer draws network maps from citation data files. Bibliometrix runs a wider battery of bibliometric measures. Both are free, with donations accepted from users. The review walks through what each tool needs to run. Programming skill, data loading, and ease of use differ. Some analyses exist in only one of the two tools. Time trends and author index scores split the pair. Spreadsheet export and thesaurus building also differ. The authors help readers pick by task and skill. Their verdict rests on hands-on feature checks of both.
fbi-roswell-teletype-1947:
Dallas wired Washington the first federal word on Roswell on the night of July 8, 1947. The teletype from Percy Wyly, the FBI chief in Dallas, sends on the Eighth Air Force report of a found disc. The wire went out at 6:17 in the evening, as the tale broke.

Wyly tells that Wright Field has not yet backed the weather balloon line the Army would soon give out. The disc, by the wire, was on its way east for study. The brisk lines catch the case at its first hour, before the cover tale set. The teletype is the Roswell story's first paper trail.
frus-1861-d147:
William Dayton sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 August 1861. It is document 147 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A second report in one day points to more than one live thread in Paris. Dayton split his points as Seward split his orders. The letter adds depth to a crowded week in the French file of 1861. Threads in Paris ranged from cotton prices to the fate of ships in French yards. Each thread he held was thin alone and strong only in the whole weave.
frus-1861-d247:
Orders from Washington reached James Shepherd Pike in a State Department letter dated 15 August 1861. It stands as Document 247 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d47:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 May 1861, the same day Seward wrote to him. It is document 47 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The two men wrote past each other across the ocean, each unaware of the other's page. Adams reported his first dealings in London while Seward drafted stern orders at home. The matched date shows how wide the gap was between the post and the capital. The British proclamation of neutrality came that same week, which raised the stakes of each page.
frus-1862-d147:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to London on 19 September 1862, addressing Charles Francis Adams, the American minister there. The dispatch survives as Document 147 in the 1862 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's printed record of its dealings abroad.

Two days earlier the armies had met at Antietam, and President Lincoln was about to act on slavery. Word of both moves would reach Europe slowly and could shift how London saw the war. A short official letter like this one was the tool Washington had for guiding its envoy through fast-moving weeks. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d247:
A second Seward dispatch to Paris followed on 28 December 1861, printed as Document 247 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France, from Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Two letters in three days mark the New Year rush of business after the Trent settlement. Dayton needed fresh guidance for a French government that was landing troops in Mexico that very month, alongside Britain and Spain. The pairing of these dispatches shows Washington trying to steady two fronts at once as 1862 began. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d347:
The Paris file in this run closes with a Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 21 November 1862, printed as Document 347 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France.

Late November found the joint-action danger past for the year and France turning its energy back to Mexico. Seward's letter of this date belongs to the winding down of the autumn crisis in the Paris channel. It ends the Dayton sequence on the steadier ground the Union had sought since spring. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d447:
Hermann Kreismann, the American consul in Berlin, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 August 1862. It is Document 447 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Consular letters rarely made headlines, but they carried the facts of everyday foreign business: trade, shipping, stranded seamen, and citizens in trouble. Kreismann wrote from a capital friendly to the Union in a month when Union arms were stalled in Virginia. A consul's report also passed along the talk of the streets and papers, which ministers sometimes missed. The letter adds a ground-level Prussian view to the volume's record of the war's second summer.
frus-1862-d47:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 14 April 1862. It stands as Document 47 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d547:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 September 1862. His note is Document 547 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, with the heading punctuated as printed in the volume.

Van Limburg wrote a week after Lincoln's preliminary emancipation order, which changed the moral weather of every diplomatic conversation in Washington. The Dutch, strongly antislavery at home, received that change with interest. The formal business of the note belonged to the usual file of trade and neutral right, but it was transacted in a new atmosphere. The letter belongs to the early autumn Dutch papers. In them the reader can sense the war becoming a different kind of war. In European eyes, it was no longer the war of the spring.
frus-1862-d647:
Writing on 5 May 1862, Robert H. Pruyn sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. Pruyn had just taken charge of the American legation in Japan, a post set up only in the late 1850s. The letter stands as document 647 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

In these first weeks Pruyn wrote home about the legation's work and his dealings with Japan's rulers. Such reports were how Washington learned what its envoys saw, weeks after the fact, since mail moved by ship. The dispatch is one link in the chain that kept a young trade link alive during a war an ocean away.
frus-1863p1-d147:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 147 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

April mail from London followed up the seizure of the Southern raider and weighed what would come next in the yards. Adams kept his reports plain and full, as Seward liked them. This dispatch is a mid-run piece of that follow-up. It shows the legation turning a win into a watch: one ship held did not end the South's hopes in Britain, and Adams knew it.
frus-1863p1-d247:
Writing from London on 24 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 247 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

In 1863 the great question in London was whether Britain would treat the Confederacy as a real nation. Adams's reports helped Washington judge that risk week by week. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d347:
The American answer to London on 31 December 1862 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 347 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

The two men met and wrote constantly, and both knew a quarrel between their countries could hand the South its independence. That shared fear kept the tone correct even when the words were sharp. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d447:
On 4 April 1863, William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d47:
Christopher G. Memminger wrote this letter to James M. Mason on 24 October 1862. Memminger was the Confederate secretary of the treasury; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 47 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The treasury's letters to London dealt with the South's thin purse: loans, cotton, and the bills that piled up in Europe. Memminger wrote to the man who faced the bankers and the British press. This letter is one of the money papers in the Confederate group printed here. It shows the war's other front, fought with credit in the counting houses of London.
frus-1863p1-d547:
On 1 June 1863 a formal note passed from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d647:
On 24 October 1863, William H. Seward, Secretary of State wrote to the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d147: A second letter from Roosevelt to Ambassador Steinhardt is dated November 20, 1943, and it stands as Document 147 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. With the secretary's letter of the same date, the day's Turkish traffic in this volume runs to three items, the heaviest for any embassy that month. The record does not divide their errands. All are printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d247:
Minutes of the Joint Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 22 November 1943, at eleven in the morning, record a session called mainly to hear the theater envoys. General Marshall opened by inviting Ambassador Winant, back from London, to describe British thinking, with Ambassador Harriman and theater representatives also present.

Winant says the British felt Allied gains in Italy were not being used fast enough, and saw chances to act and to draw Turkey into the war. On Overlord, he reports no wish to drop the operation, but strong resistance to a fixed date, since London feared a signed contract that ignored later changes. The British also wanted Balkan resistance fully used, and in Italy aimed at Rome and its airfields, not the Po valley.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d347:
Harry Hopkins sent Ambassador Kirk detailed release instructions for the Cairo communiqué from Tehran on 29 November 1943. The short telegram, approved by President Roosevelt, fixes one of the tightest press timetables of the conference.

Kirk is to give the text to the Office of War Information for publication at half past eleven at night, Greenwich time, on Wednesday 1 December, under a Cairo dateline. News services get the text at five on Tuesday afternoon in Cairo to allow transmission. They get it under strict warning. All of it stays secret until the release hour, with no advance statements or speculation of any kind. Stories must note that all the principals have left Cairo for unannounced destinations, and pictures are released at the same hour. Kirk must also notify the Chinese minister in detail and send the full instructions and text at highest priority to Steve Early in Washington.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d447:
Yet another Combined Chiefs of Staff session fell on December 5, 1943, and its minutes appear in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The chiefs, the senior American and British officers who ran the combined war effort, were meeting daily at the Second Cairo Conference. Their task was to settle the strategy that Tehran had only sketched.

The minutes lay out the session in order: attendance, the matters raised, and the decisions the chiefs recorded before passing them to Roosevelt and Churchill. Together with the day's other records, this one helps show a conference working at full speed. It is primary evidence of how the alliance made its hardest military choices.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d47: On October 19, 1943, the day the Moscow Conference opened, Stalin wrote to Roosevelt again. His message is Document 47 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The timing gives the letter its setting even though the record gives it no topic: ministers were meeting in Moscow while the heads of government kept writing over their heads. The message survives in the Foreign Relations series, in the heart of the October papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d547:
Ambassador John Gilbert Winant sent a second direct report to President Roosevelt from London on January 14, 1944. Winant's access in Britain, where he was almost a national figure, made his presidential channel unusually rich. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Two Winant reports to the President inside a fortnight show London business pressing on Washington that January. Britain was then straining under six years of war while preparing to host the invasion of France. For readers, Winant's direct reports offer the feel of the allied capital from a man both governments trusted, written while the Tehran and Cairo decisions were being put into practice.
frus-1944-quebec-d147:
Writing from Hyde Park on September 3, 1944, Roosevelt answered Churchill's latest Italian telegram, number 774. He shared the prime minister's confidence that the Allied divisions in Italy were sufficient for the task before them. Their commanders, he trusted, would press the battle unrelentingly to shatter the enemy forces on the Gothic Line.

After that breakthrough, Roosevelt insisted, the divisions must be used where they best aided Eisenhower's decisive drive into Germany. He leaned toward using American forces westward but called himself completely open-minded. The exact employment could be discussed at Octagon. He closed by crediting General Wilson and General Patch impartially for the brilliant success in southern France.
frus-1944-quebec-d247: Hopkins telegraphed Grace Tully, the president's secretary, on September 15, 1944, chasing a decision. He had sent Roosevelt the State Department's September 11 memorandum on the French lend-lease agreement. The Foreign Economic Administration and the State Department were anxious to know whether the president had initialed it. Hopkins asked Tully to help him get an answer the next day.
frus-1944-quebec-d47:
Roosevelt wrote again to Churchill on September 1, 1944. It was the second presidential message of the day. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume.

By September 1944, the two men had corresponded for five years of war. Their habits were set by then. Separate papers covered separate questions, and answers came in kind. Roosevelt's twin messages close the day's work between the capitals. For readers, the pair shows how the allies governed together. They governed at a distance and in writing. Meanwhile, armies moved faster than any conference could follow.
frus-1945-50-intel-d147:
The title "Central Intelligence Group Administrative Order No. 3" heads a text dated 19 April 1946. It is document 147 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Papers of this kind were the working stock of the system. They were drafted, read, marked up, and filed so the next office could pick up the thread. Read with its neighbors, it helps fill the gaps that grand accounts skip over. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d247:
The Deputy Director (Wright) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 4 November 1947. Readers meet it as document 247 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The shift from the old group to the CIA was fresh. The Council was still learning how to run its side of the work.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d347:
The Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum) addressed a memorandum to the Intelligence Advisory Committee on 10 June 1948. The State Department prints it as document 347 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d47:
A memorandum of a meeting held on 19 November 1945 follows the staff committee papers in the volume. It records a session rather than a single author's view. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Memoranda of meetings catch the points where plans met resistance or merged. In November 1945 those meetings came thick and fast, since the president's men wanted an intelligence plan ready for the new year. Readers tracking the endgame of the autumn fight should slow down here. The run of November papers shows the rival drafts being trimmed toward a compromise. That compromise became the National Intelligence Authority in January 1946.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d147:
Mikolajczyk explained his resignation to an American diplomat in London, and the report reached Washington on 25 November 1944. Ambassador Winant's cable passes on Schoenfeld's account of their talk that morning. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

He resigned, Mikolajczyk said, because he held a settlement with Moscow to be a necessity now. The three other main parties in his coalition wanted the frontier question left until the war ended. Without a settlement, he reasoned, Poland faced the loss of its eastern lands with no sure gain in the west. Worse, the country would face hard drives toward communism, with the Lublin Committee already largely Communist in make-up. A quick return by London Poles might still stop that.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d247:
Korea's future handling should be settled among the allies in advance, this briefing book paper argues. “Inter-Allied Consultation Regarding Korea,” dated 13 January 1945, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It poses two questions for agreement with Britain and China, and perhaps with Russia.

Who should share in the military occupation of Korea? And who should sit in an interim world administration or trusteeship, if one is set up? The Department holds that Korea's problems are of such world concern that the occupation force should carry allied representation. The seats should go to states with a real interest in Korea's future. Those are the United States, Britain, China, and the Soviet Union if she has entered the Pacific war. Care is added that American strength in the force not be thinned.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d347:
H. Freeman Matthews jotted these rough notes at the foreign ministers' lunch table at Yalta on February 6, 1945. Copied from his pencil longhand, they track the same talks Page recorded in full minutes. Stettinius backed a first communiqué. Molotov liked it and wanted "common" added before "enemy." There was no bar to naming the Black Sea area.

Then came surrender terms. All three agreed to add "dismemberment" to Article 12, after the word for demilitarization. Eden tried a softer formula about ending the German unitary state. No deal was reached on the Russian change. The shorthand scraps let readers watch a clause being born.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d447:
A Balkan federation is the ghost behind this British paper of February 10, 1945. London had already told Moscow its views on a possible Yugoslav-Bulgarian federation. In reply, the Soviet government reported knowing that Yugoslav and Bulgarian talks on a pact of alliance were proceeding. Moscow's attitude toward such a pact was favorable.

At the same time, Moscow judged a Balkan federation not a live question of practical importance just then. Britain, the paper says, was glad to learn that view. The careful courtesies hide a real fear: that Tito's Yugoslavia and Bulgaria might merge under Soviet blessing, shifting the Balkan balance.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d47: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on 8 January 1945, the same day Harriman reported from Moscow. The letter is document 47 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. Placed side by side, the two messages show the president hearing from his British partner and his Soviet ambassador within a single day.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d147:
Harry Hopkins sent a second report from Moscow on May 30, 1945, on Stalin's plans for the peace. The extract is document 147 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Hopkins had pressed Stalin on several questions that would face the three leaders at their coming meeting.

Stalin twice stressed planning at once for a formal peace conference on Europe, warning that the Allies had gone to Versailles unprepared and must not repeat the mistake. On Germany, Hopkins corrected Stalin's belief that London and Washington opposed dismemberment; the question stayed open, and Stalin said he would keep an open mind. Hopkins also expects Stalin to bring specific proposals on prisoners of war and, above all, war criminals.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d247:
A briefing paper recommended trusteeship for the Somali colonies in a paper dated June 30, 1945. The paper is document 247 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It covers Italian Somaliland, on the Horn of Africa, one of the colonies Italy stood to lose in the peace settlement.

Italian Somaliland, together with the French and British Somali territories, should go under international trusteeship, the paper holds. A workable alternative would put the Italian and British territories under trusteeship while leaving French Somaliland French, with a genuinely free port at Jibuti. The data section notes a colony of 194,000 square miles and about a million people, almost all Somalis. It was begun in the 1880s. It was folded into Italian East Africa after the conquest of Ethiopia. Its value lay in its position on the Indian Ocean near the Red Sea entrance.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d347:
Denazification is again the theme of Murphy's despatch No. 576 from Frankfurt, dated July 7, 1945, this time in extracts. General Clay, Murphy reports, had thought of holding a press conference on the purge of Nazis. Clay asked the Political Division to prepare the basic facts such a conference would need.

An informal interdivisional committee on denazification then weighed whether the conference was wise, and what form it should take. The extracts print the basic questions and the fundamental points drawn up for Clay's use. They show the occupation shaping not just a purge, but the public story it would tell Germans about that purge.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d447:
MacVeagh, the ambassador in Athens, welcomed Washington's attention to Greek election supervision in his cable of July 9, 1945. The fundamental local situation, he warns, is unchanged, and his comments rest on his reporting since December 1944. Russian participation, he believes, is essential: it would satisfy the Left and allay suspicions, and so pacify the country.

He asks what form supervision would take. Friendly observers, present to influence events and later pass on the vote's fairness, are one thing. Actual intervention at the polls, with British troops supervising, is another. That, he argues, might let Moscow charge a violation of Greek sovereignty and stir endless argument over undue influence. The British chargé, Caccia, agreed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d47:
Prime Minister Churchill protested to President Truman on June 1, 1945, that the planned Big Three meeting was set too late. His personal and top secret telegram is document 47 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had gladly agreed to come to Berlin, but not on Truman's chosen date of July 15.

July 15, he writes, is much too late for the urgent questions that demand attention, and delay would injure world hopes and unity. Even in the middle of a hard-fought election at home, he would put the meeting first. He presses for June 15 instead, or failing that July 1, 2, or 3. He also tells Truman he has sent a copy of the message to Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d547:
State Department staff wrote a top secret briefing paper on civil aviation and Great Britain for the Potsdam Conference. Dated June 21, 1945, it is document 547 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. It was meant to arm President Truman for talks with the British prime minister.

The paper lists four points to raise. Britain, it says, works to block U.S. air lines in Europe and the Near and Middle East. Britain also blocks sales of U.S. planes in sterling areas. The U.S. is ready to sign a two-way air pact, and the peace treaties should cover flying rights too. It backs the five freedoms agreed at Chicago in December 1944, of which Britain had taken only two.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d647:
Loy Henderson, director of Near Eastern and African Affairs, recorded a meeting with Zionist leaders on June 28, 1945. His memo is document 647 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Acting Secretary Grew received the group in Washington that afternoon.

The visitors were Rabbi Stephen Wise, Nahum Goldmann, Chaim Greenberg, and a Mr. Shulman. Grew said he had read with care a memo Goldmann had given Henderson days before. It set out the problems the Zionists faced and their views on Palestine's future. Grew noted a growing demand among U.S. Zionists for decisive steps on Palestine in the near future. The memo preserves the start of a lobbying push that would run through the Potsdam weeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1047:
Edwin Pauley laid out Germany's food balance for the Secretary of State in this letter of July 28, 1945. His staff worked from official statistics. In 1936, Germany within its 1937 borders lacked 5.7 million tons of food overall. The zone now held by the USSR ran a surplus of 2.65 million tons. The western zones thus faced a shortfall of 8.35 million tons.

Pauley projects the coming years. Farm collections will drop, city diets will shrink, and grain imports must fill the gap. Germany as a whole will need some 4.4 million tons of grain a year. He also arms Byrnes with a talking point for Molotov: western equipment sent east is a free gift, while eastern food would be paid for in Reichsmarks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1147:
George Kennan in Moscow wrote to Matwin, the Polish envoy there, on 23 July 1945. Kennan was the senior American diplomat in the Soviet capital at the time. His note crossed the lines of the alliance: an American writing to a Pole, inside Moscow, while Poland's fate was debated in Germany.

Embassy-level contact of this kind kept working ties alive between posts. The two men dealt with the daily business their embassies shared in the same capital. The note is a small human thread inside great-power bargaining. It shows that even as leaders argued over Poland, their envoys still had to talk to each other.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1247:
Hurley addressed this message to the President and the Secretary of State on 25 July 1945. Writing to both men at once marked the dispatch for the highest level. Hurley's China reports kept the summit's leaders tied to the Asian half of the war.

China's crisis ran on its own clock, indifferent to the German talks. A government weakening, armies watching each other, and Japan's defeat nearing made Hurley's file urgent in its own right. This message carried his word to the top at Potsdam. It is one of the threads that kept the China war inside the summit's field of view.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1347:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to Lowell Pinkerton, the American consul general at Jerusalem, on 18 August 1945. The letter came two weeks after the Potsdam Conference closed. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Jerusalem was one of the most charged posts in the American service in 1945, with the future of Palestine drawing pressure from many sides. A letter from the secretary of state himself shows the question reaching the highest level of the department. It also shows the Potsdam volume reaching past the summit's end date to follow the business the conference left behind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-147: This brief editorial note, printed without a number after document 710, comes from the Potsdam volume's editors. In the Foreign Relations series, editors' notes stand apart from the wartime texts. They supply orientation: dates, sources, and links the documents omit. The note serves readers who want to follow the paper trail with care.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-47:
A United States delegation memorandum of July 20, 1945, holds notes on a Soviet suggestion to internationalize the Ruhr. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The exchange took place in the economic subcommittee, with Maisky speaking for the Soviet side.

Maisky proposed placing the Ruhr, an area of four million people, under the four powers jointly. The body would regulate the Ruhr's production to ensure control of the German war potential. Pressed on details, he said the whole industrial area was meant, as soon as possible, and more or less permanently. A special organization, not the Control Council, would likely run it. The Western men held back in reply. Monckton and Clayton both called the scheme political as well as economic, beyond their committee's instructions. Pauley's figures put the district at twenty-five by fifty miles of coal and industry.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d747:
Cannon wrote from Lisbon to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on July 19, 1945, in document 747. The first secretary at the Lisbon embassy reported up the Department's ladder. Portugal's neutral ground made it a crossroads of rumor and quiet contact. Cannon's letter joined the second Potsdam volume.

A report to an assistant secretary travels fast. Dunn stood close to the Secretary and could act on what he read. Readers see information climbing from a listening post to the center. The document shows the Department's reach during the conference: while the leaders met, its ears stayed open in every capital that mattered.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d847:
Emilio Collado and a colleague named Rubin wrote jointly on August 2, 1945, in document 847. Collado directed the office of financial and development policy. Their letter went to an acting division chief as the Potsdam Conference closed that day. The paper joined the second Potsdam volume.

A closing-day staff letter on money matters shows the peace being costed. Financial officers had to turn summit lines into workable plans. Readers see that translation beginning at once. The document adds the Treasury-minded view to the volume's end. Potsdam's promises would live or die in offices like Collado's, and this letter shows the handoff starting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d947:
William Clayton put his reparations views on record for the Secretary of State in this memorandum of July 29, 1945. He says it confirms what he told the Secretary that morning. Clayton concedes that talk at Yalta and Moscow gave Russia reason to expect half of all reparations in kind from Germany.

Only a zonal split can work in practice, he argues. The Russian zone holds 40 percent of movable factory equipment, mostly light industry. The west holds the heavy gear Russia wants, half of it in the Ruhr. Clayton proposes a trade: Russian and Polish claims met from their zone plus a quarter of Ruhr removals. A like amount more would swap for eastern food, coal, and timber.
frus-1958-60v10p1-d147:
An editorial note in the Eastern Europe volume traces the U-2 affair from the shoot-down on May 1, 1960. Pilot Francis Gary Powers flew for the CIA. The plane fell near Sverdlovsk, 1,200 miles inside Soviet land.

The note follows the cover story of a lost weather plane. Khrushchev's May 5 speech exposed it. A last flight had been cleared for before May 1 only, per a Goodpaster memo of April 25. The note points to the summit's ruin in Volume IX. It is a rare plain record of a lie built and then overtaken.
gao-gaoreports-b-295547:
In GAO ruling B-295547, dated March 3, 2005, McKinley Construction and Excavating was the protester. The Department of Agriculture had rejected its bid on the Goose Pond Phase 2 wetland restoration project. The bid acknowledged every amendment, yet it carried only the old bid schedule. An amendment had raised the footage of pipe to be supplied. GAO denied the protest. The bid was nonresponsive because it was ambiguous. No reader could tell whether the firm bound itself to the old footage or the new.

Nine separate wetland units made up the project. A bid that leaves its core quantity in doubt cannot be accepted.
gao-gaoreports-b-296847:
Chapman Law Firm protested a sole-source bridge deal in GAO decision B-296847, dated September 28, 2005. The buyer was Housing and Urban Development. The holder was Michaelson, Conner and Boul. The work was home care and sale help for single family homes. A long-term deal for the work was stuck in court fights.

GAO denied the protest. The court delay was real, not a lack of plan by the agency. The old holder was the sole firm set to do the work at once. A bridge deal can be sole-source when a gap would harm the work. That case was made here. The bridge thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-298247:
Fabritech, a small firm, protested an Army award for gearbox overhaul in GAO decision B-298247, dated July 27, 2006. The winner was The Purdy Corporation. The gear was tail rotor gearboxes for the AH-64 helicopter. The firm's bid was cut on a view it could not get needed parts. That view went to its skill to do the work.
