GAO sustained the protest. A call on skill to do the work is a fitness call. For a small firm, that call must go to the Small Business office. That office runs the proof of skill plan. To cut the firm with no such path broke the rule. Fair talks claims rode with that core flaw.
gao-gaoreports-b-299547:
Northwest Heritage Consultants protested a National Park Service rejection of its filings. The filings were Architect-Engineer Qualifications Statements for historic preservation design work. Offices in Oakland, Seattle, and Honolulu were in play. GAO decided B-299547 on May 10, 2007.

The filings came in after the closing date. The firm sent them by Postal Service Express Mail. It said the carrier tried to hand them over in time. GAO found no proof of flawed government action. A late filing caused by the mail path stays late. The agency need not take filings that miss the date. No cure was owed. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-309947:
Central Texas College lost its protest — GAO decision B-309947, dated October 12, 2007. The Army sought foreign language training at many sites. The award went to Richard Milburn High School, Inc. The college fought two points. It said the Army should have held talks first. It said its small-firm hiring plan was wrongly judged unfit.

GAO denied the protest on both points. The call warned that award could rest on first offers alone. The choice to skip talks was fair. The call also made a sound hiring plan a must for award. A weak plan barred the win the college sought.
gao-gaoreports-b-311247:
Lisa Hartman lost her protest — GAO decision B-311247, dated May 6, 2008. She spoke for staff at the Chattanooga National Cemetery. The Veterans Affairs office gave grounds care work to DWBH Services, Inc. The work had been done by 7 staff on site. Those staff do other tasks too. None of them stood to lose a job in the shift.

GAO denied the protest. The A-76 rules ask for a race on big shifts of work. A task this small needs no call at all. A new law spares cost tests for shifts of fewer than 10 staff. Small shifts can move to firms with no race.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-547:
U.S. help in guarding the Athens Olympics is reviewed in GAO report GAO-05-547, issued on May 31, 2005. The 2004 Summer Games took place under fear of terrorism. Greece hosted a safe event with no attacks. U.S. agencies gave training and support over the four years before the Games. GAO traced the U.S. approach, agency roles and costs, and lessons carried forward.

Planning began in 2001, after the September attacks and a Greek request for advice. Help rested on a training program Greece already took part in and a U.S. military drill in March 2004. The U.S. ambassador in Athens led the effort on the ground. A Washington group chaired by the State Department lined up help at home. Nearly 20 U.S. offices gave more than $35 million in aid and support. Those lessons shape plans for the 2006 Winter Games in Turin, Italy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-747:
GAO report GAO-05-747, issued September 15, 2005, asks whether firms deduct civil settlement payments on their taxes. Some payments can be deducted, which may blunt the pain of a penalty. GAO named the agencies that struck the largest deals. It asked if tax effects shape talks. And it checked what the tax service learns about such deals.

GAO found the largest deals sat with the environmental, securities, and justice agencies, plus health fraud cases. Deal sizes ran from about $870 thousand to over $1 billion. Agency staff said they do not bargain over deductibility. They leave that call to the tax service. Most firms that replied to GAO said they did deduct such payments. GAO argued that steady data sharing would help the tax service judge these claims.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-947:
Home sale brokerage and price rivalry is the subject of GAO-05-947, issued August 31, 2005. Buyers and sellers paid an estimated $61 billion in fees in 2004. Rates stay much the same across markets and effort levels. That has raised doubts about how hard brokers compete on price. GAO studied what shapes price rivalry. It checked Internet brokers' place and blocks. And it weighed bank entry where states allow it.

GAO found the field competes more on service, quality, and reputation than on fees. Shared listing services help buyers, but they show the fee a buyer's broker will earn. That can punish any cut below the going rate. Some state rules bar rebates, which watchdogs say trims choice. The Internet has changed home searches and spawned new broker models, GAO found. Their market share stays small.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-247:
Statewide voter lists under a 2002 election law are the subject of GAO-06-247, issued on February 7, 2006. The Help America Vote Act told states to build computerized rosters of legal voters. The lists serve as the official rolls for federal elections. The deadline was January 1, 2004, but states could delay to 2006. All but nine states took the delay. GAO studied those nine: Alaska, Arizona, Georgia, Hawaii, Kentucky, Minnesota, South Carolina, South Dakota, and West Virginia.

Election officials in the nine states described the steps they took. They built the lists, checked the facts on sign-up forms, and kept the rolls clean. They also shared the snags they hit and the lessons they drew. GAO urged a study of whether jury records can flag noncitizens on the rolls. The report gives late-starting states a field guide from the first movers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-347:
Federal and state officials share blame when federal money is paid in error. In report GAO-06-347 (April 14, 2006), GAO looks at improper payments in programs that states run with federal funds. States and other nonfederal groups get over $400 billion a year. A House panel asked GAO to study state work under the Improper Payments Information Act of 2002.

For fiscal year 2005, reported improper payments topped $38 billion. That total still left out high-risk programs such as Medicaid. GAO found that state estimating was limited and uneven. It said closer federal and state coordination was needed for sound national estimates. Readers get the state methods, the gaps, and the federal help states said they wanted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-447:
Unmanned aircraft were proving themselves in war while their programs slipped at home. GAO's March 15, 2006 report, GAO-06-447, reviews unmanned aircraft systems. The Defense Department planned to spend $20 billion through 2011 to grow the fleet. The aircraft add intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and strike power. Forces in Iraq and Afghanistan already used them.

Yet programs faced cost and schedule overruns and performance shortfalls. GAO studied the two largest programs, Global Hawk and Predator. It drew lessons for the next program, the Joint Unmanned Combat Air Systems. New programs can craft better and less risky strategies, GAO said. Readers get lessons drawn from real programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-47:
Old phones and computers pile up, and dumping them can spread pollution. In GAO-06-47 (November 10, 2005), GAO studies electronic waste. Millions of used electronics become obsolete each year. Only a fraction are recycled. Export to countries with weak rules can make the harm worse. GAO was asked to sum up the scale and problems of used electronics.

GAO also examines what shapes recycling and reuse of these products. It reviews federal efforts to encourage both paths. Strengthening the federal role could help, GAO said. Readers get volumes, barriers, and program efforts in one report. The study links disposal choices to health and trade.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-547:
A program to help sick nuclear workers was itself paying contractors badly. GAO's May 31, 2006 report, GAO-06-547, examines the Energy Department's Office of Worker Advocacy. A 2000 law let the department help former contractor staff file state compensation claims. The illnesses could be linked to toxic exposure at work. Congress noted few finalized cases and asked GAO to review program costs. It focused on payments to contractors.

GAO tested whether controls were designed to stop improper payments. It checked whether payments were properly backed as valid uses of funds. Deficient controls led to millions in improper and questionable payments, GAO found. Readers get the control design flaws.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-647:
Risky federal computer projects are the subject of GAO-06-647, a GAO report dated June 15, 2006. In August 2005, the Office of Management and Budget told agencies to name their high risk information technology projects. Agencies also had to report each quarter on projects that missed cost, schedule, or performance goals. GAO was asked to count the projects by agency and judge how well agencies and the budget office spot and watch them.

GAO found that agencies named 226 projects as high risk. Processes to spot and oversee such projects were in place, but GAO saw room to improve them. GAO also found that high risk lists and management watch lists used different tests to flag a project. GAO urged stronger, shared processes so troubled projects get attention sooner.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-847:
A new global war command is assessed in GAO-06-847, issued on September 8, 2006. United States Strategic Command was created in 2002 to anticipate and counter worldwide threats. It holds seven mission areas, including nuclear deterrence and integrated missile defense. It also took on newer duties in space, intelligence coordination, and global strike. GAO judged how far the command had carried out its many missions and its new organization.

GAO found that the command had made progress in putting its new missions into practice. It had written concepts of operations and set plans, guidance, and policy. It had also gathered the people and resources to begin work. Even so, GAO said additional actions were needed to expand on that progress. The command's vision and goals, GAO warned, would not be met by structure alone.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1147:
Jobless aid still reaches few low-wage and part-time workers, GAO reports in GAO-07-1147, dated September 7, 2007. Unemployment Insurance has guarded worker income for more than 70 years. In fiscal year 2006 it covered about 130 million workers. It paid about $30 billion to about 7 million people who lost jobs.

The program began in 1935, when most workers were men in full-time factory or trade jobs. Work has changed since: more low-wage, short-term, and part-time jobs, and more women at work. Congress asked who the program serves now. GAO traced use trends, and the odds that low-wage and part-time workers get aid, beside higher-wage peers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-147:
U.S. grants aim to support peaceful democratic change inside Cuba. GAO audited that aid in GAO-07-147, a report issued November 15, 2006. From 1996 to 2005, the State Department and the aid agency gave out $74 million in grants. A presidential panel had just urged more funding. GAO studied 10 grantees holding about 76 percent of active award dollars. Most of the review focused on the aid agency's work.

The two agencies ran the aid through a joint process, GAO found. Yet their communication was sometimes poor. The aid agency has no staff in Cuba and lacked routine links with the U.S. mission there. About 95 percent of its awards came from unsolicited proposals, not competition. It also stretched most awards, lifting one set of costs from about $6 million to about $50 million. GAO said controls over grantees were too weak to assure funds were used properly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-247:
The tax agency's computer overhaul has run for years at high cost and high risk. GAO reviewed its fiscal year 2007 spending plan in GAO-07-247, issued February 15, 2007. The Business Systems Modernization program replaces the agency's aging tax systems. The plan, sent to Congress in September 2006, asked for $167.3 million. The law sets six conditions the plan must meet. GAO also checked progress on its past advice.

The plan met all six legal conditions, GAO found. The agency had also improved its management controls. It had tightened configuration management and sharpened its long-term vision. But two controls were not yet fully in place. Requirements work and reviews after systems launch still lagged. GAO asked for one more fix in future plans. Plans should state plainly how much project scope got done. It pointed to earned value management as the tool. The agency agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-647:
Military health fees frozen for a decade would rise under a Pentagon plan, and GAO-07-647, dated May 31, 2007, tests the savings claim. Defense health spending more than doubled from 2000 to 2005. The plan, called Sustain the Benefit, raises enrollment fees, deductibles, and drug co-payments for many TRICARE users. The department said the changes would save over $11 billion through fiscal year 2011 if begun in fiscal year 2007. A 2007 defense law told GAO to check the math.

GAO found real savings likely, but less than claimed. The soft spot is human reaction: no one knows how many families would quit TRICARE when fees rise. The department also lacks rich data on what cover its members hold elsewhere. Fees had sat flat for over 10 years, so some rise tracks civilian norms. GAO's caution is narrow and firm: budget the savings low, not high.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-847:
Visa wait times at U.S. posts abroad are studied in GAO-07-847, dated July 13, 2007. After the September 11 attacks, security steps lengthened visa reviews. Long waits can deter lawful travel and cost the economy billions. They can also sour views of the United States abroad. GAO checked the State Department's wait time data. It tracked steps the department took to cut waits. It judged the plan for rising demand in years ahead.

Waits generally fell over the past year, GAO found. From September 2006 to February 2007, 53 of 219 posts still hit waits of 30 days or more in some month. Posts in India cut waits from over 140 days to under two weeks. Summer peaks still strain many posts. The wait data themselves have flaws, such as late or uneven reports. GAO urged a long-term strategy for demand growth. It also urged better data and shared good practices. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-947:
Children's hospital pay under TRICARE is measured in GAO-07-947, dated July 31, 2007. The military health program pays children's hospitals a special differential. In fiscal year 2007, their base payments ran 61 percent higher than other hospitals'. That edge has narrowed since 1989. It keeps shrinking because the differential ignores inflation. Hospital groups say the pay still misses patient complexity. GAO studied claims from fiscal years 2003 through 2006. It compared diagnoses and case complexity across sites.

Children's hospital patients match medical center cases in complexity, GAO found. Both groups far exceed community hospital cases. Diagnoses at children's hospitals resemble those at medical centers. Longer stays and other signs point the same way. So the payment gap tracks real patient differences in part. A 2006 defense law ordered this study. Defense officials and hospital groups were interviewed. The report gives Congress the numbers behind the debate. Trends in where children get care close the account.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-147:
Reused medical devices labeled for one use are studied in GAO report GAO-08-147 (January 31, 2008). Some single-use devices are cleaned and sold again with federal clearance. The Food and Drug Administration oversees that trade. As of July 2007, 11 firms were marketing more than 100 types of such devices. They range from sleeves worn in surgery to tools used in open-heart work.

GAO reviewed how the agency has tightened its watch over the years. It also weighed the safety record of reprocessed devices. The title gives the balance: oversight has grown, and current data show no added health risk from their use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-47:
Medicare Part D drug coverage decisions are what GAO takes up in report GAO-08-47, dated January 22, 2008. Private plan sponsors run Part D and rule on requests to cover restricted drugs. GAO studied seven sponsors that hold over half of enrollment, plus the appeals path and federal oversight.

In a sample of 421 case files, sponsors approved about 67 percent of coverage requests, with rates from 57 percent to 76 percent. Sponsors use automated checks against set criteria to decide fast, though some felt pressed for time when doctors sent thin information. Appeals often flip outcomes: the median sponsor-level approval rate was 40 percent for July through December 2006. GAO recommended simpler appeal steps and clear definitions for the data sponsors report. The Medicare agency backed the intent of the first point.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-547:
Community colleges and one-stop centers are studied in GAO report GAO-08-547, dated May 15, 2008. The Workforce Investment Act built a one-stop system for federal job training. Community colleges supply both career training and regular academic courses. GAO visited 20 colleges and surveyed one-stop centers nationwide.

Colleges shape courses to local industry needs, train workers for named employers, and serve groups such as disadvantaged adults and one-stop clients. About 11 percent of one-stops are run solely or jointly by a community college, and 34 percent host college staff on site. Nearly half of local workforce boards, 49 percent, seat a college president. State funding and leadership help these ties; federal performance rules and funding strain them. The Labor and Education Departments generally agreed with the findings.
halliwell-archaic-1847:
James Orchard Halliwell published his Dictionary of Archaic and Provincial Words in 1847. Halliwell, a young scholar of old English texts, gathered words that standard dictionaries left out. Some were already dead, surviving only in early books, while others lived on in county speech far from London.

The entries define old and regional words and quote the writers who used them, from Chaucer onward. Readers puzzled by Shakespeare or by a grandmother's dialect could find the missing sense here. The dictionary saved thousands of words from being lost for good as speech grew more uniform. It remains a key tool for anyone reading early English literature or studying how the language changed across regions.
harvey-motion-of-heart-willis-1847:
William Harvey's On the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals appears here in Robert Willis's 1847 Sydenham Society translation. Harvey published De motu cordis in Latin in 1628, announcing that the blood circulates. Willis, a Scottish physician and scholar, gave English readers their standard version.

Harvey showed by experiment and by counting that the heart pumps far more blood than the body could make or use up. Valves in the veins, the ligature test on the arm, and the beating heart of cold-blooded animals all pointed one way. The blood must travel in a circle. The discovery remade physiology, and Willis's translation carried it to Victorian medicine in Harvey's own order of proof.
harvey-works-vol1-1847:
Robert Willis Englished Harvey's works in 1847, and this first volume holds the great anatomical writings. De motu cordis leads, with its proof of the blood's circulation. The Sydenham Society edition made the founder of modern physiology open to English readers in a worthy and lasting form for doctors and scholars.

Harvey's dissections and arguments appear here in clear, faithful prose. His letters and lesser tracts fill out the picture of his mind. Willis, a skilled translator, lets the science speak plainly throughout. The volume serves students of medicine as a classic doorway into Harvey, pairing the founding text with the anatomy that supports it.
harvey-works-vol2-1847:
Harvey on generation fills the second volume of Willis's 1847 English Works. Eggs, embryos, and the growth of chicks occupy his patient watch here. Harvey argues that all life comes from an egg, a bold claim he backs with dissections done day by day through the whole course of incubation.

The treatise pioneered the study of embryology as a true science. Deer from the king's parks supplied subjects for his royal physician's trials. Volume One gave the circulation; this book gives the beginnings of life. Together they show the founder of two sciences at work, a man whose method of close trial changed medicine for good.
heine-atta-troll-1847:
Heinrich Heine wrote Atta Troll as a verse tale in the 1840s, and it appeared in 1847. Herman George Scheffauer translated the poem into English in 1913. Atta Troll is a dancing bear who escapes his keeper in the Pyrenees and dreams of bear freedom in the wild.

Heine uses the bear's story to mock the earnest political verse of his day. Hunters, witches, and the Wild Hunt cross the bear's path in wild scenes. The verse dances even while the satire bites. Heine called the poem a last free forest song of Romanticism. It stands as his great verse satire, funny on its face and sharp underneath, aimed at German complacency.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands, complete for 1584 to 1586, gathers chapters one to eight in one file. The murder of Orange opens the work and the republic's orphanhood. Holland and Zeeland stand firm while Ghent falls to Farnese. Sovereignty is offered to France, then to England, in the opening diplomacy.

Dutch envoys suffer humiliation at the Louvre and coquetry in London. Parma's siege of Antwerp dominates the middle chapters, with Sainte Aldegonde's defence at its close. Leicester lands to a triumphal entrance as the file ends. Famine in Flanders balances the entries of princes. This compact volume holds the whole first act of Motley's drama. Readers can take the republic from assassination to English alliance in a single sitting's span of chapters, with his full narrative manner on display.
hopkins-discovery-of-witches-1647:
Matthew Hopkins defends his hunt in The Discovery of Witches, his brief tract of 1647. Hopkins had roamed East Anglia in the war years, paid by towns to find witches. Scores were hanged on his word. Foes in print charged him with fraud and cruel tests: no sleep, bound swims, and pricks for the Devil's mark on the skin of the charged.

His tract replies ask by ask, in a cool, prim tone. He died the same year, young and much cursed. The tract is the chief hunt man's own word. It is a grim self portrait.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
Part II of In the Fire of the Forge opens in Volume 5 of the Nuremberg romance by Georg Ebers. Ebers leaves the vesper bells behind and shows Heinz Schorlin still listening to an aged friar. The old man tells the story of St Francis. He covers the saint's break with everything he loved. The sorrowful start of that new life holds the young knight, who still looks out for his missing servant.

Chapter 1 meanwhile follows Biberli, who has taken the runaway maid Katterle back to the Ortlieb mansion. The servants greet her as a favorite they have missed, knowing nothing of her guilt. Biberli has coached her with a cover story about a fire scare at the fortress and a night spent waiting on papers. A saint's life and a servant's invention sit side by side, one about leaving the world, the other about surviving in it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-kolon-147:
Abba Kolon is a mythical Roman in a Talmudic legend about the founding of Rome. The tale says the first settlers found their huts fell down as soon as they were built. Abba Kolon told them nothing would stand unless they mixed water from the Euphrates into their mortar. He crossed the East as a cooper and brought back such water in wine-casks.

With that water mixed in, the new huts stood firm. A proverb grew from the tale: a city without Abba Kolon is not worthy of the name. The entry reads the story as a sign of Rome's debt to the resources of the East. It also weighs rival guesses about the strange name, and finds most of them weak.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abentrevi-josep: Joseph Abentrevi was physician in ordinary to King James I of Aragon. In January of 1271 or 1272 the king allotted him a yearly payment of 500 sueldos. The entry gives the sum in other money of its day as well. It also adds a note on the name itself. Abentrevi most likely comes from the Arabic Ibn Tarf. No other act, work, or date from the physician's life is recorded in this brief notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abodah-music-of:
Music of the 'Abodah treats the chant tied to the Day of Atonement service. The 'Abodah holds the center of that day's worship. Its core is the high priest's confession of sin, taken from the Mishnah.

Cantors turned the recital into the peak of their art. Long wordless vocal runs voiced grief for the lost Temple and hope for rest. German and Polish rites split the verses in set places. Cantor and congregation answered each other on the confessions. Modern settings later replaced much of the old plain chant, but the ornate style stayed prized.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abtalion-ben-so:
Abtalion ben Solomon was an Italian rabbi born at Consiglio about 1540. He died on October 26, 1616. He learned under Samuel Judah Katzenellenbogen, rabbi of Padua. He held his teacher in such honor that he hung his portrait in his study. He later served as rabbi at Rovigo.

A ruling by Abtalion caused a storm among Italian rabbis. The case asked if a ritual bath was fit for use. The rabbis of Venice, the most learned in the land, took the other side. Four books were written on the fight, for and against him. Their titles and dates fill much of the entry. Abtalion also fought the pilpul method of study. Leon de Modena praised him in an elegy used as his tomb text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acquittal-in-ta:
Acquittal in Talmudic law is the freeing of a charged man for lack of sound proof. A court for death cases held twenty-three judges. All were trained in the law and its lore. Their chief duty was to guard the clean from a false verdict. They had to grill the state's witnesses with great care. Proof had strict forms, and a slip could end a case.

Two eye-witnesses had to see a crime to convict. If one broke down on time or place, both men's words fell. An answer of I don't know on the core points killed the whole proof. Small gaps on side points did not. The rules did not guard theft in the same way. Theft drew a fine of twice the worth, so it counted as a suit for goods. Death cases stood apart, and the bias ran toward letting a man go.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adoniram-also-a: Adoniram was the head tax man under three kings. He served David, Solomon, and Rehoboam in turn. Other texts call him Adoram or Hadoram. The Greek form is Adoniram in both spots the entry cites. Rehoboam sent him north to take the tax from the tribes that broke away. Those tribes stoned him to death there. The hosted text gives the post, the three reigns, the name forms, and that end. It gives no birth, no town, and no other act of his long term of work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-b-rab-947: Aha b. Rab was a Babylonian amora of the third and fourth generations, in the fourth century. He was a contemporary of Rabina I. and the senior of Aha b. Jacob. His opinions were backed by his grandson, Mesharsheya. The entry is brief, and it records no teaching or event from his life beyond these links of generation, rank, and family support.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akrabbim-the-sc:
Akrabbim, "The Scorpion Ascent," is named with the southeastern boundary of Judah. It is probably one of the passes above the great Wadi-el-Fikre. Those passes lead from the wadi's north slope to the desert plateau. They form a road between Edom and Judah. No one pass can be fixed as the right one for certain.

Two candidates are offered. The Nakb-el-Safa has age and a rock-cut path in its favor. The Nakb-el-Yemen, farther west, looks like an easier road. The land around the pass took the name Akrabattene. That region, too, must not be mixed with a northern district of the same name, near Beth-el.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-mauri: Maurice Alexander Alexander was an Australian politician. He was born in London on November 30, 1820. He died in Sydney, New South Wales, on January 27, 1874. He had arrived in Sydney as a boy, in 1834. From 1863 he represented Goulburn in the New South Wales House of Assembly. He built a very large fortune by careful buying of real estate. After his death his widow founded a scholarship at the University of Sydney. She dedicated it to his memory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alkalai-judah-b:
Judah ben Solomon Hai Alkalai was a rabbi in Semlin, Croatia. He died in October 1878. He won fame for urging a return of Jews to Palestine. The entry calls him a forerunner of the Zionist cause. His book on the return came out at Vienna in 1857.

That book backs a bold joint-stock plan. A firm would ask the sultan to cede the land. Jews would hold it as a tribute land. He took up the same theme in later books. One book from 1840 defends his work on tithes. A book from 1843 praises two men who freed Jews at Damascus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anklet-1547: Anklet names an ornament worn on the ankle. Isaiah, chapter 3, verse 18, lists anklets among the jewels that women of his day wore. Some anklets were joined by a short chain. That chain forced a slow, mincing walk. The entry also notes a puzzle in the old versions. The Targum and a passage of the Jerusalem Talmud render the Hebrew word as shoes or slippers instead. An image of old and new Eastern anklets goes with the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apollonius-1647: Apollonius was one of the Judeans who went to Rome about 130 B.C. to make a covenant, a league of friendship, with the Romans. Josephus calls him the son of Alexander. That is the whole of what this short entry says in its own text. It gives no office, no speech, and no outcome for the mission. For the setting it sends the reader to the entry on John Hyrcanus, and it rests on two passages of Josephus's Antiquities, which it cites by book and section.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aryeh-loeb-ben-:
Aryeh Loeb ben Saul, also called Levi Saul Loewenstam, was a Polish rabbi born in Cracow about 1690. He died at Amsterdam on April 2, 1755. Rabbis filled his family: his father Saul had led Cracow, and his grandfather was Rabbi Hoeschl of Cracow. In 1707 he married Miriam, eldest daughter of Zebi Ashkenazi of Altona, and studied under his father-in-law in Amsterdam and Poland.

His career met storms. At Tarnopol he gained the post after officials ousted the sitting rabbi, and the congregation soon deposed him in turn. Posts at Rzeszow and Glogau followed, then a call to Amsterdam in 1740, where he stayed for life. He published no books, and his brother-in-law Jacob Emden judged his learning modest. He sided with Emden, his wife's brother, against Jonathan Eybeschutz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashirah-i-will-:
Ashirah, I Will Sing, is the first word of the Song of Moses in Exodus chapter 15, the Song at the Sea. Synagogues read it on the seventh day of Passover, on the Sabbath called Beshallah, and at the close of the Psalms in the daily morning service. A very old tune goes with it, popularly claimed as the actual chant Miriam and her sisters sang after the crossing of the Red Sea.

The entry argues that the tune may truly hold a relic of Temple music. Trumpet calls change little across centuries, since their notes rest on the nature of air in a tube. The first singers, it suggests, would shape the song's opening toward a trumpet sound. That martial coloring is still heard when the scroll reading reaches the words Pharaoh drew nigh.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-assyriology-and:
Assyriology is the study of the wedge-shaped cuneiform writing of ancient Mesopotamia. The entry shows how that young science bears on the Old Testament. It sorts the links by period: before the Flood, the patriarchs, Egypt, the early kings, Assyria's last century, and the new Babylonian age. Each part matches Hebrew records with what the stones and tablets say.

Cuneiform texts offer close matches for the creation and Flood stories and for the Sabbath. Letters found at Tell el-Amarna in 1887, more than three hundred of them, show Babylonian speech used for diplomacy in the fifteenth century B.C. Royal records name kings of Israel and Judah. Sargon II. tells of taking Samaria in 722 B.C. and carrying off 27,290 people. Such finds let readers test and fill out the Bible's own account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auspitz-rudolf-:
Rudolf Auspitz was an Austrian member of parliament and a leading manufacturer. He was born at Vienna on July 7, 1837. His family was one of the oldest Jewish families of Moravia, named for the city of Auspitz. His grandfather founded a famed woolen firm. Rudolf studied technical subjects at Vienna, Berlin, and Paris, and came home in 1858.

When beet-sugar making spread across Europe, Auspitz backed it early with land and capital. In 1863 he founded a sugar company. It soon absorbed a rival count's works and became the only sugar maker in northern Moravia. He entered politics in 1871, winning a seat in the Moravian diet. In 1873 he joined the Austrian Reichsrath. He sat in diet and chamber posts for decades, always with the German Liberal party. From 1900 he served as trustee of the Jewish congregation of Vienna.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baal-perazim-22: Baal-perazim is a place named in the tale of David's war with the Philistines. The Philistines camped in the valley of Rephaim. David pulled back to the hill fort of Adullam, then came on to Baal-perazim and beat them there. From that tale the place must have stood in the valley of Rephaim itself. Nothing more exact can be found in the sources. The entry notes a tempting link with Mount Perazim, named in Isaiah, but it does not claim the two are one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bag-2347: Bag is handled here as a Bible word-study. The Authorized Version uses that one English word for several Hebrew ones, and the entry takes each in turn. A large bag is "ḥariṭ," which could hold a talent of silver. A small bag, "kis," held a merchant's weights in his girdle, and perhaps his money too. Another small money-bag is "ẓeror," also used for a bundle. In Canticles, a bundle of myrrh is read as a small perfume-bag worn round a woman's neck.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bannaim-or-bana:
Bannaim, or Banaim, are named in one passage only, Miḳwaot ix. 6, and this entry asks who they were. The Mishnah there rules on dipping clothes for purification. Garments of the Bannaim may not bear a mud-stain even on one side, since these people are very strict about clean clothing. A tanna of the middle of the second century records the rule.

Later teachers had lost the word's sense and guessed. One reading made the Bannaim scholars of the world's building, or men who work with ax and shovel. Others took the name to mean bathers, kin to the Hemerobaptists. The entry argues, from the Tosefta and from the word "bor" meaning a pit, that the Mishnah likely means bathers only. On that view it speaks of bathing clothes, which must be spotless to be purified.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barren-barrenne:
Barren and barrenness start from the Hebrew word 'aḳar, probably "uprooted," torn away from the family stock to wither without successors. A people who counted children "an heritage from the Lord" saw childlessness as a grave misfortune. Rachel's plea, "Give me children or else I die," shows how keenly a wife felt it. Peninnah taunted Hannah with her unfruitfulness. The best return Elisha could make the Shunammite was to pray for the end of her childlessness.

In Talmudic teaching the childless man is reckoned cut off from communion with God, and counted as already dead, like the pauper, the leper, and the blind. Yet the ethical side sometimes rose above this view. "A man's good deeds are his best posterity," says one saying. The entry follows the attitude from the patriarchal stories into rabbinic teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bassus-lucilius:
Lucilius Bassus became governor of Judea after Titus took Jerusalem in the year 70. He had led the fleet at Ravenna, then betrayed Vitellius and handed the fleet to Vespasian. That service won him the Judea post and the task of taking the last forts.

Herodium gave up at once, but Macherus held out until its young leader was caught. Bassus then took the fort, killed many townspeople, and sold women and children as slaves. He died during the siege of Masada, leaving that hard task to Silva, his successor. Josephus is the chief source named in the entry for this account of his rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-moses-shab: Moses Shabbethai Beer was an Italian rabbi born at Pesaro. He served as rabbi in Rome from 1825 until his death there on May 6, 1835. On Dec. 18, 1829 he was granted a talk of forty minutes with Pope Leo the Twelfth. He used that meeting to plead for the needs of his community. The entry stresses the weight of the moment: no spokesman for the Jews of Rome had ever before been allowed to appear in person before a pope.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belteshazzar-28: Belteshazzar is the name given to Daniel by the chief of the eunuchs, in the seventh verse of the first chapter of Daniel. The entry is short and turns on what that name means. The book's writer seems to hear the god Bel in its first syllable. Scholars here read it instead as a Babylonian phrase asking that Bel guard his life. A second scholar renders it as a plea that a goddess guard the king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-2947:
Benjamin was the youngest son of Jacob, born to Rachel as she died on the road near Ephrath. She named him Ben-oni, son of my sorrow. Jacob changed the name to Ben Yamin, son of the right hand, to turn aside the ill omen. He stayed home when his brothers first went to Egypt for grain.

Joseph later forced his coming, hid a silver cup in his sack, and charged him with theft. Judah offered himself as a slave in the boy's place, and Joseph then revealed himself. The entry follows the tribe that bore his name, famed as warlike archers, and its near destruction after the crime at Gibeah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berenger-of-nar: Bérenger of Narbonne was viscount of that city in the eleventh century. In an age of wars over the worldly power of the popes, Pope Alexander the Second still found time to guard the Jews. The pope praised Bérenger for stepping in with force on their behalf when a persecution threatened. At the same time, in 1063, Alexander wrote to the bishop of Narbonne. He asked the bishop to protect the Jews just as actively in the future, should like dangers arise again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-karl-:
Karl Ilyich Bernstein was a Russian jurist and professor of Roman law. He was born at Odessa on January 13, 1842. He died at Berlin in 1894. His religion barred him from a professorship in Russia. So he built his career in Berlin instead. In 1864 he became the first Jew to earn a law doctorate there.

The entry follows his Berlin lectures from 1878 onward. He became a full professor in 1887. He also helped direct an institute training Russian students in Roman law. His writings covered delegation, alternative obligations, and Russian civil law. From 1881 he aided Russian Jewish emigration through a Berlin committee.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bezetha-3247: Bezetha was a hill north of the Temple-mound. Josephus is the entry's source for it. A valley separated hill from Temple area. After the third wall rose, it joined Jerusalem. Josephus read its name as "New City." The entry calls that reading strange. A better rendering is "house of olives." It may match Bezeth in First Maccabees. Bacchides camped there after leaving Jerusalem. There the place is called a village.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-biurists-from-c:
The Biurists were exegetes of Mendelssohn's school. Earlier commentators had distorted the Bible's plain sense. Each read passages from his own viewpoint. Mendelssohn made a literal German Pentateuch translation. He made it first for his children. Solomon Dubno undertook its "biur," or commentary. Dubno was a grammarian and fine Hebraist.

Old-school rabbis attacked the work at once. Raphael ha-Kohen and Ezekiel Landau led the critics. They feared German would seduce Jewish youth. Followers continued the work book by book. A table credits biurim on Joshua through Malachi. The school spread from Poland to Alsace and beyond. It later crossed the Atlantic with Isaac Leeser. The entry credits it with founding critical Bible study among modern Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bobruisk-3447:
Bobruisk is a city on the right bank of the River Berezina, in the government of Minsk, Russia. Jews there are first named in papers from 1511. The town grew fast in the early nineteenth century, after a fort was built.

In 1898 the city had 19,125 Jewish residents in a total of 35,177. Trade in dry goods, grain, and wood lay mainly in Jewish hands. The entry lists synagogues, schools, a hospital, and aid groups. A fire on May 3, 1902, left thousands of Jewish families homeless. The wider district held 49,858 Jews in a total of 256,095 people. Leather work, brick making, and shoe making gave many families their living there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonsenyor-astru: Astruc Bonsenyor, called Struch or Nastruch in Spanish chronicles, served Jaime I. of Aragon from 1259. He was the king's dragoman and Arabic secretary and died in 1280. A native of Barcelona, he rode with the king as interpreter on campaigns. In 1265 the king sent him to Murcia to deal with the besieged Saracens. Royal favor let him add doors and windows to his house in the Jewish quarter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brovary-3747: Brovary was a small town in the government of Chernigov, Russia. In 1898 it counted 1,344 Jewish inhabitants in a population of 5,166. Most Jews there worked in trade, while 258 followed handicrafts. Tailoring led, with 102 Jews at that trade. Others worked as day laborers or in local cigarette, tar, and chair factories. Jewish charity ran a hospital for the poor and a home for the aged. Schooling came from 12 hedarim with 136 pupils and a Talmud-Torah with 28 pupils.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burnt-offering-:
Burnt offering is the usual rendering of the Hebrew olah, which the entry says means what is brought up or presented to God. The name rests on the phrase an offering made by fire. A synonym marks the offering as complete, since the whole victim went on the altar. The entry calls it the highest order of sacrifice in the Old Testament ritual.

Levitical rules follow in detail. Victims came from herd or flock, or birds for the poor, all without blemish. The offerer killed the animal north of the altar, and priests handled the blood. Later sections trace how the rite changed over time. By the days of King Ahaz, a morning burnt offering formed part of the fixed Temple ritual.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cambridge-3947:
Cambridge, the English university town, was among the earliest English towns with Jewish settlers. One history sets the first settlement in 1073. Its old synagogue stood near the prison and later passed to the Franciscans. Two parishes still carry the name in the Jewry. The entry names a fine laid on a Jewess named Comitissa over her son's marriage.

In 1224 Henry III gave a Jew's house to the town as a jail, on the present Guildhall site. Cambridge Jews escaped the riots of 1189 and 1190 but suffered in the barons' revolt of 1266. After the return, Jews appear as university teachers. Solomon Schechter raised its Hebrew manuscript holdings with Cairo Genizah finds. Numa Hartog's top math honors in 1869 helped open degrees to Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carmi-4047: Carmi is a biblical name borne by more than one man. One Carmi was a son of Reuben who came to Egypt with Jacob, and a family later bore his name as its head. Another was a Judahite, son of Zabdi and father of Achan, who is called Achar in I Chronicles ii. 7. A third use, in I Chronicles iv. 1, is treated here as a misreading for Chelubai. Bible references are given for each use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catalonia-4147:
Catalonia was a duchy of Aragon in the northwest of Spain. Jews settled there as early as the eighth century. Cities named include Barcelona, Tarragona, Gerona, Besalu, and Vich. Crusaders coming to fight the Moors at times attacked Jews. A papal letter to bishops barred such attacks, arguing that Jews stood ready to serve.

In law, Catalan Jews gained property rights early. A rule of 1068 made Jews who bought land pay a tithe to the parish. Court rules favored Christians, though. A Jew suing a Gentile had to swear to him, never the reverse. Jews and Saracens could not testify against a Christian. On the whole, life stayed quiet. Jews traded, worked in crafts, and studied the sciences, above all medicine. That skill opened the doors of princes and counts to them, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-choba-or-chobai: Choba, also spelled Chobai, was a town the Jews fortified against the attacks of Holofernes. The entry points to two mentions in the book of Judith, in chapters iv and xv. Because Judith links it with Jericho, Reland looked for it near that city and matched it with Coabis. Conder instead proposed Al-Makhubbi as the site. The short entry reports both guesses and settles on neither one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coen-jan-pieter:
Jan Pieterszoon Coen, governor-general of Java and founder of the Dutch colonial system, was born at Hoorn on Jan. 8, 1587, and died in 1629. Trained in trade with the Piscatori firm in Rome, he sailed for India in 1607 and again in 1612. Named director-general of the Indian trade in 1613, he destroyed the town of Jacatra in 1619 and founded Batavia on its site.

Why does he stand in a Jewish encyclopedia? The entry says plainly that he was reputed to be of Jewish descent, then tests the claim. Biographies give rich detail on his rule yet stay silent on his father. His portrait could pass for a Jew, it notes. Abbing's history of Hoorn offers mostly negative signs. The entry leaves his extraction undecided.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-collins-charlot: Charlotte Collins, called Lottie, was an Anglo-American actress born in London about 1865. She first went on stage at age five as a rope-dancer. Orphaned while still a child, she joined her sisters Marie and Lizzie. The three sang and danced together in music halls. In 1890 she shot to fame with one song. Ta-ra-ra-boom-de-ay, first sung by her at the Tivoli Music Hall, swept the country. It began as a boating chant of Mississippi sailors. In 1892 Charles Frohman signed her for America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-contract-11247:
Contract, in Jewish law, means a formal agreement that binds a person to do or not do a set thing. The entry notes that Bible and Mishnah treat a promise as sacred. A broken promise draws blame even when a court cannot enforce it. Striking hands once gave a promise added force, though in the Talmud that act kept only moral weight.

Later sections cover surety bonds given in court, terms that can override set rules, and conditions tied to future events. Money matters allow more room for private terms, the entry says. Marriage terms and loans at interest face strict limits. A reader gets the main rules, sources, and cross links to deed, loans, and suretyship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-corcos-or-4647:
Corcos names a Jewish family traced back to the end of the thirteenth century. The name first appears in Spain. After the expulsion from Spain, the family rose to rank in Italy through learning, piety, and wealth. Members still lived in Gibraltar and Morocco when the entry was written. Its origin is guessed from a place called Corcos, or as a form of Carcassonne.

A long family tree follows, member by member, across several centuries. Roman rabbis in the line regulated meat sales in the ghetto and dealt with the Inquisition over Hebrew books. Others served in Italy, Spain, and North Africa. The entry works as both pedigree and group biography.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cremieux-isaac-:
Isaac Adolphe Crémieux was a French statesman, born at Nîmes on April 22, 1796. He died in Paris on Feb. 9, 1880. At his lycée he and a cousin were the only Jewish students. Admitted to the bar at Nîmes in 1817, he rose fast as an orator and advocate. His win in the Trestaillon case made his name in Paris. He defended the singers of the Marseillaise in 1819.

The long article follows his full public life. It traces his seats in government, his work for Jewish rights, and his role in the Alliance Israélite Universelle. Out of office he defended persecuted newspapers and exiled republicans across France. His clients ranged from the sultan to the viceroy of Egypt. Few entries in the set run this long.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daghestan-4847:
Daghestan is a Russian province on the eastern slopes of the Caucasus, by the Caspian Sea. Its Turkish name means mountainous country. The census of 1897 counted 12,000 Jews there, 1.85 per cent of all the people. District figures for 1894 put the largest groups at Derbent and in the Kaitago-Tabassaran and Kyurin districts. Some Caucasian tribes are thought to descend from Jewish colonists of before the common era.

In manners the Jews of Daghestan match their warlike neighbors. They speak the Tat language, a mix of Persian and Hebrew. Their writing mixes square letters with Rashi script. They wear Circassian dress and go heavily armed. A closing section sketches home life, from women carrying water jars barefoot at the well to loud laments sung in a circle on a flat roof.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-isaac: Isaac ha-Kohen's son David was a prominent rabbinical scholar who lived at Avignon in the thirteenth century. His grandson Aaron ben Jacob ha-Kohen names him in the "Orḥot Ḥayyim" as the teacher of Eliezer ben Immanuel of Tarascon. David wrote a ritual work called "Hilkot Ṭerefot," on the laws of forbidden food. Eliezer, in responsa exchanged with Samuel of Agde, often names David as his teacher and quotes his legal decisions. The entry traces the family line down to Isaac de Lattes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dehavites-r-v-d: Dehavites were one of the peoples settled in Samaria who opposed the rebuilding of the Temple at Jerusalem, as told in Ezra chapter 4. Who they were is doubtful, and this short entry weighs the guesses. They may link to a nomadic Persian tribe named by Herodotus, or to a city on Assyrian tablets. The Greek Septuagint reads the word differently in its two main copies. In one it is not a people's name at all, but part of a phrase meaning the Elamites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dobruska-moses-:
Moses Dobruska was an Austrian writer and poet born on July 12, 1753, at Brünn in Moravia. Son of a wealthy Jew, he was raised for the rabbinate with careful Talmudic schooling. A love of Hebrew poetry and German classics turned him away. He was guillotined at Paris on April 5, 1793.

On Dec. 17, 1773, Dobruska took the Catholic faith at Prague and the name Franz Thomas Schönfeld. He and his brothers were raised to the nobility in 1778. He served as associate director of the Garelli Library in Vienna. His books include pastorals, a theory of the fine sciences, and David's war songs in German. The entry admits the cause of his execution is unknown.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dubno-solomon-b:
Solomon ben Joel Dubno was a Russian poet, grammarian, and student of the Masorah. He was born at Dubno, Volhynia, in October 1738. Married at fourteen, he outgrew his local teachers. In Galicia he studied Bible and grammar under Solomon of Cholm. He died at Amsterdam on June 26, 1813.

Dubno lived at Amsterdam from 1767 to 1772, drawn by its Hebrew books. At Berlin he taught, and Moses Mendelssohn's son was his pupil. Mendelssohn became his patron and friend. Dubno wrote commentary for Mendelssohn's Bible translation, partly printed in 1778. Late in life he lived by lending books from his rich library.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eger-or-egers-5:
Eger is a rabbinical family long settled at Halberstadt, in Germany. Its first known members went by the name Gins or Ginsmann. The family's giant is Akiba Eger the Younger. He was born at Eisenstadt, Hungary, on Nov. 8, 1761. He died at Posen on Oct. 12, 1837.

Akiba showed rare Talmudic gift as a boy, and his uncle raised him at Breslau. A rich Lissa patron married him to his daughter and kept him free of want. For years he refused any rabbinical post on principle. He disliked taking pay for study of the Law. The entry prints the family pedigree and sketches of its leading members.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-b-matta: Eleazar ben Mattai, also called Matthias, was a tanna of the second century. He learned under Rabbi Tarphon. The entry places him in debates with Judah ben Illai and Simon ben Yohai. It also counts him among the skilled linguists of the court at Jamnia. One saying of his is quoted at length. A man who sees a wrong was bound to see it, he taught. A man who sees a good deed has earned that sight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-cohen-be: Elijah Cohen ben Moses ben Nissim was an Oriental scholar. He lived in the late thirteenth century. His work was a translation from Arabic into Hebrew. The source was a makamah, a tale in rhymed prose. Works of Hariri set the model for that kind. His version bears the title Megillat ha-Ofer. A handwritten copy rests in the Bodleian Library. Part of the work was printed in a Hebrew journal. The entry gives no facts of his own life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ena-rab-5747: Ena was a Babylonian scholar of the third century. He stood in the third amoraic generation of his age. Men paired him with Rab Judah as an elder of Pumbedita. Once he gave a talk at the exilarch's house. A younger man, Rabbah, called the talk a shock. He said Ena should lose his spokesman for it. Rab Nahman held a higher view of Ena's learning. Twice the two men clashed on points of law. Each fit its own case, he held in the end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-escalona-5847: Escalona was a city of Castile said to be named after Ascalon in Palestine. Jews lived there from a very early date, the entry says. A charter granted in 1130 by Alfonso VII barred Jews and Moors from judging Christians. It set a fine of 300 sueldos for killing a Jew. In 1391 many Jews of Escalona were killed, and others were forced to accept baptism. The ghetto lasted until the general expulsion. As late as 1474 it still paid a tax of 1,000 maravedis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezbai-5947: Ezbai is known only as the father of Naarai, one of David's thirty mighty warriors. That single fact, from First Chronicles, is the entry's core. A puzzle follows. The parallel list in Second Samuel reads Paarai the Arbite instead of Naarai son of Ezbai. Kennicott, in a cited work, judged the Chronicles reading correct. The entry gives no life, place, tribe, or deed for Ezbai himself. He stands in the record only through his son's place on David's warrior list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-falaquera-palqu:
Shem-Tob ben Joseph Falaquera was a Spanish philosopher and poet born in 1225 and dead after 1290. He knew Arabic and Greek philosophy well and had a sharp critical sense, the entry says. Of his own life he tells nothing. His books, listed at length, aim to wed faith and reason.

His Dialogue between an orthodox Jew and a philosopher argues that Bible and Talmud agree fully with philosophy. Reshit Hokmah treats moral duties and the sciences. Ha-Mebakkesh surveys human knowledge in rhymed prose and verse. Sefer ha-Nefesh handles the soul after the Arab Aristotelians. His Moreh ha-Moreh comments on Maimonides' Guide, and he defended that book in a letter against French rabbis who attacked it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-festivals-6047:
Festivals in Hebrew are hag, a word first tied to a circling dance around a shrine, and mo'adim, set times. The entry sorts the terms with care. Hag points chiefly to the three farm feasts, or to Unleavened Bread and Tabernacles alone. Mo'adim covers the fixed holy days apart from Sabbath and New Moon. Joy is the mark of both words.

Old traces show sacrifice leading into feasting at these gatherings. Marriage games hinting at bride capture lasted into Second Temple times, and wild revelry was not rare. The entry then lists the feasts one by one. The Sabbath comes first, a day of rest and joy. New Moon, Passover, and the rest follow in order, each with its texts and rites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fischer-bernard:
Bernard Fischer was an Austrian rabbi and author born at Budikau in Bohemia on Jan. 12, 1821. He took his doctor's degree at Prague in 1850. From 1854 to 1863 he served small congregations in the Eger district. He prepared new editions of Buxtorf's rabbinic lexicon and of Wiener's Chaldaic grammar. Those came out in 1873 and 1882.

Fischer also edited a Hebrew monthly at Leipsic in 1863. His own later books came out at Leipsic as well. One, printed in 1896, treats art and the theatre for art and theatre friends. The other, printed in 1899, sets out the ground lines of philosophy and theosophy. The entry gives no death date for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fresco-david-63:
David Fresco was a Turkish writer born at Constantinople about 1850. He came of Spanish exiles. He edited five Judæo-Spanish papers one after another. The first began in 1871 and changed its name twice in two years. Later papers of his began in 1879, 1886, and 1888. His last, begun in 1889, was the best edited and most widely read such paper in the East.

Fresco was very popular with his readers. He turned many works into the Spanish-Jewish tongue. Among them were books on the Jews and science and on natural law. He also turned Mendelssohn's Jerusalem and a Hebrew novel of Zion's love. A French tale of Paris mysteries was among his later turns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldenthal-jaco:
Jacob Goldenthal was an Austrian Orientalist. He was born at Brody, Galicia, on April 16, 1815. He died at Vienna on Dec. 28, 1868. After study at Leipsic, he became principal of the Jewish school at Kishinef in 1843. In 1849 Vienna University made him professor of rabbinica and Oriental languages. He held that chair until his death.

Most of his work was editing old manuscripts. He issued Al-Ghazali's ethics in Hebrew dress. He also edited Averroes on Aristotle's "Rhetoric" in Hebrew translation. Nissim of Kairwan's Talmud methodology and Moses Rieti's poem followed. He catalogued the Hebrew manuscripts of Vienna's Imperial Library. He also wrote an Arabic grammar in Hebrew and ran two short-lived periodicals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gracian-solomon: Solomon ben Moses Gracian was a Talmudist of Barcelona. He lived at the end of the thirteenth century and into the fourteenth. He died in 1307. He joined the synod that signed with Solomon ben Adret against Maimonides' partisans. The decree was one of excommunication. Later, after Bedersi's letter to Adret, he worked to reconcile the two parties. His name appears three times in the "Minḥat Ḳena'ot." The entry points to letters 81, 83, and 87 there. It also cites Grätz's history for the wider quarrel over philosophy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gunzburg-benjam:
Benjamin Wolf Günzburg was a Polish physician and Talmudic scholar of the eighteenth century. Unlike most Polish Talmudists of his day, he turned to secular science. He studied medicine at Göttingen without dropping the Talmud. In 1737 he asked Jacob Emden a hard question. Might he dissect dead animals on Saturdays? Emden's answer shows deep respect for him.

His medical work, "De Medicina ex Talmudicis Illustrata," appeared at Göttingen in 1743. It drew medicine from Talmudic sources. Hillel Noah Maggid thinks he may be the same Benjamin Wolf Günzburg of Ostrog. That man's notes appear in Joshua Falk's "Goral Yehoshua'." The entry leaves the identity as a scholar's judgment, not a settled fact.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hahn-august-704:
August Hahn, born at Grossosterhausen, Saxony, on March 27, 1792, was a German theologian and Orientalist who died in Silesia on May 13, 1863. He studied theology and Oriental tongues at Leipsic, with a bent for Syriac. His 1819 treatise on Ephraem the Syrian won him a chair at Königsberg.

At Königsberg he wrote on Bardesanes and, with Sieffert, a Syriac reader from Ephraem. Called to Leipsic in 1826, he fought a hard campaign against rationalism in theology and the Church. From 1833 he taught at Breslau, and in 1844 he became general superintendent of Silesia. He is best known for his Tauchnitz edition of the Old Testament text of 1833, which sold in the hundreds of thousands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hammerschlag-jo: Joseph Nathan Hammerschlag was a Moravian cabalist of the seventeenth century. The entry lists three works, all still in manuscript at the Bodleian Library. "Or ha-Ganuz" is a commentary on part of the Zohar, begun in 1648. "Sefer Mo'ade ha-Shem" treats the calendar, starting with the year 1681, and was written at Nikolsburg. The third item is cabalistic notes on the prayers, written in the margins of printed Psalms and of the prayers for the first evening of Rosh ha-Shanah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harburg-7247:
Harburg was a city on the Elbe, six miles south of Hamburg, in the Prussian province of Hanover. Jews were not admitted there until the seventeenth century. In 1621 Duke William August leased his new mint to three Jews and took their families under his protection. They could trade, travel, and settle in the town.

The entry traces the small community through the next two centuries. It records trade bans, limits on buying houses, and a tax paid by each family. A burial ground was assigned in 1690, and leave to build a synagogue came in 1776. By 1903 the community held about 50 families, or about 300 persons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hawaiian-island: The Hawaiian Islands are a group of twelve islands in the North Pacific, eight of them inhabited. Their people numbered 154,000 in 1902, with about 100 Jews among them. The islands became United States land in 1898. The first Jew known to visit was A. S. Grinbaum, who reached Honolulu in 1856. His family firm grew into a large wholesale house. More Jews settled after the queen fell in 1893. Honolulu gained its first Hebrew congregation in 1901, with forty members. Its cemetery was consecrated in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hebrew-educatio:
The Hebrew Education Society of Philadelphia was set up on July 16, 1848, largely through Isaac Leeser's work. Its charter allowed schools joining general study with Hebrew language and letters. It could even found a higher seminary with degree powers. The first school opened in 1851 in rooms over a hose house.

A legacy of 20,000 dollars from Judah Touro's estate in 1854 bought a lasting home. More schools followed across the city, and Maimonides College ran from 1867 to 1873. By the time of writing, the work centered on Touro Hall. It held night classes, trade training, baths, a reading room, and a lending library. Other Jewish groups used the buildings free.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heman-7547:
Heman is the name of two men in the Bible. The first, called the Singer, was a Levite set by David over the music of the Temple. His fourteen sons sang under him, each heading one of the Levite courses. He is also called the king's seer in the matters of God. The second Heman was a son of Mahol, famed for wisdom.

The entry wrestles with a puzzle. The Eighty-eighth Psalm is ascribed to a Heman, but which one? Its title mixes a Korah line with the name Ezrahite. That points both ways at once. The piece leaves the question open, with the evidence laid out on each side.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hess-mendel-764:
Mendel Hess, born at Lengsfeld on March 17, 1807, was a German rabbi who joined university study with Talmud training. From 1828 until his death he was chief rabbi of Weimar. He lived first at Lengsfeld, later at Eisenach.

Hess enforced a state decree for German-only services, despite Jewish anger. His post forced him to report those who missed services. He blessed mixed marriages under set terms and joined the rabbinical conferences of 1844-46. There he backed strong radical reform. After 1848 he asked the state to repeal forced attendance. He also edited a Jewish paper from 1839 to 1848 and printed sermons. He died at Eisenach on Sept. 21, 1871.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hurwitz-hayyim-: Hayyim ben Joshua Moses Abraham ha-Levi Hurwitz was a Russian rabbi of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Four books carry his name. Sefer Mayim Hayyim explains the Pentateuch and the five Megillot and appeared at Dyhernfurth in 1690. A supplement followed in 1703. Sefer Nahalat Hayyim gives novellae on several Talmudic treatises, printed at Wilmersdorf in 1713 with an index. A second Nahalat Hayyim, on the Pentateuch, came out in 1714. The entry lists sources but no life events.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ichabod-8047: Ichabod was the son of Phinehas and grandson of Eli. He was born after his father fell in battle and his grandfather died in shock. His dying mother named him Ichabod, a name read as no glory, crying that the glory had departed from Israel. His name thus kept the memory of a crushing defeat. The Greek version reads it as woe to the glory of Israel. The name appears once more, where his brother Ahijah is named as a priest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ir-shemesh-city: Ir-shemesh is a short entry, and it says only a few things, all stated plainly. Ir-shemesh was a city of Dan, named with Shaalabbin and Ajalon at Josh. xix. 41-42. Its parallel name in Judges i. 35 is "Har-Heres," rendered "the mountain of the sun." Some modern critics identify it with Beth-shemesh in Judah. The entry closes by pointing to the article on Heres. Nothing further is given: no history, no later fate, and no discussion beyond the identification question and the two biblical mentions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ise-isi-jose-be:
Ise ben Judah, also called Jose ben Judah, was a Palestinian tanna of the second century, a contemporary of Simeon ben Yohai and of R. Meir. Bacher thought him the same man as Jose the Babylonian. The Sayings of the Fathers quote his image of learning: from the young, like eating unripe grapes; from the old, like ripe grapes and old wine. He was known for his high praise of fellow scholars.

He taught that a lack of mutual respect brings early death to scholars. Against Jose ha-Gelili, he held that the command to rise before the hoary head covers any old man, not only scholars. He also ranked a father's order above a duty another person could perform instead. The entry credits him with spotting five Bible passages where a word cannot be tied firmly to what comes before or after it. That note later entered the Masorah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jedidiah-ben-mo: Jedidiah ben Moses of Recanati, also called Amadeo of Rimini, was an Italian scholar of the second half of the sixteenth century. At the request of Immanuel di Fano he translated Maimonides' Guide into Italian in 1580, under a title meaning instruction for the perplexed. Parts of that version, still in manuscript, were printed in 1892. He also made a Hebrew-Italian word book of the Bible and wrote math notes and a hymn that spells his name in its first letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jolles-zecharia: Zechariah Isaiah ben Mordecai Jolles was a rabbinical scholar and author born at Lemberg about 1814. In 1834 he married into a rich Minsk family and settled in that city. He sided with the Haskalah, the movement for wider learning, and backed school plans brought to Minsk in 1844. His printed works treat fixes to the Talmud text, a letter to men seeking the rabbinate, and readings on Maimonides, the last printed after his death. More than twenty-five other works are credited to him. He died at Minsk on May 14, 1852.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-b-jacob-: Joseph b. Jacob Isaac was a rabbi at Yampol in Russia and later at Zamoscz, and he died in 1807. He wrote Mishnat Hakamim, a book on varied subjects that included Maimonides' Maddah. Notes by his son Isaac, rabbi of Chelm, were added at the end of the book. Joseph also refers there to his son's rulings on the laws of the Sabbath and festivals. That work by Isaac bore the title Otot le-Moadim. The entry is short and rests on two later reference books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judenschreinsbu: The Judenschreinsbuch is a set of deeds belonging to Jews of the St. Lawrence parish in Cologne, Germany. Since the thirteenth century the deeds had been kept in a separate alcove, and later they were bound into book form. The deeds were written in Latin and often in Hebrew as well, with the Hebrew text sewn to the Latin paper. They run from about 1230 to 1347. Robert Hoeniger and Moritz Stern edited the set at Berlin in 1888 for a historical commission.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaula-al-yahudi: Kaula al-Yahudi was a Jewish general of the eighth century. Tariḳ appointed him to command. He fought with valor at Xerez against the Visigoths. His army was made up of Jews and Berbers. He took part of Catalonia as well. Then he rose against Al-Ḥurr, the harsh governor of Spain. Al-Ḥurr beat him near Lerida with a larger force. Kaula was taken and put to death in 718. The Jews of his army found shelter with their kin in Catalonia's cities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kirstein-moritz: Moritz Kirstein was a German physician. He was born at Filehne in 1830 and died in Berlin on July 12, 1896. He took his M.D. degree at Berlin in 1855. He then went to Vienna and Prague for post-graduate study. Kirstein settled as a physician in Berlin. In 1860 he was the first practitioner there to use the laryngeal mirror. With it he explored the larynx and the thoracic cavities. At his death he was a member of the Berlin board of health.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kolisch-rudolf-: Rudolf Kolisch, an Austrian physician born at Koritschan in Moravia on Dec. 10, 1867, studied medicine at Vienna and Heidelberg. He took his medical degree in 1891. In 1895 he became privat-docent in medicine at the University of Vienna. Alongside his lectures he practises at Carlsbad during the summer months. His writings include journal essays and two books, one on uratic diathesis dated 1894 and a textbook on dietetic therapy dated 1899. The entry lists no family or communal details beyond this career outline.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kulka-adolf-954: Adolf Kulka, an Austrian journalist born on Oct. 5, 1823, at Leipnik in Moravia, died at Vienna on Dec. 5, 1898. He studied philosophy and law at Prague and Vienna. In 1848 he took part in the unrest and was the first author whose poems were printed with no censor. From 1854 he wrote political leaders for a Vienna daily. With a partner he founded a law journal and ran it for over forty years. A book of poems named Chanuca-Lichter is singled out among his many pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lemuel-9747: Lemuel is a king named in the heading of Proverbs chapter thirty-one, a chapter addressed to him by his mother. The entry lays out rival readings of that heading. Cheyne reads the name as Jerahmeel. Others join Lemuel with the next word, massa, and read King of Massa, an Ishmaelite people named in Genesis. Toy rejects that reading and any symbolic one. The name itself, like Lael, means Godward.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levin-judah-lob:
Judah Löb Levin, called Jehalel, was a Hebrew poet born at Minsk in 1845. He studied Talmud under noted rabbis and read the whole Talmud by sixteen. Marriage into a Hasidic family turned him to the Zohar and mystic books. In 1868 he went to Kiev as a tutor in the Brodski home.

Levin began writing Hebrew verse at ten. For thirty years his poems ran in the main Hebrew journals. His 1877 book holds four long poems on the social state of Russian Jews, with a socialist bent. He also made an epic, "Elhanan," on the same theme. In 1883 he turned Disraeli's "Tancred" into Hebrew. By 1904 he worked as treasurer of a Brodski sugar refinery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-liboschutz-osip: Osip Yarovlevich Liboschütz, a Russian physician, died at St. Petersburg in 1824. He was probably a son of Jacob Liboschütz. He took his medical degree at Dorpat in 1806. He then settled at St. Petersburg, where he became court physician. He founded a hospital for sick children there. His books are botanical: a table of plant genera seen in Russia, a study of mosses near St. Petersburg and Moscow, and a flora of those two regions, all from 1811.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lizard-10047:
Lizard surveys the small reptiles of Palestine and the Hebrew words that may name them. About forty kinds are counted there, with the green lizard and wall lizard among the most common. Several Bible words for creeping things are matched to the gecko, monitor, sand lizard, and chameleon.

Talmud notes add detail on skin, eggs, and odd tales. One tale tells of a lizard thought dead and revived by cold water. Another links a lizard kind to fear in scorpions and to a cure for their sting. King Amon is said to have placed such a creature on the altar after ending Temple service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machorro-spelle:
Machorro, a Sephardic family name spelled many ways, is traced in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. The family flourished in Brazil, Germany, Holland, Hungary, and Italy. Thirteen of its members lie buried at Altona, with gravestones running from 1620 to 1782. The entry gathers scattered mentions across three centuries.

The article picks out individual Machorros from the record. Abraham and Moses flourished at Amsterdam in the mid-seventeenth century, and Abraham won praise as flutist and writer alike. Elijah lived in Brazil about the same time. Moses ben Daniel served as rabbi in Venice around 1693, and one of his legal decisions was printed at Amsterdam. A darker note names Juan Pacheco de Leon, alias Solomon Machorro, among the Maranos tried in Mexico in the 1640s. The entry shows one family's spread across the Sephardic world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manasseh-ben-jo:
Manasseh ben Joseph of Ilye, a Russian rabbinical writer, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Smorgony in 1767, he knew rabbinic sources by age seven. His father barred him from Bible and Hebrew grammar, fearing they would crowd out Talmud. He married at thirteen and settled in Ilye. He died there in 1831.

The article stresses his independence of mind. Among his disciples he criticized even the Shulhan Aruk and Rashi. He read some Mishnah passages against the Gemara's own reading. Only a powerful rabbi's protection kept the ban from him. Elijah of Wilna welcomed him yearly until hearing he also visited the Hasidic leader Zalman of Liozna. Then the gaon held aloof, though Manasseh protested that love of knowledge alone drew him. Still, he credited Elijah with teaching him the plain-sense method. The entry portrays a mind caught between orthodoxy, Hasidism, and new learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-martyrs-the-ten:
The Ten Martyrs were ten great teachers said to have been executed under the emperor Hadrian. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote their Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Tradition says the ten were killed for teaching the Law to their pupils. They taught in defiance of a Roman edict. Legend soon added detail and drama to their deaths.

The article compares the older Talmudic accounts with a special midrash on the story, the Midrash Eleh Ezkerah. That midrash survives in four versions. Where the Talmud spreads the executions over time, the midrash gathers them into a single day. It also invents the charge against them. An emperor cites the Bible's death penalty for man-stealing and blames the teachers for the ancient sale of Joseph.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medina-sir-solo:
Sir Solomon de Medina, who bankrolled Marlborough's armies, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind. A wealthy Jew who came to England with William III, he was known simply as "the Jew Medina." Through the War of the Spanish Succession he marched with the Duke of Marlborough, advancing him funds and furnishing the troops. His private couriers ran faster than the government's, so his agents often held great news before the ministers of the crown did.

That closeness made scandal. In 1711 Parliament attacked Marlborough for taking 6,000 pounds a year from Medina; the duke answered that the money bought trustworthy information. Medina was knighted for his services, the first Jew in England so honored, and he remained the largest contributor to the Bevis Marks Synagogue. The entry adds, dryly, that his descendants abandoned Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-vardima:
Menahem Vardimas ben Perez the Elder was a French tosafist and liturgist. He died at Dreux in 1224. Solomon Schechter and Isaac Broydé profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His strange second name comes from the Talmud itself. There, Vardimas appears as a by-name of a Menahem bar Jose. This later Menahem likely adopted it to stand apart. His age held many Menahems.

His authority carried weight. Moses of Coucy invokes him in the "Semag." The famous medieval discussion on the order of the phylacteries was held, by one tradition, in his own house. Samuel of Falaise called him master and "the Holy One." Gross reads that phrase as "the Pious," not "the Martyr." A liturgical poem of his treats the binding of Isaac. It found its way into the New Year ritual. A manuscript commentary cites him on the Bible as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-adolph-10:
Adolph Meyer, born at New Orleans on October 19, 1842, was a Louisiana congressman whose life is sketched in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Cyrus Adler, published in 1906. He was studying at the University of Virginia when the Civil War broke out. In 1862 he joined the Confederate army and rose to assistant adjutant-general.

After the war Meyer grew sugar and cotton and worked in finance in New Orleans, while leading the state National Guard as colonel and then brigadier-general. Elected as a Democrat from Louisiana's First District to the Fifty-second Congress, he was reelected through the Fifty-eighth. The entry notes his service on the committees on Naval Affairs and the District of Columbia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minden-judah-lo:
Judah Löb ben Joel Minden, a German lexicographer working in Berlin in the 1760s, made the first Hebrew dictionary ever produced by a Jew with German translations. Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. His Millim le-Eloah appeared in 1760 with the approval of the Berlin and Halberstadt rabbinates.

Zunz called the book the first attempt to bring High German into Jewish national literature, the article notes. Minden built on David Ḳimḥi's dictionary, added material from the Concordance, and discussed what each Hebrew letter does in grammar. Five years later he reissued Musafia's Zeker Rab as a supplement to his own work, rounding out the toolkit for German readers of Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monies-david-10:
David Monies, a Danish portrait and genre painter born at Copenhagen on June 3, 1812, is entered by Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Academy of Arts took him at twelve and gave him silver medals at fifteen and twenty. Portraits of eminent contemporaries made his start in 1830.

A public grant of four hundred rix-dollars a year sent him to Munich in 1835 to continue his studies. He entered the Danish Academy in 1848 and became professor in 1859.
