The reference standard will be an unusually thorough version of the standard stool method. Better tests are central to confirming where the disease is truly gone.
plos-pone-0350647:
Fei Liu and colleagues surveyed Chinese Super League soccer spectators to map how league quality shapes loyalty. Just under three hundred valid responses from match day surveys fed a model linking felt league quality, satisfaction, trust, belonging to a team, and loyalty. Expert review and a pilot run polished the questions first.

Felt quality lifted satisfaction, trust, and team belonging strongly, but did not lift loyalty directly. Satisfaction and trust alone also failed to move loyalty. Belonging was the bridge: fans who feel part of a team stay loyal, and quality reaches loyalty through that bond. League managers should sell identity and belonging, not just match quality and service.
plos-pone-0350747:
Robinson and colleagues presented a computing framework for fitting disease models with built-in uncertainty in a 2026 paper. Outbreak models simplify real spread, so fitting them to noisy data must allow for model error itself. Their method estimates hidden states, changing settings, fixed settings, and the simplest model structure all at once.

Letting settings drift over time absorbs some mismatch between model and reality. A penalty for complexity guards against chasing noise. The framework targets compartment models of infection, where officials need honest ranges, not single numbers. Careful handling of model error can keep forecasts humble and more useful for planning hospital and vaccine needs.
plos-pone-0350847:
Dorra Abdelmalek and colleagues went hunting for a new use for old cancer drugs: blocking the normal, non-mutated form of a growth receptor that many tumors lean on. Most approved blockers target mutated versions of the receptor, leaving patients whose tumors use the normal form with few options. From a library of approved kinase drugs first built against another target, computer screening pulled five candidates.

All five fit the receptor's fuel pocket in simulation, and one, labeled D4, gripped the key hinge and switch residues best. A hundred-nanosecond molecular movie showed the pairing held steady, and energy calculations backed it. Everything here is in silico, a ranked shortlist rather than a medicine. Still, repurposing approved compounds starts years ahead of new chemistry, so a credible shortlist is worth the laboratory tests it now invites.
plos-pone-0350947:
Soumya Ranjan Das and colleagues tackled dirty power that appears when solar panels and electric cars join the same local grid. Sun power swings with clouds, and car charging jumps without warning, so voltage waves can distort. Their fix uses a neural network controller that learns how to clean the wave, tested in computer simulation under heavy, uneven loads.

Without help, distortion sat near twenty six percent. A simple passive filter cut it by about half, and an adaptive method cut it much further. The neural network did best, bringing distortion down close to one percent with faster settling. Cleaner power protects gear, cuts waste, and helps grids welcome more solar power and cars at once.
plos-pone-0351147:
Marie A Brault and colleagues present a protocol, with no results yet, for mapping how puberty teaching for young teens is judged. Puberty shapes lifelong health habits, yet courses for eight to fourteen year olds vary widely and share no agreed skill list. The review will chart which outcomes, topics, and test tools past courses for this age group have used.

Searches will span ten sources, covering journals, theses, and broad indexes. Two reviewers will screen and extract with a shared tool, following standard scoping guidance. Results will feed a shared framework for building and judging puberty courses. A common yardstick could help schools compare courses and spot missing topics early.
plos-pone-0351247:
Namrata Ahuja and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One genome study of siphonophores. These drifting ocean colonies are made of many specialized bodies acting as one animal. The team produced a chromosome-level genome for one species, Nanomia septata. They sequenced twenty more specimens from around the world for comparison.

The genome is large. Yet it is packed into far fewer chromosomes than its relatives have. That is proof of repeated chromosome fusions. Surprisingly, nothing in the genome clearly explains the colony's elaborate division of labor. Key gene families had not expanded. Gene position rarely matched where genes are active, except in male reproductive bodies. Population data supported three known species, plus one undescribed species. Genome size had shrunk again in some lines.
plos-pone-0351547:
Sofie Jespersen and colleagues tested hard interval exercise in a hard-to-treat group. Their patients lived with both chronic hepatitis B and a fatty liver. That pairing raises the risk of serious liver harm. Patients were assigned by chance to twelve weeks of interval training or to no program. Liver fat was measured by MRI scans.

Recruitment went slowly, and the trial stopped early. Only nineteen patients joined, and fourteen finished. Liver fat fell a bit more in the training group. The gap was small and not close to firm proof. The study reads as a lesson in feasibility. The question is fair, but far more patients are needed to answer it.
plos-pone-0351747:
John Amoah-Mensah and colleagues built a math model of typhoid fever that gives dirty water a central role in spreading the disease. Typhoid thrives where sanitation is poor and clean water is scarce, yet many models skip the environment and count only person-to-person spread. Their equations track people and the contaminated water that links them.

The team worked out the threshold at which typhoid settles in for good and checked which factors push spread hardest. They then tested two levers inside the model: teaching the public about hygiene and treating contaminated water. Models like this cannot replace field data, but they help officials see which mix of education and water treatment might cut cases most before money is spent.
plos-pone-0351847:
Pinpin Jiang and colleagues chased a driver of osteoarthritis, the joint disease that wears cartilage away. Their suspect is a protein that senses low oxygen, called HIF-2α. Cartilage lives short of oxygen by design, so its oxygen sensors matter. The team measured the protein in human cartilage. They then turned it down and up in cartilage cells inflamed to mimic disease. In rats, they silenced it in knees injured to trigger joint decay.

The protein ran high in diseased cartilage. It worked by suppressing a protective chain of signals inside the cells. With that chain muted, cartilage cells moved toward programmed death. Cell and animal results line up: the protein speeds the disease rather than watching it. A named accelerator is a target drug hunters can aim at.
plos-pone-0351947:
Depression and compulsive gaming feed each other in teenagers, and Qian Li and colleagues asked whether parents are pulled into the same loop. Their 2026 PLOS One study surveyed more than twelve hundred parent and child pairs in Hong Kong, with teens answering at school and parents replying online or by phone.

Each person's low mood lined up with their own gaming problems. Teen depression also lined up with parents' gaming problems, a cross effect within the family. How warm the family relationship felt, and how long the teen gamed, carried part of these links. The authors argue help should treat the household, not the teenager alone.
plos-pone-0352147:
Eric Osoro and seven colleagues screen thousands of compounds for a kinder way to kill malaria mosquitoes. Their 2026 study targets the mosquito's juvenile hormone system. Blocking the protein that carries this hormone can derail mosquito development. The team virtually screened nearly twenty-nine hundred agrochemical compounds on the computer. Docking tests ranked how tightly each gripped the target protein. Energy calculations, chemistry checks, and toxicity predictions narrowed the list further. Fifteen lead compounds survived.

The best of them bound as strongly as the natural reference compound in simulations. Long dynamics runs tested whether those grips held over time. Electronic structure analysis favoured the same shortlist. The study pairs this computing with laboratory larvicide evaluation, per its design. Mosquito control leans heavily on a few insecticides, and resistance keeps growing. Hormone-targeted candidates, screened early for environmental safety, widen the arsenal before field resistance closes the current one.
plos-pone-0352247:
Xavier Perrier and seven colleagues collect bananas across northern Vietnam, Laos, and China's Yunnan region to rewrite the crop's origin story, in this 2026 genetic study. Cultivated banana diversity is only partly catalogued, yet new varieties with useful traits are urgently needed as diseases and climate stress mount. The team gathered ninety-one specimens, including four native wild relatives, and read their DNA for signatures of ancestry.

Farmers in the region grow many previously undescribed local varieties. Every one carried genomic traces of the endemic wild species, including the first polyploid varieties holding a complete set of genes from one local wild relative. The landraces were not domesticated on the spot. They arose when local wild plants crossed with already-domesticated bananas that arrived from farther south, possibly by an eastern route through southern China or the Philippines. Diversity, the authors say, accumulated after domestication.
plos-pone-0352347:
Jimena Fritz and seven colleagues build instruments to measure the quality of maternity care in Mexico, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Mexico lacked a thorough, culturally grounded way to judge care across pregnancy, birth, and the newborn period. Seventy-eight national experts — researchers, decision-makers, and advocates — worked through two workshops, starting from more than a thousand candidate indicators and winnowing them by structured rating.

The final set holds just under five hundred indicators across five domains, from the woman's experience to supplies and medicines. They were shaped into three tools: an interview guide for mothers, an observation checklist for births, and a hospital survey. The instruments give Mexico a common yardstick for finding care gaps.
plos-pone-0352647:
Hieu Giang Le and four colleagues tune the settings of an injection-moulding machine to make plastic parts stronger, in this 2026 PLOS ONE engineering study. Their materials were a common moulding plastic, plain and reinforced with woven carbon fibre, made by a two-step process that moulds around the fabric. Five settings — two pressures, two timings, and melt temperature — were varied systematically across a designed set of runs.

Adding carbon fibre raised bending strength modestly and pulling strength by roughly a sixth. Filling pressure dominated all others in influence. A combined statistical method picked the best setting recipe, and confirmation runs landed within a few percent of predictions. Small setting changes, it turns out, are free strength.
plos-pone-0353347:
Xiaoxi Huang and seven colleagues published this 2026 protein study on how stomach lining changes on the road to cancer. Infection with Helicobacter pylori bacteria drives a slow sequence from inflamed tissue to cancer, but the protein steps are poorly mapped. The team measured proteins in tissue from twenty-two patients across four stages of that sequence.

Protein groups tied to building ribosomes, the cell's protein factories, rose with progression and stand out as candidate warning markers. Meanwhile proteins for energy production steadily fell, pointing to failing cell power plants. Huang's stage-by-stage map may help doctors spot dangerous change earlier.
plos-pone-0353847:
Thomas and colleagues, in a 2026 study in Malaysia, compare behavior and feelings in teenage boys who were born with color vision deficiency and boys with normal color vision. Seeing color differently can complicate school and social life, yet its emotional effects in the teen years are little studied. The team screened schoolboys and matched forty-four boys in each group by age and class.

Parents rated behavior on a standard checklist. Boys with color deficiency scored higher on most problem scales, including anxiety and low mood, withdrawal, attention trouble, and aggressive and rule-breaking behavior. Attention problems showed the strongest tie. More of these boys fell into the borderline or clinical range on several scales. One twist stood out: among boys with color deficiency, those whose parents had more education showed more difficulties on some scales, perhaps because expectations run higher. The authors call for awareness and support in schools.
plos-pone-0354147:
Kennedy and colleagues, in a 2026 national survey, ask American parents whether they talk other parents into or out of vaccinating their children. The question gained urgency as the United States recorded its worst measles year in a quarter century. About thirteen hundred parents of children aged nine to twelve answered, weighted to stand for the country.

More than a third said they at least sometimes encourage other parents to vaccinate, while about one in ten said they discourage it; a small share did both. Confidence that vaccines matter for their own child's health predicted encouraging and protected against discouraging. Encouragers most often championed the measles and flu shots, speaking to family and close friends and sharing their own experience. Discouragers aimed mostly at COVID and flu shots, rarely measles. The authors suggest public health campaigns recruit the much larger pool of parent encouragers as partners.
plos-pone-0354247:
Waqar Shah and six colleagues tackle message routing in networks formed by moving vehicles, an area of research aimed at cutting road accidents. Cars in these networks relay warnings to each other, but the connections keep breaking as vehicles move, and urgent safety messages can get crowded out by ordinary traffic. Earlier routing methods, the authors argue, handle these problems poorly.

Their new protocol, called PDBFS, chooses routes using direction, the relative speed between vehicles, and how much traffic each route already carries. It also gives time-critical safety messages priority over other data. In computer simulations, PDBFS lost fewer packets, moved data faster, cut delays, and kept links alive longer than three rival protocols. The gains suggest smarter route choice could make vehicle warnings more dependable.
plos-pone-0354347:
Pavitra Jindahra, Stefano Starita, and Pinnaree Tea-makorn published this 2026 analysis of how chronic diseases cluster in Thailand. A national health survey of well over a hundred thousand people covered nine long-term conditions. Statistical grouping searched for natural bundles of illness, then linked each bundle to age, sex, residence, weight, and habits.

Four patterns emerged, from low burden to heavy combined illness. Older age raised the odds of every illness pattern, while city living and excess weight shaped particular bundles. Jindahra argues prevention should target these distinct risk profiles, not single diseases alone.
plos-pone-0354747:
Noa Gluskinos is first author on a 2026 PLOS ONE qualitative study of HIV outreach care in rural Zimbabwe. Moving antiretroviral therapy, the drug treatment for HIV, from central hospitals to local clinics brought care to millions. Its side effects on patients and providers were less clear.

Sixty interviews with leaders, providers, patients, and community members around a mission hospital were coded for themes. Participants agreed access had improved under treatment-for-all rules. But outreach also brought unintended harms. Stigma and tangled social relations shaped how care worked in practice and could raise social barriers to treatment. Understanding these local consequences, the authors argue, is needed for truly accessible care.
plos-pone-0355047:
Khanh Nguyen tackles in 2026 a control theory problem: keeping a fuzzy modelled system stable when its parts are sampled at different rates. Real controllers often read some signals faster than others, and the model's fuzzy rules may not match the controller's rules. Earlier proofs could waste useful information about timing delays between samples.

Nguyen builds a richer stability test that uses the newest readings and the delay tied to each state. A softer relaxation step makes the mismatched rules easier to handle without losing rigour. Two worked examples show the test holds in practice. The result is aimed at engineers designing sampled control systems.
plos-pone-0355547:
Linda Lait and colleagues mapped the family structure of the Plains Sucker, a freshwater fish of rivers east of the Rockies that was only recently recognized as its own species. Their 2026 study sequenced DNA from 371 fish at twenty-one sites in Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Montana, comparing two great drainage systems, the Missouri Basin and the Saskatchewan-Nelson Basin.

The basins hold clearly separate populations. Missouri tributaries were fragmented from each other, while Saskatchewan-Nelson fish mixed freely, suggesting recent connection. One population, in the Frenchman River, stood apart from all others and carried thinned genetic diversity, a fingerprint of drought-driven isolation. The authors argue Missouri populations, boxed in and genetically poor, need the most urgent protection from barriers and climate stress.
plos-pone-0355847:
Richmond Kwakye and coauthors published a 2026 case-control study in PLOS ONE on pregnant women in Ghana, examining a tolerance molecule called HLA-G alongside malaria and miscarriage. HLA-G helps the immune system accept the fetus, but that quieting may let the malaria parasite thrive and may relate to pregnancy loss. The team compared forty-six infected women with forty-six uninfected women, confirming parasite tests by microscope and measuring blood chemistry.

Infected women showed a liver enzyme pattern pointing to strain, with one enzyme still elevated after adjustment, plus higher inflammatory blood ratios. Skipping the preventive malaria medicine given in pregnancy was strongly tied to being infected. Women with a history of miscarriage carried considerably higher HLA-G levels than women without that history. HLA-G deserves prospective study as a marker of pregnancy risk in malaria regions, they suggest, though their sample was small.
plos-pone-0355947:
Rampukar Sah and six colleagues document violence in the lives of adolescent psychiatric patients in Nepal, in this 2026 study. Their sample was eight hundred ten patients aged eleven to fifteen at Kathmandu's Kanti Children's Hospital. Teenagers reported their past-year exposure to physical, emotional, and sexual abuse, neglect, and domestic violence, while parents supplied family background. The team modeled which social and family traits accompanied each kind of exposure.

Patterns were sharply social. Physical abuse fell more often on Dalit adolescents; neglect and domestic violence on Indigenous and minority groups relative to the highest castes. Girls faced far more emotional abuse, sexual abuse, and neglect than boys. Urban residence, single-parent homes, younger mothers, and parental illiteracy each raised particular risks, while rural and semi-urban settings lowered some. The authors call for culturally informed, trauma-focused prevention aimed at the families carrying the heaviest load.
plos-pone-0356147:
Gabriel Budel, Robert E. Kooij, and Michiel Tjepkema published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on the Beatles hiding in scientific paper titles. Researchers love a catchy title, and Beatles songs offer shared cultural shorthand. From a curated list of songs and lyrics, the team searched a major database, screened candidates with large language models, and verified survivors by hand.

They cataloged well over two thousand exact references to Beatles titles and lyrics, plus nearly a thousand creative wordplays bending the words into scientific puns. Use has grown over the decades faster than scientific publishing itself, and it clusters unevenly across disciplines, some fields punning far more than others. The paper is, the authors note, the first systematic cross-disciplinary account of this particular cultural borrowing. Beyond the fun, it shows how pop culture quietly frames serious work, and how language models help catch wordplay keyword searches miss.
plos-pone-0356247:
Lana Sallam and colleagues tested whether pressurised oxygen can shield healthy cells from radiation damage. Pelvic radiotherapy can scar tissue and cause lasting pain, so protection matters. Their 2026 laboratory study irradiated three kinds of surface and lining cells, then applied hyperbaric oxygen treatment.

Oxygen treatment reduced radiation-driven cell death. Radiation had lowered several protective genes, including an immune sensor and antioxidant controls; oxygen restored their activity. A drug that switches that sensor on also protected cells, while a blocker removed the benefit. Sallam and colleagues conclude the sensor pathway helps explain the protection, and they propose combining both approaches in future mucosal protection research.
plos-pone-0356547:
Xi Gong and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE that treats late-night tweeting as a public health sensor. Sleeplessness is common and worsened during COVID, yet health systems have no real-time way to watch population sleep. The team analyzed geotagged American tweets posted between ten at night and six in the morning, from March 2020 to mid 2021, against a pre-pandemic baseline, mapping state patterns and topics.

States fell into three rhythm types: single-peak, multi-peak, and smooth nighttime patterns. Links between night tweeting and daily case counts shifted by state and pandemic stage. More negative emotion in night tweets went with greater inferred sleep disturbance, while night owls talked more about local news, and states with more diverse nighttime topics suffered less emotional damage. The framework is presented as a cheap, scalable complement to sleep surveys, transferable to other nighttime behavior.
plos-pone-0356647:
Samia Yaqoob and colleagues cooked up a wound dressing gel from chia seed mucilage, a slippery natural polymer, chemically married to a synthetic building block. Their 2026 study verified the new material's structure, then put it through a battery of tests: blood compatibility, antioxidant power, germ killing, safety in animals, and finally healing speed on rabbit wounds.

The gel spared red blood cells and clotting, fought both major classes of bacteria plus two fungi, and showed antioxidant activity throughout. Rabbits dosed orally, on skin, and near the eye showed no harm, and treated wounds closed about as fast as with a standard product, reaching most of the way in two weeks. A seed-based, non-toxic dressing could suit low-cost wound care.
plos-pone-0356747:
Lin Xie, Jialian Li, Yuan Xing, and Yuhui Wang pulled apart a near-alpha titanium alloy, the kind used in jet engines. They wanted to understand an extra strengthening effect that appears when hard and soft regions deform together. Their 2026 study compared two internal architectures of the same alloy: layered plates versus rounded grains. It measured the internal stress that builds as the mixed structure stretches.

Both architectures generated the extra stress early on. The rounded-grain version kept hardening far better as strain grew. The reasons were geometric. Rounded grains offer more boundary area per volume to anchor the dislocations involved. Their larger scale gives those dislocations room to pile up. The layered version's thin plates cramped the process. Alloy designers now know which architecture to favor.
plos-pone-0357047:
Hafez Mohammad Nazmul Ahsan and colleagues assessed how much disability leprosy still causes in Bangladesh. They surveyed 176 patients at two specialist treatment centers in spring 2024. Their 2026 hospital-based study graded physical impairment with the World Health Organization scale. It also measured depression symptoms, activity limits, and experiences of discrimination.

Nearly three quarters of these patients already had the most serious grade of impairment. Claw hands, foot drop, and eye damage were the commonest problems. Almost all had the multibacillary form of the disease. Because the sample comes from referral centers, the figures describe severe, late-presenting disease rather than the national picture. The authors argue earlier detection in rural areas is the lever that prevents lifelong disability.
plos-pone-0357247:
Correction notice: Giuseppe Battaglia and colleagues amend an earlier mouse brain study on a receptor that prompts production of a neuron-supporting factor. After publication, concerns arose over two figures. In one, lanes of a protein blot had been spliced from non-adjacent positions. The splice was not clearly marked. The authors now give the original loading order in full. One lane pair also looks alike. The lead author blames a possible slip while rearranging lanes for the figure.

Original blots are supplied with the notice. The authors state that contrast handling differed between panels for display. The underlying measurements, expressed as ratios, stand. The notice keeps the study in the record with its figure history made explicit for readers weighing the evidence.
plos-pone-0357447:
Aitor Ugena and five colleagues watch sea life rebuild itself on underwater lava flows near La Palma in the Canary Islands, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The island offers a rare natural experiment: three flows of very different ages, one under a year old, one from the mid twentieth century, and one about five centuries old. The team sampled algae, tiny settling invertebrates on artificial collectors, and established rock dwelling microinvertebrates on each flow.

The parts of the community recovered on different clocks. Algae were sparsest on the newest flow but looked much alike on the two older ones, settling early. Established microinvertebrates peaked in richness on the middle aged flow, while the oldest flow favored specialized and predatory species. Recovery after a volcanic disturbance, the authors show, is not one process but several running at different speeds side by side.
plos-pone-0358247:
Keiko Ikuta led a team of eight authors studying shared work in Japanese cancer care, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Cancer services in Japan are stretched, and pharmacists could take over some tasks now done by doctors in chemotherapy care. The team used a qualitative study to ask what helps and what hinders that shift.

Ikuta's findings map the practical and cultural factors at play, from trust and training to rules and workload. Safe task sharing could free doctors for work only they can do, while pharmacists use their drug expertise more fully. Other countries facing doctor shortages face the same choice. Japan's careful evidence on barriers gives them a checklist for making the shift safely.
plos-pone-0358347:
Qunting Chen, Xinhui Chen, and Geng Chen built a gesture control system for a bionic hand, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The hand is palm-scale with fifteen degrees of freedom, meaning many joints to coordinate. Controlling that many joints with human gestures in real time is a hard mapping problem.

The team's system translates a person's hand movements into matching robotic motion as they happen. Smooth, intuitive control matters most for prosthetics, where a user needs the hand to follow intent without conscious effort. It also serves robotics tasks where an operator guides a delicate gripper. A palm-scale testbed keeps the work close to the size of real prosthetic hands.
plos-pone-0358447:
Hanna Söderström Lindström leads a team of five assessing whether flu drugs flushed into waterways could breed resistant viruses, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Ducks, the natural home of influenza A, swim in water containing traces of the same antivirals used in people. If those traces train resistance, tomorrow's pandemic strains might inherit it. The team combined new experiments on drug release and breakdown with earlier duck studies of resistance, scoring four medicines on release, stability, and resistance risk.

Release into the environment rated high for three drugs and very high for the fourth. Stability in water varied widely, with peramivir lasting longest. Two drugs, peramivir and the active form of oseltamivir, carried the highest overall risk ranking, since both persist and can drive resistance at low concentrations. The authors call for prudent prescribing that weighs this environmental ledger alongside patient benefit, especially during outbreaks.
plos-pone-0358647:
Hristo Dimitrov and three co-workers present TrackStudio, a motion tracking toolkit built for those who do not code, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Marker free tracking follows body motion from ordinary video. It has grown strong but usually demands coding skill. TrackStudio wraps proven open source engines in one visual pipeline. It covers recording, camera syncing, two and 3D pose estimation, and display, ready out of the box.

The team validated it across three settings, from cheap webcams to high resolution cameras, with awkward postures, poor light, and obstructions included. Across seventy-six participants, frame to frame consistency was very high and 3D errors stayed small, around a centimeter for hand tracking. A practical guide warns users about common setup mistakes. The pitch is simple: clinics and behavior labs can now run serious motion studies without an in house coder.
plos-pone-0358747: Huang and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how a jelly ear fungus thickens as it grows. The fungus is Auricularia polytricha, grown as food. By comparing gene activity across growth stages, the team found pathways that switch on only at certain stages. Knowing which pathways drive thickening could help growers raise meatier, higher-value crops.
plos-pone-0358847:
Zahra Aliabadi and Alireza Mohebbi simulate, atom by atom, how a powerful natural compound grips its target protein, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The protein, cyclophilin A, helps fold other proteins and is implicated in viral infection and cancer. The compound, sanglifehrin A, shuts it down at extremely low doses. Running hundred nanosecond simulations of the protein alone and with the compound bound, the authors watched stability, motion, and bonding patterns shift.

Binding stiffened the loop at the protein's active site, even coaxing part of it into a more ordered strand shape. At the same time, distant loops loosened and the protein's overall range of shapes widened, raising its disorder in a measured way. A small, shifting network of hydrogen bonds anchored the compound. The computed binding strength matched the compound's known potency, supporting a picture where it works by selecting and holding one preferred protein shape.
plos-pone-0358947:
Wenna Xu leads a team of eight speeding up the identification of germs in infected blood, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Bloodstream infections kill quickly, and standard cultures leave doctors guessing antibiotics for days. The group tested a shortcut. They spin positive culture broth through gel tubes. They identify the organism directly by laser based mass spectrometry. Then they run rapid drug sensitivity checks from bacterial membranes or the broth itself.

Across two hundred ten specimens, the rapid route named gram negative bacteria correctly about three quarters of the time, but managed only about a third of gram positive bacteria and few fungi. The sensitivity shortcuts, though, agreed with standard testing in well over ninety percent of drug checks. The mixed verdict is useful: the membrane method is nearly ready to accelerate treatment for the commonest bloodstream germs, while identification still needs work.
pmc-10652247:
Jack Morris and co-authors report a rare pregnancy case in a 2023 paper. Cushing syndrome from an adrenal cancer during pregnancy is exceedingly rare, and no firm guidelines cover its diagnosis or care. Their patient, aged 31, came in for diabetes care in pregnancy and showed clear signs of hormone excess. Tests pointed to a hormone source outside the brain's control.

She went into early labor at 33 weeks and delivered a healthy baby. Four weeks after birth, surgeons removed her left adrenal gland. The tissue verdict was adrenocortical carcinoma, a cancer of the gland's outer layer. Case reports like this give later teams a path through a diagnosis few will ever meet.
pmc-10655447:
Muench and co-authors check if mind strength shapes pain drug scripts for old hosts. Old hosts with mind loss oft get fewer pain drugs than peers. Most past proof comes from care homes, not street-level care. The team used a broad U.S. spend poll from 2002 to 2017. Hosts split in three mind tiers by their poll codes. Tier one had no mind loss marked in the poll.

Tier two had mind loss claims but no mind-loss code. Tier three held hosts with a clear mind-loss code. The team scored if a script came, and how many came. Fits held age, sex, and health traits still in the math. Pain split in three forms: any long pain, strong pain, and code-marked pain.
pmc-10668947:
Cha and co-authors test whether classroom size and window views shape young children's thinking and stress, in a 2023 study using virtual reality. Children aged about five to seven explored virtual classrooms that were large or small, with nature views or built views. The team measured executive functions, the mental skills for flexible thinking and memory. Saliva cortisol and heart rate variability tracked stress before, during, and after.

Children in the large classroom improved more on a flexible thinking task. The small classroom slightly dented spatial working memory. Stress hormones did not differ by room size, though heart signals hinted at more relaxation in the large room. Window view made no clear difference. The results suggest space itself can nudge early learning.
pmc-10669647:
Mohammad Yousefi and four co-authors review how chronic ankle instability changes the first step of walking in a 2023 article. Starting to walk is a standard test of posture control, since the body must shift balance before the step. Searching five databases, the reviewers found hundreds of papers but only six that met their quality bar.

People with unstable ankles differed from healthy controls in reaction time, in the preparatory balance adjustments before stepping, and in step execution itself. Ankle and foot motion and muscle activation also diverged. The altered preparation patterns suggest the problem reaches higher motor control, not just the joint. The authors say the thin evidence base demands caution and more research, though rehabilitation may benefit.
pmc-10670547:
Bullying leaves marks far beyond the schoolyard, and Francesca Mastorci and co-authors measure how wide those marks spread. They survey 5,390 young teenagers, average age thirteen, with a fifty-two-item questionnaire on health-related quality of life. The survey spans mood, self-image, family ties, friendships, school life, and habits.

Across all students, bullying hit mood and emotions, self-perception, and parent relationships hardest. Daily habits were touched least. Girls who were bullied fared worse than boys on every measure, and worse than girls who were socially accepted. The authors argue that strengthening emotional and social skills early could help adults spot trouble sooner. Prevention, in their view, belongs inside ordinary school life, not after the damage.
pmc-10670947:
Sergei Kosushkin, Vitaly Korchagin, Andrey Vergun, and Alexey Ryskov set out a way to compare short repeated DNA elements across species using whole genomes. Their methods paper was published in twenty twenty-three. These elements, called SINEs, copy themselves into new spots, and shared copies mark shared ancestry.

A copy found at matching spots in two genomes signals kinship, and its mutations clock the split. The authors extract the elements, match loci by the DNA flanking them, and score presence, absence, and similarity. They demonstrate the workflow on lizard genomes, where deep history is hard to read. The approach turns scattered repeats into clean markers for drawing family trees of species.
pmc-10672847:
Hilal Aydin and co-authors compare, in a 2023 rat study, two protective substances against brain damage that follows a stroke-like blockage and the return of blood flow. When flow returns to starved brain tissue, the rush itself adds injury. Melatonin and N-acetylcysteine both fight that stress, and the team asked whether using both together works better.

Forty-one rats were split into control, injury, and treatment groups. Under the microscope, untreated injury raised nearly every damage score. Melatonin alone lowered most scores, including cell death signs and swelling. The combined treatment lowered all scores further than injury alone, suggesting the pair shields the brain more than either drug by itself.
pmc-10674847:
Lai Wei and co-authors wrote a paper from 2023 on steering a small robot that checks the inside of power transformers. The robot swims in the oil that fills the device, a tight space where holding a set path is hard. The team first built math models of how the robot moves and turns in oil. They then split its motion into five parts that can be steered on their own.

Their control method looks ahead, plans the next moves for each part, and updates the plan as the robot goes. Splitting the task keeps the sums light, which matters for a small on-board computer. In computer tests, the robot held its path with high accuracy and stayed steady when pushed off course. The team sees the method as a sound way to guide robots in other tight spaces too.
pmc-10684647:
Joana Santos and Dieter Ebert tested how well the resting eggs of a tiny freshwater crustacean survive heat and drought during their dormant stage. Many pond animals wait out bad seasons as resting stages, and climate change is making summers hotter and drier. Using Daphnia from different populations, the team exposed resting eggs to combinations of wetness and temperature. Heat plus wet conditions during dormancy prevented hatching altogether.

Dry, warm dormancy allowed more hatching, but success fell and hatching slowed as temperatures rose. Eggs from populations native to summer-dry ponds did slightly but consistently better under heat and dryness, supporting local adaptation. Those eggs also carried more of a protective sugar, a possible mechanism. The authors argue that knowing these limits is essential for predicting pond ecosystems under climate change. A resting stage is a survival capsule, but the capsule has a breaking point that varies by home habitat.
pmc-10687547:
Monleón-Getino and co-authors test whether gut microbes can help diagnose bowel diseases in children in this 2023 paper. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are long-term gut inflammations. Diagnosis now needs full medical workups, so a stool or mouth test would ease the path.

The pilot study followed thirty children: thirteen with Crohn's disease, eleven with colitis, and eight healthy controls. Gene-based profiling of mouth and stool samples found different microbe patterns in the sick children. Twenty-one bacterial species were picked out as candidate markers, grouped into three sets. The authors say a stool gene test, or a small marker set, could support earlier and gentler diagnosis. They stress the small sample and the need for fuller medical checks alongside.
pmc-10688147:
Ruoyao Zou and co-authors test surgery for a hard ovarian cancer relapse pattern in a 2023 study. The cancer had returned after platinum drugs failed, but in a limited region that surgeons could reach. Records from one center between 2015 and 2022 compared tumor removal surgery against chemotherapy alone.

Of fifty two patients, twenty one had surgery and nearly all left with no visible disease. Severe problems within a month hit fifteen percent of surgical cases. Patients with complete removal went about twice as long before the cancer moved again and lived longer after relapse than the drug only group, though total survival matched. Keyhole surgery cut blood loss with like outcomes. Selection clearly matters.
pmc-10689747:
Tadahisa Inoue and five co-authors test in 2023 a scope-based fix for a swollen, stone-filled gallbladder in frail patients. Surgery to remove the organ is too risky for these patients. A stent placed through a scope can drain the organ, but late problems still occur.

The pilot study enrolls 83 patients at one center. Staff wash out the organ with a special tube, then place an inner stent tied with a thread. Placement works in about four of five cases, and nearly all placed cases improve. Early harms stay low at under four percent. Return of illness stays near five percent, which the team reads as a hopeful sign for this frail group.
pmc-10690947:
Zihe Lu, Jialin Wang, Fengqin Wang, and Zhoumin Wu use brain-wave data to predict who will respond to depression treatment, in a research paper from 2023. Picking the right treatment early matters for patient outcomes. Brain-wave recordings carry rich signals, but they are hard to classify with plain methods.

Their model turns electrode signals into a graph that mirrors links between brain regions. A special module then highlights the rhythm bands that matter most. On data from a Beijing hospital, the model separated treatment responders from resistant cases better than two known deep learning rivals. The authors say graph-based methods suit this kind of tangled signal data.
pmc-10693047:
Neelam Younas and co-authors map in 2023 how proteins that tend to clump interact with other proteins under stress in cells. Faulty stress granules, small cell bodies that form under stress, are suspected of seeding toxic clumps. The team focused on three such proteins tied to brain disease, and used a pull down method plus mass analysis in two cell types, with and without a stress chemical.

They found almost six hundred possible partner proteins, with networks that shifted under stress. Two of the target proteins were found inside stress granules marked by a known protein. The work links granule biology to clump forming proteins and names new partners whose levels change under stress.
pmc-10693547:
Sandra Fernandez and a large European team studied what drives exposure to acrylamide, a harmful chemical formed when starchy foods are cooked at high heat. Rather than ask people what they ate, the team measured breakdown products in urine, which reflect recent exposure. Data came from harmonized studies in several European countries, covering thousands of children and teenagers and more than a thousand adults. Questionnaires supplied details on diet, home setting, and social background, reported in twenty twenty-three.

Southern European samples showed higher levels than northern ones. Among young people, levels were lower for those with higher social status, those living in rural areas, and older children. Among adults, eating more fried potatoes tracked with higher levels, while higher body weight tracked with lower readings. The authors offer the pattern as a guide for food safety efforts across Europe.
pmc-10696847:
Runfeng Wang and co-authors test whether a growth factor can protect the blood-brain barrier after brain bleeding. Their 2023 study starts from patient blood data and moves to mice and lab cells. Barrier breakdown after bleeding drives much of the later harm.

In patients, higher blood levels of the factor tracked with better alertness scores. In mice, treatment eased barrier damage, brain swelling, and lesion size, and improved nerve function. In lab vessel cells hurt by blood pigment, the factor restored energy organelle shape and output. A partner protein proved required for these gains, since mice lacking it in vessel cells lost most benefit. The authors trace the effect through a known signal chain.
pmc-10698947:
Åsa Audulv and co-authors published this methods study in 2023. Qualitative longitudinal research follows a phenomenon over time to watch it change. Guidance says change should be the heart of such studies, yet published work handles time very unevenly. Some reports barely use their repeated data, while others build everything around change. The authors set out to map the options for presenting findings in this kind of research.

They analyzed the methods and results sections of 299 health research articles. From that material they built a typology with three main types and seven subtypes. The first type makes little use of the time dimension. The second arranges findings in chronological order. The third focuses directly on changes through time. The types differ in focus, depth of interpretation, and how openly they discuss time itself. The authors offer the typology as a guide for researchers choosing a presentation style.
pmc-10699047:
Lisa Knisley and co-authors report a qualitative study from two thousand twenty-three on how Red River Métis families seek health information for sick children. The work was done in partnership with the Manitoba Métis Federation. Families need resources that fit their culture and daily lives when a child is acutely ill.

The team interviewed nineteen parents and Elders by video or phone and drew out shared themes. Families stressed pride and visibility, and that Métis families are not all the same. They wanted trustworthy information in many forms, not only online. Concrete ideas included adding guidance on reaching Elders and healers, showing varied family structures and living situations, and using Métis names and languages in parent resources.
pmc-10700047:
Juliana Kuchenbecker and co-authors track in 2023 how fire changes insect communities over time on forest islands atop tropical mountains in Brazil. Insects are in steep decline worldwide, and these high forest patches may shelter species found nowhere else. Five groups, ants, bees, butterflies, dung beetles, and wasps, were sampled in rainy seasons across four years in fourteen forest islands, with fire records kept for each island.

Fire shaped how species makeup shifted over time in the groups that move least, ants and dung beetles. The stronger fliers showed no such fire effect. The authors had expected each group to respond by its power to move between islands, and the pattern partly fit. Results argue for fire care tuned to each group.
pmc-10700347:
Koonchira Buaban and nine co-authors craft new variants of a sponge compound against lung cancer in a 2023 study. The parent molecule comes from a Thai blue sponge and belongs to a family with known tumor-killing power. Chemical tweaks at one position produced a library of ester variants.

A light-driven reaction first converted the natural starting material into the target scaffold. Seventeen derivatives were then built with varied side chains, from simple alkyl groups to amino acid pieces. Each compound faced human lung cancer cells and normal cells side by side. One propanoyl variant stood out for strong cancer killing at low doses. Comparing potency against safety in normal cells guides which variants merit animal testing next.
pmc-10700547:
Cheng-Yu Tsai and co-authors predict how a deafness gene variant breaks its channel, then test the call in mice. Their 2023 study uses motion simulations of connexin 26, a channel protein hit by the commonest hereditary deafness gene. A frequent variant clogs the channel as loose ends bunch inside it.

A made-up variant was simulated next, one never seen in patients. Mixed channels of normal and variant copies stayed open in the runs, while pure variant channels blocked. That pattern predicts recessive inheritance: carriers stay healthy. Mice bred to match behaved exactly so. Only the double-copy mice lost hearing, with weaker channel currents in ear cells.
pmc-10703947:
Motoyuki Umekawa and Gakushi Yoshikawa review a washing treatment after brain aneurysm rupture in a 2023 study. When an aneurysm bursts, blood floods the space around the brain. Days later, arteries can spasm and starve brain tissue, causing delayed strokes. Flushing the blood out early might prevent that chain.

Their center treated 340 patients over nine years with irrigation between the brain's fluid spaces, started during surgery and run for days. Spasms still appeared in about half the patients on scans. Yet delayed infarction struck only about seven percent, low for this disease. Drain complications were uncommon, near one and a half percent. Early surgery, on the day of the bleed or the next, was linked to strong protection against delayed stroke. The authors pair their series with a literature review. The design is retrospective, so the case rests on comparison with known outcomes.
pmc-10704047:
Kusal Das surveys how graduate medical training differs around the world in a 2023 commentary. Medicine carries a noble image everywhere, yet the road to becoming a specialist varies wildly: entry rules, program structures, and years of training differ by country and regulator. Universities and licensing bodies each guard their own version of that road.

Das walks through the steps that shape a medical professional, from curriculum and ethics teaching to supervised practice, and notes where systems diverge. Such comparisons matter for doctors who migrate between countries and for reformers borrowing ideas abroad. A training system can only be judged fairly when its length and design are set beside international alternatives, which this piece supplies.
pmc-10705147:
A team led by Samuel Rodríguez-Zorrilla tracked tiny parcels shed by cells in the blood of patients with mouth cancer, to see if they warn of relapse. They followed twenty-seven patients for a median of just over three years around standard treatment. Parcel counts and sizes were measured with a particle-tracking tool.

Counts dropped sharply after surgery. Patients whose cancer returned had higher counts and larger parcels after surgery than those who stayed clear. Lower counts before surgery went with longer cancer-free time. A cutoff test on pre-surgery counts flagged relapse fairly well. The authors propose blood parcel levels as a watch tool after treatment.
pmc-10707247:
Shin-ichiro Kita and co-authors match hearing tests to computer models in 2023 to locate middle ear defects. Malformed ear bones dull hearing, and surgery to rebuild the chain works best when the surgeon knows which link is fixed or broken. A plain audiogram hides that detail in a tangle of interacting effects.

The team built three-dimensional finite element models of the middle ear, simulated fixations and breaks, and compared the simulated audiograms with real patients' charts. The match objectively identified where the chain was stuck or split, without leaning on a doctor's feel or scan reading. Large-scale data should power a fuller diagnostic framework, they suggest.
pmc-10707347:
Shuya Suzuki and co-authors present a 2023 study on photochromic contact lenses, which darken in bright light like transition eyeglasses. Thirty-three healthy wearers with corrected vision were tested with the lenses inactive, the lenses activated, and plain lenses matched to the dimming. Vision sharpness and contrast sensitivity were measured indoors, outdoors, and under glare.

Outdoors, the activated lenses gave significantly better contrast sensitivity at mid-range detail levels than both comparison conditions. Sharpness did not differ indoors or outdoors. The authors conclude the lenses improve visual function in bright outdoor settings while holding it steady indoors and under glare. They pitch the lenses for people facing strong sunlight and ultraviolet exposure. The benefit, they note, is in quality of vision rather than raw acuity.
pmc-10708347:
Guan-Hong Chen and co-authors review quantum dot color converters in a 2023 paper. Quantum dots glow in pure colors ideal for displays and lighting products. Turning them into stable converter films is the industrial challenge that remains.

Two embedding strategies are compared in depth across the review chapters. One disperses dots in a glass matrix through a sol-gel route. The other mixes them into clear acrylic polymer films for coating. Light scattering and stability under heat receive close attention throughout. Both routes aim at factory-scale production, not bench demonstrations alone. Readers learn how fragile nanocrystals get packaged for real products.
pmc-10708547:
Kostrov and co-authors present a magnetic rubber that can be reprogrammed after it is made. Its trick is letting magnetic grains move inside the finished material when warmed. Heat plus a magnetic field then resets how stiff and magnetic it feels.

The base is a bottlebrush polymer with two kinds of side chains. At room heat, clumped styrene chains act as links and give soft, tissue-like stretch. Warming partly undoes those clumps so grains can shift. Versions varied in link chains and iron grain load. Restacking the grains in place changed the material's response by a wide margin.
pmc-10709447:
William Laprade and co-authors build a tool that grades skin death from snake venom in mouse tests. Their 2023 paper tackles a slow, error-prone step in antivenom research: scoring dead skin patches by eye. The tool, named VIDAL, learns from images to find the patches on its own.

The software fixes light bias, scales each photo, and pulls out patch size and color shift. A new unit blends those traits into one severity grade. Scores match lab-grade tissue analysis well, the team reports. Fast, shared scoring can speed the search for better antivenoms, a need that falls hardest on poor rural regions where bites are common.
pmc-10709647:
Jacek Rogala and co-authors combine classic statistics with machine learning to sort children with autism by brain wave patterns, in this 2023 study. Autism involves social communication challenges and repetitive behavior. Brain connectivity in autism differs from typical patterns, but small past samples gave mixed results. The team re-read past EEG data with two connectivity measures and both analysis styles.

The twin approach let them check model predictions against standard tests. Machine learning also picked out a clear subgroup of children with autism whom the EEG features sorted correctly. The authors say the paired method firms up what the signals mean. It may also point toward support plans matched to distinct brain profiles, rather than one plan for all children with the diagnosis.
pmc-10709847:
Youpeng Yang and co-authors name cancers from their methylation marks in a 2023 paper. Knowing a tumor's origin guides treatment, and DNA methylation patterns differ by tissue. Flat classifiers struggle when classes are many and close.

Their tool, CHCT, classifies in a hierarchy, splitting the problem into subproblems by similarity. It trained on over eight thousand methylomes across thirty cancer types from public atlases. On a held-out test set it called 1,568 of 1,660 cases right, near ninety-four and a half percent average accuracy. A fresh set of 677 samples scored about ninety-one percent. The tool even ventured labels for cancer types outside its training scope, with care.
pmc-10710447:
Weidong Zhang and co-authors find a gut peptide loop that keeps insulin cells in the pancreas sound and at work, in a study from 2023. Those cells fail in diabetes, and what guards them in health is worth a map. The team traces a small gut peptide to a ferry that hauls food parts into the cell. The pair forms a self feed loop in the cell itself.

Loss of the ferry, by gene cut or by drug block, wipes out the guard gains of the peptide. With the loop whole, cells hold their form and pour insulin on cue more soundly. The authors call the loop a fresh self care path for these cells. They urge checks of the loop as a drug aim to slow cell loss in diabetes.
pmc-10710947:
Yan Zhang and co-authors map live HIV spread paths in a China town in a 2023 study of virus watch. The town was the first test site for web-led watch of the virus in its land. Near one thousand five hundred blood takes from fresh cases span a long decade of years.

Gene reads of one virus part build kin webs and clumps for the spread hunt in the town. Trait maths then sifts what drives clump growth in the town herd at hand. A learn model is fit to call which sparks will grow the web in time.
pmc-10711447:
Agustín Lorenzatti and co-authors study how small DNA changes can bend DNA into knots that tune genes, in a 2023 paper. Stretches rich in the letter G can fold into four-stranded knots called G-quadruplexes. When such a knot sits near a gene's start, it can raise or lower how much the gene is read.

The team scan the whole genome for changes that sit both near gene starts and inside knot-forming stretches, then link them to diseases. They test five such changes in the lab, tied to Alzheimer's disease, a bleeding disorder, skin allergy, heart attack, and deafness. In cultured cells, each change shifted how its gene was read, which fits a role in disease risk. These knot sites could become new targets for tests and drugs tailored to each patient.
pmc-10712347:
Ali F Abdelwahab and co-authors published a research paper in 2023 on a bendy hybrid carrier that delivers a diabetes drug more effectively. Repaglinide lowers blood sugar well but dissolves poorly, limiting its reach. The team blended two carrier families, fatty bubbles and surfactant vesicles, into one deformable hybrid using an alcohol injection method.

A factorial design tuned the recipe for how much drug gets trapped and how much releases over twelve hours. The best batch trapped about eighty-seven percent and released about ninety-four percent in that window. It crossed membranes better and stayed stable longer than either parent carrier. In animals it lowered glucose more and reached the blood better than the plain drug.
pmc-10713547:
Xiang Lan and co-authors test a chicory compound against hoof cell inflammation in cows. Their 2023 paper builds a lab model of laminitis risk. Hoof wall cells were grown from cow tissue and inflamed with a bacterial toxin. The team then dosed the cells with chicoric acid and tracked signal proteins and inflammatory messengers.

The acid cut three key messengers that drive swelling and pain. It also turned down the sensor and relay proteins of a major alarm pathway, while raising a brake protein that holds the pathway in check. Cell growth and purity methods are reported in detail for reuse. The authors conclude the compound guards hoof cells by quieting that alarm route, a lead for dairy hoof care.
pmc-10714447:
Yaqi Huang and five co-authors compared two anesthetics in patients with high blood pressure having breast cancer surgery, in a 2023 trial. One drug is a newer agent reported to keep blood pressure steadier. The other is the long-standard choice. One hundred twenty patients were assigned by chance to one drug or the other. Care was otherwise the same in both groups.

Dangerous pressure drops after induction were the main outcome. They occurred less often with the newer drug. The lowest pressure during induction also stayed higher in that group. Other outcomes, including drug use for pressure support and next-day recovery scores, did not differ. Side effects were similar between groups. The authors conclude the newer drug is safe in this group. It may give steadier blood pressure at induction than the standard drug.
pmc-10714547:
Kufre Okop and co-authors report citizen science projects in four African countries that designed ways to prevent heart and vessel disease, in a paper from 2023. These diseases cause a large and growing share of deaths in sub-Saharan Africa. Local people rarely help shape the programs meant to protect them.

Projects ran in Ethiopia, Malawi, Rwanda, and South Africa. Just over two hundred people took part, in rural and urban areas. Trained citizen scientists used a phone app to survey views on risk and gathered photos and voice notes in each community. The results fed joint design of prevention plans that fit each place. The teams also built support for policy advocacy. The paper shows how shared design can ground health plans in local life.
pmc-10714747:
David Ortega-Jiménez and three co-authors validated a Spanish-language technostress scale in a large sample of Ecuadorian teachers, in this 2023 study. Pandemic-era schooling pushed teaching online and strained staff, yet Latin America lacked checked instruments for the strain. The team surveyed 2,850 teachers nationwide, averaging forty years old.

Factor analysis settled on four strands: skepticism, fatigue, anxiety, and a sense of inefficiency, all under one general technostress score. The structure held steady across sex, age, and school type, and scores tracked a standard distress scale as expected. Women scored slightly higher than men. The authors offer the scale as a sound tool for spotting and studying teacher technostress in the region.
pmc-10716147:
Babariya, Gupta, and Gajjar test a one layer MoSSe sheet as a methane sensor, in work from twenty twenty-three. Using first principles, they studied how methane, or CH4, acts near plain MoSSe and near sheets decorated with palladium or platinum. Negative formation energies showed the sheets were stable. Plain MoSSe is a semiconductor with a direct band gap of 1.52 eV. That gap shrinks when a palladium or platinum atom is added.

Methane stuck more strongly to the decorated sheets, with best adsorption energies of -0.674 and -0.636 eV at the selenium site. Both the sulfur and selenium sites were favorable for CH4 adsorption. Charge transfer, work function, and recovery time also pointed to a strong sensing response. The optical response in visible light changed a lot once methane was adsorbed. The team concludes that Pd/Pt decorated MoSSe sheets could make good methane sensing nano-devices.
pmc-10716247:
Maluta, Castro, and Spotti Lopes recorded how a maize pest feeds, in a study published in 2023, and how killer fungi change that feeding. The corn leafhopper spreads viruses and bacteria as it probes plants with its needle mouthparts. What it does inside the leaf decides how much pathogen passes. The team wired insects to an electrical graph system that turns each probing act into a waveform. They matched their waveform library to earlier studies on other systems.

They then exposed insects to fungi that infect and kill leafhoppers. Feeding shifts under infection matter: a pest that probes less spreads less disease. The waveform atlas lets future studies read behavior quickly. The work supports fungus-based pest control for a worsening maize threat. It also sharpens the basic science of how this insect eats.
pmc-10716647:
Shine and co-authors measure how male and female sea snakes differ in body shape, across six species that live in the sea. Moving from land to sea changed what nature favors in these snakes, likely including how the sexes are built. Their 2023 study measures four hundred nineteen preserved snakes.

Females averaged larger than males in every species, with wider bodies, shorter and wider tails, and smaller eyes. Head traits varied: relative head length favored males in some species and females in others. The authors link the pattern to the loss of male combat at sea, and to mate searching by sight rather than scent, which favors bigger male eyes. Head gaps may reflect the sexes eating different prey.
pmc-10717147:
Yasuo Sakuma wrote a 2023 review of how two brain regions, the preoptic area and the hypothalamus, organize female rat sexual behaviour. The behaviour unfolds as linked modules in a set order: approaching, inviting, and the mating posture itself. Hormones set the odds of each module firing, tying mating to the brief fertile window of the cycle.

Oestrogens from ripening follicles support both the social and the physical parts of the sequence. Without ovarian steroids, females shun or fight males instead. The review traces how early development and surroundings shape the hormone milieu in the brain, and how the two regions conduct the timed chain from interest to mating.
pmc-10717447:
Yirui Gao, Junli Zhu, Lujia Hu, and Chen Chen compared staff loyalty across hospital types in a 2023 study in Beijing, China. Doctors in general hospitals, which treat all kinds of illness, may feel a distinct bond to their workplace than doctors in specialty hospitals. That bond can shape how hard each hospital must work to keep and spur its doctors.

The team surveyed 292 doctors in four large public hospitals. They compared total loyalty scores and each part of the score across the two hospital types. They also looked for which traits mark the doctors whose loyalty needs the most care in each type. The results aim to guide reward plans that fit each hospital's own staff.
pmc-10717647:
Nikhil Chatrath and three co-authors untangle leaky heart valves in athletes. Their 2023 paper studies aortic regurgitation with bicuspid valves. Two-flap valves are the commonest birth defect of the heart and wear out early. Training also remodels the athletic heart, blurring the line between fitness and disease.

Thirty men with the defect and at least moderate leaks were compared. Seventeen were highly active and thirteen lightly active, by phone questionnaire. Scans came from a specialist center between 2019 and 2022. Standard guidelines graded leak severity for all. The groups showed no clear scan differences at rest. The authors review how to judge such hearts without benching healthy athletes.
pmc-10717947:
How well dentists talk with patients shapes trust, compliance, and satisfaction, yet training in that skill is uneven. Salim and co-authors surveyed 305 dentists in Jordan with an online questionnaire built on a standard observation guide for medical interviews. They scored both knowledge of good communication and self-reported practice, then asked how background factors such as age, gender, sector, and schooling shifted the scores.

Knowledge averaged at a moderate level. Women scored higher than men, private-sector dentists scored higher than those in government posts, and older, more experienced dentists generally did better. Almost half had never taken a communication course, though nearly all agreed such training belongs in the curriculum. Time was the top barrier, named by 62.3 percent. The authors find a gap between what dentists know and what they report doing, and they urge schools to make communication a priority.
pmc-10719347:
Sugars coating our cells carry information, but they are notoriously hard to count. Xiao Tian and co-authors built a way to feed cells a selenium-tagged sugar and then read the selenium with elemental instruments, turning glycan detection into simple atom counting. Their strategy, SeMOE, marries a classic metabolic labelling trick with mass spectrometry imaging, so sugars can be measured and mapped in tissue at once.

The probes worked across varied biological settings, giving detection, quantities, and pictures from one experiment. A two-in-one probe also carried a conventional reporter, adding a second, optical readout. The authors present the method as a simpler doorway into the glycan world, whose signals govern immunity, infection, and cancer behaviour.
pmc-10721347:
Arnold Popkov and co-authors present a 2023 case report on leg lengthening in a teen boy. The boy, aged 14, had a thigh bone six centimeters short after an injury. The bone also bent sideways by 20 degrees. The team used a classic frame method that slowly stretches new bone. For the first time in clinic, they paired it with an implant inside the bone that breaks down over time.

The implant is made of a body-safe plastic filled with a bone-like mineral. It aims to speed bone healing while the frame does its slow work. Shortening and bend were fixed in 90 days, with no problems during lengthening. Frame time per centimeter was about half the usual span. Surgeons get a first human case for a method long tested in theory. Shorter frame time means fewer infections and stiff joints for young patients.
pmc-10724847:
Kyriakos Soulios and co-authors wrote a paper in 2023 on deepFPlearn+, an upgraded tool that checks if chemicals may cause harm. It gives its guess before any test on animals or cells. Regulators face a flood of new chemicals and can test just a few. A fast screen must pick which ones need a close look first. The old tool read each chemical through fingerprints. The new tool reads the full shape as a graph.

A graph neural network now takes in how the parts of the chemical link up. The team also split test sets by molecular scaffolds and weight, to make the tests hard and fair. The new model beat the old one by a wide mark. It still did well on chemicals it had not seen before. The team urges its use on lists of chemicals to rank them for lab tests.
pmc-10726147:
Mohamed Ferhi and three co-authors study body image among Tunisian teens in a 2023 survey. Weight gain in teens is a world health worry, and Tunisia's teen rates climb fast. How teens see their own weight, right or wrong, shapes whether health plans can reach them.

The team ran a school-based study in Sousse in the 2017 to 2018 school year. Each teen's self-view was set against true measures of height and weight. The study then weighed which traits, from sex to home means, lined up with wrong self-views. Its finds can aim school health work where it counts.
pmc-10726247:
Su and coauthors test why sound waves lose power in dirty water. Strong sound can drive chemical change that cleans waste water. Air bubbles and grit in the water can block that change. The team asks how each phase, and both at once, cut the effect.

They used argon bubbles and fine sand-like grains in pure water. A horn device sent sound at a fixed pitch through the mix. A test chemical showed how much change took place. More bubbles or grains meant less chemical change. The block grew strong once the mix passed a low share. Their math model matched the lab results well.
pmc-10728047:
Sung-Hyun Yoon and co-authors study how symptoms change after total hip replacement in patients who have both hip and spine disease. Published in 2023, the study reviews 40 patients with prior spine lesions, drawn from 417 who had a first hip replacement at one hospital between 2016 and 2022. Patients were split by whether their remaining symptoms pointed to the spine or the hip.

Pain scores fell by about half in both groups after the hip operation. The authors conclude that hip replacement helped even patients whose pain was blamed on the spine. Some older patients had spine treatment with no hip check at all, they note. They recommend a hip evaluation for such patients before further spine care.
pmc-10729047:
Xinyu Xie and co-authors check, in a 2023 study, whether mothers in rural southern Nepal recall their pregnancy care visits accurately. Counts of antenatal care visits are a key gauge of care coverage, and they often rest on what mothers say months later. The team followed 402 pregnant women at five government health posts from late 2018 to late 2020.

Observed counts served as the standard. On average, women who had a live birth attended 4.7 antenatal visits, and about 65% attended four or more, as the Nepal government recommends. Yet only about 38% of mothers reported the exact count that staff had logged. Reports of few visits ran low, while a count of four was claimed far too often. A split, under four versus four or more, fared better. Women with more visits recalled worse. The authors say recall is a weak gauge and needs better tools.
pmc-10729247:
Sirui Wang and co-authors set out a protocol to compare brain stimulation treatments for major depression by targeting method. Their 2023 paper deals with magnetic stimulation over a front left brain area. Three ways to find that spot are in use: a five centimeter rule, a scalp landmark method, and a navigation method guided by scans. Whether results differ by method is unclear.

The team will search eight databases, in English and Chinese, for trials to May 2023. Trials must give at least ten sessions of high frequency stimulation. Comparisons can be against sham stimulation or against another targeting method. The main outcome is change on a standard depression rating scale. A network method will let all three methods be compared at once, even where head to head trials are missing.
pmc-10731147:
Giuseppe Marano and colleagues review gut microbes as a key to women's wellbeing. Their review from twenty twenty-three spans mental and physical health. Gut bacteria protect, feed, and structurally support their host. Their influence reaches the brain, heart, and hormone systems.

A woman's gut community shifts across life stages. It interacts closely with the female reproductive system. Helpful bacteria may prevent or ease specific women's diseases. External factors like diet and drugs reshape the community constantly. The authors argue prevention should treat the gut as a junction organ. Pharmaceutical research is mining these links for new therapies. The review maps a fast-growing field for clinicians.
pmc-10731247:
Jiao Jiao and co-authors set out the plan for agreeing a standard outcome set for a young medical field in this 2023 paper. The field joins diabetes and heart disease care, where trials each measure different endpoints. Mixed endpoints block fair comparison, and some measures matter little to patients and doctors.

The paper describes the steps the team will follow. They will form stakeholder groups, review which outcomes past trials used, and interview patients and clinicians about what counts. From that work they will draft a candidate list of outcomes. A structured survey method will then let stakeholders vote the list down over rounds. A final consensus meeting will review and endorse the agreed set. The authors present the framework as groundwork for this field and as a model for other groups building outcome sets.
pmc-10731347:
Zhang and co-authors ask whether pairs of long non-coding RNAs, rather than single ones, track survival in breast cancer. Using data from 890 women in The Cancer Genome Atlas, the team tested how the joint levels of two such RNAs relate to overall survival. Their model adjusted for age, race, stage, treatment, and hormone receptor status. One pair showed a strong link to survival, and a related gene pair showed the same pattern.

The paper names the RNA pair as a candidate marker for breast cancer outcomes. It also frames gene pairs as a lens on tumor growth that could point to new treatment targets. The design is retrospective and rests on one public data set. The authors therefore treat the pair as a signal to test further, not as a test ready for the clinic.
pmc-10731547:
Oqba Alkuran and co-authors present a 2023 survey study of distance learning in medical teaching. Teaching hospitals mix practice with training, and some teaching had already moved online. COVID-19 forced distance electronic learning to the front everywhere. The authors ask how late-stage medical students in Jordan felt about the switch. A web questionnaire ran during the lockdown window from mid-March to May 2020. Students rated the strategy that replaced their classrooms and wards.

The cross-sectional design captures views while the experience was fresh. Medical schools get student-side evidence from an emergency pivot. Clinical training resists remote formats in ways lectures do not, so late-stage views carry special weight. The findings can guide which parts of the emergency setup deserve to survive in normal times. Pandemic-era surveys also serve as a record of how a generation of doctors was trained under stress.
pmc-10733947:
Vinicius Macedo and co-authors tuned a spongelike mineral material to pull the antibiotic amoxicillin out of water. Antibiotics wash into rivers worldwide, where they can breed resistant bacteria. The material, Al-MCM-41, is a silica riddled with tiny pores and laced with aluminum. The team varied how it is made and measured which changes mattered most for soaking up the drug.

Composition and surface area proved decisive. A silicon-to-aluminum ratio of 10.5 worked best, capturing 132.2 milligrams of amoxicillin per gram of material. More aluminum strengthened one kind of attraction to the drug, through its ring structure, while weakening hydrogen-bond links at the surface. Statistical design tools let the team find this optimum with few experiments. The authors propose the tuned material for cleaning drug-laced wastewater.
pmc-10735447:
Rules for homes that aid the old vary state by state, and a stiff rule book is not the same as stiff care. Lindsey Smith and co-authors grade that stiff grade in a 2023 study of aid home leave kinds. Ten care fields were read for reach, fine print, and teeth.

Staff counts and guest checks sat in near all kinds' books. Drug checks and chief's stamps sat in few. One north state's mind care stamp topped the stiff chart; its twin plain stamp sat near the base. One plain state wrote full reach and most fine print, yet gave the rules no teeth at all. The team say grade must be read on all three dials at once.
pmc-10735547:
Adam Perzynski, Kristen Berg, and Jarrod Dalton report early talks on digital twin neighborhoods in a 2023 paper. Poor neighborhoods face more disease and less preventive care. A digital twin is a data rich copy of a real community that can test health plans in simulation first.

The team ran studio sessions where residents and experts question the twin builders. More than thirty people took part across quarterly rounds. Worries centered on harm to real places, data privacy, and how spatial measures get picked. Residents asked for direct openness about data and for local meanings of health to shape the work. Future topics include isolation and shared life.
pmc-10735647:
Dassel and six co-authors describe building a web platform that helps people with dementia and their care partners plan future care. Their LEAD Guide walks families through values, preferences, and end-of-life wishes as thinking changes. The team turned the paper guide into an interactive online program.

Sixty community pairs took part in a pilot, working through planning talks and documents with built-in lessons. A community advisory board, including dementia experts and affected families, shaped the design through surveys and focus groups. They asked for simpler navigation, more personal messages, and easier feedback forms. The authors say end-user input at every step makes such tools workable.
pmc-10735847:
Giulia Coletta and co-authors trial live online exercise classes for older adults who sit too much. Thirty-one adults aged 65 to 80 were split into an eight-week class group or a waitlist. The classes ran live by video, not as recordings.

Attendance hit 97 percent of sessions, and nearly all participants liked the program. Step counts and activity minutes leaned higher in the class group after eight weeks but did not clear firm proof thresholds. Interviews added color on what kept people logging in. Live online delivery, the authors conclude, is workable and welcome, even if bigger trials must confirm the health gains.
pmc-10735947:
