Christina Victor, writing in 2023, reviews what is known about gaps in loneliness among older adults in the United Kingdom. Health in old age has three parts, she notes: body, mind, and social life. Social health has drawn far less study than the other two.

United Kingdom studies link higher risk of loneliness to traits such as sex, home life, poor health, and income. Yet help for loneliness rarely works well, Victor argues. She faults past work for looking at single traits alone, for using one-time surveys, and for ignoring place and culture. She calls for life-course and wider views that track how risk builds over a whole life and across places.
pmc-10736047:
Qi, Pei, Zhu, and Wu published in twenty twenty-three a study of older Americans who felt their memory slipping. Such self-noted decline can affect daily life and work. Seeking help early can lead to screening and care. The team used national survey data from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-one. They studied more than forty-one thousand adults aged forty-five and older.

Some groups were far less likely to raise memory problems with a doctor. Asian American and Pacific Islander adults were the least likely to start that talk. Black adults with limits on daily tasks were also less likely than white adults. The authors point to access gaps, stigma, language, and health knowledge. They call for tailored steps that prompt early talks with providers.
pmc-10736147:
Yuan Zhang, writing alone in 2023, studies how social ties shape disability in old age. Past work shows older adults with stronger ties tend to have fewer physical limits. What stayed unclear is how the link runs both ways over time. Zhang uses two large United States surveys of older adults that track health and social life.

For men, wider social ties came before lower physical limits later on. For women, social support seemed to guard against loss of function. For both sexes, growing limits and disability cut back later social life. The study tests whether good ties truly protect the body, or whether healthy people simply keep more ties. Its findings help explain how friendship and health feed each other late in life.
pmc-10736247:
Zhiyong Lin and Hui Liu test whether social isolation raises dementia risk differently across race, ethnicity, and gender, in a 2023 study. The data come from a long United States aging study. It ran from 2000 to 2016. Older adults were grouped as non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, or Hispanic. Isolation predicted later dementia in the first two groups. The link held after basic background factors were counted.

Among Hispanic participants, isolation did not predict dementia. The authors suggest culture and family structure may buffer the effect. Gender differences were mostly small. One exception stood out: severe isolation hit Black men harder than Black women. Money and health factors carried much of the link in both affected groups. The authors call isolation a modifiable risk worth targeting. Programs should fit the communities they serve. Diverse older adults, they argue, need tailored outreach.
pmc-10736347:
Amy Eisenstein and Ernest Gonzales present a 2023 symposium summary on research into bonds between generations. Such ties shape families and communities, yet America has grown more age-segregated, so contact across ages happens less by chance. Wording that casts older people as outsiders can widen the gap further.

The session gathers three research projects on ways to build these connections. One studies digital contact between grandparents and grandchildren during the pandemic, and what that shift meant for closeness. The others test programs that bring the strengths of both age groups into view. The shared claim is that planned contact can cut loneliness and lift well-being on both sides.
pmc-10736547:
Jennifer Morgan and co-authors study standout care workers in dementia care homes in a 2023 paper. Keeping skilled direct care staff has grown hard as shortages and turnover climb. The team followed an ongoing study of meaningful engagement for assisted living residents with dementia.

Sixty-six residents at eight communities were followed for a year, and fifty-three care workers were interviewed in three waves. Field notes came from over two thousand hours of observation. The best workers shared four approaches: knowing the person, meeting people where they are, staying in the moment, and treating every encounter as a chance to engage. Staffing stability, steady assignments, and training shaped whether those skills could grow. Findings feed training and policy ideas.
pmc-10736847:
Rashelle Hoffman, Shinobu Watanabe-Galloway, Catherine Riffin, and Joan Monin work to adapt an activity program for rural areas in two thousand twenty-three. The program is for people with mild memory loss and their care partners. Rural adults face a higher risk of Alzheimer's disease than city adults. Lack of activity is one risk that can change, and remote care can help.

The base program uses weekly talks, step counts from a wrist band, and goal setting. The team held group talks in a rural town in Nebraska. Providers, care partners, and older adults shared how to fit the program to rural life. The next step is a remote version built for pairs.
pmc-10737047:
Aung Zaw Zaw Phyo, Joanne Ryan, and five co-authors study signs of aging in blood and later frailty. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, uses data from the ASPREE trial of adults aged seventy and up. They test five scores based on marks on DNA. They also test seven proteins found in blood plasma.

The team tracked five hundred sixty people for just over five years. Faster aging on some scores meant a higher risk of frailty. One score linked to a frailty count raised risk by near half per step. The work suggests blood tests may flag who will grow frail or lose the power to do daily tasks.
pmc-10737147:
Laura Hemmy, Nichole Morris, and Kyle Shelton describe an effort to join up scattered research on older drivers. Their 2023 article notes that driving underpins independence and quality of life for many older adults, and that it draws on physical, sensory, and thinking skills together. It is also shaped by community, road design, vehicle design, and family networks. Older drivers face worse outcomes in crashes, so knowing how to keep them safe matters.

The problem, the authors say, is that interested researchers sit in separate corners of the university and rarely meet. A special interest group at the University of Minnesota, run with a transportation studies center, gave them a shared platform. Members describe how meeting across fields led to joint work on safe driving in later life, including a state-funded intervention study. The piece is a case for structured connection as research infrastructure.
pmc-10737247:
Ashley Morgan and four co-authors report a pilot trial of home strength training for older adults after a fall injury in this 2023 paper. The target group shows early mobility limits: they adapt tasks but report no difficulty yet. Such adults risk future decline, which exercise might prevent. The trial assigns participants to twelve weeks of high intensity functional strength training at home, or to a stretching program. A physiotherapist delivers both by video call. Twenty people had enrolled when the report was written.

Feasibility looks good so far. Among finishers, attendance ran near ninety-eight percent of sessions, above the seventy percent bar. Two people withdrew, for a mental health crisis and a knee pain episode. No serious training related harms were reported. The authors frame the pilot as groundwork for a full trial.
pmc-10737547:
Giuliana Casanova, Lígia Passos, Edna Rodrigues, and Oscar Ribeiro describe in 2023 how students in Portugal set up a new student chapter. The chapter belongs to the Gerontological Society of America, a group for the study of aging, and it is based at the University of Aveiro. It is the first such chapter outside the United States.

The authors tell how the group was built by and for students, and what it aims to do. Plans cover shared study, work in the local area, and links with peers and experts in the field. They also share the hard parts and the rewards, in hope that other schools will start chapters and grow a wider network for students of aging.
pmc-10737847:
Dawn Carr and co-authors trace how the pandemic's job shocks hit older workers of different races. Minoritized older adults entered COVID-19 with riskier jobs and thinner savings, and died at higher rates. Using a national retirement study with a 2021 pandemic survey, the team compared workers employed before the crisis by race and ethnicity.

Black and Hispanic older workers suffered heavier financial fallout when their jobs were disrupted, and were more likely to fall behind on rent, utilities, medical bills, food, or debts. Pre-pandemic financial weakness sharpened the link between job loss and unpaid bills, and it shaped the racial gaps themselves. The authors close with policy ideas aimed at cutting the financial fragility of minoritized workers before retirement, so the next shock lands more evenly.
pmc-10738047:
Kening Jiang and co-authors asked whether poor sleep sharpens the tie between hearing loss and dementia, in a 2023 study. Both hearing loss and broken sleep raise dementia risk, and both can be treated in later life. The team drew on a national aging survey of Medicare members, with hearing tested by tones in the 2021 round.

Among 2,383 people aged seventy-one and over, hearing loss tied to higher dementia rates only in those with sleep troubles. Sleep trouble meant taking over half an hour to fall asleep, or struggling to drop off again, at least twice a week. The pattern hints that sleep and hearing care may need to move together in prevention plans.
pmc-10738247:
Sarah Lieber and co-authors present a 2023 study of a tablet-based exercise program for older adults with chronic illness. Exercise helps old age health, yet most older adults fall short of the advised levels, above all those with long-term disease. The program, called Fittle, pairs home workouts on a tablet with team play and chat for social support. The team ran a chance-based trial of 181 adults aged 60 and up.

Among 93 adults with two or more chronic conditions, the program group felt more support and less loneliness at six months than the control group. The control group got links to exercise sites for older adults. Self-reported activity leaned higher in the program group, though the gap was not firm. Social design may be the active sauce in home exercise for sick elders.
pmc-10738347:
Haley Schneider, Maria Donohoe, Lena Thompson, and Sato Ashida followed dementia caregivers through the pandemic in this 2023 study. Care work harms health, and the virus years piled on stress. The bright side of care, its sense of meaning and family closeness, can buffer that harm. Forty-three caregivers in a support trial were surveyed at the start and three months on.

Those who began with less of that bright side saw their pandemic distress climb more steeply. The bright side itself also tended to fade across the three months. The authors argue that shoring up the positives of care early could blunt stress when hard times hit, and they call for work on how to lift them.
pmc-10738447:
Rolla Saud Mira follows older Americans for ten years to test whether the body's wear-and-tear from stress, called allostatic load, drives the pile-up of chronic diseases. The data come from six waves of the Health and Retirement Study, from 2006 to 2016. Multimorbidity was counted across five conditions: diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, cancer, and stroke. The stress score combined cholesterol, blood sugar control, inflammation, waist size, and blood pressure readings.

Higher allostatic load clearly went with faster growth in disease count, even after accounting for income, education, and habits like smoking and exercise. Part of the reason poorer and less educated Americans accumulate diseases faster ran through this stress score. Richer and poorer groups also differed in how their load changed over time. Mira argues stress biology is one concrete path from social position to failing health.
pmc-10738747:
Zih-Yong Liao, Pei-Chun Liao, and Fang-Lin Kuo study health literacy and health care use in older Taiwanese adults in a 2023 paper. Health literacy shapes health behavior, but its role in older adults' access to care was little documented. The study used the Taiwan Longitudinal Study on Ageing.

The sample covered 2,423 community-dwelling older adults between 2011 and 2015. Using mixed-effects and cumulative logit models, the team tested which personal traits tracked with care use. A significant link involved how hard people found it to manage health tasks, evidence that literacy support belongs in elder care planning.
pmc-10738847:
Yeonjung Lee, Lauren Migrino, Rochelle Deloria, and Kurt Robertson let older adults photograph their own access barriers in Calgary. Their 2023 study uses photovoice, where participants shoot images of what matters to them. Thirteen older adults across seven neighborhoods took part.

Five themes emerge from the photos and talks. Planning ahead for aging needs stands first, since aging in place takes foresight. Close, convenient access to services and resources matters next. Cultural and language supports boost safety and belonging for many. Mixed-age, mixed-background neighbors enrich community life, participants say. Affordable support rounds out the list as key to an independent life. Social connection is prized, yet thin support can leave older adults isolated.
pmc-10739047:
Jonathan Guillemot and Mildred Warner ask why so few cities in the Andes have taken up a world plan for age-friendly places. Populations in the poorer half of the world are aging fast, yet the Andean region counts only four such cities out of more than a thousand worldwide. The plan's eight themes focus on town life: streets, services, and taking part.

The authors argue that the themes fit rich lands better than poor ones. They call for more weight on two ends of the scale: state policy, where strong welfare cannot be taken for granted, and family care at home. A child-focused city plan from a UN agency offers a wider lens, they note.
pmc-10739147:
Dakota Witzel and co-authors study what shapes how older adults judge their own thinking, in work from 2023. The COVID-19 pandemic brought lasting stress that may affect mental sharpness. Less was known about what protects thinking self-views during such times.

The eight-week study followed 229 adults living in the community, with a mean age near 71 years. Each week, stress and good events were scored for strength. Stronger stress went with more self-reported thinking trouble. Stronger good events went with less trouble. Age changed the stress link, with the oldest group hit hardest. Personal toughness also shifted both links, in ways the authors discuss in full.
pmc-10739447:
Max Zubatsky and five co-authors test where a friendship circle for lonely older adults works best: a doctor's office or a community hall, in this 2023 study. Loneliness among older Americans is now called an epidemic, with real consequences for health. The intervention, Circle of Friends, is a guided group program, borrowed from Finnish rehabilitation practice, that rebuilds social life rather than medicating its absence.

Participants are over sixty, feel lonely, have been homebound or isolated recently, and have few social ties. The community arm had enrolled its first eight members when the study was reported, with primary care recruitment still underway. The researchers compare the two settings on loneliness and health risk change. The design reflects a practical question for health systems: whether the trust and reach of primary care beats the ease of a neighborhood venue for gathering the loneliest patients.
pmc-10740147:
Detlef Bartel and colleagues at Germany's Paul-Ehrlich-Institut set out the European view, from regulators, on allergen-specific immunotherapy. The practice is a century old. It treats allergy by giving the allergen in a controlled way. The team writes as staff of a national authority. They sum up the standards for regulation, and the hard points that proof from science poses for these products. Their institute checks such products through development, marketing authorization, and their whole life cycle.

Nine aspects are addressed, spanning product specificity, clinical efficacy, and treatment of adults and children, with the questions that raises when results are carried across groups. Allergen exposure chambers, biomarkers, and standardization are covered. So is real-world evidence. So is independent official batch release, with its benefits and challenges. A shared approach at the European level rounds out the agenda. The article maps where regulation presses hardest on evidence.
pmc-10741847:
Mohamad Almutairi and co-authors pool in 2023 the evidence on whether low blood platelet counts warn of severe eye disease in babies born too early. The disease, retinopathy of prematurity, can blind infants, and its worst forms need fast treatment. The team gathered studies that linked platelet counts, taken in the first two weeks or near treatment time, to severe disease.

Twenty-one studies went into a combined analysis that weighs evidence for and against a link. Low counts in both time windows tied to severe disease, with the later window giving the strongest signal. Very low counts near treatment time also tied to severe cases. When the team adjusted for the bias toward publishing positive results, only that last link kept moderate support. The authors present the tie as real but softer than the raw numbers suggest.
pmc-10742547:
Emilie Skoog, Gregory Fournier, and Tanja Bosak study how microbes in Shark Bay, Australia, gained stress-handling genes, in a 2023 paper. The bay's bumpy microbial mats resemble the life that spread across early Earth shores. The team asked whether the microbes picked up stress genes from each other, a swap called horizontal gene transfer.

They scanned eighty-three rebuilt genomes from one mat with a transfer-spotting tool. Family trees for stress genes, covering salt, oxygen damage, and arsenic, point to a long history of swaps. Many swaps seem to have happened outside the modern mat. One gene for a protective transport protein shows fresher local trading between two microbe groups. The results show that these old-style communities still evolve by sharing genes, not just by slow change within each line.
pmc-10742747:
Two plant compounds may ease gum disease in rats that also have diabetes, and a 2023 study by Georgiana Ioana Potra Cicalău and co-authors tests them in a gel. Both diseases feed on oxidative stress, which harms cells, and the compounds, carvacrol and magnolol, are natural antioxidants.

Ninety Wistar rats were split into nine groups covering health, each disease alone, both together, and treated sets. The gel was placed on the gums of rats with both conditions, using one compound, the other, or both. Blood tests tracked a damage marker and the activity of a protective enzyme. The study asks whether a natural gel can blunt the stress that links the two diseases.
pmc-10742847:
Marisa Laurila and co-authors report denture work for patients with severe tissue loss in this 2023 case series. The patients had oral cancer, major face injuries, or syndromes that left big gaps in the mouth. Each case needed full, complex rebuilding.

Care took place at Helsinki University Hospital. The team used computer-designed bar systems that hold removable dentures on implants. Forty implants were placed in all, four to seven per patient. The goal was sturdy, working teeth that patients could clean with ease. Simple care at home also cuts the need for expert follow-up.
pmc-10743047:
Yuliya Nashchekina and co-authors report a 2023 materials study on gels that could fill tissue defects. The gels mix collagen with hyaluronic acid, two natural body materials, but they can be weak and short-lived. The team adds phytic acid, a plant compound from beans and grains, as a cross-linker to brace the gel, and studies how the mix sets and holds.

Neither acid alone made collagen self-assemble, yet together the fibers kept their native form and gained chemical links. Heat and flow tests showed the phytic acid gel was steadier and stiffer, while the hyaluronic acid blunted that gain a bit. Cells grown in the gel fared slightly worse after a week, a trade-off the authors note for cancer-site repairs.
pmc-10743147:
Seonggon Lee and co-authors extend in 2023 a single-molecule X-ray scattering method to view the shapes of biological molecules. Standard methods average structures over time and over many molecules, hiding variety. Their approach uses ultrashort X-ray pulses to capture instant snapshots of single objects.

Two gold nanoparticles label each molecule, giving strong contrast for precise distance measures. They generated test images for RNAs, proteins, and a combined complex. Retrieved distances matched true values closely, often within one angstrom under realistic conditions. The analysis also weighs how particle size, X-ray traits, and detector layout affect accuracy.
pmc-10743547:
Lupi and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-three on a cone-style connection for implant-supported crowns. Screwed and cemented fittings carry known drawbacks in dentistry. Twenty-two patients receive seventy implants with the new connection. Thirty-three restorations are followed for one year. Every implant integrates with no losses or gum inflammation. Bone levels shift only slightly over the year. No screws loosen and no crowns chip in the follow-up.

Coupling stability slips in nine cases, the one blemish. Handling simplicity and edge fit are the claimed wins. Bigger samples and longer follow-up are still needed. The authors call the alternative promising.
pmc-10743747:
Jaime Rafael Barón and co-authors work on finding a rare heart disease with computer help in this 2023 paper. In the disease, the main pumping chamber of the heart has a spongy, loose wall. Spotting it matters for care, but scans are hard to read, so the team aimed to improve how software outlines the chamber.

They used heart scans from three hospitals. Using larger images helped, as did a step that removes false marks made by the network. A newer network design gave the best outlines and the best disease calls, with accuracy near nine in ten. Results differed between hospitals, which shows that making the tool work everywhere is still a problem.
pmc-10744447:
Keratoconus thins and bulges the cornea, and cross-linking treatment stiffens the tissue to stop it worsening. A six-author team reviewed records from a teaching hospital in southern Israel for patients treated between 2015 and 2019, comparing Bedouin and Jewish patients. The study covered 166 patients and 198 eyes, with at least a year of follow-up for most.

At the start, the Bedouin group had worse vision scores and thinner corneas, showing the disease had progressed further before treatment. Both groups gained in corrected and uncorrected vision over the year after treatment. Statistical analysis found that a flatter starting cornea and the standard treatment protocol predicted a stable cornea after 12 months. The patient's ethnic group had a negligible effect once starting state was accounted for.
pmc-10744647:
Milos Zivic and colleagues examined gum disease in Crohn's disease patients in two thousand twenty-three. Crohn's disease inflames the whole digestive tract. Mouth problems are one known side effect. Gum disease destroys the tissues holding teeth. The team asked whether gum severity tracks Crohn's activity. They scored bowel activity with clinical and scope indexes.

Dental checks measured attachment loss, bleeding, and pocket depth. X-rays showed supporting bone loss. Patients with active Crohn's had worse gum measures overall. One bleeding measure broke that pattern. Gum values ran higher in active disease than remission. Dentists and bowel doctors gain a reason to coordinate care.
pmc-10744747:
Grit Zahn and co-authors study in 2023 a longevity gene as a target to prevent age-related bone loss. The gene makes a transporter that moves citrate, a substance that forms a small share of bone weight. Lower activity of the gene has been linked to longer life in earlier work.

Using United Kingdom health data, variants tied to lower gene function were linked to lower osteoporosis risk. In mice lacking the gene in bone-forming cells, older females gained bone elasticity while older males gained strength. The authors propose blocking the gene as a possible route to treat bone fragility.
pmc-10744847:
Giovanni Mattioni and co-authors review when a whole lung must be removed for a rare birth defect in a 2023 paper. The defect leaves one lung's main artery cut off near its start, and the best care is not settled. The team searched the medical literature for cases where doctors chose to remove the lung, and added one case from their own hospital.

The set covered twenty-five adults and seven children, plus the team's case. In adults, coughing blood was the top reason for surgery, followed by known or suspected lung cancer, and near half the operations were urgent. Problems after surgery hit about a third of cases, with no deaths. In children, the surgery was most often a life-saving step done in haste.
pmc-10745447:
Hoang Minh Pham and colleagues simulate how electrical properties of two layers affect semitransparent perovskite solar cells. Their 2023 study concerns tin oxide and a carbon-based layer in a p-i-n device structure.

Perovskite top cells show promise for inexpensive, high-performance tandem solar cells paired with silicon. The simulation was built from real experimental data to increase model validity. Band alignment at the interface between the two layers significantly affected electron transport. The authors propose a design rule about choosing the conduction band offset between the layers. If that condition fails, raising doping density in either layer can still improve electron extraction and device performance.
pmc-10745547:
McKay Meinzer and co-authors review salt-loving bacteria that may help crops in salty soils in a 2023 paper. Soil salinization is spreading under irrigation, drought, and climate change, and it cuts yields worldwide. Salt-tolerant plants, halophytes, host bacteria around and inside their roots that thrive in salt. Those microbes may be part of how the plants cope.

Moving such bacteria onto salt-sensitive crops could let them grow where they now fail. The review focuses on two Gram-negative groups, Halomonas and Kushneria, common in very salty places. Both turn up with halophytes, hinting they can serve as growth promoters. The authors trace what is known about salt-tolerant root microbiomes. They weigh the promise of these bacteria as inoculants for salt-hit farmland. The goal is steadier harvests as soils grow saltier.
pmc-10745947:
Patrick Kottenhahn and four colleagues published a 2023 study of the defense systems of Clostridium carboxidivorans, a bacterium that turns syngas into useful chemicals. Syngas is a mix of carbon monoxide, hydrogen, and carbon dioxide from industrial waste gases. The bacterium converts it into hexanol, a fuel and chemical feedstock.

Improving the bacterium by genetic engineering is blocked by its restriction-modification systems, its built-in defense against foreign DNA. The genome encodes at least ten restriction enzymes, which cut DNA, and eight methyltransferases, which mark the cell's own DNA as safe. The team mapped the methylation patterns across the genome. Knowing the defense code is the first step toward engineering this promising industrial microbe.
pmc-10746047:
Thaissa Ribeiro and three co-authors turn waste seeds from an Amazon fruit tree into a biodiesel catalyst in a 2023 paper. They charred murici seeds into biochar, then loaded it with sodium at several levels to make a solid base catalyst, a reusable alternative to dissolved chemicals.

The fifteen percent sodium version performed best and was examined with a battery of standard material tests. Under tuned conditions it converted oil to biodiesel with about ninety seven percent ester content in the first run. Activity held up over five reuse cycles, and a regeneration step restored it for five more. The authors present the seed based catalyst as a cheap, effective use for leftover Amazonian biomass.
pmc-10746447:
Frederik Groenland and co-authors set out a registry study of blood flow readings taken right after stent placement in heart attack patients, in a 2023 paper. A pressure-based index measured after the procedure, FFR, can judge the result and guide fine-tuning. Low values after stenting predict trouble in stable patients, but in full heart attacks the small vessels stiffen temporarily, which critics say distorts the reading. The single-center registry enrolled one thousand consecutive stented patients of every presentation.

Readings were taken with a dedicated microcatheter once the operator was satisfied, with no further tweaking afterward. A resting pressure ratio was computed later from stored traces. The study compares the readings between patients with and without the major heart attack type, and between the guilty vessel and bystander vessels in the attack group. Mixed statistical models handle the nesting of vessels inside patients.
pmc-10747347:
Laszlo Papp and a large team of co-authors propose a way to restore dry grassland with native plants in this 2023 paper. The study site lies in the driest part of the Pannonian region of Hungary. Local plants there already cope with heat and drought. Imported seed mixes from other climates often fail over time.

The team screened annual and perennial herbs for seed yield, looks, and germination. Twenty chosen species were treated with a fungal partner that lives in roots. That partner, a mycorrhizal fungus, can raise drought tolerance and growth. The aim is cheap, low upkeep planting for farms, building sites, and conservation land. Native cover also fits the local ecosystem better than imported mixes.
pmc-10747947:
Daniela Díaz and co-authors build lab tests to spot a bacterium that causes canker in cherry trees, in a 2023 study. The germ, a strain of Pseudomonas amygdali, was newly found in Chile and scars the above-ground parts of trees. Later it causes sunken cankers and gummy ooze, hurting orchards.

The team read the full genomes of twelve related isolates and compared them to pin down traits unique to the target strain. From those traits they designed two tests: a standard PCR test and a faster LAMP test that works at one steady heat. Both aim to name the germ quickly and surely from tree samples. Fast, sure tests let growers act before the disease spreads through a block.
pmc-10748247:
For people with eczema, scratching is the symptom that ruins sleep and skin alike, yet clinics still grade it by asking. Cheuk-Yan Au and co-authors built in 2023 a sensor glove that counts scratches automatically.

The glove, named SIGMA, carries stretch sensors on each finger and a motion unit on the palm. A learning model reads those streams and flags scratching episodes. In lab checks the model scored up to ninety-nine percent accuracy. In a pilot with six children, it caught about ninety-four percent of scratches while worn. The authors say objective scratch counts could help doctors grade itch severity and tune treatment for each patient.
pmc-10748347:
Trachoma, the blinding eye disease caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, has long been fought with the World Health Organization's SAFE strategy: surgery, antibiotics, facial cleansing, and environmental improvement. Carla Enrica Gallenga and co-authors review the history of that campaign from an Italian point of view, tracing how the bacterium lives inside cells and how the immune response scars the eye. They revisit an old question: how much blame belongs to the flies Musca sorbens and Scatophaga stercoraria, once treated as the main carriers?

The review argues the flies look largely blameless, while sexual transmission of the same bacterium deserves more attention. The authors propose adding an S for sexual behavior, making SAFE-S, and screening people with risky sexual contact. They urge eye doctors, gynecologists, urologists, schools, and pediatricians to share the prevention work.
pmc-10750047:
Xinyang Gao and co-authors measure stretching inside a 3D-printed aluminum alloy, not just on its surface. The alloy is a workhorse of laser powder-bed printing. How its tiny grains deform and crack decides part strength, yet bulk strain at that scale was hard to see.

X-ray tomography scanned the part while software matched the images across load steps. Silicon-rich particles in the treated metal served as natural markers. The method reads strains above half a percent with fine spatial detail. Pores and grain texture can then be tied to local damage. Surface-only views miss the interior story. The technique opens the bulk to the same scrutiny the surface gets.
pmc-10753547:
Le, Chen, and Veedu reviewed modified building blocks for splice-switching drugs in this paper from twenty twenty-three. These drugs are short synthetic strands that redirect how a gene's message is cut and joined. Approved versions treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy and spinal muscular atrophy. Every approved strand is fully built from chemically altered units.

The alterations buy stability, staying power in the body, and safety. Past reviews covered such chemistry for many drug types, but none focused on splice switching alone. The authors catalogue the analogues tried for this use. A brief history of approved drugs and trial candidates follows. They hope the survey sparks work on fresh analogues.
pmc-10754247:
Kyrylo Malakhov examines in 2023 Ukraine's digital health system, eHealth, through its trends, definitions, standards, and recent legal revisions. The pandemic and then the war pushed telemedicine from the margins to the front line of Ukrainian care. National strategy stresses human-centered, accessible remote care aligned with global standards.

Telemedicine use surged most in conflict-affected regions, where clinics are hard to reach. A cloud platform for patient-centered cancer telerehabilitation grew from a national science competition project. Legal updates try to keep pace with practice. The account shows a health system digitizing under fire, and it offers other countries a case study in building eHealth that bends without breaking.
pmc-10755547:
Natalia Chechko, Elena Losse, Thomas Frodl, and Susanne Nehls study the low mood many mothers feel in the days after birth, in this study published in 2023. These 'baby blues' are common and usually pass, but their ties to a mother's past health were not well mapped. The team also asked whether the blues, and premenstrual syndrome before pregnancy, warn of later depression.

They followed 369 mothers for twelve weeks after delivery, recording health history, mood, stress, and bonding. The strength of the blues tracked closely with how severe a mother's premenstrual symptoms had been. Both the blues and premenstrual syndrome raised the odds of adjustment disorder or postpartum depression; strong blues raised the odds nearly sevenfold. Among mothers who stayed well, the blues linked to first-time birth, family mental illness, and childhood trauma. Checking both symptom sets in the first days could help flag mothers who need support early.
pmc-10755747:
Aaron Forde, Sergei Tretiak, and Amanda Neukirch hunt a recipe for loosening the grip that layered perovskites keep on their own excitons, in a 2023 study. These materials shine in optoelectronics, but trapped excitons block uses that need free charges. The team modeled two lead-bromide cousins that differ only in their organic spacer molecule. One spacer, built from naphthalene, welcomes holes.

That welcome changed the exciton's character, mixing in charge-transfer flavor. Stronger dielectric screening came along too. Together the two effects cut the binding energy well below the other compound's. The authors propose spacers that screen strongly and accept holes as a general design rule for freeing charges in two-dimensional perovskites.
pmc-10757147:
Akshit Chitkara and co-authors pool past trials to judge the risks of a cancer drug used with chemotherapy for bowel cancer that has spread, in work published in 2023. The drug blocks blood vessel growth in tumours. It is known to raise blood pressure and, rarely, to cause clots or bleeding.

The team searched major databases and gathered 26 trials that compared the drug plus chemotherapy against chemotherapy alone. Patients on the drug had about four times the odds of severe high blood pressure. In a subset of studies, the odds of a clot in an artery were more than twice as high. The authors conclude the drug adds real risk on top of chemotherapy. They urge close monitoring of blood pressure and clot signs during care.
pmc-10770647:
Tonje Holte Stea and three co-authors ran in 2023 a six-month family program for Norwegian children with overweight across twelve Healthy Life Centers. The trial enrolled 137 children aged six to twelve and their parents, without randomization. Families in the program got personal counseling, nutrition courses and activity groups. Parents reported food habits, and nurses measured height and weight.

Children in the program ate evening meals more often and kept fewer salty snacks at home. They drank more water and took in less energy, sugar and saturated fat. Their standardized body mass scores fell, and the drop tied directly to lower energy and carbohydrate intake after treatment. Age and sex worked through diet as well. The authors back such tailored programs inside local primary care. They present family habits as the lever that moves weight.
pmc-10803647:
Elizabeth Hoyos-Loya and co-authors asked front-line health workers and parents across Mexico what blocks breastfeeding promotion in primary care. The study, published in 2023, covered eighty-eight public health centers in six states. Eighty-eight professionals, from doctors to nutritionists, and eighty parents of young children were interviewed, with nine parent focus groups besides.

The qualitative design triangulates those voices to find where counseling breaks down: time, training, supplies, and mixed messages all surface in such settings. Naming the barriers precisely is the first step to fixing them. Mexico's clinics serve millions of new mothers, so even small unblocking matters.
pmc-10808647:
Yina An and four co-authors review how a growth-control pathway may steer the metabolism, and thus the behavior, of macrophages in inflamed tissue, in a paper the head dates to 2023. The catalog lists 2024, but the head's year governs. Macrophages polarize into attack or repair modes, and their fuel choices drive which mode they take.

The Hippo pathway, famous for sizing organs, increasingly looks like a metabolic traffic controller, talking with many other signaling routes. The review first maps how metabolism shapes polarization in inflammatory diseases, then catalogs the signaling pathways that tune macrophage fuel use. Against that background it argues Hippo sits near the network's center, with crosstalk that could explain disease-linked polarization patterns. The authors frame the pathway as a promising lever: adjust the signaling, and the macrophage's metabolism and mission may follow.
pmc-10809847:
Asefa Adimasu Taddese and co-authors present a systematic review and meta-analysis, published in 2023, of deep learning for diagnosing gynaecological cancers from images. These cancers threaten women worldwide, and most heavily where specialists are scarce. Human image reading is the norm, but it varies between readers and can miss disease.

Following standard review guidelines, the team searched five databases for studies from 2018 to 2022 and pooled their accuracy results. The synthesis weighs how well the models perform across cancer types and image kinds, and where the evidence is thin. The aim is a clear map of what these tools can already do and what clinics still need from them.
pmc-10822947:
Sok-Kun Tae and two co-authors report in 2023 the case of a Malaysian teenager with a rare inherited disorder of cell division. The condition stunts growth, shortens limbs evenly, and marks the face; its severest form is Roberts syndrome. The girl carried its classic signs, yet early chromosome tests came back equivocal.

Whole exome sequencing found the cause: a faulty splice in the ESCO2 gene, doubled from both parents. Across a fifteen-year diagnostic path she gained new features, diabetes, ovarian failure, eye changes, and shifting skin pigment, yet no learning disability. The report, first published in 2023, widens the known picture of the disorder in Asian children.
pmc-10825947:
Haojie Sun and colleagues reviewed records in 2024 on ozone care for diabetic foot ulcers. Such ulcers heal slowly and often lead to amputation. Most past ozone work studied long treatment courses. The team asked whether a short course could help. They compared two patient groups from hospital records. One group got ozone care, and the other got standard care. Wound state, germs, and blood markers were checked after one week. Outcomes were then tracked for twelve weeks.

After one week, the ozone group looked better on most markers. Growth and defense markers rose, while inflammation markers fell. Germ types in wounds also shrank. By twelve weeks, more ozone wounds had healed. Healing also came faster on survival-style curves. The ozone group spent fewer days in hospital. They needed shorter antibiotic courses and fewer readmissions. The authors call short ozone care a valuable option for these ulcers.
pmc-10827847:
Tzu-Yi Chia and co-authors study a signaling pair that shapes how T cells behave inside glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain tumor. Published in 2023, their work focuses on the CXCL16 signal and its receptor CXCR6. These tumors suppress immunity largely through myeloid cells that gather around them, and direct contact between those cells and T cells steers the response.

Mapping the pair showed the signal sits on the tumor-associated myeloid cells, while the brain's own microglia release it in soluble form. The team tracks how this arrangement switches T cell activity on or off by place and time inside the tumor. Their aim is a handle for waking the immune system in a cancer that resists it.
pmc-10828847: Ogallar-Blanco and co-authors compare perfectionism and passion in soccer players of two age groups. Players under 23 are set against older semi-professional players. Past work links both traits to each other and to sports performance, yet team sports such as soccer have had little study. The work tests how the two traits differ by age group and how they relate to each other in this squad setting.
pmc-10830647:
Ting Mei and four co-authors report a lung cancer case with a full clear out in a paper whose head dates it to 2023. The patient had small cell lung cancer at a stage where the disease had spread in the chest but not past it. This cancer type rarely gets surgery, and the gains of drug plus immune care before surgery were unknown for it.

The patient took five rounds of an immune drug with chemo, then had surgery. Lab checks of the removed tissue found no live cancer left at all. Six months on, scans showed no return or spread, and the patient had no side effects from the care. The authors say the path may cure some such cases, but call for planned trials.
pmc-10834647:
Asrani and co-authors report a single hard case: a 37-year-old man with a rare in between lymphoma and a badly failing liver. Gray zone lymphoma mixes traits of two better known lymphomas, and first treatment is unsettled, above all when organs are weak. Standard strong chemotherapy was too risky at first. Their case report, published in 2023, starts him on a targeted antibody drug alone.

The drug, which homes to a marker on the tumor, sharply improved his liver tests. Doctors then added a dose adjusted chemotherapy mix, and scans showed the lumps nearly gone and the swollen organs shrunk. He finished the full course, reached complete response, and returned to full time work with no relapse seen. The authors present the drug as a safe bridge to full treatment.
pmc-10867947:
Anna Jankowska, Kamil Chwojnicki, and Edyta Szurowska review how multiple sclerosis diagnosis has changed in a 2023 article. Diagnosis rests on showing disease spread across space and time in the central nervous system, while ruling out look-alike disorders. Magnetic resonance imaging joined the rules in 2001 and changed the field.

The review walks through the 2017 McDonald criteria and what changed from 2010. Spinal fluid bands can now stand in for spread over time. Symptomatic and cortical lesions now count in scans. The authors also cover Polish and international guidance and future paths. Early, correct diagnosis opens early treatment and avoids needless therapy.
pmc-10990447:
Kay de Wit and co-authors build a model that estimates how personal traits combine to raise the risk of abuse, in a 2023 paper. Past research lists many factors tied to victimization by aggressive or intimidating behavior, drawn from work on partner violence, bullying, and sexual abuse. Most studies look at one factor at a time, mainly in women.

The team joined findings from earlier studies into a single network model for girls and young women aged 12 to 24. The model shows how certain mixes of traits push the chance of harm upward, and it sorts those mixes into groups. The groups differ for physical violence, non-physical abuse, and sexual abuse. The authors offer the model as a way to spot risk patterns that single-factor studies miss.
pmc-11230147:
Asem Ali Ashraf and colleagues published a case series in 2023 on a dangerous yeast in a south Indian hospital. The yeast is Candida auris, first found in a patient's ear in Japan. It has since appeared on six continents. It spreads inside hospitals and often resists treatment.

The report describes cases seen at one large teaching hospital. Such infections cause frequent treatment failure and high death rates. Hospitals still lack settled rules for stopping its spread. The authors set out their cases against that wider background. Their aim is practical: sharper awareness among hospital staff. Early detection and strict infection control are the defenses they emphasize.
pmc-11533247:
Julie Kanter and co-authors report, in a 2024 paper, final results from a phase two trial of an antibody drug for sickle cell disease in adults. The drug blocks P-selectin, a sticky molecule that helps blood cells clump and jam vessels, causing the painful crises that define the disease.

The study was single arm and ran at several centers. Fifty seven patients, aged 16 to 70 and each with at least one crisis in the prior year, received infusions every four weeks. Two dose levels were enrolled in sequence, with or without the standard drug hydroxyurea alongside. The trial tracked how the body handled the drug, how fully it blocked its target, safety, and crisis rates. Final results from such a study decide whether a larger, controlled trial is justified. For a disease with few targeted options, that readout carries weight.
pmc-11535047:
Gaurav Arora and Hongli Feng present a 2024 study on how well farmers judge local weather change. Their survey covered corn and soybean growers on the western edge of the United States Corn Belt, where much grassland has been lost. The team compared what farmers said about past temperature, rainfall, and drought with actual weather records for the same places.

About seventy percent of farmers misjudged past weather change. Most of those who erred saw past weather as hotter and drier than records show, while many understated rainfall trends. The errors were not random: farmers who had plowed up protected grassland tended to recall weather in ways that fit that choice. The authors say such biased recall can skew farm decisions and climate policy. Their work links what people believe about weather to what they have done with the land.
pmc-11536847:
Ruifang Xu and four colleagues search ultrasound images for signs that separate a malignant thyroid tumor from its benign twin, in a 2024 study. Follicular cancers spread through the blood, but before surgery they look almost identical to harmless adenomas.

Ninety-six patients with confirmed tumors of either type had their scans reviewed against pathology. Several features appeared far more often in cancers, including mixed blood flow patterns and a star-like scar at the nodule's center. Four features together, including coexisting autoimmune thyroid inflammation, sorted the two with high accuracy, catching nearly all cancers. The authors offer the combination as a preoperative aid where tissue sampling cannot settle the question.
pmc-11536947:
Dong, Ji, Guo, Wang, and Xie study a long noncoding RNA in osteoarthritis in twenty twenty-four. The RNA, called TSIX, does not code for a protein but can regulate genes. Its role in joint cartilage decay was unclear. The team measured TSIX in patients and in a cell model of the disease.

TSIX levels were higher in patients than in healthy controls. Levels rose further in patients with worse joint damage grades. Higher TSIX tracked with worse knee function scores and higher pain scores. In cells, blocking TSIX improved survival and cut cell death after an inflammatory trigger. It also raised output of two key cartilage proteins. Tests showed TSIX acts through a small RNA that targets a gene called PTEN. The authors propose TSIX as a marker and treatment target.
pmc-11538447:
Yaru Zhang and six co-authors test an iron-based cleanup for a stubborn antibiotic in a 2024 paper. Enrofloxacin, a veterinary drug, lingers in water and soil and drives drug resistance. The team paired zero-valent iron with a persulfate oxidant to attack it.

At their best settings, the system removed about eighty-five percent of the drug in ninety minutes. Three reactive species shared the work, including hydroxyl and sulfate radicals. Over forty percent of the organic carbon was fully mineralized, and the treated water showed no clear toxicity to soil microbes afterward. The process worked across a wide acidity range and performed the same in river water as in pure lab water. Such robustness matters for real effluent. The authors offer the method as a reference point for antibiotic removal using sulfate-radical chemistry.
pmc-11572147:
Yang Bai and co-authors study a gene marker in breast cancer in a 2024 paper. A protein-coding gene called APOO shows high levels in several tumors. The team asked whether its level in breast cancer tracks patient outlook and whether it drives cancer cell behavior.

Data analysis linked high APOO levels to poorer outcomes, and the level sorted cancer from healthy tissue with high accuracy. Lowering the gene in lab cells slowed growth and movement. Lab tests tied the gene to cell death and self-cleaning pathways. Readers get a candidate marker for prognosis and a possible drug target, pending deeper proof.
pmc-11572247:
Ningning Feng and co-authors review neck spinal cord injuries in older patients in a study from two thousand twenty-four. These injuries occur without broken or displaced bones, often after minor trauma. The team compared surgery with non-surgical care in patients over sixty-five, over medium and long follow-up.

Records covered thirty-nine patients treated between two thousand ten and two thousand twenty-two. At the final check, the twenty-one surgical patients scored much better on nerve and movement scales than the rest. Scans showed the spinal canal was wider after surgery, confirming relief of pressure. Most patients were men with low-energy injuries. The authors advise active surgery when the patient's health allows.
pmc-11574247:
Xiangming Li and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, whether a waist-based score tracks with osteoarthritis in United States adults. The score, the weight-adjusted waist index, weighs waist size against body weight, so it flags abdominal fat more than bulk. Osteoarthritis, or joint wear, is a leading cause of pain and stiff joints in older adults.

The team used a national health survey from 2005 to 2014, with 12,696 participants. Models that adjusted for age, sex, race, and habits all pointed one way. Adults with higher scores faced a clearly higher risk of osteoarthritis. The link held across groups split by sex, age, and race. The score also predicted risk better than plain weight, waist circumference, and body mass index in head-to-head checks. The authors offer it as an inexpensive gauge for clinical use.
pmc-11575047:
Díaz-Madriz and co-authors take Costa Rica's antibiotic pulse for 2019, the baseline year for resistance policy. Following World Health Organization method, they merged public-sector dispensing records with private-sector sales data and converted both into standard daily doses per thousand residents. National use came to 14.32 such doses a day.

Penicillins led overall and in public care, where cautious Access-class drugs made up 83 percent of use. Private care told another story: macrolides led, and 61 percent of private antibiotics were Watch-class drugs, the ones stewardship guards most. The authors urge joint public-private surveillance and tighter rules where the Watch share runs high, offering their method to the region.
pmc-11575447:
Dominika Muršec, Sonja Šostar Turk, Urška Rozman, and a wider team wrote this scoping review, published in 2024. It surveys studies that teach hand hygiene, the simplest infection shield in healthcare, through immersive technology such as virtual reality.

The reviewers searched major databases plus dissertations and gray sources. Eleven studies from seven countries made the final cut. Ten of them used virtual reality to train healthcare workers or students. Six found immersive teaching useful for hand hygiene skills. Yet theory barely underpinned the work: only two studies leaned on any teaching framework. Engagement and knowledge retention, the technology's selling points, remain thinly measured in this niche. The authors map a young field with promising tools, patchy evidence, and clear room for better-designed trials that say why immersion should work.
pmc-11576847:
Angelika Wolman and co-authors tested how the rhythm of a task seeps into the brain and shapes decisions. Volunteers played a Go-NoGo reaction game in which trials arrived at a steady beat of about one every 1.3 seconds. Electrode recordings showed the brain's electrical activity picking up power at exactly that beat frequency, though the strength varied widely between people.

Participants whose brains locked onto the rhythm more strongly showed steadier trial-to-trial phase patterns and simpler, less complex signals. They also answered faster and showed a stronger bias to respond. The authors read the results as a chain: the environment's timing is encoded in brain activity, simpler neural dynamics follow, and behavior tilts accordingly. The study links input dynamics directly to decision style.
pmc-11579347:
Sandhya Kiran Pemmasani and co-authors search in 2024 for gene variants tied to long life in India. Genes play a real part in how long a person lives, but most studies have looked outside India. The team compared people aged eighty-five and up with younger adults, using a chip that tests many known disease-linked variants.

Nine variants stood out in the long-lived group. Some linked to a slower heart rate and lower risk of bone loss, anxiety, or schizophrenia ran higher in that group. Others tied to heart rhythm trouble and bile duct disease ran lower. A variant in a gene called FOXO3A, tied to long life in other countries, also showed up. Pathways for stress defense and energy use featured strongly.
pmc-11579947:
Monteiro and co-authors simulate how an epilepsy drug coats silver nanoparticles at the molecular level. Silver particles attract interest for killing microbes, calming inflammation, and resisting oxidation. The drug oxcarbazepine was tested as a coating at five strengths, from 500 to 2,500 parts per million. Computer dynamics tracked how drug molecules settle on the particle clusters. Special analyses mapped the weak bonds that hold the coating together.

The drug bound strongly, and binding grew as strength rose. Contact ran mainly through one nitrogen atom of the drug, at every strength. The team also describes how the coating layer is ordered. Such detail guides designs for drug-carrying particles.
pmc-11580247:
Nurse leaders carried heavy loads during the COVID-19 pandemic, and their burnout may differ by gender. Latifah Alenezi and co-authors surveyed two hundred and ten nurse leaders in the United States online in twenty twenty-three. They measured personal, work-related, and client-related burnout, plus work-life balance and the impact of the pandemic, then compared women and men.

Women reported higher personal burnout than men, with mean scores of fifty-six point two against forty-nine point three on the study scale. Men, in turn, scored higher on client-related burnout, at forty-five point three against thirty-four point eight. Work-related burnout is examined alongside these patterns. The authors argue that prevention programs should be designed with gender in mind, since the strain lands in different places for women and men in leadership roles.
pmc-11580647:
Kin Wan and co-authors describe a joint training program for optometry and education students, in a 2024 paper. Children with special educational needs often miss out on eye care. The program taught both student groups about those needs and about each other's roles. Lectures and workshops built knowledge and exam skills. The core was hands-on: mixed teams screened vision at two special schools, serving 170 children with mild to moderate intellectual disabilities.

Surveys before and after showed clear gains in understanding of special needs. Confidence in examining such children also rose firmly. Reflective writing echoed the numbers. Students valued the teamwork, felt more competent, and grasped their partners' roles better. A stronger sense of social duty also emerged. The authors present the program as a workable model for interprofessional training.
pmc-11582547:
Abiodun Lasisi-Sholola and four co-authors tested hormone therapy in rats in a 2024 study. Lead exposure and loss of estrogen after menopause are each tied to memory loss and brain cell damage. The team asked whether replacing estrogen could undo harm from both causes at once.

Thirty female rats were split into six groups, covering surgery to remove the ovaries, lead exposure, hormone treatment, and their combinations. Over twenty-eight days of treatment, the untreated harmed groups did worse on maze and object memory tests. Their front brain region showed distorted tissue, fewer pyramid-shaped neurons, and lower levels of the messenger dopamine. Hormone replacement reversed much of that damage in the combined group. The authors say estrogen protects memory circuits against this double hit, at least in rats.
pmc-11584347:
Xiaochun Xia and four co-authors sort high-grade glioma patients by genes tied to a copper-driven cell death, in a 2024 study. The death form, cuproptosis, is triggered when copper floods a cell. The team grouped patients from two large cancer atlases by the activity of fourteen such genes. Two groups emerged with sharply different survival odds and immune traits.

One group looked like an immune desert, with low defense signals across the board. The other looked inflamed and immune-rich. A score built from the genes predicted who would answer immune drugs and chemo. Lab tests flagged one gene as a driver of the tumor's harsh traits, and a candidate drug for the high-score group. The authors offer the score as a guide for personal care plans.
pmc-11585147:
Yongxiang Huang and co-authors study in 2024 how mango seedlings cope with cold, a real risk for a tropical fruit. A chemical mark placed on RNA helps plants tune their genes under stress. The team mapped that mark across the seedling's genes in cold conditions and counted which genes changed their activity.

Thousands of marks shifted and over two thousand genes changed activity, in mixed patterns. One gene stood out: HSP70, a helper that guards other proteins. Its protein latched onto marked RNAs and gathered into droplets inside cold-stressed cells, which may steady key messages. The work gives breeders fresh targets for cold-hardy mango lines.
pmc-11585247:
Yimer and a large team present an evaluation from twenty twenty-four of a diabetes care project in Ethiopia. The project shifts diabetes care to primary units with outside support. Thirty-one project sites and sixty-two control sites are compared. Data span fifty-four months across six regions and the capital. Over four in five sites now offer screening, diagnosis, and treatment. Written guidelines sit in three quarters of sites. Trained staff share rose from just over half to all staff.

Project sites hold more working glucose meters than controls. Blood sugar test counts rise notably at project sites. A key long-term blood test stays rare, though. Records still suffer gaps, over-reporting, and late filing. The authors credit the project with real service gains.
pmc-11585947:
Brad Rodu and Nantaporn Plurphanswat fill a decade-long gap in American tobacco statistics: how smoking and vaping overlap, in a 2024 short report. Federal surveys tracked each habit separately for years, leaving the substitution question data-poor.

Combining two national surveys from 2011 to 2022, the authors compute joint rates for high schoolers and adults to age 44. Smoking fell sharply, above all in teenagers and the youngest adults. Vaping climbed steeply in the same years. Former smokers made up a growing share of vapers. Quit ratios jumped among adults in their early twenties, long a low-quitting group. The numbers will not settle the gateway debate, but they frame it properly.
pmc-11586047:
Sarah Douglah and seven co-authors review whether sugar chains from tissue glue can flag cancer early. These chains shift as tumors grow, spread, and dodge the immune system. Their 2024 review keeps eleven solid studies that cover eight cancer kinds.

One chain type read kidney cancer with near perfect scores in one study. A second chain's parts looked strong for ovary cancer. A third chain split spread from contained breast cancer with fair scores, and a mixed score did better. The same chain ran high in mouth and gut cancers. The authors see real promise in the chains as early marks. Wide, mixed groups must still prove the scores hold.
pmc-11587547:
Jinbo Xu and seven co-authors read the full protein-coding DNA of 280 children whose developmental delay or intellectual disability had no explanation, in this 2024 study. Such children often wait years for a diagnosis, while whole exome sequencing increasingly delivers one by finding a single damaging variant. The question was how often it succeeds, and what predicts success.

Pathogenic variants turned up in seventy-three children, about thirty-six percent of the tested group, including twenty-five cases where whole chunks of chromosome were duplicated or missing. Almost nothing about the child predicted a positive result: not age, sex, birth history, seizures, or scan findings. Oddly, the mode of delivery did correlate. The practical message is broad access: since clinical clues barely sort the winners, offering the test widely beats trying to guess who harbors a findable cause.
pmc-11589647:
Jian Yang, Zheng-Xin Liu, and Chen Fang wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four classifying new kinds of quasiparticles in magnetic materials. Quasiparticles are the effective excitations of a material, and symmetry dictates which kinds can exist. Lattices with discrete symmetry allow more kinds than empty space does, including some with no vacuum counterpart.

The authors focus on materials where magnetic order and mobile electrons coexist, under a symmetry scheme called spin-space groups. They prove a theorem tying quasiparticle traits, such as degeneracy and how energy varies with momentum, to symmetry invariants. From it they list two hundred eighteen classes of new quasiparticles found only under these symmetries. An example with three twelve-fold fermions shows how the classes differ in practice.
pmc-11590347:
Shiyu Yang, Xia Jiang, and co-authors map the drug trial field for a slow blood cancer in a note to peers, in a 2024 letter. Key block drugs made most sick folks live near as long as well kin. Yet firm, back slide, and march cases still lack wide drug picks in wards.

A trade bank read finds more than a score and a half of trials to a set fall date. Trial counts stay high year to year with a slight late dip. Most trials sit in the first two test grades by far. Mark drugs rule the field past the first win year. New immune ways surge in late trial work.
pmc-11590447:
Alvi Muldani, Karmele Llano Sanchez, and Krista Farey report a life-threatening allergic reaction traced to the bite of a slow loris. These small primates are among the few venomous mammals, and their bites have caused anaphylaxis in the wild and in captivity. The patient, a man in his late thirties, arrived with severe nausea and vomiting about half an hour after the encounter.

The authors use the case to make a wider point. Lorises are squeezed by habitat loss and the illegal pet trade, and fragmented forests push people and animals into more contact. More contact means more bites. They also note that reactions like this are poorly counted in lower-income settings, where diagnosis can lag and records are thin. Fast recognition and treatment remain the difference between a scare and a death. The case ties one emergency to the ecology that produced it.
pmc-11593247:
Pia Göbert and co-authors survey in 2024 how German newborn intensive care units use ethics consultation. Modern perinatal care saves more fragile babies but raises harder moral calls, and consultation services exist to support teams through them. Heads of all 213 German perinatal centers were invited to answer a mixed questionnaire.

Ninety percent of respondents said a consultation service was established and available. Yet use was rare or occasional for most units, even though users rated the help highly. Ratings also split between professional groups. The authors float hurdles behind the gap, and ask whether liaison-style services would fit neonatology better.
pmc-11594147:
Svenja Kerpa and a large team build tracers that light up prostate cancer cells under X-ray fluorescence imaging, in a 2024 study. Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer in men, and current tools can miss early or tiny disease. The tracers aim at PSMA, a marker on prostate cancer cells, using a urea part that grips it. Iodine atoms attached to the tracer make it visible to the imaging method.

One design with three iodine atoms targeted the marked cells and imaged them successfully. The measured iodine uptake per cell matched values known from established tracers read by other methods. The same tracer idea can also weigh and characterize nanoparticles. A sharper tracer could one day flag single cancer cells that scans now overlook.
pmc-11594647:
Jana Luecht and co-authors study inflammation after heart surgery in a 2024 paper. Children born with heart defects often need surgery on a heart-lung machine. The machine can spark body-wide inflammation that harms recovery, and the chain of events is still unclear.

The team exposed lab-grown immune cells to blood samples taken around surgery. Blood from machine cases switched on one signaling path and raised levels of inflammation and vessel-leak factors. Longer time on the machine meant stronger responses. A drug that blocks that path calmed most of the response. Readers get a clearer target for drugs that could ease surgery side effects in children.
pmc-11595847:
Vasilii Mischinenko, Andrey Vasilchenko, and Georgy Lazorenko made porous building materials in 2024. They used coal gangue and waste concrete powder. Alkali activation turned the wastes into foams. Microwave heating sped up the process. The team varied heating time and power. Their goal was better properties with less energy.

Waste powder content also changed across samples. One mix gave the best overall performance. Strength fell only slightly in that mix. No chemical foaming agent was needed. Microwaves acted directly on the fresh mortar. Energy use dropped as a result. The work supports better waste-based foams. It also supports cleaner production methods.
pmc-11597647:
Mariuca Gartner and co-authors report a 2024 study on clear conductive films made by a gel route, with two added elements. Such films serve in screens and solar cells, where they must carry current while letting light through. How the base under the film and the added atoms shape its build and traits was not fully mapped.

The team laid five coats of film on glass, coated glass, and silicon, with niobium or zinc added in some runs. X-ray and light tests showed tiny crystals in all films, with no clumps of the added oxides. Surface shape and light traits shifted with both base and added element. Current and charge tests found traps for charge carriers in the film bulk and at the silicon face. Their counts were worked out, as was the way current flows.
pmc-11597847:
Abdessamad Ait benlabchir and co-authors dissect the essential oil of Eucalyptus globulus, a Moroccan folk remedy for breathing complaints, and test what its parts can do. Published in 2024, the study splits the oil into three fractions and profiles all four samples by gas chromatography. Eucalyptol led the mix, with globulol, cymene, cryptone, and others behind it.

Three bench assays graded antioxidant strength, and disk and dilution tests graded antibacterial action, while computer docking modeled how the compounds might bind their targets. One fraction topped the antioxidant chart in the headline assay. The team frames the oil's chemistry as a base for natural antimicrobial and antioxidant products, with fractions possibly outperforming the whole oil.
pmc-11598547:
Spasojević and nine co-authors make a silver-loaded hydrogel dressing meant to protect wounds and fight germs. Hydrogels keep wounds moist, and silver kills bacteria. The team used gamma rays both to link the gel's polymers and to form silver nanoparticles inside it, a process that also sterilizes the product.

Changing the gel recipe tuned pore size and swelling. The dressings released a quick burst of silver ions, useful against early bacterial films, then a slow tail for longer protection. Lab tests against two common bacteria confirmed killing power. Cell safety checks rounded out the case for these gels as topical dressings.
pmc-11599947:
Wang and co-authors analyze a protein control enzyme called eEF2K across many cancer types, using large public datasets. The enzyme slows protein building, above all under cell stress, and it has been tied to tumor survival. Their 2024 study maps its levels, variants, and links to patient outcomes.

The enzyme played a dual role, helping or hindering tumors based on context, and its levels tracked with prognosis. Marks on its target protein were strong at three sites, which may tune protein building under stress. One mark stayed high even where the enzyme was low, hinting at backup enzymes at work. The authors suggest targeting this enzyme and its target marks as a cancer strategy worth testing.
pmc-11600547:
Xiong-hui Xu, Chao-yang Luo, and Yuan Mu publish the first full mitochondrial genome of a marine worm, in a 2024 paper. The worm, Loimia arborea, belongs to the terebellid family of tube-building polychaetes. Its mitochondrial genome runs sixteen thousand twenty-three base pairs. It holds thirteen protein-coding genes, twenty-three transfer RNA genes, two ribosomal RNA genes, and one control region. Unusually, two copies of the methionine transfer RNA gene sit side by side.

Using the thirteen protein genes across thirteen species, the team rebuilt the family tree of the order Terebellida. Two main branches were strongly supported, and the terebellid family came out as a single natural group. The genome gives future studies of worm evolution a solid reference point.
pmc-11600747:
Polke and co-authors gather what is known about an ultra-rare lung disease in a 2024 cohort paper. Pulmonary lymphangiomatosis spreads abnormal lymph vessels through the lung, chest lining, and nearby tissues. No agreed diagnosis or treatment path exists, so a specialist center reviewed its twelve cases found across more than two decades.

Patients skewed female and younger, averaging forty-two years, and most had never smoked. Breathlessness on effort and coughing blood or milky fluid were the lead complaints, and lung capacity ran well below normal. Scans most often showed central chest involvement and fluid around the lungs. Eight patients took sirolimus, and every treated patient improved on clinical and scan measures. One needed a lung transplant, and survival stood at ninety percent over follow-up.
pmc-11602247:
Mansi and co-authors study new prescriptions of sleep and calming drugs given after critical illness in the United Kingdom. Survivors often face poor sleep and mental health strain, yet how often family doctors start such drugs was unclear. Their 2024 study follows nearly 53,000 adult survivors who had not taken these drugs before their hospital stay.

About one in twenty got a new prescription within ninety days, and half of those kept refilling for months. A past record of insomnia nearly doubled the odds, and anxiety, depression, and recent opioid use also raised them. Older patients were less likely to get a new prescription. A small share of the variation sat with the practice itself. The authors call for work on where in the care path these starts happen.
pmc-11602647:
Raymond Spiteri and seven co-authors upgrade the numerics of a land surface model in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Land models simulate heat and water in soils and plants, but sloppy solvers quietly corrupt results. The team's model had used a low-order method with no real error control.

They wired in a solver suite that estimates error and adapts its step size and order on the fly. Continental runs over half a million land cells showed the change clearly. At the same computing cost, the new model's output sat orders of magnitude closer to fully converged answers. The authors argue reliable, efficient simulation sharpens understanding of the land's role in the Earth system. The upgrade is freely available to other modelers.
pmc-11603147:
Sick farm animals in Taiwan can carry gut germs that shrug off strong drugs, and Nan-Ling Kuan and co-authors checked how widespread that trait is in work from twenty twenty-four. Samples came from pigs, cattle, and goats with loose stools, plus birds with a gut illness. Lab tests sorted which germs could break the strong drugs.

About one in eight farm samples and one in twelve bird samples made the drug-breaking trait. Pigs were hit hardest among farm stock, and chickens most among birds. One gene type turned up most often in both groups. All trait carriers passed the gene to a test germ in the lab, which shows how fast it can spread. The authors warn that food animals form a real store of drug-proof germs.
pmc-11603647:
Aruna Gummadi, Divya Muppa, and Venakata Yella map unusual DNA shapes in gene regions in a 2024 study. The regions before and after a gene's coding part shape how the gene is used. DNA there can fold into shapes other than the standard double helix, and those shapes affect cell function. Their spread across species was not well documented.

They compared both regions across hundreds of species from many branches of life. Some orders of animals and plants favored curved motifs, while others favored four-stranded knots. Patterns were broadly shared across related classes, with species-level differences on top. The authors say the map hints at deep roles for these shapes in evolution.
pmc-11606047:
Alessandra Pereira and co-authors published a 2024 pilot study of a supplement mixture for a rare brain disease where iron accumulates in the deep hubs of the brain. The disease wears down movement, speech, and sight in steps. Its root is a flaw in a gene that starts the production of a core cell food, coenzyme A. With that food in short supply, cell pathways that need it sag. No cure currently stands.

The mixture holds four parts: the base of the food, its relative, a fish oil fat, and a protective vitamin. In dish cells from patients, the mixture cut iron accumulation and raised cell markers. Three patients then took the mixture with their standard brain drugs. The study is a first look, not a proof. The team sets out the dose and the scores used, for the next, larger trial.
pmc-11607047:
Zhining Kou and co-authors map bacteria around a desert sand-fixing shrub in winter. Their 2024 study samples soil beside the roots, soil near them, and the plant inner tissues of Ammodendron bifolium in the Takeermohuer Desert. The shrub is fading under human pressure and harsh climate, and its bacteria may aid survival.

Root-zone soil runs richer in organic matter, carbon, nitrogen, and potassium than outer soil. Five bacterial phyla dominate the desert set. One phylum leads near roots, another in far soil, and a third inside the plant. Depth and compartment each reshape the community. A root-loving genus peaks inside roots. The authors chart a winter baseline for protecting a pioneer desert plant.
pmc-11607447:
Jianwen Song and co-authors build a cancer-seeking nanoparticle in a 2024 paper. Tumors often lack oxygen, and their probe stays dark until it enters such low-oxygen tissue. Once lit, it glows in deep-tissue imaging and makes sound waves for photoacoustic scans, while light treatment heats and poisons the tumor.

A vessel-disrupting drug deepens the oxygen lack, and a coating from immune cells steers the particles to cancer. The light attack killed tumor cells in a way that alerts immunity, waking a defense pathway. In mice, treated tumors shrank, distant tumors slowed, and rechallenge failed. Readers get an image-guided immune therapy design.
pmc-11607947:
Abd El-Fatah and co-authors read bursa germ strains from hen flocks in Egypt in 2023. The germ crushes guard force in hens and costs farms a lot. In sum, 52 flocks gave bits: broiler, layer, and home hens. Flocks sat in more than one state of Egypt in the set. Signs span low mood, kidney marks, and bursa marks in birds. Pool bits from bursas went through a gene test for the germ.

That test used VP2-tied starts to flag the germ in bits. In sum, 20 flocks flagged germ-true in the test runs. Six prime bits went to egg growth for lone germ pulls. Egg marks span blood spill, skull swell, and liver death. Thick films on the egg sac joined the mark set there. VP2 reads from the six pulls then fed tree reads.
pmc-11608247:
Many old buildings have sound walls but rotten timber floors. Ahmed Shamel Fahmy and co-authors test a replacement floor built from cold-formed steel, thin steel shaped without heat.
