Their design is a box section: a concrete slab poured on trapezoidal steel decking, two sigma-shaped steel members, a steel plate, and stiffening angles, all joined with self-drilling screws. It is meant to install quickly and cheaply in restoration work.

The team loaded four full specimens to failure and recorded how they bent and strained. The floors proved stiff and strong, reaching full capacity without the thin steel buckling locally. Failure came instead from distortion at the end supports. Hand calculations matched the test results well, and a computer model of the system reproduced its behavior, supporting the design for reuse in old buildings.
pmc-11608547:
Liying Ren and co-authors review how image mining and gene-linked imaging can sharpen liver cancer care, in an overview from two thousand twenty-four. The cancer ranks sixth in frequency and third in cancer deaths worldwide. Scans guide screening and follow-up, yet what image patterns say about tumor biology stayed murky.

Radiomics extracts hard numbers from scans, widening what doctors can measure. Radiogenomics then ties those numbers to genes and pathways, giving them biological meaning. Reading the links, checking they hold across peoples, and handling varied causes remain hard. The authors map uses, strengths, and limits across the care path.
pmc-11610547:
Xinyue Wang and six co-authors show that a common sugar helps Salmonella thrive inside host cells in a 2024 study. Salmonella lives and multiplies inside macrophages, the immune cells meant to kill it, and from there it can spread through the body. Xylose is the second most common sugar in nature, and the germ can grow on it alone, yet its role in infection was unknown.

Infected macrophages held more xylose, and the germ switched on its xylose-eating genes inside them. Mutants that could not use xylose grew poorly in macrophages and spread weakly in mice. A sensing system that fires when glucose runs low turned the pathway on. The authors name xylose a backup fuel for the germ.
pmc-11611747:
Robert Edward T Ang and eleven co-authors published a study in 2024 on one-year results for a replacement lens that also corrects astigmatism. Cataract surgery swaps the cloudy lens for a clear implant, and a toric implant can fix the eye's uneven focusing at the same time. The lens tested here uses a double C-shaped support meant to hold it steady against rotation.

One hundred eighteen patients received the lens in both eyes, 236 eyes in all. A year out, three quarters of eyes landed within half a diopter of target, and nearly all patients saw well enough at distance without glasses. Night-time measures stayed strong for most. The support design kept lenses well aligned, a key to lasting correction.
pmc-11612447:
Alexa Lupi, Ana Vazquez, and Gustavo de los Campos present a 2024 method for mapping where gene risk scores travel well across ancestries. Most gene studies rest on European roots, so scores built there often fail in other groups. Past work blamed gene frequency and linkage gaps, but the loss may vary along the genome.

Their method splits the loss by genome zone and builds maps of local travel worth from UK Biobank data. Even in groups with low overall travel, some zones score high. Six traits back the maps, since zones the method flags do in fact travel well in real scores.
pmc-11613547:
Pallavi Singh and co-authors show that swapping in a certain ion makes a solar-cell material heal its own light damage faster, in a 2024 paper. The material is a halide perovskite, a crystal family prized for cheap solar cells and lights, and already known for self-healing. Real devices, though, use mixed recipes rather than the pure forms studied before, so the team tested healing in a mixed crystal used widely for such devices.

Replacing at least 15 percent of one building block, methylammonium, with guanidinium or acetamidinium sped up recovery after damage. A same-sized stand-in, dimethylammonium, changed nothing, so size alone is not the cause. The authors link the speed to strain inside the crystal, the swapped ion's electric tilt, and hydrogen bonds it forms. Fast self-repair matters because a device that heals overnight or between uses lasts far longer.
pmc-11613847:
Qian, Zhang, and Jiang mine U.S. drug harm reports for the cancer drug selpercatinib. The drug blocks RET changes found in some cancers. Trial data leave gaps on rare harms seen in wide use. The team pulled reports from the FDA adverse event system. Four math methods flagged harms tied to the drug.

They found 464 reports covering 1,007 harms. Three new harms stood out: trouble swallowing, fluid around the heart, and weakness on one body side. Abnormal liver tests were more common in Asian reports, mostly at doses above 160 mg. Allergy reports also ran high in Asian patients and in those under 50 kg. Dose, weight, and sex each shaped the harm pattern.
pmc-11615247:
Jun-yi Zhu and co-authors compared a protein from the original COVID virus strain with the same protein from the Omicron variant, to see why Omicron causes milder disease. The protein, called Nsp6, was already known as one of the most harmful parts of the virus. The team switched it on in fruit flies and in mouse heart cells.

The original protein damaged heart, muscle, and airway tissue in flies, both in structure and function. It also broke the cell's sugar-burning pathway and harmed its energy factories. The Omicron version did little of that damage. The contrast helps explain Omicron's milder course. It also points to Nsp6 as a target for future drugs.
pmc-11615547:
Housing trouble leaves traces in clinic notes, but pulling those facts out by hand is slow. Alexandra Ralevski and co-authors tested large language models for that task in work from twenty twenty-four. Notes came from hundreds of pregnant women, in both raw form and a cleaned form with names stripped.

The stronger model beat its older sibling and a name-finding tool, and it caught more cases than human readers did. Human readers were more exact when they did flag a case. Cleaning the notes barely changed the stronger model's exactness, though it caught fewer cases. The team sees such tools as a way to speed studies and to help clinics reach patients who need housing aid.
pmc-11615647:
Jonathan King and ten co-authors published a 2024 analysis of the Australian HIV epidemic using a ratio that works without firm population counts. For some groups, Australia lacks solid denominators, so trends are hard to track. The incidence prevalence ratio compares new transmissions with the number of people living with HIV, judged against a benchmark from life expectancy after infection.

The team modeled ratios for three groups: men whose HIV came from male to male sex, women, and people who inject drugs. Data came from notifications, cohorts, and health records. Each ratio was set against an Australia specific benchmark built from mortality data. A ratio below its benchmark signals a shrinking epidemic. The method gives public health teams a gauge for groups that headcounts miss.
pmc-11616347:
Haemophilus influenzae keeps evolving past ampicillin, sometimes without the usual enzyme to blame. Margo Diricks and co-authors re-examine the alternative route: changes in the drug's target protein, PBP3. Pooling 291 isolates, they confirm that two substitution patterns track with ampicillin resistance, while only one tracks with resistance to the stronger cefotaxime. Most unclassified isolates stayed susceptible, though one pattern proved a leaky predictor.

Genome-wide scans of two further cohorts hunt fresh determinants and trace how resistance evolves. Getting genotype and phenotype to agree matters at the bedside, where a wrong call wastes the first, best dose.
pmc-11616447:
Aleksandra Zamljen and Blaz Likozar review sponge-like goods that catch and hold ammonia in a 2024 piece. Ammonia could serve as a clean fuel and energy store, much like hydrogen but easier to ship. The catch is making it in small local plants from green power that comes and goes.

Old plants split ammonia from gas mixes by chilling, which wastes energy. Salt-like solids can soak it up instead and let it go on call. The piece walks through how those solids work, how fast they fill, and how heat shapes the trade. It also shows how math models help design fresh solids. Green local output is the end goal.
pmc-11616647:
Dale J Hu reviews Anthony Fauci's memoir On Call in a 2024 piece on a life in public service. Fauci led the main United States institute for allergy and infectious disease from the mid-1980s until early 2023. Hu notes that the book mixes triumphs and errors with personal stories, sports, and family roots.

The review traces Fauci's path from Jesuit schooling and medical training to leading the response to HIV and later threats such as Ebola, Zika, and Covid. It stresses his skill as a researcher, manager, speaker, and mentor, and his ties with seven presidents. Hu also notes the hostility Fauci faced in hard times, and the lessons in leading that readers in disease work can draw.
pmc-11621347:
Chunyu Song, Teer Guo, and Jianghua Sui set out to plan safer ship routes through crowded, complex seas. Their 2024 paper improves the A star search method, a standard route finder, by adding a ship collision risk score and by working on sea charts drawn at several scales at once.

A line-of-sight step smooths out the zigzag paths the search can produce. The risk score reshapes how the method prices each node, so the chosen route weighs both length and danger. Tested on the Zhoushan Islands sea area, the new method cut planning time by thirty percent, expanded nodes by eleven percent, and path length by about six percent against the plain method. The authors offer it as a fuller plan for smart ship safety.
pmc-11622547:
Eunkyung Han and co-authors report a 2024 study of immune cells inside triple-negative breast cancer. This form of breast cancer lacks the usual drug targets, so the immune response matters a great deal. Cells that enter the tumor, called tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, can shape how the disease grows and how treatment works.

The team profiled tumor samples with a gene panel to find immune genes tied to high cell counts. They then stained tissue samples to check protein levels for key markers. Tumors rich in these cells showed more killer T cells and natural killer cells, by gene and by stain alike. The authors built a combined score from five markers to sum up this killer cell presence. Their work links where the cells sit in the tumor to the outlook for patients.
pmc-11623947:
Se-Hyung Park led a large team comparing two ways to block fructose metabolism in a 2024 paper. The first enzyme in the pathway is a target for fatty liver disease, and excess fructose drives obesity. One approach silences the enzyme's gene in the liver; the other blocks its activity with a drug. Both improved liver fat in mice on a rich diet, but by different routes: silencing cut fat making, while the drug raised fat burning.

The drug also hit a second enzyme, causing a sugar-phosphate pile-up, liver swelling, and worse glucose tolerance. Silencing fully stopped fructose breakdown and improved tolerance. The authors warn that how one blocks the enzyme matters.
pmc-11624247:
Yeast colonies carrying the [PSI+] prion grow white, but treatments that cure the prion leave red sectors inside the white, like slices of a pie. Jordan Collignon and co-authors build the first computer pipeline to measure those sectors. Sector sizes and counts carry clues about how curing works at the molecular level, yet older lab routines ignore colony patterns.

Lacking hand-labeled examples, the team trained their neural network on synthetic colony images, then turned it loose on real ones. On hand-checked experimental images, the pipeline named the state of about ninety-five percent of colonies correctly and judged sector frequency correctly in about eighty-nine and a half percent. The authors note the tool can be extended across growing conditions, letting experiments be compared in fine detail. They offer it as a way to turn colony photographs into hard numbers on prion curing.
pmc-11624747:
Jonathan Ka Ming Ho and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on a handheld heart test for chest pain. When a person comes to an emergency room with chest pain, doctors check blood for a protein that rises when the heart is hurt. Lab tests are exact but slow, so a bedside device that gives fast results could speed up care.

The team compared the handheld device with a standard lab test in five hundred eighty-five Chinese patients at one emergency department. Blood was drawn at arrival and again three hours later, and both tests ran on each sample. They checked how well the fast test found heart injury, overall and in groups split by sex and age. A device that matches the lab this closely can help staff rule out heart attacks sooner.
pmc-11624947:
Story-based nursing, where patients tell and reshape their illness story, may ease the load of gut cancers. Yan Zheng, writing alone in 2024, reviews records of 103 patients with cancers of the food pipe, stomach, or bowel. Half got routine care, and half got the story-based care on top.

After care, the story group scored higher on drug, exercise, diet, and mood habits. Anxiety and sadness fell in both groups, but fell more in the story group. Felt burden and side effects also dropped more there. Life quality rose on body, family, mood, and function scales. Zheng notes the small, single-site sample as a limit.
pmc-11625047:
Khadija Sarwer and co-authors review a thickened-heart illness that blocks blood outflow, from its genes to new drugs. Their 2024 review covers obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Faults in muscle protein genes drive excess growth, stiff filling, and poor blood flow in the heart muscle.

Imaging with sound and magnetic scans remains the main way to grade thickness and blockage. Standard drugs such as beta blockers ease symptoms but do not change the disease course, and results vary by patient. New heart myosin blockers, two of which the review names in depth, mark a shift in care. The authors weigh a combined plan that joins gene insight, imaging, and layered drug therapy.
pmc-11625247:
Mona-Lisa Coutinho, Ricardo Portela e Silva, André Postiga, and Valentina Almeida report, published in 2024, a bronchoscopy that turned into an emergency in a woman of sixty-one. She carried an undiagnosed case of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a rare disease where inflamed blood vessels attack organs, airways included. During the camera exam of her airways, her voice-box area swelled badly. Her vocal cords barely moved. Air stopped flowing well, her oxygen crashed, and her heart arrested.

The team presents the case as a warning about hidden airway disease. The illness had given no signs beforehand, only unexplained breathing symptoms. A scope that is safe in most patients can trigger disaster in a swollen, stiff airway. The authors urge doctors to keep this disease on the list when breathing trouble has no clear cause. Airway checks before procedures, and a skilled airway team on hand, are their practical lessons.
pmc-11625747:
A schizophrenia drug that also fights coronaviruses gets its mechanism pinned down in a 2024 study by Sara Baroni and co-authors. The drug, lurasidone, had already shown activity against both SARS-CoV-2 and a common-cold coronavirus in earlier work.

Lab tests now point to two targets. The drug blocks a viral cutting enzyme shared by both viruses, which the virus needs to copy itself. Against SARS-CoV-2 it also strikes the spike protein, hindering entry into cells. Infected cells treated with the drug carried far less virus. The authors pitch the borrowed medicine as a dual-action candidate worth developing further, since future coronaviruses would likely share the same weak points.
pmc-11625947:
Farid Haghdadi and colleagues save a snapped front tooth without surgery, in this case report from twenty twenty-four. Horizontal root fractures usually spare the tip segment, which stays alive. Their patient's upper central incisor broke that rule: the apical segment had died, an unusual necrosis that normally invites root-tip surgery.

Age and the tooth's stability argued against the knife. Instead, the team sealed both segments, tip and crown side, with mineral trioxide aggregate, a bioactive dental cement. The conservative route worked across a two-year follow-up, preserving the natural tooth. The authors offer the case as evidence that MTA sealing can substitute for apical surgery in this rare fracture-plus-necrosis combination. It keeps intervention proportionate for a tooth with life left to live.
pmc-11626047:
Ali Ghassabi and co-authors test a paired drug plan in rats in a 2024 study of a kidney ill. The ill swells the kidney filters as the body shields turn on the self. Two arms of that shield, one that stirs attack and one that calms it, fall out of step in the ill.

Rats were made ill with a shot, then split into groups that got one drug, the other, both, or none. Blood tests and spleen cell reads tracked the shield arms. The pair aims to right the balance better than each drug alone. Such rat work can shape dose picks before human trials are weighed.
pmc-11627247:
Nino Sharvashidze, Matteo Valsecchi, and Alexander Schütz study, in twenty twenty-four, how the eye system judges blur and distortion across quick eye movements called saccades. Vision at the edge is coarser than at the center, yet objects at the edge have been judged less blurry than at the center in past tasks. The team asked if that overcorrection also happens across a saccade, and if it biases change detection. They altered the blur and distortion of simple shapes with a special algorithm.

Objects looked less blurry before a saccade, at the edge, than after, at the center. Distortion showed no such gap. In change tasks, people tended to report that both blur and distortion grew across a saccade. A brief blank after the move sharpened judgments.
pmc-11628247:
Giang H Ta and Max K Leong look for a safer way to give a key COVID-19 drug. Paxlovid pairs nirmatrelvir with ritonavir, and ritonavir clashes with many other drugs, which can cause harm. Their 2024 study asks whether nirmatrelvir alone could be given through the skin instead. Computer models predicted how well the drug crosses skin, using several standard tools to check the same question from different angles.

The models agreed that skin delivery looks feasible for this drug. A skin route would skip the gut and liver pass that forces the pairing with ritonavir. That could cut the clash risk for patients on many other medicines. The authors stress that the work is a computer-based first step, and lab and human tests would need to follow.
pmc-11628547:
Four researchers measure high lung blood pressure among lung disease patients in Ethiopia in a paper from 2024. The lung disease is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, often shortened to COPD. High pressure in the lung vessels is a serious problem that can follow it. The team reviewed records and surveys from public hospitals in Addis Ababa in mid-2024.

Just over half of the four hundred twenty-two patients had the high pressure problem. Risk was higher in men, in patients over fifty-five, and in those who smoked or drank alcohol. Heart failure also raised the odds. The authors urge early checks for these high-risk patients. Their findings fill a gap in local data on the problem.
pmc-11629147:
Tirlet and co-authors build a flexible data scheme for joining gene activity and gene control data across studies. Modern biology piles up layered data sets that are hard to combine and query. Their 2024 scheme uses a web-style data format and a shared location scheme, so records can be found by where they sit on the genome.

The scheme can be filled in whole or in part, which lets teams start small and grow. To prove it works beyond one field, the team rebuilt two published studies, one in medicine and one in environmental science. Both rebuilds succeeded, which the authors take as proof of breadth. They offer the scheme as a tool for handling wide multi-layer data sets.
pmc-11630847:
DeBord and a large team ran tests in twenty twenty-four on shade and capped feed for young beef cows in heat stress. Heat can cut growth, raise thirst, and strain the herd. They split near nine hundred cows into high-fuel capped feed or free rough feed, with or without shade.

Capped cows ate less but gained more per feed unit than free-feed cows. Shade cows also gained more per feed and drank less than no-shade cows. Pant scores were lower with shade and with capped feed both. In gut tests capped feed raised food break-down, and shade kept gut sour lower.
pmc-11631347:
Thiemo Frank and co-authors track drug resistance in a germ that causes ear, nose, and throat ills in Germany, in a 2024 study. Such ills drive much of the antibiotic use in clinics, so fresh counts of what still works guide sound care.

Labs in a watch network sent in two hundred fifteen samples from 2019 and 2020. The top rates of resistance hit three common drugs, each near one in six or one in seven samples. Gene reads traced most cases to known shields: an enzyme that breaks one drug and tweaks in a target that blunt the next. Two samples held fresh tweaks not yet tied to resistance. The authors set the counts and gene maps as a base for treatment rules.
pmc-11631747:
Shuangfeng Ding and co-authors join gene-chip reads with gene-lot draws to hunt guard genes at the root of multiple sclerosis. The ill is a self-guard strike that strips nerve wraps in the brain and cord. Their 2024 study pulls blood cell script sets of sick folks from a world bank. Guard-tied genes that shift in the ill are sifted by a guard gene list.

Path reads name what the shifted genes do as a crew. A web map lifts the hub genes of that crew. Score forms and curve tests weigh how well the hubs call the ill; mouse ill reads back the hubs in flesh. Lot draws then test if the hubs drive the ill or just ride it.
pmc-11631847:
Carlo Ronsini and co-authors pool studies on lymph node removal in advanced ovarian cancer. Their 2024 review follows standard reporting rules, searching two databases from the first reports to June 2022. Node spread appears in about half to three-quarters of advanced cases, so the value of routine removal is a live question.

Eighteen direct comparison studies with near twenty-seven thousand patients enter the sums. Overall survival runs higher in the node removal group by a clear margin. Disease-free survival tilts the same way but without statistical firmness. Recurrence rates read as comparable across the studies. The authors judge node removal protective in advanced disease. They still note the pooled set mixes study designs, so care in reading is warranted.
pmc-11632947:
Hei Hang Edmund Yiu and co-authors sit down with Hong Kong patients to learn what they actually want from cholesterol drugs. Their 2024 focus group study interviews twenty Cantonese-speaking patients with high cholesterol at a university hospital. Non-adherence to these medicines is common and quietly dangerous, yet patient preferences were barely mapped.

Four themes emerged: management struggles, medication preferences, and how the choice tasks themselves were structured and understood. Barriers included thin knowledge, heavy pill burdens, weak communication with providers, little say in decisions, scarce drug information, side effects, and plain forgetting. The sessions also fed a discrete choice experiment design, so the traits patients weigh can be measured at scale later. The authors aim to build preference evidence into prescribing.
pmc-11633747:
Sorting single cells by their chemistry, without dyes or damage, has long been slow, because the light signal each cell returns is faint. Jing Zhang and seven co-authors speed the process up sharply in this 2024 paper. Their system first sharpens the signal with a stimulated form of the scattering, images the cells, reads their chemical fingerprints on the spot, and then ejects chosen cells with a laser pulse.

The sorter handled live bacteria and fungi, and picked fat-rich yeast cells from a mixture at about thirteen cells per second, with gene tests confirming the catch. It also works on tissue slices, not just loose cells, and a feedback loop lets it image, judge, and eject in real time. The authors pitch the machine as a general tool for single-cell biology.
pmc-11634047:
Sónia Alves and co-authors test a fall risk score from a phone health app, in a 2024 paper. Falls are a major public health worry as populations age, with high death rates and lasting harm to body, mind, and social life. Spotting high risk people early is key, most of all for those over sixty in care homes.

The study used real world records for 617 older adults in German care homes, with a mean age over eighty. The app score at first check was tested against falls at follow up. The team also sought threshold values and the smallest change in score that matters in clinic. Such a score could guide personal fall plans.
pmc-11634147:
Eric Michael Lander and co-authors study in 2024 whether DNA from a tumor, found in the blood, can warn that cancers of the food pipe and stomach will come back. Their patients had local cancers and got drug or radiation treatment before surgery. In many, the tumor seemed fully gone after treatment, yet up to a third of those patients still saw the cancer return.

The team drew patients from 11 centers who had finished pre surgery treatment. Their tumor response was graded as complete or near complete. Blood tests after surgery checked for scraps of tumor DNA. The question was whether a positive test foresaw a return of the disease. A blood test that flags hidden risk could guide extra treatment for those who need it, and spare others who do not.
pmc-11634547:
Halime Gulle, Dylan Morrissey, Abdulhamit Tayfur, Dilber Karagozoglu Coskunsu, Stuart Miller, Aleksandra Birn-Jeffery, and Trevor Prior map what tracks with heel pain severity in a paper from 2024. Only about half of plantar heel pain cases recover within a year. The study gathered two hundred thirty-five people, split between heel pain and other foot pain. Dozens of demographic, body, mind, social, and activity measures were tested in regression models.

Quality of life, education, gender, and morning pain length all linked to severity. Heel pain patients more often had systemic disease and fear of movement. They also reported worse morning and standing pain. The authors urge clinics to assess the whole person, not just the foot.
pmc-11635247:
Liu and seventeen co-authors test stem cells against lung injury from seawater drowning, in this two thousand twenty-four study. Breathing in seawater can trigger severe acute lung injury, a complication that sharply raises the death rate for drowning victims.

In mice given artificial seawater into the lungs, the team traced the damage to an inflammatory signal, TNF-alpha, which switched on a cell-shape change pathway through the Snail protein. They then delivered mesenchymal stem cells as an inhaled mist through the windpipe. Treated mice showed better lung function and less damage on scans and tissue tests. The work identifies both the injury pathway and a possible cell therapy worth developing for drowning care.
pmc-11635647:
Yang Liu and co-authors tie a simple blood index to early worsening after mild stroke. Their 2024 study examines the triglyceride-glucose index, a stand-in for insulin resistance computed from two routine labs, in four hundred two Chinese patients with first-time mild ischemic stroke.

About a quarter deteriorated within seventy-two hours by a standard stroke scale. Those who worsened carried clearly higher index values. After full adjustment, each step up the index more than tripled the odds of deterioration, and the top quarter of patients faced over twice the risk of the bottom quarter. The relationship ran straight, with no bend. The authors propose the index as a cheap early warning to flag mild strokes that will not stay mild.
pmc-11636247:
Lina Wang leads a team on COVID outcomes in blood cancer patients. Their study from twenty twenty-four is set in the late phase of the pandemic. Blood cancer folks face high risk from this virus.

Data came from one hospital in Shanxi over one month. The group held just over two hundred inpatients. Life span was the main outcome the team tracked. Stats tests sought traits that raised death risk. Cases spanned leukemia, myeloma, and like blood diseases. Late stage virus still shaped outlook for these folks. Risk traits are listed for care teams.
pmc-11638047:
Brendan Moloney and co-authors report early work on standardizing a breast MRI measure across hospitals in a 2024 paper. Quantitative contrast MRI can predict how a tumor will answer chemotherapy given before surgery. Most proof came from single centers using one maker's scanners.

Three sites ran the same protocol on three different scanner brands, with a test phantom for quality checks. Fifteen patients finished the study during treatment. The team compared two math models of contrast flow and two ways of setting baseline values, whole-tumor versus per-point. Their early results map what it takes to run the measure evenly across centers.
pmc-11638247:
Felix P Lützenkirchen and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four study of a protein called neurobeachin at inhibitory brain synapses. These synapses use the signal chemical GABA to calm nerve cell activity. Their strength changes when receptors move into or out of the synapse surface.

The team found neurobeachin sitting at these synapses and binding their anchor protein, gephyrin. Its arrival depended on activity, and it drove receptor removal through a protein kinase A pathway. Neurons missing one copy of the gene failed at this removal unless normal neurobeachin was restored. The work names a player in how inhibitory synapses scale down.
pmc-11638347: William Novotny, Pam Fox, and Dynita Haislip report a grave case in a 2024 paper. A child with croup and asthma got a calming drug through the nose at a dose in the normal range for such care. The child's breathing then failed in a sudden and severe way. The authors warn that the drug, though safe for most, holds a small but real risk of such a crash when a child's airways are already strained.
pmc-11639047:
Olha Bezsmertna and eleven co-authors present a 2024 study of magnetic states in tiny three dimensional structures shaped like flowers. Bending magnetic films into curves is a fresh way to tune magnetic whirl patterns. The team built neat arrays of these nanoflowers with a template method.

The flowers repeat every 400 nanometers across areas of square centimeters, with few flaws. Advanced imaging and computer models then mapped the magnetic states inside. The interplay of surface and volume charges in the curved shapes steadies odd states: lopsided and shifted vortices, and states with paired defect lines. The work shows how shape alone can set magnetic behavior.
pmc-11639847:
Sanan Raza and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on whether a silk protein can keep rabbit semen in better shape during chilled storage. Breeders store semen for days at cool temperatures, and quality fades with time. The team added sericin, a glue protein from silk, at two low doses and stored samples at fridge and cool-room temperatures. They tracked sperm motion, survival, and the state of the sperm's membranes and caps over three days.

Sericin, temperature, and storage time all shaped the results. The protein improved motion patterns and protected membranes and caps, with the clearest gains at the colder setting over longer storage. It also slowed bacterial growth in samples kept at the warmer setting for three days. Pregnancy results with three-day stored, treated semen looked promising, though not clearly better in the count. The team credits the germ-fighting effect as part of the benefit.
pmc-11639947:
Linfeng Liu and co-authors probe why some brain aneurysm walls light up on scans in a 2024 study. Wall enhancement on vessel MRI may flag weak spots in unruptured aneurysms at the middle cerebral artery fork. The flow cause behind the glow was unclear.

They studied 104 aneurysms in 95 patients and modeled blood flow in both patient shapes and silicone copies. A high aspect ratio, a tall sac on a narrow neck, predicted wall enhancement. Tall aneurysms held slower flow, lower wall stress, and wider low-flow zones, with stronger glow. In the models, contrast pooled under the dome. Slow near-wall flow is their proposed driver.
pmc-11640047:
Lioba Lendl and Ann Kristin Barton review how horse asthma is diagnosed in this 2024 article. Horse asthma ranges from mild, hidden disease to severe attacks, and the quiet forms are the hardest to confirm. Standard checks include listening to the chest, a rebreathing test, blood work, and a scope view of the airways, plus fluid samples washed from the windpipe and deep lung.

Cell counts in the deep lung fluid set both the severity grade logic and the inflammatory type, yet that fluid can look normal when disease rests or runs low. The review sorts factors that can sway results: recent exercise, cold or chlorinated air, long training, and bleeding from hard work. Stress tests that challenge the airways may unmask hidden cases, the authors suggest.
pmc-11640347:
Anna Michalska-Foryszewska and co-authors review imaging in multiple myeloma in a 2024 article. The disease is the second most common blood cancer and mostly strikes older people. Scans track bone damage, catch complications, and judge risk across its stages, from early quiet forms to full disease.

The authors ask whether number-based image analysis, called radiomics, can sharpen that work. Such tools mine scans for patterns the eye cannot score, and may yield markers that predict outlook and treatment response. Artificial intelligence methods are entering the same space. The review argues the promise is real but unproven in daily care. Standard tests and more studies are needed first.
pmc-11640547:
Michał Miciak and co-authors sort thyroid cancer patients in a 2024 study by where their tumors sit. For well-behaved thyroid cancers, whether the tumor is one-sided or both-sided, single or multiple, may shape how far it has spread and what surgery is wise. The team reviews nearly seven hundred patients treated over fifteen years.

The biggest group, one-sided single tumors, shows the lowest rates of spread beyond the gland, node involvement, distant spread, and vessel invasion. Both-sided multiple tumors show the highest rates. The authors argue these simple features, read before surgery, help stage the disease and pick treatment.
pmc-11640747:
Kamil Candan and colleagues published a 2024 study of a small Anatolian lizard. The species had never had its life history measured. Samples came from Iğdır Province in Türkiye. Bone growth rings revealed each lizard's age. Males and females were compared directly.

Males averaged larger and older than females. Body size rose with age in both sexes. Survival rates also favored males. Females matured into shorter expected adult lives. The growth curves differed clearly by sex. Such baseline data supports future conservation work. It also feeds comparisons across related lizard species.
pmc-11641047:
Haoqing Yang and co-authors map chemical change in fat tissue of mice fed capsaicin in this 2024 study. Capsaicin, the heat in chili peppers, can switch on brown fat that burns energy. A layer of white fat over the brown fat makes clean sampling hard. Standard chemistry on ground tissue misses where each change happens. Spatial methods instead read chemicals in place, slice by slice. The team fed mice the compound and imaged a key fat depot.

The depot sits between the shoulder blades and mixes both fat types. Spatial readings showed which chemicals rose or fell in each layer. That view avoids blending the two fat types into one average. The authors aim to clarify how capsaicin reshapes this tissue. Obesity research uses such maps to find drug targets. The work is a methods-driven look at a classic diet compound.
pmc-11641547:
Seung Hwan Kim and co-authors published a study in 2024 on how fumes from common chemicals affect skin disease genes in mothers and babies. Solvents such as toluene, xylene, and benzene are linked to eczema, but their effect across a pregnancy was little studied. The team measured gene activity and DNA marks in exposed mothers and their infants.

Exposure to toluene switched on a water-channel gene tied to skin cell trouble in mothers. In infants, two immune and skin-barrier genes stood out. Xylene raised a histamine receptor gene in mothers, while infants showed a shared immune pattern across xylene forms. The results suggest babies may answer chemical exposure with a narrower, more uniform defense than adults.
pmc-11641747:
Hasan Nisar and co-authors studied how low oxygen changes the radiation response of lung cancer cells in a 2024 paper. Tumors short of oxygen resist radiation, which limits care. The cells used also lack a gene, p53, that is often lost in this cancer type.

Cells were kept at low oxygen for two days, then given X-rays. They survived better and formed more colonies than cells in normal air. Breaks in DNA formed and healed at the same pace, so repair speed was not the cause. Instead, cell cycle timing, swelling signals, and gene activity all shifted. The authors conclude that resistance can grow even without that gene, through these other routes.
pmc-11641947:
Francesca Serapide and co-authors review a possible hidden driver of long COVID in a 2024 article. Long COVID lasts at least three months after infection and can bring fatigue, brain fog, and breathing trouble, but its causes stay unclear. The review weighs the idea that dormant viruses wake up after the COVID infection and keep the body inflamed.

The dormant viruses named include Epstein-Barr virus and two herpes-family viruses that most adults carry for life. The authors ask whether these woken viruses act on their own or team up with other factors, such as virus that lingers and a mis-tuned immune system. Shots and antiviral drugs in the acute phase may cut long COVID risk, they note. Tests that spot viral waking could guide care for high-risk groups.
pmc-11642047:
Wanzhen Chen and six co-authors identify a wheat protein that holds back the making of the waxy coat on leaves. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. That wax seals the plant surface and guards against dry air and other stresses, so breeders want to know how it is controlled.

Quieting the gene for the protein, called TaCFL1, raised leaf wax by about fifteen in each hundred parts and made the leaf skin less leaky. Two partner switch proteins pushed wax the other way: quieting either cut wax, and quieting both cut it by nearly a third. A third protein was shown to be a core part of the wax-making chain. The results sketch a control circuit that wheat breeders could tune for tougher crops.
pmc-11642147:
Tzu-Chieh Hsu, Chun-Hsien Chiang, and co-authors run yo-yo diets in male zebra fish to read liver and muscle marks, in a 2024 study. Weight drop and gain loops hit many folks in a year span. What those loops do to liver fat and muscle was not yet traced in this fish.

Three feed sets split to rich, lean, and swap plans for months. Rich feed fats the liver in two months of the runs. Swap feed holds liver fat low at first, then matches rich by late checks. Long swap makes liver harm worse than plain rich in the end. Muscle size and burst speed hold strong on swap plans.
pmc-11642247:
Anna Balzer and co-authors test if delirium on arrival at a rehab hospital predicts worse motor gains after hip fracture surgery. Their paper from 2024 deals with older patients, in whom delirium is common after surgery. Its effect on motor rehab in this group was little studied.

Of 143 patients admitted for rehab, thirty eight, about twenty seven percent, had delirium. They scored lower on a mind test and had far higher rates of sedative drug use. Rehab gains were measured by three motor scores at discharge, built from a standard independence scale. Stay length and other results split by delirium state are set out, to weigh how much the early delirium costs in function.
pmc-11643447:
Linjiang Xu, Chunming Wang, Fei Yan, Zhuangxi Hu, and Wei Zhang improved laser cutting in 2024 of stainless steel grid plates from nuclear fuel assemblies. To take fuel rods apart, a ten-kilowatt fiber laser must cut a stack of four plates, each a few millimeters thick with gaps between. Cut width served as the quality score for the stack.

Under the right settings, all four layers cut cleanly, with seam widths growing from the top layer down in the values reported. Gas pressure faded layer by layer: the top plates' melt pools were blown clear by the assist gas, while the bottom plates had almost no gas help. Cut zones were mainly austenite with some ferrite. Readers get process settings and a layer-by-layer account for a hard industrial cut.
pmc-11643747:
Jianxia Gu and co-authors build a sensor that measures two body chemicals at trace levels. Their 2024 paper fuses a metal-organic framework with carbon nanotubes. The targets are acetaminophen, a common painkiller, and dopamine, a brain messenger. Finding both at once, at tiny doses, is analytically hard.

The framework MOF-5 grew directly on the nanotubes in one heated bath. The blend offers wide surface, layered pores, and strong conductivity. Its detection ranges span wide bands for both targets. Detection limits fell far below a tenth of a micromole for each. Repeat runs agreed, and common interferents barely disturbed readings. Spiked urine and tap water samples returned honest values. One device could serve clinics and water checks alike.
pmc-11643847:
Engineering ceramics shrug off heat, wear, and corrosion, but they crack where metals bend. Alaa Almansoori and co-authors review in 2024 how stirring graphene or carbon nanotubes into five workhorse ceramics changes that bargain. The review covers alumina, silicon carbide, zirconia, aluminum nitride, and silicon nitride, the staples of automotive, aerospace, and friction-heavy uses.

Adding the carbon reinforcements, sometimes paired with a second filler, can blunt the brittleness that limits these materials. The authors survey the main ceramic families, their strengths, and the usual fixes for their weaknesses. Their aim is a map for choosing and toughening ceramics for demanding jobs where failure is not an option.
pmc-11644347:
Hongying Li and co-authors report nine years of conservation farming trials. The trials sat on the sloped farmland of China's Three Gorges Reservoir area. Soil quality there is in decline. Orchard plots set standard citrus planting against three other ways. Those ways were citrus with white clover, straw mulch, or daylily hedgerows on contour lines. Crop fields set a standard wheat-peanut rotation against hedgerow intercrops and a ryegrass-sesame rotation. The team took soil samples at upper, middle, and lower slope spots.

The green practices raised soil traits at all three slope spots. The effect of the practice beat the effect of slope spot itself. A soil quality index summed up the gains. The authors read the long trial as proof of a clear point. The right planting system, more than terrain work alone, rebuilds soil on sloped farms.
pmc-11644447:
Raffaele Borghini and co-authors wrote a 2024 review asking whether gluten-free eating is medicine or fashion. For people with celiac disease the diet is required. Many others now follow it for hoped-for benefits, sometimes on weak advice. The authors weigh the trend against its costs: price, poor taste, social strain, and possible nutrient gaps.

They also raise a less known risk. Cutting gluten can stir up bowel disorders that mimic irritable bowel syndrome in prone people. Reactions to nickel in food, to certain fermentable carbs, and to histamine may each play a part. The review urges a careful medical check before starting the diet, so real disease is not missed.
pmc-11644947:
Five authors present a study from two thousand twenty-four on a neural network for weather forecasting. Good forecasts matter for daily work, disaster warning, and care of the environment. Older data-driven methods often miss how weather patterns grow and move across a region over time.

Their network joins two designs: convolutional layers that read spatial patterns, and a transformer that tracks change over time. A spatial attention block first pulls out the layout of a weather field and rebuilds it. The design also tracks how variables such as heat and wind affect each other. The aim is forecasts that are both fast and accurate enough for real use.
pmc-11645047:
Yujing Wang and co-authors review, in 2024, the hard problem of aligning laser range data with camera images for spotting objects. Cars, robots, and augmented reality tools pair these two sensors, yet their data differ in format, detail, and response to weather. In moving scenes, lining them up in space and time is harder still.

The review compares more than twenty alignment methods from recent years for three-dimensional object detection. It sorts the methods, weighs their strengths and limits, and names open problems such as sensor fusion, scale, and real-time demands. Earlier reviews focused on fusion math, so alignment gets overdue attention here.
pmc-11645247:
Kai Wang and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on a joint care for severe sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection. The care pairs hybrid blood filtering with a drug, ulinastatin, drawn from urine protein. One hundred fifty patients form the look back, split by which care they got. Scores of illness depth, two small RNA marks, and inflammation factors are tracked.

After care, all marks fell in both groups. The joint group fell more on each count. Their pain eased sooner, gut enzymes settled faster, and hospital stays ran shorter. The team says the pair lifts short term odds in severe sepsis.
pmc-11647247:
Junjie Xie and four co-authors study a copper handling gene in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in this 2024 paper. The gene, ATOX1, helps move copper inside cells and ties to cuproptosis, a copper driven cell death. Data mining of lymphoma samples showed the gene switched on higher in tumors than in normal tissue. Lab tests then cut the gene down in lymphoma cells. Growth slowed, and cells stalled at one cell cycle checkpoint. A growth signaling pathway, MAPK, also dimmed when the gene fell.

Adding copper restored that pathway's activity, tying the effect to copper transport. A copper blocking drug killed lymphoma cells in a dose dependent way, and gene knockdown made it stronger. The authors read ATOX1 as a driver that keeps the MAPK pathway fed with copper. Blocking copper flow, they suggest, could be a route against this common lymphoma type.
pmc-11648047:
Wan Ying Tan and co-authors compare hospital stays of men and women with neuroendocrine tumors in a 2024 paper. These rare tumors arise in hormone-making cells, and sex is known to color their frequency and drug side effects. The team mined a national sample of United States hospital discharges from 2019, covering over seven thousand patients with primary or spread tumors.

About half the patients were women. Race, ethnicity, and insurance mixes differed by sex. During admission, women drew more mouth and nerve diagnoses, plus nausea and vomiting in every tumor group. Men drew more fluid buildup in the belly, swallowing trouble, bile duct blockage, and jaundice. Background conditions also split: women carried more joint, mood, thyroid, and weight problems. The authors say sex-aware care could sharpen management of these admissions.
pmc-11648247:
Moliterni and a large team of co-authors study why palmitic acid, a saturated fat, harms liver cells while oleic acid, an unsaturated fat, largely does not. Excess fatty acids can poison cells, a process called lipotoxicity, and the difference between fat types is central to fatty liver disease.

In a human liver cell line, palmitic acid triggered cell stress, blocked the cell's recycling system, and sharply lowered DGAT1, an enzyme that safely stores fat. Blocking DGAT1 directly killed cells even with the gentler fat. A drug that activates the PPAR alpha pathway reversed the damage. The work points to DGAT1 protection as a possible treatment angle for fatty liver.
pmc-11648747:
Alexander Park, Aditya Khurana, Roger Wang, and Adam Eltorai track Medicare pay for pain procedures in this 2024 study. Interventional pain care is common and costly, yet how its reimbursement moved over two decades had not been charted.

Using the federal fee schedule tool, the team pulled pay for thirty-two frequent procedures from 2000 to 2023, in both facility and office settings, and adjusted for inflation. Average pay fell about sixty-one percent in facilities and sixty percent in offices over the period, shrinking several percent per year. Statistical tests compared the two settings' declines. The steep, steady erosion frames current debates about access to pain care.
pmc-11649047: Salihou Aminou Sadjo, Florence Muller, and Jean-Louis Lemelle report a hip injury case in a child in a 2024 paper. The injury, a closed degloving lesion, separates skin and fat from deeper tissue after a shearing blow. It is rare in children's surgery and easy to overlook. Their patient was an eleven-year-old girl with a lesion on her left hip. Treatment used a compression bandage rather than surgery, and her outcome was favorable. The report pairs the case with a review of past writing on this injury.
pmc-11649647:
Juan Tang and co-authors trace a chain of molecular switches that helps head and neck cancer grow. This cancer type, mostly squamous cell carcinoma, is common and deadly. At the chain's end sits a signaling protein called 14-3-3 zeta, long tied to tumor advance. The team sequenced tumor and healthy tissue from five patients to find circular RNAs that control it.

One circle, CircRNA_036186, stood out. It works by soaking up a small RNA, miR-193b-5p, that would otherwise hold the 14-3-3 zeta gene down. With the sponge in place, the protein's levels rise and the cancer's program runs freer. The authors propose the circle as both a biomarker and a drug target, and as a foothold for deeper study of circular RNA in this cancer.
pmc-11650347:
Zhang and six colleagues track a complement protein in kidney cancer tissue and during immunotherapy in twenty twenty-four. The protein, C3a, showed in most tumor samples from over one hundred cases. Bigger tumors and higher stage carried more of it. Blood levels were then watched in thirty advanced patients on immune drugs.

After four cycles, levels fell in patients whose disease shrank or held. Levels rose in those whose disease grew. Patients with falling levels stayed progression free longer. Other traits like age and grade showed no link. The marker may mirror treatment effect to some degree, they conclude.
pmc-11651547:
Amanuel Yoseph, Lakew Mussie, and Mehretu Belayneh present a 2024 study on undernutrition in pregnant women in Ethiopia. Poor maternal nutrition is a major public concern there, but local proof for the south was thin. The team surveyed 515 pregnant women in one district in June 2024. Interviews and body measures fed a multi-level analysis.

About 42 percent of the women were undernourished. Planned pregnancy lowered the risk. Household food insecurity raised it sharply, as did poor diet variety and weak nutrition knowledge. At community level, low literacy and low wealth each raised risk. Literacy showed the largest effect of all. The authors urge action on food access, diet variety, and nutrition teaching, plus community literacy and wealth.
pmc-11651947:
Brain scans after stroke track a diffusion measure that falls, then rises again, and the standard story credits shifting water between cells. Yì Xiáng Wáng offered in 2024 a different reading, built on a three-band link between that measure and the tissue's T2 relaxation time.

On his curve, tissues read the lowest diffusion when their T2 sits near a middle sweet spot, and higher when it strays either way. The same curve explains puzzles elsewhere: why spleen and liver differ, why muscle beats richer-perfused liver, why cartilage reads so high. Applied to stroke, the natural course of the measure follows the tissue's T2 journey, no extra mechanism needed.
pmc-11652047:
Ziwen Wei and four co-authors build a sturdier way to align chest CT scans taken at different times. Aligning lung images is hard: breathing moves tissue, metal objects streak the picture, and low-dose scans add noise. Fast deep learning aligners often break under those conditions.

Their 2024 method splits the chest into regions and treats each by its own features and motion. A special curve, the Welsch function, reshapes how strongly mismatches are punished, with settings that adapt from coarse to fine stages. That design tolerates sliding motion at organ borders and heavy noise. A stepwise solver keeps the math manageable. Tests on a public four-dimensional CT set from a deformable registration lab checked the gains.
pmc-11652947:
Ho Sung Jeon and co-authors compare in 2024 two ultrathin stents used to hold heart arteries open after blockage treatment. Both stents slowly release the same drug and use a coating that dissolves over time. One is made in Korea, the other is a widely used rival. The team drew on a single-center registry of real-world patients.

The registry held 751 patients with the first stent and 931 with the second. After matching the groups on patient traits, 483 pairs remained. Over about two years, the combined rate of cardiac death, heart attack in the treated vessel, and repeat repair was nearly identical, at about three percent in each group. The authors call the two stents comparable in safety and effect for daily practice. They add that only a large randomized trial can settle the match for good.
pmc-11653547:
Gashaye Melaku Tefera explored how lack of trust shapes primary care for Ethiopian immigrant women in the United States. Distrust is a known driver of unequal access among minority and disadvantaged groups. Tefera interviewed twenty-one women who had arrived within the last five years, living across six states and Washington, DC.

Five forces wore trust down: the system's heavy reliance on medication, a preference for home remedies, the role of faith in care choices, poor openness from providers, and discrimination at several levels. Tefera urges clinicians to explain care plainly, be transparent, ask about patients' home-country systems, and practice culturally aware care. At the policy level, the study calls for workforce diversity, training reform, and teamwork across health, education, and immigration sectors.
pmc-11653647:
Xiuqing Lu and co-authors published this breast cancer study in 2024. A protein called TBL2, part of a large regulatory family, had unclear roles in this disease. The team measured it in patient tumor samples and linked it to outcomes. TBL2 was selectively overproduced in breast cancers. High levels tracked with worse clinical features and poorer survival for patients.

Experiments in cells and animals confirmed the protein drives growth. Silencing TBL2 slowed cancer cell multiplication, while boosting it sped growth up. The mechanism runs through partnership: TBL2 acts as a scaffold bringing two other proteins, PRMT5 and WDR77, together. That pairing strengthens PRMT5's chemical activity, which switches on AKT, a master growth signal. More AKT activity means faster tumor cell proliferation. The authors propose TBL2 as both a warning marker and a drug target. Blocking its scaffolding could, in principle, cut the growth signal at its source.
pmc-11653747:
Qian Zhu and co-workers study why a cancer drug works less well in throat cancer linked to Epstein-Barr virus, in a 2024 paper. The drug cetuximab targets a growth receptor and helps patients live longer. Yet tumor levels of that receptor do not predict who responds.

The team found that infected cancer cells raise a protective protein called CD55. That protein mainly blocks one immune attack route, in which killer cells destroy antibody-tagged tumor cells. A viral protein drives the rise through a known signaling pathway. The authors suggest that drugs blocking CD55 could restore the treatment's effect, giving a clear next step to test.
pmc-11653847:
Negar Narimisa and co-authors test in 2024 two compounds against the slimy films that a food-poisoning germ builds on surfaces. The germ, Salmonella Typhimurium, shelters in these biofilms, which shrug off many drugs. Both compounds were picked because they block a protein the germ uses to manage stress.

One compound, the antibiotic nafcillin, stopped films forming at a low dose and wiped out set films at a higher one. Microscope views showed thinner films and changed cell shapes. Both compounds also turned down a set of toxin-control genes in the germ. The results point to fresh ways to fight stubborn films on food plant surfaces.
pmc-11653947:
Ramona Marasco and co-authors show how desert bacteria help plants bear salty soils in a 2024 study. Microbes from harsh places may shield crops as climate stress grows. Two Pseudomonas strains from date palm roots were already known to ease drought.

Both strains settled on roots and reshaped them: main roots grew shorter while root hairs lengthened. The bacteria also shifted the plant's auxin balance, the hormone system steering root form. Cell, body, and gene-level checks traced how tolerance improved under salt. Harnessing root microbes could cut the chemical burden of farming dry, salty land, if field trials confirm the greenhouse promise.
pmc-11654347:
McDonald Nyalapa and three co-authors study what helps or hinders nurses learning about diabetes in Malawi in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Studies across sub-Saharan Africa report low diabetes knowledge among nurses. Yet little work asks why. These nurses staff tertiary hospitals in the center and south of the country. They both treat patients and teach them how to manage the disease.

The team ran focus group talks with twenty-six nurses from two hospitals. They sorted the answers into themes using a standard qualitative method. The themes cover barriers, such as time and training gaps, and supports, such as motivated peers. Knowing these factors is a first step toward better training. The findings can guide hospital leaders and educators who plan nurse education in low-resource settings.
pmc-11655547:
Zhen Qi and co-authors test a milk thistle compound against tearing of the aorta in a 2024 study. The tear, called aortic dissection, is a grave threat to heart health. Muscle cells in the vessel wall die or change form as the tear grows, and no drug has yet proven able to stop it.

The team found signs of an iron-driven cell death, ferroptosis, raised in patients and in mice bred to model the tear. The compound, silibinin, eased vessel widening, swelling, and cell death in the mice. In human vessel cells it kept cells alive and cut harmful oxygen bursts. Gene scans pointed to iron balance and cell stress paths, and tests pinned one protein, HMOX1, as a direct target.
pmc-11655847:
Mi-So Park and co-authors identify a long non-coding RNA that helps colorectal cancer grow and spread, in this 2024 study. These RNAs do not build proteins, but they can steer how genes behave. Computer analysis of patient data flagged one RNA, named LINC02257, at high levels in tumors, where it tracked with worse survival and later stages.

Lab tests showed the RNA pushes cancer cells to multiply and move. It works in two ways: it soaks up a small RNA that normally holds tumors back, and it binds a protein called YB1 and helps switch on its target genes. The team proposes the RNA as a target for future treatment.
pmc-11655947:
Qiu and eight co-authors show the enzyme A20 mediates brain ischemic tolerance by blocking neuron death signaling, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Brief low-oxygen preconditioning protects brain tissue from later ischemia. Immune cell polarization after stroke shapes the damage outcome. A20 edits ubiquitin tags on the death protein RIP3.

Preconditioning raises A20 and strengthens its binding to RIP3. Tag removal then blocks the necroptosis death pathway. Inflammatory M1 polarization of immune cells falls accordingly. Extra neuronal A20 reproduces the protection in rats. Brain injury after global ischemia is ultimately reduced.
pmc-11656047:
Neeti Nadda and co-authors study gene variants in an immune checkpoint gene and their links to liver cancer in an Indian population, published in 2024. The gene, HLA-G, helps tumors escape the immune system. Variants in a regulatory tail region of the gene may change how much of it is made.

In a case-control study, patients with liver cancer and healthy controls were genotyped at a set of positions in that region. Most patients also received locoregional therapy, so treatment response could be checked as well. Three of the variants tested were associated with both cancer risk and treatment response. Those three sit where small regulatory RNAs bind, a plausible route for their effect. Blood levels of the protein also differed in the study, the authors report.
pmc-11656547:
Yian Chen and co-authors published a 2024 survey study on stress among nursing students during the COVID-19 pandemic. Nursing students are the reserve force of the health system, next in line for frontline work. The strain of the pandemic years weighed on them in particular. The team asked how two emotional traits, empathy and emotional intelligence, relate to that stress.

They surveyed 1,126 students at one medical university between March and June 2023. Students filled in scales for pandemic stress, for how strongly they feel others' emotions, and for how well they read and manage their own moods. Stress scores differed by where students lived. Emotional empathy rose together with emotional intelligence. Statistical models then examined whether mood skills mask or soften the link between empathy and stress. The study aims to guide support for students whose empathy, a strength in care, may also expose them to strain.
pmc-11656647:
Dong-Qi Wu and co-authors study how two enzymes from a liver fluke change the immune behavior of buffalo blood cells. Their 2024 paper concerns fascioliasis, a parasitic disease that threatens both people and livestock worldwide. The parasite secretes many products to soften host defenses, but the role of this enzyme family was unknown.

The team profiled the family in the parasite and picked the two most active members across its life stages. They made those enzymes in a lab system and exposed buffalo immune cells to them. The tests covered cell growth, movement, nitric oxide output, signal molecule release, and engulfing of particles. Mapping which parasite products dial immunity up or down helps explain how the fluke survives in its host, and may reveal drug or vaccine targets.
pmc-11657147:
Pierre Laloux and co-authors published a study in 2024 on counting people with many health conditions at once. Such counts often list body diseases only and skip mental health. Yet mental illness carries a heavy burden and shapes daily life. The team asked what changes when mental health joins the count.

They used data from a Belgian health survey from 2018. Adding mental health raised the share of people counted as multi-ill from thirty-five percent to about forty-two percent. Links between the count and quality of life grew stronger with mental health included. Two short scales for anxiety and low mood gave the best fit of all. The authors say counts without mental health understate the true load on people's lives.
pmc-11657647:
Lindsay Nettlefold and a team of co-authors report on streamlining a health program for older adults, in two thousand twenty-four. The program, Choose to Move, helps older adults be more active through a consultation and group meetings with a coach. Scaling such programs is hard when health funds are tight, so the team cut coach hours by forty percent.

More than a thousand older adults joined the leaner version across many local programs. Delivery stayed faithful to the design, coaches reported. Activity rose in both age groups, and mobility and social isolation improved. Gains matched or beat the older, costlier version for several measures. The authors argue that careful trimming can aid scale-up.
pmc-11657747:
Otonicar leads a large team presenting a method to profile DNA and RNA in the same single cells, in work from twenty twenty-four. Single cell DNA sequencing decodes cancer variation cell by cell. Existing methods are low throughput or cannot be paired with transcriptome data from the same cell.

Their assay, HIPSD and R seq, profiles low coverage DNA and RNA in thousands of cells in parallel. It builds on a modification of a standard protocol, keeping it simple and accessible. Joint profiles let researchers link a mutation to its expression effect in the very same cell, a key step in understanding tumor evolution.
pmc-11658247:
Yingting Jiang and six colleagues published a survey study in two thousand twenty-four on phone addiction among nursing students in China. Heavy phone use harms students' health and training. Social anxiety and loneliness were suspected drivers, with sleep possibly in the mix.

Four hundred thirty-seven students in a career resilience programme were surveyed in late two thousand twenty-three. Students sorted into low, middle, and high social anxiety profiles. Loneliness carried a clear share of the path from social anxiety to phone addiction. Sleep length did not significantly change those links. The authors say anxious students differ in kind, not just degree. They suggest loneliness-focused support to curb compulsive phone use.
pmc-11658347:
Zhuoran Yin and co-authors published a 2024 study of how surgery affects microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, in young and old mice. Surgery in older patients can bring short-term thinking problems, and inflammation is a suspect. The team gave young and aged mice anesthesia and abdominal surgery, then read the gene activity of their microglia at six and 48 hours, expecting a fired-up, inflammatory state.

Blood and brain signals of inflammation did rise after surgery. Yet the aged microglia themselves turned quieter at six hours, switching off genes that are usually active in diseased brains. The quiet state had faded by 48 hours. Age alone, more than surgery, raised the number and staining of microglia in the memory region. The authors say the response is brief and more complex than simple inflammation.
pmc-11658747:
Albert Anastasio and a large team published a surgical outcomes study in twenty twenty-four on Haglund syndrome, the painful heel bump that frays the Achilles tendon. Operations split and clean the tendon, remove the bump, and reattach it. Some surgeons also transfer a toe tendon to add strength, but whether that adds complications was unstudied.

The review covered three hundred ninety patients operated between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty-three, fifty-two of whom had the tendon transfer. Over about ten months of follow-up, persistent pain affected ten percent and wound breakdown eight percent, with infections rare. Complication rates did not differ notably between the groups. The transfer appears safe to add when surgeons judge it useful.
pmc-11658947:
Mason Manning and co-authors test which spread rules can keep folk ways split across crowds. Mass-copy was long held the key: copy the crowd and ways freeze in place. Fresh lore says mind skews blunt that key. Their 2024 model adds two more rules: gain-copy, where pay rules the pick, and norm back-up, where rule-break draws push-back. Each rule's hold on split ways is raced in the model.

Gain-copy keeps split ways just when pay ties to land facts. Norm back-up breeds and holds chance splits with ease. Back-up also makes ways path-bound: old ways steer new acts past crowd shifts. Land split may drive work ways; chance ways more like spring from back-up.
pmc-11659247:
Abiodun Azeez and co-authors map fungi on oil palm trees with leaf spot disease in 2024. Plants and their microbes act as one living unit, yet microbe effects on palm health are little studied. The team compares fungi on sick and healthy trees across leaf, root, and soil.

Gene reads from twenty-nine samples found fourteen fungal groups, with two groups dominating. One genus led on healthy leaves, while another led overall on sick trees. Soil from healthy trees held the richest marker set. Both sick and healthy leaves shared fungi linked to the disease, a surprise the authors flag for follow-up.
pmc-11660147:
Indrė Misiūnaitė and co-authors present a 2024 chemistry study aimed at Parkinson's disease. In that illness, a protein called alpha-synuclein clumps into fibers that harm brain cells, and current drugs only ease symptoms. The team made a family of small ring-shaped compounds, building them with a gold catalyst in a waste-lean reaction.

Several of the new compounds changed how the protein clumped. Some slowed the first step of fiber formation and kept the protein in a harmless loose state. Others trapped small clusters or steered growth toward fibers with unusual shapes. The findings mark these compounds as promising starting points for drugs that attack the clumping process itself rather than only its symptoms.
pmc-11661547:
Bushra Kaleem, Sadaf Shahab, and Tahir Sultan Shamsi published a study in 2024, written in Spanish, on a mutation that blunts the main drugs for chronic myeloid leukemia. The mutation, called T315I, changes the target protein so standard inhibitors fail to bind. The team asked how often it appears in patients already failing treatment and what it means for their future.

Among 102 patients responding poorly to therapy, about one in five carried the mutation, detected by a targeted test and confirmed by sequencing. Carriers were followed for up to ninety-six months. Nearly sixty percent of carriers progressed to the dangerous blast phase, and progressors were more likely to carry the mutation. Overall survival among carriers was about eighty-two percent across the study period.
pmc-11662147:
Nils Schmidt and co-authors show, in 2024, that a chemical mark on DNA controls pigment making in a cyanobacterium. Such marks guide gene use in complex organisms, but their role in bacteria was murky. Removing the enzyme that places the mark in this microbe turned it bluish, because a key pigment fell.

The chain ran through a gene for an enzyme in the pigment pathway. Without the mark, that gene misbehaved and raw materials piled up. Mutations and engineered gene versions proved the mark is needed for proper gene expression. The authors present this marking as a real gene-control layer in cyanobacteria, not a leftover.
pmc-11662447:
Agnieszka K. Banaś and co-authors watched seedlings wake up their photosynthesis in 2024, weighing red light against blue. Seeds germinating underground build pale precursor chloroplasts that cannot photosynthesize. Once light hits, these etioplasts transform into working chloroplasts during de-etiolation. The team illuminated etiolated Arabidopsis seedlings with monochromatic red or blue light at equal photon levels for twenty-four hours.

Both colors made working young chloroplasts, hence the title's joke that the process is almost color blind. But the steps did not proceed evenly: single stages of the transformation were tuned by one color or the other. Blue light sped the disassembly of the internal storage form, the prolamellar body, according to ultrastructure study. Fluorescence readings tracked the assembly of photosynthetic complexes. The fine print matters for controlled-setting farming, where light recipes are a design choice.
pmc-11662647:
Deng and co-authors switch genes on and off with light inside an industrial bacterium, in a 2024 biotechnology study. Corynebacterium glutamicum is a factory workhorse for amino acids and chemicals, but balancing growth against production needs nimble control. Chemical switches can be toxic or blunt. The team built the first optogenetic systems for this species, using light-sensitive RNA-binding proteins to form light-driven transcription factors, plus a light-guided gene silencing system.

With light as the dial, they steered the cell's metabolism to make two valuable sugar chains for the first time in this host. A light-controlled fermenter reached the highest reported yield of one product, 6.2 grams per liter. The circuits are programmable and portable to other production strains, the authors argue.
pmc-11663647:
Xiaoyan Zhang and co-authors tune how a Chinese medicinal root is processed after harvest in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The root, Astragali Radix, is used in clinics and health foods. Fresh processing can save active compounds that drying loses, and it costs less.

Samples varied by moisture, kneading, and sweating steps. Kneading and sweating raised key compound levels at the same moisture. A scoring method picked the best mix: thirty-five percent moisture, one hundred kneading cycles, and twelve hours of sweating. Fresh-processed root beat the traditional kind on sugars, flavonoids, and one marker compound, and its flavonoids woke immune cells more strongly. Saponin levels did not differ.
pmc-11664247:
Manon Barthe and co-authors map how damaged skin loses its protective barrier, in a 2024 study. Healthy skin keeps water in and germs and chemicals out. Detergents, sunburn, scratching, and the pandemic era's constant washing and sanitizers all wear that barrier down.

Working with human skin kept alive outside the body, the team applied chemical and mechanical insults that mimic daily harms. They then measured how leaky each damaged sample became and how its layers changed. Comparing damage types side by side shows which injuries break the wall worst and how the wall fails. Such models let companies test creams and cleansers for barrier harm without human trials.
pmc-11665147:
Laureen Raelly-Muze, Rafael Vega, and Leslie Hutchins report a rare case combining penetrating brain injury with electrical injury. Their illustrative case from twenty twenty-four involves a man hurt by a welding spike. The spike entered through the orbit above the eyeball. Current passed through his body and exited at his toe.

Scans showed air inside the skull and a bleeding track through deep brain tissue. Remarkably, the eye itself escaped injury. The spike path also missed major organs and key brain structures. That lucky path let the patient recover with minimal deficits. The authors draw lessons for teams facing several injury types at once.
pmc-11666647:
Marieke Woensdregt and co-authors draw lessons for theory building in fields where evidence is thin or indirect, in a paper from 2024. Their guiding case is the study of how human thought evolved. The past left only sparse traces, such as fossils and old tools, that hint at language and other skills.

From work in that field, the authors distill five good practices. State your assumptions openly. Set out rival theories in plain view. Build formal or computer models to test ideas. Check that a theory fits what is known about related topics. And combine many kinds of evidence so weak strands can support each other. They argue that thin evidence can spur better theory, not just block it, and that the lessons apply in many fields.
pmc-11666947:
Huo and co-authors give a step-by-step protocol for coating glass with a clear, conductive tin oxide film. The film is doped with tantalum to carry charge well. It shows low surface roughness, low resistance, and high carrier counts, making it a strong stand-in for standard clear conductors.

The method uses hollow cathode gas flow sputtering to lay the film down. Steps cover preparing and cleaning fresh float glass before coating. Later steps detail how to measure the film's light and electric traits. Full use notes point back to the team's earlier paper on this film.
pmc-11667047:
Olexandr Kuryata and co-authors review, in a 2024 paper, a body compound called 5-ALA as a possible help for metabolic disorders. The compound is a building block for heme, the iron holding part of blood pigment, and it plays a role in many body tasks. The review pulls together the latest work on how it acts.

The compound seems to affect swelling, immune response, cell stress, and the work of the cell's energy plants. It also bears on how the body handles sugar and fats. The authors trace these effects to gene switches that it calms or rouses, and to products made as heme breaks down. Those products may shield cells from harm. The review sets out what is known, and what trials should test next.
pmc-11667147:
Nehal Shata and three co-authors tell of a young boy whose stiff neck was an early sign of skull base sink. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The boy had slow growth, lost motor gains, and stiff low limbs, with a right head tilt that grew worse. Gene tests found a variant that did not full tell his state.

Scans at last showed the skull base bone pushed in, with cord squeeze and swell at the top joint. A skull hole cut eased the press, and team care ran the rest. The boy got back motor skills and rose to the mid weight line. Late finds came from the plague years.
pmc-11668547:
Necrotizing enterocolitis is a gut disease that strikes premature babies, mixing poor blood flow with fierce inflammation. Yunfei Zhang and three co-authors asked what role a low-oxygen sensor protein plays, using mice bred to lack it in the gut lining. They triggered the disease in newborn mice and measured gut damage, stress, inflammation, and cell growth and death.

Without the sensor, the gut suffered more damage, more stress, and more cell death, and healing growth slowed. A known inflammation pathway also switched on harder in those mice. The authors conclude the sensor normally guards the gut, and they point to that pathway as a treatment target.
pmc-11668747:
Noorah Alnaghaimshi and co-authors wrote a review from 2024 on the quality of Arabic mental health apps. Anxiety and depression disable many people across Arab countries, yet services are thin. Phones could help close the gap, but the region's app shelf had not been mapped. The team searched the app stores of fifteen Arab countries and rated what they found against standard quality and safety guides.

Twenty-two apps passed their screen. Most showed no sign that mental health experts helped design them. Most leaned on live calls or chats with specialists rather than proven self-help methods. Quality scores ran low across design, engagement, information, privacy, and support. Set against recommended Australian apps, the Arabic set lacked core tools such as structured self-help therapy and crisis lines. The team calls for design frameworks that bring users and clinicians into the process from the start.
pmc-11669747:
Kristy Lau and a team of co-authors compared drugs for COVID-19 in the Omicron wave. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, set antiviral drugs against lab made antibodies.
