Antivirals were thought to still work on this variant. The antibody drugs had lost much of their power to block the virus. The team pooled trials that set each drug class against no drug or other drugs.

They searched many databases in mid twenty twenty-two, with updates later that year. They rated bias risk with standard tools. Readers who treat this disease get a ranked view of which drugs helped most in acute care. The work guides drug choice when a variant dulls one class.
pmc-11671047:
Abir Bouhamdi and co-authors published this sleep study in 2024. It asks how much hospital-based fitting of CPAP gear helps people with hard sleep apnea, a state where breath stops again and again at night. CPAP blows a soft stream of air that keeps the throat open. Getting the pressure right takes a night of close watch.

The team looked back at the records of sixty-nine patients, most of them women, who had the fitting done in hospital. After fitting, scores for stopped breath and drops in blood oxygen fell, and sleep grew longer and more sound. A third of the patients still needed a stronger mode, such as a two-level machine. The authors say in-hospital fitting is worth its cost, since it tailors care and picks out those who need more help.
pmc-11671747:
Marta Camici, Giulia Del Duca, Anna Clelia Brita, and Andrea Antinori propose a linked explanation for long COVID in a 2024 article. Long COVID still lacks a clear cause and a proven treatment. The authors argue the key lies in lasting harm to three systems that calm inflammation. These are reflexes run by the vagus nerve, a hormone axis from brain to adrenal glands, and the energy parts of cells.

They trace how the virus could damage each stage of this linked axis, directly, through immune attack, or by waking dormant viruses. Two chemical messengers get close attention for their shared calming roles. If the calming systems are weak, cell damage from the virus may go unchecked. The authors call for studies of hormone receptor sensitivity in people with long COVID.
pmc-11672247:
Yi-Sheng Lu and co-authors cage a useful enzyme inside tiny silicon particles to help it break down a nerve agent, in work published in 2024. The enzyme can split organophosphate compounds, a class that includes the agent VX. On its own, though, the enzyme is fragile and hard to recover after use.

Placed in the cage, the enzyme worked about twice as fast on a stand-in compound as the free enzyme did. The cage also shielded it from heat and from being cut up by other enzymes. The loaded particles kept working through seven cycles of use and recovery. In a gel on rabbit skin, and in tests with human blood, the construct stayed active against VX.
pmc-11672447:
Yulei Guo and David Fennell compare visitor codes of conduct in Chinese zoos and zoos in English-speaking countries, in a study from 2024. Zoos worldwide post such codes to steer visitor behavior. Yet the ethics of managing visitors has drawn little research.

The team read close to nine hundred statements from forty-nine zoos in all. The two groups shared much in structure and content. Most rules took a duty-based form: plain bans and duties for guests. Few codes drew on animal welfare science or used the visit to teach conservation. The authors suggest adding both, and designing rules that reason about outcomes and fit each zoo's setting. That shift could raise guest engagement and ease management.
pmc-11672547:
Ylenia Mazzocato and ten co-authors reported in twenty twenty-four a way to design ring-shaped peptide drugs with the help of machine learning. Such design tools tend to need large sets of test data, which are hard to build in the lab. The team worked with a small data set on blockers of a protease linked to tumors.

They chained three tools in turn: a random forest model, a method that reads how pairs of sites in a chain change together, and a sim-based search. The ring peptides shaped this way were then made and tested in glassware. They blocked the target more strongly than the best past blockers. A crystal view of one peptide bound to the protease showed a wide contact face and a stiff ring shape. The work shows that smart pairings of methods can stretch small data sets a long way.
pmc-11672947:
Ji-Soo Oh and five co-authors report the first human use of a new catheter device for a thickened heart, in a 2024 trial. In hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, the wall between the heart's chambers grows too thick and blocks blood flow. Drugs, open surgery, and alcohol injection each have limits.

Their device reaches the thickened wall through a vein of the heart and burns it from inside with radiofrequency energy. Four patients were treated and followed for a year with scans and walking tests. Average wall thickness fell from 22.6 to 18.9 millimeters, and the pressure gradient blocking flow dropped substantially at rest. Only two patients, though, showed clear gains on ultrasound and walking distance. No serious side effects, such as rhythm problems or vessel injury, appeared. The authors call for larger studies.
pmc-11673047:
Seul Bi Lee and co-authors report a 2024 study on CT scan consistency. Radiomics reads hundreds of numeric traits from a scan. Scanners and settings vary across hospitals, which shifts those traits. Shifted traits break the reproducibility that clinic use demands. The team tests a deep learning harmonization tool on belly scans. A pre-trained algorithm was applied to 63 dual-energy scans. Each scan was rebuilt in four ways, and ten regions per scan were analyzed.

Of 455 traits per region, 387 survived a cleanup of redundant ones. Traits before and after harmonization were compared for stability. Hospitals could share radiomics models if scans agree across sites. That sharing is the prize: one model, many scanners. The feasibility design keeps claims modest. Still, stable traits after harmonization would mark a real step toward multi-site radiomics trials.
pmc-11673247:
Gabriela Sequeda and co-authors review third generation therapies for substance use in young people in a 2024 scoping review. These therapies rest on acceptance, mindfulness, and psychological flexibility. They aim to help young people change drug related behavior, cope with hard emotions, and maintain abstinence over time.

The review covered a five year window across major databases. Eight studies were found, most on mindfulness, with one each on dialectical behavior therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy. Results were promising, with reductions in substance use and in problems such as anxiety and depression. The authors call the evidence emerging rather than settled.
pmc-11673347:
Leonardo and four co-authors graded AI-made research ideas in twenty twenty-four for a teen spine curve ill. Doctors face tight clinic days, so fast idea tools could aid the field. Four chat models got the same prompt and gave ten to fourteen ideas each.

Each idea was checked in a paper bank and scored for how new it was. Mean newness scores sat close across the four models. A few ideas from three models had no past papers at all. One model gave no fully new idea in its set. AI can spark fresh study paths, they find.
pmc-11673547:
Yong Wu and seven co-authors present a particle-based method to model and visually simulate blood flow in bifurcation aneurysms, bulges where a brain artery splits. Their study came out in 2024. Such simulations support surgical training, diagnosis, and treatment planning, but flow in these bulges is hard to model.

The method treats blood as an incompressible fluid made of interacting particles, an approach called smoothed particle hydrodynamics. Vessel geometry follows a classic law relating branch sizes, with an adjustable split structure. The model covers aneurysm formation, growth, and rupture, including interaction between blood, tissue fluid, and the artery wall. It also computes and displays wall shear stress, the friction of flow on the wall, in a new particle-based view. Numerical experiments supported the method's feasibility.
pmc-11673747:
Shrivastava and coauthors test a fat-like compound in mice bred to mimic Alzheimer disease. In that illness, brain swelling fails to clear and nerve cells die. The compound helps the brain calm swelling and heal. The team gave it to the mice for a long time and then checked their brains.

Treated mice had less of the sticky protein that builds up in the illness. Fewer nerve cells died, and fewer showed signs of cell death. Brain immune cells also shifted to a calmer state. The results back more tests of calm-down compounds for this brain illness.
pmc-11673847:
Jiayi Sun, Kai Cheng, and Yanyun Xie review molecule based detection of urinary tract infections in a 2024 paper. Urine culture stays the gold standard test, but it loads hospital labs heavily, and faster options like flow tools or strip assays lose accuracy or time. The hunt for dependable biomarkers is therefore urgent.

The review sorts known markers into three groups, those in clinical use, promising candidates, and disputed ones. Infection types, simple versus complicated and lower versus upper tract, organize the survey. Nucleic acid, metabolite, and lipid markers get special attention. The closing section weighs the hurdles and the outlook for marker based testing.
pmc-11674047:
Babies born before twenty-eight weeks, or under a kilogram, face their highest death risk before ever leaving the hospital. Zhenyuan Dai and six co-authors searched records from Guangzhou hospitals, 2013 to 2024, for first-day signals that predict which of 211 such infants would not survive to discharge.

Twenty-six factors from the first twenty-four hours went into the screen. A penalized regression picked thirteen, and a leaner final model kept six, mixing the expected, gestational age, five-minute Apgar score, and twins or more, with fresh markers the abstract flags. Accuracy stayed strong in training and validation sets, with area scores above 0.80. The authors aim the model at early, honest counseling and triage in Chinese units.
pmc-11674347:
Raluca Vlad and colleagues reported a fabricated illness case in 2024. A caregiver invented symptoms for a child. Tests were also altered by the caregiver. Doctors now call it factitious disorder. It counts as serious child abuse.

The child had prolonged reported fever. Hospital checks never confirmed the symptoms. Stories and test results never matched. Frequent visits raised early alarm signs. The mother stopped returning after attitudes changed. Staff distance replaced earlier empathy then. The authors stress careful communication skills. Unexplained stories deserve gentle questioning. Prolonged fever was the central puzzle.
pmc-11674447:
Sanam Meraj and co-authors tested in 2024 whether common bed bugs can host a parasite called Trypanosoma rangeli. That parasite spreads through kissing bugs and can infect people alongside the related parasite that causes Chagas disease. Whether bed bugs could carry it too was an open question with clear public health weight.

The team fed the parasite to bed bugs and also injected it, then tracked where it went in the body over time. No live parasites turned up in the bugs' blood space, saliva glands, or waste by either route. The bugs did switch on immune defenses soon after infection. The results argue that bed bugs do not serve as hosts that pass this parasite on.
pmc-11674647: Sylvie Fraitag fronts a second run of a journal set on skin disease study in children, dated 2024. The short head notes that child skin care is still a growing sub-field. A rise in books and papers on the topic in recent years backs that growth. No more detail on the set's contents is given in the head, so this note stays at that scope.
pmc-11674847:
Yu-Ting Lee and co-authors (2024) report a case where a distant treatment effect was planned, not stumbled upon. The abscopal effect, in which radiation to one tumor shrinks others elsewhere, is usually a surprise. Their patient was a 53-year-old man whose bladder cancer had spread to liver, lungs, and bones after chemotherapy failed. His tumor carried a marker score suggesting immunotherapy could work. He received four cycles of the immune drug pembrolizumab.

Meanwhile, the team aimed ablative, high-dose radiation at selected lung metastases, deliberately trying to trigger the immune system against the rest. The result was complete remission, which held after the drug was stopped. The authors also review the literature on this effect. They argue that with the right tumor marker and aggressive local radiation, the abscopal effect can be pursued as a strategy rather than hoped for as an accident.
pmc-11674947:
The authors review Gaucher disease, a rare inherited disorder, with an eye on the Mexican population, in this 2024 overview. A faulty gene starves cells of an enzyme that breaks down a fatty substance, which then piles up inside scavenger cells, swelling the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. The review covers how common the disease is, how it shows itself, and how it is treated.

Replacing the missing enzyme remains the mainstay, with a second drug class that slows production of the accumulating fat. Early diagnosis plus individualized therapy markedly improves outlook, especially for the common type without brain involvement. The brain affecting types still lack good options. The authors call for better epidemiology in Mexico and continued work on the neurological forms, where families wait longest for progress.
pmc-11675047:
Siying Liu and co-authors test a blood-based way to track a rare disease in children in a 2024 paper. The disease, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, creates lesions that are usually followed by imaging. Tumor DNA in the blood may offer another signal of how the disease responds.

In this retrospective study, the team compared molecular response in blood with what scans showed. They used data displays and survival models to check how well the two agreed. If blood signals match imaging, children might be monitored with fewer scans, though the authors frame this as a first examination.
pmc-11675447:
Periodontitis inflames the gums and eats away the bone that holds teeth, and its roots lie in a failing mucosal barrier. Shuhong Kuang and co-authors map that barrier in a 2024 study that joins single-cell and spatial methods across humans and mice. They compare which cells and signals the two species share in diseased gums.

One pathway stood out: gum lining cells use a signal called JAG1 to steer macrophages, the immune cells that drive inflammation. Blocking JAG1 calmed inflammation in the lining cells and eased disease in animal tests. The team argues that pairing human tissue data with mouse models points to targets that fit human biology. JAG1 now stands as a candidate for new periodontal treatments.
pmc-11675547:
Min-Kyung So and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on re-reading disputed BRCA1 gene variants. ClinVar, the public variant database, holds clashing calls on the same variants, which stalls care for families facing breast and ovarian cancer risk. The team re-read 450 BRCA1 missense variants with conflicting entries, using an automated tool and British gene-specific guidance.

Grouped into three bands, the two methods agreed on about fifty-nine percent of variants. Neither method ever called a variant harmful that the other called harmless. By May 2024, only seventeen of the 450 had settled in ClinVar itself. The authors urge using both tools together.
pmc-11675747:
Wenxiang Jing and co-authors forge a sponge from bamboo in a 2024 paper that traps heavy metals in water. A ring compound at its core grabs set metals with care, but it costs much and is hard to get back. That pair of flaws caps its use in foul streams.

The team stuck the rings on a light bamboo foam, made with a blast cook and a lined freeze. Tests read the foam build, its pores, and its pull on lead, copper, and cadmium in lone and mixed baths. The aim is a cheap trap that can be fished out and used again. Water teams gain a green sponge with a sharp grab.
pmc-11675947:
Silvia Pérez-Piñero and co-authors put a persimmon extract through a proper placebo trial for weight management, in a 2024 study. Seventy-one overweight but healthy adults took either four hundred milligrams of the standardised fruit extract or a placebo daily for one hundred and twenty days, with neither side knowing which. Body composition was measured by X-ray absorptiometry and electrical impedance.

Among the strictly overweight subgroup, the extract group lost significantly more fat, in both kilograms and percentage, than the placebo group. Lean mass held steady, so the loss was fat rather than muscle or water. Between-group differences were strong statistically. The authors present the extract as a candidate aid for weight management, while the trial's modest size invites larger confirmation before any shelf claims.
pmc-11676147:
Zhengang Liang and co-authors make ceramic armor in 2024 by 3D printing plus microwave heating. Armor ceramics with complex shapes are hard to mold or machine, so printing opens new forms. The team prints a zirconia ceramic from a light-cured resin, then hardens it in a microwave kiln rather than a standard kiln.

They tuned the resin recipe until one mix cured with little shrinkage and low flow resistance. Microwave heating at a set peak temperature gave dense ceramic with fine grains, denser than standard heating. Nearby resin mixes left pores or clumps, which weakened the parts. The best recipe yielded hard, tough ceramic with high bending strength, suited to armor shapes.
pmc-11676247:
Marcin Zemła and co-authors study how foam structure and density shape the products of recycling rigid polyurethane foams. Their 2024 paper makes foams from oil based and plant based building blocks. Five target densities ran from forty to one hundred twenty kilograms per cubic meter. Standard tests measured cell structure, strength, heat flow, and water uptake. The foams were then shredded and broken down with a glycol and a catalyst.

The breakdown products were checked for amine and hydroxyl values, thickness, and molecular weight. Hydroxyl numbers of the recycled polyols ran from 476 to 511. The plant based starting material strongly affected the amine number and thickness of the product. Closed cell content ranged widely, from twenty to ninety five percent. Strength also spanned a wide range. The work links foam design choices to the quality of what recycling returns.
pmc-11676347:
Natsuki Yamaguchi and co-authors review in this 2024 paper the promise and peril of making stem cells immortal. Mesenchymal stem cells repair tissue and calm immune responses, and trials worldwide use them. Yet they age fast, vary by donor, and run scarce, which blocks steady supply. Engineered immortal lines grow forever and can feed both cell therapy and cell-free products made from their secretions.

The catch is safety: the genes that grant endless growth can also destabilize the genome and seed tumors. The review weighs guardrails such as chromosome checks and built-in suicide genes that kill cells on command once their job ends. Careful testing, the authors argue, decides whether the supply fix is worth the risk.
pmc-11676447:
Camille Eyssartier and co-authors measure how the spine aligns during a handstand in a 2024 study. Gymnasts use the handstand in many sports, but how the back balances upside down was little known, which can hamper coaching. Nineteen national-level gymnasts had low-dose X-rays taken from front and side, both standing and in a handstand. The images were rebuilt in three dimensions.

Most gymnasts tucked the pelvis backward during the handstand. The lower back curve, the upper back curve, and the offset of a mid-back point all shrank on average. Standing posture showed the lower curve tied to pelvis angle, while the handstand showed a different link. The data give coaches a first map of spine strategy in this pose.
pmc-11676647:
Alessandra Rigoli and co-authors reviewed what is known about dancers' energy and diets in a 2024 scoping review. Dancers train hard from a young age, and too little food for that workload harms growth, health, and performance. The team searched nine databases plus grey sources for studies of pre-professional and professional dancers.

Twelve studies qualified, covering mostly ballet and one contemporary group. Young dancers often ate less than they burned, with low energy availability. Professionals ate more than students but still raised concerns in several reports. No studies covered musical theatre or opera dancers at all. The authors map a thin evidence base and call for better support and research.
pmc-11676847:
Gabriela Kot and co-authors ask what dialysis cramps cost patients in daily life and movement. Their 2024 study surveys sixty-seven people on regular in-center hemodialysis, whose quality of life already trails healthy peers. Muscle spasms during treatment are common, yet their wider burden was little studied.

A validated nine-question cramp survey was paired with standard activity and health questionnaires. The team relates the presence and severity of cramps to self-rated quality of life and habitual physical activity. The aim is to move cramps from an accepted nuisance to a measured factor in how dialysis patients feel and function, which could argue for treating them more aggressively.
pmc-11676947:
Jorin Overwiening and co-authors build a population level model of the thalamus to show how brain state reshapes its responses, in work from twenty twenty-four. The thalamus relays nearly all sensory traffic to the cortex. Its behavior shifts between waking and sleep, but cell level and population level views rarely meet.

Their mean field model holds relay cells and reticular cells with real cell traits. A brain chemical's presence or absence sets awake and sleep like modes, steering burst firing. Sensory input drew straight responses when awake and bent ones in sleep. Cortical input flipped roles by state, damping replies when awake and waking the system in sleep. Noise leveled the difference.
pmc-11677047:
Merve Küçükoğlu Keser, Dilek Şahin, and Sıddıka Songül Yalçın measure a protein called osteopontin in mothers with and without diabetes in pregnancy. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The condition, gestational diabetes, is growing more common and endangers both mother and baby.

The team enrolled one hundred sixty-five women, about half with the condition. At birth they sampled the mother's blood, cord blood, and later her breast milk. Cord levels of the protein, and of a second marker, did not differ between groups. The mother's blood and milk, though, carried more of the protein when she had the condition. Higher bands of the protein tracked with higher odds of the condition. The authors suggest it reflects body changes tied to the disease.
pmc-11677147:
Dhinu Jayaseelan and co-authors map how the ways of past studies of pain in tendon ills range, to bare the lack of one way. Their scope review is from two thousand twenty-four.

Tendon pain curbs use of the limb. Proofs hint the pain paths work awry, in arm and leg ills alike, but in unlike ways. Five stores and gray works were searched to a spring cut. Near three thousand works came up; a small set was kept. They split near even twixt arm and leg themes. The team reads the tests, tools, and groups each used. The aim is to show the spread, so a shared way can be built.
pmc-11677347:
Shan Gao and colleagues studied a traditional Chinese herb for depression in two thousand twenty-four. The herb is a daylily species used historically for mood. Its active ingredients and mechanisms stayed unclear. Chemical profiling found dozens of compounds in the plant. Stressed mice modeled human depression for testing. Computer network analysis predicted likely targets.

Gene activity studies in brain tissue added more clues. Protein tests then verified key pathway changes. Several plant compounds emerged as likely active ones. Dozens of depression-related targets were implicated. The herb seems to act through many routes at once. Such multi-target action fits traditional medicine patterns. Modern checks now support further study.
pmc-11677447:
Ju-Yeong Kim and Gyu-Min Kong measure in 2024 how the thigh bone bows in Korean adults, and how that bow shifts with age and sex. Bow of the thigh bone tends to be stronger in Asian groups. Surgeons need good norms when they plan bone work.

Five hundred fifty X-ray films were read from three view angles. Women showed more bow than men in a front view at first pass. Once height and weight joined the model, age stood out as the main driver. Each year of age added a small, steady rise in the bow angle.
pmc-11677747:
Andrius Masedunskas and co-authors lay out in a 2024 trial protocol a test of whether draining the body's sugar stores before a fast deepens its cellular cleanup. Twenty-four healthy adults will cross over between a three-day water-only fast alone and the same fast after glycogen-depleting exercise. The main readout is autophagy, the cell's recycling flow, in blood immune cells.

Side measures span body composition, heart rhythm variability, vessel function, and layers of molecular profiling from blood to stool. Fasting is popular but its human biology is half-mapped; this design isolates whether an empty tank changes the cleanup signal.
pmc-11677847:
Peter Murray, Jonathan Coffman, and Franklin Garcia-Godoy wrote a 2024 review arguing that mouth infections drive a large share of disease across the whole body. The review sums up 252 studies linking gum disease and tooth decay germs to systemic illness. People with such mouth disease were, on average, about 3.3 times more likely to develop body-wide diseases or poor pregnancy outcomes.

The review ranks the main oral germs by how often studies name them, and lists the linked conditions: cancer, heart disease, diabetes, Alzheimer's, and many more. Mouth conditions affect roughly a quarter to nearly half of Americans. Dental treatment, the authors note, can clear the infections and ease the linked diseases. They frame the burden as a public health crisis hiding in plain sight.
pmc-11678147:
Rebecca Rossetti, Vittoria Strinati, and Alessandra Caputi lead a team piloting a ketogenic diet for women whose polycystic ovary syndrome has thinned their periods. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-four. The syndrome is a common hormone disorder of fertile-age women. Diet is one of its few non-drug levers.

Eighteen women ate ketogenic for forty-five days, then reintroduced carbohydrates gradually. Twelve finished the six-month course. Periods became more frequent, and ovarian volume shrank. Key hormones shifted in favorable directions. Those gains did not depend on how much weight was lost. Testosterone and excess hair, by contrast, improved only with weight loss. Even normal-weight women benefited on cycles. The authors read this as evidence for a direct metabolic effect. A controlled trial is the clear next step.
pmc-11678547:
Ewa Szczepanska-Sadowska, Agnieszka Cudnoch-Jędrzejewska, and Tymoteusz Żera review two hormones that talk to each other, in a paper published in 2024. Vasopressin mainly guards blood pressure and body water, while insulin controls sugar and energy storage. The review gathers evidence that each shapes the other's release and action across the body.

In the liver, vasopressin frees stored sugar and promotes fat making. In the pancreas, it boosts release of insulin and a partner hormone. Insulin, in turn, raises vasopressin release from brain centers. This two-way link helps match blood supply to tissue needs. When the link goes wrong, it feeds insulin resistance in obesity and diabetes, the authors argue. The pair may be a joint target in heart and metabolic disease.
pmc-11678647:
Dorantes-Heredia and co-authors count faulty DNA repair in advanced tumors at one Mexican center in a 2024 study. Repair status guides prognosis and drug choice in several cancers. Records and tissue from bowel, stomach, gullet, and womb cancer patients treated from 2017 to 2020 were reviewed. Protein stains on tissue showed whether repair crews were present.

Faulty repair appeared in about one in eight bowel cancers. Rates were lower in stomach cancer and higher in womb cancer, while gullet cancer showed none. Rates looked alike in women and men, peaking in the forty-something age band. The authors offer the counts as a base for wider Mexican studies.
pmc-11678747:
Maria Paço and co-authors review in 2024 how therapy can ease a common problem after knee ligament injury or repair: the thigh muscle will not switch on fully. That failure, called arthrogenic muscle inhibition, slows strength gains and recovery. The team gathered trials from four databases and graded their quality with standard scales.

Twenty studies qualified. Fifteen tested exercise, and exercise clearly helped. Seven tested treatments that pass current into the muscle, and two forms paired with exercise improved strength, pain, and joint movement. Nine more studies covered mental rehearsal, cold packs, taping, and vibration. Mental rehearsal and cold used before exercise aided muscle recovery, and taping cut swelling and pain better than exercise alone. Vibration results were mixed. The authors put structured exercise first, with add-on therapies to lift results further.
pmc-11678847:
Venkata Thunuguntla and seven co-authors test a cactus extract on the blood vessels of obese mice in a 2024 study. Obesity stiffens arteries and dulls their ability to relax, seeding heart disease. The extract, from Caralluma fimbriata, is known for curbing appetite, but its vessel effects were uncharted.

Eighty mice grew fat on sixteen weeks of rich food, then received the extract, a prescription diet drug, both, or neither. The team weighed fat, then tested artery rings in baths for their relaxing response and stained them for stress signals. The extract improved the vessels' relaxation and shifted the stress markers, standing beside the drug as a gentler candidate worth clinical attention.
pmc-11679247:
Anna Voziki, Olga Deda, Melania Kachrimanidou, and Victor Gault wrote this review paper, published in 2024. It gathers mouse studies on fecal transplants as a treatment for a stubborn gut infection, judging success by the chemistry of the gut rather than symptoms alone.

The infection, caused by the Clostridioides difficile bacterium, often returns after antibiotics. The reviewers screened 460 papers and kept five that profiled metabolism in treated mice. In all five, transplanting gut microbes from healthy donors restored the gut community and shifted its chemistry. Levels of short fatty acids and processed bile acids rose, and both are known to hold the germ back. The transplant beat antibiotics and probiotics at rebuilding a healthy gut. Results still varied with donor and method, so the authors urge careful reporting over rushed standardization.
pmc-11679347:
Valentina Focaroli, Marina Chiaro, Maria Vittoria Battaglia, Laura Guidetti, and Andrea Velardi reported a training program for teachers on health-damaging behaviors in two thousand twenty-four. The focus was doping, which reaches beyond elite sport into schools and gyms. Pressures for strength, beauty, and status drive much of it.

A sixteen-hour online course taught high school teachers about doping and its mental and social roots. It also gave tools to build students' self-esteem and self-management. Teachers were tested before and after with standard scales. Their self-efficacy and emotional regulation improved clearly, and they applied those gains with students. A later youth survey will help design future prevention events.
pmc-11679447:
Bauder and co-authors sharpen vehicle position data after the fact with Kalman filters in this 2024 study. Connected vehicles broadcast awareness messages with their GPS position up to ten times a second. Meter-level errors in those positions weaken tolling and accident reconstruction.

Two obstacles stand out: the messages arrive at uneven time steps, and filtering must run retrospectively. The team built extended and unscented Kalman filters with two motion models. They adjusted the filter's noise settings step by step and inserted interpolation points to even out the timing. Driving tests with two connected vehicles compared the variants. The study shows how much accuracy post-processing can recover from standard broadcasts.
pmc-11679547:
Jacob Schmidt and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-four, ChatGPT as a support tool for informed consent before penile prosthesis surgery. The patients have erectile dysfunction after prostate removal. ChatGPT-4 answered twenty common questions in four areas: the condition and treatment, the surgery, complications, and aftercare. Three senior urologists rated the answers with the DISCERN quality instrument, on a one to five scale. Readability was scored with two standard formulas. Agreement among raters was good.

Mean quality scores sat in the moderate range across all four areas. Clarity and relevance scored high, above four. Complex issues, such as risks and alternative treatments, scored lowest, below two. The authors conclude the tool can support, not replace, consent talks.
pmc-11679647:
Farm insecticides can train malaria mosquitoes to resist the sprays meant to kill them, and Massioudou Koto Yérima Gounou Boukari and co-authors measure that effect in northern Benin in this 2024 study. They surveyed vegetable growers around Malanville and Parakou and tested local Anopheles mosquitoes against two families of insecticide.

Nearly all growers used fertilizers, and all used pesticides. One mosquito species dominated in Malanville while another was the only kind found in Parakou. Lab tests on standard treated papers and bottles showed strong resistance to pyrethroids and to DDT. Helper chemicals that block detox pathways, plus gene tests for known resistance mutations, helped the team trace how the resistance works. The findings warn that farm and health spray programs must plan together.
pmc-11679747:
Wenzhuo Ma and co-authors present a 2024 paper on vehicle positioning in cities. Satellite signals alone can drift in built-up areas, where tall blocks weaken the fix. The team adds camera vision to judge how the car is moving. A filter then adjusts its method to the state of the drive, such as moving or parked.

When the car sits still, a zero-speed rule tightens the fix. Tests in models and in real drives checked the method. It beat a standard filter and a multi-model rival on accuracy. Gains over the rival ran from about a fifth to near a third across three axes. The work targets safe, exact city driving.
pmc-11679847:
Laia Miralles-Llumà and ten colleagues published a clinical trial report in two thousand twenty-four on weight loss in people with severe sleep apnea and obesity. Sleep apnea stops breathing briefly during sleep and is closely tied to body weight. The trial tested whether a year-long intensive programme changed body makeup, not just weight.

Thirty-four patients were split into a programme group and a standard care group. The programme used a low-calorie Mediterranean diet with close support. After a year, the programme group had lost over eight percent of body weight, while the control group lost almost none. Scans showed the loss came mostly from body fat, including deep belly fat. Breathing during sleep also improved, along with blood measures linked to heart risk.
pmc-11679947:
Eric Bunnell and Matthew Stratton review whether functional training helps balance and the inner ear sense of motion in a 2024 paper. Functional training builds movements used in daily life, and it has grown popular in gyms and clinics. The authors gather human studies that touch on balance, vestibular function, or functional movement.

The evidence suggests general fitness training can improve balance and vestibular function, and training built around functional movements may help even more. Age and sex may shape the gains. Few studies, though, test vestibular function directly alongside balance, so the authors call for work that pins down how the benefit arises.
pmc-11680047:
Amine Ben-Daoued, Frédéric Bernardin, and Pierre Duthon compare, in a 2024 review, a light simulation program called SWEET against rival simulators to check its accuracy. Faithful light modeling matters because small errors in how rays scatter add noise and artifacts to images. SWEET traces rays backward using random sampling.

The authors detail updates since SWEET's first report and line it up against well-known tools, notably Mitsuba. They compare brightness values across settings of thickness and scatter direction to expose bias from random sampling. The use case in view is car camera imaging for self-driving, where true-to-life scenes matter. SWEET kept noise low, which supports its use for high-grade imaging work.
pmc-11680147:
Di Bao and colleagues studied a pig diarrhoea virus in gut cells in 2024. The virus causes enteritis in piglets. It can kill young pigs quickly. Mitochondrial DNA can fuel inflammation responses. Inflammasome involvement was unclear before this work. Cultured pig intestinal cells were infected.

Infection damaged mitochondria inside the cells. Mitochondrial DNA escaped as a result. That escape switched on the NLRP3 inflammasome. A second signal boosted a key inflammatory protein. Reactive oxygen from mitochondria helped that signal. The protein interleukin was then secreted. The authors claim a first full mechanism. Pig virus inflammation is now clearer.
pmc-11680347:
Yuhang Zhang and co-authors send a gene message to the lungs to fight the MERS virus. Their 2024 study builds on mRNA tools proven in COVID-19 vaccines. The message codes for a nanobody, a tiny antibody that can block the virus, and is packed in fat bubbles tuned to land in lung tissue.

In dishes, the system made the nanobody, which bound the virus and blocked a test version of it. In mice, the message reached the lungs and kept making the blocker for a full day. The authors pitch the platform as cheap, scalable, and quick to retarget. It may serve against other lung infections and fresh viral threats.
pmc-11682847:
Emanuella Brito and seven colleagues published an evaluation in two thousand twenty-four of ChatGPT as a patient education source on breast reduction surgery. The operation is common and relieves real burdens, but patients arrive with many questions. Whether chatbot answers are trustworthy was the concern.

Fifteen typical patient questions were put to ChatGPT. Five board-certified plastic surgeons graded each answer as appropriate, too thin, or inaccurate. Of seventy-five gradings, ninety-two percent called the answers accurate. Six responses worried the experts: four lacked needed detail and two were wrong. The authors say the tool is broadly reliable for basic education but not flawless. They advise professional oversight of AI patient materials.
pmc-11683647:
High phosphate levels in the blood have been linked to higher death rates, and one phosphate compound, sodium hexametaphosphate, is known to interact with proteins. Malik, Alamri, Altwaijry, Alamro, Alhomida, Ayub, and Odeibat test what this compound does to clumps of trypsin, a digestive enzyme, at gut acidity. They track the clumps with light-based tools and microscope images across a range of doses.

The clumps began to dissolve once the dose passed one millimolar, and at six millimolar they broke up the most. At that dose the freed enzyme also folded back into a shape close to its normal form, and the microscope images showed the shapeless clumps gone. The authors suggest the compound could serve as a general tool for dissolving protein clumps. Uses could include freeing proteins trapped in cell-made pellets and refolding them afterward.
pmc-11683747:
Wazzan Aljuhani and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on how common kneecap pain is among adults in Saudi Arabia. The syndrome brings pain behind or around the kneecap and mainly strikes active people. No firm count existed for the kingdom. The team sent Arabic questionnaires online to adults across the country, mixing background questions with a standard knee pain scale.

Two hundred seventy-eight adults took part, most of them young and just over half of them men. About one in four reported knee pain of some kind. Applying the standard scale put the syndrome's rate at nine percent. Two traits linked to the syndrome stood out: being out of work and having knee pain at all. Age, sex, and body weight showed no clear link. Calling the rate low next to some past reports, the team still urges larger, firmer studies to pin the number down.
pmc-11684547:
Jessan Jishu, Saad Hanan, Farhan Shahid, Alexandra LaForteza, and Sanjay Shrestha argue, in a 2024 review, that family doctors should be welcomed into interventional pain medicine. That field uses procedures to ease pain in patients whom standard care has failed, and demand for it keeps growing. Pain is among the top reasons patients see a family doctor, yet no pain fellowship is set up to favor family medicine graduates.

Residency training in family medicine gives only a small slice of time to pain care, and little of it covers procedures. The authors set out the rising need and make the case that family doctors are well placed to offer the full range of pain care. They urge pain fellowships to treat family physicians as strong candidates and to credit their skills in hands-on treatment.
pmc-11686447:
Ben West and six co-authors present a 2024 study on predicting the sugar coating patterns of lab made therapeutic proteins from gene activity data. The coating, built of sugar chains, shapes how a drug protein moves through the body and how safe and stable it is. The process has no template, so outcomes vary a lot between cell lines.

The team asked whether bulk gene reads, taken before a production run starts, can forecast the coating a cell line will give. They found real signal in the data. One gene, Alg5, flagged lines likely to yield proteins with higher levels of a certain sugar form. Such forecasts could save costly trial runs.
pmc-11687947:
Guo leads a large team improving variant calling in exome data, in work from twenty twenty-four. Whole exome sequencing reads the protein coding parts of the genome for cancer diagnosis and association studies. Results depend on mapping reads to a reference genome.

A single standard reference may fit some populations poorly, causing missed or false variants. Using a population matched reference can sharpen mapping and calls, the team argues. Their work tests that gain directly. Better calls matter most for patients whose ancestry differs from the reference builders, a known source of genomic medicine inequality.
pmc-11688747:
Tracey Gendron, Alyssa Camp, and Amateau Gigi study, in a paper published in 2024, whether taking age bias to heart raises the risk of suicidal thoughts in later life. Their frame is a known theory that such thoughts grow when people feel they are a burden and feel cut off from others. Ageism can feed both feelings at once.

The team surveyed 454 volunteers aged sixty-five and over, drawn from more than thirty states. Twelve percent said they had had suicidal thoughts in the past month. In their models, older age and internalized ageism both raised the odds, and internalized ageism showed the strongest link of any factor tested. The authors argue that fighting age bias is part of suicide prevention for older adults.
pmc-11688847:
Nuo Sun screened this 2024 hunt for drugs that switch on the cell's cleanup of worn-out mitochondria. That cleanup, mitophagy, fades with age and may feed heart decline. Using a glow reporter that changes color with acidity, Sun's team imaged cells exposed to over ten thousand compounds at fifteen doses each. A custom algorithm sorted the flood of images.

Several selective inducers emerged, with one, Mito-I, strongest. It switched on cleanup in human heart cells grown from stem cells and in mouse hearts. The effect ran through a receptor protein the drug raises; without it, the cleanup failed. Treated worms lived longer. Old mice given the drug kept better heart function. The work links a single cleanup switch to both lifespan and heart health in aging.
pmc-11689047:
Sadaf Milani and co-authors explore paths from highway exposure to cognitive health in older Mexican Americans in work from 2024. Living near many major roads has been linked to worse thinking, but the routes of that effect were unclear.

Using survey data on 1,723 adults aged seventy-five and over, the team tested mental and physical mediators. More roads in a tract linked to lower mental test scores. Limits in daily living activities carried about forty percent of that link. Depression, neighborhood satisfaction, and physical performance did not mediate. The authors call for work on the steps involved.
pmc-11689147:
Dowden, Morhardt, and Lucca explore how men experience caring for a spouse with primary progressive aphasia, in a 2024 qualitative study. The syndrome begins with language loss and later brings behavior and personality change. Most dementia caregivers are women, so the male path is poorly charted, and no prior study had asked about gender in this specific condition. The team analyzed deep interviews with 17 male caregiving spouses who attend a monthly support group.

Questions covered coping strategies, how the men approach the role, whether they seek help, and which services they use. The analysis traces their needs across the illness course. The authors aim for a finer picture of a gendered role inside one clinical profile, rather than dementia care in general. Services can use the findings to reach men earlier.
pmc-11689347:
Brystana Kaufman and co-authors present a conference abstract mapping palliative care for American veterans with life-limiting illness. Using national health-system and Medicare records from 2014 to 2017, they found 120,249 veterans who received specialist palliative care. Two thirds received it only as hospital inpatients; one third had at least one outpatient visit.

A third of veterans first met palliative care within two years of qualifying by illness. Outpatients were more likely to have cancer and less likely to be highly frail, while rurality and housing instability looked similar across settings. Hospice stays ran similar lengths in both groups, but were shortest for those with a single encounter. The authors say the contrast between settings raises questions about how timing and place shape outcomes.
pmc-11689947:
Alexandra Lee and Sei Lee study bladder leakage in adults with diabetes in this 2024 paper. A drug class now advised as first-line care for many such adults protects heart and kidneys, but it also raises infection risk in the urinary tract. Leakage is common in older adults and raises that same risk, yet its rate in this group was little known.

Data came from a national health survey from 2013 to 2020, with 2,366 adults with type 2 diabetes. The share advised to take the drug rose with age. Among those aged 70 and over who were advised it, 41 percent reported frequent leakage. The authors urge care when starting the drug in patients with leakage.
pmc-11690047:
Vera Gallistl takes a social view of a clear question in long-term care, in twenty twenty-four. When AI tools are used in care, can people grasp how they reach a choice? Most work treats that as a tech fix. Gallistl argues it is also a social issue, shaped by who asks and why. She bases the work on two tools, fall sensing and social robots.

She draws on thirty talks and fifty hours of watching care in action. Coders, care staff, and older adults meant quite different things by a clear AI choice. Their needs went well past the code itself. The paper shows why care settings must define clarity for all three groups.
pmc-11690247:
Sheryl Zimmerman and Sam Fazio review lessons from a summer training institute for early dementia researchers in this 2024 paper. Across its first three years, the Alzheimer's Association program drew strong reviews: nearly all respondents were satisfied, and most said it deepened their grasp of the disease and sharpened research skills.

Feedback still reshaped the program. Sessions split by track, public health versus psychosocial, turned out to matter to both audiences, so content was rebalanced. Recruitment and flow were refined too. The authors share planned improvements and advice for other groups building similar institutes, plus guidance for mentors of individual trainees. The piece treats training design as something to study and improve like any intervention.
pmc-11690347:
Stipica Mudrazija and co-authors present a 2024 conference abstract tallying what dementia costs African American and Latino families in the United States. The count covers lost wages for patients and caregivers, extra medical spending, the value of unpaid care, and wider losses such as tax revenue.

In 2020 the bill reached about 94 billion dollars, two thirds of it unpaid family care. By 2060 the authors project 1.4 trillion dollars, with forgone wages swelling as caregivers grow younger and better educated on average. They urge policies that keep working-age caregivers attached to their jobs.
pmc-11690647:
Megan Huisingh-Scheetz and co-authors presented this talk paper in 2024 on exercise for frail older adults. Movement is called the ideal frailty cure, and trials back it as the best fix known. Yet frail adults face steep blocks: weak bodies, few resources, low confidence, and payers who will not fund long programs. The team review those blocks from past trials and a local survey.

Their survey of 101 older adults, mostly African-American, spans the non-frail to the frail. They then set out a fresh trial, EngAGE, which beams exercise into the home through a voice-run device. It will face off against paper-based routines in 124 frail, homebound adults. The authors close with the gaps that must close: payment, access, and programs built for the frailest.
pmc-11690847:
BoRin Kim and co-authors track the digital gap among older adults across the plague years in a 2024 study. Survey waves from 2018 to 2022 covered more than seventeen hundred people over seventy. Five tech habits were checked: mail, search, food shopping, banking, and social feeds.

Four groups stood out, from near-non-users to heavy mixed users. The near-non-users were the largest band, and more than nine in ten in both that band and the heavy band stayed put across the years. Money and schooling split the groups before the plague. After it, social support was the key that helped elders widen their tech use.
pmc-11691047:
Esha Chakravarty studies ovarian cancer outcomes in older women treated in east India. Her 2024 paper reviews five hundred elderly patients at a gerontology institute in Kolkata. Ovarian cancer is called a silent killer because it is usually found late, and its incidence climbs with age.

Most patients were diagnosed in their sixties, with a mean age of sixty-nine. One-year relative survival fell steeply with age: fifty-seven percent for the youngest group, down to twenty-one percent past eighty. Four factors drove the worse outcomes: aggressive tumors, drug resistance, body and mind decline, and other illnesses. Chakravarty suggests decision aids to sort who benefits from major surgery and chemotherapy.
pmc-11691247:
Amy Rauer and four co-authors published a study in 2024 on older adults' leisure activities, done alone or with others, and their associations with well-being over time. The benefits of leisure are well documented, and social networks create opportunities for it. Whether leisure with particular companions, or alone, is more advantageous was unclear.

The researchers followed 136 adults in the United States, aged fifty to ninety-one, across three time points from the summer of 2021 to the winter of 2022. Leisure was most often spent with a romantic partner, followed by time alone, with friends and family least common. More leisure overall was associated with better well-being, including fewer depressive symptoms and a stronger sense of purpose. The gains came chiefly from leisure with others. Leisure done alone was associated with a weaker sense of self-worth. Time with partners and family fell when COVID-19 cases peaked.
pmc-11691347:
Saanvi Lamba, Pranjal Tyagi, Diana Ruiz, and Stuti Dang published a study in 2024 on the technology-related COVID-19 experiences of older veterans in the United States. A survey was sent to twenty thousand veterans living at home, from five Veterans Affairs medical sites. It asked about their experiences during the pandemic.

One open-ended question invited veterans to share anything about their COVID-19 experience. Close to two thousand men and eighty-eight women responded, but twenty-three responses concerned technology. The most common themes were trouble accessing technology, difficulty using the tools, and using technology to communicate during isolation. Some veterans used technology for health appointments, while others were unable to see providers in person or preferred to do so. On the positive side, technology helped many stay connected with family, friends, and church from home. The authors urge support with devices and training for older adults.
pmc-11691947:
Moyosoreoluwa Jacobs, Peter Lichtenberg, and Wassim Tarraf study self-reported memory decline across racial and ethnic groups, in this 2024 paper. Subjective cognitive decline, feeling one's memory slip, can precede Alzheimer's disease. It also comes in different patterns, and rates differ by group. The team used two waves of a national risk survey.

They studied 44,152 adults over fifty who reported decline: white, Black, and Hispanic respondents. A latent class analysis found three patterns, from uncomplicated decline to decline mixed with daily-life limits. Hispanic and Black respondents were far more likely to fall in the mixed-limits group, 38 and 41 percent against 22 percent for white respondents. Social and health factors explained only a small share of the gap. Since two thirds of the high-risk group had raised memory concerns with a clinician, the authors see a ready point for early help.
pmc-11692347:
Quynh Vo and co-authors compare the money strain of family caregiving across generations, in work from 2024. Unpaid care for older relatives drains savings and adds debt for many families. Whether younger caregivers suffer more than older ones had not been mapped nationally.

Data came from the 2020 Caregiving in the United States survey. Adult caregivers of older adults reported hits to savings, debt, and bill paying. Millennials showed far higher odds of each hit than baby boomers. Generation X caregivers also reported stronger savings hits than boomers. Models adjusted for background and care load. The results argue for aid aimed at younger caregivers.
pmc-11692847:
Julie Robison and four co-authors study care goals in a home care program in a 2024 paper. The Medicaid program helps older adults live at home despite disability. Care plans should match what each person wants, but little was known about whether goals are met across groups. They interviewed diverse adults, with and without dementia, months after enrollment.

Most people said they had as much say as they wanted in setting goals. Three quarters felt they had met their goal, and nearly half did better than expected. Meeting goals was just as likely for people with dementia and across racial and ethnic groups. Other experiences did differ by group, the authors note.
pmc-11692947:
Gavin Green and six co-authors test an online therapy program for dementia caregivers in 2024. The program teaches skills from acceptance and commitment therapy in a self-guided format. Caregivers of people with dementia face heavy stress, and a flexible online offer could reach many of them.

Eighty-three caregivers finished the post-program survey. Its ease-of-use score averaged eighty-six of one hundred, a high mark. Most said the content helped, that they would use it again, and that they would recommend it. Interviews with twenty-eight caregivers backed the scores. They praised the work-at-your-own-pace design and the hands-on exercises, and many kept using the skills later.
pmc-11693047:
Katyayani Strohl and a team of co-authors interviewed health workers about end-of-life care for people with dementia who prefer a language other than English, in two thousand twenty-four. Such patients face a high risk of poor palliative care. The team spoke with social workers and medical interpreters who serve Chinese, Spanish, or Vietnamese speakers.

Four themes emerged from the talks. Interpreting grew hard when patients seemed not to make sense, and family dynamics complicated decisions. Talks about the course of dementia and quality of life often came too late. Culturally fitting resources in the patient's language were lacking. The authors name training, pre-meetings, and better staffing as targets for change.
pmc-11693347:
Nursing homes cannot keep staff, and Ahmad and co-authors argue the reasons sit in workers' whole life stories, not just their shifts. A life course lens ties career stage, family roles, and past disadvantage to the choice to stay or go.

Survey data from 678 staff in 23 nursing homes fed a model of intention to stay. Career stage, being a household's main earner, and benefits status all mattered. So did accumulated disadvantage, emotional burnout, and holding other care roles outside work. The authors urge managers to move past one-size retention plans. Mental health access, leave for caregiving, decent insurance, and small grants or tuition help could steady a workforce that is itself often vulnerable.
pmc-11694047:
Naruse and colleagues check muscle loss and body strength in younger adults with type two diabetes in this twenty twenty-four study. Muscle loss is well logged in older adults with the disease, but facts for young and mid-age adults are thin. The team drew patients from hospital stays for blood sugar care.

Inside, about one in five men and fewer than one in ten women in the group showed muscle loss. Men with the disease had less muscle than men with no disease, while women showed no such gap. Both sexes with the disease walked more slowly and stood on one leg far less long. Body weight index tied most strongly to muscle loss in the checks.
pmc-11694647:
Fish skulls evolve fast in the great African lakes, where cichlid species have multiplied into hundreds of forms with distinct feeding styles. Andrew Conith, Sarah Pascarella, Sylvie Hope, and Craig Albertson study one skull bone, the parasphenoid, in this 2024 paper. The bone braces the braincase and soaks up the forces of biting, so its shape may track where a fish lives and feeds.

In one group that has moved between deep and shallow water many times, the bone's depth and length differed by habitat. To find the genes behind the shape, the team crossed two species with unlike bones and mapped the offspring. Two genome regions explained much of the variation. The same regions also shape the jaws and braincase, hinting that adaptive change reuses a small set of genetic levers.
pmc-11695047:
Anbazhagan, Krishnan, Divya, and Sureshkumar study gut bacteria that resist carbapenem drugs in a South Indian hospital, in a study from twenty twenty-four. How strong this resistance is shifts with place and with how drugs are used nearby. The team gathers over two thousand samples across two years. For each one they note growth, species, resistance, and the genes behind it.

About a third of the samples grow bacteria, and two hundred fifty are Enterobacteriaceae. Twenty-two isolates, about nine percent, resist carbapenems outright. Escherichia coli and Klebsiella species make up most of the resistant set. The NDM gene shows up in nearly two-thirds of the resistant isolates. Labs must track how the drugs fail, so they can curb spread in the hospital and guide sound drug use.
pmc-11696647:
Dong Ho Kang and co-authors test whether antibodies against an immune sensor can ease nerve pain in rats, in a 2024 paper. The sensor, called Mincle, sits on immune cells and has been tied to nerve pain and spinal cord inflammation. A related sensor family may interact with it. The team delivered antibodies into the spinal fluid of rats whose leg nerve had been tied, a standard model of nerve injury pain.

Three different antibodies were tried, plus a drug that blocks the related sensor. Pain was gauged by how the rats reacted to light touch on the paw. Every treatment eased the pain response, and stronger doses worked better. A combined dose analysis probed how the two kinds of blocker interact. Lab mapping also found which part of the sensor the antibodies grip, guiding future drug design.
pmc-11697047:
Blood medicine has long lacked doctors who mirror the patients it serves, and a society program set out to change that pipeline. Margo R Rollins and co-authors evaluate the program in a 2024 paper. The American Society of Hematology's recruitment effort ran from 2004 to 2022 with over four hundred awardees. Dropout rates and career paths were compared with national figures.

Graduate awardees finished at rates far above the national minority average. Medical student awardees also dropped out less than peers nationwide. Many stayed in blood medicine, well above expected shares. Early career awardees overwhelmingly remained in the field. The authors call the program a success while urging more work on equity.
pmc-11697147:
Teketel Ermias Geltore and co-authors review what is known about family planning uptake after childbirth in Ethiopia in a 2024 paper. Deaths and illness around the postpartum period remain high, and family planning is an underused lever for spacing births safely. Earlier reviews covered pieces of the topic, but no synthesis of syntheses existed.

Using an umbrella review method, the team gathered systematic reviews from four databases under standard reporting guidelines and graded their quality. The outcome of interest was how many postpartum women use family planning and what drives that choice. The paper sets out to give programs and policymakers a single consolidated picture rather than scattered estimates. Findings sections detail the pooled magnitude and the associated factors across the included reviews.
pmc-11697547:
Mitra Ashayeripanah and Jose Villadangos offer a lab protocol from 2024. It tests how spleen cells prime T cells outside the body. The cells at the center pick up bits of germs. They then show those bits to young T cells so the T cells learn to respond.

Step by step, the protocol tells how to inject mice with tagged germ material. Next it shows how to pull out the cells that took it up. Those cells are then mixed with T cells in the lab. Notes explain how the setup fits many mouse models. A reader gets a clear recipe for testing how well these cells start a response.
pmc-11698047:
Emily D McParland and co-authors wrote a 2024 study on how fruit fly cells hold their shape while tissues grow and move. Cells link their inner skeleton to the seams between cells, and a protein called Canoe helps keep that link strong. Canoe has two side-by-side parts that bind Ras-family switch proteins, and both parts were known to matter.

Using fly mutants, the team found the two parts do unlike jobs. Both bind the switch protein Rap1 with like strength in test tubes. Yet losing the first part nearly wiped out Canoe's work in the animal, while losing the second part left flies alive and fertile. Flies without the second part showed weak seams in embryos and in the growing eye. The split in roles reshapes views of seam control.
pmc-11698547:
Senapati, Kattamuri, and Deoker describe a carotid body tumor found by chance in a 75-year-old woman. These rare tumors grow near the split of the carotid artery and often cause no symptoms. Scans, not biopsy, are used for diagnosis, since biopsy can cause bleeding.

She came to the emergency room with nausea, vomiting, and a severe headache. Her blood pressure was very high and her heart rhythm was irregular. Neck imaging showed a stable mass of 38 by 53 by 15 millimeters. Given her age and other illness, radiation was planned instead of surgery.
pmc-11699047:
Jatziri Mota-Gutierrez and co-authors published a 2024 study on how much Belgian consumers care about sustainable beekeeping. Honey buyers increasingly meet claims about culture, environment, and ethics on the label. The team surveyed 1,100 Belgian respondents about their honey habits and their interest in the wider benefits of sustainable hive management.

Age and purchasing habits significantly shaped interest levels. The analysis sorted which consumer traits predict concern for each class of benefit, from pollinator ecology to global fairness. Such segmentation matters for producers deciding what to certify and advertise. If younger buyers reward ethical claims while older buyers prize origin, labels and campaigns should differ. The study also probes the gap between caring and paying, a standing question in food research. Its data help beekeepers and marketers aim honest claims at the audiences most ready to value them.
pmc-11708947:
Alireza Khabbazi and co-authors review the odd two-way pull of smoking on vessel swelling in a 2024 paper. The ills in view are a clan of rare states where the walls of blood vessels swell and starve the organs they feed.

Smoke bears a load of poisons that can stir or blunt the body's guard cells. The review weighs proof on risk, on how each ill shows, on how care works, and on how quitting shifts the course. For two ills the proof on risk stays in doubt. For one named ill, smokers in fact run a lower risk, a firm and strange result. Smoke also bends how that ill and its kin show and end. The authors set out the clash in full.
pmc-11709347:
Thamires Magalhães and co-authors tracked how sex hormones relate to brain volume change in aging adults, in work published in 2025. Ninety one people across middle and older age had brain scans and saliva hormone tests about a year apart. The team focused on a memory hub and the cerebellum.

Higher starting testosterone and progesterone each predicted larger volumes a year later in parts of those regions. In women, the progesterone link with the memory hub held firm, above all in the middle aged group. The authors read the pattern as a protective effect of both hormones against age related shrinkage. Work continues on hormone stage detail.
pmc-11709647:
Jillian Joyce and co-authors add memory checks to routine women's health visits in a 2025 report. Alzheimer's changes start earlier in women, yet women are diagnosed later. The EMPOWER program folds cognitive screening into the yearly gynecology visit to close that gap.

Women fifty and older at a Columbia center took two screens. One asked about everyday memory slips; any slip flagged a positive. The other was a digital task with word recall and clock drawing, scored from impaired to normal. Early results from 130 women begin to show how self-report lines up with the task score. The mapping matters: a cheap survey only helps if it tracks real performance.
pmc-11709847:
Chengju Tian and co-authors study how a memory pathway weakens in a tau disease model in a 2025 paper. Two linked brain areas handle non spatial memory and falter early in Alzheimer's disease. Input from the first area reaches two subtypes of cells in the second. Whether tau harms both subtypes alike was not known.

Light pulses fired the incoming fibers in slices from model mice. One cell subtype showed much weaker incoming signals than in healthy mice. The other subtype kept its incoming strength at normal levels. Inhibitory signals are covered in the fuller results beyond the early findings.
pmc-11709947:
Sedigheh Zabihi and co-authors present a 2025 conference review of symptoms that appear before an Alzheimer's diagnosis. Non-thinking symptoms can surface years early, and spotting them could speed detection. The team searched three databases for long-term studies that linked such symptoms to later diagnosis, then pooled the results.

Thirty studies qualified, most on mood and behavior symptoms. Depression was tied to a later diagnosis across fourteen studies, with odds near double. Evidence for anxiety, sleep trouble, and personality change was mixed. Body signs told a clearer story: low blood pressure, weight loss, bladder trouble, and fainting all appeared up to ten years ahead.
pmc-11710047:
Pedro JDMR Pinho and five colleagues use a national Brazilian aging study, published in 2025, to test how memory complaints match real memory loss. Many older people say their memory is poor. Such complaints may warn of later dementia, but they do not always match test results. The link is poorly studied in mixed populations like Brazil's.

The team used data from over nine thousand Brazilians older than fifty. People rated their own memory, and all took a word list test. Among those with complaints and full data, about a quarter had true memory loss on testing. More schooling, more trouble with daily tasks, and more signs of depression went with true loss. Higher household income went with less loss. The authors note that most people with complaints test normal, so complaints alone should not drive care.
pmc-11710247:
Hiranya Pintana and co-authors tested a heart drug in rats with drug-linked memory harm, in a study published in 2025. The cancer drug doxorubicin can cause a foggy state often called chemobrain. The team asked whether ivabradine, a drug used for chest pain and fast heart rates, could protect the brain.

Twenty male rats were split into four groups, with some given the cancer drug and some also given the test drug for a month. The cancer drug hurt memory, brain signaling, and the energy parts of brain cells. The test drug eased oxygen stress in those cell parts but did not fix the memory loss. That split result helps show which brain harms may need a different kind of help.
pmc-11710347:
Monika McAtarsney-Kovacs, Shahina Pardhan, Raju Sapkota, and Ian van der Linde test a memory skill, published in 2025, that may flag early decline. The skill is binding: holding together the traits of an item, such as its shape, color, and place, for a few seconds. Earlier work hints that binding fails early in mild cognitive impairment. If so, quick binding tests might catch decline sooner.

Three groups took computer tests: young adults, healthy older adults, and older adults with mild impairment. Tasks paired items with places, names with places, and colors with places or words. Healthy older adults scored below the young on some tasks. The impaired group scored below healthy older adults on three more. Binding scores also matched standard thinking tests well. The authors argue that the weakest tasks may serve as early markers of decline.
pmc-11710447:
A large team describes NIAGADS, a national data store for gene studies of Alzheimer disease, in this 2025 paper. The store holds gene and sequencing data and gives qualified researchers a way to reach it for work on Alzheimer disease and related brain disorders.

The site works with big research groups and centers that run gene studies, and it is backed by the National Institute on Aging. Data from funded gene studies of the disease are meant to be placed there or in a like approved site. The paper sets out how the store is run and why shared data matters: pooled sets are far larger than any one lab could build alone.
pmc-11710647:
Sarah Marzi studies how gene risk for Alzheimer disease shows up in the brain's immune cells, in work published in 2025. Those cells, called microglia, help defend the brain. Genetic risk for the disease clusters in the switch regions that control microglia genes. Marzi asked how risk burden changes those switches, using both a mouse model and human brain tissue.

Human microglia grown from stem cells were placed into mice bred for the disease. The cells carried different forms of APOE, the strongest common risk gene. As risk rose from the safer form to the riskiest, the cells turned up inflammation signals. Helpful cell states linked to defense were turned down. In donated human brains, microglia showed wide changes in the same switch regions. Some changes could be tied straight to gene variants. The work links inherited risk to the cell changes seen in disease.
pmc-11712047:
Mariana Albuquerque de Luna and co-authors describe dementia care at a specialist clinic in Recife, Brazil, in 2025. Dementia is rising fast, above all in poorer countries, yet reports from Brazil's northeast are scarce. Recife is a large city in a region marked by deep inequality and low literacy.

The team reviewed records of patients seen from 2018 to 2023, keeping 137 of 168 charts. Patients averaged sixty-six years old, and over a fifth could not read. Alzheimer's disease was the top diagnosis at a quarter of cases. Family care fell mostly to adult children, the record shows, for both women and men in the clinic.
pmc-11712147:
Kimberly S VanHaitsma and co-authors study pain and activity choice in nursing homes in a 2025 report. Knowing what residents like is the base of person-centred care, yet how matched activities affect health was unclear. The team used a tracker that counts how many attended activities match each resident's stated likes.

The study followed 586 residents with varied thinking ability, using survey and care record data over one year. Pain eased over time on average. Residents with sharper thinking and those new to the home reported more pain. After other factors were weighed, joining activities went with less pain. The link was strongest for activities the resident had marked as liked. The authors suggest chosen fun can distract from pain.
pmc-11712247:
Arshia Khan and co-authors build a soft robot pal that breathes with its user to calm and sharpen the mind. Paced breaths can ease stress and feed the brain air, a path to clear thought. Their 2025 build hides two push rods in a plush form, run by a small board through a motor card. The rods swell and shrink in turns, four ticks to a stage.

Push caps in the shell spread the move like a chest rise. A user who hugs or holds the pal can sync breaths to its pace. The pitch is a calm tool with no screen and no drill tone. Mind scores would be the next test of the claim. Soft form may draw in kids and old folks who shun hard gear.
pmc-11712347:
Melissa Knox, Megan Witbracht, Joshua Grill, and Jennifer Lingler report early work from the PARADE study in this 2025 paper. The study concerns how Alzheimer's disease and related dementias are now diagnosed. Biomarker tests can confirm the biology behind memory loss, but families from groups long left out of research may face the news with distinct needs.

The authors aim to learn how such families live through biomarker-based diagnosis. They want care that answers cultural needs and respects each family's context. Online focus groups, led by a trained facilitator over a secure video platform, form the core method. Participants are a chosen subsample of families already enrolled in PARADE. The talks trace the full path, from first concern to hearing the result. Lessons from these voices should shape fairer support after diagnosis.
pmc-11712447:
Julie Chandler and co-authors report a 2025 study on health care use before Alzheimer testing. The study looked at older adults with no signs of memory loss. One group had raised amyloid in the brain, a marker tied to the disease. A second group did not. Records covered the five years before their brain scans.

The two groups had much the same common health problems. Both had less high blood pressure and diabetes than matched peers. The raised-amyloid group used more hospital, emergency, and doctor care than the second group. They also showed more mood, adjustment, and sleep diagnoses than matched peers. The work may help spot early signs of the disease stage.
pmc-11712547:
Diego Bustamante-Paytan and co-authors review in this 2025 paper how well a common thinking test fits Spanish-speaking Latin America and the Caribbean. Dementia in the region may triple by 2050, and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment is widely used to screen for it. Yet one fixed version may not suit the region's varied cultures and schooling. The team searched seven databases plus grey sources for local validation studies.

Twelve studies passed their rules. Only two reported real changes to the test, and just one explained the cultural reasons in depth. Reports on translation steps were thin in most. Schooling skewed scores wherever low-education groups were tested. The authors urge standard adaptation steps and cut scores tuned by education.
pmc-11712647:
Mengjin Dong and co-authors present a deep learning method that measures brain shrinkage linked to Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 paper. Tracking shrinkage of the hippocampus over time is a known marker of the disease. Standard tools compare scans directly and can mistake head motion or image flaws for real tissue loss.

Their method, Regional Deep Atrophy, learns from pairs of scans taken at different times. It learns to tell which scan came later and whether the gap in time matches the change seen. The network also marks the regions that drive its judgment, then measures volume change only there. Trained and tested on hundreds of participants, it matched prior tools. The design aims for cleaner measures in early disease.
pmc-11712747:
Min Seok Baek and co-authors study walking problems in Alzheimer's disease in this 2025 paper. Gait changes may track how the disease advances in the brain. The team enrolled patients with full dementia from the disease and patients at an earlier stage. A third group had no impairment of thinking. In all, more than one hundred people took part over about a year and a half. Each had brain scans, amyloid imaging, and tests of thinking and mood.

Walking was measured on a short mat fitted with pressure sensors. The team linked gait measures to skill scores and to amyloid load in brain regions. Thickness of the brain's outer layer in each region was also measured. A gene test for a known risk variant was included. The aim is a map of how walking, thinking, and brain change connect. Such a map could support earlier, fuller checks of patients.
pmc-11712847:
Kelly Johnston and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on what people with early Alzheimer's disease hope a new drug would do for them. The team spoke with people who had just finished a phase 1 trial of an antibody drug, along with the partners who joined the trial at their side.

Twenty-eight pairs took part in long talks after the trial ended. Almost all named memory and thinking trouble as their worst burden, and many spoke of getting lost or low mood. Nearly nine in ten said the best a drug could do was keep the disease from getting worse. Holding on to daily skills, and still knowing loved ones, ranked high too. Drug makers can use such hopes to shape what trials measure.
pmc-11712947:
Dianxu Ren, Lisa Tamres, and Jennifer Lingler study how faith in one's own coping power links to low mood and worry in pairs of patients and care partners. Their 2025 study deals with mild cognitive impairment, an early slide in memory and thought. Most past work looked at the patient alone, not the pair.
