The team used the first-round data of a funded study, with 82 pairs in all. Each side filled in scales for coping faith, low mood, and state anxiety. A paired model then split two kinds of pull: how one's own faith tracks with one's own mood, and how a partner's faith tracks across the pair. Age, sex, and schooling were held steady in the math.
pmc-11713047:
Chadsley Wessinger and co-authors link diet quality to thinking skills in middle-aged women at risk of Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 study. All the women had a family history of the disease and led inactive lives. A gene variant that raises risk sharply was tested as well. The question was whether better diet goes with better executive function, and whether the gene changes that link.

Just over one hundred women gave diet records, saliva for gene tests, and thinking test scores. Better diet scores predicted better working memory across the group. The benefit, though, showed clearly only in women without the risk variant. For carriers, diet quality showed no clear tie to test scores. The authors note the work is a baseline look from an ongoing trial, not a final word.
pmc-11713147:
Rashidi-Ranjbar and co-authors report early findings from a small trial of light therapy for mild memory impairment, in this 2025 paper. The treatment shines near-infrared light through the skull to boost cell energy. It targets the cell's power units, whose failure has been linked to amyloid build-up.

Fifteen patients were split between real and sham devices that looked the same. Each person used the device at home daily for six weeks. Before and after, the team ran thinking tests, brain scans, and blood work. The paper shares first results on whether the treatment is safe, workable at home, and worth testing in a larger trial.
pmc-11713247:
Dinghao An and Yun Xu test whether a blood sugar marker also flags risk of Alzheimer's disease, in work from 2025. The disease is known to travel with faulty sugar handling, but the drivers were murky. Gene studies let the pair test cause and effect rather than mere correlation.

They screened a vast pool of data sets for sugar markers tied to the disease, then ran two-way genetic tests. One marker, used to track blood sugar, stood as a genetically driven risk factor. No other sugar measure or sugar disease explained the link as a middle step. Brain gene data pointed to hub genes, and pathway checks tied them to drug targets for the disease.
pmc-11713347:
Erin Abner and three co-authors probe the odd inverse link between cancer and Alzheimer's disease in donated brains, in a 2025 conference paper. Some cancers go with a lower chance of a dementia call in life. Whether a cancer past also means less brain damage at death was not known.

The team matched 785 autopsied volunteers from a Kentucky aging center to the state cancer registry. About a quarter had a cancer call. Those with cancer had lower odds of mild loss or dementia and higher test scores near death. Brain checks weighed plaques, tangles, and vessel harm, with math care for bias and missing data. The authors repeat the tests on those who began the study thinking clearly, to guard the result.
pmc-11713447:
Diny Thomson and co-authors study a gene variant that may speed Alzheimer's decline, in this 2025 paper. The variant affects a protein that feeds and supports brain cells. People with high amyloid who carry the variant seem to lose ground faster than those without it.

The team compared twenty-six carriers with sixty-eight non-carriers from a national imaging study. All had amyloid and tau scans plus memory tests. The authors check tau levels stage by stage across the brain, along with memory scores. If carriers build tangles faster in key areas, the variant could help doctors predict each patient's course and pick who joins trials.
pmc-11713547:
Turner and co-authors test an online picture tool that helps people with thinking problems talk about care choices, in this 2025 paper. Memory and language trouble can make it hard to state what kind of help one wants. The team built the tool to ease those talks.

Interviews ran over video calls with people who had mild impairment or mild to moderate dementia. A shared screen canvas let the interviewer drag icons for people, places, safety, and feelings into view. Three stories guided each talk, one past choice and two made-up ones with growing care needs. The design team kept the tool simple to hold down mental effort.
pmc-11713647:
Zhe Sun and co-authors chart how a small brain fluid factory ages, in work from 2025. The choroid plexus makes spinal fluid and clears waste from the brain. Its size shifts in aging diseases, but its inner tissue and blood flow changes were less clear.

Scans covered 641 healthy adults aged 36 to 90 years from an aging data set. Diffusion scans gauged tissue texture, and flow scans gauged blood supply and arrival time. Values were read inside the plexus and compared with gray and white matter. Age links were tested across the full span. The maps give a baseline for spotting disease change against normal aging.
pmc-11713747:
Kellen Petersen and co-authors run the leading Alzheimer's blood tests head to head against brain scans, in a 2025 study. Blood tests could replace costly scans and spinal taps for spotting amyloid, the protein clump that marks the disease. Six makers' assays were run on stored plasma from study volunteers who also had amyloid PET scans.

Each test's measures, and mixes within each platform, were scored on how well they sorted scan-positive from scan-negative people. The comparison covers the amyloid proteins and several forms of phosphorylated tau, plus damage markers on some platforms. A shared, independent benchmark like this helps clinics and regulators judge which blood test deserves trust as screening moves into practice.
pmc-11713847:
Blood-brain barrier leak after COVID-19 is measured by Zhe Sun and co-authors in work dated 2025. Mind fog after the illness may ride on a leaky barrier. Sixty-seven people split by past infection and by mind test state took a water-exchange brain scan. Blood marks tied to Alzheimer risk were drawn the same day. Leak scores were set side by side across the groups.

Past-infection groups leaked more than the clean group. Mind-impaired people leaked more than the sharp, in turn. Leak scores tied to some blood marks as well. Barrier harm may link the virus to mind loss.
pmc-11714047:
Ying Luan and five co-authors test whether links to tau hot spots predict where the brain loses synapses in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. Synapses are the tiny joins where nerve cells pass signals, and their loss tracks thinking decline. Tau is thought to poison these joins, and harm may spread along wired paths.

The team scanned 45 people with mild loss or dementia who had amyloid in the brain, plus 23 healthy adults without it. One scan gauged synapse density and one gauged tau. They found the areas with the most tau and mapped how strongly each other area links to them. Areas wired tightly to the hot spots showed more synapse loss. A control check with a random map did not show the pattern.
pmc-11714247:
Mara ten Kate and fourteen co-authors test whether busy brain hubs gather amyloid faster in healthy older adults. Their 2025 study draws on a Dutch cohort of cognitively healthy monozygotic twins. Amyloid buildup is one of the first steps toward Alzheimer's disease, starting decades before symptoms, and active hub regions have been suspected as early targets.

Resting brain scans gave each of 100 regions a hub score based on its count of connections. PET scans measured amyloid at the start and again about 4.4 years later. The team checked whether hub scores forecast a shift to amyloid-positive status, and whether hubness tracks amyloid change region by region. Family ties between twins were handled in the statistics. The design speaks to whether brain wiring helps explain where the disease begins.
pmc-11714447:
Anjan Bhattarai and six co-authors measure tau in the brain from scans alone, with no blood draws, in a 2025 conference paper. Tau scans track a core protein of Alzheimer's disease. The usual math needs blood samples over time, which adds pain and cost.

The team used a new whole body scanner that can read the blood signal straight from the images. Fifteen adults, most thinking clearly and all free of tau build up, had ninety minute scans. The team pulled the blood curve from a large chest vessel in each scan. They then fit the brain curves with a standard model for three areas at risk in the disease. The work tests whether scan length changes the answers.
pmc-11714647:
Ramiro Eduardo Rea Reyes and co-authors test cold storage of blood in a 2025 study on Alzheimer marks. Blood marks could bring the ill hunt to rural and poor groups, with blood drawn far from labs. But a long, warm trip can rot the marks before they are read.

Dry ice is not always at hand in the field, so the team asked how plain cold packs treat the marks. The study tracks mark drift when blood is chilled in the common way. Such lore sets fair rules for field draws. Brain teams gain bounds for hunts that must start far from a freezer.
pmc-11714847:
Apoorva Safai and eight co-authors link neighborhood disadvantage to altered brain cortex patterns, in a 2025 study. Poor neighborhoods track with worse health and thinking scores. The team used a network method that maps how alike brain regions look in shape. Data came from Wisconsin Alzheimer's research groups and held 526 adults with sound thinking.

People in the most deprived areas scored lower on word flow, symbol, memory, and combined tests. Shape networks in front and side brain regions differed by group. Two hub measures in those regions partly carried the link between deprivation and test scores. The authors say such patterns may help explain later-life decline risk in poor areas.
pmc-11714947:
Brain scans can predict Alzheimer's dementia early, but the best models sit in labs instead of clinics. Yong Fan built a web tool to close that gap, described in a 2025 paper. A browser viewer shows the scans, while cloud computers do the heavy work behind it. The system splits the brain into parts, rebuilds the cortex surface, and runs a learned prediction model. Results flow back to the browser for display.

The tool accepts the two standard scan file formats used in hospitals and research. Its parts run state-of-the-art deep learning methods in real time. Fan frames the tool as a bridge from research to daily care. Fast, shared access could let more clinics test scan-based prediction. The paper describes the build rather than a clinical trial.
pmc-11715047:
Masashi Kameyama and co-authors examine why early phase images from amyloid PET brain scans lose contrast, and how to win it back. Published in 2025, this entry presents the same study in a second journal record. The first minutes of an amyloid scan can stand in for a blood flow image, flagging both amyloid buildup and nerve cell loss.

Strictly, the early image shows tracer delivery, not blood flow itself, so its contrast is weaker than a true flow image. The authors derive a contrast recovery method and a principled way to set its parameter from the literature. A check against glucose scans showed strong agreement, with mild underestimation in high flow zones. The aim is sharper diagnosis from scans already being taken.
pmc-11715347:
Chanda Simfukwe, Young Chul Youn, and Seong Soo An wrote this 2025 paper on brain wave tests for Alzheimer's disease. EEG is a safe test that records the brain's electric signals from the scalp. Measured with care, those signals may serve as a marker that helps spot the disease and its stage.

The team studied resting EEG from 534 adults in South Korea, 265 with the disease and 269 healthy peers. Each person was tested with eyes open and with eyes closed, using 19 scalp sensors. The group with the disease showed a strong rise in slow delta waves, most of all at the front, side, and top of the head. The authors also checked how well brain areas stayed in sync, to round out the picture.
pmc-11715747:
Lindsey Kuchenbecker and co-authors hunt in a 2025 study for blood protein marks of Alzheimer's disease in African Americans. Blood tests are easier to reach than brain scans, but most candidate marks were found in narrow groups. This group faces higher risk yet sits in few studies, a gap this work fills.

A broad scan measured thousands of proteins in blood from 142 patients and 144 healthy peers. Models held age, sex, and batch in the count while hunting for split proteins. A risk gene was added in a second pass to check the finds hold. Top split proteins were then tested for how well they sort patients from peers. The set forms a fresh candidate list tuned to this group.
pmc-11715847:
Kirk Erickson presented work in 2025 on aerobic exercise, brain health, and Alzheimer's disease markers in blood. More activity links to lower dementia risk, and exercise improves several brain measures in later life. Yet the pathways behind those gains, and the factors that shape them, remain poorly understood.

The presentation covers recent studies and levels of possible mechanism, including effects on the hippocampus, brain networks, and metabolism. It also describes early results from a large trial of supervised moderate exercise. Six hundred forty-eight adults aged sixty-five to eighty, all cognitively normal, exercised three times a week for twelve months. Blood markers, thinking tests, and brain scans tracked change.
pmc-11715947:
Carles Falcon and a team of co-authors used a multi-delay scan method to catch early blood flow changes across the Alzheimer's path, in a 2025 study. The method, arterial spin labeling, tags blood water to measure flow without injections. Flow readings depend on how long the tagged blood takes to arrive, and a time-encoded version samples several delays at once.

Fifty-nine adults aged 60 and over took part, split among healthy amyloid-free, healthy amyloid-positive, and impaired amyloid-positive groups. The team compared the multi-delay readings with single-delay ones in brain areas known to run low in the disease. They also matched flow values against spinal fluid markers of amyloid, tau, synapse harm, and nerve loss, plus thinking scores. The aim was to show the richer scan finds early change that the plain scan misses.
pmc-11716047:
Stroke risk for people with dementia who take risperidone is the target of a 2025 study by Nalamotse Joshua Choma and co-authors. Risperidone is the only drug of its class approved in the United Kingdom for the agitation and aggression that dementia can cause. It also carries a known risk of stroke, so the team wants risk judged person by person.

The project uses records for more than 358,000 patients from a national primary care database. It compares stroke rates in dementia patients who took the drug with those who never did. It then tests whether heart and vessel history changes each person's risk. Those patterns will feed personal prediction models for safer prescribing.
pmc-11716247:
Sam Asher and co-authors report a long study from 2025 on teeth, mouth care, and loss of thinking skill over time. Past work linked tooth loss to weak memory, but it left open what role tooth decay itself plays. The team also asked how daily mouth care and use of dental care fit in.

The study followed 2,958 adults in Finland who took part in health checks in 2000 and again in 2011. Dentists checked teeth and plaque at the start, and people told how often they brushed and saw a dentist. Poor mouth care, shown by plaque on two or more teeth, linked to loss in word skill and recall. Tooth decay alone showed no such link.
pmc-11716647:
Shruti Durape and fifteen co-authors link head injury to later mortality in a 2025 study. Traumatic brain injury is known to raise short term death risk. Its long shadow over decades, and over dementia deaths in particular, was murkier. The Framingham Heart Study's long running cohorts supplied the data.

Injury histories were assembled from records, exams, and self reports across lifetimes. Severity followed standard rehabilitation and veterans criteria. Each injured participant was matched with three uninjured peers by age and sex. Dementia diagnoses used established clinical standards. The design isolates injury's association with all cause and dementia related death. Findings speak to lifelong follow up after head trauma. The cohort's span, back to 1948 recruits, gives rare statistical depth.
pmc-11716747:
Ferrante and co-authors present a 2025 study on spotting thinking problems in Parkinson's disease from brief word tasks. Memory and thinking symptoms are common in the disease, yet standard tests are long and rely on judgment calls. The team used automated word analysis on fluency tasks, where patients name animals, shop items, or words with a set first sound.

The sample held 384 Spanish speakers with the disease. Software scored each word on six traits, from rarity to concreteness. A learning model used those traits to predict scores on a standard dementia rating scale. The aim is a fast, objective screen for mild impairment. Clinics could run it without specialist staff, the authors suggest.
pmc-11716947:
Vamshi Krishna Kancharla and Neelam Sinha repurpose an object-detection network to stage early Alzheimer's decline from brain scans, in this 2025 paper. The corpus callosum, the great fiber bridge between the brain's hemispheres, shrinks as neurodegeneration advances. Distinguishing early from late mild cognitive impairment is a step toward timely care.

Their model adapts YOLOv5, a fast detector built for everyday images, to find the callosum in structural MRI slices and classify the scan as early or late impairment. Unlike earlier texture-only approaches, it uses the callosum plus its surrounding context inside the bounding box. The data came from the ADNI cohort, one hundred subjects split evenly, eighty percent for training. On the test set the model reached ninety-seven percent accuracy. Heat maps from an interpretation method showed where it looked. The authors suggest detection networks deserve a place in neuroimaging toolkits.
pmc-11726747:
Takuya Hasegawa and four co-authors set up a mouse model that serves two cancer syndromes at once in a 2024 paper. Cancer cachexia wastes muscle and fat and saps strength, and good animal models for testing treatments are scarce. Cancer-induced bone pain, by contrast, is well modeled. The team injected lung cancer cells into the thigh bone of mice, the standard pain model, then checked whether cachexia features followed.

The features did follow. The mice lost weight, muscle, and fat, hurt at the tumor site, and showed anxiety-like behavior. Pain and mood, usually studied apart from wasting, appeared inside one model. The authors offer the setup as a platform for cachexia research that honors its physical and psychological sides together, and for screening therapies against both.
pmc-11726847:
Paula Cristina Martins and Vitor Hugo Oliveira study child well-being in poor families in this 2024 paper. Their families receive several forms of welfare support at once. The study asks how poverty strains family life and children's emotions and behavior. Parental stress and day-to-day family dynamics are central suspects. Ninety-nine children aged eight to twelve took part. All came from the Porto area of Portugal.

Standard forms measured stress, parenting views, family function, and child outcomes. The team also weighed the role of cash transfer programs with conditions. Contact with child protection services was another factor in the mix. Such programs aim to help, but they add demands on parents too. The findings speak to how support can be shaped to protect children. Social workers and policy makers are the intended readers.
pmc-11727247:
Luca Marsili and co-authors describe seven years of experience running a genetics clinic for rare movement disorders, in a 2024 paper. Many such disorders are inherited, and modern sequencing can find the cause, but clinics must choose among several test types wisely. Their program, launched in 2017, offered whole-exome sequencing to patients whose disorders looked genetic in origin.

Of eighty-two unrelated patients, twenty-seven percent received a firm genetic diagnosis. Those with a found cause had fallen ill significantly younger. Unsteady gait and parkinsonism were the most common presentations, and a few symptom groups accounted for most diagnoses. The authors lay out a full protocol. It includes a decision tree for escalating to whole-genome or long-read sequencing. It also covers how results are returned and re-analysis of unsolved cases. All of it aims at raising the diagnostic yield for rare brain disorders.
pmc-11727347:
Gregor and a team including Mirolo and Brandes reported in twenty twenty-four the first known case of a cat leukemia virus gut ill in a wild Eurasian lynx in Germany. The lynx is at grave risk in that land, so new germs matter for its care. The young female fell ill with gut signs and died in a week.

Her gut showed bleed and tissue death, with worn lymph parts and thin bone marrow. Tests proved the virus, a first for this lynx kind. Two gut germs had also moved in as second ills. The case warns that pet cat germs can reach rare wild cats.
pmc-11727647:
Janis Opincans and co-authors test a pain block after stomach removal surgery. The head text dates their trial to 2024, though the catalog lists 2026. Patients were split at random into two groups of 30. One got a steady infusion of a local anesthetic into the belly wall layers. The other got plain salt water the same way.

The drug group reported lower pain scores at every check after surgery. None of them needed rescue opioid painkillers. They also passed gas sooner, moved their bowels sooner, and got out of bed sooner. Their hospital stay was shorter. The trial ran from 2021 to 2023 at their center. The authors judge the block effective for pain control and for cutting opioid use after this surgery.
pmc-11727747:
Merve Berika Kadioglu, Mirac Sezer, and Bulent Elbasan compared hands-on manual therapy with a home exercise program for young adults who grind their teeth. Bruxism can bring jaw pain, poor sleep, and stress. Writing in twenty twenty-four, they ran a small randomized trial over eight weeks. Patients filled in standard scales for sleep quality, stress, jaw function, and quality of life before and after treatment. The team counted sore trigger points and rated pain during activity, at night, and at rest.

Both treatments improved nearly every measure, including sleep, stress, and quality of life. The home group alone failed to improve rest pain. Manual therapy did better than home exercise on sleep quality, jaw function scores, and trigger point counts, while pain, stress, and quality of life gains were similar between groups. The authors present both options as useful care.
pmc-11728047:
Repair surgery for a loose pelvic floor often includes a tightening step whose best use has never been proven, yet nearly every specialist performs it. Esther van Swieten and co-authors survey that gap in a 2024 study of urogynecologists worldwide. Members of the field's global association answered questions on when they operate and how.

Almost all who replied perform the step, most often to draw one muscle pair together with a few dissolving stitches. A wide opening found on exam and the patient's own sense of looseness ranked as the strong reasons to operate. Pain during sex and pelvic pain ranked as reasons to hold off. Technique varied widely from surgeon to surgeon. The group rated the need for real trials near the top of the scale.
pmc-11728247:
Mateusz Gutowski and co-authors test whether measures of blood flow to the limbs and organs can predict outcomes in severe COVID-19. Published in 2024, the prospective cohort study followed 102 patients in the first 48 hours of hospital care. Tools included capillary refill time, finger heat imaging, oxygen saturation, and a Doppler measure of kidney cortex flow.

Forty patients worsened and 24 died. Those who worsened or died started with slower capillary refill and lower kidney flow, plus worse lab values. In adjusted analysis, only kidney flow and capillary refill stayed linked to both worsening and death. Cutoff values for each marker are given. Two other measures did not predict outcomes.
pmc-11728347:
Six authors, led by Marija Boskovic Cabrol, report in 2024 on how growth faults in broiler chickens change breast meat. They looked at three faults, called white striping, wooden breast, and spaghetti meat, and checked meat traits such as color, water loss, protein, fat mix, and taste.

Wooden breast stood out most. Meat with that fault lost more water when cooked, had less protein, and showed a changed fat mix, while taste scores stayed much the same. The other two faults had smaller effects. The work helps meat plants and food firms judge how much these faults lower the worth of the meat they sell.
pmc-11728447:
Daniel Polterauer and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on a gentler test for cochlear implant candidates whose hearing nerve may still work. Before implant surgery, doctors check whether the nerve exists and can fire. The standard electrical test needs the eardrum opened under anesthesia, which burdens patients.

Their variant places the stimulus at the eardrum without that surgical step and records the brain's late response. Sixteen patients were tested, and seven showed a clear positive response shaped like those from older methods. Electrical artifacts ran stronger than in rival tests, a flaw the team flags. Still, the approach may spare some patients an anesthetized procedure.
pmc-11728547:
Xianda Sun and co-authors study how added polymers clump clay in rock and trap leftover oil, in a paper from 2024. Oil fields pump in soap-and-polymer blends to push out more crude. As pumping grows, wells have begun to yield less, not more. Slices of frozen core show much oil clinging between grains in the rock.

The team watched the process in a see-through model of rock pores. They flowed a clay slurry, crude oil, and blends of the two through the model. The polymer acted like a glue that bunched the clay flakes into clumps. Those clumps thickened the oil mix and blocked the pores. The trapped mix then resisted further pushing. The authors say this clogging helps explain the yield drop in late-stage floods.
pmc-11728647:
Wang and six co-authors compare two cotton varieties to learn why some plants resist lodging, the bending or falling of stems before harvest. The resistant variety had stronger stems, more lignin and cellulose, and higher activity in lignin-making enzymes. Gene activity tests pointed the same way.

Genes for lignin, cellulose, and sugar building ran hotter in the resistant variety. When the team silenced two lignin genes, plants lost lignin and lodged more easily. The authors conclude that these three stem materials support standing strength. They propose the related genes as breeding targets for machine-picked cotton that stays upright.
pmc-11728747:
Amararathna and co-authors test in 2024 whether a dark berry can blunt a tobacco-linked cancer chemical in mice. The chemical, known as NNK, turns harmful once body enzymes process it. Past work showed the haskap berry cuts lung harm from the chemical in lab and animal tests.

Mice got the berry in food, then the chemical, and the team checked liver enzymes and the chemical's by-products. With the chemical present, the berry lowered two enzyme genes and steered breakdown toward safer by-products, they report. Computer docking hinted the berry parts fit the enzymes well. The results suggest one route by which the berry may guard the lung, by slowing the step that makes the chemical dangerous.
pmc-11728847:
Six authors present a survey in two thousand twenty-four of sand flies and a parasite at Europe's northern edge for the disease they spread. The parasite, Leishmania infantum, causes leishmaniosis in dogs and can infect people. Switzerland is not yet a homeland for the disease, but imported dog cases appear often, and the flies live in its southern canton.

In two thousand twenty-two and twenty-three, the team trapped flies and tested dogs and cats for signs of past infection. Three quarters of the southern sites held sand flies, and one known carrier species was the most common. No flies were caught in the northwest survey.
pmc-11730247:
Koshiro Nagata and co-authors report saving a young mother's womb after severe bleeding from a stuck placenta, in a 2024 case report. A placenta that will not detach can cause deadly bleeding, and removal of the womb is the usual rescue. That saves life but ends fertility, a heavy loss for a woman aged twenty-eight with her first child.

Doctors first inflated a balloon inside the main artery to slow blood flow, a method borrowed from trauma care. The placenta was then removed by hand, and a balloon inside the womb held pressure to stop bleeding. The womb was saved and her condition stayed stable. The authors say the artery balloon buys time for fertility-saving steps.
pmc-11732347:
Kaiming Peng and seven co-authors build a survival prediction chart for older patients with esophageal cancer treated before surgery. Esophageal cancer grows commoner as populations age, and elders' outlooks vary widely. Their 2024 study mines a United States cancer registry for patients over 60 who received chemotherapy, with or without radiation, before an operation.

The 1,392 patients were split into building and checking groups. Being male and having higher tumor, node, and spread stages each predicted worse survival on their own. Chemotherapy alone fared about the same as adding radiation. The resulting nomogram sorted patients into three risk bands with moderate accuracy. The authors present it as a planning aid for doctors and families.
pmc-11734047: Nuno Cotrim and co-authors report a giant heart tumor as the cause of a stroke, in a 2024 case paper. The tumor is a myxoma, the most common primary tumor inside the heart. Such tumors are benign under the microscope, yet they can shed fragments into the blood. Sound imaging of the heart is the key tool to find them and map their size, shape, and attachments. Surgery to remove the tumor cures most patients, and return of the tumor or fresh clots is fairly rare.
pmc-11736347:
Taiyang Liao and a team of co-authors test whether lowering a stress protein can slow osteoarthritis. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The protein is called Nupr1, and the team links it to a form of cell death driven by iron, named ferroptosis.

In mouse cartilage cells, a trigger of inflammation raised the protein and the death pathway. Silencing the protein kept cells healthier, with less iron buildup and less fat damage in their membranes. Protective proteins tied to the pathway also held up better. The team then used knee surgery in mice to model the disease and delivered the silencing tool by virus. The work frames the protein as a lever on cartilage cell death in worn joints.
pmc-11742347:
Erythropoietin treats anemia in kidney failure, but clinicians worry it may also thin bones. The seven authors used Taiwan's national insurance database to compare dialysis patients who received the drug against matched non-users. There were 2,839 patients in each group, drawn from diagnoses between 2000 and 2014. They tracked major osteoporotic fractures of the hip, spine, and wrist.

Users suffered every fracture type more often. Adjusted hazard ratios ran from 2.19 for hip to 2.50 for spine fractures, and 2.41 for major fractures overall. Risk climbed with dose, with a clear trend for major, spine, and wrist fractures. The authors conclude that erythropoietin treatment in hemodialysis patients is associated with a raised risk of osteoporotic fracture.
pmc-11749547:
Ekaphan Shatsnimitkul and six co-authors run a fluids trial around a gut procedure in a paper whose text is dated 2024. The procedure, called ERCP, threads a scope to the bile duct. A painful pancreas flare is its most feared side effect. Heavy fluid intake beforehand may lower that risk.

Three hundred patients were assigned by chance to two fluid plans. One plan gave a large volume of Ringer's solution plus albumin. The other gave a standard volume of Ringer's alone. Staff who judged outcomes did not know the assignments. Flare rates came out nearly the same in both groups. About six to seven percent of each group developed pancreatitis. The extra albumin plan showed no clear edge in this trial.
pmc-11771747:
Julia Castellanos Segado and co-authors profile who gets sent for brain testing at a Madrid hospital in a 2024 study. The neuropsychology clinic at Hospital Universitario La Paz assesses how brain trouble affects behavior and thinking. Six years of referrals were reviewed.

Records covered 394 adults seen from 2018 to 2023. Women outnumbered men, 232 to 162, and averaged a little older. Suspected dementia was the top reason for referral in both sexes. Most patients had finished schooling by age eighteen, and that trait tied significantly to being assessed at all. The typical patient, the authors conclude, is a middle-aged adult with mid-level education and a dementia question.
pmc-11772547:
Paul Scott and co-authors track how often single chamber atrial pacemakers are still used in England after a key Danish trial. Their paper from 2025 deals with sinus node disease with intact lower conduction, where one lead in the upper chamber can keep a natural rhythm. The Danish trial found no survival gain for that type and double the redo risk, so guidance now ranks it second line.

National device records were used to find first implants of the type and to track trends over time. The study also tests whether redo risk stays high in daily practice, where careful patient choice might soften the trial result. The paper works from registry data, not a new trial.
pmc-11788847:
Gary Hodge and colleagues gathered the views of patients, families, and professionals on what blocks good palliative and end of life care in South-West England. Care at the end of life is widely reported as patchy in Britain, and the region adds rural and coastal distance, an older population, and little prior research. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team ran focus groups across the region with health and care staff, people nearing the end of life, family caregivers, and the bereaved. The groups were asked what gets in the way of good care.

Five barriers stood out: too few specialist staff, especially out of hours; poor communication and coordination between services. The rest were unequal access, lingering strain from the pandemic, and reluctance to talk about death and dying. The authors say hearing all three viewpoints together shows where fixes must aim.
pmc-11790447:
Jeong Min Song and co-authors ask whether high CA125 blood levels should push otherwise low-risk womb cancer patients toward node removal, in this 2024 paper. Korean criteria mark younger women as low risk for spread to lymph nodes. The marker, though, also rises from harmless conditions, which clouds the call.

Charts from seventy-three premenopausal patients at seven Korean centers were reviewed. Only two of sixty-two who had nodes removed showed spread. Five women saw recurrence over about five years of follow-up, and five-year recurrence-free survival reached just under eighty-nine percent. The aim was to sharpen guidance for this narrow group.
pmc-11794547:
Tianli Wang and co-authors predict how much phosphorus crop shoots take up, in work dated 2024 in the text. Heavy phosphorus fertilizer harms soil, and a fair uptake read helps farms feed crops with less waste, yet field scale reads are hard to take.

Their combined model sums uptake by leaf, stem, and grain, each part fit on a small set of samples. Light spectra from the crop canopy feed the model in a Henan test zone. Accuracy beat plain fit models by a wide mark. A training scheme that picks the most telling samples keeps data needs low. The tool suits region wide nutrition watch.
pmc-11799247:
Mengjie An and co-authors rank cotton lines for salt tolerance at sprouting in a 2024 study. Cotton tolerates some salt as an adult, yet seedlings suffer badly and yields drop. Breeders lacked a clear, small set of traits for early screening.

From over three hundred varieties, clustering sorted lines into five tolerance classes. A standard salt dose was first tuned on a sample subset. Weight and shoot measures proved the most telling traits, with total fresh weight the single most reliable. Tolerant lines kept sodium low in roots and moved ions more selectively. Three scoring models let labs trade accuracy against workload.
pmc-11805047:
Ankita Kondhalkar and four co-authors measure iodine in the food of mothers in India's Vidarbha region. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, sits inside a newborn screening program. A baby in the womb depends wholly on the mother for iodine. Too little iodine can stunt brain and body growth for life.

Salt, water, and staple foods from mothers in rural and town areas are tested. The work runs with several departments at a medical college in Wardha. Even mild lack in the mother can dull a child's school path later. The data can show where diets fall short. Local fixes, like salt checks, can then be aimed well.
pmc-11852247:
Claudia Hernandez and six co-authors describe a face treatment method in this 2024 paper. The method uses a filler based on calcium hydroxylapatite, a mineral-like material. The filler does two jobs: it lifts soft tissue and it prompts the skin to make more collagen. The authors treat several face layers in one session, using the filler at different strengths.

Six patients aged forty to sixty, with mild loose skin, took part. Strong filler went deep along the cheek bone, jaw angle, and jaw edge. Weaker mixes went to the back temple area and the cheek side. After at least ninety days, raters judged most patients improved on a standard scale. The paper gives doctors a one-visit plan that pairs lift with skin renewal.
pmc-11855047:
Hye Jean Hwang rebuilds how British doctors argued suicide out of the crime books after the war, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. In the late nineteen forties and fifties, doctors alone pressed for law change. Their tack framed suicide as a plain, neutral fact, not a moral fault.

Set causes like illness, isolation, and family strain made the act read as beyond control. Cases of attempts, not deaths, led their pitch. Reform, they argued, would sharpen control, not loosen it. The line of talk ends at the Suicide Act of nineteen sixty-one. Readers get a rhetoric that moved a statute.
pmc-11862847:
Hui Zhang and five co-authors test whether 3D CT scans help doctors agree on knee fracture types. Fractures around the knee are sorted by standard systems that guide surgery. If doctors read the same scan differently, care can drift. Their 2024 study gathered twenty-three patients with fractures near the knee and gave three radiologists both flat and 3D scan views. Each doctor classified breaks of the thigh bone end, the kneecap, and the shin bone top, twice over.

Agreement scores were computed within and between readers for both scan types. The question is practical: 3D rendering costs time and software, so it must earn its place with steadier calls. Clearer agreement means treatment plans rest on shared facts. The study adds evidence from a real hospital caseload, not test images.
pmc-11867947:
Wenpeng Cao and colleagues test a plant flavonoid against stroke damage in mice, tracing its target, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The compound is cynaroside, known for calming inflammation and oxidation. The injury modeled is the harm done when blood flow returns to a blocked brain artery.

Treated mice woke from the model stroke with milder deficits, smaller dead zones, and less swelling, and their brain immune cells stayed calmer. Computer docking and binding tests pointed to one target: Alox15, an enzyme the compound appears to grip directly. With it suppressed, the inflammatory alarm chain quieted and the markers of ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death, fell. Toxin signals such as interleukin-1 beta dropped in both mouse brains and dish-grown immune cells. The authors propose cynaroside as a stroke candidate working through this enzyme.
pmc-11881647:
Krista Louise Alexander, Katharine Hall, and Yuling Max Chen ask whether having a librarian on a review team lifts the work's reach. Knowledge syntheses, such as systematic reviews, rely on expert searching, which is a librarian's craft. Their 2024 study took five hundred fifty-one syntheses from one year in clinical psychology journals. Each paper was coded by whether a librarian was a co-author, was thanked, or had no visible role. Citation counts and journal impact factors were then compared across the groups.

If librarian-backed reviews gather more citations, the case for funding their role grows. The study uses one field and one year as a clean test bed. The authors aim to move a familiar claim, that librarians improve reviews, from belief to measurement. Editors and funders are the intended readers.
pmc-11883247:
Tuba Yuce Inel and Sadettin Uslu describe a single hard case from two thousand twenty-four. A woman aged thirty-seven came in with swollen, red eyes and short breath. Scans showed a tight narrowing of her airway just below the voice box. Tests pointed to a rare illness in which the immune system attacks small blood vessels.

Doctors first gave steroid drugs and a drug to calm the immune system. When her breath got worse, they added a stronger drug called rituximab. The narrowing still grew, and during a scope test she stopped breathing. Surgeons had to open a new airway in her neck at once. The case shows how fast this illness can threaten life.
pmc-12007547:
Yann Bihan-Poudec and co-authors study how the heartbeat distorts high detail brain scans of macaque monkeys in a 2023 paper. The monkey brain is a key model for the human brain, but clinical scanners cannot easily reach the fine detail that dead brain scans allow. Heart pulses cause phase errors between scan shots, which create ghost images and signal loss.

The team compared scans with and without timing the shots to the heart. The losses hit the brainstem, thalamus, and cerebellum hardest. Timing to the heart restored signal in white and gray matter and cut ghosting. With that fix, living monkey brains could be scanned at a detail once limited to dead tissue.
pmc-12008347:
Rabab Fouad and seven co-authors tested in 2024 whether blood markers of vessel growth can flag liver cancer arising from hepatitis C. They compared 25 patients with the cancer, 25 with cirrhosis and 25 healthy volunteers. Cells called Tie2-expressing monocytes were counted by flow methods, and two angiopoietin proteins were measured in serum. All three signals ran higher in the cancer group.

The share of the special monocytes, the Ang2 level and the Ang2-to-Ang1 ratio each separated cancer from cirrhosis and health clearly. Ang1 alone rose only against the healthy group. The authors suggest the monocytes help feed tumor vessels through this pathway. Blocking that signal could one day support existing treatment. For now they propose the markers as candidates for earlier detection. Blood tests of this kind would be cheaper than scans for screening.
pmc-12040747:
Xuewei Li and co-authors report a 2024 study in mice with scarred livers. Part of the liver was cut away, a common step in liver care. Scarred livers grow back poorly after such cuts. The team tested whether stem cells from human cord tissue could help the liver grow back and cut down scar tissue.

The treated mice showed better regrowth and less of the tough scar protein. The team links the gain to a known growth signal path in cells. That path helps cells divide and build new tissue. The work is in mice, not people, so care in humans is still far off. Still, the results point to a clear next step: test safety and dose, and check whether the same signal path drives the gain in larger studies.
pmc-12056447:
Kajal Nehra and co-authors look back at records in a 2024 study on late hospital arrival for breast cancer in India. Breast cancer made up a large share of new cancers in the country, and many deaths follow late first visits. The team measured how long the delay ran and what drove it.

The study covered 138 patients aged 18 to 60 at a cancer clinic in central India. Each had waited more than two weeks between first noticing symptoms and first seeing a doctor. By naming the main causes of delay, the work points to where public teaching and referral fixes could save the most time.
pmc-12199947:
Paulina Kluszczyk and six colleagues present a 2024 case report on a hip fracture that barely announced itself. A forty-four-year-old, professionally active patient was receiving palliative treatment for a rare vessel-born sarcoma that had spread through the pelvis and spine. Years of scans, biopsies, chemotherapy, and targeted drugs had kept the disease mostly stable, and the patient walked with crutches.

Without any injury, a routine scan in 2023 revealed a fracture just below the ball of the left thigh bone, already knitting together. Given the stable fracture and the widespread pelvic disease, the team chose not to operate. The authors note this nearly silent fracture as a rare complication of bone cancer that vigilance, not surgery, served best.
pmc-12288947:
Qingmiao Shi and co-authors build a gene-based risk score for liver cancer from the Notch signaling pathway, a pathway that helps steer the cancer's growth. Their study, whose head dates it to 2024, mines public gene data from liver tumors. Patients first split into three clusters by Notch gene activity, and the clusters differed in survival and in how much immune activity their tumors showed.

A five-gene signature then formed the score: SPP1, SMG5, HMMR, PLOD2, and CFHR4. The score estimated survival well, and high- and low-risk patients differed in immune makeup and in how they might respond to immune therapy. Tools such as a decision tree and a nomogram refined the grouping for clinical use. The authors offer the model as a guide for judging immune traits and likely treatment response in this cancer.
pmc-12315747:
Nadine Herzog and co-authors probe the gate of short-term hold in a 2024 brain study. Day life asks us to hold a goal through noise, yet drop it when the world turns. A gate in the mind runs that trade, but its beat and flow were thin lore.

Rest brain waves gave two marks of the push-pull poise of brain nets: how long waves stay linked, and the slope of the wave spread. The ask is how those marks track with gate acts. Such ties hint that rest poise sets how the gate swings. Mind teams gain a flow view of a core thought act.
pmc-12662847:
Peter Wühr, Bianca Wühr, and Gerhard Rinkenauer test how hand skill leaks into attention tests in this 2025 study. Two paper tests, the d2-R and the FAIR, ask people to hunt targets among distractors. Both demand marking answers by hand, so motor skill may sway the scores.

In one test, each target gets a short stroke. In the other, a steady line runs under the row and spikes up at targets, which reveals the search path. The team gave both tests to 120 people, plus five motor subtests like pegboard and tapping. The study asks how much of an attention score is really hand speed.
pmc-12663147:
Elena Sproviero and co-authors studied two drugs that block a key step in how cancer cells build their parts in 2025. The disease in focus is multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that still has no cure. The drugs target an enzyme that starts the making of ribosomes, the cell parts that build proteins.

One drug, called BMH-21, helped natural killer cells attack the cancer and release more attack signals. The other drug, CX-5461, caused cell damage and aging that raised a shield protein and calmed the killer cells down. Both drugs also helped a known antibody drug work better. The results point to new ways to pair these drugs with immune care.
pmc-12663447:
Xinyi Yue and co-authors chart how killer immune cells differ in people with Parkinson disease, in a study from 2025. The cells are natural killer cells, a front-line arm that kills sick cells. Past long studies hint they play a part in the disease, but fine facts on blood cells were scarce.

The team drew blood cells from patients and healthy donors, then grew and woke the killer cells with a set method. Patient cells were more apt to die and a bit more apt to kill tumor test cells. Gene reads showed broad sameness with shifts in immune and fuel paths. Subtype mixes also split the groups. The map gives labs fresh marks to test for early calls and for cell-based care of brain disease.
pmc-12663547:
Wei Chen and co-authors map how age and sex write themselves into the DNA drifting free in blood, in this 2025 study. Methylation, chemical tags on DNA, shifts with age and differs by sex, but older datasets sampled only a slice of the genome. The team sequenced the whole genome's tags in blood plasma from ninety-eight healthy adults aged twenty-two to seventy-seven. Cell-free DNA makes the test a simple blood draw.

They found just over three thousand age-linked sites and about a thousand sex-linked ones, tied to hundreds of genes. A complete map sharpens tools that guess age from blood and warns test makers where sex skews results. Liquid biopsies for cancer and aging all lean on baselines like this one.
pmc-12664147:
Zexiu Lu and co-authors trace a chain of molecular switches that helps a common breast cancer grow. The cancer type, estrogen receptor-positive, leans on sugar-burning metabolism, and the protein CUEDC1 is unusually abundant in its tissues. Lab tests showed that a regulator called MAZ switches the gene on, and that high levels of the protein speed tumour growth and predict worse outcomes for patients.

The team found the protein works through a partner channel protein, CACNG4, which turns up a growth pathway known as PI3K and its partner AKT. That pathway in turn drives the sugar-burning program the tumour depends on. Patient data backed the chain: the two proteins rose together and both tracked with poor prognosis. Screening a compound database for blockers of the first protein, the authors point to the whole axis as a treatment target.
pmc-12664847:
Wanyi Fang and co-authors find that an immune signal can protect the diabetic retina by waking its resident cleanup cells. Diabetes slowly damages retinal nerves before vessels fail, and early protection is scarce. In diabetic mice, injections of interleukin-12 into the eye partly spared the nerve fiber and ganglion cell layers from thinning.

Gene profiling pointed at microglia, the retina's immune cells, and their eating activity. The signal switched on a pathway through STAT4 that raised two partner proteins, TREM2 and DAP12, boosting the cells' growth and appetite even in high sugar. Lab tests confirmed the chain. The authors propose this route as an early treatment target before vision is lost.
pmc-12666047:
Scarred lungs make breathing a daily negotiation, and patients often feel under-informed. Thomas Riegler and co-authors interviewed eleven people with pulmonary fibrosis about the information, services, and self-management support they actually experience. Conversations lasted up to seventy minutes and covered staying well, exercise, oxygen use, and symptoms such as breathlessness, cough, and fatigue.

Doctors and nurses were the main source of information, yet for hard topics like life expectancy patients searched the internet, mostly in vain. Guidance on drug side effects and diet was missing, home exercise lacked structure, and cough and fatigue had few workable strategies. The authors recommend blended programs that pair digital resources with human contact rather than replacing it.
pmc-12666147:
Julia König and co-authors interview German cancer doctors about money's pull on medical choices in a 2025 study. Cancer care keeps getting pricier, and reimbursement rules can reward or punish specific decisions. Hard data on where money actually bends judgment was scarce.

Sixteen physicians with budgeting experience described their workplaces in depth. The team distilled twenty-one concrete decision situations where finances intrude. They sorted into four patterns: care not reimbursed at all, care paid below its cost, care paid above its cost, and costly care of doubtful value. The findings confirm that financial pressure reaches real bedside choices. The authors offer the catalog as a base for measuring how widespread the effect is and which patients it endangers.
pmc-12691347:
Yulia Shifrin and Sabine Mai review chromosome-end profiling as a risk marker in a blood cancer, in this 2025 paper. The cancer, multiple myeloma, grows in the bone marrow and varies widely between patients. Better risk sorting is needed at each stage of care.

The ends of chromosomes, called telomeres, can be counted and mapped in three dimensions inside the cell nucleus. Their number, brightness, clumping, and layout track with relapse risk in new patients and with the chance that early disease will advance. Blood and marrow cells gave like profiles, which hints that blood tests could track leftover disease. The authors urge wider tests of the method in care.
pmc-12692347:
Shingo Kishi and co-authors report a lab study, published in 2025, on osteosarcoma, a bone cancer seen most often in teens and young adults. The team asked whether blocking creatine kinase, an enzyme that helps cells store and move energy, could slow the cancer. Survival for this disease has changed little in decades, so new drug targets are badly needed.

Blocking the enzyme cut growth in cancer models and killed cells mainly through a form of cell death called apoptosis. The treatment also weakened the cells' energy stores, harmed their power centers, and reduced their spread and movement. In mice, it slowed tumors and their spread. The authors argue that this energy pathway is a weak point worth targeting, perhaps alongside standard drugs.
pmc-12692547:
Beatrice Risso and co-authors review brain disorders tied to one sugar ferry gene in a 2025 paper. The gene's product moves a sugar building block inside cells. Without it, proteins and fats miss their sugar coats. Faults can be inherited or arise in patches of brain tissue.

Disorders range from whole body sugar coat defects to local brain malformations. The review sorts symptoms by variant type and tissue spread. Lab assays and animal models fill in how the faults harm cells. Sugar dosing and tailored medicine lead the treatment outlook section.
pmc-12692647:
Ochratoxins are poisons made by molds that contaminate food. Testing and rules focus almost entirely on one of them, ochratoxin A, leaving its close cousins B and C unchecked in tricky foods like coffee and spices. Jiaojiao Xu and co-authors first confirmed that commercial test columns built for ochratoxin A also catch the other two at high rates. They found that the usual extraction fluid destroyed ochratoxin C, and developed a stable shared extraction using a mix of acetonitrile and water.

A new washing step with a mild detergent solution tamed the heavy interference from these foods. The finished method was validated in roasted coffee and pepper on two instrument platforms, showing clean linearity, sound recovery, and tight precision. Testing forty shop samples found ochratoxin A in nearly half. One spice group showed the A and B forms together.
pmc-12693347:
Lianao Zhang and co-authors dope rare-earth crystals with antimony to make them glow across the spectrum, in a 2025 paper. These zero-dimensional halides are stable and trap light energy well, but rare-earth ions absorb weakly and emit in narrow lines. Adding antimony creates glowing defect centers that both shine broadly and hand energy to the rare-earth ions.

Across nine host metals the doped crystals brightened and their colors tuned widely. Some hosts kept the broad glow, others passed the energy on for sharp rare-earth emission, and two showed their own electron-transfer quirks. Mixing terbium and europium hosts produced a dual color-and-spectrum code the team proposes for anti-counterfeiting tags.
pmc-12693547:
Abdullah Amini and co-authors study in 2025 how glaucoma and cataract relate to a blocked main vein in the retina. The block harms blood flow in the eye and can cost sight. Past links with other eye diseases were not fully clear in time order.

The study matched more than four hundred confirmed cases with a larger control group of like age and sex. Both glaucoma and cataract were far more common in the ten years before the block than in controls. After the block, new glaucoma rose sharply and new cataract also rose. The authors read this as a sign that poor vein flow builds over years.
pmc-12693847:
Han and co-authors design a soft touch sensor that uses magnets arranged in a special pattern to feel bending over a wide range. Soft magnetic sensors suit wearables and robots, but the sensing chip usually sits in the bending layer, which tangles the signal. Their 2025 design splits the parts: small magnets sit in a soft rubber sheet, while the chip stays fixed at a distance on a firm base.

Computer models show the magnet pattern boosts the field and makes it more even, staying readable even fifteen millimeters away. The pattern also flattens the field's shape, which makes the signal simpler to read and allows faster sampling. The authors offer the design as a guide for future touch sensors in wearables and smart robots. The study is based on modeling rather than a built device.
pmc-12694947:
Dirk Holst and co-authors build a reporting checklist for studies that use artificial intelligence to run systematic literature reviews, in work from twenty twenty-five. Reviews anchor evidence synthesis but eat time and staff. Language models can speed the work, yet hidden AI use threatens trust and repeatability.

Existing guidance mostly covers AI as a research topic, not as a review tool. The team mined trial and prediction reporting frameworks for items, then sorted them into a modular add on to the main review reporting standard. The checklist spans the whole review, from title to discussion. It asks authors to name the tools, describe human and AI teamwork, report performance checks, and state limits.
pmc-12695147:
Ali Karami, Vida Naderi Boldaji, and Fatemeh Khalili report in 2025 an airway rescue in a man whose windpipe was far wider than normal and had never been diagnosed. The rare condition, Mounier-Kuhn syndrome, stretches the windpipe and main airways. During heart surgery, the breathing tube leaked badly at two sizes, and repositioning did not help.

Old chest images, reviewed in hindsight, showed the dilation plainly. The team borrowed a trick from fistula care. They slid the tube into one main bronchus and eased it back until both lungs sounded even. Gauze packing sealed the gap, and ventilation held. The authors urge teams to spot the syndrome before surgery. A wide windpipe on any chest image, they say, should change the airway plan.
pmc-12696047:
Watermelon growers graft their vines onto a wild cousin's roots to dodge soil disease, but the favorite rootstock flowers late and drags the crop's fruiting with it. Venkata Rao Ganaparthi, Patrick Wechter, Amnon Levi, and Sandra Branham mapped the flowering-time genes in that wild relative, Citrullus amarus, in 2025.

A cross of two inbred lines gave 129 descendant lines, trialed over two years and two seasons. The trials scored days to female flowering and days to fruiting, two traits that move almost in lockstep. Two steady spots on chromosome 3 together explained about forty percent of the flowering spread. The authors hand breeders the markers needed to build early-flowering rootstocks that keep the disease armor.
pmc-12698547:
Hou studies how vocational college students accept an online English course in twenty twenty-five. The course is a MOOC, a large open online class. The study uses a model that links ease of use, usefulness, attitude, and intent to use. A survey of four hundred thirty-four students provides the data.

Ease of use raised how useful students found the course. Usefulness in turn improved attitude and raised intent to use the course. Stronger intent linked to a better learning experience for students. In a surprise result, a positive attitude alone linked to a worse experience. The author argues that course content and teaching design shape the experience more than first impressions. The findings offer tips for building MOOCs for vocational learners.
pmc-12699547:
Nina Trinks and five co-authors present a 2025 study checking whether a newer machine measures metabolism as reliably as the established one it might replace. Indirect calorimetry infers energy use from breathed gases and guides nutrition care. Five volunteers with type 2 diabetes from a German study each underwent sixteen measurements per device over four days, in randomized order, with recalibration after every session.

The two machines' repeatability differed only slightly across oxygen use, carbon dioxide output, and the derived energy figures. Confidence intervals were wide, reflecting the tiny sample, but centered near zero difference. Extra calibration did not consistently change the results. The authors conclude the newer device measures reliably and can stand in for the older standard in clinic. They frame the study as a validation step for equipment turnover in metabolic units.
pmc-12699847:
Valji, Valji, and Lam survey fairness, diversity, and inclusion in Canadian anesthesiology training in twenty twenty-five. No prior study had charted who trains in the field there or what programs do on inclusion. An anonymous online survey went to residents in all seventeen programs. One hundred twenty-three replies came from fifteen programs.

Near parity held for gender among respondents. Some ethnic groups fell well below their share of the national population. Most residents called inclusion important, yet over half knew of no program efforts. Two in five had no training on the topic at all. The authors urge programs to name, run, and track their efforts. Barriers to action need study next, they add.
pmc-12700547:
Shuai Ma and a large team of colleagues published a 2025 study on breast tumors and a drug called auranofin. Auranofin is already approved for joint disease. The team asked whether it could also weaken the way tumor cells cope with stress when they copy their DNA.

Cancer cells face stress as they copy DNA, and a protein called TOPBP1 helps them survive it. The study shows that auranofin binds to TOPBP1 and blocks its work with partner proteins. That leaves tumor cells with more copying faults and a weaker stress response. In tumor models, this made standard drug treatment work better, which points to a new use for an old drug.
pmc-12700947:
Yan Hu and Chuntao Liu studied regulatory T cell control in asthma in 2025. Asthma harms many people worldwide. Regulatory T cells balance immune reactions. Boosting them may calm airway swelling. Gene network analysis flagged sugar-tagging steps. Fat burning pathways also stood out strongly.

One protein tag ran the pathway. Animal tests backed how it works in living animals. More of these cells slowed asthma growth. Both major asthma types were blocked. Sugar tagging of proteins was carried out. Fatty acid burning supplied the route. Aimed treatments gain a base in theory. Boosting these cells is the plan.
pmc-12701347:
Lea Herschbach and co-authors evaluate an AI chatbot that gives doctors real-time feedback while they practice communication for mental health care. Good communication is essential in medicine, and mental health visits are rising. Feedback is the engine of improvement, yet trainers cannot watch every practice session.

The proof-of-concept study asks how accurate the chatbot's feedback is and how trainees receive it. The chatbot comments as the conversation unfolds, rather than after the fact. That timing lets learners adjust on the spot. The authors check the tool's judgments against human standards. Early evidence of this kind guides whether AI coaches belong in medical training.
pmc-12703047:
Gravina and co-authors profiled, in a 2025 study, the cargo of large extracellular vesicles in the blood of people living with HIV. These drifting sacs carry messages between cells and may feed the chronic inflammation that shadows treated HIV. The donors showed clear signs of that background inflammation.

Against healthy controls, their vesicles carried one standout microRNA, 31 long non-coding RNAs, and 45 proteins at altered levels. Four named proteins tied into the microRNA's regulatory web, pointing at known inflammation pathways. In dish tests, vesicles from the HIV group stirred bystander immune cells to release more inflammatory signals. The work names candidate molecules through which vesicles keep the immune system simmering, and possible points to cool it.
pmc-12704847:
Zoey Verdun, writing alone in 2025, asks whether a health scare changes how people live. Using panel data from a large British household study, Verdun compares a hard health shock with a softer warning.

To handle the fact that a diagnosis is not random, people were matched on their starting health risks. A big event, such as a heart attack or a diabetes diagnosis, led people to improve their overall lifestyle score. A softer signal, such as being told of high blood pressure or chest pain, brought no change. The gains came from smoking less and from not drinking. Diet and exercise did not move by a clear margin.
pmc-12704947:
Farhana Rahman and co-authors study blood pressure control and genes in this 2025 paper. Grade 1 hypertension is the mildest stage of high blood pressure. The team asked how lifestyle habits and one gene variant shape control of the condition. They recruited 447 patients who had taken pressure drugs for over a year.

Patients who kept up lifestyle changes had better pressure control. A variant in the ACE gene linked significantly with having hypertension at all. Drug response also split by gene form: one common drug worked best in one group, another drug in the other. The authors back pairing healthy habits with gene-matched drug choice.
pmc-12705047:
Gelaw and co-authors report a surgical case from Ethiopia in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A woman aged twenty, who also had epilepsy, developed a cancer of the lower lip. Such cancers are rare in young people and are more often tied to sun, tobacco, or genes.

Surgeons removed the tumor with a wide cut and cleared glands on both sides of the neck. They rebuilt the lip using tissue from the forearm, joined by fine vessel work, plus a tendon sling. The flap lived, healing went smoothly, and she regained lip closure and speech. The authors say the case shows such complex repair can work even where resources are limited.
pmc-12706047:
Mohamed Saleh and four co-authors study how thyroid problems and diabetes jointly affect a fatty liver disease. Their study is from two thousand twenty-five, at a hospital in Egypt. Four hundred patients with the liver disease were split into four groups of one hundred. The groups covered all mixes of diabetes and thyroid trouble.

Patients with both conditions had the most advanced liver scarring. Severe fat build-up in the liver was most common in those with thyroid trouble but no diabetes. Low thyroid function, even in mild form, went with higher scarring scores and worse fat levels. Tests included blood work, ultrasound, and a stiffness scan for high-risk patients. The authors urge joint screening of thyroid and sugar in these patients.
pmc-12706247:
Colin Halverson, Samantha Vershaw, Clair Francomano, and Tom Doyle study self-doubt in people with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in two thousand twenty-five. The connective tissue disorders bring pain and odd symptoms that doctors often wave off. The team asked what that dismissal does inside patients' own minds.

Forty-three patients in Europe and North America filled a survey, and thirty-nine sat for deep interviews, split between the hypermobile type and gene-defined types. Nearly three in four doubted the extent, even the reality, of their own pain. Many traced the doubt to years of being brushed off, above all in childhood. Self-doubt warped how they noticed and voiced symptoms; some quit standard care entirely, while others built coping tactics.
pmc-12707747:
Fast proof of drug resistance guides tuberculosis care, but no single test catches every resistant strain. Marcela Bhering and co-authors compared three rapid tests on samples from forty suspected drug-resistant lung cases in Rio de Janeiro. Cases came from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-two. Lab-grown drug testing served as the standard, and a deeper gene reading method settled disagreements.

Two rapid tests caught rifampicin resistance in about nine of ten cases. One test missed more isoniazid resistance, and it weakened when samples held few bacteria. The deep reading found resistance the other tests missed, plus mixed infections in some samples. The authors back layered testing where resistance is common. Their counts show where each tool earns its place.
pmc-12708347:
Timothy Huerta and a large cross-institution team describe, in a 2025 paper, how they built a learning health system that spans several covered institutions. Such a system feeds daily care data back into research, yet putting one into practice has proved hard for many centers.

The paper lays out the leadership structure, data rules, and technical tools that made their version work at scale. It also proposes a wider data vision matched to team-based and translational research. Extra materials give practical detail for other centers that want to copy the model. The account treats governance, not software alone, as the core of the system.
pmc-12708747:
Zhentao Lao and colleagues used single-cell data in 2025 to find a cell group that marks where head and neck cancer spreads in lymph nodes. This cancer type is common and often deadly because it reaches the nodes, yet the spread mechanism is poorly understood. Gene activity was read cell by cell to map interactions inside metastatic nodes.

A macrophage group carrying a distinctive marker clustered close to blood vessel lining cells in spread nodes. Vessel density was also higher there, confirmed by tissue staining and spatial imaging. The authors suggest signalling between these macrophages and vessel cells helps build a niche for metastasis, offering leads for prognosis and precise treatment.
pmc-12709747:
Lingjie Fan and co-authors link movement patterns to pain at body sites in older adults. Movement is a drug-free way to ease pain, but its tie to pain at each site was murky. The team used a national aging study from 2021 and 2022. Wrist sensors logged total activity, sitting time, and how often activity broke into short bursts.

Mid-level sitting time tied to more back and neck pain. Bursts of stronger activity tied to less leg pain, while broken sitting tied to more foot pain. Over time, burst patterns tied to head pain that stayed, though checks weakened that link. Machine models guessed foot and back relief fairly well. The authors urge pain plans tuned by body site.
pmc-12709847:
Some pregnant women in the Netherlands decline the care guidelines recommend, often after hard past births, and some plan to birth outside the system. Marene Dimmendaal and four co-authors studied a special clinic in 2025 that was set up to keep those women in hospital care on terms they could accept.

The researchers interviewed eight women and partners who used the Nijmegen clinic. Parents described an unexpectedly positive experience, built on shared effort and flexibility from staff. Care felt joint, yet on the woman's own terms, and many found the birth healing after earlier trauma. The clinic's approach, the authors argue, shows how services can meet parents halfway instead of losing them entirely.
pmc-12710247:
Raymond K Wong, an editor, writes a Thanksgiving reflection on gratitude toward the peer reviewers of his journal. His 2025 essay opens the journal's final issue of the year, where all reviewers from the past twelve months are named. Review work is unpaid and unseen by readers. Wong argues it sits at the heart of what the journal does. Authors trust the journal with their work, and sound reviews shape whether that trust is repaid.

Good reviews, he notes, are detailed, creative, and generous. Even a harsh verdict can leave authors with clear guidance and the will to try again. The reviewer pool spans fields beyond the journal's own specialty, which strengthens each paper. Senior reviewers also mentor newer ones, which keeps standards alive. Wong closes with an open call for past authors and keen readers to join the pool.
pmc-12710447:
Jian Deng and co-authors present a 2025 journal article using genetic methods to test whether diet habits cause age-related cataract. The team used gene variants as stand-ins for 83 eating and drinking habits from a British biobank, and checked them against cataract data from Finland. Several statistical routes, including two-way and multi-factor checks, guarded the causal claims.

One habit stood out: drinking alcohol with meals, rather than apart from meals, cut cataract risk by about a third among current drinkers. Part of the effect ran through inflammation markers, with one marker carrying about eleven percent. The pattern also held for cataract surgery in separate data.
pmc-12711047:
Priscilla Kapombe and co-authors report what killed people with HIV who died at home across Zambia from 2020 to 2023, in a 2025 study. Treatment coverage has raised life expectancy in this group, but recent cause-of-death data were scarce. Health workers interviewed relatives of the dead using a standard verbal autopsy tool, and a computer program assigned a probable cause. The sweep covered 33 districts and more than 67,000 community deaths.

Of those deaths, 11,475 were people with HIV, dying at a mean age of 45. Half were assigned to HIV-related causes, with heart disease next at about 13 percent and lung tuberculosis at 7.5 percent. Among decedents without HIV, heart disease led. Over the four years, the HIV share of deaths fell while the heart disease share rose.
pmc-12711147:
Dhouha Bacha and co-authors searched in 2025 for factors that predict how stomach cancer responds to drug treatment given before surgery. Chemotherapy around surgery is the standard curative plan for stomach adenocarcinoma that can be removed, and it improves survival. The tissue response to that treatment strongly shapes outlook, so an early predictor has value.

The team reviewed patients who had surgery after pre-treatment from 2015 to 2020. Response was graded on the Mandard scale, which scores the share of live tumor cells left against scar tissue across five grades. Grades one to three counted as a response. Clinical and tissue factors were then tested against that grade. Readers get a focused hunt for signs, visible before or at surgery, that tell which tumors the drugs are truly shrinking.
pmc-12711947:
Inherited cancer risk in Indonesia is nearly unmeasured, leaving families unsure who should be tested. Muflihatul Muniroh and nine co-authors ran a 113 gene panel in 2025 on 159 people from fifty-five families with cancer histories, including relatives still healthy. Breast cancer dominated the family stories.

Harmful variants turned up in about nineteen percent of families, spread across eight genes, and most positive families were confirmed as hereditary cases. Early onset cancers carried the variants far more often than late onset ones, fifty-four against fifteen percent. Unaffected relatives also carried findings that change their care. The authors say the data gives Indonesian clinics a first local base for testing rules.
pmc-12712047:
Milk thistle is a top-selling medicinal plant, and it asks little water, a virtue in dry northwest Iran. Jafar Ghaffarzadeh and co-authors test how irrigation and living fertilizers shape the plant's growth and chemistry. Their two-year field trial near Lake Urmia crossed two watering regimes with five fertilizer options.

Full irrigation and no irrigation formed the main split, while subplots ranged from no fertilizer to a combined nitrogen, phosphorus, and potash biofertilizer. The pairing of water and fertilizer mattered most for total yield, seed head count, and antioxidant strength. Biofertilizers improved most measured traits over the untreated control. The authors frame the crop as a way to shift the region from thirsty crops to low-water ones, raising farmer income while easing pressure on the shrinking lake.
pmc-12712547:
Ibrahim Canbey, Tulay Ozcan, and Ozan Gurbuz review how plant essential oils interact with fermented foods in a 2025 paper. Yogurts, pickles, and cured meats rely on lactic acid bacteria, yet the helpful microbes die off fast, shortening shelf life. Aromatic plant oils bring strong scents plus antibacterial, antifungal, and antioxidant powers. The review asks what happens when the two meet in one product.

The oils can suppress spoilage germs and pathogens while, at the right dose, sparing or even supporting the starter cultures. Pairing them with prebiotics may stretch probiotic survival further. Dose is the tightrope: too much oil can kill the very bacteria the food needs. The authors map the evidence for formulators.
pmc-12712847:
Hesti Lina Wiraswati and colleagues test a lab-made compound against a stubborn breast cancer type, in this study from twenty twenty-five. The cancer is luminal B, nearly forty percent of breast cancers, and hard to treat well. The compound, pyrazoline B, had already hurt several cancer cell lines. Here it faced BT-474 cells, a standard model of this subtype.

The compound hit from several sides at once. It froze the cell cycle by cutting a key growth protein, lowered two growth signal receivers, and killed cells through oxidative stress by a route that skips the usual executioner enzymes. Paired with the standard drug paclitaxel, it strengthened the drug's brake on growth and movement. Computer forecasts of how the body would handle it looked better than for paclitaxel. The authors name it a multi-target lead, with animal tests the clear next step.
pmc-12714247:
Ariyan Ayati Firoozabadi and co-authors join two ills in one grand count in a 2025 review. One ill is a fat-clogged liver; the next is a slow neck gland. Each is wide spread, and lore hints each feeds the next.

The team pooled near thirty-nine million souls from past work. A slow gland nearly doubled the odds of a fat liver, and of its worse scar form. The link held for the mild, half-woke form of the slow gland. Turn the pair round and the fat liver also nearly doubled the odds of a slow gland. Near all in the pool were women, a skew the authors own as a cap on how far the marks reach. They urge joint care of the two ills and more work on the root they share.
pmc-12714847:
Gjermund Almås, Martin Stangebye, Lars Slørdal, and Olav Spigset track drug company mailings to Norwegian doctors over two decades in 2025.
