Written promotion to general practitioners must meet legal rules. Past studies doubted the honesty of such material. The team checked mailings from three periods: 2004, 2012, and 2023-24. Claims were matched against cited sources and the law.

Mailing counts fell sharply over time. The share of claims judged correct and clinically apt rose from under half to over three quarters. Common faults were vague claims, claims beyond the cited source, and missing sources. Conflict notes held steady near sixty percent of references. The authors urge continued skepticism despite real gains.
pmc-12715247:
Fardin Talebi Sarokolai and Yousef Shiri describe a new additive for drilling fluids in this 2025 study. Drilling deep wells in hot, salty ground is hard on the mud that cools the drill bit and carries rock chips up. The pair built tiny particles with a mineral core and a special polymer coat, then mixed them into a clay-based fluid.

Tests showed the mix flowed better and held its shape under heat. Fluid loss through the well wall fell by about a third in mild tests, and the mud cake left behind grew much thinner. The fluid also stayed stable in very salty water and after rounds of hot aging. The coated particles beat the plain polymer on gel strength and salt tolerance, which points to use in deep, harsh wells.
pmc-12715947: Candela Romano and nine co-authors published a correction in 2025 to their review comparing synthetic and biological mesh in keyhole hernia repair. Three figures in the review had appeared in wrong form. The notice replaces those figures and prints the old and new versions side by side for openness. The corrected figures are the forest plots of risk ratios for recurrence, complications, and adverse events, plus the funnel plots used to check for publication bias. The original review itself has been updated.
pmc-12716547:
Lakew Mussie, G Mutwiri, and Amanuel Yoseph set out a 2025 protocol for a review of rheumatoid arthritis among older adults in Canada. The disease is a long term autoimmune condition that swells joints, causes pain, and erodes function. It hits older adults hard, yet Canadian proof on how common it is in this group, and what drives it, is scattered.

The planned review will pool past studies to estimate the overall rate in adults aged 60 and older. It will also name the key factors tied to the disease, and test for gaps between ethnic groups. The team will search six databases plus grey sources, for studies from 2000 to late 2025. Two reviewers will screen, extract, and grade each study on their own. The protocol fixes those rules in advance, so the later review can be checked.
pmc-12717047:
Lorenzo Maso and co-authors build antibodies that turn a cancer drug's mark on a tumor protein into an immune target. The drug sotorasib sticks to KRAS G12C, a common cancer driver, but tumors often resist it over time. Fragments of the drug-tagged protein appear on cell surfaces as neoantigens, though in tiny counts. Their 2025 study first measured those fragments directly with mass tools.

One engineered antibody grips the tagged fragment with extreme strength and holds it on the surface far longer. That boost let T cells kill resistant cancer cells in dishes and in animals. A second antibody covers a wider set of tissue types and a second drug. Structure work explains how the grip breaks old limits.
pmc-12717247:
Jenny Geiger and co-authors modelled cell death in a 2025 study of how mitochondria vary in their response. A key step in apoptosis opens the outer membrane of mitochondria. When only a few open, the cell may survive and cancer risk can rise; when a few escape, cancer cells may recover.

The team built a particle model of a full cell, tuned with lab data, covering a small set of interacting proteins. Random effects strongly pushed small, broken mitochondria toward opening under low stress. Under high stress, small ones were more likely to escape. Measures of real mitochondria sizes in lab cases matched the model, supporting a real role for chance.
pmc-12717347:
Muffato and co-authors study how people explore a new place and what they remember of its layout, in a 2025 psychology study. Survey knowledge is the map-like grasp of how places relate, and it varies widely between people. A sample of 234 adults explored a virtual city freely inside an immersive display. The team measured how often each person revisited spots and how widely they roamed.

Women revisited and roamed less than men on average. People who felt confident and enjoyed exploring revisited less, and joystick familiarity helped people roam wider. Exploration style helped explain the link between those traits and accuracy on a map drawing task. Spatial working memory also predicted map accuracy directly. The results show free exploration is a skill with its own habits.
pmc-12717747:
A retraction notice withdraws a rat study on healing taste buds after nerve injury. The study had tested whether parcels from bone marrow stem cells, alone or with zinc, could restore a taste bud area after both glossopharyngeal nerves were cut. After publication, concerns arose about the images.

In one figure, parts of a micrograph appeared to overlap. In another, two graphs seemed to overlap while claiming to show different conditions. The authors could not answer the concerns well enough, and the editor lost trust in the results. Five authors disagreed with the withdrawal, while three did not reply. Readers should not rely on the reported healing claims.
pmc-12717847:
Green and coauthors ask how elephant seals change their dives when food is rich. Past studies gave mixed views on that link. Sex, sea habitat, and study scale all seemed to shift the result. A core snag is that food gain at sea is hard to gauge as dives unfold.

The team built a large set of dive records from 609 seals over many years. Shifts in body fat gave a proxy for food gain on each trip. They tracked dive time, rest time, and swim speed. Seals changed dives in the same way when food gain rose. Sex and habitat did not change that core pattern.
pmc-12717947:
Özlem Bakan Demirel and Hatice Yıldız test staged sex counsel in a 2025 trial of women on birth control. The staged plan grants talk room step by step, from plain leave to speak up to full care for hard cases. Two-stage in shape, the trial first screened a large group of women with a set score for sex function.

A round hundred with scores in the ill range split into counsel and plain arms. The score was read again a year on to see if the talk held its gains. The plan is cheap and needs no drug. Health teams gain a year-long check on talk as cure.
pmc-12719347:
Most stroke patients arrive awake, but about one in eight arrives with clouded consciousness. Palazzo and co-authors study that group in a 2025 single-center cohort paper covering more than six thousand ischemic stroke patients admitted over eighteen years. They ask where such strokes sit, what causes them, and how the patients fare.

Strokes in the upper brainstem, the thalamus, or the temporal lobes most often clouded awareness. The pattern also tracked with damage in several territories at once, strokes at the back of the brain, right-sided strokes, and unwitnessed onset. These patients were more often misdiagnosed at first. Body temperature and blood pressure related to the symptom in a U-shaped way. Outcomes at three months and survival at a year were compared after adjustment, completing a clinical portrait of a high-risk presentation.
pmc-12721547:
Wunderlich and co-authors survey people who took part in studies where healthy volunteers are infected on purpose with a germ that causes diarrhea. Such studies help test vaccines and treatments, but they raise clear ethical questions. The 2025 survey covers 48 past volunteers at one Baltimore research center, from studies run between 2009 and 2020.

Most volunteers said they were glad they joined and would do so again. They praised the staff, the pay, and the food most often. Before joining, many rated the study as risky, but after finishing they rated that same risk lower. Most were Black or African American, and many had low incomes, a fact the authors report in full. On balance, volunteers judged the benefits to outweigh the harms.
pmc-12722647:
Gloria Vaghi and co-authors report a real-world study from 2025 on a drug used to treat migraine attacks as they happen. The study, called DART, ran in sixteen headache centers in Italy. It asked how well the drug worked and how well people bore it outside a strict trial.

Fifty-eight people took part and logged one hundred attacks in a phone diary. They noted pain at the start and then every half hour for two hours after each dose. About one third were free of pain at two hours, and those who treated a mild or mild-to-strong attack did best. The paper also tracks side effects, so readers can judge both gain and cost in daily care.
pmc-12722747:
Yukang Zeng and co-authors map the gene spread of a prized edible fungus and build ID cards for its strains. The fungus breeds without sex, so strains blur and rights over new strains are hard to guard. Their 2025 study re-reads the full gene code of thirty-six stock strains and sorts them by shared marks. Three mark types are used: lone swaps, swap clusters, and small gaps.

At a two-group split, strain kinship stands out clean and matches tree and plot checks. Core mark sets are picked for each type, just over two hundred marks in all. Cards built from mixed sets tell strains apart, though near twins score near full match. The cards give growers and breeders a firm way to name and guard stock.
pmc-12723847:
Fareeda Abo-Rass and Jesse Bump argue that academic publishing quietly polices which truths global health may speak, in this comment from twenty twenty-five. Peer review is meant to guard rigor. For scholars from marginalized and colonized communities, the authors say, it also guards the vocabulary, and with it the reality, that journals will print.

Their case is concrete: an article recommended for publication was then pressed by editors to swap politically accurate terms about Palestinians for state-approved labels. They read this language policing as control over knowledge itself. The cost is an evidence base that edits out occupation, violence, and segregation, the very forces shaping health, and wears the edit as neutrality. The authors demand structural change: protect scholars' right to name their own communities' experience, and treat political conditions as data, not as bias.
pmc-12723947:
Teferi Mekonnen and eleven co-authors track how survival with Down syndrome has changed across half a century in Norway, in this 2025 study. Using linked national registries covering more than three million births from 1967 to 2018, they compared people with Down syndrome against everyone else up to age forty. About one in a thousand births carried the diagnosis.

Survival improved markedly across the decades, yet a gap remained in every cohort, widest before age five. Babies born in the earliest decade faced over six times the mortality risk of those born in the latest one, with each later cohort stepping down. Low birth weight raised risk at every age. Being born into a below-median income household or having siblings also raised risk, and the income effect grew stronger after childhood. The authors show progress and inequality side by side.
pmc-12725547:
Adila Dias and co-authors test whether a red cell enzyme flaw raised COVID risk in the Brazilian Amazon, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Near four thousand men from four health data systems were tracked. Two hundred six carried the confirmed flaw.

No clear tie showed for catching the virus, hospital care, or death. Age drove all outcomes, as elsewhere. One ethnic group showed higher catch odds in the data. The team calls for care with ethnic and gene mix in such studies. Regions rich in the flaw need not fear it for this virus. Readers get a big, calm negative from a high-flaw region.
pmc-12727747:
Andrew Snelling and co-authors described in 2025 how they built a register of pregnancies inside a large British health database. Records based research is vital for pregnancy, since pregnant women are often left out of trials, and a clean register makes such research far easier.

The team linked GP records to hospital data and used a three stage method to find pregnancy episodes and their start dates. The register holds more than 279,000 pregnancies in about 267,000 women, for outcomes recorded from late 2020 to late 2022. Most were deliveries with live births, and about one in six ended in loss. Loss rates varied by ethnic group. Most records came from hospital maternity data.
pmc-12727847:
Roni Kankaristo and seven co-authors count and explain a rare birth defect of the colon. Their 2025 Finnish study covers colonic atresia, a blocked segment of large bowel in newborns. National registers supplied cases from 2004 to 2017. Five matched controls stood against each case.

Thirty-six cases appeared in the registers. Total prevalence ran near zero point four five per ten thousand births. Half the babies carried other anomalies as well. About a fifth were lost to termination or newborn death. Maternal diabetes showed a link to the defect. Rates held steady across the study years. Small numbers demand care, but registers give this rarity a full national picture.
pmc-12729247:
Phosphorus is hard for lentil plants to get from soil, yet they need it to grow and set seed. Ankita Chakraborty, Arpita Das, and Joydeep Banerjee catalogued a family of enzymes in lentil that help free phosphorus, in a 2025 study. They found 22 such genes spread across the plant's chromosomes, studied their shapes and control regions, and compared them with the same family in soybean, rice, and a model weed.

Most of the proteins appear built for export out of the cell, and their control regions carry switches tied to hunger signals for phosphorus. The authors say the catalogue points to genes worth testing for breeding hardier lentils.
pmc-12729347:
Ten authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five on marital status and outcomes in older patients with a very early lung cancer. The cancer is small cell lung cancer caught at the smallest stage, in patients aged seventy and older. Marital status can shape the support a patient has for hard treatment choices.

From a national cancer database covering two thousand to two thousand twenty-one, the team took one thousand three hundred ninety-one such patients. Analysis tied sex, marital status, and receiving surgery or chemotherapy to overall survival. After matching the groups to even out other factors, widowed patients lived shorter lives than married ones on both measures used.
pmc-12729447:
Justin Touchon and Myra Hughey raise young treefrogs under three housing setups to see how captive conditions shape growth and microbes. One group lived in natural style boxes in groups. A second group lived in cleaned boxes in groups, and a third lived alone in cleaned boxes.

Frogs were raised for more than eight months, with growth tracked and samples taken from feces, gut, and skin. Frogs housed in groups grew fastest, and natural style housing also improved survival. Microbe diversity on skin and in gut did not vary much with housing, but fecal diversity did. Community make up varied most by sample type, then by housing and time.
pmc-12729647:
Kamil Bijowski and co-authors test whether zinc can guard rat jawbone against cadmium in a 2025 study. Cadmium is a toxic metal that builds up in bone and stirs harmful oxygen stress. Rats drank water with cadmium levels like moderate to high human exposure for a full year, with or without extra zinc.

Cadmium alone weakened the bone's antioxidant defences and damaged its DNA, proteins, and fats. Extra zinc, raising intake by at least seventy percent, blocked the metal's build-up in the jawbone. It also kept the oxidative balance steady and spared the cell building blocks. The authors offer this as first proof that zinc intake can blunt long-term cadmium harm to this bone.
pmc-12729747:
Yiran Wang and co-authors study a gene that holds back fat formation in cattle, in a 2025 paper. The gene, SCD5, was tested in young fat cells from Xinjiang Brown cattle, a breed valued for meat quality.

Turning the gene up slowed cell growth and cut fat storage, along with the master fat genes. Turning it down did the reverse. The gene acts through a signaling route: more SCD5 meant less of the messenger WNT5B, which in turn lowered the pathway's main switch. Silencing that messenger reproduced the downstream effect. The authors name SCD5 a new brake on fat cell development in livestock. The finding could inform breeding and feeding for marbling.
pmc-12729847:
Vastolo and Cutrignelli review studies on feeding farm animals forage grown in water rather than soil. Hydroponic sprouts, mostly barley, promise fresh feed with little land. The review covered 28 studies that met standard reporting rules.

Barley sprouts ran rich in protein but held much water and little dry matter. Dairy cows on the feed made milk with better fat profiles at the same yield. Buffalo cheese quality rose, though costs rose too. Sheep and goats did well at moderate shares of the diet, and lambs on the feed emitted less methane. The authors call the forage a useful supplement, not a full replacement.
pmc-12731247:
Sicheng Huang and co-authors track, in 2025, what predicts relapse in a rare scarring disease around the kidneys and aorta. Ninety-six patients with idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis were followed for a median of two and a half years, with visits every few months recording symptoms, labs, and treatment.

Twenty-one patients relapsed, and the cumulative risk climbed steeply with time. A swollen kidney at diagnosis predicted relapse strongly, and stopping maintenance therapy tripled the hazard. Steroid treatment during maintenance protected against relapse, with dose mattering too. Among swollen-kidney patients, quitting steroids raised relapse further. The authors back long, low-dose steroid maintenance.
pmc-12732047:
Zicheng Huang and co-authors map a research field in this 2025 paper. Fatty liver disease tied to metabolism now affects about a quarter of people worldwide. Fatty acids from food may help treat it without drugs. The team counted and charted more than four thousand five hundred papers on the topic.

Output peaked in 2022, with China publishing most and the United States holding the most influence. Early work chased disease mechanisms such as insulin resistance. Recent work runs clinical trials of omega-3 and short-chain fatty acids. The authors see the field moving into proof-testing. They point to less-studied oils and fatty acid types as next frontiers.
pmc-12732247:
Young-Hwa Hwang and co-authors survey the global state of cultured meat technology to forecast when it can be industrialized. Published in 2025, the review draws on papers, patents, regulations, and media reports from 2023 to 2025. Cultured meat has moved from early lab concepts to approvals and first sales in a few places.

Asia leads as a hub, with China, Japan, South Korea, and Singapore strong on scaffold cultures and serum free media. The United States pairs advanced tech with a clear approval path, though state bans loom. Europe and the United Kingdom stress defined media and structured novel food rules. The authors expect premium and hybrid products first, with whole cuts staying premium into the early 2030s.
pmc-12732447:
Aleutian disease devastates farmed mink, and Ilona Mazurkiewicz, Andrzej Jakubczak, and Marek Kowalczyk hunt for gene variants that might confer resistance. Their candidate is a gene involved in immune response and virus handling. They sequenced its eight exons in fifty farmed mink from Latvia and twenty wild mink from Poland, and checked the animals for viral DNA.

Two variants turned up. One swaps a building block in the protein and is predicted to moderately change its function; the other is silent. Both appear in farmed and wild animals, but one allele was nearly twice as common in farmed mink. The authors propose the gene as a candidate for breeding programmes that select for disease resistance. They frame the results as a first characterisation meant to guide molecular selection, not yet proof of protection.
pmc-12732647:
Shouxia Xiao, Yuelin Hu, Xin Wang, and Hongsong Yu published a review in twenty twenty-five on epigenetic mechanisms in autoimmune thyroid diseases. The group covers Hashimoto's thyroiditis, which lowers thyroid function, and Graves' disease, which raises it. Genes alone do not explain these diseases; environment matters too.

Epigenetic changes sit between genes and environment, reshaping how genes are read without changing the DNA itself. The review covers DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs, and how each steers disease course. Because these marks can be measured and sometimes reversed, the authors present them as tools for earlier diagnosis and more personal treatment.
pmc-12733047:
Vela Sancho and co-authors report that a cell-grip protein runs high in the blood cells of people with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, in a 2025 study. MS inflames and strips the insulation from nerves, and it strikes women three times as often as men, though men often fare worse. A signaling protein called pleiotrophin runs high in these patients. The team measured the gene activity of its receptors in blood immune cells from patients and healthy people.

One receptor gene, ITGB3, was clearly overactive in patients' cells. Computer docking then showed the signal protein could latch onto that receptor, held by metal ions, even more tightly than the receptor's usual partner. The authors suggest this receptor is actively tuned in the disease and may carry the signal's inflammatory push in the blood.
pmc-12733147:
João Oliveira and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on checking pacemakers from home versus in the clinic. Pacemakers can send their data remotely, which saves patients a trip. In Portugal, the state pays for patient transport, and those trips cost a great deal each year. The team asked whether remote checks pay off at one district hospital.

They surveyed forty-one patients who used paid transport for clinic visits. They compared the transport bills with the cost of the remote equipment, and asked patients how they felt about each route. Small studies like this test whether a policy that looks good on paper works for real patients, whose views decide whether remote care gets used at all.
pmc-12733247:
Heavy coursework tires the minds of online students, but feeling that a course is worth taking fights back, finds a 2025 survey study. The authors collected complete responses from 415 online undergraduates in the United States and modeled how demand, course value, engagement, and mental fatigue connect.

Demand raised fatigue directly. Course value lowered it in a roundabout way, by lifting engagement, and engagement itself cut fatigue. The authors suggest colleges can protect students by tuning workload, making the point of each course plain, and designing for involvement. They frame the advice as both a teaching and a public health matter.
pmc-12733347:
Michal Markiewicz and co-authors relate blood factors to quality of life in progressive supranuclear palsy in a 2025 study. The disease, an atypical parkinsonism, brings eye movement failure, falls, stiffness, and thinking problems. Swelling in the brain may drive it, though cause and effect stay unclear. The team measured swelling and growth factors in eleven patients and ten controls.

One growth factor, GDNF, told the story: lower blood levels tracked with worse clinical scores and worse quality of life ratings. The swelling factors showed no such links. The authors stress the small sample and call for larger studies before any clinical use.
pmc-12733447:
Yuping Jiang and a team of co-authors isolate a fungus living inside ragweed and show it boosts tomato growth. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Ragweed is a tough invader, and the microbes that evolved inside it may carry useful traits.

The fungus, a Chaetomium strain named V3, was identified by shape and DNA. Tomato plants treated with it grew taller, with longer and more branched roots and greener leaves. Fruit yield rose, and the fruit carried more vitamin C and lycopene. The strain makes plant hormones itself and switches on tomato genes that answer to those hormones. The authors offer it as a candidate growth promoter for farming.
pmc-12735147:
Mega Septiana and five co-authors checked lung function in one hundred Indonesian children who had recovered from COVID-19, in this 2025 study. Reports on children's lungs after the infection are still rare. The children, aged five to eighteen, took breathing tests, and the team weighed factors from illness severity to nutrition.

Nearly half showed impaired lung function, mostly a restrictive pattern where the lungs cannot fully expand. About eighteen percent had long COVID, with fatigue the most common complaint. Lingering symptoms nearly doubled the odds of a bad breathing test. Being undernourished and having had moderate-to-critical illness each raised the odds about fivefold. The authors call for follow-up studies to confirm the links and find the mechanisms.
pmc-12735347:
Hong Zheng and co-authors test how a pipeline steel breaks under mixed pulls. Their 2025 study uses L360QS steel, a tough grade that resists cracking from sour gases. It is seeing more use in pipe networks, yet its fracture behavior has been little studied.

Bars of many shapes were pulled, sheared, and pressed to cover a wide span of stress states. A computer model then read off the strain at which each break began. The team built a two-part rule that matched fresh tests within five percent. The curve of a notch shaped the results most of all shape traits. The rule feeds safety checks for pipes on steep slopes.
pmc-12735447: Daniele Orsucci, writing alone, reviews the genetics of movement disorders in a 2025 paper, drawing lessons from essential tremor. Movement disorders form a mixed group of brain conditions shaped by genes and environment together. The piece uses essential tremor, one of the most common of these conditions, as the lens for what genetic studies have and have not delivered.
pmc-12735647:
Min Li and co-authors report a 2025 study on making better organic solar cells. Most high-performing cells use a polymer that pairs an electron donor part with an electron acceptor part, but that design loses too much voltage. The team built a new polymer, called M1, that joins two acceptor parts instead, giving it lower energy levels and broader light absorption.

When a small amount of M1 was added as a guest material to a standard cell blend, the films formed a better structure for splitting and moving charge. The resulting device reached a power conversion efficiency of 19.70 percent and held up better in light. The work offers a practical route to stronger, steadier solar cells.
pmc-12736047:
Wei Fan and co-authors test whether tiny sacs shed by a lung germ can shield mice from harm. The study appeared in 2025. The germ can cause deep liver sores, lung harm, and death. Its shed sacs had shown promise as a base for a new shot.

Shots of the sacs shielded up to four in five mice from the germ. Gene data hinted the shield works through immune cell shifts. Lab and live tests bore that out. The sacs steered one immune cell type toward a calm state and shaped helper cell growth. The team checked the shifts with gene, stain, and blood tests.
pmc-12736147:
Yulianna Minutti-Calva and co-authors studied extracts of the horsetail plant Equisetum hyemale in 2025. The plant has a long folk medicine history. The team soaked its aerial parts in three solvents and mapped the chemistry of each extract.

The extracts scavenged one standard radical target strongly, yet fought bacteria poorly. They showed moderate kill power against liver and colon cancer cell lines. In worm tests, the extracts cut survival after two hours of exposure. Computer docking found strong binding of two plant compounds to a bacterial enzyme target. Safety and uptake predictions round out the profile for drug work.
pmc-12736447:
The authors detect conveyor roller faults with a transformer framework in a 2025 paper. Belt conveyor rollers fail quietly before they fail loudly. Existing monitoring scales poorly and detects late. Cheap sound and vibration sensors offer another route.

Their system, MIRA, learns normal patterns without fault labels. A masked transformer autoencoder reconstructs healthy signals. Deviations in reconstruction flag anomalies automatically. The framework also infers which roller is failing. A custom testbed carried sensors at each roller station. Four fault types were tested across fourteen locations and six belt speeds. Detection accuracy approached ninety-nine percent overall. Localization accuracy topped ninety-six percent. Variable conditions did not break the system. Spatially aware alerts let crews target repairs precisely. The authors pitch the approach for industrial conveying at scale.
pmc-12736547:
Vienna has tracked pollen in its air for decades, and one city tree leaves a clear record in that data. Maximilian Bastl and co-authors use 48 years of pollen counts, from 1976 to 2023, in a 2025 study of the tree of heaven, an imported tree now common across Austria. They matched the counts with city weather records.

The tree's pollen season runs from early June to mid July, with a peak near mid June. Over the study years the season grew more intense as the climate warmed. Heat and hours of sunshine had a direct effect on flowering in the city trees. The authors link the shift to climate change and warn of harder pollen and allergy seasons ahead for city residents.
pmc-12736847:
Collins Dormena, Obed Appiah, and Taher Ghomian sense a stubborn pollutant with carbon nanotubes in a 2025 paper. The target, PFOA, is a forever chemical that will not react or glow, so labs need pricey gear to find it in water. Carbon tubes shift their electric flow when molecules land on them, which makes them fine noses for such quiet compounds.

Their sensor lines a few tubes across gold gaps rather than a messy net, which keeps the read steady. More PFOA in the water dropped the device's resistance in a clean trend. A small gate voltage pulled the charged molecules in and lifted sensitivity near ten fold. Wave tests gave each compound its own mark, which aids picking PFOA out of a mix.
pmc-12736947:
Eberto Rodríguez and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-five, new cassava varieties bred for better nutrition in Colombia. Cassava is a starchy root crop. Boosting its pro-vitamin A content can help cut vitamin A deficiency in at-risk people. The team grew five yellow-fleshed types with higher beta-carotene, the orange pigment the body turns into vitamin A. They tested them at four sites in the Cauca River Valley and the Pacific region. Checks covered yield, farm traits, and cooking quality.

Two types stood out, one for each region. Both matched or beat the local check varieties and adapted well to their zones. Their roots held high carotene levels, low toxic cyanide levels, and cooked in under half an hour. The team proposes them for release as new varieties.
pmc-12737547:
Christian Poitras and Benoit Coulombe use artificial intelligence to predict which human cell surface proteins the H5N1 bird flu virus may grab onto. The virus's surface spike, hemagglutinin, decides which hosts and tissues it can enter, mainly by binding sugars on cells but perhaps also specific proteins. Since 2023 the virus has spread widely in birds, spilled into mammals including cattle, and infected a few people, raising pandemic concern.

Their pipeline blends structural modeling, interaction prediction, and biological filtering to rank likely protein partners of the spike. Such partners could help explain how the virus enters cells and picks its targets. They would also be candidates for lab testing and for drug design aimed at blocking entry. The authors stress the output is prediction, not proof: each candidate needs experiments. They present the work as a way to speed the hunt for host factors in high-risk flu viruses.
pmc-12738547:
Junrui Liu and others put out a 2025 chemistry study showing a molecular attraction missed before. Alkynes are triple-bonded carbon units used widely. Their sideways pulls were largely unmapped. Two cage-shaped metal mixes provided the test bed. Crystal builds showed a surprise stacking pattern.

Shake signals shifted just as foretold. Computer work showed a real interaction. A data bank search found it in hundreds of crystals. The force is weaker than classic ring stacking, yet it shapes traits. Its shake signature could flag useful builds. Imaging probes might exploit the signal too. A missing piece of how molecules are built is now named.
pmc-12738647:
Bowman compares the mouthpart dentition of seventeen free-living mite species from bird nests, in a study from twenty twenty-five. These astigmatan mites share one commensal community. Explaining their coexistence requires knowing how each one feeds. Bowman decomposed the chewing digit patterns into functional groups.

Two morphotypes emerged: hook-like tearing digits and nibbling digits. The default chewing surface design is described in fine detail, likened to fine grinding grades. Angles of the surface features suggest adaptation to aggregate material. Various species show gripping, bladed, scooping, or scraping specializations. One species is classed a crusher, another a chewer, and some approach saw designs. Miniaturization, Bowman notes, limits how far feeding designs can diverge. The atlas explains how seventeen species partition one small habitat.
pmc-12738747:
Linxiu Qu and Lujun Li measured how cooling towers lose water as wind-blown mist, in this 2025 study. In mechanical draft wet towers, fans pull air through falling water to cool it, and some droplets escape with the exhaust. That escaped fraction, the drift ratio, decides how much water a plant wastes and how far chemical mist spreads.

Using a model tower and absorbent filter paper to catch the escapees, they ran ninety-six experiments varying the hardware and the flow. Drift rose in a curved, non-linear way with air speed, and nozzle size mattered most of all: small nozzles behaved differently from large ones as wind increased. Water density and air speed also regulated each other's effects. The authors fitted a three-variable prediction model. Tower operators can use it to pick settings and nozzles that keep the water, and the cooling, in balance.
pmc-12739147:
Seven authors, led by He Yiping, wrote this 2025 paper on squeezing more oil from a tight reservoir in the Jiyuan oilfield. The Geng 60 area holds an ultra-low permeability reservoir, rock that lets oil move only with great effort. Uneven rock quality has made water flooding harder year by year, and more wells now produce water.

The team based their plan on the reservoir's architecture, its inner layout of rock layers. They built a set of linked methods tuned to that layout. The set covers mapping the best rock zones, fine control of injection and output, plugging water paths, reshaping flow profiles, and enhanced recovery steps. The paper sums up the methods and judges how each one performed. Its aim is steady oil output while water rise is held back.
pmc-12739847:
A gut parasite that shrugs off the standard drug yields more when friendly bacteria join the attack. Mona Mohamed and co-authors prove the pairing in dishes and mice, in work from twenty twenty-five. The parasite is common and its harm debated, yet infections linger. Three arms were run: drug, bacteria, and both.

In dishes, the pair cut parasite counts and life by about ninety-five percent, past either arm alone. In mice, stool cysts fell near ninety-nine percent on the pair. Gut tissue healed best there too, and flare signals fell most. Probiotics earn a supporting role, the authors conclude.
pmc-12739947:
Wenjian Li reviews drugs that block the interleukin-4 signaling axis in type 2 inflammatory diseases, published in 2025. This immune pathway drives conditions from eczema and asthma to nasal polyps and a swollen esophagus. Antibodies against the shared receptor, above all dupilumab, shut down two signals at once, interleukin-4 and interleukin-13. Trials and real-world studies show better disease scores, improved lung function, and fewer severe flare-ups across the indications.

Not every patient responds, and primary resistance occurs. Side effects are usually manageable but distinctive: injection site reactions in up to a fifth of patients, eye inflammation in eczema patients, colds, and temporary rises in eosinophil counts. The author points to biomarker monitoring, dual-target antibodies, and precision dosing as the next refinements. The review gives clinicians an evidence map for a drug class still expanding into new diseases.
pmc-12740847:
Hyemin Jeong and a large team of co-authors published this microbiome study in 2025 on ankylosing spondylitis, a long-lasting inflammatory disease of the spine. Gut microbes are suspected of feeding the immune dysfunction behind it. The team sequenced stool samples from 44 patients and 50 healthy controls, then compared the microbial mixes and checked them against how active each patient's disease was.

Overall diversity was similar between patients and controls, but the mix differed. Patients carried more Proteobacteria, including Escherichia types, and fewer of several groups seen as beneficial. Among patients, those with highly active disease had lower gut diversity than those with quiet disease. One genus, Coprobacter, rose in step with two standard disease activity scores. The authors suggest it as a possible marker for tracking the disease.
pmc-12741847:
Xinjing Chen and Jingxuan Hong test a blood protein as a forecasting marker for heart patients who had artery-opening treatment, in work from 2025. The protein reins in a cell signal path and shapes immune cell balance. Prior work tied its loss to worse artery disease.

The study held 173 patients with acute coronary syndrome and thirty-two healthy adults. Protein levels ran lower in patients than in healthy adults, then rose a month after treatment. Higher levels went with fewer of one inflammatory T cell kind. The team also tracked fitness scores and major heart events after care. They propose the protein as a cheap aid for judging outlook in this group.
pmc-12742147:
Selamawit Girma Tadesse and co-authors measure how common sexual dysfunction is among new mothers visiting a hospital in northwest Ethiopia. Problems with desire, arousal, or pain after childbirth are frequent yet often ignored. The team surveyed 420 postpartum women at Debre Tabor Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in spring 2024.

Using a standard questionnaire with a set cutoff, they found that about fifty-two percent of the women met the mark for sexual dysfunction. Several factors raised the odds. Women in paid work were more likely to report problems than housewives. A bad outcome in the recent pregnancy more than tripled the odds. Tears to the perineum during delivery doubled them, and depression nearly tripled them. The authors say the burden is high and largely hidden. They urge postpartum care to ask about sexual health directly and watch high-risk women more closely.
pmc-12743547:
Liver cancer is hard to treat, and a plant compound called rutin has shown anti-tumor hints. Weifeng Yao and co-authors study whether rutin fights liver cancer through ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and fat damage. They combine cell experiments with large public cancer data sets.

In lab dishes, rutin slowed liver cancer cell growth, movement, and division in step with dose. Data mining tied five genes to both rutin and the death pathway. A risk score built from those genes split patients into groups with clearly different outlooks, and it held up in two outside data sets. One gene stood out in single-cell data, and computer docking showed it binds rutin most stably. The authors propose the score as a tool for judging patient outlook.
pmc-12743847:
Yue Yu and four co-authors test a biologic drug, ustekinumab, in Crohn's disease, with a focus on cases limited to the small intestine, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Crohn's disease inflames the gut, and disease in the small bowel alone often needs stronger drugs and more surgery. Few studies had checked how well this drug works by disease site.

The team followed patients for a year, using scopes, scans, ultrasound, and lab tests to judge healing. They compared patients whose disease sat in the small bowel with those whose disease reached the large bowel. Outcomes included full remission, healing of the gut lining, and healing through the whole bowel wall. The study gives site-by-site evidence for planning care.
pmc-12745047:
CAR-T cell therapy raises response rates for people whose multiple myeloma returned or stopped responding to treatment. Only about one in five patients stays free of progression for five years. The authors used flow cytometry to track immune cells in the blood of fifty-three patients, sampling at cell collection, before infusion, and after the cells were given. They mapped how the CAR-T cells grew, counting over sixty-five populations at the peak near two weeks.

No feature of the CAR-T cells themselves predicted who stayed in remission. What mattered was the patient's immune state at cell collection, plus how much tumor was circulating before infusion. Combining these measures with disease stage gave a risk score that separated likely responders before treatment started. The authors conclude the patient's immune state and tumor burden shape long-term control more than the infused cells.
pmc-12745247:
Yingpin Cao and co-authors study glasses wear and focusing function in nearsighted adults with dry eye in a 2025 paper. Dry eye and focusing strain often travel together, and regular correction might ease both. The team compared adults who wore glasses regularly with those who wore them little or not at all.

Over one hundred patients had tear and focusing measures taken. Regular wearers showed longer tear break-up time and lower symptom scores, with no gap in tear height. Links between tear stability and focusing measures were also tested. The results support steady correction as part of dry eye care, not just vision care.
pmc-12745447:
Elif Zapsu proposes a view of the brain shaped by quantum physics and a sense of unity. The essay opens with Carl Jung's idea of one world that joins mind and matter. Zapsu asks who we are, and notes that labels for our traits can divide people and feed power struggles.

From that start, the paper sketches basic quantum ideas in plain terms, such as matter being mostly empty space and energy coming in small packets. It then links those ideas to the self, identity, and therapy. Zapsu writes as a psychologist without formal training in physics and admits that limit. The aim is to spark research on a post-material view of the mind and its use in care.
pmc-12745647:
Wenjing Liu, Ning Jiao, and six co-authors tune feed energy for a new green-shell laying hen. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, works with Wenshui hens at peak lay. No feeding standard exists yet for this breed. Six hundred hens, aged thirty-three weeks, split into five groups for a six-week trial.

Each group ate feed with a set energy level, from low to high. Output rose then fell as energy climbed, a curved pattern. The second-highest level gave the best laying output and nutrient use. Blood fats rose steadily with energy, while one mid-level group led on antioxidant strength. The results name a target energy for peak-lay diets of this breed.
pmc-12747947:
Neilmegh Varada, Olivia Yang, and David Savage report a melanoma patient hit by four immune side effects in this 2025 case report. The eighty-year-old man received a two drug checkpoint combination for stage four disease. A month in, his liver enzymes rose mildly. After the second cycle they worsened, eased on steroids, then flared past three times normal after the third. A rash appeared, and his thyroid failed. Treatment stopped and hormone replacement began. A month later he was admitted with heart failure from heart muscle inflammation.

Steroid tapers kept failing as the liver flared again. A second immune suppressant finally let him taper off fully. Liver, skin, and heart all recovered, and he moved to surveillance without further cancer therapy. The case shows how one patient's toxicities can stack and stagger over months.
pmc-12748247:
Frances Ouyang and seven co-authors review why the so called good cholesterol can go bad and fuel heart risk. High levels link to low heart risk, in part by pulling cholesterol from artery walls. Yet shape and task of the particles matter as much as count.

Swelling, from illness, habits, or harsh oxygen, can rework the particles into pro swelling forms that harm vessel walls. One charged form is a stark case. Pull strength may beat raw level as a risk mark. Care should aim at both count and quality of these particles.
pmc-12748547:
Siqing Xiang and colleagues improved ghost imaging under noise in 2025. Ghost imaging builds pictures from light patterns. Compressed sensing cuts the needed measurements. Noise usually degrades the final image. A Bayesian method was proposed here. Sparse coding used a learned dictionary.

A three-level graph structured the estimation. Messages passed between levels during solving. Simulations and bench tests both succeeded. Complex objects imaged accurately despite noise. Sampling stayed very low throughout. Solving ran faster than rival methods. Precision stayed high at the same time. Biomedical imaging is one suggested use.
pmc-12748647:
Eren Bas and Erol Egrioglu present a 2025 paper on forecasting that runs itself and can explain its choices. Practitioners dislike methods that demand subjective tuning at every step. The authors build their automation around a deep dendritic recurrent network, a brain-inspired model whose inputs can be tested one by one for real significance.

Significance tests decide which inputs enter the model, and validity tests check the fitted result, all framed as explainability tools. Simulations probed how well the tests behave. The full automatic method then faced famous forecasting rivals on the M3 and M4 competition series, thousands of real-world tracks from business and economics. The authors report a method that needs no hand-holding yet keeps its reasoning visible. Automation plus audit trails is the pitch.
pmc-12749047:
Xianyao Jiang, Yongjin Huang, Changwu Li, and Hongyan Jiang tracked a stomach germ in the throat in a 2025 study. The germ, Helicobacter pylori, was long tied to stomach ills, and hints said it may also help start head and neck cancer. They enrolled two hundred twenty high risk people and the same count of patients with that cancer.

The germ showed up more in the cancer group than in the high risk group. In high risk people, carrying it raised the odds of the cancer, and strains with strong harm genes raised the odds more. Patients who carried it saw more returns of the cancer and more deaths. The authors urge care teams to weigh throat carriage in risk checks.
pmc-12749747:
Zheng Wang and co-authors build an explainable AI that judges skin spot risk from full-body 3D photos plus medical facts, in a 2025 paper. Skin lesions vary wildly in look, and judging them taxes even experts. Black-box AI may score well yet leave doctors unable to see its reasons.

Using a public data set of 1,075 patients, the team extracted 41 clinical and lesion features and full-body 3D images. A plain regression model handled the facts, while image networks read the photos; explanation tools then showed which features and image areas drove each call. Image models reached about 87 percent accuracy on their test task. Transparent risk scores could help dermatology teams triage moles with more trust.
pmc-12749847:
Ephrem Habyarimana and six co-authors tested gene-based selection for iron and zinc in sorghum grain in a 2025 study. Breeding sorghum rich in these minerals is a cheap way to fight poor diets. Lab tests of grain are slow and costly, so gene forecasts can save time and money.

Forecasts that used many traits at once beat those using a single trait across tight breeding budgets. The biggest gain came when cheap, easy traits scored in a few places fed the model, rather than when the two target minerals were scored in more places and years. The authors say borrowing strength from easy traits can lift genetic gain per dollar and per season. The work suits programs with thin resources.
pmc-12750547:
Six authors present a study in two thousand twenty-five on predicting which emergency patients will come back. Return visits strain emergency departments, and the dangerous ones, ending in intensive care, arrest, or emergency surgery, matter most. Earlier prediction work leaned on fixed facts and rarely used changing vital signs.

Using records from a major Taiwan hospital across four years, the team built a hybrid deep learning model. It joins a temporal network for the vital-sign streams with a transformer for fixed facts like age and triage level. The model scored well at flagging the rare high-risk returns.
pmc-12750747:
Mohd Hazim Ahmad Fuad, Ely Zarina Samsudin, Nik Nairan Abdullah, and Ahmad Nazim Aimran set out a study protocol in twenty twenty-five on how hospital staff in Malaysia cope with workplace violence. Violence against health workers is a known hazard that harms mental health and care quality. The protocol centers on psychosocial safety climate, the degree to which a workplace guards mental well-being, and asks how it shapes coping.

The plan runs in two phases. First, a survey of at least four hundred forty workers in public hospitals will gauge safety climate, violence exposure, and coping styles with standard scales. Then, six to twelve workers with recent violence experience, drawn from high-climate wards, will be interviewed in depth. The two strands will be merged to guide climate-based steps that help staff cope and soften the impact of violence.
pmc-12751547:
Yeeun Jun and eleven co-authors edit a rice gene to resist bacterial blight in a 2025 study. The blight bacterium hijacks rice sugar-export genes, turning them into doors for infection. Knocking out one such gene, a SWEET family member, has protected other rice varieties.

The team used gene editing to disable the gene in Samkwang, an elite Korean variety. The edited line resisted the test strain better than the parent line. Gene activity scans showed defense genes quieter in the edited plants after infection, a sign the bacterium gained less foothold. The authors also chart plant traits to check for yield costs. Their care reflects a breeding rule: resistance must not drag down the harvest.
pmc-12751747:
Medical students and residents learn by treating real patients, but patients can refuse them, and refusals skew what trainees get to practice. Sarah de Bever and four co-authors review the literature on how outpatients feel about trainee care in this 2025 paper. They searched four databases through April 2024.

Of nearly nine thousand studies found, thirty-eight qualified, most of them surveys, and the average quality score was low. Two themes ran through them: satisfaction and willingness. Satisfaction was strikingly high, often above ninety percent, and most patients reported having accepted a trainee. Yet acceptance varied, and the review maps the factors that sway it. The authors aim the findings at clinics that want patients to welcome the doctors of tomorrow.
pmc-12751847:
Shabnam Shahabi Nejad and seven co-authors test whether the blood fluid of obese mice speeds aging in lean mice, in this twenty twenty-five study. Obesity brings long-term swelling in the body and early aging of cells. The team asked if factors carried in blood alone can pass that aging on.

Lean mice got weekly shots of pooled blood fluid from fat or lean donors for four weeks. The team then weighed fat pads and immune organs and read aging marks in fat tissue and blood cells. Genes tied to cell aging and swelling were also measured. The design tests blood as a carrier of obesity's aging effect.
pmc-12752047:
Nihan Kaya Acar, Enes Bardakci, Merve Pelin Dur Sarıgüzel, and Peris Celikel survey dental students in Türkiye in this 2025 study. The question is how clinical anxiety and self-confidence relate during the hands-on training years of dental school.

The cross-sectional survey reached 548 fourth and fifth year students across several faculties, about two thirds of them women. Each student rated ten items on anxiety and ten on confidence. Anxiety peaked around fear of making mistakes, named by nearly four in ten. The team used rank correlation to test how the two scales move together, aiming to help schools ease anxiety and build sound professional confidence.
pmc-12752347:
Yu Liu and co-authors published a 2025 study on gene activity in the livers of monkeys with obesity-related diabetes. The monkeys, cynomolgus macaques, are close models of human metabolism. The team read out which genes were active in liver cells from diabetic and healthy animals. They paid special attention to long non-coding RNAs, stretches of RNA that regulate other genes without making proteins.

Protein-coding and non-coding RNAs showed distinct patterns between the groups. The coding genes clustered in metabolic pathways, above all in fat transport. Genes for breaking down alcohol were turned down in the diabetic livers. The non-coding RNAs followed their own separate pattern, hinting they help steer the metabolic changes. The study widens the molecular picture of how obesity leads toward diabetes. The authors suggest the patterns could guide precision treatments aimed at specific RNA targets in the liver.
pmc-12752747:
Isamu Matake, Tomoya Yasujima, and co-authors pin a cell trash port as the urate exit from cell bins, in a 2025 study. Urate is the end waste of a food break path, and its build forms gout stones. Wall ports for urate were known, but bin clear paths stayed in the dark till now.

The port moves urate out of bins by a push from sour cell juice. Bench tests rate it as a low grip, high flow port for urate. In eater cells, less port slows clear of gout stone bits. Less port also cuts a fire chem tied to a food signal. Gout risk may ride on port health.
pmc-12752847:
Nolan Fox and co-authors report an unusual chest case in a 2025 paper. Their patient, a 68-year-old man with bladder cancer that had spread, came in with stubborn hiccups and chest pain. He also had a blocked urinary tract. Imaging showed fluid around one lung and signs of infection in that fluid.

Tests found germs in the fluid but no cancer cells, and the fluid's creatinine level topped that of his blood. That pattern marks a rare condition called urinothorax, where urine leaks into the chest space, here paired with an infected collection. Care drained the chest but did not fix the blockage, and the outcome was poor. The case warns against treating the leak alone.
pmc-12753547:
Danni Zhou and co-authors compare two ways of giving estrogen before frozen embryo transfer in a 2025 study. The hormone prepares the womb lining, and it can be swallowed as tablets or absorbed through the skin as a gel. Across 244 transfer cycles, 123 used tablets and 121 used gel.

Implantation and clinical pregnancy rates were statistically alike. The gel group showed a slightly higher live birth rate and lower miscarriage rate, though neither gap reached significance. Blood tests at twelve weeks showed clearly higher liver enzyme levels in the tablet group, since swallowed estrogen passes the liver first. The authors call the gel a safe, workable alternative.
pmc-12753747:
Ziwen Lv and four co-authors built a chart to predict sudden breathing failure in lung cancer patients, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Breathing failure is common after surgery and in cancer care, yet few tools forecast it for this group. They mined a large intensive care database for risk factors.

About a third of the patients in the data developed breathing failure. Ten factors fed the final chart, including clotting time, blood sugar, kidney markers, breathing and heart rates, lung disease, shock, and race. The chart sorted patients with fair accuracy, and repeat checks showed its risk estimates lined up well with real outcomes. The authors offer it for bedside use in judging individual risk.
pmc-12753847:
A nerve block beside the spine, called the erector spinae plane block, eases pain by bathing spinal nerve branches in local anesthetic under ultrasound guidance. Shengfang Du, Qianqian Xie, Tingting Liang, and Yinhua Feng reviewed its use for chronic pain in 2025. The technique began in acute care and spread because it is simple to perform and has a strong safety record.

The review walks through the anatomy behind the block, how it spreads across several segments, and the evidence in cancer pain and nerve pain. It also weighs the method's limits and unsettled questions. The authors aim to fix the block's place in chronic pain care and point to where trials should go next.
pmc-12754947:
Hang Zheng and co-authors compare rest patterns in taekwondo interval training. Their 2025 study puts 13 trained athletes through rounds of roundhouse kicks under two work-to-rest plans. One plan rests half as long as the work burst, the other five times as long.

Heart rate, oxygen use, blood lactate, and effort scores all climbed round by round under both plans. The oxy-fuelled share of energy grew across rounds while the sugar-fuelled share fell late. The long-rest plan kept heart rate, oxygen use, and effort lower throughout. Jump height tracked muscle fatigue between rounds. The authors offer the contrast as a guide for setting session design for coaches who use kick-based interval work.
pmc-12755747:
Divya Nair Narayanan and Samsiah Awang published a study protocol in two thousand twenty-five on measuring foot self-care in Malaysians with diabetes. Foot ulcers cost patients money and quality of life, and painless damaged feet mean problems get missed. Clinics lack a standard local tool to score how well patients care for their feet.

The protocol runs in two phases. First, the team drafts questions from the literature, checks them with experts, translates them, and pre-tests them with patients and clinic staff. Second, a pilot and a larger field test across urban and rural clinics will validate the tool. Scoring bands and their meanings will be set. The aim is a simple instrument for daily use.
pmc-12757247:
Sumin Kim, Jaehak Jeong, and Sojung Kim build a growth model for greenhouse cherry tomatoes under long heat stress. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Heat in glass houses cuts yields as the world warms, a key fear for this top Korean crop. Two breeds were grown in heat and their shape traits taped to feed a yield model, with cast warm paths laid in.

One breed put more growth in leaf and stem and bore less fruit share; the other bore more. In warm casts, the leaf-heavy breed gained yield while the fruit-heavy one lost. Its leaf mass kept food make high in heat. The team offer the model for yield casts.
pmc-12764247:
Hongxia Chai, Ruiting Ma, Feifei Cheng, Dandan Chen, and Yan Zhang compare pregnancy risks after lab-assisted conception with natural conception in two thousand twenty-five. The study is a matched look back at births in Lanzhou, China, from two thousand nineteen to two thousand twenty-four. Each assisted case was paired with a natural case by admission month and pregnancy length.

The assisted group had higher rates of twin or more pregnancies, anemia, and bleeding after birth. High blood pressure of pregnancy, pregnancy diabetes, and a liver bile condition also ran higher. The gaps held for single babies alone, bar one trait. The authors tie the added risk to embryo handling, hormone use, and the mothers' own health ground.
pmc-12766847:
Yona Lunsky and a large Canadian team set out the plan for testing a national brain health course for people with intellectual disabilities, in this protocol from twenty twenty-five. The course was built with this group, not just for it. Adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities face higher dementia risk than others, yet brain health programs usually leave them out.

The course, Brain Health-IDD, is a virtual class co-designed and co-taught by clinicians and people with lived experience. Three groups from across Canada will take it: adults with disabilities aged forty and up, family caregivers, and health and social care providers. Surveys and focus groups at the start, at course end, and three months later will track attendance, satisfaction, knowledge, and confidence. Health habits, wellbeing, and whether memory screening gets started are also on the list. Findings will be shared with advocacy and policy groups.
pmc-12767147:
Liang Chi and eight co-authors trace how a beef cow's body fat echoes in her calf's gut in a 2025 study. A cow's condition score grades her fat cover. Plump mothers may hand their calves a skewed gut flora and a stirred immune system, with costs that last past birth.

Dung and blood were drawn around calving from Hereford cows sorted by score. Gene reads of the gut flora showed the mothers' own flora barely moved with score. Calves told another tale: those of high-score cows carried more of a germ group tied to gut upset. Their blood also ran high on two swelling signals.
pmc-12767247:
Adam Burke, Adekunle Sanyaolu, and Amitabha Ray review how bacteria touch cancer, with a focus on a childhood kidney tumor, in this 2025 note. Bacteria can spark cancer, set the stage for it, infect patients during care, or supply parts for targeted drugs.

In children, gene faults drive most tumors, yet infections during care still drive much sickness and death. Drug designers pair a homing antibody with a bacterial toxin to strike cancer cells. The tumor in focus is Wilms tumor, the most common kidney cancer of childhood. Its key protein also shows up in many adult cancers. The note surveys the tumor's traits and its infection risks.
pmc-12768747:
Ana Carolina de Freitas Lopes and co-authors report on Brazil's national horizon scanning system for health technology, in a 2025 paper. The system hunts early signs of new health tools so the public system can plan. It grew from 2008 roots and settled inside the national assessment body in 2011.

Over one year, the team logged one hundred thirty-one scanning studies. Most backed calls on whether to adopt new tools into public care. Others fed court-order alerts, clinical guide updates, emergency readiness for threats like COVID-19 and mpox, and research funding picks. The authors call the system a key evidence source for state health planning.
pmc-12768847: Leidy Anne Teixeira and co-authors make a systematic review, in a 2025 paper, of the domains teams use to judge medical device technologies for adoption into health systems. Their structured searches covered five databases for work from 2017 to mid 2023, and they also drew on documents from international assessment networks and the World Health Organization. Two reviewers selected and extracted studies on their own, with a third to settle disputes. Mapping the domains in use shows health systems what a full evaluation should cover.
pmc-12770347:
Yu-Chiu Kao, Her-Bang Huang, and Chau-Hwang Lee combine red light with a gentle electric field to make nerve fibers grow farther and straighter. Their 2025 study works in three-dimensional collagen gels, closer to real tissue than the flat dishes of earlier work. Each stimulus alone was known to encourage neurite outgrowth; together, in 3D, they were untested.

Two nerve cell lines grew longer, better-aligned extensions under tuned doses of both. Gene sequencing pointed to neuropeptide Y and its receptors as mediators, and electrical recordings showed the neurons maturing functionally. Paired physical cues could one day coach regrowth after nerve injury, where direction matters as much as length.
pmc-12771047:
Enrico Ragni, Laura de Girolamo, and Dimitrios Kouroupis review how the physical setting around stem cells shapes the healing parcels they release, in a paper from 2025. Cell free therapy with these parcels, called extracellular vesicles, is a rising rival to transplanting stem cells themselves. Stem cells of the mesenchymal type are a leading source because they are easy to gather and calm immune responses.

How good the parcels are depends on the setting in which the cells are grown. Forces and stiffness in three dimensional culture steer cell behavior and change the parcels that come out. Trials now test parcels from force conditioned cells for joint, heart, and nerve repair. The review weighs that growing work and highlights a study that shows the effect in practice.
pmc-12771847:
Sarem Khilji and co-authors chart gene activity in growing cattle in 2025 across three tissues. Which genes are on, which version of each is used, and which DNA stretches lie open together define how a tissue works. Humans and lab animals have such maps; cattle largely lacked a joint one.

Brain front, liver, and thigh muscle came from four young Angus steers. Two scans read gene activity and open DNA side by side. Thousands of genes differed in activity between each tissue pair, the team reports, and version use shifted too. The joint map gives breeders and biologists a base for tying traits like growth and meat quality to the switches that set them, tissue by tissue.
pmc-12771947:
Xingyu Fu and co-authors hunt gene marks for a clogged-artery ill in a 2025 study. The ill turns deadly when dead cells pile up un-swept in the wall, which swells the soft core till the cap tears.

The sweep of dead cells has its own gene crew. The team read gene marks from a big bank and found four-teen crew genes set apart in the ill. A smart sort picked five as test marks. Four of the five ran high in fresh checks. Maps of guard cells in the wall and dish tests backed the picks. The authors say the marks could flag the ill in time, and the crew's work in the wall is now a path for new care.
pmc-12772547:
Mangala Samarawickrama and two co-authors wrote a 2024 study on what diabetes costs patients at a military hospital in Sri Lanka. Diabetes is a long-term disease that is growing more common worldwide. It lowers quality of life and brings costs to patients, families, and the country.

The team surveyed 200 outpatients, most of them men, with an average age near 42 years. Patients had lived with the disease for about five years on average. The mean cost came to about 55 dollars per patient per year. Direct medical costs made up 65 percent of that bill, and tests were the most common cost. Travel and other non-medical costs made up the rest. The study gives a clear picture of the load patients carry out of pocket.
pmc-12775747:
Practicing a diagnostic interview on a real patient is risky, so one Spanish team let students rehearse on AI patients instead. Daniel García-Torres and co-authors logged 1,832 interviews in 2025, where 156 psychology students questioned thirteen virtual patients set to different randomness levels. After each chat, students rated the session and noted strengths and flaws.

Ratings averaged near nine out of ten, with women rating higher than men. Glitchy connections dragged scores down, and the liveliest setting, the highest randomness, was liked best. Nearly all students felt their diagnostic skill had improved, though exam scores matched the prior year's class. The authors see such patients as a well-liked rehearsal tool whose real learning payoff still needs proof.
pmc-12777647:
Souptik Barua and co-authors study how faithfully older heart patients wear activity trackers during phone-based rehab, in this 2025 paper. Cardiac rehabilitation delivered by mobile health tools is growing, and wearable accelerometers log the activity that drives it. Whether patients keep the devices on, and whether that faithfulness tracks with getting fitter, was understudied. This analysis reuses data from a randomized trial.

An AI clustering method sorted patients into behavioral types by how they wore the trackers. Those types were then set against gains in functional capacity. Distinct wear patterns may flag patients who need a nudge before they drift away. The work shows how passively collected wear data can guide human coaching in remote rehab.
pmc-12780147:
Youngsik Oh and co-authors built a two-way immune drug in 2025 that feeds killer T cells while it traps a signal that holds them back. The feed signal, IL-7, grows those cells but has disappointed in the clinic, in part since tumors raise the brake signal after care. Their fused drug joins the feed to a trap for the brake in one molecule. Each half was checked for grip and work in dishes and in mice.

In a mouse colon cancer model, the fused drug beat each half alone. More armed killer T cells poured into tumors. In a breast model it cut spread to new sites. Paired with radiation or a second immune drug, it did better still. The team pitches it for clinic tests.
pmc-12784447:
Kumutha Nadaraj reports a tricky diagnosis in a pregnant patient in this 2025 case report. The patient arrived with double vision, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. Her pattern of signs fit Miller Fisher syndrome, a rare variant of a nerve disease, but it also looked like a stroke.

The syndrome is marked by eye movement failure, unsteady balance, and lost reflexes. It is far more common in Asia than in the West, as a share of its parent condition. A vitamin-deficiency illness can also mimic it closely. Nadaraj walks through how the team sorted the look-alike causes. The case stresses that spotting the syndrome early matters, since prompt treatment improves outcomes. It also flags pregnancy as a setting where the trap is easy to fall into.
pmc-12784747:
Ji-Min Choe and co-authors review in 2025 sixty-five dogs that had a diseased gallbladder removed at a Seoul hospital. The disease, a mucus-filled gallbladder, strikes mostly older and small-breed dogs. The team checked bile germ tests, drug resistance, and tissue findings to guide care after surgery.

Only about a fifth of bile samples grew germs, most often two common gut germs. Near a fifth of those germs resisted many drugs, though two drugs still worked well. Toy Poodles appeared far more often than chance suggests. Tissue checks showed a thickened gallbladder lining in most dogs, often with liver swelling too. The authors urge routine bile testing.
pmc-12785347:
Jihan Ke and co-authors review a clot-control protein that also steers stem cell fate and cell aging, in work from two thousand twenty-five. The protein blocks the system that dissolves clots, its classic job. Fresh work ties it to fibrosis, clotting disorders, and tumor growth as well.

The review builds a signaling network centered on the protein for cell fate choices. It then weaves that network into known aging pathways. The two processes, choosing a fate and growing old, talk through this protein. The authors frame it as a drug target for chronic diseases that mix both threads.
pmc-12785947:
Yuxia Fan and co-authors compared the non-volatile chemistry of strong-flavor baijiu at high and low alcohol levels, in a 2025 study. Alcohol content shapes the taste and mouthfeel of this Chinese spirit and steers buyer choice. The team used untargeted chemical profiling on samples from the Jiangsu region.

They quantified 647 compounds that do not evaporate, then screened for the ones that separate the two strength groups. About 110 key compounds differed clearly, and most ran higher in the stronger samples. A pattern model could also tell brands and origins apart. The results link alcohol level to the heavier flavor compounds that linger on the palate.
pmc-12786047:
Uysal Yeler and co-authors studied two plant compounds in fat cells grown in the lab, in a paper published in 2025. The compounds are natural pigments found in herbs and vegetables. The team asked how they affect the making of fat cells and the burning of fat for heat. One master switch drives fat cell growth, and it turns on a partner protein as cells mature. A third protein, found in heat-making fat, lets cells waste energy as warmth.

The researchers dosed mouse fat precursor cells with each compound at three strengths during their maturation. They then measured the switch, its partner, and the heat protein, as both gene activity and protein levels. Shifts in the first two would signal slower fat making. A rise in the heat protein would signal more energy burning. The results inform the search for plant-based aids against obesity.
pmc-12786447:
Paulina Tomecka and co-authors report, in a 2025 case study, a rare birth defect in a thirteen-year-old girl that is often missed until the teen years. The syndrome combines a doubled womb, a blocked half-vagina, and a missing kidney on the same side. It tends to surface as a pelvic mass, painful periods, and lasting pelvic pain.

Scans revealed the pattern in this patient. Surgery cut the blocking wall inside the vagina and drained the trapped blood, which cleared her symptoms and reopened the tract. The authors urge doctors to weigh this syndrome when teen girls have cyclic belly pain plus a kidney anomaly. Early surgery can prevent grave harm and protect fertility.
pmc-12786647:
Binrong Zhu and co-authors study 3D-printed low-carbon concrete for reusable building formwork in this 2025 paper. Printing turns digital models directly into physical parts, enabling complex shapes. The team tested how printed concrete strength varies by direction. Layers in printing can make one axis weaker than another. Steel slag and iron tailings replaced part of the mix in some batches. Compression, bending, and splitting tests measured each mix.

Carbon emissions of the mixes were also counted. A ranking method weighed all results to pick the best printable recipe. The goal is formwork that can be used again and again at large scale. Reusable forms cut both cost and waste on building sites. Direction-aware design matters for printed parts under load. The study joins digital construction with lower-carbon materials.
pmc-12786947:
Castro and six co-authors try to make a plant-based plastic film work better for food packaging in a 2025 paper. The plastic, PLA, is stiff and breaks down in compost, but on its own it is brittle.

The team mixed PLA with treated gelatin and a solvent blend that softens the mix. They compared two ways of adding the gelatin and checked structure, heat behavior, strength, and how fast the films break down. Adding the gelatin directly gave a smoother, more even film. The softener lowered the softening point and improved how the film could be shaped, though the films grew weaker than plain PLA. One blend stood out for stretch and ease of making. All films took up more water and broke down faster.
pmc-12787747:
Wanxin Hou and co-authors tracked cracking and healing in clay soil treated with a natural gum in a 2025 study. Silty clay cracks as it dries and can partly heal when wet again, a cycle that weakens roads and slopes. Guar gum, a plant-based polymer, is a green candidate for steadying such soil.

The team ran four wet-dry cycles outdoors under real weather, filming the crack patterns as they formed and closed. Image software measured crack density, width, depth, and how the cracks linked up. Fine imaging and mineral tests then revealed how the gum binds the soil at small scale. The results guide low-cost, low-impact soil treatment for regions with strong seasonal swings.
pmc-12789547:
Wanglong Wan and five colleagues fuse several machine learning models to diagnose faults on electrical distribution lines. Single-model classifiers lean on one feature type and need lots of simulated training data, while real fault records are scarce and noisy. The team extracted time-frequency features across multiple dimensions from real-world data.

A Dempster-Shafer evidence theory method then combines the models' judgments, weighing conflicting evidence formally. Experiments on collected field data reached an average accuracy of 74.6 percent across four grounding fault types, including tricky intermittent arcing. The authors present the fusion framework as a practical step toward faster, more reliable fault handling that keeps power supply stable.
pmc-12794347:
Shu Liu and five co-authors report a 2025 case of a two-year-old boy in China with a rare gene fault. Both copies of his TOMM7 gene carried the same change, passed down from related parents. The gene keeps a gateway complex in the cell's power plants working, and faults in it cause a syndrome with dwarfism and slow development.

The boy's growth had nearly stopped by age two. From thirty-one months he got long-acting growth hormone shots. Over ten months he grew 3.8 centimeters, and his growth score slid far less than before treatment. The authors offer the case as a lead for treating growth failure tied to faulty cell power plants.
pmc-12795847:
Adrianna Jebrzycka and eight co-authors studied how the loss of a thymus gene dims alarm signals in young immune cells, in research published in 2025. The gene, Aire, shows body tags to young T cells so they learn self from foe. Its gland cells also release alarm calls of two kinds. Single-cell gene readings spanned thymus, marrow, and lymph nodes in normal and gene-free mice.

In the thymus, late young T cells and gland cells alike showed low alarm gene activity with no Aire. Marrow cells showed no such link. So the alarm role of the gene sits in the thymus, not the marrow. The findings tie the tag display of the gland to its alarm release. They help explain why Aire loss breeds self-attack.
pmc-12797347:
Raghu Yelugam and co-authors build a way to explain disease clusters in 2025. Grouping patients by signs and symptoms can yield several plausible answers, with no single right one. Reading meaning into those groups is the hard part, above all without ground truth.

Using dementia cases as the test bed, two spectral methods each found five plausible subgroups. The groups differed between methods, as expected. Their formal explanation space then laid both answers side by side for comparison. It scores group quality, flags which traits drive each group, and supports keeping rival answers rather than forcing one.
pmc-12797947:
Zeynab Pirmoradi and co-authors present a 2025 study of a plant compound against essential tremor. Essential tremor causes persistent limb shaking and has no effective treatment. Quercetin is a plant flavonoid with protective hints. Packing it into a nanoemulsion should raise how much reaches the brain. The team tests the formula in mice whose tremor is triggered by harmaline, a drug that overexcites the olive-cerebellar circuit. Thirty-two male mice split into four groups of eight.

Groups cover control, harmaline alone, the nanoemulsion alone, and both together. Behavior tests and molecular measures track tremor and brain inflammation. Neurologists get early evidence on a delivery upgrade for a common natural compound. Behavior plus molecules is a stronger readout than either alone.
