Mouse tremor models are imperfect mirrors of the human disease, yet they remain the standard first gate for candidate treatments.
pmc-12801547:
Yukiko Yamazaki, Shuko Matsuda, and Yuka Matsuki published a 2025 study fixing the cutoff for a noninvasive fluid-responsiveness measure used in anesthesia. When blood pressure dips during surgery, doctors must judge whether fluids will help. The measure, estimated stroke volume variation from a continuous cardiac output system, lacked an agreed threshold. The team ran fluid challenges in patients under general anesthesia and sorted responders by how much their stroke volume rose.

The best cutoff for the estimated measure was 7.3 percent, with fair accuracy. The standard variation measure's cutoff came out at 12 percent, with weaker accuracy. The authors say the estimated measure, now with its own threshold, can guide circulation management during surgery. The study offers a concrete number where clinicians previously guessed.
pmc-12804247:
Akhil Mohan and co-authors present in 2025 a cheap way to clean up crude oil made by heating plant matter. Such bio-oil holds many oxygen-rich compounds that spoil its use as fuel. Their method pairs low-cost soaking materials, some drawn from factory waste, with a common solvent to strip those compounds out.

The oil split into a clean upper layer and a heavy lower layer in the solvent. With calcium hydroxide as the soaking material, oxygen-rich parts fell from about forty percent of the oil to near zero. Careful tests charted the chemistry, stability, and heat traits of the cleaned oil. The route is simple enough to scale.
pmc-12804747:
Zhongze Chen and co-authors test a cockroach extract against fatigue in mice in a 2025 study. The extract is a glycoprotein from the American cockroach, an insect long used in Chinese medicine. It is known for antioxidant action and for shaping gut microbes. The team first confirmed its antioxidant strength in lab tests, then tired mice out with swimming.

Treated mice swam longer before exhaustion. Their livers showed less injury, stronger protective enzymes, and lower damage markers. Waste products in blood and muscle fell, and fuel stores in liver and muscle rose. Gut microbe mixes shifted, and helpful short-chain fatty acids increased. Links among microbes, those acids, and fatigue signs supported one connected pathway. The authors conclude the extract fights fatigue by easing oxidative stress, tuning energy use, and steering the gut. They propose it as a candidate for fatigue care.
pmc-12805647:
Ha Eun Shin and co-authors study the role of one fibroblast type in asthma in a 2025 mouse study. Fibroblasts repair tissue and drive scarring, so they are a tempting drug target in lung disease. Yet their day to day role in keeping lungs calm was unclear, and removing them might do harm rather than good.

Using engineered mice, the team deleted most of the target fibroblasts for months. Even without a trigger, lungs showed altered matrix genes and more inflammatory cells. When asthma was induced with dust mite allergen, the loss led to more mucus and stronger inflammation. The results warn that these fibroblasts help hold immune balance in the lung.
pmc-12805747:
José Bretones-Pedrinaci and co-authors survey Spanish hospitals on whether malaria drugs are on the shelf when an imported case lands. Their 2025 study starts from the pattern: local transmission is long gone, yet imported cases, mostly the deadliest species, keep rising. Fast access to artemisinin-based treatment is what keeps such cases from turning grave.

Pharmacy leads at 46 hospitals answered on stocks and ordering times between late 2023 and early 2024. The first-line vein drug for severe malaria sat in three quarters of hospitals. But only three in five could fetch more within a weekday if the shelf ran dry. Bigger hospitals and those with a malaria protocol fared better. The authors call the patchwork a patient risk.
pmc-12808447:
Javier Arranz-Herrero and co-authors show that a child cancer drug can switch on a core germ alarm part by a direct grip, in a study from 2025. The alarm part wakes when loose gene scraps float in the cell, and drug hunts prize new ways to wake it. A vast screen of drug forms flagged the old drug as a fit.

Heat reads prove the drug grips the alarm part in a bare tube. A twin flaw form of the part, built to drop the grip, kills both grip and wake. The wake needs no gene scrap sense parts at all. Sim runs show two drug forms grip as a pair. Reuse of the drug as an alarm wake is the pitch.
pmc-12812647:
Yangyang Mei and nine co-authors tested whether a leftover cholesterol measure can flag a blood-flow form of erectile dysfunction, in this study published in 2025. The measure, called residual cholesterol, rides on fat-rich particles left after digestion and has been tied to heart risk. Its link to erection problems tied to artery health had not been charted.

The team recruited men with erectile problems and healthy controls at three hospitals, using scans and night-time tests to find the artery-based form. Residual cholesterol ran higher in the patient group and stayed linked to the artery form after other factors were weighed. It also beat standard fat measures at picking out those cases. The authors suggest it may help sort men by vessel risk, pending longer studies.
pmc-12812947:
Paolo Brustio and co-authors test a well-known bias in elite football in work published in 2025. Players born early in a selection year are often favored in youth talent searches, a pattern called the relative age effect. The team measured the bias in Italy's Serie A and asked what it buys.

They checked the bias by age group, playing position, and team ranking. They then asked whether early-born players actually got more match appearances or playing time. The title states the core finding: the selection bias did not turn into a playing-time advantage at the top level.
pmc-12814747:
Hamza A Mahmood and co-authors surveyed doctors and medical students in the United Kingdom about high vitamin B12 levels, in a 2025 study. A very high B12 reading in blood can point to cancer, liver disease, or other serious illness. Yet the sign gets little teaching time, and two tricky look-alike states can mislead care.

The survey covered 46 family doctors and 50 students. Nearly nine in ten doctors named at least one illness linked to high B12, against only about two in ten students. Most in both groups said they would test further, but neither group knew the look-alike states. The authors call for better training on this test result.
pmc-12815447:
Yangjun Liu and co-authors wrote a review and pooled analysis, published in 2025, on exercise, belly fat, and inflammation in older adults. Belly fat and chronic swelling are twin marks of aging tied to many diseases. Exercise is thought to blunt both, but the size and shape of the effect needed a firm tally.

Six databases were searched to February 2025 for trials in healthy older adults or those with obesity, diabetes, or metabolic syndrome. From 7,622 hits, 19 trials with 1,130 people made the cut. The pooled results weigh aerobic, resistance, and mixed training against belly fat and swelling markers. Bias checks used a standard Cochrane tool.
pmc-12815747:
Li and co-authors rank traditional Chinese exercises for knee osteoarthritis using a network of trial results. Knee arthritis burdens many middle-aged and older adults. Four exercise forms entered the comparison: Tai Chi, Baduanjin, Wuqinxi, and Yijinjing. The team gathered 20 randomized trials with 1,457 patients from six databases. Outcomes covered pain, function, walking distance, and life quality. A Bayesian network method let forms be ranked even without head-to-head trials.

For pain relief, Yijinjing ranked at the top of the network. Rankings for stiffness and function differed by outcome. The layered result helps clinics pick an exercise by the patient's main complaint.
pmc-12815947:
Alaa Alaerjan, Ayman Mostafa, Alshimaa Mahmoud, and Mohamed Ezz present a faster way to identify people by the veins in several fingers, in work from 2025. Vein patterns are hard to fake and need no touch, which suits secure login. Heavy models and single finger sign up have held back use on small devices.

Their two stage system pairs a light mobile network with a new matching network. The first part is tuned layer by layer to stay small yet sharp. The matcher gives a calibrated chance score instead of a fixed margin rule. Users can sign in with any finger, which adds ease without losing speed.
pmc-12816247:
Yi Dong and co-authors wrote a clinical trial, dated 2025 in its text, on pairing eye drops with tiny plugs for dry eye tied to Sjögren's syndrome. The autoimmune disease dries the eye surface, and cyclosporine drops are a standard answer. Plugs that block tear drainage keep both tears and drops on the eye longer. Twenty-one patients joined a paired-eye trial: one eye got drops plus a dissolving plug, the other drops alone.

After three months, both eyes improved on every measure. The plugged eyes gained more: tears lasted longer before breaking up, the tear layer stood taller, and surface immune cell counts fell further. Symptom scores also dropped more on the plugged side. Patients' two symptom scales moved together only in the paired treatment. The team reads the pairing as a stronger strategy for this hard-to-treat dry eye.
pmc-12816647:
Fengchai Wang and Kun Wang present FL-TEAR, a routing frame for fog cloud Internet of Things networks that learns trust by federation and weighs energy in path choice. Safe, sound, low energy links are hard across mixed, weak nodes. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Static trust scores give way to shared learning: nodes train one global trust and energy model without baring raw data. Trust scores update from behavior, link soundness, and leftover energy. Paths are picked by a score that blends trust, energy, delay, and link steadiness. The layered design spans things, fog, and cloud, cuts chatter, and guards privacy. Tests beat strong baselines.
pmc-12816747:
Samanvitha Sudi and co-authors present a 2025 study of a gut-made compound and its effect on heart valve cells. The valve disease at stake has no drug cure, only valve swap surgery, and its roots stay murky. The compound, a breakdown product of food parts, is tied to many heart ills, yet its valve role was untested.

Using resting valve cells grown by a new lab method, the team found the compound wakes the cells into a scar-forming state. Stress inside the cell's protein workshop drives the shift, and blocking that stress path blunts it. Resting cells proved more touchy than standard-grown ones.
pmc-12817147:
Samitha Senevirathne and four co-authors cover an infected, exposed leg artery graft with a rotated thigh muscle, in a 2025 case report. A graft left bare or infected threatens limb and life, and soft tissue cover is the rescue.

The patient had an open fracture and a femoral artery injury, repaired with a vein graft. Repeated trauma infected and exposed the graft. The team cleaned the wound thoroughly, targeted antibiotics, and rotated the vastus medialis muscle over the site to seal it with living, blood-fed tissue. The graft survived. The authors propose this flap for exposed exploration sites along the inner lower thigh. Muscle, they show, is both bandage and blood supply.
pmc-12817447:
School closures during the COVID-19 lockdown hit Nigerian girls and women hard, yet some turned the time toward growth. Chinyere Cecilia Okeke and Ifeoma Maureen Obionu surveyed 339 females aged ten to twenty-four in 2025, during the 2020 lockdown period, using a resilience framework. Most respondents were in their early twenties, and many said housework and home tension had cut into their learning.

At the same time, many reported learning new skills, building businesses, earning income, and caring for their physical and mental health. The authors read this as resilience worth building on, not just a crisis response. They urge schools and support systems to foster such adaptive strength for long-term empowerment.
pmc-12817547:
Dalia Younis and co-authors ask, in 2025, whether dialysis itself is to blame for odd trace element levels in patients' blood. Dialysis patients might lack essential elements or carry too much of toxic ones. To separate the treatment from the environment, the team compared one hundred thirty-seven Egyptian patients with their own relatives from the same area.

Blood levels of twenty-two elements were measured, along with dialysis and tap water. Only a few elements differed between patients and relatives, while blood pressure, diabetes, city living, and nearby factories each left their own marks. One element, zinc, predicted hemoglobin levels in patients. Place, more than dialysis, explained most patterns.
pmc-12817647:
Zohreh Alinasab and co-authors explore what drives infections that patients pick up in hospitals in Iran. Published in 2025, the qualitative study used grounded theory and in-depth interviews with 30 experts in the field. Recruitment ran by snowball sampling until no new themes emerged. Such infections are a major burden, above all in developing countries.

Analysis found three main themes: the patients, the hospital environment, and the service providers. Patient factors covered health status and care processes. Environment factors covered management, building layout, and hygiene. Provider factors covered how work is organized and managed. In all, six subcategories and 54 key statements were drawn out. The authors say the map can guide control programs and cut costs.
pmc-12820047:
Atefeh Zeinali and Leila Moradi published a catalysis study in twenty twenty-five on a three-part nanocomposite built to make complex drug-like molecules quickly and cleanly. The composite marries a carbon nitride sheet, chitosan, and a zinc-based porous framework. A battery of imaging and spectroscopy checks confirmed the hybrid's structure.

It then catalyzed a one-pot, four-component reaction assembling phenazine-fused products in a water-ethanol mix. Yields ran from seventy-seven to ninety-six percent within two hours at most. The catalyst survived six reuse cycles without appreciable loss of activity. Green credentials, speed, and recyclability are the selling points. The authors present the design as a template for rationally assembled catalysts rather than lucky finds.
pmc-12820247:
Alessandro De Santis and co-authors presented a 2025 case study on soil near Foggia in southern Italy. Heavy metals in soil can harm soil life and food safety, yet common risk scores rest on chemical tests alone. The team sampled twelve soils near the city and checked them for seven toxic elements. They also read the DNA of the microbes living in each soil.

The group built a new risk index that keeps the ranking of older scores but softens the pull of extreme values. Their index matched a known score closely while staying more stable. As risk rose, some microbe families grew more common and others faded. Simple tree models could sort soils into risk classes from microbe data alone, which may help target clean-up work.
pmc-12821047:
Hongyu He and co-authors studied lung ultrasound patterns in patients on breathing machines in a 2025 paper. The patients were at high risk of failing to come off the machine. Ultrasound images of the lung fall into patterns: dense, tissue-like patches or widespread hazy lines.

The team reviewed 97 such patients whose lung scores showed severe loss of air. They grouped patients by pattern and tracked how lungs regained air after routine care. They also compared failed weaning, days on the machine, and deaths. A quick bedside scan pattern may help doctors judge who is ready to breathe alone.
pmc-12821447: Mohammad Ullah and Sadeka Tamanna published a 2025 case report on stubborn headaches caused, apparently, by a statin. Statins cut heart risk for millions; their known side effects center on muscles and the liver. This patient developed relentless headaches after years on simvastatin. Standard painkillers failed. Other causes were ruled out, and a companion drug was paused without effect. When the statin was stopped, the headaches vanished. The authors warn that a drug-induced headache can hide for years behind a familiar prescription.
pmc-12821647:
Anastasiia Bakhchina and co-authors test eye gaze measures of cognitive load in a driving simulator, in a 2025 paper. Driving taxes attention and working memory, and a secondary task can push load higher. The team compares eye tracking against a standard self report scale for telling load levels apart.

Close to seven hundred people drove highway and urban routes in a fixed simulator, with a memory task as the added load. Self report split load levels well on the highway. Eye measures split the driving stages best, and gaze transition entropy hit very high accuracy for that split. Eye measures linked to self report in urban driving but not on the highway.
pmc-12821847:
Manish Shah and a large research network describe in 2025 how they will run a trial on seizures in children. Ambulance crews now dose a calming drug, midazolam, by weight, which takes math steps and can lead to low or late doses. The trial tests a simpler plan that sets the dose by age group instead.

Crews in twenty cities will switch to the age-based plan in steps, so sites can be compared fairly. The main check is whether seizures have stopped when the child reaches the hospital. The team will also track breathing problems to confirm the simpler plan stays safe. Full results will show if age-based dosing should replace weight-based dosing.
pmc-12821947:
Maria Paroikaki and co-authors report drug resistance patterns for hard to treat Helicobacter pylori infections in a 2025 study. The bacterium is a common cause of stomach inflammation, and standard two drug cures can fail. Fresh local data for the United Kingdom after the pandemic were lacking.

The team reviewed biopsy samples sent to a London laboratory between 2018 and 2023, covering 193 isolates. Resistance was low for two drugs, moderate for two others, and very high for one common agent. The authors compare the pattern with European registry data. They argue that regional testing should guide drug choice when first cures fail, rather than relying on habit or distant data.
pmc-12822047:
Jingjing Hou and co-authors report, in a 2025 case paper, a windpipe skin that choked a man soon after his tube came out. The skin, a fibrin sheet, is a rare ill of tube use and can grow in a day. The man had end-stage kidney ill and was on blood wash. A heart stop from high potassium brought a tube for 23 hours. Once it was out, his breath grew hard, then whistled, then blocked. A new tube went in. A scope then proved the sheet in the pipe. His CT scans showed the pipe's shift in step with his signs.

Fast scope work is the cure path. The team warns: new breath strain after a tube, in kidney folk most, should raise this thought.
pmc-12822147: Ramya A and co-authors report a case illustrating the Renbok phenomenon in a 2025 case report. The phenomenon is the withdrawal of one skin lesion when another appears. An eleven year old girl had multiple dark, scaly plaques of psoriasis across her scalp, trunk, and limbs. She also had patchy hair loss from alopecia areata on the scalp, and those patches were strikingly spared from the scaly plaques. The authors discuss the immune mechanism between the two autoimmune diseases.
pmc-12822247:
Azar Esfehani and eight co-authors hunted for fungicide resistance in the wheat pathogen that causes Septoria leaf blotch across Iran. The main fungicides strike an enzyme called CYP51, and Iranian fields lean heavily on one of them, propiconazole. The team tested twenty-eight fungal isolates from six wheat provinces for drug sensitivity, then read the target gene in detail.

They found two mutations never reported anywhere, plus rare ones seen only a few times worldwide, alongside the well-known resistance changes. The variants combined into seven patterns with differing resistance levels, and whole-genome sequencing confirmed the targeted reads. The most resistant isolate also switched the gene on harder when challenged. Computer models of the enzyme suggest the new mutations reshape its surface or drug pocket. The authors warn that resistance in Iranian populations is more inventive than surveys assumed, and they recommend routine molecular monitoring.
pmc-12822847:
Saba Bashir, Pulwisha Mustafa, Aasia Nawaz, Sabahat Hamid, and Marvi Qazi studied women who still leaked urine after a successful repair of a birth-related tear between bladder and birth canal. Their study, published in 2025, ran at a hospital in Hyderabad over one year. Such leaks can persist even when the tear itself is closed.

Ninety women took part, most from rural areas and with little schooling. About eight percent still had leakage after surgery. Of all the factors checked, only the type of tear mattered: tears that ran in a full circle carried the highest risk, roughly seven times higher after full analysis. The authors stress skilled surgery and prompt care to protect continence.
pmc-12824247:
Bethany Anderson and co-authors probe enzyme activity in bowel disease in a 2025 study. Cathepsins are enzymes that cut proteins, and one of them, cathepsin S, has been tied to gut pain in inflammatory bowel disease. The team asked whether it drives other symptoms too.

Using activity probes in human samples and mouse colitis, they found cathepsin S raised sharply in stool and gut fluid during disease, though not in gut tissue itself. Mice lacking the enzyme bled less and had milder tissue scores, but most other signs stayed alike. A drug blocking the enzyme gave mixed effects. The work maps where these enzymes act in the inflamed gut.
pmc-12824347:
Meletiadis and co-authors read wild boar genetics to explain a fever's spread in Italy in a 2025 study. African swine fever swept the northwest, and how boar populations connect may have steered it. The team genotyped 578 boars from twenty six hunting districts at thirteen markers. Clustering and spatial methods mapped the population's structure and its mixing zones.

Where boar groups blend, the fever found bridges; where they are cut off, it stalled. Disease control in wildlife usually maps fences and roads, not genes. This work argues the animals' own family geography belongs on the outbreak map, and it shows how to draw that layer.
pmc-12825247:
Xiupan Wei and four co-authors measured brain to muscle talk in patients healing from stroke in a 2025 study. The coupling between cortex and muscle shows how the central and outer nerve systems coordinate movement. How that coupling shifts in early stroke recovery during arm tasks was unclear, so the team recorded both sides at once.

Twenty five patients in the subacute phase and twenty age matched healthy peers held a wrist push at half strength for fifteen seconds. Light based brain scans and skin muscle sensors ran together. Patients showed weaker phase and rhythm coupling in key brain muscle pairs. Their cortex fired harder with tighter inner links, while muscle signals ran simpler and weaker. The authors map the shift as a mark of early recovery strain.
pmc-12827147:
Ying Huang and co-authors link liver scarring scores to heart disease in people with prediabetes, in a 2025 study. Fatty liver can scar over time, and that scarring travels with clogged arteries. Whether the link holds before full diabetes sets in was unclear.

The study covered 7,409 patients aged 40 to 80 with prediabetes. Three blood-based scarring scores, FIB-4, NFS, and APRI, each tied to higher odds of artery disease after other risks were weighed. Curved fits probed whether the link bends at high scores. Head-to-head curves compared how well each score sorts patients. Clinicians may gain a cheap liver-based flag for heart checks in the prediabetes clinic.
pmc-12828047:
Chunpeng Wu, Xingguo Jiang, and co-authors share cloud, edge, and end gear work in power nets with a deep learned scheduler, in a 2025 study. Green power growth floods nets with sense data from scores of end points. Schedulers must place that load with low wait and high yield at once.

A long term goal is split into live slot picks by a queue trick. A tuned deep net then picks slots with rich past plays to learn from. Sim runs show the plan bends well to dense, fast loads. Queue waits stay curbed while most data still gets through in full.
pmc-12830647:
Doggui and co-authors track COVID-19 outbreaks in long term care homes in Quebec, Canada, in a 2025 study. The period runs from May 2022 to September 2024, during the Omicron era. Residents of such homes face a high risk of severe illness, so the team counted outbreaks, cases, and deaths across 471 active homes.

In all, 2,501 outbreaks and 39,089 cases among residents and staff were logged. The odds of an outbreak, the rate of new cases, and the death rate all fell in the 2023 to 2024 season compared with wave seven. Large homes were more likely to have an outbreak, but spread and deaths inside homes were much the same by size.
pmc-12830747:
Squeezing and releasing sandstone over and over changes how water flows through it, Zhenwen Liu and co-authors show in a 2025 study. Deep rock projects face stress and water pressure at once. Bench tests cycled load on sandstone while water seeped through under set pressures.

Raising side pressure lifted peak strength by about eight percent and stiffened the rock. Higher water pressure weakened it instead. Side pressure suppressed swelling and microcracks, guarding flow paths. The coupled results map how tunnels and storage caverns may leak or hold as loads cycle. Engineers gain numbers for judging rock safety under real ground stress.
pmc-12830947:
Haotian Chi and five co-authors described in 2025 a new enzyme that resets a bacterial immune system. In type III CRISPR defense, bacteria sense invader RNA and release ring-shaped signal molecules that switch on helper weapons. Ring-cutting enzymes clear those signals once the threat passes. The team characterized one such enzyme, Crn4, from a less-studied CRISPR subtype.

Its crystal shape showed a small paired protein with a fold unlike any known before. The enzyme cut a wide range of ring signals in lab tests and calmed CRISPR defense in living cells. Viruses and plasmids carry their own copies, which may act as counter-weapons against bacterial defense. The finding widens what is known about how these immune systems switch off.
pmc-12831047:
A large team of trainers from ELIXIR, the European life-science data network, surveys online teaching across its member groups in this white paper from twenty twenty-five. Bioinformatics skills are in demand far beyond any one campus, so the network has leaned on e-learning to reach more people. The paper maps what exists now and what good online training needs.

It profiles shared platforms such as the Training e-Support System and a Slovenian e-learning platform, and notes how course files in a shared format can move between sites for reuse. It also covers blended courses that mix online work with live sessions, and set learning paths that guide a student step by step. The closing part looks ahead: better trainer skills, more open materials, and training records that follow open data rules. The aim is steady, shared growth of skills across Europe.
pmc-12831247:
Catalina Medina and six co-authors mapped street food stalls near public schools in Mexico City, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Food sold around schools shapes what children eat, yet street stalls had been little studied compared with shops. The team surveyed stalls within a short walk of dozens of public schools.

Well over a thousand stalls were found, and more than four in ten sold only unhealthy fare by their scoring tool. Stalls in the poorest areas were not always the worst scorers, and distance from school mattered too. Unhealthy stalls cluster near schools in at-risk areas. The authors note new rules now aim to cut this exposure, and their effects need study.
pmc-12831347:
Anesthesia without muscle relaxants for a patient with Lou Gehrig's disease is reported by Yongxin Sun and co-authors in a 2025 case study. The patient, a man in his mid-fifties, could not lie flat without breathlessness due to weak breathing muscles. He needed a scope procedure to break up a ureter stone.

The team used vein-only anesthesia with two fast drugs and a throat mask for breathing, skipping relaxants entirely. Low opioid doses aimed to spare breathing drive after surgery. The procedure finished smoothly, with stable vital signs and a quick wake-up. The case shows how tailored plans can carry fragile patients through routine surgery safely.
pmc-12831947:
Fatin Nabila Mat Nawi and Mae-Lynn Bastion describe allergy cases from a glaucoma eye drop in a 2025 paper. The drop lowers eye pressure well and is usually gentle. Allergy to it can appear quietly, long after treatment starts.

Five cases came from one eye doctor's records over two years. Patients had used the drop for nine to sixteen months before redness and swelling began. Itching, often expected in allergy, was not prominent here. Signs included eyelid follicles and mild surface swelling, with pressure staying steady. No patient had stopped the drop on their own. Symptoms cleared quickly once the drug was withdrawn. The series warns clinicians to suspect the drop even after many calm months.
pmc-12835047:
Jing Guo, Zhenli Wang, and co-authors grade a built wetland that cleans acid mine waste water in China, in a 2025 study. Mine waste is sour and rich in metals, which harms streams and land. The wetland runs in four linked parts with three kinds of reed and grass.

Water left the wetland near neutral, up from a sour start. Iron was wiped out in full, and zinc fell by most of its load. Germ checks show a rich mix that turns sulfur and nitrogen in key loops. Plant and germ work join to clean the flow in a green way.
pmc-12835447:
Seyeon Park, Sukhee Ahn, and Hyunjin Cho report a 2025 study that translates and tests a childbirth fear form in Korean. Fear of birth can drive hard labors and low mood after birth, yet Korea had only broad anxiety forms to gauge it. The team rendered a known birth expectancy form into Korean by a back-and-forth method.

Two hundred women took the form in face-to-face surveys. The Korean form settled at twenty-six items in four groups, from fear to felt risk. Scores held together well and matched kindred measures, which backs the form for use with Korean mothers.
pmc-12836447:
After keyhole surgery, a nerve block in the abdominal wall can dull pain for hours. Two helper drugs can stretch that relief, and doctors debate which works better. Vinisha S and co-authors randomly split sixty patients into two groups. One block mixed the numbing drug with magnesium sulphate. The other used a sedative called dexmedetomidine instead.

The magnesium group went about an hour longer before needing rescue pain relief, thirteen hours against twelve. Pain scores ran slightly lower with magnesium at every check, though not decisively. That group also used less backup medicine over the first day. Blood pressure and side effects stayed similar. The authors call magnesium's edge real but modest.
pmc-12836847:
Weitao Jiang and co-authors engineered the root-zone microbes of apple trees to fight replant disease in two thousand twenty-five. Replant disease strikes young apple trees planted where old ones grew, and a Fusarium fungus is a key cause. Rootstocks differ in how well they resist it.

Comparing resistant and sensitive rootstocks, the team found the resistant ones boost a lysine-making pathway when infected. Lysine leaking from roots drew in helpful Bacillus bacteria, which rose sharply in share. Those bacteria made antifungal compounds that blocked the fungus. In pots and fields, pairing Bacillus with lysine cut disease, raised seedling weight, and steadied the root-zone community.
pmc-12836947:
Ting-Chieh Huang and eleven co-authors present a 2025 study on gut infections in bowel disease patients taking biologic drugs in Taiwan. These drugs calm inflammation but can open the door to opportunistic infections, and Asian comparisons across drug classes were scarce. Six hundred fourteen patients on three drug classes were followed for nearly a thousand patient-years combined. Three infections were tracked: two bacterial and one viral colitis.

Rates of the two bacterial infections were similar across all three drug classes. The viral colitis, caused by cytomegalovirus, was clearly more common on the anti-TNF class, at about six percent, than on the other two. A disease flare, and having one of the other infections, strongly predicted the main bacterial infection. The authors advise heightened watchfulness during flares. They clear two drug classes of extra gut infection risk on this evidence.
pmc-12837047:
Chuanzhen Yang and co-authors studied why growing cotton with mustard helps hold back a soil disease that wilts cotton, in work published in 2025. A three year field trial compared cotton grown alone with cotton grown beside mustard. The mixed plots had less disease and higher yield.

Mixed growing changed the microbes around cotton roots and boosted a core set of helpful strains. The team built a mix of five such strains, and that mix gave the best control in tests, far above single strains. It also switched on defense genes in the cotton plants. The authors say microbe mixes drawn from mixed cropping could be a greener way to fight soil disease.
pmc-12837347:
Siqi Liu, Young-Eun Noh, and Jeonghyo Kim gather qualitative studies on how injury reshapes an athlete's sense of self, in a 2025 review. For committed athletes, being an athlete is a core identity, and injury can shake it hard.

Twenty-four studies were synthesized under standard review guidelines. Two themes emerged. In seventeen studies, injury disrupted identity: limits on the body, withdrawal from competition, and distress shrank the athletic self. In seven, athletes rebuilt identity through new roles such as coaching, volunteering, or switching sports. Quality and confidence ratings were applied to the findings. The authors call for longer-term and mixed designs, and for attention to culture and context.
pmc-12838347:
Camilla Morosini and co-authors review the health record of heated tobacco products, in this 2025 paper. The devices warm tobacco instead of burning it, cutting many toxic outputs. Makers pitch them as a safer step for smokers who cannot quit.

A growing stack of studies, though, ties their use to cell stress and inflammation much like smoke. Animal work flags risks for lungs, heart, and fertility in both sexes. Human data are still young but point the same way. The authors weigh the claimed harm cut against these signals. They call for care in treating the products as safe swaps.
pmc-12839047:
Guangying Shao and co-authors wrote a 2025 review of urea transporters, proteins that move urea across cell membranes, and their roles in the heart and blood vessels. These proteins were long studied for their work in the kidneys, where they help concentrate urine. Newer work finds them in heart muscle and vessel lining cells as well.

In the heart system they help control cell water balance, a gas signal that relaxes vessels, the heart's electrical rhythm, and responses to stress. Faulty transport is now linked to high blood pressure, heart thickening and failure, rhythm faults, and vessel disease. The review weighs the promise and the hurdles of targeting these proteins with drugs.
pmc-12840547:
Dragoș Lazăr and co-authors chart eye damage in adults hospitalized with measles in Romania. Measles surged across Europe in 2023 and 2024, and Romania was hit hard. Eye signs are known in the disease but poorly counted in adults.

Records from a Bucharest hospital covered 250 laboratory-confirmed cases over one year. Eighty-eight patients saw an eye specialist, and nearly all of them had eye lesions. Inflammation of the cornea was the commonest form, in about two thirds of examined patients. The team compared the cornea group with other eye cases to find linked traits. Knowing the pattern helps wards order eye checks early. Adult measles is not just a rash and fever.
pmc-12840947:
Han Wu and co-authors test green soil inputs on yellow farm soil in southwest China in a 2025 study. The soil is sour and holds food poorly, which caps crop yield. Plots got less nitrogen feed plus rice husk and seed cake, with or without charred plant matter.

The green mixes raised soil pH, food stores, and maize yield by a modest share. Gene reads of soil life showed more helpful germ types and a shift in nitrogen-cycling genes. One soil nitrogen form stood out as the main link to gene change, the team reports, and more trials are urged.
pmc-12843247:
Binxing Li and co-authors published this study in 2025 on carotenoids, the pigments in foods like leafy greens and corn that the eye needs. The pigments ride to the eye on HDL, the so-called good cholesterol. Low stores are tied to a higher risk of age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of sight loss in older adults. The team asked what pigment pills do to blood fats.

They checked blood from women in a trial where half took lutein and zeaxanthin pills while pregnant. By late pregnancy, the pill group had higher HDL, with no shift in other blood fats. Mice fed any of three pigments for a month showed the same HDL rise, plus lower blood fats of the harmful kind. The authors think the HDL lift may be one way pigments guard the eye.
pmc-12845347:
Abdulkadir Bahadir Alkan and seven co-authors ask whether a sugar coat can steer how cancer cells swallow drug carriers. The carriers are tiny balls of a body-safe plastic, a common drug ferry. Which door a cell uses to take them in shapes where the drug lands. Their 2025 study coats the balls with two unlike sugars and tests them on breast cancer cells.

Uncoated balls went in mostly by a bulk gulp path cells use to drink their surroundings. One coat kept that path but added two finer doors. The other coat cut the bulk path and leaned more on a guided door. The team calls it a proof of concept for coat-based steering. More cell types and finer tests must come next, they note.
pmc-12846247:
Lin and co-authors test a weakened live vaccine against a gut disease of pigs. The bacterium Lawsonia intracellularis causes a thickening of the pig gut that harms growth. Few vaccines against the disease are on the market. The team weakened a strain by growing it through 90 rounds in lab cells. The tamed strain, JS-G90, was then given to pigs by mouth.

Vaccinated pigs shed fewer bacteria and showed no gut tissue damage, which signaled safety. The team then exposed pigs to the wild bacterium. They checked shedding, tissue harm, and both antibody and cell-based immune responses. The work weighs whether JS-G90 can anchor a new vaccine for pig farms.
pmc-12846347:
Qiqi Zhang and a team of co-authors mapped HIV types and drug resistance in Wuhan, China. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, used blood samples kept from twenty twenty-two. HIV types vary by region and shift over time. China now has many types in play at once. The team took one hundred forty-nine samples from a Wuhan hospital. They drew out cells, pulled the virus code, and read three key gene regions.

The reads showed the local mix of virus types and where drug resistance marks sit. Such maps guide which drug mixes to use first. Readers who plan HIV care in central China get a local view of type spread and resistance. The work backs care choices with lab proof from the city itself.
pmc-12847747:
Yutao Yan and co-authors build a network that tells real faces from fakes in a paper published in 2025. Face recognition systems can be fooled by photos, screens, or masks, so anti-spoofing checks are vital. Many past methods ignore useful clues across sensing modes or are too heavy for real use.

Their network, DAH-FAS, combines three branches: color images, infrared, and depth. A custom block sharpens fine detail in the color branch, while a thermal enhancer helps the infrared branch read heat patterns of living skin. An attention step aligns features between the infrared and depth branches so they reinforce each other. On three public benchmark sets, the method separated real from fake faces with clear advantages over rivals.
pmc-12847847:
Xiaoyue Ma and colleagues published a 2025 study on ultra-fast wireless links using light. Radio spectrum is crowded and limited. Laser beams offer a huge alternative bandwidth. Steering light beams without moving parts is the challenge. The team used a chip of thin-film lithium niobate.

Their phased array steered beams electronically. Multiple targets could connect in real time. One channel reached extremely high data rates. That pace exceeds current mobile network peaks. Uncompressed high-definition video streamed stably in tests. Chip-scale light links could serve dense data centers. Vehicle and indoor networks may follow.
pmc-12848547:
Jun Yamazaki and co-authors track a protein in the spinal cords of normal mice as they age. The protein is a known mark of the fast, easily tired nerve cells that move muscles. Those cells die early in ALS, a disease that wastes the nerves that drive movement. Their 2025 study asks how the protein's pattern shifts between youth and middle age in healthy animals.

The team counted nerve cells in mice at six and twelve months of age. Both the total count and the count of marked cells fell with age. Marked cells also showed a stray buildup of a second protein tied to ALS harm. The authors suggest the mark may flag cells prone to wear out. They urge checks in ALS patients and disease models next.
pmc-12848847:
Weakness and numbness climbing up the limbs often points doctors toward Guillain-Barré syndrome, but a missing nutrient can mimic it. Albright, Pitter, and Benameur report two women whose spinal cord trouble traced back to copper deficiency. One, fed through a gut tube after esophagus surgery, lost feeling and balance over six months; the other, a long-time zinc user with denture adhesive, worsened over two weeks.

Both cases turned on history: past surgery, feeding routes, and zinc exposure, which blocks copper uptake. The authors urge doctors to weigh diet and surgical history, plus exam, lab, and scan clues, before settling on a nerve diagnosis.
pmc-12851847:
David Heath, Natasha Patrick, Christine Li, and Fiona Lee report a rare twisted gut emergency in a teen girl in a 2025 case study. A pouch present from birth on her small bowel, usually silent, triggered one gut segment to telescope into another.

She arrived with one day of sharp pain low on the right side, matching appendicitis. Scans hinted at the telescoping but missed the pouch. Surgery found the folded segment, a full twist of the mid gut, and the pouch as the lead point. Doctors untwisted and removed the pouch; the bowel survived and she recovered smoothly.
pmc-12852247:
Hannah Gidl, Sara Binder, Anna Osiecka, and Barbara Klump follow how young carrion crows grow voices that mark them as individuals, in a 2025 paper. Social animals benefit from telling group members apart, and calls often carry a signature of who is calling. What was unclear is how early such signatures appear and how steady they stay as a bird grows. The team hand-raised crows and recorded them for four weeks, across the nestling and fledgling stages.

Signatures of identity were present from the start, carried by several features of the calls. The same features stayed in charge as the birds aged, even as the calls themselves changed. Crows also grew more distinct from one another over time, though the pace of change depended on the situation in which they called. The authors link this shifting vocal identity to the birds' social development in their first weeks of life.
pmc-12853847:
Jinyan Chen and five colleagues map a three-way RNA rivalry in the blood cells of new diabetics, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Long noncoding RNAs can sponge up microRNAs in the cell. That frees the genes those microRNAs hold down in their work. Such networks may yield blood tests for type 2 diabetes.

Blood cells from newly diagnosed patients and healthy controls went through microarray and sequencing screens. RNAs that split in their levels were built into a competing network. Its named axis links the noncoding RNA PRNCR1, a microRNA, and the gene SSTR3. Laboratory assays validated the levels of the molecules in the axis. Accuracy analysis tested how well it could sort cases, set against clinical parameters. A leukocyte-based signature would be an accessible window into diabetes biology. It can be drawn from an ordinary blood draw.
pmc-12853947:
Yuzhu Fan and co-authors report a sly case in a 2025 paper of a gland ill masked by pregnancy. The ill pours out a salt hormone that drives blood pressure up. In pregnancy that pressure can fall to plain, since a second hormone blocks the first, and the true ill hides.

Their patient was a young woman with dizzy turns and wild pressure swings. First checks missed the gland cause. After birth, the block lifted and pressure leapt back, which at last gave the game away. The case maps the trap step by step. Birth teams gain a warn tale for pressure that calms too well.
pmc-12855947:
Pietracupa and a large team scan in twenty twenty-five the brains of newly diagnosed Parkinson's patients to see whether early network changes forecast decline. Several dozen untreated patients and healthy peers had brain scans and motor and thinking tests, and about half the patients were rechecked after roughly five years. Structure measures covered grey matter and deep brain volumes, while resting scans mapped how networks talk.

Patients showed no structural loss yet, but their resting networks were already quieter across many systems, from movement to attention. Those quiet patterns did not match symptoms on the day. They did predict who worsened over the follow-up years. The authors pitch resting scans as an early tracking tool for the disease.
pmc-12859847:
Boyang Zeng and a large co-author team link, in 2025 work, a famed gene's forms to a blood index of swelling in a large Chinese sample. The gene shapes fat handling and risk for heart and brain disease. One of its forms is thought to fan low-grade swelling, but no single blood mark had caught that trait well.

Close to fourteen thousand adults at one hospital were typed for the gene and had the index worked out from three blood counts. Carriers of the risk form held a higher index than the base group, while carriers of the guard form held a lower one. The links held across sex, age, pressure, and sugar groups. The team reads the gene as a driver of chronic mild swelling.
pmc-12864547:
Eline Hooijman and colleagues check whether labs worldwide can spot decay in a radioactive prostate cancer drug, and what that decay does in the body, in this study from twenty twenty-five. The drug carries lutetium-177 to PSMA on tumor cells. Its own radiation slowly chews it up, a process called radiolysis, and broken drug may wander off target.

Hospitals compared their liquid chromatography methods and could each measure the damage consistently, with only small spread between labs. One official method separated peaks better but lost more sample, with no gain in the purity verdict. In mice bearing prostate tumors, batches made at three purity levels behaved as feared: the more degraded the drug, the less it favored tumor over kidney. The authors say quality control for radiolysis is trustworthy across sites, and worth keeping tight.
pmc-12864647:
Tian Guolin and seven co-authors pooled studies on giving hormone therapy before prostate removal surgery, in this 2025 review. The question is whether shrinking and calming the tumor with neoadjuvant hormone treatment first makes the keyhole operation safer and more successful. Surgeons have debated the practice for years on conflicting small studies.

Searching six databases up to February 2025, the team found fourteen cohort studies comparing surgery with and without pre-treatment. The combined results favored hormone therapy first: fewer positive margins, meaning less cancer left at the cut edge, fewer biochemical recurrences, less blood loss, and shorter catheter time. A subgroup using robot-assisted surgery gained further on operating time and margins. The authors conclude the add-on improves surgical outcomes, while noting the evidence comes from cohorts rather than randomized trials.
pmc-12868647:
Paolo Cocomazzi and a large team of co-authors study the antibody-like receptors on cancerous white blood cells. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The cancer is a slow leukemia of B cells. In many patient groups, these receptors switch themselves on without any outside trigger, which helps the cancer cells grow. One large patient group was untested for this trait.

The team built receptors from three patients in that group and studied their shapes. The receptors reacted to many self targets, a shared pattern for the group. But they did not clump together or switch on signals in a test cell line. That sets this group apart from the others. The cancer in these patients must grow by some other route, the authors argue.
pmc-12868747:
Wenkai Zhu and sixteen co-authors report a magnetic tunnel junction built from atomically thin materials that produces large spin signals, in this 2025 paper. The device is a p-n junction only nanometers thick, and it generates, steers, and detects electron spin without any applied voltage. Such effects feed low-power spintronic electronics.

The junction's tunneling magnetoresistance reached eleven hundred percent at a tiny bias current. Stranger still, at zero bias the device produced a spin voltage effect above thirty thousand percent, far beyond any magnetoresistance signal reported before. The team traces the effect to uneven diffusion: spin-up and spin-down electrons cross the junction at different rates, pushed by its built-in electric field while it trades energy with its surroundings. They call the state a spin-engine regime. The findings suggest new ways to transform and amplify spin information for electronics that sip power.
pmc-12869947:
Kongkong Cui and co-authors study children whose neuroblastoma, a childhood cancer, was found before birth and treated with surgery, in work from 2025. Better ultrasound has made such early finds more common. Yet most past knowledge came from single case reports, leaving gaps on long term health and quality of life.

The team reviewed forty-nine cases from one major center over more than a decade. They added just over one hundred cases from prior studies. Most tumors began in the adrenal glands. Data covered tumor traits, treatment, complications, and survival. Follow up also checked later health problems and daily quality of life.
pmc-12874847:
Young Gyu Kwon and co-authors find what drives unmet health care needs in South Korea in a 2025 paper. Even with national insurance, many people miss needed care. The team compared five machine learning methods to rank the barriers.

Data covered nearly 1.5 million adults from a community health survey spanning 2016 to 2022. Factors were grouped as predisposing, enabling, and need-based. One method, LightGBM, predicted best, with high accuracy and strong recall. Age, income, self-rated health, drinking, schooling, work status, and walking habits mattered most. The authors frame the results for precision public health.
pmc-12875547:
Mehtap Gunes and co-authors report a rare birth condition in a teenage girl, in a 2025 case report. The condition joins three traits: a blocked half of the vagina, a doubled womb, and a missing kidney on the same side. Late diagnosis can lead to trapped blood, tissue growth in the wrong place, and loss of fertility.

The patient, aged fourteen, came in with belly pain and irregular periods. Scans showed the doubled womb, trapped blood on the right side, and the missing right kidney. Surgeons opened the blocked passage while keeping the hymen intact, drained the blood, and placed a short-term tube to keep the path open. She recovered well and went home on the second day. The authors stress early scans when such pain appears in teens.
pmc-12892847:
Rusinova and six colleagues strip rat sciatic nerves of cells to make graft scaffolds for wide nerve gaps in twenty twenty-five. A day long wash of enzymes and detergents clears the cells while sparing the nerve's frame. Rats then got the scaffold or their own nerve graft across a long defect. Recovery was scored at ninety days.

DNA fell to a fifth of native levels, and no nuclei stayed. Skin tests showed no macrophage attack on the scaffold. Fiber counts in scaffold grafts trailed the own graft gold standard. Small myelinated and motor fibers regrew, though. The team calls the scaffold a promising graft stand in.
pmc-12905847:
Xinjie Li and thirteen co-authors test blood sugar chain profiles as a no cut way to spot major liver harm in chronic hepatitis B. Early spotting of harm guides when to start virus drugs. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Standard no cut tests miss hidden harm, most of all when liver enzyme levels look normal. The team studied over six hundred patients who had never had virus care and whose harm was proven by liver biopsy. Sugar chain profiles came from an automated read method. About two thirds had major swelling and over half had major scarring. Set peaks rose or fell in a clear pattern with harm, the authors report.
pmc-12906747:
Community programs can curb high blood pressure, but whether they pay for themselves is less clear. Reshu Agrawal Sagtani and co-authors set out a review plan for that money question in a 2025 protocol paper. Their review will gather full cost studies of community programs for preventing and managing hypertension. Six databases plus grey sources will be searched up to January 2025. Two reviewers will screen the finds on their own.

Quality of each study will be graded with set checklists. A pooled math summary will run only if the studies match closely enough in method and outcome. The team aims to compare cost results across countries and program styles. The paper is a plan, published before the review itself is run.
pmc-12907447:
Marie Warny and co-authors present a study, published in 2025 per the text, on predicting outcomes after stem cell transplants from donors. A successful transplant needs the immune system to rebuild. Two cell types that return early, natural killer cells and gamma-delta T cells, may attack leukemia without harming the patient's own tissues.

The team followed 105 patients at one center, measuring two growth signals and many cell types over time. High levels of one signal, interleukin-15, soon after transplant linked to worse survival and more graft-versus-host disease. The signal also tracked inversely with the protective cell counts. The findings suggest that this signal could flag patients at risk early, when extra care might help most.
pmc-12918047:
Wei Han and co-authors report a case of an infant carrying two different cancers at once. The head of the record dates the report to 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. The four-month-old had a malignant rhabdoid tumor of the kidney. Simultaneously, the child had a neuroblastoma of the adrenal gland. No guideline covers so rare a pairing.

After surgery, protons delivered fourteen gray in ten sessions to the abdominal-pelvic tumor bed. Strict sparing of growing organs was the aim throughout. A literature review backs protons for such cases, since they stop inside the target. One year on, the child stayed disease-free. Kidney function and skeletal growth stayed normal. The authors present the case as support for protons where photons would tax development.
pmc-12926447:
Kexin Cheng, Weihong Li, and five co-authors review plant scents sniffed as a cure for depression. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, covers essential oils given through the nose. Depression is common and disabling, yet standard drugs act slowly and often cause side effects. The nose offers a direct path to the brain that skips a key barrier.

The team pools forty studies from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-five. Plant oils hold many small fat-loving compounds that act on several targets at once. The review sums up dose plans and timing used in the studies. It also lays out how the oils may lift mood. Gaps that block clinic use are flagged for future work.
pmc-12946147:
Kotaro Matsuura and six co-authors tested in 2025 whether showing elderly patients objective measures of their movement keeps them exercising. Rehab works only if people stick with it, and quitting is common. The team used camera-based motion capture with artificial intelligence to estimate arm joint forces in 31 older hospital patients. Half got a feedback report midway through eight weeks of exercise; half did not.

A short questionnaire tracked motivation, self-understanding of progress and intent to continue. Patients with Parkinson's disease scored worse on change than the other groups. Among the rest, the feedback group tended to gain in willingness to keep going. The authors read visible progress as a nudge that supports long-term rehab. They note the design was not randomized, so larger trials should confirm the effect.
pmc-12977547:
Wenxiu Chen and co-authors hunt in 2025 for genes that drive the hormone imbalance of polycystic ovary syndrome. The team sequenced RNA from patients' ovarian granulosa cells and from two mouse models of the condition, then merged the gene lists to find shared suspects.

One gene, PLAU, stood out. It runs high in the syndrome's granulosa cells, and the study links its rise to disturbed steroid hormone production and to more cell death in the ovary. The harm runs through a known inflammatory switch, the NF-kB pathway named in the title. The work marks PLAU as a candidate driver worth targeting in future studies.
pmc-12985347:
Two surgeons in Mexico report a rare hip injury from a car crash and how they fixed it in one operation, in a case report published in 2025. The patient, a thirty-three-year-old man, arrived with many injuries, including a hip dislocated forward with the thigh bone's neck trapped in a pelvic opening. Such combined injuries are exceedingly rare and usually follow high-energy trauma. The team planned a single procedure with two surgical approaches.

Through one approach they removed the trapped femoral head, and through another they fitted a total hip replacement. The operation finished without complications. The patient bore full weight within two weeks of rehab. Two years later his strength was preserved, scans showed a stable implant, and his hip score was strong. The authors offer the dual-approach operation as a safe, effective answer to this rare pattern.
pmc-12997447:
Animal disease laboratories across Southeast Asia were scored with a standard mapping tool between 2012 and 2020, and Morgane Gourlaouen and co-authors analyzed the results for thirty-two labs in ten countries. The tool grades five areas, from organization to disease surveillance quality. The regional average landed at sixty percent, with wide spread.

Most labs improved steadily across the decade. Those already strong held their level. Labs targeted by support programs climbed the most, in some cases sharply. Persistent gaps cluster in the same categories across the region. The authors use the map to aim future investment, arguing the tool itself is a fair way to watch progress. The study was published in 2025.
pmc-13021147:
Meredith Franco and co-authors study coaching that helps teachers run equity and social-emotional lessons. Schools were split by lot into two arms of a trial. One arm taught a standard social-emotional curriculum with coaching. The other added equity-focused lessons plus coaching for both sets. The team checked 106 coached teachers for how well coaching matched its plan.

Coaching in both arms ran as designed, and the equity arm's coaching looked distinct. Teacher traits, such as background, tied to how much coaching each teacher used. Teachers in both arms rated work with their coaches well. The authors draw lessons for coaching that can carry equity aims into daily class work. They urge care in how coaches are matched and supported.
pmc-13084047:
Rehab Salah Eldeen and three co-authors tuned a power filter controller with a hybrid search. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, deals with hybrid active power filters, which clean harmonic junk from power lines. Their control rests on a fractional order PID, a five knob scheme with tight links between knobs. Plain tuning goes shaky on such a set. The team joined two nature drawn searches: a pelican method and a grey wolf method.

The pelican side adapts the hunt; the wolf side adds pack smarts. Joint, they tune all five knobs with more balance than each alone. Aim marks are firm dynamic acts and deep harmonic cuts. Readers in power electronics get a steadier way to set a hard controller.
pmc-13084147:
Li Liu and co-authors set out a plan to study visiting in intensive care units in China, in a 2026 protocol paper. Past work on in-person and video visits leans on numbers for safety and effect. Far less is known about how visits feel to patients, families, and staff.

Interviews will be held with all three groups at three large public hospitals in the southwest of the country. People will be chosen on purpose to cover varied roles, and talks will run until no new themes emerge. Responses will be sorted with a set seven-step method for lived experience studies. The team hopes to surface gaps between the two visit modes and guide better family visiting practice.
pmc-13096947:
Gabriela Galarza-Arévalo, Myriam González, and Maria Romero published a review in twenty twenty-six on metallic nanoparticles already at work in clinics, as diagnostics, therapies, and both at once. Iron, gold, hafnium, gadolinium, silver, copper, titanium, and zinc particles are surveyed across cancer, infection control, coatings, and imaging.

Clinical numbers anchor the survey. Iron oxide particles heated glioblastoma tumors during magnetic therapy. Gold shells ablated most treated prostate lesions. A gold particle ferried a potent cytokine safely through the body. Silver fluoride cut children's dentin caries progression notably. The authors argue the field has crossed from promise to practice in specific niches, while integration of diagnosis and therapy in one particle remains the frontier.
pmc-13127247:
Akhil Nair, Lucas Foppa, and Matthias Scheffler present a clearer way to search for new catalysts in this 2026 paper. Catalysts speed up chemical reactions, and computer-guided search can test many candidate materials. Standard search tools need a few key physical traits in advance, but for these reactions the right traits are unknown.

Their framework picks the key traits as it searches, using a method that builds short formulas from physical quantities. It can catch curved links and interactions between traits that simpler screens miss. In simulated hunts, the method found surface sites of one- and two-atom alloys that can activate carbon dioxide. It beat widely used feature-picking approaches. The authors aim to make guided discovery work where expert traits are not known ahead.
pmc-13128247:
Thamyris Maia and Mariana Cunha translate a cancer navigation scorecard into Brazilian Portuguese in a 2026 study. Nurse navigators guide cancer patients through complex care. An American academy defines thirty-five metrics to judge navigation programs; Brazil needed them in its own language and culture.

Permission secured, the team followed standard adaptation steps. A ten-expert committee checked meaning, idiom, lived fit, and concepts across three rounds to ninety percent agreement. Thirty-five nurse judges then pretested every metric for clarity and local sense. The content validity index reached 0.97. The adapted set is offered as ready for Brazilian oncology services to evaluate their navigation work.
pmc-13132647:
Yudai Fujimoto, Yoshimi Yuri, and Hironari Tamiya reported in 2026 a case of using a wearable tracker to manage activity during intensive treatment for leg lymphedema. Decongestive therapy is the standard care for this chronic swelling, but how much activity is best during it was unclear. Their patient was an older woman with swelling in both legs after cancer treatment.

Over a two-week hospital program, a wrist device tracked her steps, distance, energy use, and sleep against a daily step goal set together with her team. Swelling measures, skin quality, and mobility all improved, as did her quality of life scores. The authors say wearable data can support shared goal setting and engagement during therapy.
pmc-13134347:
Ahmad Madankan and co-authors report a case where appendix pain turned out to be endosalpingiosis, fallopian tube lining growing where it does not belong. Published in 2026, the case concerns a 21-year-old Iranian woman with severe right lower abdominal pain, nausea, and a sense of fever. Scans looked normal, yet the pain demanded action.

Surgery removed the appendix, and tissue study found the stray ciliated lining inside it. Her symptoms cleared fully afterward. The condition usually appears in ovaries or the uterus, and appendix cases are rare enough to count. The authors add it to the list of appendicitis mimics and advise a gynecological check after such a find, given its links to pelvic disease.
pmc-13135447:
Yoshihiro Miyake and four co-authors report a leak between a neck artery and a vein behind the eye, in this 2026 case report. The cause was a car crash that barely touched the patient's face. A carotid-cavernous fistula is a direct shunt from the internal carotid artery into the cavernous sinus, usually the price of severe head injury. Arterial pressure then floods the eye's veins.

Their patient was a seventy-six-year-old woman whose injuries were mostly to her chest and abdomen, with a facial bruise. Fifteen days later she reported a pulsing noise in her ear, and her right eye developed drooping, redness, and frozen movement; scans confirmed the shunt, and symptoms mirrored on the left. Doctors sealed the left-sided fistula by embolization, threading a catheter to the leak. The lesson is vigilance: even minimal facial trauma can hide an injury that threatens sight.
pmc-13135547:
Dervla Quinn and four co-authors track post-traumatic stress disorder among women giving birth in United States hospitals, in a 2026 study. Using a national inpatient database covering 2016 to 2020, they measured how often PTSD appeared in delivery records and what it meant for mother and baby.

Recorded PTSD more than doubled over the period, from about 236 to 546 per hundred thousand deliveries, growing roughly twenty-three percent per year. Women with the diagnosis carried more other health conditions. Their odds of preterm delivery ran about thirteen percent higher, and of restricted fetal growth about nine percent higher. Stays were longer and hospital costs greater. The authors call for research into why diagnoses are climbing and whether the stress disorder itself, or its causes, drives the added risk.
pmc-13136747:
Salma Hashem, Roméo Murhega, and Patient Migabo report a misplaced pituitary in a 2026 case paper. The back lobe of the gland sometimes forms in the wrong spot during development, a rare quirk often tied to other brain differences. A seventy-two-year-old woman's scan, taken during a balance workup, found it by chance.

Her gland lobe sat away from its usual seat, with no hormone faults to show for it. The report details the scan signs that mark the condition. A review of bright-spot lesions on the same scan type helps readers split look-alikes. Chance finds like this test a radiologist's calm and knowledge.
pmc-13138247:
Varsha Rathore and co-authors show a mitochondrial protein driving prostate cancer in a 2026 study. The protein plays both sides in other cancers, suppressing some and feeding others. In prostate tumors its levels climb under stress, and the team traced what it does there.

Silencing it slowed growth in one cell line, curbed migration and invasion, and pushed stressed cells toward death. The protein grips a key growth switch directly, keeping two signal paths lit. Blocking those paths reproduced the silencing effect. Tumor data tie high levels to worse outlook. The authors name the protein a candidate biomarker and a possible drug target for aggressive disease.
pmc-13139647:
Tama Ray and seven co-authors test how the definition of forest canopy changes measured links to productivity in a 2026 paper. Canopy structure controls light capture, and fuller canopies usually mean more productive stands. But researchers define canopy space differently, and no universal definition exists.

Using laser scanning data from a tropical tree diversity experiment, the team computed a space filling index under four canopy definitions. The index varied strongly with the definition chosen. Still, fuller canopies predicted higher productivity under all definitions. Cutting off the top layer and adding the lowest layer weakened the link notably. Filling mattered more in mixed species stands than in single species ones. Layer choice, the authors argue, deserves care in forest studies.
pmc-13140947:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome turns injured lungs stiff and starved of oxygen, and it still kills many trauma patients. Manuel Castillo-Angeles and Ali Salim review how to manage it in their 2026 paper. The core of care, they stress, is lung-protective ventilation, careful fluid balance, and a team approach across specialties.

New work is reshaping the edges of that core. Sorting patients into phenotypes promises care matched to the kind of ARDS at hand, and precision medicine pushes the same way. Advances in ECMO, the heart-lung bypass that can rest ruined lungs, widen the options for the worst cases. The authors survey adjunctive therapies as well and argue that the clearest gains now lie in these emerging tools.
pmc-13141247:
Shujie Wang and co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol paper, a study of whether a blood chemical can flag older patients at risk of delirium after gut surgery. Delirium strikes about thirty percent of older adults after such operations, bringing confusion that can last and harm recovery. Gut surgery is known to raise production of serotonin, the chemical in question, but its tie to delirium is unproven.

The single-center study will enroll 314 patients aged sixty and over having planned gut surgery in Qingdao, China. Serotonin will be measured before anesthesia and again after surgery. The main outcome is delirium within three days, scored by trained assessors. Recovery quality, gut function, pain, and complications are also tracked, with a preset causal map guiding the analysis. Consent and ethics approvals are in place.
pmc-13142147:
Pulkit Mehrotra and colleagues reported an adult Wolfram syndrome case in 2026. Wolfram syndrome usually starts in childhood. Diabetes and optic nerve wasting define it. Brain degeneration progresses alongside both. Adult cases are easily missed clinically. A thirty-eight-year-old woman presented late here.

Her diabetes needed insulin from early on. Antibodies were absent in her tests. Vision loss advanced from optic atrophy. Brain scans showed cerebellar shrinkage too. Genetic testing found a novel variant. Both gene copies carried the fault. Suspicion and imaging guided the diagnosis. Trial eligibility may now follow.
pmc-13144347:
Ari Dienel and co-authors report a 2026 mouse study on bleeding around the brain, a condition called subarachnoid hemorrhage. Some patients get worse days after the bleed, a problem known as delayed neurological deficits. Tiny clots in small brain vessels are thought to play a part, but trials of anti-clot drugs in people have given mixed results.

The team tested cause and effect in mice. After the bleed, clot-related factors rose, small clots formed, and animals with more clots did worse. Boosting platelet action made outcomes worse, while removing platelets cut clots and improved results. Some anti-platelet drugs also helped, and they calmed platelets taken from human patients. The authors call platelets a promising treatment target.
pmc-13144747:
Mohamed Ibrahim and co-authors pilot a noninvasive way to measure kidney vessel responses in Black adults in a 2026 study. They expected standing, hand grip exercise, and cold to raise blood pressure and lower kidney blood flow conductance. Pressure was recorded without pause, and kidney artery speed was read by ultrasound.

Eleven adults took part, and each stimulus raised pressure as expected in first visits. Hand grip also lowered kidney conductance in the data. Repeated visits let the team check how stable the measures are. A reliable bedside method could help study vessel health in groups at high risk of kidney and heart disease.
pmc-13144947:
Rafia Zaman and co-authors reported in 2026 a stroke patient whose scans turned up an unexpected lump: a rare tumor of the carotid body, the tiny sensor where the neck artery forks. Such tumors are usually harmless and silent, found in only one or two people per hundred thousand.

The sixty-three year old man came in with slurred speech and weakness on one side; brain scans confirmed a stroke in the right middle artery territory. Neck ultrasound found no artery narrowing but spotted a solid mass wedged between the fork's branches, and a follow up scan confirmed the tumor at two centimeters wide. A vessel team advised removal, since the tumor can grow, press on nerves, or rarely turn malignant.
pmc-13145447:
Siobhan McLernon and co-authors ask young Black and minority ethnic adults in London what they know about stroke risk. Their conference abstract from 2026 notes that stroke under age sixty five is rising, with Black and South Asian groups hit earlier. The study joins group talks with a survey.

Six talk groups held 43 people, and 241 people filled in the survey. Knowledge of common risks such as high blood pressure was strong. Knowledge was weak for diabetes, heart rhythm faults, kidney disease, poverty, air pollution, and risks tied to sex. Women scored higher on awareness than men in the tests. The authors use the gaps to shape local prevention work.
pmc-13145547:
Federico Marrama and co-authors asked in 2026 why some stroke patients who gain ground fast still end up disabled. A clot-pull procedure can restore flow, and a sharp drop in stroke scores in the first day is a good sign. Yet some such patients never regain free daily life. The team read a national registry of clot-pull care from 2015 to 2022 and kept patients whose scores fell fast.

Near one in five of those fast gainers had a poor outcome at ninety days. Age past seventy-five, diabetes, and brain bleed after care each raised that risk. A longer wait from last well time to the procedure added risk by the hour. Full flow restore cut the risk. The authors say a good first day is not the whole tale.
pmc-13145847:
Veltkamp and a large team (2026) studied why some patients suffer strokes despite blood thinners for atrial fibrillation. Such breakthrough strokes are poorly understood. The team used a multicenter study of 2,737 patients with a fresh stroke. They checked CT scans for hardening of the neck arteries, including soft, risky plaques, and grouped patients by their pre-stroke anticoagulant.

Scans were available for 1,464 patients, and 81 percent had some carotid atherosclerosis. About 17 percent had a narrowing of at least half, or a full blockage. Among patients with one-sided stroke and no big narrowing, risky plaque on the stroke side appeared in about a third of cases, far more often than plaque on the opposite side only. In patients on the newer oral drugs, same-side risky plaque was over four times as likely as in patients on no anticoagulant. The authors call this plaque an underestimated partner in breakthrough strokes.
pmc-13146047:
Tho Phung and co-authors report a 2026 conference study on spotting severe sleep apnea in stroke patients. The standard screen is a questionnaire, but stroke can leave patients unable to answer well. The team instead measured throat length on the brain scans these patients already receive.

In one hundred three adults treated for acute stroke, a combined throat length measure ran longer in those with severe apnea. The scan measure sorted patients better than the questionnaire score, and a cutoff caught most severe cases while clearing about half of the rest. The questionnaire cleared far fewer. The authors say the scan route is fast, objective, and adds no cost or new steps to care.
pmc-13146447:
Shih-Syuan Wang and co-authors compare two ways to keep stroke patients still during clot removal, in a 2026 review. Full anesthesia gives stillness, while conscious sedation may speed the work and keep blood pressure steadier. Which is better for acute stroke care has stayed unclear.

The review pooled nine trials with close to fifteen hundred patients. Full anesthesia gave higher rates of successful reopening of the blocked vessel. Yet rates of living on one's own at ninety days did not differ in a clear way between the groups. Death rates were also a safety check. The trade off can guide teams that must choose fast in the suite.
pmc-13146647:
Michele Malesani and co-authors report a 2026 conference study on seizure-like brain wave spikes after stroke and whether faster vessel reopening prevents them. The spikes show on brain wave tests in the first days and mark higher risk of later epilepsy. All patients in the study got drug or device reopening care.

Among more than two hundred patients with wave tests within three days, about a quarter showed the spikes. Drug start times matched between those with and without spikes. Times to device start and to full reopening, though, ran clearly longer in the spike group. The authors read the gap as a sign that faster device care may cut spike risk, while calling for more study.
pmc-13146747:
Yingchao He, Yongkun Li, and Yinzhou Wang present a 2026 conference report on an unexpected benefit of one way to treat brain aneurysms. Patients with unburst aneurysms often also carry heart and brain vessel disease, leaving them open to strokes and heart attacks. One repair method, stent-assisted coiling, forces months of strong blood-thinning therapy afterward.

The team reviewed nearly two thousand such patients across three strategies: open clipping, simple coiling, and stent-assisted coiling, the largest group. The main measure was the rate of vessel-blocking events in the six months after treatment. The question is whether the forced thinning therapy protects the whole body, not just the repair site. Results compare the mid-term safety of each route.
pmc-13147647:
Three Nordic societies for anaesthesia and intensive care write a joint letter in 2026 pushing back on new goals set for emergency medicine in their region. A working group had proposed that emergency doctors take first charge of all acute patients, including the sickest, both in hospital and before arrival. In Nordic lands that first charge now sits with anaesthesia teams, who fear the shift could put patients at risk.
