The letter notes that sparse populations and high public safety mean few critical cases reach each doctor, which makes deep skill hard to keep up. Handing rare, high-stakes work to a broader group could thin that skill further. The societies ask that patient safety anchor any change.
pmc-13149747:
Ten authors, led by Mahboobeh Ghasemzadeh Rahbardar, wrote this 2026 cohort study on blood inflammation scores and later death. Simple ratios built from routine blood counts have been proposed as signs of future risk. The study tests four of them: counts that mix neutrophils, lymphocytes, and platelets in varied ways.

The data come from the MASHAD cohort, drawn from adults aged 35 to 65 by a stratified cluster method. Baseline records held background facts, health data, and the inflammation scores. The team then followed the group for ten years. Deaths from all causes, from cancer, and from cardiovascular disease were tracked. Survival models weighed how each score linked to each outcome. The work asks whether a cheap blood score can flag high-risk adults early.
pmc-13154547:
Xingwei Jiang and co-authors feed soy compounds to dairy cows in 2026 and track the effects at many levels at once. Milk yield and feed thrift matter for greener dairy, since the gut vat where cows ferment feed sets how much energy and nitrogen they use. Whether plant compounds from soy shift that vat, body hormones, and yield together was unclear.

Fifty-six Holstein cows split into high and low yielders, then by diet: plain feed or feed with a pinch of the soy compounds. In all, four groups of fourteen formed. The soy diet lifted milk yield by 8.75 percent, they report, with fat-corrected milk, intake, and feed thrift all up a few points, and more for some groups. Multi-level reads aim to show why.
pmc-13155147:
Zhao, Ckurshumova, Ettehadolhagh, Liu, Fefer, and Hoare deliver a crop protectant switched on by light, carried in nanovesicles, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Light-driven killing can wipe out plant germs of many kinds once light hits them. What holds the method back in the field is getting the activator to the crop. Tiny vesicles carry magnesium chlorophyllin in their skins.

Added agents tune how the load comes out: fast when the vesicle gets wet again, or slow, by seeping through the skin. The load tops sixty percent, with vesicles near ninety nanometers wide. Killing of a bacterial plant germ under light improves a lot. Uptake into plant roots also improves with the carriers. Other crop agents that love water could ride the same platform.
pmc-13156247: Ji Sun and co-authors report advanced gastric cancer that appeared as a giant growth under the stomach lining, in a case report from 2026. Stomach cancer can at times mimic a stromal tumor that sits below the surface. When that tumor type is suspected before surgery with no firm tissue proof, a frozen section check during surgery is advised, so the wrong operation is not done.
pmc-13156547:
Grant M. Pham and Roger N. Pham published a 2026 case series on an unusual shingles pattern. Shingles usually strikes one skin strip on one side. Two young healthy men broke that pattern. Their lesions crossed several skin regions. Neither man had immune problems.

Ages were thirty-five and twenty. Psychological stress preceded both cases. A skin microscope tool aided early recognition. Antiviral treatment started promptly for both. Supportive care included stress reduction advice. Both men recovered fully. Stress may help reactivate the dormant chickenpox virus. Doctors should not rule out shingles in young, healthy patients.
pmc-13157347:
Njira Lugogo and co-authors report, in 2026, on deaths among adults in the United States who had severe asthma cared for by lung experts. Their data come from the CHRONICLE study, which enrolled 4,366 adults from 2018 to 2024. Patients joined if they used strong biologic drugs, used steroid pills for much of the prior year, or stayed uncontrolled on strong inhaled care. The team describes who died, what doctors named as the main cause, and what care each person was on.

Over about 14,758 person-years of follow-up, 130 people died, or about 3 percent of the group. That rate was 8.8 deaths per 1,000 person-years. The report fills a gap, since fresh data on death in this group have been scarce.
pmc-13157447:
A parvovirus of horses, first tied to fatal liver disease after serum treatments, turns out to circulate quietly in healthy animals too. Picetti and co-authors sampled one thousand healthy horses across forty municipalities in the north of Brazil's Rio Grande do Sul state. They pooled the blood samples five at a time and searched each pool for the virus's DNA with a sensitive nested test.

The virus showed up in 69 of the 200 pools, spread over twenty-six of the forty municipalities, and age made no clear difference to the rate. Sequencing a gene fragment from five pools showed the local strains closely match those found worldwide, with small spelling differences shared with Argentine strains. The authors conclude the virus is widespread in the region's horses and should be on the list when a horse shows signs of hepatitis.
pmc-13157747:
Andriko Palmowski and co-authors pool patient-level data from rheumatoid arthritis trials to price two years of low-dose steroids in bone, in a 2026 analysis. Five trials with 1,112 patients compared doses up to seven and a half milligrams of prednisone equivalent against standard care, with spine and hip density and fractures as the joint outcomes.

The steroid groups lost a small but real amount of spine bone density, while the hip held steady. Fractures were uncommon and equally frequent in both arms, and no subgroup stood out as especially fragile. Repeated checks kept the result. The authors conclude the bone cost of low-dose treatment is real but confined to the spine over two years.
pmc-13159947:
Hongxu Zhu and Qi Jin build a risk chart for heart patients in a 2026 paper. Two blood proteins form a ratio that tracks artery risk. The team asked whether that ratio forecasts major events after stenting. Their patients had coronary artery disease treated with a stent procedure.

Records covered nearly two thousand five hundred patients. About eight percent had a major event over roughly three years. Each step up in the ratio raised event risk measurably. A chart blending ten factors sorted patients into three risk bands. Five year event free rates fell steadily from the low to the high band. Checks on a held back group confirmed the chart's accuracy. The authors offer it for clinic risk talks.
pmc-13164147:
Wiset and six co-authors optimize infrared roasting for immature rice, in work from twenty twenty-six. Immature rice is eaten across Asia for its green color, soft texture, distinct flavor, and nutrition. Its fragile grains and sensitive pigments make processing tricky.

Roasting temperature and time in a rotary infrared roaster were varied across wide ranges. Effects on physicochemical traits, nutrition, and cooked rice quality were measured. Infrared heat is fast and even, but too much destroys color and texture. Optimized settings give small processors a recipe that keeps the qualities consumers pay for while making the product shelf ready.
pmc-13166247:
Cancer care in Tanzania must meet more than body needs, and Veronica Bernard Mkusa and co-authors asked patients what faith and meaning mean during treatment. Their twenty twenty-five study took place at Ocean Road Cancer Institute in Dar es Salaam. The team spoke one to one with patients and taped the talks for close study.

Twenty-four patients took part, with equal shares of men and women and a wide age range. Six themes came out, among them what gives life meaning, beliefs about what causes cancer, and how faith helps people cope. Some beliefs about cause and care were wrong and may delay sound treatment. The authors urge care staff to ask about faith needs as a routine part of care, to lift quality of life.
pmc-13171147:
Leonardo Adriano Ragacini and Omar Chávez-Martínez trace the past of a Brazil homeopathy library in work dated 2026. The Virtual Health Library on Homeopathy gathers, scans, and shares homeopathy knowledge for Latin America. In the seventies and eighties the field was near invisible in data banks. A home index and a term list grew first, then the library took shape through deals with health bodies.

Now it stands as the field's main digital store in the zone. Fresh tech updates and AI tools mark its next phase. Its life will rest on steady use and on fit with new ways of knowing, the team finds.
pmc-13172847:
Sudeshna De, Kharma Foucher, and Lawrie Zhang describe a bootcamp for new research staff in this 2026 conference abstract. Their center at the University of Illinois Chicago offers a certificate that takes about eighteen months, but new hires needed a fast, hands-on start.

The team built a one and a half day workshop for staff with up to two years of experience. Day one mixed talks on project management, safety, and ethics with a choice of hands-on sessions, and day two covered local policies. Of 38 who signed up, 34 came for at least one day. Surveys before and after tracked confidence and sense of belonging to the research community.
pmc-13175947:
David Goodman-Meza and co-authors tested language models in 2026 for spotting people who inject drugs in hospital discharge summaries. This group faces high infection risk, yet standard diagnosis codes miss most of them. Text models could extract the needed facts from free-text notes instead.

Summaries from an infectious diseases service in Sydney, covering 2018 to 2022, were hand-labelled by a reviewer. Eight language models were compared. The best model scored far above diagnosis codes, which caught under a third of cases. Detection of heroin, methamphetamine, cannabis, and methadone use was near perfect, while some prescription drug misuse was harder. The authors urge tuning and outside validation.
pmc-13176947:
Chen Zhao and five co-authors studied what makes surgical margins too thin in small lung cancer operations in a 2026 paper. Removing one lung segment, rather than a whole lobe, works as well for tumors under two centimeters, but only if the cut clears the tumor by enough. The team reviewed 667 such operations from 2019 to 2023.

About 87 percent achieved a sufficient margin, defined as at least the tumor's width. Bigger tumors, tumors deeper from the surface, and tumors sitting between segments raised the risk of a thin margin, as did a shorter distance to the segment's airway. The authors give cutoff values for each factor to flag risky cases before surgery.
pmc-13178547:
Kaiqiang He and co-authors build a heat proof fuel cell membrane from stacked nanosheets in a 2026 paper. Hot fuel cells run better, but standard membranes dry out and stop conducting protons, the hydrogen ions that carry the current.

Thin sheets pass protons through ripples and tunneling, yet stacked sheets stall between layers. The fix bridges sheets with pockets of phosphoric acid, giving protons both a through sheet path and a hopping path along the acid. A graphene and boron nitride pair hit top tier conductivity at 250 degrees and strong power, even on methanol.
pmc-13179347:
Credit card fraud detectors can be accurate and still useless to the humans who must act on their alerts, if nobody can explain the flags. The authors compare four supervised learning methods for fraud detection: logistic regression, random forest, and two boosting ensembles, XGBoost and LightGBM. To test generalizability, they run all four on three different public transaction datasets. Standard scores cover accuracy, precision, recall, and ranking quality.

Tree-based ensembles, led by XGBoost, give the best predictive results, while the linear method still improves clearly over baselines. The authors then apply the SHAP explanation framework to the top models, ranking which features drive the verdicts. The study pairs every performance figure with an interpretability readout, model by model and dataset by dataset. The authors offer the combined picture as a guide to building fraud systems that stay transparent and accountable.
pmc-13179447:
Yuanyuan Jia and co-authors build a cheap gene test for thyroid cancer in a 2026 paper. Papillary thyroid cancer often carries a change in the BRAF gene or in a gene switch called TERT, and finding them aids diagnosis. Standard sequencing is slow and costly for many clinics.

Their method pairs a mutation-specific amplification trick with glowing probes to catch three named changes in one workflow. In lab checks it beat commercial kits on accuracy and sensitivity. On 40 stored tissue samples, it found the BRAF change in more than four of five cancers, matching sequencing where it counted. Fast, cheap mutation checks could widen molecular diagnosis.
pmc-13179747:
Evans Luvanda, Rashid Heri, and Menti Ndile interview stroke survivors about recovery in Tanzania in a 2026 study. Stroke leaves many people disabled, and cases are rising in sub-Saharan Africa, yet little is known about how survivors there manage care. The team spoke in depth with twenty survivors who attend follow up at a large referral hospital.

Four themes emerged. Money strain made care and prescribed food hard to afford. Survivors adapted with personal beliefs and home remedies when services fell short. Family support and steady contact with providers mattered greatly. Long waits, paperwork hurdles, and changing providers broke the flow of care. The authors urge better discharge planning and family centered rehabilitation.
pmc-13179947:
Mahmoud and co-authors test a birch-bark compound against aggressive breast cancer cells in this 2026 study. Betulinic acid is a fatty plant compound known to push cancer cells toward death. The team paired it with the standard drug doxorubicin.

They treated triple-negative breast cancer cells, a type with few targeted options. Viability assays and flow cytometry measured killing and death mode. Treatment raised cell death, lowered the growth signal miR-21, and shifted four target genes in a tumor-suppressing direction. Computer docking suggested both compounds can bind the PTEN and PDCD4 proteins. The authors link the combined effect to growth arrest and cell death through these pathways.
pmc-13180147:
Matthew Brewer and nine co-authors study patient reported scores in shoulder and elbow care in a 2026 paper. Clinics use a survey system called PROMIS to grade pain and function. Scores at the first visit help set care plans. The team asked which patient traits line up with those starting scores.

Records covered adults seen between 2022 and 2025 with shoulder or elbow pain. Each patient took adaptive tests on pain interference and physical function. The team sorted scores from within normal limits to severe impairment. Sex, surgery status, body weight, age, and injury site were all tested. A second pass on shoulder patients added the main diagnosis. The study helps clinics read baseline scores in context.
pmc-13181147:
Christopher Anderson and Matthew Lazio report, in twenty twenty-six, a case of rat-bite fever that was missed on a first emergency visit. The fever is caused by germs that live in rats. It is rising as more people keep rats as pets. Signs vary widely, and the germs are hard to grow in the lab, so diagnosis often rests on the story and symptoms. Their patient came back a second time with fever, rash, and joint aches.

Doctors then made the diagnosis on clinical grounds and started antibiotics. The patient had a penicillin allergy, so other drugs were used. Full recovery followed with no complications. The authors stress a full, careful history, since delay can bring severe harm.
pmc-13181247:
Juan Mariano Statti and a large team of co-authors report in 2026 the repair of a false bulge in the aorta that appeared years after a gunshot wound. Such bulges are rare after injury but can burst and kill. This one sat near the branches that feed the gut organs, which made repair harder.

The team reached the bulge through the blood vessels rather than open surgery, sealing it from inside. Careful scans before and during the work guided each step of the plan. The authors present the outcome as a success for this less invasive route. They stress how layered imaging supports the diagnosis and safe handling of such tangled vessel injuries.
pmc-13182247:
Xiangjun Liu and a large team of co-authors published a study in 2026 on how a high-iron diet can feed colon cancer. Too much iron is tied to this cancer, but the chain from iron to tumor was murky. The team found that iron wakes up a set of gut stem cells marked by a protein called Hopx, rather than the better-known stem cell pool.

Inside those cells, iron switches on a growth pathway whose key messenger the Hopx protein then protects. It does so by blocking a second protein that normally tags the messenger for disposal. With the messenger spared, colon cells multiply and tumors form. The authors suggest that cutting iron or targeting Hopx could join existing prevention plans.
pmc-13183747:
Yohei Iimura and Seiichiro Kuroda map treatments for skin harm from cancer drugs. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, covers three known side effects. One is the rash tied to a class of targeted drugs. The others are sore hand and foot syndromes from two drug families. These harms cut life quality and can make patients quit treatment.

Fifty-one clinical studies enter the map. For the rash, antibiotic plus steroid cream plans cut severe cases. For one hand-foot form, blocking an inflammation enzyme helps by mouth or skin. Barrier care and strong steroid creams serve the other form. Each harm has its own mechanism, so care must match the drug.
pmc-13184247:
Lobna Abdelrauf and co-authors test in 2026 an olive compound against heart scarring in diabetic rats. In diabetic heart disease, scar tissue stiffens the heart and weakens its pumping. A growth signal drives that scarring through a known relay. The compound, oleuropein from olives, is a strong antioxidant with heart-protective hints.

Diabetic rats given the compound pumped better and laid down less scar material than untreated diabetic rats. The compound turned down the growth signal, its relay, and several scar proteins, while lifting a brake protein in the relay. It also eased oxidative stress and blood sugar. A standard blood pressure drug served as the comparison.
pmc-13184547:
Fan Xu and co-authors find a way to make lung cancer cells more sensitive to a targeted drug by blocking their recycling of damaged mitochondria, in work dated 2026. Combination care is key to making such drugs work longer. A cleanup process tied to a protein called FUNDC1 was protecting the cancer cells.

A plant compound from a traditional pill worked with the drug to disrupt that cleanup. The pair caused mitochondrial failure and a build up of harmful oxygen species in the mutant cancer cells. Both agents lowered a key oxygen sensing protein, which cut FUNDC1 levels. Cells that had grown resistant had already lowered FUNDC1 and were extra sensitive to the compound.
pmc-13184647:
Mark Powell and Eric Ebel argue in a 2026 critique that a published risk model for Salmonella in ground turkey holds major errors. The model aimed to estimate illnesses from the meat and guide control efforts. The critics focus on three flaws they say are large enough to change the findings, rather than a full review.

The largest flaw sits in the home cooking heat input, where a spreadsheet error set the lowest heat far above the stated value. Fixing that error cuts the cooking benefit sharply and, by their account, means the original study overstates illnesses from ground turkey by more than tenfold. A second input also draws fire in the critique that follows in the text.
pmc-13185047:
Yi Zhang and co-authors reviewed rescue valve-in-valve procedures during catheter-based aortic valve replacement at one Chinese center, in a 2026 study. The bailout, placing a second valve inside a failed first one, rescues cases with heavy leakage or a slipped valve. Records covered 1,597 patients, nearly half with two-leaflet valves, whose outcomes in this rescue setting were little documented.

About six percent needed the bailout, at similar rates in both valve shapes. A larger valve ring and strong residual leakage after the first deployment predicted trouble everywhere. The team also weighed early and mid-term survival with statistical balancing to compare groups fairly.
pmc-13186147:
Aditi Sharma, Rajesh Kaushal, Naveen Chitkara, and Ekkarat Boonchieng design a blockchain-based system for remote patient care. Body sensors can track vital signs at home, but the flood of data raises safety and privacy worries. Medical images, in particular, had not been tied into such record systems. The team's model stores images off the chain and the rest on a shared ledger with set access rules.

In tests with twelve hundred transactions, the system kept pace with the send rate up to a high load and lost no transactions. Delays stayed short, and reads were near instant. The paper shows the design can be both safe and fast enough for live care.
pmc-13189047:
Liliana Belgioia and co-authors asked whether radiation after partial voice-box removal helps patients live longer and freer of disease, in a study published in 2026. The multicentre review covered 312 patients treated between 2005 and 2022 with laser or open partial surgery for throat cancers. One hundred thirty-seven also received post-operative radiotherapy; they tended to have worse disease features. Statistical matching and weighting balanced the groups for fair comparison.

Radiation clearly improved disease-free survival and local control, and it improved disease-specific survival too. Overall survival, though, did not differ significantly between the groups. The authors read this as support for radiation in carefully selected high-risk cases after partial laryngectomy. They caution that the benefit concentrates where recurrence risk is real, not across the board.
pmc-13189647:
Eleni Galanis and Nicholas Ogden warn doctors in Canada about diseases emerging with climate change. Their 2026 piece notes that shifts in temperature and rain are driving such diseases into new regions. Tick and mosquito borne illnesses pose a rising risk. Two papers in the same issue cover tick borne diseases that can be caught in Canada.

Climate change helps germs, carriers, and animal hosts survive and spread, the authors say. It also shifts human behavior. Lyme disease, already common in Canada, is a case in point. Its range has grown. Doctors play a key role, they argue. They spot where and when diseases emerge and alert public health staff. New regions face diagnostic challenges, since local doctors may not expect these illnesses.
pmc-13190447:
Thomas Aston, Georgios Machtsiras, and Filipe Teixeira-Dias benchmark deep learning models for head pose estimation in sports impacts in a 2026 study. Measuring head movement from video, called videogrammetry, can quantify collisions, but standard training data lack the big rotations, speed, and blocking views of real play. Ten participants performed controlled football headers.

Fast infrared cameras gave true head orientations while two video cameras filmed front and side views. All three models estimated pose with mean errors in single digits of degrees. A full-body mesh recovery model scored lowest and coped best with blocked views, beating dedicated head-only models. Errors grew for side views, rotational headers, and low face visibility.
pmc-13191247:
Xinghua Wang, Iqra Anwar, Richard Pratt, Victor Dzau, and Conrad Hodgkinson turn scar cells into heart muscle by holding one signal on, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Stem cell routes need that signal on, then off, to make heart cells. Direct conversion was probed for the same logic.

Blocking one brake enzyme early kept the signal on, with no later off-step needed. Yield rose and the new cells matured better, as calcium maps showed. Gene reads grew richer in muscle terms, and side paths stayed quiet. The split from the stem route is stark. Readers get a timing rule for building heart cells direct.
pmc-13191647:
Federica Bono and co-authors test whether a second fungus virus carries a working movement protein, in a 2026 study. One such virus was recently shown to infect plants naturally. Its movement protein let it slip between plant cells. Whether that trick is common among kin viruses was unknown.

The team examined a related virus found in a Trichoderma fungus. Structure prediction showed its candidate protein holds the classic folded module of movement proteins. Shape alone, though, did not prove function. Assays in plants tested whether it could rescue movement of a crippled plant virus. It could not. The plant-crossing gift, it seems, is a rare trait of one isolate, not a family habit.
pmc-13192047:
Lindsay Mullin and co-authors study mild mental traits in parents of autistic children in a 2026 cohort paper. Traits like anxiety or focus problems can run below the level of any diagnosis. Because autism has a strong genetic side, parents may carry faint forms of related traits. The team measured those traits in both parents and compared family types.

The study covers 189 families with an autistic child and 100 families without one. Families with more than one autistic child were split out for a closer look. Trait scores were compared between mothers and fathers and across groups. Links between the two parents' traits were also tested. The patterns help show how genetic liability passes quietly between generations.
pmc-13192347:
Frank Post and ten co-authors pool nine trials in 2026 on kidney safety of a daily HIV drug combo. The three-drug pill is a mainstay of HIV care, but kidney strain is a standing worry in people whose kidneys already work poorly. The team gathered patients with mild to moderate kidney impairment at the start.

Across 1,069 people followed for up to 240 weeks, kidney function stayed broadly stable. Kidney side effects were rare, and almost no one stopped the drug for kidney reasons. The pooled record supports the combo's kidney safety in this group, within the trial settings studied.
pmc-13194947:
Rongyang Xu and co-authors fine-tune light circuits by depositing carbon spot by spot in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Photonic chips guide light for communication and computing, but tiny build errors throw them off. Post-build trimming must be exact and local.

A focused ion beam lays carbon only where aimed. Test couplers, parts prone to build error, took trim without harm to the light path below. Tuning steps ranged across a wide band of signal levels. Each quarter-turn of phase shift cost only a small extra loss. The tuned response held steady over two months after a brief settling. The authors see a base for wider trimming schemes.
pmc-13196147:
Kantor, Morrison, Ko, Semenov, and Fortgang build and test in twenty twenty-six a scale that measures public attitudes toward AI in medicine. Whether patients accept medical AI shapes how much good these tools can do. The team drafted questions from past studies, expert panels, and open surveys, then tested them on representative samples in the United Kingdom and the United States.

Analysis settled on twenty items in four themes: benefit, trust, comfort with specific tasks, and concerns. The scale proved highly consistent in both countries and matched general AI attitudes well. Higher scores also predicted a lower wish for human-only care. The authors offer it to track acceptance in trials and health system rollouts.
pmc-13196547:
S Boisbouvier and co-authors test whether radiotherapy patients fare better sitting up. Their 2026 pilot compares upright and lying positions in fifteen breast and lung cancer patients already receiving standard lying treatment, tracking comfort, breath holding, and lung measures across five visits each.

Discomfort moved with position: lying hurt lower backs, standing hurt knees. Nine patients preferred upright for comfort and eight for breath holding, and rising after upright sessions hurt less. Lung volumes shifted by position, with reserve volume larger upright, while total capacity stayed the same. Breath holding worked in both postures for everyone. The authors say upright delivery, also cheaper to house, deserves fuller trials on comfort and lung sparing.
pmc-13197347:
Chendong Li, Oi-Man Kwok, and Timothy Lawrence wrote a 2026 guide to a hard problem in data work: data sets where far too many values are zero. Counts like these show up often in health and mind research. Older models for such data give two sets of results, which makes the overall effect on a whole group hard to read.

Their guide first sets out the theory behind a newer type of model that gives one clear, group level effect. Then it presents a free software package the team built for the R language. The package fits two forms of the model, one for each common count type. Worked examples show how to run the tool and how to read what it gives back. The aim is to make the newer models easy for working researchers to use.
pmc-13197647:
Elsafy and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a rare benign lung growth, with a review of all published cases. Their patient, a 69-year-old woman, had a slow-growing nodule by the lung lining found by chance. Biopsy showed lung tissue with scarring and extra smooth muscle. Surgery confirmed the rare diagnosis after look-alike diseases were ruled out.

The review gathers fourteen cases from the literature. Typical diagnosis age sits near fifty-five, and men outnumber women sharply. Every followed case ran a benign course. Slow growth on scans is the clue, the authors stress, but tissue proof must exclude mimics such as solitary fibrous tumors before the label sticks.
pmc-13197847:
Miguel Vicente and co-authors reported a heart valve case in a 2026 paper, read with live 3D ultrasound. Infective endocarditis, a germ attack on the heart's inner lining, kills many patients, above all in poorer lands. One germ, Enterococcus faecalis, drives a large share of cases.

Their patient was a 59-year-old man with high blood pressure and diabetes who came in weak, feverish, and aching. Blood tests showed severe anemia and high white counts. A new heart murmur led to scans that showed growths on the mitral valve, a bulge in its leaflet, and a hole through it. The 3D reads guided the care team.
pmc-13198447: Heather L Gelhorn and colleagues are authors of a study corrected in a 2026 note in Quality of Life Research. The study used mixed methods to define meaningful change for patients with tenosynovial giant cell tumor, drawing on exit interviews and trial data. During publication, spacing, capitalization, and table and figure header and footer errors crept in. The note states that the original article has been corrected.
pmc-13198547:
Manon Giraudier and colleagues tested nerve stimulation to aid recall of emotional memories in a 2026 study. The vagus nerve links the gut and brain and helps set arousal. It shapes how emotional memories form, but its role at recall was less clear, so the team applied gentle ear stimulation during a memory test.

Volunteers had viewed unpleasant and neutral scenes a week before, with no task attached. During recall, real stimulation was compared with a sham version. Real stimulation selectively boosted vivid recall of the unpleasant images. The effect was modest in size. The authors offer first human proof that this nerve helps retrieve emotional memories, a lead for future therapy work.
pmc-13198747:
Liane Wagner and four co-authors trace how roundworm infection reshapes a pig's chemistry, in a study dated 2026. The worm, Ascaris suum, is the costliest gut parasite in pig farming and a stand-in for the worm that infects people. Its effects on the host beyond the gut wall are little known.

Pigs got either one large dose of worm eggs or small daily doses, and gut contents and blood were sampled over seven weeks. A magnetic resonance method read hundreds of small molecules at once. Daily low doses changed the chemistry more than one big dose, with the strongest upset mid-course and partial recovery later. The colon showed the biggest shifts in acids made by gut bacteria and in protein building blocks.
pmc-13199647:
Softened and pureed diets keep care-home residents with swallowing problems safe, but the food often falls short on nourishment. Erica Deasy and co-authors audit those meals in a 2026 study of one Irish long-term care facility.

Every dish and drink served over two typical days was weighed and analyzed for the four standard texture levels. Energy and protein landed below recommended standards at nearly every level. Fat ran high, while fiber, vitamin D, and several minerals ran low. A few bright spots appeared at the least-modified level. The authors conclude that texture safety and nutrition must be planned together, not traded off by default in the kitchen.
pmc-13199847:
The cushions between spine bones wear out with age, and a tag that marks proteins for the shredder helps steer the wear. Xuening Liu and Xuewen Kang review in 2026 how that tag, ubiquitination, touches each strand of the ill. It bears on the drying of the cushion's gel and the many ways its cells die. It also touches cell aging, rust-like stress, and swelling. The tag can speed or slow each strand by marking the right protein up or down.

Cures that aim at the tag fill the back half of the review: plant goods, small drugs, cell-sent parcels, and smart stuffs laid into the disc. The enzymes that set and lift the tag make neat drug targets, the pair say. They weigh the gains against the hard road from bench to back clinic.
pmc-13200247:
Fernando Soto, writing solo in 2026, uses computer runs to ask how small added chemicals steer the first skin that forms inside a lithium battery. That skin shapes how well the battery works, and two common additives are known to help. What stayed in dispute is whether they tweak one shared path or open wholly new ones.

Soto ran many short atom-level runs for a plain mix and for mixes rich in each additive. A learning tool then mapped the shapes that formed. Each mix filled its own zone of shapes, with unlike patterns of atoms around the lithium. The split grew as the runs went on, not just from the starting mix. He reads this as proof that additives pick the path itself.
pmc-13200547:
Yuhua Fan and three colleagues regularize deep neural networks for genomic prediction, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Genomic datasets hold far more markers than they hold samples to learn from. Residual networks can catch nonlinear gene effects in that data. But they overfit with zeal when the data is set up in that way.

Proximal regularization is their cure for that flaw. It is folded head-on into the optimization algorithm at the heart of the work. The team extends a stochastic adaptive proximal gradient method for residual networks of this kind. Both convex and non-convex penalty shapes have support in the frame. Convergence gets a fresh analysis in the paper as well. Breeding and genetics applications drive the work. To predict traits from DNA is just where samples are precious and features are legion. A network that holds up there earns its complexity.
pmc-13202547:
Anna Dornisch and co-authors put out the protocol in 2026 for RadTARGET, a multicenter phase two trial rethinking how prostate cancer is irradiated. Modern radiation cures many intermediate and high-risk cases, but escalating dose to the whole gland injures the bladder and bowel in the process. The trial's wager is geographic: most recurrences after radiation start in the dominant visible tumor, so dose should be concentrated there and on purpose lowered everywhere else in the prostate.

Patients are randomized between that image-guided plan, boosting the dominant lesion while de-intensifying dose to non-suspicious tissue, and standard radiation. The immediate question is toxicity, whether the reshaped dose reduces acute urinary and gastrointestinal side effects, with imaging by advanced magnetic resonance methods and molecular scans guiding the targeting. The results are clearly built as the base for a larger phase three trial of efficacy and safety.
pmc-13202747:
A questionnaire about how people trust information gets a skeptical audit in a 2026 psychometric study authored by Nicola-Hans Schwarzer. The research article evaluates the German version of the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust, and Credulity Questionnaire in 567 university students, comparing its original structure with published shortened models.

Confirmatory factor analyses found that neither the fifteen-item nor the twelve-item version fit the data acceptably. Reliability and variance measures fell below accepted thresholds for all three subscales in every model tested. Links with related traits behaved as theory expects for mistrust and credulity but diverged for trust, leading the authors to recommend thorough item revision before wider use.
pmc-13203947:
Lukman Abiola Oluodo and co-authors test feed additions for crossbred goats in this 2026 study. Sunflower oil and a probiotic bacterium were given alone and together to young male goats, to see effects on growth, meat quality, and fat makeup. Twenty-eight goats, about four months old, were split into four groups of seven.

Growth did not change, but feed use efficiency improved in all supplemented groups, most in the combined group. Carcass traits were unchanged. Meat from the oil groups was more tender and had a lower early pH. The combined diet raised healthy fat shares in the meat, including total polyunsaturated fats. Blood fat and enzyme values rose over time in supplemented groups.
pmc-13208147:
Anastasiia Bolikhova and co-authors fish plant extracts for compounds that switch on cell cleanup in a 2026 study. The cleanup process, autophagy, guards against age-related disease when it runs well. Plants are rich in candidate activators. The team paired fraction testing on human cells with high-resolution chemical analysis to name the active compounds fast.

Five plants known for such activators validated the pipeline: it found their main active compounds correctly. A wider screen then flagged woolly milkvetch, Astragalus dasyanthus, as a producer of glabrol, an autophagy inducer, for the first time. The authors call the method effective for sorting complex extracts. They propose it for high-throughput hunts for new cleanup-activating compounds. Such finds could seed therapies for diseases of aging.
pmc-13208347:
Ten researchers led by Adiyadolgor Turbat review how fungi that live inside plants make a key plant hormone, indole-3-acetic acid. The hormone steers plant growth, root shape, and branching. Many inner fungi make it too, shaping how plant and fungus get along, yet the fungal routes are less mapped than plant or bacterial ones.

The review gathers work from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-five on which fungi make the hormone and by what paths. It weighs how to prove the fungus, not the plant, is the maker. It then covers gains such as growth boosts and stress tolerance, noting effects hinge on dose and setting.
pmc-13208447:
Rahma Alshamrani and co-authors screened twenty wheat varieties for the ability to yield in salty soil, in a study published in 2026. Salt stress caps wheat harvests across dry regions. The team grew the varieties at two salinity levels and measured yield, spike and kernel counts, grain weight, and the balance of sodium and potassium in the plants. Varieties differed significantly on every trait.

Four stood out: Bhan 2000, a local variety, P7, and Sakha 93 kept the best yields under salt. Yield tracked strongly with kernels per spike and with a favorable potassium-to-sodium ratio, while sodium content dragged it down. The winners kept their ionic balance, the likely tolerance mechanism. The authors recommend the four for salty fields and as parents in breeding programs. Their combined yield-plus-ion scoring, they say, sharpens selection accuracy.
pmc-13208747:
Ieva Vienazindyte and co-authors study the eye nerve layer in multiple sclerosis in this 2026 paper. The retinal nerve fibre layer thins as the disease harms nerves. Its thickness can be measured quickly with an eye scan. The team asked how well it tracks disability and brain scan findings.

Records covered 84 patients at a Lithuanian university hospital neurology clinic. Diagnosis followed standard McDonald criteria. Eye scans were taken at diagnosis, with repeat scans for some patients. Disability was scored on the standard expanded scale. Cross sectional links between layer thickness, disability, and scan reports were tested with rank and regression methods. Follow up data probed whether thinning foreshadows worsening disability over time.
pmc-13208947:
Wenlu Zhang, Chunfa Huang, Shengjun Xia, Xing Hu, and Qiulin Li optimize a ceramic slurry for light based 3D printing, in work dated 2026. The method builds silicon based ceramic cores layer by layer as a slurry hardens under light. If the slurry is unstable, particles settle unevenly and the part loses strength and accuracy.

The team tuned particle size mix, a nanopowder additive, and solid loading. The aim was a slurry that flows well yet stays even for a long time. Their best mix held a high solid load and stayed stable after a long settling test. Parts printed from it test the recipe in practice.
pmc-13209047:
Wenhao Dai and co-authors study dust particles thrown off by train power contacts in this 2026 paper. Electric trains draw power through a sliding contact between a carbon strip and a copper wire. That rubbing contact wears down and sheds fine particles into the air, which can harm health.

The team ran a lab rig that mimics the contact under set loads and electric currents. Without current, heavier loads wore the strip more and raised particle counts across sizes. With current, heavier loads cut how often electric arcs sparked between the pair. Stronger current deepened arc damage to the surface. Each arc burst out a sharp spike of particles, and more or stronger arcs meant dirtier air nearby.
pmc-13209147:
Shaohuai Xia and co-authors build a bedside score for death risk after a brain bleed in a 2026 study. The bleed type studied starts without injury and carries high risk in hospital. Standard risk models often ignore clotting problems in the wider body, which this team puts at the centre.

The score blends a clotting time measure with platelet count, two values from routine blood tests. It was built on 287 patients at one hospital and checked on 621 patients from a large public database. A clear cut point marked where risk jumped sharply. Age, coma score, and one drug also helped predict outcomes. Combined models scored well on tests of accuracy. The authors present the score as a simple aid for sorting patients by risk.
pmc-13210047:
Nabeel Israr and colleagues used first-principles computation to vet a new family of lead-free double perovskite crystals for solar and heat-to-electric uses. Perovskites are tunable light absorbers, but the best contain toxic lead. The candidates swap in rubidium, indium, and copper with one of three halogens. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team ran density functional calculations, including spin-orbit effects, to check stability, electronic bands, light absorption, and thermoelectric behavior across a wide photon energy range.

The crystals passed stability checks and showed direct band gaps in or near the useful solar range, shrinking as the halogen grows heavier. Absorption was strongest in the ultraviolet. Heat-to-electric performance was promising for the fluoride member, whose efficiency figure neared values of practical interest. The authors present all three as candidates for sustainable optoelectronics.
pmc-13210647:
Vyas Jigar and co-authors review frames built to mimic the body's own scaffolds so new tissue can grow blood vessels, in this 2026 survey. Poor vessel growth is a top block to healing grafts, since cells need air in and waste out. Fake frames can now mix the stiff tune of made plastics with the live signs of raw body stuff. The survey weighs the main ways folk coax vessels into such frames.

The tricks held shaping the face, lacing in growth signs, and seeding vessels before the graft goes in. Make ways ran from spun mats to printed forms in three and four planes, plus chip flows. Cell and animal reads grade how well each works. Bone, heart, nerve, and skin uses lead the move to clinic. Scale-up and stiff rules still bar the way, and smart stuff tuned per patient is the next aim.
pmc-13210947:
Mingju Chen and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how image generators can be controlled by many kinds of input at once. Diffusion models once worked mainly from text. Newer systems take sound, three-dimensional data, and body signals as well, and the review organises how those mixed signals are mapped and injected into generation.

Coverage follows the shift from older U-Net designs to newer transformer-based generators, and from single inputs to combined multi-source control. The authors sort evaluation measures and describe trade-offs between image quality and control. They close by pointing to hardware testing, physics-based limits, and causal reasoning as routes toward faster, more reliable controllable generation.
pmc-13212647:
Muhammed Kara, Mehmet Ali Cengiz, Emre Dünder, and Talat Şenel present a 2026 paper on a Bayesian upgrade to a regression method for grouped body data. Populations like patients or athletes split into subgroups that share some patterns and differ in others. The existing method separates shared from group-specific components but cannot express uncertainty or use prior knowledge. The Bayesian version adds full probability distributions over its answers, with intervals that show how sure the model is.

Estimated by simulation sampling, the method was tested on synthetic scenarios and on a public data set of elite athletes' physical and blood measures. It beat traditional approaches on prediction accuracy, interpretability, and robustness, especially where samples are small. The authors pitch it for medical imaging and other fields with naturally mixed groups. Uncertainty, they argue, is not a luxury in such data.
pmc-13212847:
Abdirasak Sharif Ali and Augustus Osborne chart in 2026 how stunting among Somali children under five changed over nearly twenty-five years. Stunting, meaning a child is far too short for their age, reflects long-running malnutrition and carries lifelong effects.

Using World Health Organization modelled estimates, the pair found national prevalence fell from about a third of children in 2000 to under a quarter by 2024. Boys stayed consistently more affected than girls throughout, and the relative gap barely narrowed. The authors call the remaining level a serious public concern. They urge sex-sensitive nutrition action plus wider measures on mothers' schooling, household wealth, and climate resilience.
pmc-13213047:
Zhaoran Su and a large team investigate in 2026 why some colorectal cancer cells resist a therapy that uses alternating electric fields to wreck cell division. The treatment, already used for a brain cancer, had never been tested systematically across many bowel cancer cell lines.

Across a broad panel of patient-derived lines, the fields damaged cells through several routes, from scrambled division machinery to DNA damage and cell death. One gene stood out as switched on in resistant lines. Silencing it made cells sensitive again, and computer screening nominated two existing drugs that might block its product and boost the therapy. The gene could become a target for combination treatment.
pmc-13214447:
Ayodhia Pitaloka Pasaribu leads a very large group reporting in 2026 on an Indonesian stakeholder meeting about curing relapsing vivax malaria. A multi-country trial had tested a single-dose drug and a shorter high-dose course against the standard two-week regimen.

Officials, clinicians, and programme staff met in May 2025 to weigh the Indonesia-specific findings for national policy. Gaps remain around pairing the single-dose drug with the malaria combinations used locally, they agreed. The high-dose week-long course looked ready to adopt sooner, provided testing for an enzyme deficiency that makes these drugs risky is strengthened. Attendees stressed tailoring plans to Indonesia's varied regions and keeping political commitment to elimination.
pmc-13214547:
Shi Tang and co-authors review a 2026 approach to immune care that joins tiny adjuvants with organic materials. Adjuvants boost immune response, but most organic materials are weak at that task on their own. The goal is a strong, lasting response with less harm to the rest of the body.

The review sets out how the joined materials are sensed by immune cells and how they are taken in and processed. It sorts the main material classes and adjuvant types, and it weighs traits such as size, surface traits, and release timing. Uses span vaccines, immune therapy, and tissue repair.
pmc-13214947:
Martínez Briseño and co-authors test a year of recreational exercise for older adults living in Mexican welfare homes. High blood pressure and type 2 diabetes are common in this group, and drug treatment alone leaves room to improve. Two hundred sixty residents over sixty joined; one group kept drugs only, the other added five supervised activity hours a week.

After twelve months, the exercise group's blood pressure fell further than the control group's, on both readings. Blood sugar control also improved more, and body fat dropped in both groups. Muscle mass, though, was hard to preserve either way. The authors argue that structured, playful activity belongs in routine care for such homes, even where budgets are tight, because the gains came on top of standard medicine.
pmc-13215047:
Kelnner Portela Luz and Danilo Lopes Ferreira Lima report in 2026 a first field test of a digital platform for endometriosis care inside Brazilian public primary care. Diagnosis there often takes seven to ten years, hitting poor, rural, Black, and Indigenous women hardest.

Sixty women and health professionals used the platform for eight weeks across ten clinics. Usability and acceptance scored high, and users finished most educational modules. Pain and anxiety eased while knowledge, treatment adherence, and referrals rose, though with no comparison group those shifts count as exploratory signals only. Subgroup patterns hinted at equity-relevant differences. The authors frame the tool as feasible for low-resource settings.
pmc-13215747:
Jarzabek and Denny reviewed tests for cutaneous leishmaniasis in twenty twenty-five, a skin disease caused by a parasite spread by sand flies. The World Health Organization has set target goals for a better test: more accurate and cheaper than current tools. Knowing the exact species matters more now as drug resistance grows.

Blood tests cannot identify the species, while gene tests need costly machines. Heat-based gene tests called LAMP are promising, but few are species-specific so far, and Ethiopia is neglected in this work. Cheap devices built during the COVID-19 pandemic await testing for this disease. Image analysis by AI offers another route. The authors map both the chances and the hurdles ahead.
pmc-13216147:
Víctor López-López and co-authors present a 2026 multicentre study of bile leakage after robotic liver surgery in expert Spanish centres. Bile leaks are among the most troublesome complications of liver resection, and robotic series with solid numbers have been scarce.

The database covered 492 consecutive patients in three high-volume centres, most operated on for cancer. Bile leakage occurred in just nine patients, a rate of 1.8 percent, and none of the leaks reached the most severe grade. All were handled without reoperation. Overall complications within ninety days affected 29.3 percent of patients, mortality was 1.6 percent, and the typical hospital stay was three days. The authors credit centralization in expert hands.
pmc-13216547:
Mostafa A. Gouda and co-authors present a 2026 food science study comparing Grison, the air-dried cured meat of Swiss tradition, made from three different animals: cattle, buffalo, and camel. Rising cattle prices and interest in alternative proteins motivated the head-to-head test.

Topside from each species was dry-cured under controlled conditions and tracked through processing and in the finished product. Camel meat and its Grison ran moister, with higher pH, residual nitrite, and redness, but less protein, fat, and lipid oxidation than the others. Tasters gave camel the best colour and flavour scores. Cattle Grison was fattiest and lightest in colour. Buffalo Grison was toughest and least juicy. The authors judge camel a genuine rival to the traditional product.
pmc-13216647:
Wessam M. Salama and co-authors present a 2026 wireless engineering study on estimating the radio channel in MIMO systems. Many antennas talk at once there, and the channel must be measured before data can flow. Deep learning estimators usually need retraining whenever conditions change, which limits their use.

Their hybrid framework combines a Transformer network, zero-shot learning that maps channels into a shared attribute space, and the Muon optimizer. In simulations it beat classical least-squares and MMSE estimators and several deep learning baselines, especially in channel conditions never seen during training. Growing the array from 2 to 128 antennas at high signal quality cut estimation error by about 94 percent. The authors present the design as ready for next-generation networks.
pmc-13217447:
Ahmed Omar Siyad and co-authors present a 2026 case report of severe lung failure after measles in a two-year-old unvaccinated girl treated in a resource-limited setting. Measles pneumonia can escalate into acute respiratory distress syndrome, a complication seldom documented where intensive care is scarce.

The child arrived after a week of fever and worsening breathlessness following a measles-like illness, critically ill with oxygen saturation far below safe levels and depressed consciousness. Chest imaging showed diffuse infiltrates, and heart ultrasound excluded a cardiac cause. She spent fourteen days on a ventilator with antibiotics, vitamin A, transfusion for severe anaemia, and careful fluid management. She left intensive care on day eighteen and went home well after twenty-seven days. The authors stress vaccination and early referral.
pmc-13218147:
Yi Chen and colleagues describe a 2026 protocol for a randomized trial of a symptom-monitoring system for pemphigus vulgaris. The disease is a rare autoimmune blistering condition with recurring sores on skin and mucous membranes, heavy symptom burden, and relapses that are hard to predict. Care still leans on medication plus hospital follow-up, leaving home monitoring thin.

The multicentre trial will randomize 160 adults with confirmed disease and active lesions to the Intelligent Multimodal Symptom Assessment and Response System or to standard care. The system combines patient-reported outcomes, wearable body-signal data, and photographs of lesions on one platform over twelve weeks. The main goal is better symptom alerting and management. Secondary goals cover self-management, sticking with treatment, and quality of life. The team will ask patients how usable the system feels, since people with a rare disease must keep using a tool for it to help.
pmc-13219247:
Burcu Kamaşak Arpaçay and Kenan Aycan map variations in the brain's venous drainage channels, in this 2026 cadaver study. These channels, the dural venous sinuses, carry blood out of the brain. Their layout varies a lot where several meet, and a harmless variant can look like disease on scans or trip up a surgeon.

The team dissected fifteen adult cadaver brains, mean age seventy, and measured the main sinuses with calipers. The meeting point itself was missing in twenty percent of cases. One or another sinus was often small, missing, or drained in an unusual pattern, and dural folds sometimes stood in for the meeting point. Widths of the top channel averaged about 6.7 millimeters. The authors urge radiologists and surgeons to expect such variants before calling pathology.
pmc-13219347:
Erika Spada and co-authors map image search tools for radiology in a 2026 review. Content-based search finds past scans that look like the one at hand. Such finds can back a hard call or teach a new reader. The review sweeps the field's state: what works, what stalls, and what comes next. A fresh form, trajectory search, tracks how an ill moves through scans over time.

Real clinic use lags the lab work, the team find. Mixed data forms, privacy walls, and weak time sense block the path. Fixes pair path search with mixed data feeds and human checks in the loop. That blend fits how doctors think: by case arcs, not lone snaps. The authors see search as a core aid once those bars fall.
pmc-13221147:
Limeng Sun and co-authors find that several animal coronaviruses need the same sugar decoration on their doorway protein before they can enter cells. Without the enzyme's modification, the pig receptor failed to bind the spike of transmissible gastroenteritis virus, and entry depended on one specific sugar site on the protein. Protein-wide sugar mapping confirmed the site is decorated in normal cells and nearly bare when the enzyme is knocked out. The same requirement held for dog and cat coronaviruses, at matching sites on their versions of the receptor. The authors name FUT8 a possible broad-spectrum antiviral target.
pmc-13221647:
Kexuan Ma and co-authors study how a gene-switch complex called NF-Y works with machines that open and close DNA packaging. NF-Y binds a short DNA pattern found near many genes, in fungi, plants, and animals alike. How it reshapes DNA packaging, though, was not clear.

Working in two fungi, the team fished out two large packaging machines, called SWI/SNF and RSC, using NF-Y parts as bait. They found four subunits seen only in thread-like fungi, and pinpointed which parts touch NF-Y directly. Tests showed the partners share control of growth, development, and enzymes that break down plant walls. The results suggest NF-Y borrows the strength of real packaging machines to switch genes on and off.
pmc-13221747: Jacob P Thönes and colleagues publish a 2026 correction in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders that fixes the title of their earlier article. The notice is a correction only: part of the original title was missing, dropping the words covering knee extension strength. The full title concerns estimating knee joint angle and extensor strength from electrical impedance during concentric knee extension. No data, methods, or conclusions change; the journal record and the article itself have been updated to carry the complete title.
pmc-13222347:
Izadora de Souza and colleagues review the double-edged role of the NRF2 pathway in ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, in a 2026 article. NRF2 coordinates genes that shield cells from oxidative stress. In cancers, constant NRF2 activity helps tumors resist chemotherapy by boosting detoxification and antioxidant defenses.

Many NRF2 target genes also control ferroptosis through glutathione production, fat metabolism, and iron handling. Depending on cell type and metabolic state, the pathway can guard against ferroptotic death or set it up. The review traces how this network was discovered and flags the pivotal target genes. Tuning NRF2 deliberately might push resistant tumors into ferroptotic death.
pmc-13222847:
Kasinathan Rakkammal and ten co-authors present a 2026 review on making finger millet, a hardy but neglected grain, withstand climate stress. The crop already tolerates poor conditions, yet the basis of that toughness is poorly mapped. The review gathers what is known about its responses to drought, salt, heat, cold, and toxic metals. At the body level it reshapes roots, saves water, and adjusts leaf structure.

Chemically it stockpiles protective compounds and boosts antioxidant defenses. Genes and signaling proteins orchestrate these responses, but the wiring diagram is incomplete. Modern tools, from gene sequencing to CRISPR editing, could connect traits to genes and speed breeding. The authors argue the pieces are rarely combined in real field breeding. They propose finger millet as a model for breeding climate-ready cereals, if physiology and gene work are finally joined.
pmc-13222947:
Andarva leads a large team studying an immune enzyme and fat droplets in prostate cancer cells, in work from twenty twenty-six. Secreted phospholipase A2 group IIA is an innate immune mediator, an enzyme that cuts fat molecules. Lipid droplets inside cells store fat and support tumor growth.

The enzyme modulated lipid droplet formation in prostate cancer cells, the title reports. How an immune related enzyme reshapes fat storage in cancer cells links inflammation with tumor metabolism. That link could suggest new drug angles, since starving cancer cells of stored fat is one route to slowing their growth and spread.
pmc-13223647:
Jessica M Jarvis and co-authors ask caregivers how confidently they could report rehabilitation use after a child's traumatic brain injury, in a 2026 qualitative study meant to shape a new measure. Fourteen caregivers of hospitalized children up to age eighteen joined remote semi-structured interviews. Sampling sought variety in factors tied to service use, and sessions ran until no new themes appeared.

They felt confident reporting services and satisfaction by setting, with rough dosage, though confidence varied between care settings. They endorsed a full reporting form with built-in meanings and guided prompts, ideally electronic, to fill in from home. A caregiver-report tool spanning the whole care path looks acceptable and feasible on this evidence.
pmc-13223947:
Newly hatched chicks ride trucks in the dark, and nobody had tested whether light on the road helps or harms. Deliah McGregor and co-authors simulated transport in 2026 for more than eleven thousand broiler chicks, under darkness, white light, or blue light, for four or seven hours. They then tracked blood chemistry, growth, feed use, and welfare signals to market age.

Light changed nothing measurable. Trip length mattered instead: seven-hour chicks showed stress chemistry after the ride and slower early growth, though mortality stayed flat. The authors conclude the industry's dark trucks need no retrofit, while shorter trips remain the kinder goal.
pmc-13224347:
Stephanie Denise M. Sison and colleagues analyse a 2026 Medicare study of how frailty and dementia, alone and together, shape costs and time spent at home. Home time loss counts days spent in hospitals or facilities rather than at home, serving as a rough quality-of-life measure. The team used fee-for-service claims for older beneficiaries and grouped people by both conditions.

Both spending and lost home time climbed as frailty grew more severe. Dementia behaved differently depending on physical state: it came with higher costs among robust beneficiaries, yet lower costs among the frail. Those contrasting patterns suggest the two conditions drive distinct kinds of care, and the authors call for better recognition of frailty in planning services.
pmc-13224747:
Dawn M. Holman and colleagues analyse a 2026 national survey report on sunburn among United States high school students, using 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Survey data. Sunburn raises skin cancer risk, and teenage rates have stayed stubbornly high for years. The team estimated how many students burned at least once, and how many burned five or more times, in the previous year.

Just over half of students reported at least one sunburn. Among those who burned, about twenty-three percent burned frequently. After statistical adjustment, rates differed by sex, race and ethnicity, body weight, substance use, diet, activity, and social media use. The authors argue that persistently high figures justify continued prevention work in schools, clinics, and communities.
pmc-13225447:
Karla Kotková and Yvona Angerová compare in 2026 how young and older women learn balance skills on a training platform. Relearning movement matters in rehab after injury or disease. Age may slow learning, but how much is less clear.

Both groups train on a platform that tracks the body center of weight and shows it on a screen. Speed and accuracy of weight shifts improve in both groups. Older women start and end slower in raw time, yet early gains follow the same pace as the young group. After week six, gains slow for both, and more so for older women. Both groups carry gains to a surprise random task, which shows true learning.
pmc-13226047:
Murray Baron and colleagues test a 2026 workaround that lets artificial intelligence analyse older lung scans saved as sparse slices. AI tools for interstitial lung disease need continuous high-resolution CT stacks, but many archived scans survive only as about thirty separated slices. The team rebuilt full stacks from fourteen systemic sclerosis patients by inserting copied slices between the real ones.

Both original and rebuilt scans went through the same commercial AI program, which scored honeycombing, reticular pattern, ground-glass change, and total disease. Agreement between versions was excellent on nearly every measure, judged by several statistical checks. One pattern score showed a weaker result on a single test. The trick could unlock large archives of legacy scans for modern analysis.
pmc-13226147:
Mingzhou Jiang, Fandi Mo, and co-authors review how wild oxygen bits drive chest aorta wall splits, in work from 2026. The split tears the wall in and rots its mid coat, a swift death risk. Wild bits now look like a core spark in that rot path.

The review maps where wild bits form and how they feed rust stress. Fire signs and wall stuff breaks ride that stress in the tale. Rule webs span gene, mark, and fuel shifts that tune bit acts. Cure paths aim at bit birth blocks, guard boosts, and path tweaks. Weak spots are named too: low aim, thin ward proof, and blunt cut needs.
pmc-13226247:
Yifan Chen and colleagues review a 2026 synthesis of how skull and facial bones develop under two kinds of control at once: molecular signals and physical forces. Unlike trunk bones, craniofacial bones arise from neural crest tissue and form through distinctive patterns, so lessons from limb bones transfer imperfectly. Chewing, growth stresses, and other mechanical loads feed back into the signalling that shapes them.

Recent work maps where force-sensing and classic developmental pathways meet, and how imbalance between them produces congenital and acquired disorders of the face and skull. The authors argue that treating the mechanical and genetic sides as one system opens new preventive and therapeutic angles for craniofacial disease.
pmc-13226347:
Cyanide can poison people through drinking water and through foods such as cassava, a root crop eaten in many parts of the world. The sensor uses a dye-like chemical that glows under light, and the glow fades when cyanide is present.

Tests showed that the sensor reacts to cyanide far more than to other ions in the mix. The team checked how it works with two lab methods and found that cyanide joins one part of the sensor and cuts its glow. The sensor can spot very small amounts and works across a wide range of acid levels. It also gave good results on real food samples. Simple tools like the sensor could help check food safety without costly gear or deep training.
pmc-13226447:
Genet Shifera and co-authors report a 2026 study of a glowing sensor for a toxic form of chromium in water and fish. This form of chromium is a pollutant that harms health even at low levels, so cheap and sharp tests are needed. The team built tiny crystals of zinc oxide laced with silver.

The crystals glow under a set wavelength, and the glow drops in a steady way as the pollutant rises. The sensor picked out the target over other substances and found very small amounts. Tests on river water and fish samples, spiked with known amounts, gave results close to the true values. The method is simple and repeatable.
pmc-13226647:
Muhammad Irfan Afridi and Agnieszka Chacinska wrote a 2026 news piece on a stress switch inside mitochondria, the cell parts that make energy. When cells face stress, a cutting enzyme called OMA1 wakes up in the inner membrane. It was known to snip proteins that control how mitochondria split and how cells sound a stress alarm. What else it cuts was less clear.

A study by Nishigori and team found a new target: AIFM1, a protein tied to the inner membrane. Under stress, OMA1 cuts it loose, and the cell's breathing and growth slow down. The piece explains how this clean cut helps cells tune energy use to hard times, and why the find matters for stress biology.
pmc-13226847:
Fares Chaabouni and seven co-authors report a 2026 case study of a rare birth defect in a newborn girl. The defect is a swollen lower end of the tube that drains a kidney. Most cases are found before birth or by chance, but this one slipped out through the birth canal.

The baby was 13 days old and came in with a red mass that was first thought to be a sealed membrane. A scan of the pelvis showed a doubled right kidney with the swollen tube end, which fit the rare form. Surgeons cut and then removed the swollen part with no problems after the operation. The case warns doctors to keep this cause in mind for such masses.
pmc-13226947:
Hong Yao, Shourong Shi, and Ruqian Zhao test in 2026 whether a chlorogenic acid complex protects broiler chickens against gut oxidative stress, and which component does the work. The acid is a natural plant polyphenol, but its forms differ in strength. They combined animal trials, network analysis, docking, and lab antioxidant assays to sort the mixture out.

In birds, the complex reversed stress-induced losses in weight and gut enzyme activity. Network results singled out one form as the key component, binding stably to three core targets. Another form scavenged free radicals best in vitro. The key form also protected gut cells and boosted protective proteins.
pmc-13227947:
David J Irwin and a large team localise a 2026 brain-pathology signature in globular glial tauopathy, a rare protein-clumping disease that can present as progressive aphasia, the slow loss of language. Earlier work had spotted iron-rich inflammation in mid-to-deep cortical layers without mapping it against symptoms. pmc-13233447:

pmc-13233647:

pmc-13233847:

pmc-13235447:

pmc-13236847:

pmc-13236947:

pmc-13238247:

pmc-13238647:

pmc-13239147:

pmc-13240247:

pmc-13240947:

pmc-13241247:

pmc-13241647:

pmc-13241747:

pmc-13242447:

pmc-13242847:
Yan Zhang and co-authors offer a 2026 review of histone methylation in the shift from fatty liver disease to liver cancer. pmc-13243247:

pmc-13243547:

pmc-13243847:

pmc-13244847:

pmc-13247847:

pmc-13254847:

pmc-13255947:

pmc-13257647:

pmc-13258047:

pmc-13259447:

pmc-13260447:

pmc-13260647:

pmc-13263347:

pmc-13263647:

pmc-13263847:

pmc-13264347:

pmc-13264447:

pmc-13264747:

pmc-13264847:

pmc-13266047:
