Position change linked clearly to width change for both measures. The link was stronger in females for the fixed-location measure, with a slope of 0.19 versus 0.11 in males. A smaller 4-year check found responsiveness held despite poor position values.
pmc-13352947:
A 2026 correction in Molecular Oncology repairs a figure error in a 2014 paper on the HPV-18 E6 oncoprotein and its effect on the cell polarity protein Par3. During figure assembly, the western blot images in Figure 4C were issued with the wrong tubulin control, after an unintentional flip and an incorrect crop of that blot. The authors are Facciuto, Valdano, Marziali, Massimi, Banks, Cavatorta, and Gardiol.

Inspection of the first tubulin blot shown that the mistake gave no advantage to the paper's interpretation, and a corrected figure now replaces the faulty one. The correction therefore preserves the study's ends while fixing the record. Readers can use the corrected figure with confidence that it reflects the first experiment.
pmc-13353647:
Konstantin Drach, Carsten Leven, and Olaf Cirpka present a method to find and measure groundwater discharge in work from 2026. Discharge is hard to pin down because it needs data on how rock conducts water and on the slope of the water level.

Their approach uses a small set of pumping and watch wells set across a line about one hundred meters long. A smoothing method infers the pattern of water conduction, with uncertainty, from drawdown data. Tests in a made-up valley aquifer show the method beats standard pumping test fits and can locate discharge patterns at well spacing scale.
pmc-13355247:
Nelson Mills and co-authors test whether a gene repeat count shapes low testosterone severity and treatment response in men, in work from twenty twenty-six. The androgen receptor gene holds a repeat stretch whose length tunes hormone sensitivity. Testosterone therapy works unevenly, and the repeat may explain part of that spread.

One hundred sixty-two men with symptoms gave surveys and blood tests before and after therapy. The average repeat count sat in the normal range. Longer repeats linked weakly but firmly to higher testosterone after therapy. Men with symptoms yet near normal base levels held longer repeats on average. Men who needed higher levels to feel better also trended longer. The authors see the repeat as a useful gauge.
pmc-13355647:
Mariam Ait Oumelloul and co-authors searched in 2026 for gene variants that shape blood chemical levels in people with HIV. People with HIV age faster and face more age-related illness despite good virus control, for reasons not fully known. The team linked genome data to about 1,930 blood chemicals in 1,244 people in a Swiss cohort.

They found 27 chemicals tied to 12 gene regions, including genes for metabolic enzymes. Most known links from general studies were confirmed, and gene activity data overlapped strongly with chemical levels. Further analysis hinted that some chemicals may cause age-related diseases. The authors see paired genome and chemical profiling as a path to personal care.
pmc-13355847:
Amy Pham and co-authors report a 2026 case of acetaminophen overdose in one of the smallest premature infants yet described. The baby was born at about 24 weeks and weighed 640 grams when a medical record error led to two intravenous doses ten times too large. Overdose in such tiny infants is rare, with only four prior cases in print, and their drug handling differs from older children.

Blood tests showed high drug levels and brief clotting problems, but no liver cell injury. Treatment with the antidote N-acetylcysteine brought clotting back to normal and cleared the drug. The authors urge study of safe limits for this age group as the drug's use grows in newborn units.
pmc-13358847:
Jinbing Liu and co-authors test a traditional plant remedy against flu in a 2026 study. Fagopyrum acutatum, a buckwheat relative, has long been used in Chinese medicine for lung and breathing complaints. The team asked whether its extract can calm the inflammation that influenza A virus triggers, which can injure the lungs badly.

They identified 103 compounds in the extract and tested it in cells and in animals. Gene and protein checks traced which pathways the extract quiets, while animal tests measured survival, lung damage, and inflammatory signals in blood and lung tissue. The results support the plant's traditional use and point to compounds worth isolating.
pmc-13359847:
Giulio Cantù reviews the unsettled questions around salivary gland tumors in a 2026 paper. These tumors are uncommon but come in many types and grades, which makes firm rules scarce. Drawing on about 100 past and recent studies, Cantù separates what the field knows, what it doubts, and what it merely believes.

Debates include how to grade the most common cancer type. Another asks whether one reported cancer form truly exists, or is usually a spread from skin cancer. A third concerns how much of the parotid gland surgeons should remove for each case. The review gives clinicians a clear map of where judgment, not evidence, still rules.
pmc-13360047:
Kevaun Altamon George Wilson and co-authors review a delivery idea for animal feed in a 2026 paper. Sulforaphane, a healthful compound from cruciferous plants, fights oxidation and inflammation but breaks down easily, so little survives in feed. The review examines wrapping it in tiny particles made by ionic gelation from two natural polymers, chitosan and alginate.

The shell should shield the compound through the stomach and release it where it can be absorbed. The authors cover particle size, loading efficiency, release control, and safety rules, and weigh the potential for poultry, pigs, and cattle. Most proof so far comes from human and rodent work, a gap they flag for farm studies.
pmc-13360147:
Ting Li and co-authors published a 2026 study of breath acetone as a painless way to track ketones in the body. Ketones are chemicals the body makes when it burns fat, and high levels can be a risk in diabetes. The team tested 4,000 people with normal blood sugar, prediabetes, or diabetes. They compared breath acetone with ketones in blood and urine.

People with ketones in their urine had higher blood ketones and higher breath acetone. Breath acetone rose step by step as urine ketone levels rose. The link between breath and blood ketones was strong in people with diabetes and moderate in the other groups. The team also set early breath cutoff values for spotting ketones in blood. They say breath tests could one day offer a needle-free way to watch ketone levels.
pmc-13361047:
Boyeon Kim and Jee-Hyung Lee review the inner diversity of pancreatic cancer in a 2026 paper. This cancer, called PDAC, is among the hardest to treat, with only about one in ten patients alive at five years. It almost always resists immune checkpoint drugs. The authors blame two partners: the tumor's own patchwork of cell types and a surrounding tissue that shuts immunity down.

Drawing on multi-omics data and maps of gene activity across the tumor, they show how layers of difference let the cancer adapt and hide. Dense scar tissue and suppressive immune cells add physical and chemical walls. The review ends with plans for precision immune therapy tuned to each tumor's makeup. It aims to guide researchers hunting for cracks in this cancer's defenses.
pmc-13361447:
Małgorzata Ponikowska and co-authors tracked a biologic drug in children with severe eczema in a 2026 study. Dupilumab is a shot that calms the immune signals driving atopic dermatitis. Long-term results in children, outside of trials, are still scarce. The team looked back at 55 young patients with moderate to severe disease treated at one center.

They followed skin scores, affected body area, and quality of life across the whole course of treatment. The main goal was the share of children reaching a 75 percent cut in a standard eczema score, and how fast that gain came. Deeper gains, safety, and how long the drug kept working were also tracked. Real-life paths show families what to expect over years, not just trial months.
pmc-13362247:
Nga Ngoc Quynh Nguyen and co-authors fortified tofu with a wild termite mushroom in a 2026 food study. Termitomyces albuminosus is a valued edible mushroom that grows with termites. Its dried powder was added to soy tofu at three levels, either mixed in directly or swapped for part of the soy. The team measured yield, color, texture, inner structure, nutrition, and antioxidant power in fresh, cooked, and lab-digested tofu.

More mushroom made the tofu darker, softer, and lower in yield, as the protein network grew coarser. The swaps hurt quality more than the straight additions at high levels. Still, every sample kept its gel-like spring. The lowest swap level held up best overall. The work tests whether a prized wild mushroom can lift a staple food's nutrition.
pmc-13362347:
Ivana Herak and co-authors describe who gets a collapsed lung and what their care involves in a 2026 Croatian study. Pneumothorax lets air leak around the lung so it partly collapses. The team reviewed 60 hospitalized patients over three years at one center. Cases struck mostly older men. Chest drainage, a tube that lets the air out, was used in about three quarters of admissions and in every case caused by medical care itself.

Age 60 or over was the only trait that independently predicted who received drainage. Dependency at admission and sex did not. Nursing workload was heavy: each patient carried on average about two formal nursing diagnoses, and nearly a quarter left hospital functioning worse than they arrived. The authors say care plans should build nursing dependency in from the start.
pmc-13364147:
Chenxi Liu and colleagues present a 2026 field study on drip fertigation for dense summer maize in Shandong, China. Over two years, two hybrids grew under border flooding or drip lines that deliver water and nitrogen together, across eight planting densities up to very tight stands. The team tracked where nitrogen sat in the soil and how plants moved it from leaves to grain.

Drip fertigation raised yield for both hybrids and lifted water and nitrogen efficiency by larger margins. It kept nitrogen in the top root zone, left less nitrate deep down, and pushed more nitrogen into grain after silking, while uptake efficiency itself barely changed. The gain, the authors say, comes from better placement and remobilization, not from pulling in more nitrogen.
pmc-13365447:
Dong Yeol Kim and three colleagues present a 2026 study on a sugar-based protein coating that may calm brain inflammation in Alzheimer's disease. The coating, called O-GlcNAcylation, tunes how proteins behave under stress. In Alzheimer's, the brain's immune cells, microglia, lean toward an aggressive state that harms neurons.

The team found the coating sharply reduced in patient hippocampus tissue, alongside stronger inflammatory signaling. In mouse and cell models of inflammation, the coating fell as microglia turned aggressive. Feeding glucosamine restored the coating, quieted the inflammatory switches, and shifted microglia toward a calmer state. Treated mice also kept their memory and neurons better. The authors propose raising this coating as a fresh treatment strategy.
pmc-13366947:
Mohammad-Hasan Imani-Nasab and others studied crisis care of COVID-19 at primary healthcare level in Lorestan Province, ran the story-based study in 2026. The pandemic, beginning in December 2019, became a global challenge needing effective crisis care, yet primary care events in given regions were unstudied. Local solutions counted for frontline response.

Twenty-five healthcare managers at senior, middle, and operational levels were interviewed through purposive and snowball sampling, using semi-structured face-to-face interviews studied phenomenologically. Challenges and solutions in primary care crisis care were found. Health system planners gain grounded lessons from managers who navigated the pandemic at the local level.
pmc-13367147:
Wu and colleagues discuss glycosylated RNAs, RNA molecules decorated with sugar chains, as a sorting signal for the tiny parcels cells exchange, in a 2026 commentary on extracellular vesicle biology. Cells load RNAs into exosomes, vesicles that carry messages between cells, but how particular RNAs get chosen was unclear. A recent study using sugar-tagging found these RNAs enriched inside exosomes rather than on the cell surface, as earlier work had suggested.

Experiments showed glycoRNAs enriched in membrane-bound compartments in the cytoplasm and inside the exosome lumen, the vesicle's interior. The ESCRT machinery, the cell's vesicle-building apparatus, sorts them there for protected long-range delivery. Wu lists three glycoRNA classes by location: surface-displayed, exosome-luminal, and surface-associated on vesicles. The commentary argues RNA chemistry itself, not just RNA sequence, helps decide what cells send, opening a layer of communication biology.
pmc-13369447:
Rui Zhao, Desheng Zhou, Wenpei Xu, and Yanjun Zhang cook up two-faced magnetic particles that thin extra-heavy oil under microwave heating. Their 2026 study attacks a thick problem: the oil's extreme viscosity blocks efficient pumping, while standard heat and chemical methods burn energy and strain reservoirs. Their Janus catalyst splits its jobs by side.

An iron oxide core gives magnetic grip for recovery after use. Molybdenum disulfide sheets on one face supply the catalytic sites, and graphene quantum dots drink in microwaves to make nanoscale hot spots. Long chains on the magnetic face orient the particles at the oil boundary. The system cut viscosity by over 95 percent at 100 degrees, and core flooding tests added more than 18.5 percent recovery after water flooding. The particles survived repeated cycles.
pmc-13371547:
Aditi Tiwary and co-authors profile breast tumors in a 2026 study from a hospital in southern India. A newer drug works on tumors with even low levels of a growth protein called HER2, so the old yes-or-no split has widened into a spectrum. The team sorted three hundred tumors into four groups along that spectrum.

The low group was the largest, at just over half the cases. Those tumors more often carried hormone receptors, had lower grades, and grew more slowly than the other groups. The high group came second, while the ultralow and negative groups were small. Age, tumor size, and stage are also compared across groups. The authors say such profiles help match patients to the new drug options.
pmc-13372347:
Yunqin Zhao and colleagues seek a label-free, numeric marker of embryo quality for in vitro fertilisation in a 2026 study. Embryo grading by eye is subjective, yet choosing the best embryo matters greatly for pregnancy chances. The team applied dynamic optical coherence microscopy to mouse blastocysts, measuring intracellular fluctuation spectra.

Full-band measures showed no clear difference between low- and high-cell-count embryos. Band-specific analysis did: higher-cell-count embryos showed higher mid-band mean frequency, wider mid-band bandwidth, and less low-frequency variance. Using cell count as a stand-in for quality, these frequency-specific signatures emerge as candidate markers. The work is exploratory, but it points toward objective embryo selection without dyes or labels.
pmc-13374247:
Muslim Alanoglu and co-authors test how school air shapes teacher feel through a sense of say. The study appeared in 2026. A warm, kind school air may lift how well staff feel at work. The path may run through how much say staff feel they hold.

Near five hundred staff at state schools in one Iraq city filled the forms. School air linked to well feel at both the staff and school tiers. Air at the school tier tied strong to the sense of say. That sense in turn tied to well feel and bore part of the air's link. The team backs kind school airs in ruled-from-top school webs.
pmc-13374347:
Annie Bunce and others analyse health results for people using expert home abuse services in England in a 2026 study. Domestic abuse harms health widely, yet how abuse type, added weaknesses, and social background shape results was not fully mapped. Second analysis used Women's Aid On Track, the largest national data set on home abuse in England.

Statistical models linked abuse types to health results. Abuse types included bodily, sexual, feeling, money, coercive control, tech-aided abuse, and threats to kill. Weaknesses included impairment, substance support needs, and being pregnant. Results included injury, choking attempts, self-harm, low mood, and suicidal thoughts. The analysis, corrected for housing, leaning, and background, can help services target health support to victims at highest risk.
pmc-13375947:
Zhongwei Cao and co-authors model HIV with cells that hide in a 2027 math study. Some sick cells rest and hide the virus from drugs, then wake and seed it anew. Air-like swings in the body's state can sway those wakes, the team holds.

Their model lets growth and wake rates swing in a way that pulls back to a mean. Math proves one true path for the sums and gives cut lines for the virus to stay or to die out. Strong swings can kill the virus off in the sums, even when a still model says it would stay. The work is sums alone, a guide for next lab tests.
pmc-13376547:
Cristina García-Florentino and co-authors test whether a Mars clay can shield a building block of life. Their 2026 paper studies L-histidine, an amino acid, tucked into nontronite clay. Mars sunlight breaks down organic matter at the surface, which hides signs of life. Yet a rover found organics in clays, hinting these minerals guard them.

Under Mars-like ultraviolet light, histidine slipped between clay layers at acidic levels and degraded only slightly. At basic levels it formed stacked layers and showed no breakdown at all. Pure histidine fared worse. Infrared and X-ray tools showed how the clay held it. The authors name nontronite a prime target for hunting organics on Mars.
pmc-13376747:
M M Mundu and co-authors bring a deeper math check to the control of solar power and battery systems in 2026. A home or small grid must store solar power and release it as needs change. Basic methods find a best plan but say little about how stable that plan is. Small shifts in sun or demand could push the plan off course.

Their method uses a class of math tools that track how a plan bends under small shifts. Tests on a one day system show weak points in the plan. The checks also flag where the best plan stops being best. The work gives guidance on battery size and control settings. It aims for more robust plans in small solar grids.
pmc-13377147:
Vankova and colleagues ask whether sex hormones or sex chromosomes set the anti-inflammatory power of HDL, the good cholesterol particles, in 2026 heart research. Hormone therapy offers an experiment: 14 transgender men and 17 transgender women were tested at baseline, after hormone suppression, and after 11 months on hormones. The assay measured how well each person's HDL suppressed an inflammatory signal in blood vessel cells grown in the lab, alongside detailed lipid profiling.

The HDL anti-inflammatory capacity stayed largely unaffected by the hormone changes across all time points. Neither HDL cholesterol level nor particle number correlated with function. Instead, composition mattered: rises in core lipids tracked with worse anti-inflammatory function, while rises in membrane lipid species tracked with better function, each at the significance threshold. Vankova concludes neither sex chromosomes nor hormone shifts fundamentally determine this HDL function; what it carries does.
pmc-13377847:
Mehdi Fallah and seven co-authors search walnut genes for markers tied to spring leafing, in a study dated 2026. Late frosts harm walnut orchards when trees leaf out too early. Breeders want trees that wake later in spring, and gene markers would speed the search.

The team studied 85 walnut types from Iran and abroad over three years. They read tens of thousands of small gene differences and matched them with the day each tree reached half budburst. Strong signals turned up on six chromosomes, and the best ones held across years and models. A second test method confirmed the markers. The results give breeders firm targets for raising frost-safe walnuts.
pmc-13378047:
Mukta T Killedar and Suraj B Kanase describe a 2026 case report on shoulder problems after stroke. Their patient was a 45-year-old man whose left side was weak after bleeding inside the brain. Four months later he had shoulder pain, stiff and tight muscles, limited movement, and the shoulder had slipped partly out of place.

The gap between the shoulder bone and the arm bone measured 18 mm at the start. Over four weeks he did active shoulder exercises using a sling for support, plus exercises to steady the shoulder blade and activities that put weight through the arm. The program was stepped up over time, and the report follows his individual response in detail.
pmc-13378147:
Xinqi Guo and co-authors report a 2026 study on a brain pathway that may drive high blood pressure. Certain nerve cells in a small brain region release a hormone that raises activity in nerves controlling the kidneys and blood vessels. In rats bred to have high blood pressure, those cells were overly active.

The team traced the problem to a chain of proteins that controls chloride, a salt component, inside the cells. Too much chloride made a calming signal act in reverse, so the cells fired more. Blocking parts of that chain calmed the cells and lowered blood pressure in the rats. Quieting the brain cells directly had the same effect.
pmc-13378347:
Chen-Xi Yang and colleagues report a 2026 study on a fat-carrying protein in pancreatic cancer. This cancer is highly aggressive and has a very poor outlook. The protein, called FABP4, had been linked to cancer growth and to a related signalling protein, but its exact role here was unclear.

Levels of FABP4 were much higher in pancreatic cancer cells than in normal cells. Tests showed it binds directly to that signalling partner, called PPARγ in the work. Raising FABP4 made cancer cells grow, move, and use fats more, and made tumours grow faster in mice. A drug that blocks the partner protein largely removed those effects.
pmc-13378647:
Marius Brühl and co-authors measure how people with haemophilia walk at three speeds, in a 2026 study. Bleeds into the elbow, knee, and ankle slowly deform the joints, a condition called haemophilic arthropathy. Thirty patients and 31 healthy controls walked at three, four, and five kilometers per hour in a motion lab. The team recorded foot pressure and knee and ankle angles, and split patients by how severe their joint damage was.

Speed alone changed little between the groups. Patients with major damage, though, pressed less through the second half of each step. Their ankles also bent less in both directions, while knee motion looked mildly reduced. The authors read this as weak push-off power, well compensated for now. They say the pattern confirms gait suffers most when joint damage is advanced.
pmc-13379547:
Zhi Zhen Lim and co-authors add up the full cost of spinal muscular atrophy in Singapore, in a 2026 study. The disease weakens muscles from birth and needs lifelong care. The team count not just hospital bills but also private care, home help, transport, gear, and the paid work that caregivers give up.

Records covered 61 patients, and 15 caregivers were surveyed. Hospital stays cost about 1,664 Singapore dollars a day, while breathing gear and mobility aids added large fixed sums. Lost paid work came to about 42,933 dollars per family each year. All told, the burden averaged about 62,004 dollars per patient per year from society's view, most of it falling on families. The authors argue that policy on this disease should weigh the whole burden, not just clinic costs.
pmc-13381647:
Jing Wang, Yongbo Zhou, and Ning Liu present a method for gathering upkeep data from electrical substations, the yards where power lines meet and voltage changes. Their 2026 paper notes that fast, safe data gathering helps crews spot faults before they grow. Substation gear speaks in many formats and over many links, which makes one clean feed hard to build.

Their design has three layers. Gear at the site sends readings to the nearest edge server. The cloud layer picks which edge server should gather each batch of data. A swarm-based smart algorithm makes that pick, aiming to cut both delay and energy use. In tests, transfer speeds stayed steady, the longest wait was a few seconds, and nearly all data arrived whole. The authors say the method is ready for real use.
pmc-13381747:
Kate Feloy, Brian Powell, Tobias Friedrich, and Hannah Barkley model future heat stress on Hawaiian corals. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with regional ocean dynamics. The islands stir Pacific flows and create local variety.

Global climate models miss that fine local detail. A downscaled model resolved daily states at fine scale. Three emission paths ran to the end of the century. The big island faces the greatest heat stress ahead. Yet adaptation could let corals persist in all paths. Local forecasts guide reef management choices.  Three paths span varied emission futures.
pmc-13382747:
Sandra G. Barbosa-Muñoz and colleagues present a new family of pyrrolyl quinone compounds and test how they bind DNA in 2026 work. The compounds were built from a simple quinone through a series of addition and substitution steps. Further reactions with other building blocks widened the set of structures for testing.

Light-based tests, gel runs, thickness measures, and computer docking all pointed to real contact with DNA. Such binding matters because compounds that sit on DNA can block copying enzymes tied to fast cell growth. The authors frame the scaffold as a useful starting point for later drug design and for tools that detect target molecules.
pmc-13383447:
Yingman Liu and nine co-authors report, in two thousand twenty-six, a pilot test of a new way to save teeth judged hopeless from gum disease. Rather than pull and discard such teeth, the plan takes each tooth out, cleans it, and puts it back. A robot helps reshape the socket so the tooth fits well.

Scans fed a robotic system that planned each case before surgery. Out of the mouth, the root was cleaned and its canal was sealed from the tip end. The tooth then went back into the reshaped socket and was tied to nearby teeth. At three months, bleeding and swelling had eased and pockets were shallower. The teeth felt firm and worked well with new veneer fronts.
pmc-13385447:
Florine Roussange and colleagues flip drug screening by matching drug effects to disease signatures in stem cells in 2026 work. Fifty drugs were tested on mesenchymal stem cells grown from a human pluripotent line. Over half shifted gene activity, many in pathways tied to single-gene diseases.

One hit stood out: the blood pressure drug prazosin raised levels of SQSTM1, a gene halved in one ALS and dementia form. Checks in patient skin cells, depleted motor neurons, and a zebrafish model backed the effect. The authors argue the reverse-mapping route can surface repurposing leads that target-first screens miss.
pmc-13385647:
Bear and colleagues mapped the research in 2026 on artificial nutrition, feeding by tube into the gut or by vein, for pregnant patients who are acutely ill. Care must weigh the mother's needs against the baby's, yet little was known about what studies exist. Following standard scoping review methods, the team searched five databases for work on hospitalized pregnant adults given such feeding.

Only 24 studies qualified, and most were single case reports or small case series, with just one randomized trial. Severe vomiting of pregnancy was the commonest reason for feeding, and vein feeding was the commonest route. Reports varied widely in how they gave energy and protein targets, vitamin cover, weight change, and outcomes for mother and baby. The authors call the evidence base thin and urge strong trials so guidelines can set a shared standard for this complex care.
pmc-13385847:
Junhao Wang and colleagues rebuild 3D views of uterine fibroids from routine multi-angle MRI scans in 2026 work. Standard care uses three flat scan planes with uneven spacing, which fragments any 3D picture. Models trained at one center also tend to fail on outside data, a gap their method targets.

Their framework, FGAS, uses anatomy-guided draft labels plus cross-view consistency checks to cut false alarms. Accuracy jumped from a baseline overlap score near 43 percent to about 71 percent on clinical datasets. The authors present the system as annotation-free help for diagnosis, surgery planning, and treatment review.
pmc-13386247:
Andreas Antzoulas and co-authors report a case in 2026 of a gallstone blocking the small bowel, a rare turn of gallstone disease. Such blocks make up one to four percent of mechanical bowel blocks, the authors note, and they strike older people most. The stone slips from the gallbladder into the gut through an abnormal channel, then lodges where the bowel narrows.

Care must join antibiotics, fluids, and surgery, they write. Options range from an emergency cut to free the bowel alone, to a one-stage fix that also removes the gallbladder and repairs the channel. Suspecting the cause in an older patient with gallstone history and sudden blockage is half the battle, backed by a classic trio of scan signs. The case adds one worked example to a thin record.
pmc-13386447:
Nadia Maaroufi and three co-authors present, in a 2026 data paper, half a century of crop and soil records from Swedish field trials. The trials test how nitrogen dose and straw management affect yield and soil properties in a cereal-only rotation. Four sites span the country, one maintained since 1970 and the other three since 1980.

Each site runs the same design: four nitrogen fertilization levels, from zero to 150 kilograms per hectare per year, crossed with straw removed or straw incorporated into the soil. Crop biomass has been collected annually since the trials began. Topsoil was sampled often in the first decades, then every four years. The dataset gives grain and straw yields, nutrient content, and soil carbon data. The authors offer the long series to track how cereal-only farming, straw fate, and nitrogen shape soil carbon and yield over decades.
pmc-13387747:
Basil Zia Khan, Andrew Wigham, and Daniel Kearns report a filter clot emergency treated by large-bore clot removal in a 2026 case report. A 55-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer carried a vena cava filter placed to block lung clots. The filter itself clogged completely, causing both cava syndrome and spontaneous bleeding behind the belly lining.

Clotting and bleeding arriving together in this way is very uncommon, and few such cases appear in print. Mechanical thrombectomy through a large catheter cleared the blockage successfully, the team reports. The case aims to give clinicians a workable path for this dangerous complication.
pmc-13388347:
Hironobu Nishijima and six co-authors simulated how air moves through children's noses in a 2026 paper. Smell depends on air reaching the olfactory lining high in the nose, and children's noses change shape as they grow. How that growth affects smell airflow has been poorly understood.

The team rebuilt the nasal passages of eleven patients aged three to eighteen from CT scans and ran airflow simulations. The smell region and its airflow grew steadily until about age fifteen, then jumped in late teens. Young children got far less air to the smell lining, and scent tracers arrived later and weaker. The authors conclude that an immature nose limits smell efficiency in early childhood.
pmc-13390147:
Pernille Lindholm Heidemann and colleagues describe, in 2026, a five-month-old Chow Chow puppy whose sudden seizures traced to a blood vessel tumour in the brain. Cerebral hemangioma is a known but rarely reported cause of seizures in dogs, with risk usually rising with age and peaking near nine years.

After causes outside the skull were ruled out, magnetic resonance imaging showed a large, well-defined bleeding mass spanning the right frontal lobe area. The mass matched the puppy's between-seizure deficits. Those deficits pointed to the right forebrain. Veterinary neurologists gain an age-outlier case that widens the expected range for this diagnosis. They also get a clear imaging description. That description can help others recognise the same pattern in young dogs.
pmc-13390347:
Amanda Maria Rydgren Thomsen, Danillo Oliveira Alvarenga, and Kathrin Rousk compare, in 2026, the microbes living on mosses in forests receiving very different nitrogen pollution. Moss microbes fix nitrogen from the air and supply it to nutrient-poor ecosystems, so shifts in that community matter.

Three common mosses were sampled in a temperate forest with high nitrogen deposition and a northern forest with low deposition. The authors test whether the moss host or the environment shapes the microbiome more, and whether nitrogen fixation follows the same pattern. Pollution made the microbiomes more alike overall, yet each moss species still answered in its own way. Ecologists gain evidence that air pollution can narrow natural variety even among microbes.
pmc-13390547:
Tejaswini Malapati and colleagues present, in 2026, a hybrid flap method for rebuilding the nipple and areola after breast reconstruction. Rebuilding this complex is the final step of reconstruction and strongly affects appearance and satisfaction, but rebuilt nipples tend to flatten over time.

A 28-year-old woman had both sides rebuilt three months after implant-based reconstruction, using a method that merges C-V and star flap designs to add central bulk, support height, and preserve blood supply. Healing was smooth with no flap loss, symmetry was kept, and the patient was satisfied, though some height loss occurred and height was not measured objectively. Plastic surgeons gain an honest single-case account of a combined design.
pmc-13391347:
Hadi Hadi and colleagues quantify, in 2026, how degraded land widens the gap between the harvests farms achieve and the harvests they could achieve. Concern that land degradation cuts farm output over the long run is old, but global empirical proof has stayed inconclusive.

Across world croplands, the team finds that each ten percent rise in degradation is linked on average to about a two percent wider yield gap. In the worst hotspots, including parts of India, northeastern China, and the United States Midwest, the penalty reaches about six percent. Agricultural policymakers gain a global figure that turns soil restoration into a food security investment with a measurable return.
pmc-13392047:
Jacquelyn Turcinovic's team tested lab-made Bombali ebolavirus in cynomolgus monkeys to gauge its human disease risk. These included vessel leak, lymphopenia, neutrophilia, and swelling.

Virus appeared in liver, lymph nodes, and adrenal gland at peak virus load, yet all animals survived and mounted strong IgG and blocking antibody responses. Bombali virus thus looks weakened beside Ebola, Bundibugyo, Sudan, and Tai Forest viruses, and may serve as a model of resolving Ebola virus disease.
pmc-13392247:
Zeyu Wang's team reworked seeding theory for zinc aqueous cells, which lacked a zinc-exact account of plating at the zinc-water edge. Without it, blocking hydrogen evolution and dendrites, the barriers to practical zinc cells, stayed trial-and-error.

Adapting classical spherical seeding to zinc's six-sided close-packed crystal and adding edge drag, the team defined a unit-free marker, Wf. It merges angle driving force with drag, where higher values aid uniform plating. A high-Wf liquid ran over seven hundred hours at full depth of discharge and 7,660 cycles at high current in a zinc-sodium V oxide cell.
pmc-13392447:
Feng Chen's team applied causal logic linking upstream gene changes to serum marker patterns in gut-gland ductal gland cancer. The cancer carries poor outlook and weak aimed-treatment response. Their Mutation-Upstream-of-Metabolomic-Signature approach tests whether blood markers capture cross-talk among gene-change-driven networks.

A nine-marker serum panel model life span across several cohorts, and analysis found GRPEL1 as a tumour-feeding gene whose energy-use-linked pattern meets mTOR, PI3K, and Akt signals. GRPEL1 softened cancer cells to growth halt under mTOR blocking, giving a system for new targets and reasoned combination therapies.
pmc-13392647:
Thammacharoen and colleagues review, in 2026, how a high dietary cation-anion difference diet might act as a biological coolant for dairy goats and cows in hot climates. The review gathers physiological, behavioral, and hormonal evidence on animals under natural high temperatures, then evaluates feeding diets richer in minerals such as sodium and potassium.

Summer heat cut milk yield by roughly 16 percent in cows and about half in goats compared with winter. Animals on the high-DCAD diet drank more water at night, held larger body water reserves, and showed smaller daytime rises in rectal temperature. Rumen fermentation, digestibility, and feed intake improved too. The authors argue the diet supports the body's own cooling machinery rather than merely buffering acid, a partner to shade and ventilation.
pmc-13392847:
Hyelim Lee and a large team set out to strengthen how the Korean military handles infectious disease, since crowded barracks and field training make outbreaks easy to start and hard to stop.
