The team interviewed thirty-seven recent graduates of an epidemiology investigator course, built problem-based lessons around seven diseases, and piloted a tabletop exercise with forty Navy and Air Force infection staff.

Trainees named four pain points: vague guidelines, missing tools, double reporting that doubled work, and knowledge fading fast after short courses. Pilot feedback ran strongly positive on every rated point, with clear procedures and swapping experience across units singled out as the most valued parts. The authors call for standardised military reporting, standing joint bodies with civilian partners, and regular hands-on drills.
pmc-13393147:
Narumitsu Kagoshima, Uchida Takayuki, and Matsumoto Takashi describe a 66-year-old woman with six weeks of worsening back pain. The cause was an abdominal aortic aneurysm that had leaked slowly and sealed itself, masquerading as a tumour behind the belly. Scans showed an irregular mass hugging the aorta and squeezing the left ureter, which had swollen the kidney with backed-up urine. Density readings fit an organised blood collection rather than solid growth.

Detailed angiography confirmed a bulging infrarenal aorta with a wall defect but no active leak, plus an extra kidney artery branching low. Because a stent approach threatened further leak and kidney blood flow, the team chose open repair with the extra artery reimplanted directly. The operation freed the ureter, excluded the aneurysm, and kept the kidney perfused, and the authors urge doctors to keep contained rupture in mind for such masses.
pmc-13393247:
Rodi Ertogrul and co-authors probe in 2026 whether shoulder socket shape variants link to loose joint position on dye-enhanced scans. One hundred ninety patients with no tears or clear instability form the group. Scan reads grade socket rim forms, capsule attach types, and head shift.

Undergrown rims appear in near three in ten patients, and absent rims in a small slice. Grooves under the rim show in just over half the group. Head shift backward grows with undergrown rims and deep grooves. Capsule attach type also predicts head position on its own.
pmc-13393847:
Wei-wei Chen and colleagues evaluate integrin-binding sialoprotein as a glioma prognosis marker in a 2026 study. This bone-related protein has been tied to metastasis in breast, lung, and prostate cancers, but its role in brain glioma was poorly characterized.

Gene data from Chinese glioma databases were linked to clinical features, with Cox models testing prognostic value and staining used to confirm expression. Pathway analysis connected high IBSP levels to adverse biology, and drug screens suggested agents that might target it. Neuro-oncologists gain a candidate marker for stratifying glioma risk.
pmc-13393947:
Tamir Velner, Zohar Rubinstein, and Bruria Adini evaluated a seventy-hour programme designed to build resilience inside an Israeli emergency medical service. The service works under decades of security pressure. That pressure sharpened after the October 2023 attacks. Staff completed a validated seven-domain resilience questionnaire before the programme, just after, and six months later, with roughly two hundred respondents per wave. Internal resilience trustees delivered training plus a longer organisational embedding phase.

Overall resilience rose significantly right after the programme and kept climbing at six months. Situational awareness showed the cleanest gain, with adaptive capacity and learning processes also improving. Paramedics gained far more than other staff groups. The effect survived adjustment for background variables. The authors offer rare long-term trial evidence that resilience in pre-hospital services can be built on purpose rather than merely hoped for.
pmc-13394147:
Yafen Wang and seven colleagues trace how breast tumours export a tiny RNA, named piR-hsa-28212, in exosomes to grow the lymph vessels that carry cancer to lymph nodes. The RNA ran high in blood exosomes of patients whose cancer had reached their nodes. Laboratory and animal work followed its two-pronged action on the VEGF growth signal family, the master switch for lymph vessel growth.

Delivered into lymphatic vessel cells, the RNA stabilised the message for a transcription factor that raises the VEGF receptor. That boosted the cells' migration and tube building. The RNA also drove lymph vessel growth and node spread in a mouse footpad model. Back inside cancer cells, the same RNA protected a methylation enzyme that marks the VEGF ligand's message, raising its output and secretion. The authors nominate the RNA as a target against lymphatic metastasis.
pmc-13394247:
Danny W Walmsley and Damian M Bailey reviewed artificial intelligence in contact sports research in 2026. Sports like rugby and American football carry a known risk of brain injury. A hard blow can cause concussion, a mild brain injury with headache, sickness, and foggy thinking. Most cases clear in weeks, but some athletes face months of symptoms and faster mental decline over time.

Diagnosis still rests largely on what athletes report, plus early-stage blood and saliva tests. AI tools could scan brain images, sensor data, and large test result sets for patterns people miss. The authors also warn of real risks: weak data, hidden bias, and tools sold before they are proven. Both sides shape their advice for teams and researchers.
pmc-13394547:
Imdadul Haque and colleagues describe, in 2026, three copper compounds built on Schiff base frames. Each frame joins a benzophenone part to a ring that carries a methoxy or ethoxy group. Copper acetate turned the frames into compounds with two frames per copper atom. Crystal studies showed the copper sits in a square pyramid shape, with a long fifth bond.

Powder tests confirmed that bulk samples match the crystals. Heat tests showed plain melting with a lasting phase change. Electric tests found two stepwise transfers of single electrons. The free frames beat the copper compounds at mopping up test radicals. Computer models matched the light and shape data well.
pmc-13394847:
Rajyk Bhala, Sriram Ambadi, and Reid Oldenburg study, in 2026, online talk about sun protection and false claims. Searches that doubt sunscreen have grown in recent years. The team pulled top TikTok clips for three search terms and checked search volume on Google from 2020 to 2025. Clips were sorted by stance and by whether a doctor made them.

Clips by non-doctors drew like levels of likes and shares. Yet raters scored them lower on quality and viewer experience than doctor clips. Search interest in anti-sunscreen terms rose while sound advice spread less well. The authors warn that reach and truth do not travel together online.
pmc-13395347:
Sara C. Handley leads a 2026 study of whether higher levels of maternity care guard mothers from grave harm. Guidelines sort birth hospitals from basic to regional centres, aiming to match risk with skill. Records covered more than three million births in four states over about a decade. Harm was counted without blood transfusion cases, to sharpen the measure.

Raw harm rates rose with hospital level, since sicker mothers go to bigger centres. After adjustment, basic hospitals showed slightly lower harm odds than regional centres for all patients. Among women with common treatable problems, mid-level hospitals fared worse. The authors say triage and transfer habits blur the picture and need work.
pmc-13395447:
Denisse Bustos and co-authors profile, in 2026, the fitness of volunteer firefighters on a treadmill test. Thirty-one men ran in steps that rose in speed, with short rests between. Breath, heart rate, energy use, and blood lactate were tracked from start to after the test. Fire work demands high fitness, so the team checked men against guidance from a national fire body.

Oxygen use and heart rate climbed steeply as speed rose. The share of energy from oxygen fell while the burn-without-oxygen share grew. About half the men missed the oxygen mark advised for their age. Heavier men showed lower heart rates at hard stages, a pattern the authors flag. They urge set training and food guidance.
pmc-13395847:
F. L. Menezes and co-authors weigh, in 2026, gene links between early breeding and growth in Nellore cattle. Records covered weights at four ages, muscle area, back fat, and age at first calving. The team split gene effects from herd, year, season, and sex effects. Heritability ran high for weights and low for first calving age.

Breeding values for weights moved together strongly. First calving age tied in complex ways: genes for faster growth went with later maturity in one read, yet carcass traits pointed the other way. Picks based on muscle or fat gave small shifts in calving age. The authors give breeders a map of trade-offs. Early breeding need not cost carcass finish, their data hint.
pmc-13396347:
Zhang and team test, in 2026, whether intensive blood pressure control helps real-world patients as much as trials suggest, by emulating a randomized trial in Hong Kong's territory-wide public health database. They followed 118,271 adults with uncomplicated hypertension managed either to an intensive target below 130/80 or to a standard target in the 130-to-140 over 80-to-90 range. They watched for complications and deaths over up to 11 years.

Patients managed intensively ran a lower risk of hypertension-related complications, including heart events and end-stage renal disease, and lower all-cause mortality. Crucially, the intensive group showed no significant increase in the serious adverse events that make clinicians cautious about aggressive treatment. Benefits held broadly across subgroups in the analysis. The authors argue the results support adopting the below-130/80 target in primary care guidelines, since trial benefits, such as the 27 percent event reduction reported earlier, appear achievable in routine practice.
pmc-13396447:
Zihan Xu and co-authors profiled 60 cancer cell lines cell by cell. They measured both gene activity and which stretches of DNA lay open, hunting for rules that set a cancer cell's state. Their 2026 atlas spans 16 tissues of origin and 20 cancer types.

The collection holds about 241,000 gene-activity profiles and 223,000 chromatin profiles. Across that spread, the team found shared regulatory networks and one conserved axis tied to a change called EMT, where cells loosen and become mobile. Amplified control genes appeared to push cells between states. A rare skin melanoma subtype showed a shared program that damps inflammation, set against its common cousin.
pmc-13396547:
Fatima Zahid and co-authors packaged artemisinin, a plant-derived drug, inside microscopic silica sponges and tested the package against colon cancer in rats, in a 2026 study. Artemisinin dissolves poorly and clears fast, so a carrier that ferries it to tumors could sharpen its effect.

The particles were made by a sol-gel route, loaded with the drug, and coated with polyethylene glycol to help them circulate. Size and structure checks came first, with the standard drug gemcitabine as the yardstick. Rats were then given a chemical that induces colon tumors, and the team tracked how different doses of the package slowed the disease, probing the mechanism as the doses rose.
pmc-13396747:
Wang and team present, in 2026, a case of eruptive halo nevi appearing after melanoma excision in a 36-year-old man with a family history of melanoma on his father's side. Halo nevi are moles ringed by a pale circle where immune cells, chiefly CD8 T lymphocytes, destroy pigment cells in the mole and nearby skin. Sudden crops in adults are rarely reported but linked to underlying malignancy, so the picture carries weight beyond cosmetics.

The patient's back lesion was biopsied and returned as a melanoma of 0.8 millimeters thickness without ulceration, and the halo nevi erupted after removal. The authors review the phenomenon, noting that in the Lorentzen case series, patients with eruptive or multiple halo nevi averaged 39.6 years of age. They discuss how immune activation against melanocytic antigens, the mechanism exploited by melanoma immunotherapy, likely drives the reaction, and they advise malignancy evaluation when adults develop eruptive halo nevi.
pmc-13398147:
Shova Aryal and co-authors report a rare bleeding source found late after a caesarean birth, and the vessel-blocking fix that stopped it. Their 2026 case concerns a woman with repeated vaginal bleeding after her caesarean, managed at first with medicines and several blood transfusions. Late postpartum bleeding, beyond the first day and within six weeks, strikes about 0.21 percent of mothers in the figures cited.

Only on day 48 did imaging name the culprit: a pseudoaneurysm, a ballooned weak spot, on the uterine artery, likely from vessel injury during surgery. Doctors closed it by embolization, threading material into the vessel to seal the leak. The case presses teams to hunt rare causes when bleeding keeps returning.
pmc-13399447:
Brenda Salley and a large team describe a study protocol, published in 2026, for testing Talk With Me Baby for Well-Child Care in rural and underserved clinics. The program coaches caregivers, during ordinary pediatric checkups, in habits that enrich a baby's language environment. Yet families in rural and low-resource areas have rarely been included in rigorous trials.

At least 66 child-caregiver pairs, with babies aged two to six months at enrollment, will be recruited over five months from two primary care clinics. Every family receives the program across well-child visits for twelve months. The protocol notes a key design point: because all participants receive the intervention, the study tests preliminary efficacy signals rather than comparing against a control group. The trial was registered prospectively as NCT06479278 in June 2024.
pmc-13399647:
Pablo Cañete San Pastor and M Inmaculada Prósper Ramos describe a fully arthroscopic bone block repair for recurrent posterior shoulder instability with socket bone loss. Their 2026 technical paper targets a hard problem: restoring socket concavity while also treating damage inside the joint, through small incisions. Posterior instability with bone loss often defeats soft-tissue repair alone.

The method uses a tricortical iliac crest autograft, bone taken from the patient's hip, fixed with independent cortical buttons from a commercial instability system. An adapted anterior guide helps place tunnels accurately from the back, with careful capsular mobilization, a bleeding bone bed, progressive button tensioning, and capsular reconstruction leaving the graft outside the joint. The paper offers surgeons a detailed blueprint, pending outcome follow-up.
pmc-13399847:
Kyle S. Ardavanis and colleagues describe repairing a talar body fracture that never healed, working entirely from behind the ankle through the arthroscope, in a 2026 technique article. Talus fractures are uncommon, roughly one to four percent of foot fractures. Their candidate is a nonunion inside the joint but with the talus shape and cartilage still preserved.

With the patient face-down, the surgeons view from the posteromedial portal and work from the posterolateral one, clearing debris from both the nonunion and the subtalar joint beneath it. An awl punches channels into both surfaces to provoke bleeding and fusion. Bone graft is packed in under direct vision, and headless compression screws finally fix the talar body and fuse the subtalar joint in the same pass. The authors present the approach as a way to salvage the talus while skipping the osteotomy and its wound risks.
pmc-13400047:
Yu-Ting Kuo and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six prospective comparison of two endoscopic fixes for cancer-blocked stomach outlets. One option props the blockage open with a metal stent. The other builds a new bypass channel using ultrasound guidance.

About one hundred fifty patients with inoperable blockage were split evenly between the methods. Technical and clinical success and side effects were similar early on. The main measure was how often patients needed another procedure later. Follow-up ran until death or a set closing date. Long-term results favoured the bypass approach, informing comfort-focused choices.
pmc-13400247:
Jessica Buck and colleagues worked out how to irradiate a mouse's whole brain and spine the way oncologists treat children with medulloblastoma, in a 2026 methods study. The team compared four fractionated strategies, focal, regional brain, whole brain, and full craniospinal, across seven widely used models, including patient-derived xenografts and a mouse allograft.

Only the full craniospinal approach matched the clinic. Focal treatment barely controlled disease. Regional brain targeting extended survival but tumors regrew fast. Whole brain treatment delayed progression yet let spinal metastases declare themselves, exactly the failure the clinical routine exists to prevent. The full treatment clearly improved survival in every model, with recurrences appearing at the original site, matching human relapse patterns. The authors publish the protocol, with optimized dosing per model, as a shared resource so that drug candidates are tested against the real standard of care.
pmc-13400347:
Nicole Zeky leads a team examining, in 2026, food insecurity and diet in children newly diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease. Food insecurity means a household lacks steady access to enough food. It often goes with lower diet quality and more ultra-processed food, both relevant to bowel inflammation.

The cohort held 120 patients aged 5 to 17 years at one center, followed for 12 months. Fourteen percent of families reported food insecurity, and those families lived in more deprived areas and more often had public insurance. A data method grouped patients mainly by how much unprocessed food they ate. The group eating more unprocessed food gained more healthy body mass, while remission and healing rates did not differ.
pmc-13400647:
M Ketzer leads a team reporting, in 2026, that methane seeping from beneath the north Greenland Ice Sheet comes mainly from rock, not microbes. Meltwater methane has drawn attention as ice sheets shrink, because methane is a potent warming gas. Most earlier Greenland work, at southern and western edges, found microbe-made methane.

The team measured methane levels and carbon isotope fingerprints in meltwater draining the northern ice sheet. Levels were far lower than in other Greenland catchments, even though water clearly came from under the ice. Isotope values and local geology pointed to a heat-formed, underground source largely independent of microbes. Geological stores, the authors warn, must count in Arctic carbon budgets alongside biological ones.
pmc-13401147:
Francesca Fazio and colleagues survey, in 2026, how Italian blood cancer centers treat multiple myeloma that has returned or stopped responding, for a national research group. Care has grown complex because patients now meet many drug classes in their first treatment line, narrowing later options. A shared national picture was missing.

Seventy-one centers contributed data, pooled in aggregate, on regimens, treatment lines and clinician views. Daratumumab-based combinations dominated first-line use. Resistance to a key drug class and to anti-CD38 antibodies emerged early, squeezing choices at second and third lines. Newer immune therapies targeting BCMA were broadly endorsed by respondents. The authors call for shared guidelines and genuinely new therapies.
pmc-13401247:
Raghuram Manickam and Vijaya Nirmala Subramani wrote a 2026 mini review on protease-processed amnion, a birth membrane material prepared with enzymes, and its possible uses in dentistry. Amnion is valued for calming inflammation, limiting scarring, and helping wounds heal.

Processing the membrane with proteases may keep its structure and active components better than conventional methods, and early evidence hints at faster wound healing. The authors weigh its role in extraction socket healing, gum regeneration, and repair of openings between mouth and sinus. Support in the mouth is still mostly preclinical, they caution, and problems with processing consistency, sterilization, storage, and regulation remain. Well-designed clinical trials are needed before routine dental use can be recommended.
pmc-13401547:
Koichi Sugimoto and many co-authors present a 2026 multicentre retrospective study of metastatic kidney cancer treated with two first-line immunotherapy combinations, asking whether ordinary host factors predict survival differently under each. One pairing doubles immune checkpoint inhibitors; the other mixes one with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

The analysis covered 493 patients, 205 on the double immunotherapy and 288 on the mixed regimen. In the double immunotherapy group, several host factors independently predicted worse survival: body mass index under 25, abnormal blood lipids, use of proton pump inhibitors. Opioid use, with hazard ratios roughly between 1.6 and 2.9. The pattern in the mixed-regimen group differed, which is the study's point: the same everyday patient characteristics do not carry the same prognostic weight under both treatments.
pmc-13402347:
Li and co-authors build, in 2026, molecular switches that respond to X-rays at doses far below earlier radioswitches, opening remote control through barriers that light cannot cross. Existing switches needed multi-gray doses to flip fully. Their design routes X-ray energy through triplet excitons: a copper iodide scintillator absorbs the radiation and hands energy to a hydrazone photoswitch of lower triplet energy by triplet-triplet transfer.

Films of the pair reached their photostationary state at about 0.18 gray and showed a detection limit near 0.01 milligray, roughly two orders of magnitude more sensitive than previous systems in the authors' comparison. Switching quenches fluorescence, dropping quantum yield from 18.43 percent to 0.27 percent across the transition, which enables optical readout. They demonstrated high-resolution radiography at 3251 dots per inch with patterns retained for at least two months, helped by the switched state's thermal half-life of over 300 years in solution.
pmc-13402647:
Two labels in a published figure were swapped by mistake, and a correction notice now sets the record straight for a quality study of optical coherence tomography scans in neuromyelitis optica. Figure 4 of the original article showed rejection rates for two scan types, peripapillary and macular, with the labels exchanged during manual labeling. The corrected figure accompanies the notice.

Because the labels flipped, two paragraphs on pages 587 and 588 read the rejection pattern backward, and the notice removes both paragraphs in full. One had compared scan types across levels of visual impairment; the other had explained the higher peripapillary rejection rate by routine clinical use. The underlying dataset, the statistical analyses, and the main conclusions of the study all stand unchanged. The authors close with an apology for the error.
pmc-13402747:
Jinhua Hong and co-authors chart how excitons, bound electron-hole pairs that govern light response, move through freestanding sheets of hexagonal boron nitride. This insulating two-dimensional material absorbs in the deep ultraviolet, where ordinary optical tools struggle, and momentum-resolved views of its excitons were missing. The team used electron energy loss spectroscopy with fine momentum resolution on single and few-layer flakes.

The first bright exciton band split into two close features, labeled A and A prime, visible only at small momentum and absent from standard frozen-nuclei calculations. A new optical conductivity approximation let them pull deep ultraviolet conductivity at zero momentum straight from the spectra, and the fine structure there matched earlier light emission reports. The authors offer the method as a general way to read exciton detail, including phonon sidebands, in thin materials.
pmc-13402847:
Peng Tian and co-authors follow a Chinese aging cohort to test whether cardiometabolic multimorbidity, carrying two or more of heart disease, diabetes, stroke, and high blood pressure together, raises hip fracture risk. Data came from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study across 2011 to 2020. After exclusions, 6314 adults aged 45 and older entered the analysis, 544 of them with multimorbidity at baseline.

Over nine years, 287 new hip fractures occurred, and the multimorbidity group fractured at a clearly higher rate. Full adjustment still left a hazard ratio of 1.70, a 70 percent risk lift, with a confidence interval from 1.318 to 2.47 in the reported model. The link ran stronger in people under 60 and in those with a fall history. The authors urge fracture prevention to treat stacked heart-metabolic disease as a bone risk in its own right.
pmc-13403447:
Wei Lu and co-authors asked in 2026 whether rerouting a cut nerve into muscle could help the spinal cord recover in rats. The surgery joins the nerve stump to a calf muscle so stray fibers gain a target. Thirty rats were split into control, nerve-cut, and treated groups.

Treated rats walked better and kept more muscle weight than rats with a plain nerve cut. Their muscle also held less scar tissue. Gene signals tied to synapse building rose in the spinal cord, while one growth signal fell. The team reads the shift as helpful rewiring, though cell-death markers moved in a mixed way that needs more study.
pmc-13404847:
Nils Laurenz and co-authors present SMART-MILS, a 2026 trial protocol on 3D maps for liver surgery in Aachen, Germany. Liver removal is hard because anatomy varies and flat scans force surgeons to rebuild shapes mentally. Patient-specific 3D reconstruction promises clearer planning, but its effect on speed in theatre is unproven.

Adults booked for keyhole liver resection will be assigned evenly to standard planning or standard planning plus a 3D map. The map, built with approved MeVis software, is available before and during surgery. Groups are balanced by how hard the planned resection is on the Iwate difficulty scale. Outcomes centre on how efficiently operations proceed with the extra map.
pmc-13405647:
Satoshi Yamakawa and colleagues bend knee ligament grafts at different angles to test their strength, in 2026 laboratory work. In ACL reconstruction, the graft bends where it exits the thigh bone tunnel, and that bend may weaken it. Pig grafts of bone, tendon and bone stood in for human tissue.

Fourteen constructs were split between two bone plug arrangements and loaded repeatedly between 10 and 50 newtons. Each was tested straight and bent at 30, 60 and 90 degrees. Stiffness and stretch rose sharply in the first ten cycles under every angle. Sharper bends reduced stiffness in one construct type but barely affected the other, showing graft geometry matters.
pmc-13405747:
Jingjing Zhou and colleagues listen to graduate students narrating their supervisor relationships online, in a study published in 2026 on a Douban community group. Students increasingly use digital spaces to share real experiences and seek emotional support. Their stories reveal how they make sense of a key academic bond.

Online ethnography and thematic analysis sort the posts into four themes: identity formation, emotional exchange, experience sharing and social connection. Posting helps students clarify who they are, vent feelings, gather practical tips and feel they belong. The authors read the group as a self-help channel filling gaps where institutional support falls short. Findings point to weaknesses in offline supervision that universities could repair.
pmc-13406047:
Chun-Hsien Wu, Chih-Yi Lin and Yi-Chun Du build a video cleaner for keyhole surgery footage, in a 2026 engineering paper. Smoke from burning tools clouds the camera view, lengthening operations. Earlier programs cleaned single frames but left flicker, brightness drift and colour wobble between them.

Their system, DCP-TS, joins a smoke-removing network guided by a dark channel prior with a stabiliser that runs only at viewing time. Flow alignment, brightness smoothing and gamma correction steady the sequence without retraining. On colorectal surgery videos the method scored a PSNR of 23.39 decibels in the reported tests, beating rivals on image quality measures. The authors claim a first joint fix for smoke and flicker.
pmc-13406747:
Lea A Wehrli and Federico G Seifarth review keyhole against robotic surgery for Hirschsprung disease in children, in a 2026 systematic review. In the condition, a segment of bowel lacks nerve cells and must be pulled through and rejoined. The Yancey-Soave technique is performed with either standard keyhole tools or a robot.

Seven studies covering 556 children met the criteria from seven hundred screened reports. Keyhole surgery accounted for 338 cases and robotic for 218 in the reported totals. Technique, age at operation, operating time and bowel function outcomes were extracted under PRISMA rules. Wide variation between reports limits firm ranking, a gap the authors highlight for future trials.
pmc-13406947:
Bor Luen Tang argues in a 2026 letter that declaring generative AI use in biomedical writing should be compulsory and thorough. Authors, reviewers, and editors all now use these tools, Tang notes, while open declaration remains rare across journals.

One cited study found only 5.7 percent of submissions to a large journal group disclosed AI help. A wider count found about 76 explicit disclosures among 75,000 papers published since 2023, even though most journals had a policy in place. Some scholars favour voluntary reporting, and detection tools are unreliable, Tang concedes. Even so, the letter holds that mandatory, detailed disclosure is the steadier path to keeping published work trustworthy.
pmc-13407847:
Vishal Chettry, Rakshak Kumar, and Riccardo Testa introduce, in 2026, a journal collection treating biodiversity as natural capital in ecologically sensitive regions. Conservation planning usually stares at visible forests, wetlands, and farmland, while the collection pushes attention underground to soil life and outward to the seam where rural land meets fast-growing cities.

Contributions examine how species, communities, and microbiomes answer environmental gradients, management, and climate limits, and what those answers mean for productivity and ecosystem services. Highlights are varied. Climate-matched seed sourcing keeps grand fir forests growing and storing carbon. Diverse multi-crops in northern conditions raise biomass and energy yields with lower pressures. Other papers build habitat quality indices for wetland waterfowl. Soil networks in shaded coffee systems are also covered.
pmc-13408447:
Ou Jiang, Zichen Cao, and co-authors identify in 2026 a nitrate sensor that can switch white fat toward burning energy as heat. Browning white fat is a hoped-for route against obesity, yet how a simple dietary anion triggers it inside cells was unknown. The sensor, a protein called Sialin2, sits on both the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria of fat cells.

There it tightens contacts between the two organelles and opens a calcium relay that raises mitochondrial calcium uptake. In parallel it links up with fat-handling enzymes that route droplet fat into mitochondrial burning, feeding the heat-producing machinery. Mice lacking the sensor's gene lost all nitrate-driven browning, while nitrate feeding improved fat heat production and wider metabolic measures in obese mice without adrenaline-like stimulation.
pmc-13408747:
Weijian Pang, Jun Zhou, Jingwen Xu, and Xinian Zhi tackle in 2026 a spacecraft problem: spotting thermal faults aboard a microsatellite when only a trickle of data reaches the ground. Thermal control telemetry arrives through one or two downlink passes a day, channels are numerous and redundant, and labelled fault examples barely exist. Supervised tools starve, while single-sensor checks miss how channels move together.

Their framework first scores how strongly temperature channels inform one another and keeps only the informative few, cutting dimensionality by more than four fifths. A two-level seasonal decomposition then separates orbital rhythms from daily cycles, and paired convolutional and memory networks predict each component. Weighted prediction errors feed an adaptive alarm threshold. On real satellite telemetry the system flagged several fault types accurately within a single day of data, beating existing approaches.
pmc-13408847:
Abdallah AbuJlambo and colleagues profiled chronic pain, mental health, and catastrophic thinking among Palestinian patients at Gaza's Al-Shifa Hospital. Their 2026 cross-sectional study surveys 272 patients, median age 43 and 57.7 percent female, most married, half unemployed, and 94.1 percent living on under 1,974 shekels monthly. Chronic pain in conflict settings intertwines with trauma, yet Gaza-specific data had been scarce.

Lower limb pain predominated, with knee pain in 26.8 percent and median duration of four years. Depression affected 83.1 percent, anxiety 83.8 percent, and stress 88.6 percent, with 56.3 percent showing extremely severe anxiety, and catastrophic thinking correlated strongly with distress. The paper calls for integrated, trauma-informed pain care addressing biomedical and psychosocial factors together, with future work on sociopolitical stressors.
pmc-13409547:
Michalina Nowakowska and Leszek Szalewski survey Polish dentists in 2026 about their feelings toward artificial intelligence entering the surgery. AI tools increasingly read dental radiographs, assist diagnosis and planning, and run practice administration, yet attitudes in Central and Eastern Europe were undocumented. One hundred eighty-three licensed dentists answered fifteen attitude statements through professional social media groups.

Acceptance landed in the moderate middle overall, though enthusiasm ran highest on two items: AI's potential to improve how a practice is managed, and openness to adopting it in dentistry generally. The questionnaire itself proved highly consistent, and the analysis probed whether sex, age band, or specialty shifted the answers. For policymakers and vendors, the picture is of a profession willing in principle and waiting for tools that earn trust in the clinic rather than the brochure.
pmc-13410547:
Mengyi Shan and colleagues simulate in 2026 how an enzyme unravels collagen, the tough protein of bone and skin. The enzyme, cathepsin K, is unusual: with help from a sugar-like partner it can unwind collagen's triple helix and cut it up. Blocking it is a hope for bone disease drugs, yet the unwinding steps were unclear.

Computer runs lasting millionths of a second followed the enzyme pair, a collagen segment, and the sugar partner in water. Unwinding began when six key links between the collagen strands broke. The sugar partner curved across both enzyme and collagen, holding the trio steady. Two enzyme spots helped pry strands apart, offering targets for future drug design.
pmc-13410647:
Yumin Dai leads a long author list in 2026 on a soft contact lens that watches eye pressure through the night. Pressure inside the eye often rises during sleep, when clinic checks cannot see it. That blind spot matters for glaucoma, a disease of slow vision loss.

A flexible circuit built into a standard soft lens bends with the eye and turns pressure shifts into readable signals. The team reports the highest sensitivity yet for such a lens, with steady readings while wearers lie flat with eyes closed. Trials in rabbits and dogs, plus pilot wear by healthy and glaucoma patients, showed the lens was tolerated and could track posture-linked pressure rises. Home night monitoring is the goal.
pmc-13410947:
Klein, Kronfli, and Young argue that hepatitis C elimination has a doing problem, not a knowing problem. The world has curative drugs and 2030 targets, yet progress stalled. Thirteen countries are on track for the World Health Organization goals, and two of the twenty burden countries are among them. Their 2026 commentary lays out the stalled numbers, then replaces target talk with a stepwise list along the cascade, starting with prevention and testing.

New infections in 2024 ran near the number cured that year, and deaths from hepatitis C liver disease stayed high, down only slightly since 2015. Injection drug use drives cases, so the authors push opioid agonist therapy first where neither it nor needle programs exist, and prison needle programs as drug use shifts beyond opioids. Later steps press testing and treatment access for people current programs miss. Political will and funding, they conclude, are the intervention.
pmc-13411047:
Jing Chen leads a long author list in 2026 sorting polymer electrolytes for solid-state batteries into three honest families. Such batteries promise more energy with better safety, using plastic-like materials instead of flammable liquids. Papers, though, lump very different materials under one label, which muddies comparisons.

The families split by how ions actually travel: soaked gels, nearly solid mixes with some liquid help, and true solids run by the polymer alone. Each family has its own transport route, surface behavior, and built-in limits. Priorities differ by family, from gel stability to solid contact with electrodes. Clear labels and tests matched to real use would make claims across studies comparable at last.
pmc-13411147:
Dianlong Hou and co-authors examine in 2026 whether kidney function and a neuron injury marker together flag thinking problems in type 2 diabetes. Brain decline is a common, under-spotted complication of the disease. Kidney and brain share delicate small vessels, so damage in one may mirror damage in the other.

Eighty patients were split evenly by a standard thinking test score into groups with and without cognitive dysfunction. Blood measures included the kidney estimate eGFR and neuron-specific enolase, a protein that leaks from injured neurons. The analysis weighs how each marker relates to test performance and whether pairing them sharpens detection. Such a blood-based pairing could help clinics screen diabetic patients earlier without brain scans.
pmc-13411647:
George Galea and co-workers uncover in 2026 a holding bay for DNA repair: the Golgi apparatus, the cell's shipping hub, parks a repair protein until damage calls it into the nucleus. How the Golgi and nucleus coordinate was poorly understood. Systematic screening of proteins living in both places exposed a whole repair network.

The repair protein RAD51C sits anchored to a Golgi giant called giantin during quiet times. DNA damage flips a signal through the ATM kinase, cutting RAD51C loose for nuclear import. Timing and place thus gate genome protection, with the Golgi acting as a regulated reservoir. Disrupting the anchor or the release signal would predictably leave cells exposed, a vulnerability the study maps for future work.
pmc-13412147:
Anaïs Delhomme and colleagues present in 2026 a fast DNA test for parasitic worms hiding in krill. Anisakidae nematodes pass through zooplankton before reaching fish and, sometimes, people who eat them raw or undercooked. Krill are thought to be major hosts, yet checking them has been slow and fiddly, leaving an ecological blind spot. The team calibrated a PCR assay followed by sequencing, practising on krill they had deliberately seeded with larvae.

Applied to North Sea krill, the assay found infection rates between 2.5 and 4.5 percent, higher than older reports gave. The authors credit the method's sensitivity, while allowing that ecosystem change may also play a role. They offer the test for wider parasite surveys.
pmc-13412547:
Yiwei Chen and co-authors compare the safety of immune checkpoint inhibitors in melanoma in 2026 by pairing trial evidence with real-world harm reports. These drugs work well against melanoma, yet their side-effect profiles differ and head-to-head safety data are thin. A Bayesian network meta-analysis covered 31 randomized trials with 11,937 patients, and a parallel search mined the United States FAERS database for reports filed between 2004 and 2023.

Ipilimumab, nivolumab, and pembrolizumab ranked lowest for treatment-related harms of any grade in the trial network. The reports database held 5,974 adverse events among 4,599 treated melanoma patients, with 236 event terms significantly tied to the drug class. The authors offer the signals for monitoring, not firm prescribing rules.
pmc-13413947:
Yibo Zhang and co-authors coat a fibre-optic interferometer with silicone film in 2026 to make a thermometer that thrives below freezing. Electrical sensors struggle where interference, tight spaces, or wiring burden measurements, while fibre sensors shrug those off. Their device sandwiches multimode fibre between single-mode leads, its sides polished flat with a carbon dioxide laser, then wraps the sensing stretch in a temperature-sensitive silicone blend.

Polishing more sides steadily sharpened the response: sensitivity rose from 0.73 to 2.15 nanometres per kelvin as polished facets went from one to four across the tested range of 223 to 273 kelvin. The sensor stays compact and cheap to build in their design. Biomedicine, aerospace, and energy storage are named as candidate homes for it.
pmc-13414447:
Haili Wang and co-authors fine-map in 2026 the exact spots where antibodies grip p54, a surface protein of African swine fever virus used in diagnosis and vaccine design. With no vaccine available, early blood detection carries the fight against this near-uniformly lethal pig disease. The team built the protein, raised three monoclonal antibodies in mice, and shaved the target down residue by residue with mutant proteins.

Two minimal epitopes emerged: one shared by two antibodies, a seven-residue stretch starting at position 56, reported here for the first time. The third antibody pinned a stretch at positions 108 to 114 in their mapping. Ten single residues proved critical for recognition. Both epitopes stay conserved across at least the two major virus genotypes, suiting them for tests and epitope-based vaccines.
pmc-13415547:
Jinzheng Bai and colleagues designed mine layouts in 2026 for pits threatened at once by rock bursts and water inrush. Water-rich rock above the worked seam can crack as mining grows, flooding the pit while stored rock energy bursts outward. The team joined theory, scaled models, and computer simulation to compare layouts.

Their analysis set safe ranges for key layout measures and used a support-vector model to score each scheme on both hazards together, naming one layout as best balanced. Mine planners gain a joint design method for ground where water and rock energy must be controlled as one problem.
pmc-13416447:
Jingran Liu and colleagues review patient journey maps as a tool to keep people with several chronic diseases on treatment, in a 2026 narrative review. Journey maps draw the patient's path through care, exposing where adherence breaks. Searches of three databases plus reference lists yielded eight studies on chronic comorbidity care.

Four barrier zones stood out. Care lacked combined management pathways, and continuity broke when patients moved between institutions. Chances were missed at key care moments. Stigma and poor pain control pushed special groups to leave care. The map gives nurses a clear picture for designing fixes at each weak node.
pmc-13417347:
Sohaib Arshad Mayo and co-authors present a transformer model that picks its own frequency focus for diagnosing gearbox faults under noise, in a 2026 engineering study. Fault signals live in certain frequency bands, while noise spreads everywhere. Fixed filters cannot adapt to each fault or noise level, so their model learns a soft frequency mask for every sample.

Filtered signals pass through attention across sensor channels, with signal statistics injected at each layer. On one benchmark with nine fault types, accuracy held above 95 percent at very high noise, and clean accuracy neared 100 percent on two datasets. The model also runs fast on small edge graphics hardware.
pmc-13417647:
Jian-Yong Wang and co-authors link bone thinning patterns to thinking problems in Parkinson disease, in a 2026 clinical study. Brain and bone signal to each other, yet which bone pattern matters for cognition was unclear. Bone density was measured at the hip, wrist, and spine in 120 patients, alongside symptom checks.

A grouping method split patients into spine only thinning and whole body bone loss clusters. Cognitive problems were far more common in the whole body group, with roughly ninefold adjusted odds. The link ran stronger in older and male patients and in longer illness. Protecting bone broadly might also help protect thinking, the authors suggest.
pmc-13417847:
Kailu Zhao and colleagues pooled ten animal trials in 2026 to test whether umbilical cord stem cells repair the ovaries of mice with premature ovarian failure. The condition ends fertility early by depleting egg follicles and skewing hormones, and stem-cell transplants have been proposed to restore the ovarian environment.

Treated mice grew far more follicles at every stage, with higher estrogen and anti-Mullerian hormone and lower follicle-stimulating hormone, all with strong statistical signals. The paper supports moving this approach toward careful human study, while noting that animal results alone cannot promise fertility gains in women.
pmc-13418047:
Jing Wu and colleagues pair two kinds of nucleic acid drugs to treat pancreatic cancer in patient derived tumour models, in a 2026 study. One drug switches tumour suppressor genes back on, while the other silences cancer driving genes. Single target nucleic acid drugs often fail in complex cancers, so the team profiled each tumour's genes and proteins to pick personal combinations.

Tailored pairings beat single agents through coordinated control of several genes at once. Certain pairings also worked across different tumours sharing genetic features, hinting at broader use. The flexible design shows how personal and shared combinations can coexist in precision cancer care.
pmc-13418147:
Erica Mascarenhas and colleagues outline how United States health care can cut its large climate footprint as federal rules roll back, in a 2026 article. The sector leads the world in per person health emissions, and its 2022 output was tied to heavy losses of healthy life years. Cuts are grouped under buildings, supply chains, and daily operations.

Proven steps include renewable energy, less medical waste, and lower emission anaesthetics, inhalers, and food services. Two overlooked sources get fresh attention: conference travel and the growing energy appetite of artificial intelligence. Cleaner care also promises better air, lower costs, and stronger resilience for vulnerable groups.
pmc-13418747:
Olivier Bergeron-Boutin and colleagues measure how much content from untrustworthy sources reached adults on two large social platforms during 2020. Their study covers all active adult users in the United States on Facebook and Instagram. Sources counted as untrustworthy had shared misinformation again and again, as judged by outside fact-checkers of that period.

Exposure turned out to be tightly packed among a small slice of users rather than spread across everyone. Most people rarely met such content in their feeds at all. Those who saw the most of it often held firm views before they ever logged on. Surveys tied to the platform data showed no clear shift in attitudes from the exposure itself. The results suggest that reach alone overstates the power of low-grade sources to move public opinion.
pmc-13419347:
Lubin and colleagues analysed in 2026 how malpractice litigation around suicide shapes Israeli healthcare policy. The team searched national court databases for psychiatry malpractice cases and pre-trial settlements about suicides from 1985 to 2023. They recorded patient, lawsuit, and care-quality details for each case.

Over 38 years they found only twenty court lawsuits over patient suicides, seventeen deaths and three life-threatening attempts. Plaintiffs won three in five of those cases. Fourteen suicides happened in inpatient units and six in community care. Settlements before trial rose sharply over time, from seventeen in the first period to fifty-six in each later period. The authors warn that rising legal pressure may push psychiatrists away from high-risk public-sector work. They propose stronger safety systems, clearer documentation, and less adversarial compensation routes to protect both families and prevention work.
pmc-13419847:
Alejandro Cortés-Meda and colleagues follow households in a dengue-endemic town in Oaxaca, Mexico, to learn what keeps the dengue mosquito living around homes. The mosquito thrives in urban and suburban yards, above all in poorer areas with stored water. Their year-long cohort study ran seven indoor and outdoor checks for the insect.

Teams made 476 visits in total and found 494 breeding sites holding larvae or pupae across the rounds. House traits, resident habits, and season were each tested against how often the mosquito appeared and how long it stayed. Standing water habits that families can change stood at the center of the analysis. Season-aware control aimed at the flagged household factors could cut spraying waste and dengue risk together.
pmc-13420347:
Zhang and Liu studied in 2026 a gene switch called SPI1 in age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of sight loss in older people. The disease damages the retina's support layer, whose cells can undergo a harmful identity shift known as EMT. Using patient data and a cell model stirred up with an inflammatory signal, the team traced levels of SPI1 and two linked factors, ALKBH5 and NURR1.

Zhang found SPI1 and ALKBH5 ran high in the stressed cells while NURR1 ran low, and SPI1 levels in patients tracked age and disease stage. Turning SPI1 down restored the cells' epithelial marker, lowered a mesenchymal marker, cut harmful reactive oxygen, and slowed cell migration. The chain runs in order: SPI1 raises ALKBH5, which uses a chemical RNA tag to lower NURR1. Restoring either downstream step partly undid the benefit of silencing SPI1, confirming the axis as a candidate drug target.
pmc-13420647:
Emma Glajchen and colleagues present ForeSight-HF in 2026, an AI decision aid built for heart failure care in skilled nursing facilities. Nursing homes juggle complex patients with thin specialist access and patchy records, while existing AI tools were designed for hospitals.

The language-model system reads unstructured notes to score heart-failure likelihood and flare risk and suggest tailored steps, illustrated by one congested patient needing stronger diuretics and one dry patient needing diuretic cuts. Nursing teams gain a post-acute aid aimed at cutting the readmissions that follow one in four heart-failure hospital stays.
pmc-13420747:
Daniel Wittrock and co-authors set out in 2026 the protocol for a review of airway pressure support given before hospital arrival. Keeping a small positive pressure in the lungs, PEEP, can ease breathing in acute respiratory distress. Ambulance systems apply it through varied devices and for varied conditions, from lung disease flares to heart failure.

The scoping review will search five databases for studies of adults treated before arrival with pressure-based ventilation. Two reviewers will screen and chart the studies, with a third settling disputes, and quality will be graded with standard scales. The map aims to show what outcomes and safety data exist.
pmc-13420847:
Tshegofatso Seabi and colleagues describe a training strategy for the staff of 17 health and demographic surveillance centers across sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. These centers track births, deaths, and movement house to house in regions where civil registration is weak, producing rare long-run population data. Their value depends on the data, analysis, and writing skills of local teams.

The program targeted data managers and analysts, the staff who turn field rounds into publishable findings. Pandemic disruption sharpened the need, since sites with strong pre-crisis counts could measure the crisis itself. Rounds every three to twelve months capture deaths, pregnancies, and migration in the covered populations. Stronger local analysis means findings reach policy while they are still current.
pmc-13421247:
Kenji Miyazawa, Hojjat Bazzazi and Wei Gao built a whole-body mathematical model, reported in 2026, that follows lipid nanoparticle mRNA medicines through the body. Such medicines instruct cells to make a protein inside the body, yet their journey involves tissue entry, cell uptake and several steps inside the cell that are hard to measure directly.

Calibrated on detailed rat data covering both the mRNA and the protein it produced, the model includes liver uptake, lymph circulation and the fate of mRNA inside cells. Sensitivity tests showed that breakdown inside cellular compartments, mRNA stability and translation efficiency mattered most for liver protein output. Scaled to humans by body-size rules, the model matched published clinical blood measurements.
pmc-13421347:
Manzano and Mars developed in 2026 a mathematical framework for studying horizons, the null surfaces in spacetime that bound regions such as the edge of a black hole. A horizon carries a chosen direction field, and its deformation pattern sets how isolated the horizon is from its surroundings. Their formalism encodes that pattern and its first sideways change on the surface itself, detached from any surrounding spacetime.

Manzano introduces two tools: a tuple that captures the pattern's base level, and a non-isolation tensor that measures departure from perfect isolation. That tensor vanishes for the classic horizon types. From it they derive a general near-horizon equation linking the tensor, a torsion term, and curvature, which recovers known equations for special cases. They also prove two existence theorems giving exact conditions for a horizon with any chosen isolation profile to sit inside a spacetime obeying given field equations.
pmc-13421447:
Alexander Posis and colleagues studied brain markers and mood change in 2026 among 225 participants of the LifeAfter90 study, whose average age was 93. Depression touches more than one in ten of the oldest old, yet how brain health steers mood over time was unknown.

Larger occipital brain volume at baseline tracked with slower rises in depression scores. More free water, a sign of white-matter injury, tracked with faster rises, and amyloid scans did not behave as expected. The paper links preserved cortex and healthier white matter to steadier mood even in the tenth decade of life.
pmc-13422247:
Anne F. Klassen leads a ten-author team introducing, in a 2026 paper, a short questionnaire built for valuing obesity treatment outcomes in patients' own terms. A global consensus had named eight domains that matter — from self-esteem and body image to stigma and excess skin — yet standard economic measures skip several of them.

Drawing items from the established BODY-Q questionnaire, the team built the BODY-Q-7D and tested it in an international online sample. Statistical modelling trimmed the instrument to seven items that fit well, with reliability above the usual bar across three coefficients. Most of their validity and responsiveness checks passed. The next step is attaching preference values so the scores can feed cost-effectiveness decisions.
pmc-13422847:
Ibrahem-Altwijri and colleagues test in 2026 DizzyVR, an immersive virtual reality system for vestibular rehabilitation, the balance retraining used after inner ear disorders. Standard exercises bore patients, and boredom kills adherence.

Ten patients with various vestibular disorders each completed eight weekly sessions in the headset. Attendance and completion stayed high, above ninety percent of scheduled sessions in this small group of ten participants who finished the program and rated it afterward. Usability and satisfaction ratings came out good to high. Three participants reported mild nausea or disorientation that eased over time. Before-and-after comparisons showed exploratory gains in walking speed, balance confidence, and gait stability, while the dizziness handicap score improved only as a trend. The authors call the system feasible and safe, and ask for larger controlled trials.
pmc-13422947:
Stian Andersen leads a seven-author team explaining, in a 2026 Norwegian study, why so many adults have a heart murmur despite healthy valves. Systolic murmurs without significant valve disease are common and commoner in women, yet what makes a murmur audible was unsettled.

In the Tromsø population study, 1,680 adults without significant valve disease had echocardiograms and heart-sound recordings; about a fifth had an innocent murmur. One factor dwarfed the rest: the pressure gradient across the aortic valve, with murmur odds rising steeply as it grew and passing fifty percent in the six-to-eight millimetre range. Female sex more than tripled the odds, and age, blood pressure and haemoglobin contributed smaller effects. The authors say the sex gap tracks physiology, not disease.
pmc-13423047:
Chucai Peng and colleagues examine the soil pressure acting on inclined support structures built close to existing buildings, a common problem in crowded excavation work. Their 2026 study pairs laboratory model tests with fresh theoretical derivation, varying the support angle from upright to 20 degrees while holding the soil width-to-height ratio fixed.

Cameras tracking particle movement and pressure sensors mapped how failure surfaces formed in the confined soil. The team then split the soil into zones and wrote balance equations for thin horizontal slices in each zone. Their formulas for pressure size, total force, and force position matched the measurements well, especially in the main compression zone low in the soil mass.
pmc-13424347:
Adam Gorski and colleagues tested drought effects in 2026 on enzyme activity in deadwood and soil across temperate forests. Microbes drive wood decay through enzymes that harvest carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus, yet simulated moisture deficit may throttle that work unevenly by species and season.

Two years of drought cut all five measured enzymes in deadwood, often by more than half, with smaller soil declines and weaker responses in beech and spruce. The control-drought gap widened in year two. Forest ecologists gain evidence that prolonged drought slows nutrient recycling from deadwood, with cumulative effects.
pmc-13424947:
Gai Liang and Feng Yuan write to the editor about the WISE trial. In that trial, a 24-week home walking plan aimed to head off joint pain from aromatase inhibitor drugs in early breast cancer. Recruitment and sticking to the plan were strong, and walkers logged far more steps than controls, yet pain did not clearly fall.

The letter argues the dose may explain the flat result. Brisk walking for 150 minutes a week sits above the range tied to pain relief in a cited synthesis of 25 trials with 1899 patients. Trial readers get a sharp caution: a null result can fault the dose, not the walking, and the next trial should test gentler amounts.
pmc-13425647:
Nathalia Bordeira Chagas and colleagues refined hormone cutoffs for nonclassical congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a 2026 diagnostic accuracy study of children with premature pubarche. Early pubic hair prompts endocrine testing, and 5 to 20 percent of such children carry 21-hydroxylase deficiency in its nonclassic form. The cohort held 203 children with median age 7.5 years, most of them girls, all receiving ACTH stimulation testing.

Genotyping of CYP21A2 served as the reference standard and confirmed the condition in 32 children. Basal 17-hydroxyprogesterone showed excellent discrimination, and genotype-based thresholds should reduce both missed cases and unnecessary follow-up testing. Clear cut points help staff spare most young kids long tests while still catching the few who need full care and close watch.
pmc-13425947:
Aart Jan Teunissen and co-authors look back at a failed rollout of spinal morphine for joint replacement surgery in a 2026 study. Pain after hip or knee replacement still slows recovery, and expert guidance backed a small dose of morphine in the spinal fluid. At their teaching hospital, results did not match that advice, so the team reviewed its own records.

The review covered 854 patients who had spinal anesthesia for hip or knee replacement over about eighteen months. Of those, 414 got the morphine dose. The team compared pain scores on the day of surgery and the two days after, plus side effects such as trouble passing urine. The mismatch between local results and guidance frames the paper's lessons for other hospitals.
pmc-13426347:
Fares Alrefai and coauthors studied keratoconus severity and follow-up in a tertiary referral cohort in a 2026 analysis of Pentacam records from 2014 to 2021. Screening 21,157 charts used corneal shape thresholds to flag the cone-shaped corneal disorder, followed by manual review to confirm diagnosis and grade severity. The focus included self-identified minority patients, risk factors for progression and surgery within two years, and loss to follow-up.

Regression and mixed models linked demographic, socioeconomic, and clinical factors with presentation severity and later outcomes. Eye services gain equity-relevant evidence on who arrives with advanced disease and who disappears from care. Some young men and women reach the chair with eyes far gone, and the facts here may help staff find them at a far earlier stage.
pmc-13426447:
Li and colleagues reported in 2026 on a membrane, a thin selective barrier, that can switch which gas it lets through more easily. Gas plants need to separate carbon dioxide from hydrogen to make cleaner hydrogen fuel, but the two directions of separation normally rely on opposite methods. The team built the membrane from a water-rich gel combined with tiny zirconium cages that have a defined pore structure.

Li found that the wet membrane strongly favoured carbon dioxide, with a separation factor of 44 and very high gas flow. When the membrane dried, it shrank and the cages shifted, exposing tight sieve-like openings that favoured hydrogen instead, with a factor of 798 in that direction. The switch could be reversed and also tuned by acidity, which points to one device that can serve both separation tasks.
pmc-13427047:
Coelho and colleagues describe a 2026 surgical technique for rebuilding the medial patellofemoral ligament. That band keeps the kneecap from slipping sideways, a common problem in young active patients. Their approach uses the patient's own gracilis tendon but leaves its lower attachment in place, preserving the graft's blood supply.

The graft is routed behind the adductor magnus tendon, which acts as a pulley copying the ligament's natural path on the thigh bone. That trick avoids drilling a tunnel in the thigh bone and needs no implants. At the kneecap, the graft is fixed through two converging bone tunnels with high-strength sutures. The authors present the method as less invasive and biologically favorable, especially for patients whose bones are still growing and cannot tolerate large tunnels or hardware.
pmc-13427247:
Cook and team crossed mice lacking one copy of the progranulin gene with mice expressing human TDP-43. The cross mimics the human cause of frontotemporal dementia. TDP-43 is the protein that clumps in that disease. They asked whether low progranulin triggers TDP-43 clumping. Or does it instead worsen the damage TDP-43 causes through other routes?

Progranulin shortage never switched on clumping in mice whose TDP-43 levels stay clump-free. It did not increase clumping in high-expressing mice either. But it deepened social dominance impairment beyond either single condition. It also brought joint effects on dendritic spines in the medial prefrontal cortex. The shortage altered the RNA splicing changes driven by TDP-43. And it skewed inflammation, raising markers of disease-linked microglia while dulling signs of adaptive immunity. The authors point to prefrontal neuron dysfunction and scrambled inflammation as forces that drive the disease forward.
pmc-13427447:
Taylor Wilcox, Julie Hansen, Andrew Blanker, and Michael E. Widlansky review disrupted mitochondrial quality control in atherosclerosis in a 2026 article. Heart muscle needs constant ATP to contract and keep ion balance, and vessel cells need efficient energy to preserve lining integrity and tone. Mitophagy, the selective recycling of damaged mitochondria, sits at the center of that upkeep, governed by several pathways still being mapped.

When recycling falters, dysfunctional mitochondria accumulate and drive vascular injury in the authors' synthesis. Pinpointing which regulatory steps fail in atherosclerotic tissue could reveal drug targets beyond cholesterol lowering. Heart and vein cells burn fuel at a high rate all day and all night, so worn fuel plants hit them first and hit them hard in this ill state.
pmc-13427647:
Qianlong Li and a large team use, in a 2026 study, machine learning to read which animal a dangerous bacterium came from, based only on its genome. Pasteurella multocida causes fowl cholera in birds and other diseases in cattle, pigs, and cats, and it can infect people. The team gathered 814 checked bacterial genomes from those four hosts in a public database. Family trees built from the genomes grouped largely by host.

Five learning models then predicted host origin from tiny genetic letter changes, scoring high accuracy on held-out strains. A method that credits each clue showed which changes mattered most, pointing to genes for metabolism, cell signaling, and drug resistance. Some strains looked misclassified because they may truly have crossed between hosts. Early host clues could warn farms before an outbreak spreads.
pmc-13427747:
Sheikh Sunzid Ahmed and colleagues design, in a 2026 computer study, candidate vaccines against tularemia, a highly infectious disease carried by animals. The bacterium's Schu S4 strain is the most dangerous form, and no licensed vaccine exists. Rather than growing the germ, the team mined its proteins for short pieces, called epitopes, that immune cells recognize. Two target proteins tied to virulence supplied most of the pieces.

Two stitched-together vaccine designs, TulaVac1 and TulaVac2, scored well on predicted safety, stability, and immune strength in simulations. Their parts are nearly identical across strains, and predicted population coverage reached high levels worldwide. Docking and motion simulations suggested firm binding to immune sensors, with the first design ahead. Everything here is computational, so lab and animal testing must follow before any claim of protection.
pmc-13428147:
Wang and colleagues gathered real-world results in 2026 for surufatinib, a targeted pill, in advanced grade 3 neuroendocrine tumors, a fast-growing cancer of hormone-making cells. The drug was proven in slower grades of this cancer, but grade 3 disease lacks clear treatment standards. The team asked how long the drug holds the cancer back and which patients gain most.

Records covered 77 patients treated at fifteen Chinese centers. The middle time before the cancer grew again was just over nine months, and about one in five patients saw tumors shrink. Patients whose Ki-67 index, a measure of cell division speed, sat at or below thirty percent stayed progression-free far longer. Adding other drugs raised shrinkage slightly but did not extend control.
pmc-13428247:
Hotmaria Julia Dolok Saribu and co-authors map, in a 2026 scoping review, how digital tools and standard routines work together to keep hospital patients safe. Falls, drug errors, and missed deterioration still harm many inpatients. The team searched five databases for studies from 2006 to mid-2025 that paired a digital technology with a set protocol. Twenty studies made the final cut across many hospital types.

Four themes emerged: early warning algorithms for decline and sepsis, barcode and electronic systems for drug safety, digital checklists for handovers, and electronic monitoring for hand hygiene and fall prevention. Reported results covered deaths, stays, errors, and rule-following. Since the review mapped evidence without grading study quality, its findings read as a landscape, not a verdict. Hospitals gain a menu of pairings that multidisciplinary teams can adapt.
pmc-13428447:
John Pooley and colleagues tracked where a gene therapy virus spreads inside the brain's fluid spaces after injection into one side chamber. The target was the choroid plexus, a tissue lining those chambers that makes the fluid bathing the brain.

The team tested an engineered virus shell in mouse, rat, and pig tissue, and in living mice. It homed to the choroid plexus lining cells in all three species, carrying a glowing marker gene. Loaded with gene-editing tools, the virus also cut levels of a water channel protein in those cells. Spread was uneven, favouring the injected side's main chamber over the middle and rear chambers, a dosing problem Pooley flags.
pmc-13428547:
Jeannine Diur Yav and colleagues assess, in a 2026 study, what caregivers and health workers know about tuberculosis in children in one Congolese health zone. Childhood TB is often missed where resources are thin, and late care-seeking makes it worse. Interviews in 2024 covered 163 caregivers and 27 health providers in the Kabondo-Dianda zone. A structured questionnaire scored knowledge of spread and prevention and asked where families turn first when a child falls ill.

Caregivers scored poorly, averaging under 3 of 11 knowledge points, while providers averaged above 8. Many caregivers blamed evil spirits or household animals for transmission. Only about half went first to a health facility, and nearly two thirds delayed seeking care. Half used informal care at some point. The authors see community teaching and faster referral habits as the clearest levers for earlier diagnosis.
pmc-13429047:
Ibrahim Abubakar Abdi writes, in a 2026 commentary, that child malnutrition in Somalia will not yield to endless emergency aid. An estimated 1.7 million Somali children under five faced acute malnutrition in 2025, including nearly half a million severe cases. Decades of conflict, climate shocks, and weak institutions keep levels at emergency marks despite large aid flows. The author argues the response model itself is part of the problem.

A proposed framework joins stronger health systems, changed food systems, social protection with nutrition in mind, gender-responsive programs, and community-based treatment. Each strand targets a structural driver rather than the latest crisis spike. Funding would shift toward national strategies built to last. The piece frames child nutrition as a foundation for national development, not a side program of relief work, and calls on partners to fund accordingly.
pmc-13429547:
Francesco Maria Carrano and a large team follow, in a 2026 study, hernia repair done alongside sleeve gastrectomy for up to ten years. A hiatal hernia lets the stomach slide upward through the diaphragm, and it is common in severe obesity. Records covered 111 patients operated at several centers in 2014 and 2015, with 108 patients assessable at follow-up averaging nearly eight years. Recurrence meant the sleeve had migrated upward by more than two centimeters.

About 13 percent of patients had an anatomical recurrence. Of those, about two thirds were managed without another operation. Large hernias at the first surgery and reflux disease afterward each multiplied recurrence odds about fivefold. About one in ten patients overall needed reoperation, always tied to reflux symptoms rather than anatomy alone. Freedom from recurrence looked near total at five years but fell by ten, a late estimate the authors treat cautiously.
pmc-13430747:
Priscilla Abrafi Opare-Addo and colleagues measure gaps in care for repeat strokes at a Ghanaian teaching hospital. Repeat strokes make up as many as one in four strokes in low- and middle-income countries and worsen outcomes, yet prevention workups often fall short.

Cases admitted to Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital from 2023 to 2025 were reviewed for diagnostic testing and treatment. Repeat strokes formed 17.8 percent of stroke admissions over two years, and ischemic strokes formed 76.2 percent of those repeats. The registry shows where subtype testing and prevention drugs lag, so hospitals can close the most costly gaps first.
pmc-13432447:
Kistan and co-authors check kidney safety of an HIV prevention drug in African women around pregnancy. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, used as PrEP, prevents HIV infection in people at risk. Its effect on renal function during pregnancy and after birth has been understudied, despite wide use in women.

The analysis draws on the CAP016 randomised controlled trial. It follows kidney measures in women who took the drug while pregnant and into the postpartum period. Tenofovir can strain kidneys in some users, so pregnancy-specific data matter. Results inform safe PrEP programs for mothers and future pregnancies.
pmc-13432547:
Sethmi Ranasinghe and co-authors trialed a new nose adaptor in 2026 that lets a measured-dose puffer spray steroid mist for hay fever and for sinus disease after surgery. Standard nose sprays work well, yet drip down the throat and raw noses push many users to quit. Two swap-over trials each held sixteen users, who tried both tools for three weeks apiece.

Symptom gains tied between the two tools. In both groups, eleven of sixteen users picked the puffer with adaptor, citing fewer harsh feelings. The sinus group also logged a sharper jump in satisfaction scores with the new tool. Users said they would more likely keep up daily use with the adaptor. The authors read the warmer welcome as a path to steadier long-term control.
pmc-13434047:
Bingfeng Wu and co-authors built a shoot-in gel in 2026 that hunts gum disease germs both outside cells and in their hiding spots inside cells. Gum disease wrecks teeth roots through germ fire plus immune drift. Lead germs sneak into cells and jam the cell's waste pits, which lets them dodge stock care.

The gel self-builds from three parts: a body collagen, a germ-cut chain, and a plant drug. Loose build lifts the plant drug's melt and pass rates. Outside cells, the chain and drug team to tear germ skins and stall their fuel. Inside cells, the drug pools in waste pits, cuts harsh oxygen stress, and resets pit sourness. Live tests showed calmer gum tissue and fresh repair.
pmc-13434547:
Sandeep Kaur and Akashdeep Singh Chauhan challenge the idea that ultra-processed foods are cheap, once full costs across life in poorer countries are counted. Under the NOVA system, these factory foods now supply a large and growing share of daily energy worldwide.

They are built from low-cost refined inputs plus cosmetic additives, tuned to taste great, last long, and earn profit, and shoppers see them as handy low-price picks. The commentary argues that view misleads, since diet-linked disease, unequal access to healthy food, and damage to nature all add hidden bills. Food-policy readers get a full-cost challenge to the cheapness claim.
pmc-13435347:
Munseok Choi, Seok-Jae Heo, Yu-Jin Kwon, and Chang Moo Kang link a combined heart, kidney, and metabolic syndrome with pancreatic cancer risk, in a 2026 study. Pancreatic cancer is usually found late and kills most patients.

The team followed 326,148 UK Biobank participants for an average of 13.5 years. The syndrome is staged from 0, no risk factors, to 4, full disease. Cancer rates climbed from 9 to about 49 cases per 100,000 person-years across the stages. Against stage 0, the risk roughly doubled at stage 1 and stayed near double at the top stages. The pattern held across subgroups. The authors argue that the combined syndrome, not just single risks, deserves weight in prevention planning.
pmc-13435647:
Jenet Narzary, Sayed Golam Mohiuddin, and Aslan Massahi uncover a cleanup enzyme that helps E coli survive cell wall drugs in 2026. A wide screen for active promoters flagged several cutting enzymes. Knocking out one, called Tsp, sharply cut survival under beta lactam drugs.

Some skin leaks did not cut survival, so leak and death part ways here. Balance, not bulk, guards the wall during drug attack. New drugs might tip that balance on purpose.
pmc-13436447:
Gen Yang's team studied iron and alkaline soil responses in 2026 in Arabidopsis thaliana and its close relative Arabidopsis halleri. Soil pH shapes nutrient access, and chalky alkaline soils limit iron, yet how iron-starvation genes respond to pH alone was unclear. Root gene profiles were taken under low iron, alkaline pH, and both together, comparing species and halleri lines from soils of differing pH.

One gene group led by PYE tracked iron shortage even at pH 7.5, while a second group led by FIT responded to alkaline pH even when iron was available. Halleri lines from high-pH soils tolerated both stresses better, with longer, less branched roots and steadier mineral profiles. Plant breeders get a split regulatory map for breeding crops that handle alkaline ground.
pmc-13437647:
Valentina Daponte and co-authors deleted a signaling gene in mouse bone-eating cells to learn how they help build bone. Strength comes from teamwork: osteoclasts dissolve old bone while osteoblasts lay new, and the two swap chemical messages. Their 2026 study removed the WNT5A gene only from the osteoclast line, leaving the osteoblast supply intact, then read bone structure, cell counts, gene activity, and cell movement.
