Gene readings in builder cells showed tangled programs for sticking to surfaces and talking to neighbors, plus stress signatures. Direct tests confirmed builder cells gripped poorly, moved badly, and matured a weaker matrix without the osteoclast signal. The authors crown osteoclast WNT5A as a true coupling factor.
pmc-13437747:
Elina Üveges's team mapped copper handling in 2026 across colorectal cancer cells carrying different KRAS codon twelve mutations. Copper supply is a candidate target in KRAS-mutant bowel cancer, where options are thin, but whether mutation subtype changes copper biology was unclear. Isogenic lines with G12C, G12D, and G12V mutations were compared on copper levels, uptake, toxicity, transporter expression, and chelator sensitivity.

G12V cells changed most, with lower copper, higher uptake, more ATP7A transporter, and protection against chelators, G12C sat in the middle, and G12D barely differed from controls. Yet a copper chelator slowed growth in all mutants. Oncologists get a subtype-specific copper story that argues for mutation-aware trials of copper-targeting drugs.
pmc-13439247:
Xiaobing Zhai and colleagues ask whether blood metabolites can sort people with obesity by their future risk of major depression, in a 2026 analysis. Obesity raises depression risk, yet risk varies widely between people with similar weight. The team followed more than 41,000 adults with obesity for a median span beyond fourteen years. Blood profiles were fed into several machine learning methods to forecast depression at three, five, and nine years.

About 3,600 new depression cases appeared during follow-up. The best model, a gradient-boosted tree method, sorted future cases well and beat standard clinical scores, though accuracy eased in later checks. Genetic analyses suggested some metabolites sit on the causal path from obesity to depression. The authors propose blood-based sorting to aim early help at the people most likely to benefit.
pmc-13439447:
Deyu Li and co-authors test a traditional plant against Alzheimer's-like cell damage in a 2026 study. The plant, Cuscuta chinensis, is used in Chinese medicine. The team asked whether it protects nerve cells from the oxidative injury that a toxic amyloid fragment causes, and how that protection works.

First they identified the plant's chemical components with advanced mass spectrometry. They then injured HT22 nerve cells with the amyloid fragment and measured survival and cell death markers. Showing protection in a cell model is an early step toward judging whether the plant's compounds merit animal studies.
pmc-13440047:
Piotr Fabrykiewicz and colleagues chart how an unusual magnetic pattern in the crystal DyFeO3 changes with temperature, reporting neutron work in 2026. DyFeO3 is the sole rare-earth orthoferrite known with a ground state whose magnetic order does not match the crystal grid, a so-called incommensurate state. That state appears below about four kelvin and brings strong coupling between magnetism and electric polarisation. How its higher harmonic ripples evolve with warming was the open question.

Their measurements follow those harmonics across temperature and set them beside published results on a cousin material, TbFeO3. In that cousin, an applied field organises the ripples into a soliton lattice, a train of spaced magnetic kinks. The comparison helps separate traits driven by the dysprosium ions themselves from traits any such lattice would show. The work sharpens the low-temperature magnetic map of a model multiferroic crystal.
pmc-13442647:
Arshpreet Kaur and colleagues map a gene family that feeds scent and pigment paths in orchids in a 2026 computer study. The genes make an enzyme called 4CL, a gate step for a broad plant chemical path. Searches across eight orchid species found 29 such genes in total.

All 29 proteins sat in one cell part, the peroxisome, and shared a set of built-in motifs. A family tree split them into three groups. Switch zones ahead of the genes held 54 types of control marks, which hints at wide roles across plant life. Root tissue showed high use for 11 of the genes. The authors frame the map as groundwork for lab tests that tie each gene to its chemical goods, work that may guide orchid breeding in time.
pmc-13442847:
Seung Ju Kim and colleagues show tiny ion devices that hum at the edge of chaos in a 2026 paper. Brains may gain their thrift from that edge state, where order and wildness meet. Past chips reached the edge through heat shifts that burn much power. Their devices move ions through a film, much as nerve cells move ions.

At currents near a hundred nanoamperes, the devices showed sharp drops in flow ease, noise gains, and self-born pulses. A compact model tied those signs to ion drift, thread growth, and circuit play. Power thrift beat heat-based edge devices by more than a thousand-fold in the report. The authors pitch the parts as low-power bricks for brain-like chips. Much work stays ahead, from part spread to circuit tests at scale.
pmc-13443047:
Xiaochen Huang and colleagues vet a kefir microbe strain, Pediococcus pentosaceus K6, for food use in a 2026 study. The strain came from Tibetan kefir, a fermented milk. Gene maps and dish tests checked both safety and guest-gut skills that mark a good probiotic.

Safety screens came back clean, with no blood harm, no bad waste goods, and no move-ready drug defense genes. The strain lived through acid at a survival share of 83.83 percent after two hours at pH 3.0 in dish tests. It also stuck to its kin at high rates and curbed Listeria growth with a clear zone near 29.83 mm wide. Gene clusters for microbe goods may explain that punch. The authors back K6 as a food-grade lead.
pmc-13443647:
Daniel Ashipala and colleagues ask health students in Namibia how joint team work feels in real wards in a 2026 study. Team care across trades lifts patient results, yet Namibia held little work on student views. Sixteen health science students at the national university sat for deep one-on-one talks in the Khomas region.

Three themes rose from the talk records. Students read team work as a joint learn and care chance that builds skill. Blocks spanned weak trade ties, poor talk, and rank walls in wards. Fixes named by students spanned shared tasks, early team drills, and staff who model joint care. The authors say the will is there, while ward culture lags. Schools and hospitals must fix ties between trades to cash the gains students see.
pmc-13443747:
Taiana de Alencar and coauthors report a 2026 pragmatic trial of pharmacist-led comprehensive drug management for adults with hypertension in Brazil's public primary care network. The team randomized 128 adults to the drug program or usual care and followed them for 12 months across medical, body, humanistic, and cardiovascular risk results.

Between-group differences were not significant for most results, though cardiovascular risk trended more favorably with the program. Within the program group, systolic pressure fell by 9.47 millimeters of mercury alongside gains in cholesterol measures, risk, quality of life, and disease knowledge, while controls improved mainly in knowledge and self-rated quality of life. The program shows medical promise but needs stronger between-group evidence.
pmc-13443947:
Theresa Antwi and colleagues investigate a 2026 survey of how bullying erodes exam performance through psychological safety among senior high school students in Ghana. The team surveyed 585 students at 12 public schools across three regions, testing direct, indirect, and interaction effects with multivariate methods.

Psychological safety fully carried the bullying effect: once it was accounted for, bullying's direct link to scores vanished, while safer students scored markedly higher. Counseling accommodations softened bullying's blow to safety, and girls suffered the bullying-performance link more than boys. The authors urge gender-sensitive, regionally tuned policies and formal counseling support during high-stakes exams.
pmc-13445347:
Zachary Grand and colleagues test whether an artificial intelligence scribe shortens visits and eases workload in a busy hip and knee replacement clinic, in a 2026 study. Note writing eats a large share of clinic time and feeds doctor burnout. One surgeon ran the trial at a single center from late 2024 into early 2025.

Timers watched one hundred twelve visits, split between the AI scribe and standard note taking by doctor and assistant. Visits with the scribe ran about a fifth shorter on average. Workload ratings, scored on an index first built for flight research, leaned lower with the scribe across all six fields, though that gap fell short of firm proof. The gain in time was clear even at one site.
pmc-13446347:
Georgina Fröhlich and colleagues describe a program that turns radiotherapy into a heroic mission for children, run across seven Hungarian centers, published in 2026. Treatment with big machines, tight masks, and time apart from parents frightens young patients and can force sedation. The program wraps preparation in story and play, with a hero named Brave at its heart.

From May 2023 to May 2026, two hundred fifty-six children took part. Each got a themed box with a toy model of the treatment machine, storybooks, games, a mask to decorate, comfort items, and markers for milestones passed. Staff from many trades ran the plan together. In five cases, growing ease with the steps removed the need for general anesthesia altogether.
pmc-13446647:
Berken and the Transpacifier Endoscopy Research Group tested a 3D-printed pacifier that guides an ultrathin endoscope through a baby's mouth. It lets doctors inspect and biopsy the upper gut of young infants without general anesthesia. Anesthesia worries delay infant endoscopy. The transnasal route used in older children is impractical at this age.

In the single-center study at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, six infants aged 2 to 6 months underwent the unsedated procedure using their own suck reflex. All procedures were completed with adequate views and diagnostic-quality biopsies. Findings changed management in two of the six cases reported. No major adverse events occurred during or after the examinations in this early series. Parent and provider feedback supported the approach. In a related survey, over 85 percent of clinicians agreed performing endoscopy outside the operating room is a major advantage.
pmc-13447147:
Xiuling Luo and colleagues report a 2026 trial of ongoing nursing care after stroke. Many survivors leave hospital with lasting limits in movement, thinking or self-care, and family carers often lack training. Care that continues at home through linked community services might improve recovery and cut return trips to hospital.

Sixty patients with after-effects of stroke were split evenly between routine ongoing care and a model using community medical teams at home. The community group scored higher on daily living tasks, quality of life and satisfaction with nursing. That group also had fewer complications, fewer readmissions and lower medical costs. The authors present the linked model as a practical way to support recovery while using shared local resources more fully.
pmc-13447247:
Juan Carlos Chávez-Autor sets out a teaching framework called the System 3 Method in a 2026 conceptual analysis of deep learning. Students now reach vast information and smart tools, yet access alone does not build durable understanding or transfer. The method aims to train learners to build, check and reshape their own knowledge in cycles, with creativity kept in view.

Cycles move among gut orientation, active construction, rational checking, integration and transfer, under both quiet and deliberate self-monitoring. A five-step classroom routine gives the idea practical form, from generation through reflection to time-aware control. Creative progress is judged on novelty for the learner, usefulness and diversity, alongside mastery. Artificial intelligence may serve as a scaffold or critic only when a human keeps charge of authorship and checking, the author insists.
pmc-13447647:
Ndidiamaka Ijeoma Favour Eneojo and colleagues present a 2026 narrative review of suicide literacy in The Gambia, where knowledge of warning signs and help-seeking shapes prevention. The team searched broadly for Gambian evidence on suicide knowledge, attitudes, and literacy, synthesizing themes and gaps.

No published surveys of suicide-specific knowledge or attitudes surfaced, marking the field as scarce and under-researched. Help-seeking faced barriers from limited services, cost, access, cultural expectations, stigma, and law. The authors call for burden and risk-factor research to ground prevention strategies in the country.
pmc-13447847:
Moones Honarmand and coauthors build a 2026 solar-driven magnet light catalyst that removes at once toxic chromium and the drug cefixime from water. The cobalt ferrite and cadmium oxide layered mix on clay lifts spread, contact, and soaking while splitting charges well.

Under sunlight, the tuned mix cleared chromium in 25 minutes and cefixime in 60 minutes, beating single parts tenfold in rate. An S-scheme charge pathway drove scores, and magnet reuse held across cycles. Real water tests removed 85 to 94 percent of cefixime and all chromium in factory effluent, backing real-world dirty water use.
pmc-13448547:
Maren Landsem, Gunnar Morken and Morten Schou audit first antipsychotic choices in first-episode psychosis at a Norwegian university hospital in a 2026 cohort study. Guidelines advise against starting with drugs carrying high weight-gain risk, since weight gain distresses patients and drives stopping treatment. All two hundred thirty-eight patients treated from 2012 to 2016 were traced through records at start, one year and two years. Over half began on a high weight-risk drug, about a third on a lower-risk option, and the rest on none at initiation. Older age, emergency referral and greater illness severity each raised the chance of a high-risk start. Focused effort on those groups is urged to bring practice in line with guidelines.
pmc-13449347:
Huaze Ding and colleagues engineer in 2026 a nanoparticle treatment for acute kidney injury that rebuilds two depleted energy molecules inside mitochondria. Injured kidney tubule cells lose NAD+ and see their coenzyme Q oxidized, driving a flood of damaging reactive oxygen species. Supplying either molecule alone fails in practice: NAD+ breaks down fast and crosses membranes poorly, while coenzyme Q lacks a homing signal for mitochondria.

Their carrier-free particles co-assemble NAD+ with a pre-reduced, mitochondria-targeted form of coenzyme Q. Small enough to pass the kidney's filtration barrier, the particles gather in injured tubules and release their cargo in response to reactive oxygen. In cell oxygen-deprivation and cisplatin injury models, treatment cut reactive oxygen buildup, restored mitochondrial energy production, raised protective autophagy, and eased iron-driven cell death. The authors offer the approach as a platform for other mitochondria-linked diseases.
pmc-13449647:
Kaifei Wang and colleagues introduced pAnno in 2026, a workflow that hunts for hidden protein-coding regions by joining genome, transcript, and protein data. Proteogenomics can reveal coding elements that standard gene lists miss, but building custom protein databases usually slows searches and risks false hits. Even with a fifty-fold larger database, it added only about three percent processing time while keeping sensitivity high. It found far more novel proteins in pear and far more non-canonical immune peptides in lung cancer than prior methods. Researchers gain a practical tool for uncovering overlooked coding regions at scale.
pmc-13450447:
Edith Yeung and colleagues demonstrate in 2026 a chip-scale device that coaxes single photons out of a quantum dot in two directions at once. Reliable single-photon sources are basic currency for quantum information, and semiconductor dots inside grown nanowires already emit excellent photons, but usually upward, off the chip. The team set a dot-bearing nanowire across a gap in a curved silicon nitride waveguide, letting the wire's glow leak evanescently, through its fading near field, into both waveguide arms.

Correlation measurements at the device's output facets confirmed true single-photon emission from both ends, for neutral and charged excitonic states alike. The authors present the geometry as groundwork for architectures that route quantum light in several directions across a photonic circuit.
pmc-13450747:
Andrew Medford and David Sholl ask in 2026 whether learned computer models of atom forces will replace quantum chemistry or simply speed it up. Quantum methods give true energies and forces for groups of atoms, yet they cost so much time that many real problems stay out of reach. Learned models promise near-equal accuracy at a small share of that cost.

Speed gains could reach a million fold, which would open far larger and longer simulations to chemists. The authors weigh what that shift means for materials and drug work, and where learned models still fall short, such as new kinds of chemistry far from their training data. They close with a research plan for using the tools with care.
pmc-13451347:
Sage and six co-authors test fluid replacement levels during long cycling in the heat, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Each trial replaces sixty or eighty percent of fluid losses with matched sodium.

Body mass loss is greater with lower replacement at all time points. Blood sodium stays stable across both trials by design. Water deficit itself, not sodium, drives the impairment.
pmc-13452147:

A newer trial hinted at benefit in a stage II subgroup, though its main endpoint missed significance. The authors blame uneven assays, variable shedding, and timing problems, and they demand proof of patient benefit before wider use.
pmc-13452547:
Bruno and colleagues turn lavender leaf waste, left after essential oil is drawn out, into a catalyst for making a bio based fuel additive called solketal. A catalyst speeds a chemical change without being used up. Their 2026 study cooks the waste in hot water under pressure, then adds acid groups to the carbon that forms. Tests with X-ray and infrared tools confirmed the acid groups had attached to the char.

It reached a 97 percent conversion of glycerol with a 98 percent share going to solketal, the product wanted. Best results came at low heat for just half an hour. pmc-13453047:

Treated livers showed restored protective enzyme phosphorylation, less inflammation, and quieter Kupffer immune cells compared with untreated cirrhotic animals. Stimulating the receptor made human stellate cells contract more, an effect the blocker reversed.
pmc-13453647:
Gil-Barturen and nine co-authors study lab perfusion checks for lungs donated after circulatory death, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Lungs from such donors face warm damage and scant checks before transplant. Use of these lungs lags behind brain-death donor lungs. Perfusion outside the body lets teams inspect lungs for hours first.

One center reviewed over two thousand transplants from twenty oh seven to twenty twenty-four. About one in five used circulatory-death lungs, and over half of those had perfusion checks. Checked lungs came from riskier donors yet matched unchecked lungs on survival. Intensive care stays were shorter with checked lungs. Wide perfusion use lifted the share of such transplants sharply over time.
pmc-13453947:

Cutting out these sarcomas often takes flat muscles and the inguinal ligament with it, leaving a weak spot where a hernia can push through. Their 2026 paper sets out a repair that places mesh outside the belly lining to rebuild the region's natural opening.

Standard polypropylene mesh served in 11 cases, with a titanium coated version in two. Four patients got a wound infection and two a fluid collection, yet only one developed a hernia in the long run. The authors call the method simple, cheap, and repeatable.
pmc-13454047:

Their 2026 study compares tolerant and resistant strains of two species, Candida glabrata and Candida krusei, across gene, protein, and metabolite layers. The focus falls on mitochondria, the cell's power plants.

Tolerant and resistant strains carried higher ATP, the cell's energy coin, and showed distinct metabolic rewiring. Protein scans flagged changes in mitochondrial and energy proteins, while metabolite scans tied resistance to shifts in purine handling and the main energy pathway. Gene reads found mutations in ATP binding genes in the resistant strains. The authors present the power plant changes as fresh targets for drugs against hard to treat yeast.
pmc-13454247:
Limin Hu and five co-authors open a journal collection on the tumor microenvironment in solid cancers with this 2026 editorial. That setting shapes how tumors start, spread, dodge immunity, and resist drugs.

The collection gathers 15 studies, reviews, and analyses across target discovery, immune and stromal control, matrix remodeling, stress adaptation, and biomarker work. Machine learning for patient sorting and translational platforms also feature. The editors frame a field wide shift: away from hunting single driver mutations and toward treating the whole tumor ecosystem. Earlier reviews often took one path or cell type; this set aims for the integrated view. The pieces run from cell level faults to clinic ready tools.
pmc-13454347:
Zhenyu Du, Siyuan Cheng, Qi Zhao, Xiongfeng Ma, and Xiao Yuan prove, in a 2026 theory study, fresh limits on copying groups of quantum states. Reading the fine details of such systems, though, amounts to cloning a whole ensemble of states.

A loophole then appears for ensembles made by finite-time processes, where the ban can be dodged in principle. pmc-13454547:
Tian and colleagues ask whether body shape measures can act as a clock for aging, much as blood tests now do. Their 2026 study used a 3D body scanner to take 171 measures from 302 adults in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. A machine learning method picked the measures that best predicted real age. The team then compared each person's body based age with their true age, with follow up over about twenty years.

The model found 22 measures that predicted age well, with error near four and a half years, and thinner thighs and calves marked older age. People whose body age ran ahead of their true age had worse thinking scores tied to motor planning, weaker physical function, and less leg mass. Over time they also lost dexterity, balance, and muscle strength faster, and shed more leg lean and fat mass.
pmc-13455247:
Fatima Inusa Anga and others read COVID-19 knowledge and cautions in pregnant women in Abuja, Nigeria, in 2026, at a tertiary antenatal clinic. The team polled one hundred twenty women from July to September 2021 by multi-stage sampling.

COVID-19 awareness hit ninety-five point eight percent. Knowledge of spread and prevention was sound. Hand hygiene scored ninety-nine point two percent, crowd dodging ninety-two point five percent, and isolation steps ninety point zero percent. A structured face-to-face form scored knowledge, views, and caution habits. Results were summed by descriptive stats in SPSS version 28. False beliefs and habit gaps in the full results steer aimed antenatal teaching. Mum-health teams gain base data for COVID-19 prevention in pregnancy.
pmc-13456947:
Nishmitha Poojary and four co-authors probe how the plant Vitex negundo might act against polycystic ovary syndrome, a hormone disorder marked by irregular cycles, high androgen levels, and ovarian cysts. Standard drugs for the syndrome often bring side effects, which has turned interest toward plant remedies. The plant's exact molecular action was unclear.

The team first fingerprinted the plant's chemicals with mass spectrometry, finding 186 metabolites, of which 122 were secondary metabolites. Network analysis then linked those compounds to 910 possible body targets, and 50 of them overlapped with known syndrome targets. Central targets included P53, AKT1, and IL6. Computer docking picked out three compounds, among them syringin and isovitexin, as the most promising leads. The authors propose these for lab and animal testing next.
pmc-13457047:
Mohammadreza Kariman, Christoph M. Augustin, and Gernot Plank show, in a 2026 computer study, that judging heart pacing by one number can crown the wrong winner. One style, biventricular pacing, prettied the ECG, narrowing its main spike from 120 to 90 milliseconds, and sped activation. Yet its activation maps strayed furthest from the natural pattern. The rival style, conduction system pacing, drew maps close to a healthy heartbeat while hiding leftover unevenness in its speed profile. The authors conclude that each metric tells a partial truth. They propose patient-specific simulation with many measures as the honest way to choose and tune pacing.
pmc-13457147:

Only six of twenty-three centers had tried ECMO in preterm infants, treating twenty-two babies in all. The median baby was born at thirty-four weeks and ran on the machine for about 112 hours. About 82 percent were weaned off, and about 77 percent survived to go home. Complications were rare beyond the cannula site. Worryingly, over half the survivors showed brain injury on later scans, and about 41 percent had developmental delay by age two. Results did not differ clearly by whether birth came before or after thirty-four weeks.
pmc-13457247:
Geqi Zhu and colleagues test whether adding modified biopsy forceps to a tiny camera threaded through the mouth improves the diagnosis of malignant bile duct narrowing. Tissue proof is essential for biliary strictures, yet standard forceps samples are small. Their 2026 two-center retrospective study covers 158 inpatients with suspected extrahepatic cancer treated between 2020 and 2025, split evenly between the modified-forceps method and scope-guided biopsy alone.

The modified approach detected far more carcinoma in situ, 32.9 percent against 6.3 percent for scope alone. Overall accuracy reached 93.7 percent versus 72.2 percent, sensitivity 93.2 percent versus 71.4 percent, and both methods kept perfect specificity. Adverse events were similar, at 7.6 percent and 8.9 percent in the two groups. The authors conclude that the modified forceps raise diagnostic yield for malignant strictures without a safety penalty. That gain could spare patients repeat procedures or surgery for what turns out to be benign disease.
pmc-13458447:
Xinming Hu and a large team trace a three-step relay by which a long non-coding RNA pushes kidney cancer toward spread. XIST is famous for silencing one X chromosome, yet tumors repurpose it. Their 2026 study uses two renal cancer cell lines, 786-O and Caki-1, stimulating them with TGF-beta, a signal flipping cells into the mobile epithelial-mesenchymal transition state.

Blocking miR-141-3p partly undid the silencing benefit; restoring ZEB1 cancelled the protection of miR-141-3p, closing the loop in rescue experiments. The authors present the XIST/miR-141-3p/ZEB1 axis as an in vitro regulator of TGF-beta-driven malignancy and a drug target.
pmc-13458547:
Dapi Menglin Chiang and colleagues profile vesicle proteins in staph-spiked blood and sepsis patients in a 2026 study. Spiked samples showed more staph-linked vesicles after low-dose piperacillin-tazobactam and high-dose vancomycin, despite stable vesicle size and counts, with host defence proteins and a staph ribosomal protein rising. Patient vesicles carried acute-phase proteins such as CRP and SAA2 regardless of culture result, mirroring a shared systemic response. Vesicle profiling thus captures infection signals even when cultures fail, pending larger diagnostic trials.
pmc-13458747:
Shaowen Lyu and colleagues test a simple question: does a bigger biopsy core give a truer picture of a lung tumor's immune landscape? Their 2026 study takes resected tumors from 29 patients with stage I to III non-small cell lung cancer. It stains them for nine immune markers, and carves out simulated cores from one to four millimeters.

Measured scatter shrank as cores grew, for every marker, supporting the intuition that larger samples average out patchiness. One marker refused to behave: PD-L1, the protein that gates checkpoint therapy, stayed heterogeneously distributed in 58.8 percent of patients even inside four-millimeter cores. Ten patients had prior treatment, adding messiness. The authors advise sampling strategies that respect PD-L1's patchiness and call for larger validation before heterogeneity metrics guide biopsy practice.
pmc-13459047:
Xinyu Li and co-authors ask in 2026 whether blood uric acid predicts new hardening of blood vessels in people with type 2 diabetes. Their hospital cohort in Dalian followed 665 patients who began with no visible calcification on chest scans and later had repeat imaging. Over a median follow-up a little beyond two years, 315 patients developed new calcification in the coronary arteries, the aorta, or both.

Higher uric acid tracked with higher risk in a fairly straight line, and patients in the top quarter faced roughly twice the risk of the lowest quarter after adjustment. Adding uric acid modestly improved prediction. A cutoff near 300 micromoles per liter is offered only as a starting point needing outside confirmation.
pmc-13459347:
Xiaoxia Zeng and co-authors report the first known case linking antibodies against contactin-2, a protein at the gaps between nerve insulation segments, to an autoimmune nodopathy mimicking Guillain-Barré syndrome. Their 2026 case report describes a 48 year old woman admitted to intensive care unconscious with high fever after heat stroke and blood clotting failure. Cooling, ventilation, and fluids revived her. When the ventilator stopped, she showed limb weakness and slurred speech. Nerve testing revealed axonal type peripheral nerve injury.

Cerebrospinal fluid showed the classic protein cell dissociation pattern, protein raised without extra cells. Antibody testing identified anti-contactin-2 as the culprit, an association never before documented anywhere. The authors argue that limb weakness, speech and breathing problems, fluid findings, and early axonal damage on electrical testing should prompt thoughts of this diagnosis in antibody positive patients. The case expands the known spectrum of autoimmune nodopathies.
pmc-13459447:
Elif Ayşe Tamtekin Erdoğan and co-authors compared two ways of teaching preschoolers dental care: live demonstration on a model versus an educational video. Their 2026 trial enrolled 282 children aged three to five at six private kindergartens in Istanbul, Turkey. Children were assigned to model teaching, video teaching, or no training. Dentists examined the children's teeth and gums with standardized indices and surveyed parents at the start. Both checks were repeated six months later to see which method changed habits and reduced new cavities.

Both methods produced significant positive changes in the children's oral health behavior and knowledge compared with baseline. Improvements in dental and gum health measures also appeared after the education period, the authors report. The head to head comparison favored the hands on approach for the hardest outcome: model education proved more effective than video in reducing new caries over the six months.
pmc-13459647:
Mylavarapu and a large team pool studies on heart risk in women with endometriosis in this 2026 meta-analysis. Endometriosis, where womb-lining-like tissue grows elsewhere in the body, affects roughly five to ten percent of women of reproductive age and causes chronic inflammation. Because earlier reviews disagreed, the team systematically gathered studies comparing cardiovascular outcomes in women with and without the condition.

In the pooled data, women with endometriosis had about a 21 percent higher risk of cardiovascular disease overall. Their risk of major adverse cardiovascular events was about 23 percent higher than women without the condition. Risks were higher still for ischemic heart disease, at about 57 percent, and for the combination of angina and heart attack. The authors conclude endometriosis should count as a sex-specific factor when judging a woman's heart risk.
pmc-13459847:
Isheeta Madeka and colleagues asked in 2026 whether patients whose lung cancer vanishes completely after pre-surgery treatment live longer depending on which treatment they received. Using the National Cancer Database, the team found 584 patients treated between 2017 and 2020 whose resected non-small cell lung cancers showed a pathologic complete response, meaning no cancer remained. Most had stage three disease and underwent lobectomy.

Five-year survival after chemotherapy plus immunotherapy reached a level in the mid-eighties percent, significantly above chemoradiation at 70 percent. Chemotherapy alone, however, posted a similar survival figure to the combined immune approach, with no significant gap. The authors conclude that complete response after chemoimmunotherapy carries an especially strong survival association, while cautioning that treatment groups were not randomized.
pmc-13460047:
Ziyang Zhang, Yunxia Li, Tie Li, Hongfeng Wang, and Yanxin Wang mapped in 2026 two decades of research on artificial intelligence in heart failure care. Bibliometrics counts and networks publications rather than testing patients. Searching the Web of Science for work from 2005 to 2025, the team screened more than four thousand records and charted output, countries, journals, and keywords with visualization software.

Publication surged after 2019 and passed a thousand papers in 2025 alone. The United States and China led production, and hot topics clustered around machine learning, medical image analysis, and extracting features from clinical records. The authors recommend stronger multicenter validation and better sharing of multimodal datasets so models prove themselves beyond the hospitals that built them.
pmc-13460347:
Shuhui Li and a large team examined in 2026 how the mitochondria, the cell's energy factories, malfunction in blood cells from people with schizophrenia. Quality control for these parts involves building new ones, reshaping them, and clearing damaged ones. The study compared 42 patients with 43 healthy controls using imaging, gene activity, DNA checks, and oxidation measures, plus a neuron model damaged with peroxide.

Patient mitochondria appeared fragmented into many small pieces. Building signals were turned up while the clearance receptor was suppressed, and their DNA copies ran low despite extra damage. Defenses against oxidation, including coenzyme Q10 and an enzyme called SOD, were depleted, and energy metabolism faltered. The authors trace this imbalance largely to oxidative damage.
pmc-13460547:
Darwazeh, Duong, Panchal, and Abou-Zamzam present a 2026 review of fifty years of change in vascular surgery. The field has shifted from open reconstruction alone to a broad specialty covering veins, aorta, carotid, and limb arteries, plus dialysis access. Imaging leapt forward in step, from plain scans to live guidance inside the operating room.

The deepest shifts hit three territories: aortic disease, carotid disease, and peripheral arterial disease. Thread-based endovascular tools rewrote how blocked or bulging vessels get fixed. Drugs backed by trials now stand beside scalpels and catheters. The authors trace how each wave of tools reshaped outcomes across five decades of practice.
pmc-13461447:
Patrick Manser and five co-editors introduce in 2026 a research collection on whether serious digital health technologies can finally move physical activity habits. Global inactivity keeps rising despite a World Health Organization target of cutting it by fifteen percent by 2030, proving that generic advice fails. The collection's central claim is that apps, wearables, and games are delivery platforms, not interventions in themselves, so their worth depends entirely on design and support.

Evidence gathered across the papers shows self-monitoring alone fades, while well-timed, personal, interactive coaching built on behavior theory produced more durable gains. Technologies can build habits at scale when they supply clear cues, quick rewards, and repeated practice. A bibliometric anchor paper charts nearly three thousand articles and the wearable boom of the 2010s.
pmc-13461547:
Mark Katson and co-authors present a 2026 comparison of three ways to score hand-drawn spirals in people treated for essential tremor. Essential tremor causes shaking, often in the hands, and the treatment studied here uses focused ultrasound guided by magnetic resonance imaging to treat one spot in the brain. Clinicians rate spiral drawings by eye, so the team tested whether computer measures could match those ratings.

The analysis used 410 spiral drawings from 106 patients treated with the ultrasound procedure. Two newer image-based scores showed no clear link to the clinician ratings. A far simpler measure, the total length of the drawn line, did track worse ratings, with longer lines going with more severe tremor. Improvement after treatment appeared only in the treated hand, and the authors suggest simple, clear measures deserve more testing against daily function.
pmc-13461847:
Binbin Yu, Shimin Zhao, and Jun Wang report, in a 2026 cell study, how a protein around tumor cells lowers a protective molecule inside mouth cancer cells. The cancer type is oral squamous cell carcinoma, which starts in flat cells lining the mouth. The protective molecule, glutathione, shields cells from oxygen-based damage, and tumors lean on it. The outside protein, OSF-2 or POSTN, is common in many cancers and helps spread.

Treating cancer cells with POSTN cut glutathione levels, while its spent form and harmful species rose. A second protein, PRKRA, fell after treatment. Forcing cells to make PRKRA raised glutathione and lowered harmful species, yet POSTN reversed that protection. Gene and chemical surveys pointed to pathways behind the shift, including cell death signaling. The authors conclude POSTN drains glutathione by lowering PRKRA. They suggest glutathione control could become a treatment angle for this cancer, pending more work.
pmc-13462047:
Shu Yan and Fei Zhou survey, in a 2026 review, metal-based nano-drugs designed to strengthen cancer immunotherapy. Such therapy helps a share of patients, partly because tumors hold immune cells back. Metals such as iron, manganese, copper, and zinc shape how immune cells work, a field called metalloimmunology. Free ions reach tumors poorly, can poison the body, and clear fast.

The review maps designs that release their load on tumor conditions, home in on targets, or combine jobs in one particle. Metal ions can kill cancer cells in ways that alert the immune system, switch on an alarm pathway, STING, and rewire the tumor's chemical setting. Pairing nano-drugs with checkpoint drugs, heat therapy, or light therapy may add gains. The authors link each immune pathway to the design it needs. They flag safety hurdles: the safe window and the body's habit of balancing metal levels.
pmc-13462147:
Yibei Yu and colleagues test, in a 2026 imaging study, whether extra scan measures can sharpen a risk score for ovarian growths. The score, O-RADS, sorts such growths into five risk levels using magnetic resonance imaging traits. Sorting matters: ovarian cancer is a leading cause of cancer death in women. The team added measures of how water moves in tissue, drawn as a spread of values, plus a blood marker.

Records covered 196 patients with 235 growths, all checked against tissue results. Most water measures differed between harmless and cancerous growths. The score alone sorted risk strongly. Adding the mean and shape of the water spread, plus the marker CA-125, lifted accuracy and caught more cancers. Sensitivity rose while false alarms held steady. The authors conclude the added measures improve how the score classifies these growths, helping teams decide who needs surgery and who can be watched safely.
pmc-13462847:
Minseok Kim and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, the first Korean detection of Japanese iris necrotic ring virus in Narcissus plants, the daffodil family grown from imported bulbs. Bulb imports into Korea rose over fivefold in a decade, and infected bulbs carry viruses silently into new fields. The team screened 75 Narcissus plants with gene reading and tests. The virus turned up in 22 samples, all from the Shinan area, where over half the local plants carried it.

One isolate's full genome was read: just over 4,000 letters with five working genes. Narcissus isolates matched each other exactly in coat protein, while differing more from older iris isolates abroad. Rubbing infected sap onto squash plants passed the virus on, proving mechanical spread. Every positive plant carried other viruses, a sign of the mixed infections common in Narcissus. The authors expect the work to support bulb quarantine checks and cleaner planting stock.
pmc-13462947:
Congcong Ma and colleagues map, in a 2026 literature analysis, global research on gut microbe interventions for children, from autism to obesity and poor nutrition. The field has grown fast, yet its structure and gaps were unclear. The team searched a citation database for work from 2010 to mid-2025 and charted it with mapping tools. 1,915 articles by over twelve thousand authors across 546 journals were found.

Output accelerated after 2018. China and the United States formed a dual core of production. Fewer than three in ten studies crossed national borders, showing thin international teamwork. Hotspots centered on autism, obesity, and nutrition disorders, while development and behavior outcomes sat in the shadows. Rising themes included personal nutrition plans, links between gut microbes, brain, and behavior, and gene and chemistry profiling. The authors urge wider multinational collaboration and fuller attention to developmental endpoints in future trials.
pmc-13463047:
Venkata V. B. Yallapragada and colleagues built a design-build-test pipeline for synthetic proteins that seek out targets in the body and glow on arrival. Each protein joins a tiny antibody piece, which steers it, to a light-making reporter enzyme.

The team designed proteins against two targets: a staph germ surface factor and a cancer marker called MUC1. Computer screening picked the best designs, which were then made in the lab and confirmed to bind their targets. Injected into mice, the proteins gathered at infection and tumour sites, glowing in proportion to dose and target cell count. Yallapragada presents the platform as a fast route to imaging agents for infections and cancers alike.
pmc-13463247:
Raeesah Fakier and colleagues map, in a 2026 scoping review, the factors that help or hinder good pain control after surgery. Pain after operations stays poorly managed despite better treatments, suggesting the problem lies beyond drug strength. The team searched three databases for work published through September 2025, with two reviewers screening and extracting data. Barriers and enablers were organized with a behavior framework, then matched to intervention strategies.

Enablers included patients who feel empowered and take part in their pain care, good rapport between clinicians and patients, and structured support from teams and policy. Barriers ran wider: poor knowledge and false beliefs about pain, skill gaps in judging and treating it, weak talk between professions, thin policy, and short staffing. The authors conclude fixing surgical pain needs a many-sided push at personal and system levels. Their map aims to guide programs at each level of care.
pmc-13463647:
Zhi-ping Long and colleagues pooled trial evidence in 2026 on folic acid for adults with high homocysteine, a blood marker tied to heart risk. Folic acid should lower that marker, but how far it moves blood pressure and cholesterol, and at what dose, stayed unsettled. The team screened four databases to October 2024 and combined 36 randomised trials of folic acid alone against placebo or usual care.

Homocysteine fell in a dose-linked way, most at 5 to 15 milligrams daily and after six months or more, while folate levels rose and blood pressure and cholesterol shifted modestly. Yet results varied widely and leaned on small studies, so true effects may be smaller than pooled figures suggest. No heart events appeared at doses up to 10 milligrams daily, but events rose at 15 milligrams, and no trial tracked hard outcomes like heart attack or stroke.
pmc-13464047:
Perevedentseva and co-authors test a protein fragment as a trap for rare earth elements in this 2026 study. These elements, the lanthanides, are essential for wind turbines and other clean-energy technology, yet mining and recycling them pollutes heavily. The team studied EF4, a loop from the protein calmodulin that naturally grips calcium, and checked how it binds lanthanide ions instead.

Using heat measurements, laser fluorescence, magnetic resonance, and computer simulations, they found the loop binds the whole lanthanide series strongly, with small differences between elements. The isolated loop proved far more flexible than it is inside the full protein. It formed complexes with either one or two metal ions, depending on conditions. Fixed onto a support, the loop successfully pulled samarium ions out of a laboratory solution.
pmc-13465547:
Lyu and co-authors compared a 2026 genomic comparison of skeletal muscle in newborn calves and adult steers, hunting the switches that steer growth after birth. Muscle growth matters directly for beef yield and quality in cattle production. Gene activity and the enhancers and transcription factors that control it were profiled in both age groups.

Muscle biology shifted markedly from birth to adulthood in Lyu's analysis of the two groups. Newborn muscle emphasised protein building and energy metabolism, the machinery of rapid early growth. Adult muscle instead emphasised cell differentiation and migration, blood vessel growth, fibre forming activity, and immune response. Coordinated shifts in transcription factor networks and enhancer programmes drove those changes, the authors conclude. The findings point to genomic strategies for improving muscle growth and meat quality.
pmc-13465647:
Ilkim Karakapici and Nuket Ornek Buken explored this 2026 look at the ethical strains inside cosmetic dentistry. Veneers and whitening sell partly through social media and consumer culture, which pulls against a dentist's duty of care. Theory on this clash abounds, but everyday evidence from practicing dentists was thin. The team interviewed nineteen dentists in Ankara, from specialists to general practitioners.

Four themes emerged: ethical responsibility, views of the cosmetic field, the slide from care toward commerce, and how system pressures land in the clinic. The deepest tension sat between not harming patients and the market's pull to sell more treatment. The study gives ethics teaching a ground-level view of where principles bend under commercial pressure.
pmc-13466647:
Tian and co-authors tested in 2026 whether change in loose mitochondrial DNA in blood around heart attack treatment predicts later trouble. Mitochondria are the cell's power plants; their DNA leaks out when heart muscle dies. The team measured levels before and after emergency artery opening in 236 patients, followed them one year, and grouped them by how much their level changed.

Events were common: 58 patients, about a quarter, suffered a major cardiovascular event within the year. Risk climbed steadily with the size of the DNA change. Each standard step up in change meant roughly a quarter more risk, and the highest-change third fared worst, a clean dose-response pattern. The signal came mostly from returning chest pain rather than deaths or new heart attacks. The authors call the marker exploratory: it may flag patients headed for symptom flare-ups, but must still prove itself against established risk scores.
pmc-13466847:
Akad and colleagues compared bone health markers in 2026 between 50 long-term kidney transplant recipients and 56 people without transplants who had low bone mass. Bone disease is a major late problem after transplantation. The team measured blood markers of bone building and bone breakdown alongside density scans.

Transplant patients had lower density scores at the hip and spine even though they were younger. One bone formation marker, called BALP, stayed clearly higher in transplant patients after adjusting for age, sex, body size, and menopause status. Other markers did not differ, and the blood markers barely tracked with scan results inside the transplant group. BALP also separated the two groups best in a screening test, which the authors say deserves follow-up over time.
pmc-13467247:
Raluca Maria Badila and colleagues pool research on a brain injury blood marker used to forecast recovery after cardiac arrest, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. The marker, neuron-specific enolase, is among the most studied for this grim task, yet modern care that cools the body may change how the marker behaves and which cutoff counts as hopeless. Searches ran across three databases for studies from 2000 into 2026.

Twenty-one studies passed the entry rules for the qualitative set, with a homogeneous subset feeding the pooled accuracy numbers. Quality was graded with standard scales for observational work and trials. The synthesis aims to give intensive care teams thresholds they can defend.
pmc-13467747:
Laura Figà and a large Italian team present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one newborn with intermediate osteopetrosis. This is a rare inherited disorder. Bone is not broken down properly in it. Bone becomes abnormally dense as a result. The baby presented with low blood calcium in the newborn period. The head was progressively enlarging.

Brain imaging confirmed obstructive hydrocephalus. This is fluid build-up inside the brain. A shunt relieved it. Genetic testing found no causative variant. Whole-exome sequencing was included in the testing. Yet the clinical and scan picture supported the diagnosis. The child received calcium and vitamin D treatment. A stem cell transplant followed. The donor was matched but unrelated. The authors highlight it as successful despite the negative genetic results.
pmc-13468147:
Shakila Parveen Asrafali, Thirukumaran Periyasamy and Jaewoong Lee published this 2026 review of polybenzoxazines, high-performance thermosetting plastics, and how molecular structure shapes composites. The review moves from monomer design and the ring-opening curing reaction through reinforcement with carbon nanofillers, fibres and hybrid fillers. It then covers processing routes from compression moulding to 3D printing, and uses in aerospace, high-frequency electronics and coatings.

The numbers explain why: engineered versions keep working above 350 degrees, leave char yields up to 92 percent in fire, and reach dielectric constants as low as 2.67 for electronics, with near-zero curing shrinkage and no volatile byproducts. Lasting weak points include brittleness, high cure temperatures and being hard to recycle. The authors highlight dynamic covalent networks, vitrimer chemistry and self-healing designs as the routes past those barriers, and frame their map as an engineering guide for new composites.
pmc-13468447:
Juan Wang and co-authors build in 2026 a flexible film that pulls the antibiotic tetracycline out of water, made from two plant-derived carbons. Nanocellulose forms the self-supporting film, while carbonized lignin, treated with phosphoric acid to carve a hierarchy of pores rich in mid-sized channels, does the capturing. Structural checks confirmed the carbonization and plentiful oxygen-bearing surface groups that grab the drug.

The carbon reached a maximum uptake of 21.06 milligrams of tetracycline per gram within two hours, following kinetics that point to chemical rather than purely physical capture. Loading the film with too much carbon weakened it, so an optimized 30 percent loading balanced strength and performance. Antibiotic residues in farm and hospital wastewater drive resistance, and a compostable film filter made from wood waste streams is an appealing answer.
pmc-13468647:
José Roberto Vega-Baudrit, Mary Lopretti, and Felipe Orozco review in 2026 how to trace nanoplastics in drinking water back to their sources. Finding particles under one micrometer is only step one. Regulators need to know whether they came from source water, treatment works, mains pipes, packaging, or the lab itself. The review examines fingerprinting: the chemical marks that survive each stage of the water chain.

Polymer type, particle shape, surface oxidation, and additive and breakdown profiles can be combined into solid source assignments. So can heat-breakdown markers, read across tools from enhanced Raman spectroscopy to atomic force microscopy with infrared. Quality control counts as part of the proof, since a fingerprint that might be lab background contamination is worse than none. As nanoplastic monitoring spreads, naming the source decides who must act. That makes this synthesis a practical reference.
pmc-13469047:
Kongkong Cui and colleagues tested tumour size in 2026 as a predictor of spread and survival in Wilms tumour, the most common childhood kidney cancer. Size effects on outlook, metastasis, and treatment response stayed murky. The team analysed 1,916 United States registry patients from 2000 to 2022 plus 237 hospital patients for external validation.

Tumours over 10.4 centimetres fared worse, with size independently raising death risk at a hazard ratio of 1.79. Metastasis struck 187 of 880 large-tumour patients against 87 of 762 small-tumour patients, and large tumours cut five-year survival by 9.8 points among chemotherapy recipients with distant spread. Size offers a simple extra risk marker, especially where genomic testing is scarce.
pmc-13470147:
Davis and Clibbens ask what mental health workers gain from their own past mental illness in this 2026 systematic review. About one person in eight worldwide lived with a mental health condition in 2019, which includes many professionals themselves. Even so, such experience is often undervalued at work and carries stigma, so the authors gathered studies on how it shapes daily practice.

They combined findings from 10 papers using thematic analysis, a method that groups repeated ideas. Two broad themes emerged. The first was value within the person, covering attitudes, beliefs, and deeper understanding of illness. The second was value between people. It covered stronger connection with patients and a different approach to care. The authors conclude that services should treat this experience as an asset and work to reduce stigma around it.
pmc-13470247:
Tiwari and Kujan's 2026 scoping review maps how oral cancer is taught to healthcare practitioners and students around the world. The authors gathered studies describing any delivery mode for oral cancer education, from lectures and case discussions to hands-on head and neck examination practice, and looked for gaps in current teaching.

Thirty-nine studies qualified for inclusion across the databases searched. Every teaching method improved oral cancer knowledge over baseline, though the gains varied in size. Time devoted to the topic ranged widely, from none at all up to 50 hours in some programs, with a median of just 2 hours per course. Biopsy practice and clinical observation also appeared among the approaches catalogued. The authors found no consensus on the best delivery mode and argue that curricula urgently need more time on oral cancer.
pmc-13470347:
Shayesteh Tabatabaei built a low-cost fuzzy logic irrigation controller in 2026 for vineyards in semi-arid Malekan County, Iran. Water scarcity demands irrigation that responds to field conditions in real time. An Arduino Uno controller reads soil moisture, air temperature, and a light-derived solar index, applies fuzzy rules to set irrigation duration, and gates pumping during rain.

MATLAB surface analysis plus a March to August 2024 field pilot against conventional irrigation cut water use 34.6%, from 520 to 340 cubic metres per hectare. Cluster weight, sugar content, and rotten cluster rates improved descriptively. Single-season, unreplicated pilot limits mean larger multi-season trials must confirm the gains before growers adopt widely.
pmc-13470947:
Qiyuan An mapped sesame floral organ gene readings in 2026 to clarify flower growth in a key oilseed crop. Gene-reading landscapes of sesame floral organ growth were largely unmapped. RNA reads read sepals, petals, stamens, and carpels, finding 5,685 to 10,253 unlike expressed genes between organ pairs.

Focus pointed to energy steps, speeding action, hormone signal relays, MAPK signals, ABC pumps, and starch and sucrose energy use. Eighteen MIKC-MADS genes showed organ-own patterns backing the old ABCDE model of floral type, with hormone- and stress-tuned switch parts. The atlas gives breeders genetic stock for working gene work and gene breeding.
pmc-13471247:
Luisa Enria and colleagues reflect in 2026 on a workshop method for exposing power inside communities before health emergency work begins. Responders from Ebola to COVID-19 have learned to work through trusted local leaders, yet programs often treat each community as uniform and miss who really holds authority. The team ran participatory power mapping workshops in Sierra Leone to surface those structures.

Participants charted who holds power and who trusts whom, producing fine grained maps that changed from place to place. The exercise showed trust is neither uniform nor fixed, and it reframed residents as co designers of interventions rather than passive recipients. Making power visible also lets responders watch how their own programs shift it. The authors recommend systematic power mapping as part of emergency preparedness.
pmc-13471347:
Babolin and co-authors test whether a computer model can spot autism spectrum disorder from the chemicals that gut bacteria are predicted to make. Their 2026 pilot study combined two large databases, GMRepo v2 and Agora2, to estimate each person's microbial metabolite output.

A random forest model, a machine learning method that votes across many decision trees, separated autistic participants from healthy controls with a mean accuracy of 85% in validation testing. When the team checked the most influential metabolites against published lab studies, 40% matched findings already reported in living subjects. Short-chain fatty acids, amino acid derivatives, and volatile organic compounds ranked among the strongest signals. The authors frame the work as a proof of concept for cheaper, earlier screening research.
pmc-13471647:
Mondal and co-workers in the United Kingdom and India built in 2026 a machine learning tool for a make or break pill trait. The trait is how well a drug seeps through the gut wall. Lab tests of that seep rate are slow and dear. Their tool tried four ways to write a drug's build as numbers, each fed to three learner types. The best pair hit a firm score on held out drugs.

They then asked the tool to show its work. A fat versus water split score and the count of base type atoms drove most calls, and some build bits pushed the score up or down. A wrap method, named jackknife plus, put honest bounds on each guess. At the top setup, the bounds held near all true scores in fresh tests. The team pitches the tool as a firm first screen.
pmc-13471947:
Chuan Zhao and colleagues built a facility-level model of phosphorus recovery from sewage sludge across Japan, testing what real plants could actually deliver. Phosphorus is a finite fertiliser ingredient, and import-dependent countries face supply risks from concentrated world reserves.

Engineering limits cut the theoretical recovery sharply, by 34 to 63 percent depending on the route, the model found. Pairing local water-phase recovery at small plants with central ash leaching still met about 63 to 67 percent of Japan's farm phosphorus target. Only a limited share of treatment plants would need to take part to reach that level. Costs varied widely between facilities, so Zhao argues for targeted incentives and planned redistribution of recovered products.
pmc-13472247:
Ajay Gautam and colleagues report a battery materials study, published in 2026. It improves a solid electrolyte for all-solid-state lithium batteries. These sulphur-based argyrodite materials conduct lithium ions well. They degrade in humid air, though. The team replaced part of the arsenic in one material with germanium. They studied effects on structure, ion movement, and air stability.

Simulations showed the substitution freed the bottleneck step in ion transport. This was the long-range step. Conductivity rose sixfold over the unmodified material. Softer acid elements can stabilise sulphur, the authors argue. That is the key. High ion mobility and better air stability can then coexist in this electrolyte family.
pmc-13472447:
Masud and co-authors blast brain progenitor cells to study blast injury mechanics. Blast waves can tear cell structures in the brain. The team hit adult hippocampal progenitor cells with shock waves. Single blasts ran at 14.5 psi, and double blasts at 29.0 psi. Waves came from above or below the dish.

Atomic force probes read stiffness, roughness, and flow traits after blasts. Double blasts from below cut stiffness and roughened cell skeletons most. Cell survival, growth, and fate choice all shifted by blast path. One path cut young neurons and oligodendrocytes. The reverse path raised young neuron share instead.
pmc-13472847:
Liu and colleagues review in 2026 whether plant-derived compounds can help sexual dysfunction tied to depression or caused by antidepressant drugs. The two problems are often confused, yet they need different care. The review sorts candidates by how direct their evidence is for drug-caused dysfunction.

Saffron shows the most coherent signal, backed by small randomized trials in men and women whose problems followed fluoxetine treatment. Maca shows a narrower signal in women on common antidepressants, mainly after menopause. Rose extract remains preliminary, and ginkgo evidence is inconsistent with interaction concerns. Ginseng, pomegranate, and dietary nitrates are plausible through blood vessel pathways but lack direct trials. The authors frame all of these as investigational add-ons, not proven treatments.
pmc-13472947:
Jung and colleagues report a 2026 study building a mouse model for skin infection by Mycobacterium abscessus, a fast-growing bacterium that causes chronic, hard-to-treat wounds. Existing animal models inject the germ under intact skin, which poorly mimics real infection through broken skin. The team infected open excision wounds instead and compared the two routes in mice.

Wound infection produced persistent lesions whose tissue pattern matched human disease: pyogranulomatous inflammation, with foamy macrophages and giant fused cells around the germs. Lesions lasted and could be sampled for bacteria counts, local signal molecules, and blood profiles over time. Subcutaneous injection gave a weaker match. A faithful skin model matters because this germ resists many antibiotics; testing new drugs in a model that behaves like human wounds raises the odds that results carry over to patients.
pmc-13473547:
Aneesh Vijayan and thirteen colleagues tested in 2026 different vaccine schedules against Ebola in macaques, using two viral vectors that carry the Ebola glycoprotein. How vector vaccines are combined can change the immune response, and the current Ad26 plus modified vaccinia Ankara platform faces manufacturing difficulties, so alternatives are wanted. The team compared same-vector and mixed-vector regimens built from human adenovirus 26 and a next-generation vaccinia virus called Sementis Copenhagen vector, focusing on order.

Starting with Ad26.EBOV and following with SCV.EBOV strengthened antigen-specific memory CD4 T-cell responses well beyond a same-vector Ad26 regimen. Binding antibody levels matched the same-vector regimen, while neutralising antibodies ran briefly higher at peak for the reverse order. The authors present the Ad26-first mixed schedule as a promising alternative that could ease factory limits, while stressing that monkey immune responses must still translate into human protection.
pmc-13473747:
Danae Laina and co-authors studied how the scent of a deceptive flower shapes the community of small dung flies that visit it, in a 2026 paper. The plant, Arum maculatum, tricks flies with smells that mimic their breeding sites, and it relies on them for pollination. The team tracked which fly species and sexes visited ten plant populations north and south of the Alps.

The lesser dung flies were the second most common visitor family. In one southern population where they were abundant, the team tested whether the counts of the two main fly species tracked each plant's scent mix and fruit output. The work links scent traits to visitor makeup and to the plant's breeding success.
pmc-13474547:
Opening a breathing hole in the neck is routine critical care, but whether to guide the needle with a camera, with ultrasound, or by feel is unsettled. Filippo Sanfilippo and co-authors weigh in with a 2026 letter to the editor, responding to a trial that found routine camera guidance added time and cost without cutting major complications.

The letter warns against generalizing: the trial's operators were experienced hands. A pooled analysis they cite suggests camera guidance helps most where operators are newer, anatomy is distorted, or centers do few cases. pmc-13474747:
Baldo and co-authors followed 23 patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 treated with selumetinib. It is the first drug shown to shrink plexiform neurofibromas, the congenital nerve tumors that disfigure roughly half of people with the condition. pmc-13474847:

pmc-13474947:

pmc-13475347:

The data come from Pennsylvania streams. The package serves the state's Unassessed Waters Initiative. That programme samples fish communities and stream conditions. pmc-13475447:

Rates of the bone splitting open and of wound infections were low and much the same in all three groups. Older age, obesity, and longer surgery raised the risk of surface infection. pmc-13476347:
Sudhakar Rao and co-authors present a 2026 hospital study on heart involvement in leptospirosis, a waterborne bacterial infection common in coastal India. The average stay ran about ten days, and two in five patients stayed longer. Diabetes and high blood pressure each affected about one in six patients. pmc-13476947:
Amadou Gaye, Vence L. Bonham, and Tesfaye B. Mersha argue in 2026 that trust must anchor artificial intelligence in genomics for African populations. African ancestry holds the deepest human gene diversity, yet forms barely one percent of genome study members. Models trained elsewhere can misread risk and drug response for African patients. pmc-13477247:
Jingwen Zhang and co-authors review ways to tune the marriage of light and matter inside atom-thin materials. Sheets of transition metal compounds just one layer thick hold excitons, paired electron states that bind light strongly. Placed in tiny optical cavities, they form hybrid light-matter states called polaritons, the basis of proposed new devices.

Fixed cavities cannot adjust once built, so researchers have developed live tuning methods. The review covers tuning by squeezing, electric fields, heat, and light pulses, and what each can change, from energy levels to response speed. Live control would let one device switch jobs on demand. The authors close with the hurdles to stable, chip-scale polariton tools and where the field may go next.
pmc-13477347:

Scans were graded for white matter changes, old silent strokes, tiny bleeds, and widened fluid spaces around small vessels.

Tiny bleeds and brain shrinkage did not differ clearly. Two scan readers agreed closely on the gradings. pmc-13478047:
Min Wu and colleagues report a 2026 case of eye damage in a seven-year-old boy infected with both H1N1 influenza and Mycoplasma at the same time. Both germs commonly cause pneumonia, yet eye complications are rare. The boy already lived with an inherited retinal splitting condition diagnosed at age three.

Treatment against the virus and the Mycoplasma resolved the detachment and brought eye pressure under control. The authors warn clinicians to consider this combined infection when similar eye findings appear, especially in children with short eyes.
pmc-13479347:

Normative models chart typical growth and flag atypical development before birth. Scanning a moving fetus makes image quality uneven, and larger samples are often prized over cleaner ones.

Adding lower-quality scans shifted growth centiles in a systematic way, most at the lowest tail. Bias grew as standards relaxed and varied by brain structure, even when segmentations looked fine.
pmc-13479547:

pmc-13479647:

The case series shows how a change class that routine workflows miss can mislead lab reports. The authors urge insertion-aware checks when two standard methods clash in family cancer testing.
pmc-13479747:

Knowing which cells are dividing matters in cancer, repair, and inflammation research. Existing tools force cells into three broad states and have shaky accuracy on modern droplet datasets.

pmc-13479947:
Robert E. Steinert and coauthors published a 2026 laboratory fermentation study of carotenoids, the pigment antioxidants in colorful vegetables, and their interaction with gut microbes. Most carotenoids escape absorption and reach the colon, yet what they do there was poorly known. Carotenoids alone changed the communities only slightly, as the reported results describe. The paired tests with inulin show whether pigments steer fiber fermentation toward different metabolite outputs in each health group.
pmc-13480047:
Kelli K MacMillan and co-authors describe a 2026 profile of women who used a tailored birth plan service in Western Australia. pmc-13480247:
Zhendong Lu and co-authors report a 2026 model for spotting which thymoma patients face trouble after surgery. pmc-13482647:

pmc-13483547:

pmc-13483647:

Filtering out background sound, low energy, and movement sensitivity showed the largest gaps.

pmc-13483747:

pmc-13483847:

pmc-13483947:

pmc-13486647:

pmc-13487247:

pmc-13487347:

pmc-13489147:

A control group of 150 patients got the standard approach. Image quality scored higher in the preselected group, most clearly in patients with fast heart rates. Radiation doses were recorded for both groups.
pmc-13490447:

pmc-13491347:

pmc-13493847:

pmc-13495047:

pmc-13495447:

pmc-13498747:

pmc-13499047:

pmc-13499347:

pmc-13499447:

The authors conclude that approved-center care leveled results by health plan, while aid programs still sped up access.
pmc-13499847:

Trials ran briefly and excluded many complex patients, such as those already on preventives or with severe other illnesses, though two named exceptions widened entry. Across both streams the drug cut monthly migraine and headache days from the first month onward, with gains sustained in longer follow-up.
pmc-13499947:

Shared viewing turns a solo emergency skill into supervised training.
pmc-13500647:

pmc-13500747:

Past studies hint that threads may hold less toxin than fruiting bodies. The authors gather all work on food-relevant toxins of this fungus family. Their findings feed into safety checks in the European Union and beyond.
pmc-13500847:

In the ridges, an undulation index for the junction correlated with epidermal thickness, with how the outer horny layer stacked, and with ceramides, fats that protect the skin barrier. The authors present the combined imaging and AI approach as a non-invasive way to track age-related change.
pmc-13502747:

pmc-13503747:

The peaks partly overlap the range soaked up by a mystery absorber in the Venus clouds, whose source is unknown. The authors say fungi like these should stay on the list of possible cloud life until probes learn more.
pmc-13503847:
Maryam Azad, Mohammad Akbarzadeh Pasha, and Hossain Milani Moghaddam report a layered material that sniffs out triethylamine gas at room temperature, in a 2026 study. The gas is used in industry and marks spoiling fish, yet it is toxic and can ignite. A cheap sensor that works without heat would aid safety checks.

The team grew a conducting polymer over a mix of graphene sheets and ruthenium oxide grains. The blend reacted more strongly to the gas than the mix without polymer. At low levels it gave a clear signal, and it largely ignored six other test gases. At high heat the response was very fast, and the material flipped its electrical type near that point. Repeated tests showed steady behavior over time.
pmc-13503947:
Sugandha Sharma leads a team forecasting pollen outbreaks that strain people with breathing illness, in a 2026 paper. Timely warnings let clinics and patients prepare. The team built a network that takes many inputs and gives many outputs at once, covering tree, grass, and weed pollen.

A tuning method modeled on firefly glow set the network's knobs. Trials ran on data sets from twenty thousand to one hundred thousand cases. The model reached accuracy near 92 percent, with precision and sensitivity both above 96 percent. Per-class checks showed strong calls across all three pollen types. The authors say the system could back public alerts in India, where their data focus lies.
pmc-13504347:
Rebecca Fluri leads a large team linking new variants in the LDB1 gene to brain development disorders, in a 2026 study. The gene makes a helper protein that partners with other regulators as the brain forms. Only a few cases, with enlarged brain fluid spaces, had been reported before.

An international effort gathered sixteen people with fresh variants in the gene. All showed some mix of slow development and behavior differences. Variants near the gene's tail end also came with enlarged fluid spaces, which marks a second pattern. Lab work showed two fault paths: head-end variants break the protein's pairing with itself, while tail-end variants block its grip on a key partner and act in a dominant harmful way. Fruit fly tests backed both paths.
pmc-13505047:
Zeng-chun Wang and four co-authors studied brain oxygen levels in young children during heart surgery. Their 2026 study followed 104 children who had surgery for heart defects present at birth. The group split the children by age: six months or younger, six to twelve months, and over twelve months.

Sensors tracked brain oxygen at five points around the surgery. Levels dipped and then rose in all groups, but the youngest babies stayed lowest the whole time. The team also checked blood markers of brain and heart strain after surgery. Their results suggest babies under six months face the highest risk, so oxygen checks matter most for them.
pmc-13505147:
Lida-Alkisti Xenaki leads a large Athens team studying people in their first episode of psychosis, one month into follow-up. They asked whether poor insight, meaning weak awareness of being ill, changes the link between reading emotions on faces and everyday social functioning. The analysis covered 175 participants drawn from an Athens first-episode cohort.

Face-reading was tested with degraded images of emotional expressions, while insight and functioning were scored on standard clinical scales. No interaction between insight and face-reading reached significance for overall functioning. One exploratory result for aggressive behaviour also faded once many tests were taken into account. Poor insight and stronger negative symptoms tracked worse functioning more steadily than face-reading did. Clinicians reading the study get a caution against treating emotion recognition as the main lever on early social recovery.
pmc-13505747:
Andrea Batchev, Widana Kaushalya, Chashitha Padukka, Janya Subasinghe, Alice Walker, and Matthew Allen champion a ligand family for studying the space just outside a metal's grip. Their 2026 paper concerns cyclen tetra-amides, ring-shaped molecules that hold large ions such as lanthanides. The chemistry that matters for sensing and imaging often happens in the second sphere, the shell of nearby water and partners beyond the direct bonds.

Surveying known variants, the authors show this family steers three distinct second-sphere settings. They then use that control for the first step-by-step oxidation study of a europium complex in solution. Oxygen access, gated by hydrogen bonds to second-sphere water, set the oxidation pace. The mechanism points toward sensors that quantify low oxygen.
pmc-13506247:
Sachiko Ishikami and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a liver tumor that held two cancer types inside one mass. The cancer, arising in the bile ducts within the liver, comes in small-duct and large-duct forms. A rare benign growth linked to the large-duct form was also present.

The patient was a 75-year-old man with no symptoms. A 35-millimeter mass turned up during checks for prostate cancer. Surgeons removed part of the liver, and lab study found both cancer types side by side in the single lesion. Such mixed cases are exceedingly rare, the authors note. Documenting them sharpens how pathologists read tumors that refuse to fit one label.
pmc-13506547:
Tadayoshi Hashimoto and colleagues outline a 2026 proposal to expand SCRUM-MONSTAR, a large cancer profiling program in Japan, toward treatment of spread itself. Their plan adds profiling of circulating tumor cells, meaning live cancer cells found in blood, to tissue tests and blood DNA tests. The authors argue that DNA alone cannot show how living cells change state and survive travel.

The expanded platform would pair single-cell readings, metabolism studies, and lab models such as organoids with computer-aided review. One focus is a shift that lets tumor cells detach, float, and seed new sites. Finding weak points in that process could guide new trials aimed at stopping metastasis.
pmc-13507047:
Kenan Kütükde reports 2026 tests of abrasive water jet cutting on compacted graphite iron, a strong iron used in diesel engines. Plates 10 millimeters thick were cut while three settings varied: abrasive flow rate, nozzle distance, and cutting speed. Outcomes were surface roughness, cut width, and taper angle of the cut edge.

A structured test plan with 27 runs let the author weigh which setting mattered most for each outcome. Abrasive flow led for roughness and taper, while cutting speed led for cut width, and nozzle distance mattered little. Best finish came at a stated flow, distance, and speed combo. The method cut this hard iron with precision and little heat harm.
pmc-13507147:
Matheus Phellipe Brasil de Sousa leads a 2026 modeling study of two neuron types in the globus pallidus externa, a basal ganglia hub for movement control. Prototypical and arkypallidal neurons fire at different rates and respond differently to voltage dips. The team varied two ion flows in a cell model: a steady leak flow and HCN flow, which turns on after voltage dips.

Measured traits such as firing rate, sag ratio, and trough depth were matched to lab benchmarks.
