Valid settings revealed a trade-off curve where leak and HCN strengths balance each other in opposite directions. Staying on that curve preserves healthy firing through varied channel mixes. Drifting off it may explain faulty firing in Parkinson disease circuits.
pmc-13507247:
Alessandro Soncini leads a 2026 team studying a molecular ring of ten iron and ten dysprosium atoms. The ring can hold a detectable toroidal moment, a closed swirl of magnetism with no net poles. Such swirls could let electric fields steer spins, yet equal clockwise and counterclockwise states normally cancel, hiding the effect. Heat usually washes out delicate magnetic order as well.

Their calculations, tuned to measured data, map a vast low-energy landscape rich in swirl character and define how strongly the swirl responds at real temperatures. A pulse train design would build up swirl polarization and convert it into a readable magnetic signal through magnetoelectric coupling. Molecular toroics move closer to practical spin-electric devices.
pmc-13507347:
Kenni Wojujutari Ajele and others compare mental behavioral therapy with mindfulness-based programs for low mood, anxiety, and stress in adults with chronic states. In 2026, the stratified subgroup meta-analysis pools 107 randomized trials covering 23,585 adults with blood sugar illness or cancer, following PRISMA guidelines and searching four databases through October 2025. Mental distress affects about twenty-four percent of blood sugar illness patients and thirty percent of cancer patients.

Both approaches clearly improved results overall, with same-form mean difference minus 0.78. Mental behavioral therapy showed larger effects, mainly for low mood at minus 0.95 and blood sugar illness at minus 1.21, though comparisons were indirect and heterogeneity large. Group programs lasting at least eight weeks, with at least eight contact hours plus homework or boosters, worked best. Mindfulness may offer scalable benefits mainly in cancer care.
pmc-13507547:
Julian Okorocha, Fiona Ashton, Flavia Stettler, and Joideep Phadnis review published measurements of a bend in the upper ulna bone near the elbow, in 2026 work. Surgeons need to know this angle when they fix fractures there or design implants that fit the bone. The review followed standard reporting guidance and searched three major databases for studies from 2000 to late 2024. Only studies of healthy adults with measured values were kept.

Twenty-one studies covering more than 2,000 bones made the cut. The weighted average angle came out near six degrees, yet results differed sharply by method. Studies of cadaver bones gave higher values than scans or X-rays, and landmark choices varied a great deal. The authors argue that a shared measurement method would make future work more reliable and more useful in the clinic.
pmc-13508347:
Anqi Liu, Linfeng Xi, and Min Liu report a 58-year-old woman whose fifty years of coughing blood traced back to a birth defect in a lung vein, in a 2026 case report. She had been labeled with chronic clot-related lung disease from a standard single-phase scan and put on blood thinners, which made her bleeding worse. Her scans showed sweeping blockage, yet her heart and lungs stayed oddly stable. That mismatch triggered a second look with a two-phase scan. The new images showed delayed filling and missing lung veins on one side.

The supposed clot proved to be a flow illusion caused by sluggish blood movement. A procedure then blocked the backup vessels feeding the area, and her symptoms settled. The case warns that when scan drama and patient stability disagree, a two-phase scan can prevent dangerous treatment for a clot that is not there.
pmc-13508447:
JiMin Kim leads an eleven-author team testing a small molecule that tackles several toxic forms of the amyloid protein behind Alzheimer disease, in 2026 work. Antibody drugs now exist, yet each hits only some amyloid forms and reaches the brain poorly. The compound, YIAD-1003, was checked in dishes against three amyloid variants, including a modified form found in plaques. Two mouse models followed: one dosed with amyloid directly, and a genetic strain that builds plaques.

In dishes, the compound both blocked fiber growth and dissolved ready-made clumps across all variants. In the acute mouse model, dosing alongside amyloid spared memory. In the genetic strain, oral dosing improved learning and memory scores, cut plaque load and loose amyloid, and calmed inflammation markers. The authors argue for broad-spectrum small molecules as a complement to narrow antibody shots, and they move this candidate forward for development.
pmc-13508647:
Banaszkiewicz and co-authors report registry results in 2026 on catheter-directed mechanical thrombectomy for pulmonary embolism in patients with cancer. The procedure threads a catheter into the lung arteries and vacuums out the clot, and it is now often used for serious embolisms. Cancer patients are often left out of such studies, leaving their outcomes unclear, so this registry set them against patients without cancer.

The study included 290 patients, of whom fifty-three, or 18.3 percent, had active cancer, and the strain measure of the heart's right side improved by twenty-seven percent in both groups after treatment. Major bleeding was seen in 1.9 percent of cancer patients and 0.8 percent of the others, a gap that was not significant, and the in-hospital death rate was 9.4 percent versus 6.4 percent, also similar. The authors conclude the approach is safe and works well in cancer-associated embolism.
pmc-13509247:
Yuen-Sing Lee, Sin-Min Li, Hui-Ju Chen, and Jih-Jung Chen profile the chemistry of a traditional herb, Polygonum aviculare, hunting its active ingredients, in 2026 work. The plant has long served in folk medicine for inflammation and urine flow. Extracts from its above-ground parts were tested for antioxidant power, blood sugar enzyme blocking, and calming of inflammation. Pure compounds were then isolated and run through the same tests. Computer docking checked how the winners might grip their target enzymes, and a drug-likeness screen judged their promise.

Five compounds beat the standard antioxidant control by a wide margin. One, kaempferol, blocked the sugar enzyme hundreds of times more strongly than the clinic drug used as comparison. It also quieted two inflammation drivers in immune cells and nudged those cells toward a healing state. A sister compound, quercetin, matched it on several tests.
pmc-13509747:
Ao Sun and Yulin Yuan use eye tracking to study how readers handle Chinese separable words, in 2026 work. These word units can appear whole or split apart, with other material sitting between the parts. Thirty native speakers read sentences holding split separable words, ordinary verb-object phrases, or a borderline class of quasi-separable words. The team also factored in how often each split pattern appears in large text collections and how surprising each word was in context.

Split separable words cost readers no more effort than ordinary verb-object phrases in acceptance judgments or eye measures. The borderline class fared worse, drawing lower acceptance, slower judgments, and harder reading at the target spot. Frequent patterns eased those costs, and surprising words drew more repeat looks. The authors say split forms lean on learned patterns, so readers join the parts much as they join a normal phrase.
pmc-13511547:
Iolanda Masalskiene Costa and six co-authors review web-like traps cast out by neutrophil immune cells as a driver of brain inflammation, in 2026 work. These traps, made of loosened DNA studded with inflammatory proteins, catch germs yet harm tissue when made in excess. The review links faulty trap formation to injury in Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, and related conditions.

Traps appear to break down the blood-brain barrier and amplify inflammatory signaling, tying front-line immune activation to nerve cell damage. Several treatment ideas aim at this pathway: blocking the enzyme that loosens DNA, using enzymes that chew up traps after release, and calming the oxidative signals that trigger trap casting. The authors present trap targeting as a promising route to temper brain inflammation and limit vessel damage, pending proof in patients.
pmc-13511747:
Álvaro Farfán-Díaz and co-authors compare in 2026 standard body measure formulas for body fat and muscle in young Chilean soccer players. Formulas built on other groups and other body models can skew food and sport judgments. Records from fifty male under fifteen and under sixteen players, gathered in 2018, were run through five fat formulas and four muscle approaches.

Agreement among the fat formulas was judged with standard tests and difference plots. Muscle approaches were compared across repeated measures, with care taken since they target different muscle parts. The study warns that two formulas naming the same output can give quite different numbers. Coaches and team doctors get guidance on which estimates to trust for teen players.
pmc-13512147:
Rui-Han Liu, Yun-Qian Lin, and Yu-Han Ma present a physics study, published in 2026. It is theoretical work on batteries. It examines the trade-off between power and efficiency during discharge. Pulling energy out faster wastes more of it inside the battery. The authors derive the exact shape of that compromise. They also derive how best to schedule discharge over several stages.

Their analysis shows a universal curve. The trade-off follows this curve. Efficiency at maximum power is exactly one half. This echoes a known heat-engine limit. For staged discharge under a deadline, the best rule is simple. Each stage runs at its required current. All other stages share one uniform baseline current. The deadline sets that baseline.
pmc-13514847:
Antonio V Vega, Arnold Solano, Fausto Acosta-Fiallos, and Raúl Dávalos Monteiro examine, in a 2026 study, a polymer coating meant to protect medical steel from corrosion inside the body. Implants face salty, oxygen-bearing fluids that can free metal ions and harm tissue, so a barrier layer could extend their safe life. The coating blends polyvinyl alcohol with a small share of chitosan, a shellfish-derived polymer, applied by dipping.

Over 216 hours soaking in a balanced salt solution mimicking body fluid, the coated steel's electrical resistance climbed several-fold, signalling a stronger barrier than bare steel offers. Circuit modelling showed the defence shifting over time from a simple blocking layer toward behaviour shaped by fluid slowly seeping through. Vega's team concludes that the coating delays corrosion well under body-like conditions.
pmc-13515147:
Montini and colleagues report a 2026 study of a new silver-based material made to kill Acinetobacter baumannii, a hospital germ that often resists nearly all antibiotics. The team made it with a green method, using fluid from bacterial cultures. Tests confirmed it combined metallic silver, silver chloride, and silver phosphate at nanoscale size.

In broth and time-kill tests, it killed every isolate tried, even strains classed as extensively drug-resistant or pan-resistant, terms for germs that resist almost all or all drugs. Tests on human red blood cells showed low toxicity, giving it a high selectivity score. The authors present it as a candidate control strategy for infections where treatment options have nearly run out.
pmc-13515347:
Sarah Tournayre and twelve co-authors asked whether app engagement foretells who stays on a weight drug, in this 2026 study. Fewer than half of patients persist with such drugs at a year. Adults with severe obesity starting a weekly drug through a French early-access scheme were tracked for forty-eight weeks, and their use of a digital assessment platform was graded at the start.

Engagement came in three levels, from never opening the platform to finishing all its forms. The team tested whether that grade foretold staying on the drug, reaching full dose, and weight lost, and whether staying on the drug carried the engagement effect into weight. Clinical and behavioral predictors of response were hunted alongside. The authors frame engagement as an early sign worth acting on.
pmc-13516347:
Sarah A Neller and five colleagues map levels of active engagement inside an arts-based programme for dementia care partners in a 2026 qualitative study. Engagement is thought to power such programmes, yet nobody had pinned down its stages. Nine care partners joined six focus groups about a programme using multisensory activities and caregiver-informed story vignettes to work through dementia behaviour challenges. The team coded the talk for process patterns across twenty-seven activities.

Four levels emerged, in rising depth: participating, clarifying, contributing, and applying. The levels varied by person, by session, and by activity. From them the authors built a conceptual model linking what comes before engagement to the levels themselves, then to the programme's expected effects on coping and stress. Neller's team offers the framework as a way to measure engagement honestly in future trials, sharpening ideas about dose and fidelity.
pmc-13516447:
Shuli Wei and co-authors test whether rotating crops over many years helps wheat weather drought. Their 2026 study draws on a field trial in the foothills of the Greater Khingan Mountains, running since 2016, where spring wheat follows potato, rape, both, or itself year after year.

In 2022 all plots grew the same wheat variety, and drought was imposed from late jointing. Against wheat grown in the same ground nonstop, the potato rotations raised yield by more than seventy percent under drought. Rotated plants also built up less cell damage and calmer defense chemistry. One rotation guarded leaves best, another tuned root responses. The authors urge multi-site trials to confirm the pattern.
pmc-13517047:
Mohannad M Fallatah leads a twelve-author review of next-generation carriers for RNA vaccines in a 2026 article. RNA cargo is fragile: enzymes shred it, cells admit it poorly, and it can stall inside cellular compartments. Tiny carriers shield the cargo and escort it in. The authors compare the families on offer, from the clinically proven fatty nanoparticles to structured lipid carriers, polymer systems, and cell-derived exosomes.

Each family trades stability, targeting, body-friendliness, and release control differently. Making them at scale under drug-grade rules, batch after batch, is the shared bottleneck the review stresses. Newer tricks include acidity-tuned lipids, homing ligands, carriers that react to triggers, self-amplifying RNA, computer-guided design, and needle-free delivery. Fallatah's team argues that solving stability in storage and transport will decide how far RNA vaccines reach beyond rich health systems.
pmc-13517547:
Magdalena Długosz-Lisiecka leads a six-author study of how radioactive contamination behaves on skin in a 2026 paper. Spills in labs, hospitals, and nuclear clean-up leave isotopes on workers' skin, and scrubbing hard can do its own damage. Using fresh pig skin kept at body temperature, the team spread europium-152 in four carrier liquids, from plain water to strong acid, alkali, and alcohol, let it dry, then tried cleaning methods.

The carrier and the drying decided how deep the isotope sank and how well cleaning worked. Harsh chemistry changed the game far more than the scrubbing style. The winning kit combined a soap solution, a metal-binding agent called DTPA, and an absorbent swab, lifting the most radioactivity with the least force. Długosz-Lisiecka's team argues decontamination plans must start from the contaminant's chemical form, not from habit, a lesson aimed at emergency and CBRN responders.
pmc-13518847:
Pavithra Mahesh and Rajkumar Soundrapandiyan build a 2026 soil fertility predictor that takes soil enzyme activity seriously. Enzymes drive nutrient cycling and organic matter breakdown, yet many machine learning tools underuse them amid noisy, tangled data. Feature picking and model tuning are usually done apart, which caps accuracy.

Their framework unifies both steps under an improved sand cat swarm optimizer, a search method modeled on hunting cats, with escape moves and cosine-shaped exploration to avoid early traps. Enzyme-linked features were kept in view, and redundant ones filtered out. Gradient boosting reached 98.48 percent accuracy across cross-validation. A crop mapping step then turns fertility predictions into planting advice.
pmc-13518947:
Hung N Do, Joe McKenzie, and S Gnanakaran stress-test a 2026 workflow that bounces molecular simulations between detailed all-atom and simplified coarse-grained views. Each view has strengths, so cycling between them sounds attractive for sampling protein shapes faster. The team implemented the cycle in OpenMM and tried four systems, from folding soluble proteins to membrane protein encounters.

Cycling did shake two soluble proteins out of stuck shapes so they could fold, though the benefit came from random distortions during conversion rather than smart sampling. The most reliable win was faster mixing of membrane lipids around proteins. Do and colleagues conclude plain iteration, without constraints or model tweaks, has narrow practical uses, and they share the workflow openly.
pmc-13519047:
Xuze Lin and co-authors report a man whose heart valve flap swung shut past a burn cure for a spare heart path, in a case report from 2026. The burn kills the spare path that made his heart race. In rare cases the cure frees the flap to swing and block the heart out path.

Chest tight strain and swoons came past his cure. Scans showed the flap swing, a high out path push grade, a bent wall, and a small heart room. Gene tests cleared the thick heart ill the swing oft rides with. A pulse slow drug eased his signs and the swing went in time. Wall shape and room size may flag the risk ere cure.
pmc-13520147:
Guihao Zeng and four colleagues weigh costs and benefits in 2026 of a newer chemotherapy regimen, BrECADD, for advanced classical Hodgkin lymphoma from a United States payer's view. The HD21 trial showed the regimen works, pairing brentuximab vedotin with five other drugs. Whether the gain justifies the price needed a formal model.

A Markov model cycled every 3 weeks across a 50-year horizon, discounting costs and health gains at 3 percent yearly. BrECADD added 2.24 quality-adjusted life years at an extra cost of about 113,134 dollars, giving a ratio near 50,412 dollars per quality-adjusted year, well under the 100,000 dollar threshold. Every sensitivity scenario stayed below the threshold, and all 1,000 simulations agreed.
pmc-13520347:
Ayse G Keskus and colleagues introduce in 2026 TP53-META, a free web tool for comparing gene activity datasets through the lens of TP53, a gene often altered in cancer. Researchers can upload their own RNA data or reuse public sets to see which changes depend on TP53.

Charts cover grouped gene patterns plus networks linking genes, pathways, diseases and treatments. Two worked examples show the workflow, covering silencing of a target gene in breast cancer cells and shared TP53-linked genes in liver scarring. The tool fills a gap, since earlier databases listed TP53 targets without offering joint analysis across studies.
pmc-13520547:
Panatda Jannoey and co-authors test zinc oxide and chitosan nanoparticles as a shield for rice against the brown planthopper, in a 2026 study. The pest drains seedlings and spreads virus. A coating that wakes the plant's own defense genes could cut spray use.

Two forms were compared: a fused composite particle and the two ingredients applied apart. The apart form won. Seedlings grew taller with longer roots, took up more zinc, and switched on defense genes along two hormone pathways. They also withstood pest attack better. The composite, by contrast, muted gene activation and zinc uptake alike.
pmc-13522347:
Elder and co-authors compared in 2026 how V2a interneurons, a class of spinal nerve cells involved in movement, develop from two different embryonic routes. The cells can arise from hindbrain-like progenitors lower in the brainstem region or from spinal-cord-like progenitors. Whether the birth route leaves a lasting mark on the mature cells was unclear, so the team profiled both populations side by side.

The two routes produced interneurons with different transcription factor motifs, the DNA patterns that switch genes on, and different gene activity for axon growth and calcium handling. Forcing the cells to form by direct transcription factor induction created a third population unlike either natural route. Two regulators, CREB5 and TCF7L2, proved specific to the spinal lineage in network modeling, and knocking them down confirmed their role. The authors conclude that developmental origin shapes interneuron identity.
pmc-13522547:
Carlsson and colleagues proposed a 2026 theory for steering quantum materials with empty cavities, using vacuum energy rather than light. The Casimir effect means the zero point energy of surrounding electromagnetic fields can push a material toward one state. They apply that idea to nematic order, where electrons align in stripes but heat keeps the pattern fluctuating.

As a test case, Carlsson considered quantum Hall stripes placed near a crystal that bends light differently along different axes. That uneven environment creates an orientation dependent Casimir energy favouring one stripe direction. The calculated effect was about a thousand times stronger than other known stabilising mechanisms at feasible setups. The authors link the idea to recent stripe experiments and to wider cavity control of materials.
pmc-13522747:
Mei Yang and co-authors reframe a signal protein as a two faced governor of kidney disease. Their review from 2026 deals with interleukin-33, long classed as a simple alarm freed by cell harm. It can guard tissue or drive swelling and scarring, and the setting decides which.

What tips the balance is the kind of harm, the disease phase, and the local mix of immune and kidney cells. The signal path steers innate lymphoid cells, macrophage states, and T cell groups, with a stress on helper T cells that calm immune attack. The review spans fast kidney harm, diabetes kidney disease, lupus kidney swelling, and one more immune kidney type, and weighs repair against lasting scar growth.
pmc-13522947:
Lucian Bahrin and co-authors make twelve new flavonoid compounds and test them against bacteria. Each carries a bromine atom on one ring, placed at one of three spots. Four structures were proven by X-ray analysis.

The team screened all twelve against four problem bacteria, including staph and a common gut species. Activity depended on both the compound and the strain. One, named 5h, hit broadly and looks most promising; three others struck hard at chosen strains. At low dose, all compounds left over 90 in a hundred test cells alive, with harm rising by dose. The study maps which tweaks help.
pmc-13523147:
Sameh M Said leads a team reporting removal of a giant benign heart tumor in a young woman in a 2026 case report. The twenty-year-old patient had worsening breathlessness and palpitations. Imaging revealed a large mass inside the wall of the left ventricle consistent with a fibroma, a rare benign fibrous tumor that can still trigger dangerous rhythms or block blood flow.

Surgery removed the entire mass by enucleation, meaning it was shelled out while preserving heart muscle. Recovery was uneventful, and the patient left hospital on the fifth day after surgery. Tissue examination confirmed a fibroma with no malignant features. The authors stress early recognition and complete removal as the preferred approach for symptomatic cases, even in young adults.
pmc-13523247:
Guanhua Yu and collaborators review a chemokine signaling pair in autoimmune disease and cancer in a 2026 article. CCL20 is a small signaling protein that guides immune cells, and its only receptor, CCR6, sits mainly on immune cells. Together they help maintain immune balance and direct cells to tissues under normal conditions.

When the pair is dysregulated, it contributes to the development and progression of autoimmune diseases and to cancer growth through several routes. The review gathers evidence on those roles across diseases and surveys recent attempts to block the axis with drugs. The authors argue that a systematic grasp of this signaling pair is essential if targeted interventions are to improve outcomes, and they present the axis as a promising therapeutic target.
pmc-13523747:
Ashfaq and colleagues probed how water organizes itself inside mixtures of water, a helper solvent, and an oil, in a 2026 spectroscopy study. Such three-part mixtures are common in chemistry and biology, yet most earlier work used single solutes at low strength. Using Raman spectroscopy, which reads molecular vibrations from scattered light, the team tracked water's hydrogen bonding as oil replaced helper solvent at constant water content.

Ashfaq found that adding oil shrank the amount of disturbed water sitting in shells around water-fearing surfaces. That happened even as the number of dangling hydroxyl groups rose in every mixture tested. Those groups are water arms not bonded to anything. The acetone-based mixture showed the strongest light scattering. Together the results suggest the oil gathers into oil-rich droplets dispersed through the water. They do not spread out molecule by molecule, a finding that informs solvent design and separation science.
pmc-13524147:
Tsung-Pi Lien and others examine, in a 2026 retrospective study, the risk of low blood sodium with antidepressant use, comparing a newer drug, agomelatine, with three established options. Serotonin-based antidepressants are linked with hyponatremia, a sodium drop that can be dangerous, while mirtazapine seemed safer. Evidence on agomelatine was limited.

Records from Kaohsiung Veterans General Hospital covered patients starting a single antidepressant for at least two weeks between May 2013 and April 2023. Raw rates of low sodium ranged from 5.8 percent for mirtazapine to 10.2 percent for venlafaxine. After adjustment for patient factors, differences between drugs were no longer significant. Older age, cancer, diabetes, and anticancer drug use independently predicted low sodium. The authors stress individualized prescribing that weighs illness and interacting medicines.
pmc-13524847:
Thies Nicolaisen and co-authors test in 2026 how the way air is sampled changes gas readings in a piglet nursery. Ammonia and carbon dioxide can harm young pigs and the staff who tend them, and barns offer many rival meters and rules. The team ran three devices side by side across four production rounds in six pens.

Readings differed a lot by device for both gases. Sampling height, pig height against human height, did not change ammonia values but did change carbon dioxide values. The pen chosen within the room shifted both gases, which shows how patchy barn air is. The authors advise using two systems and picking spots with care.
pmc-13524947:
Amare Kebede and six co-authors scan the wheat genome for DNA markers of performance under heat and combined drought-plus-heat stress, in a two thousand twenty-six plant genetics paper. Compounding stresses at sensitive growth stages slash yields.

Nearly eighteen thousand markers were tested across one hundred eighty-seven diverse bread wheat genotypes for thirteen phenology, architecture, and kernel traits. The scan found marker-trait associations of several pleiotropy types, constitutive, adaptive, and conditional, plus two robust markers. Thirty-five candidate genes emerged, twelve highly expressed under the stresses and nine of them transcription factors regulating stress responses. The authors offer the markers and genes to breeders building climate-resilient wheat.
pmc-13525547:
Lin and colleagues pooled fixed-dose trials of antipsychotic drugs to map how dose relates to gains in the two core symptom groups of schizophrenia. Positive symptoms include hallucinations and delusions, while negative symptoms include flattened emotion and social withdrawal. Their 2026 review and dose-response meta-analysis searched the Cochrane schizophrenia register and earlier reviews for randomized trials of 21 antipsychotic medicines used alone in acute illness.

Lin pooled 112 studies with 385 dose arms and about thirty-seven thousand patients. For most drugs the dose-response curves for positive and negative symptoms ran roughly side by side, rising then leveling off or falling past a turning point. Partial dopamine agonists, drugs that partly switch on rather than fully block dopamine receptors, stood apart, matching their positive-symptom effects on negative symptoms. The curves give clinicians a practical guide to doses beyond which extra benefit is not likely.
pmc-13525947:
Ivana Baranova and co-authors give an early profile in 2026 of tiny RNA strands in the blood of COVID-19 patients. Such strands help steer gene activity and can be hijacked by viruses. The Delta and Omicron variants of the virus led to different illness paths, so the team asked if their RNA marks differ too.

A chip that reads thousands of these strands at once compared both variant groups with healthy controls. Sixty-five strands shifted in both variant groups, they report. The team also hunted strands tied to how bad symptoms got and to stages of Delta illness, and mapped the genes those strands may target. Early maps like this can point to blood marks that sort patients by likely course.
pmc-13526347:
Beibei Li and four co-authors rank, in 2026 work, paired pulse-wave plans for the nerve pain that can trail shingles. The pain drags down life's quality, and the pulse tool is oft paired with a second arm, yet which pair wins was murky. The team ran a web-style pooled test of past trials, with pain as the lead score.

Seventeen studies fed the pool. At one week, pulse plus a heat-cut tool topped the rank for pain. At one and three months, pulse plus a steroid led. For sleep, a vein drip drug won early and a mood drug late. That mood drug also topped the rank for low mood, while the drip won for worry. More trials are owed, the team says.
pmc-13527947:
Rebecca J. Thomas and eight colleagues describe in 2026 how people with multiple sclerosis helped design a feasibility trial of CIRCuiTS, a computer-based cognitive remediation program delivered with a therapist. Thinking problems are common in MS and drag down quality of life, yet proven treatments are scarce.

Consultation ran in three phases, including a two-day workshop that produced 24 practical recommendations. The planned trial will recruit 24 people with MS and cognitive difficulties from a UK health service, giving half the twelve-week program at once and half after a thirteen-week wait. Sessions can be remote and adapted for dexterity problems. Feasibility and acceptability come first, with goals, cognition, fatigue, and mood also tracked.
pmc-13528047:
Yingying Ye and eight colleagues build machine learning tools to spot a dangerous immune overreaction in children with Epstein-Barr virus in a 2026 study. The condition, called EBV-HLH, can turn a common infection deadly. Records came from 1,026 children treated at a hospital in Suzhou between 2017 and 2024. The team compared simple glandular fever cases with HLH cases.

Six learning methods plus standard regression were trained on selected features. A boosted tree model called XGBoost won clearly. Its accuracy score reached about 0.98, with high sensitivity and specificity. Five measures drove its calls: D-dimer, swollen neck glands, and three blood values. The authors say the tool could support early decisions. They stress it still needs testing in other hospitals.
pmc-13528147:
Deniz Gezgin Yıldırım leads a nationwide Turkish team cataloging autoimmune side effects of TNF blocker drugs in children in a 2026 study. The drugs treat rheumatic disease but can spark the very kind of illness they calm. Records covered ten years and 2,450 children on these drugs. Seventy-one children developed such reactions. That is a rate of about 2.8 percent.

Eye inflammation without infection was the top reaction, at thirty-eight percent. Paradoxical psoriasis followed at twenty-five percent. Lupus-like illness, multiple sclerosis, and surface eye inflammation were rarer. Most cases arose on etanercept, the most used drug. The median time to reaction was about twenty-two months. Over half switched to another TNF blocker. Others moved to different drug families. About sixty-three percent cleared fully. The authors advise watching for these flips during long treatment.
pmc-13529147:
Xu and colleagues reported a 2026 case of pulmonary embolism days after hemorrhoid surgery, an operation rarely linked to this complication. A pulmonary embolism is a lung artery blockage by a blood clot. The patient was a 55-year-old woman treated at a Chinese hospital in June 2025 for a rectal mass. She had no history of clots, vein disease, hypertension, or diabetes, and she was discharged without problems.

Xu recounts that five days later she returned with right-sided chest pain and a dry cough. Lung artery imaging showed an embolism together with pulmonary infarction, death of lung tissue downstream of the blockage. Oxygen, anti-inflammatory treatment, and blood thinners shrank the damaged area on follow-up scans, and her outlook stayed favorable under review. The authors use the case to argue for vigilance and clot prevention after colorectal surgery, since missed embolism is fatal.
pmc-13529247:
Antoine Cribellier leads a team on swarming in malaria mosquitoes. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses three D flight tracks. Mating swarms look complex, as if rich rules drove them.

Tracks came from two past lab data sets on one species. Bugs flew under fake sunset over a visual mark. Each bug swapped straight flight with fast turns called saccades. Turns fired at the swarm edge and leaned toward sunset. Lone bugs did much the same, the team found. A plain agent model with three rules copies the swarm.  Small to mid size swarms were the focus.
pmc-13529647:
Sudipta Saha and three co-authors study bacteria that live inside three food plants: turmeric, ginger, and white radish. Such inner bacteria might yield new germ-fighting compounds, but they could also carry drug resistance into the food chain. The team drew twenty-four bacterial strains from the fresh roots. A third of them slowed the growth of tough, drug-resistant germs from hospitals.

Extracts from one strain kept that germ-fighting power. Yet the same inner bacteria resisted many common antibiotics, across several drug classes. The paper frames these plant dwellers as a double-edged find: a source of new compounds and a possible route for resistance to spread.
pmc-13530047:
Giuseppe Anzillotti and eight colleagues report two-year results for injecting calcium phosphate cement under damaged knee cartilage to treat painful bone marrow lesions in mild-to-moderate osteoarthritis. Ninety-two knees received the subchondroplasty procedure in a prospective multicenter study, with pain, function, quality of life, and imaging tracked for twenty-four months.

Pain scores improved dramatically and held: the main knee score rose from about forty-six to eighty-one, and simple pain ratings more than halved. Over ninety percent of knees avoided further surgery at two years, and joint structure stayed radiographically stable. No serious device-related harms appeared. The authors conclude the procedure gives durable relief for this lesion type.
pmc-13530147:
Zhen-Gang Liu and colleagues report in 2026 a molecular brake on nerve regrowth in the brain and spinal cord. An enzyme called OTUD7A normally steadies a partner protein named HINT1 by trimming certain tags from it. Steady HINT1 appears to hold back a growth program driven by mTOR signaling.

Removing the brake changed outcomes in animal injury models. Lowering HINT1 alone helped retinal nerve cells survive and regrow after optic nerve crush. A broad enzyme-blocking drug likewise preserved tissue after spinal cord injury. Combining several gene changes strengthened regrowth further, marking the pathway as a candidate treatment target.
pmc-13530247:
Sehar Shahzad Farooq and colleagues design a 2026 seizure detector for long brain-wave recordings that works on patients it has never seen. Seizures are rare in hours of scalp recordings, electrode setups vary, and false alarms quickly exhaust clinicians. Their hybrid system learns normal brain patterns first, then classifies suspect windows.

Each patient in a public Boston dataset took a turn as the sole test case while all training used the rest. Accuracy and specificity ran very high, with a few false alarms per hour. Sensitivity stayed modest, showing the hard trade-off in catching rare events quietly.
pmc-13530547:
Jinyi Zuo and co-authors studied, in a 2026 paper, whether an implanted vagus nerve stimulator helps patients who live with both a disorder of consciousness and epilepsy. Few therapies move such patients toward awareness. The device is standard for epilepsy but untested for this combined group.

Ninety patients either received the implant or were managed without it. Matching balanced the two arms at 23 patients each for the main comparison. After one year, about 35 percent of implanted patients had gained a meaningful step on a coma recovery scale, against 4 percent without. Gains in the implant group pulled ahead from month three onward. The authors present the result as a real signal for a group with almost no options, while noting the data are retrospective.
pmc-13530947:
Tomita and colleagues present a 2026 methods study on staining lymphatic vessels in frozen tissue sections. Lymphatics are thin-walled and hard to see in routine processed tissue, so their true spread is undermapped. The team froze normal monkey tissues and stained frozen slices with LYVE-1 for lymph vessels and a blood vessel marker, von Willebrand factor, then compared patterns with routine processing.

In the liver, the lymph marker stained the sinusoids, the organ's blood channels, across the whole lobule in frozen sections, while routine processing showed staining only near the lobule's center. In the small intestine, milk-carrying lymph vessels sat ringed by scattered blood capillaries. The large intestine revealed a few lengthwise lymph vessels that routine methods miss. Frozen staining thus unmasks vessels that standard preparation hides, a caution for anatomy built on processed tissue alone.
pmc-13531747:
Oluwadamilola D Thompson and co-authors survey eating habits among 235 male academics in Ibadan, Nigeria, in 2026 reporting. Questionnaires based on world health tools plus a day-recall diet record measured meal patterns, diet variety, job stress, and mood. Participants came from universities and research institutes across career ranks.

About seven in ten skipped breakfast weekly, while over half still ate a varied diet. Severe job stress tripled the odds of skipping breakfast, and senior rank raised those odds further. Moderate depression lowered the odds of a varied diet. The authors urge workplace nutrition programs for university staff.
pmc-13531847:
Yi Wang and co-authors propose in 2026 a conceptual circuit for waking up cold tumors that ignore immune therapy. Cold tumors admit few immune cells and answer checkpoint drugs poorly. The review reframes them as stuck below an activation threshold rather than fully inert, with failures sorted into priming, travel, and entry problems.

An iron-driven cell death process can release danger signals that switch on an internal alarm pathway, and that alarm in turn makes cells easier to kill by the same process. Crossing the threshold resets the immune setting. Timing, dose, and tumor variety bound the idea.
pmc-13532647:
Three cheap blood marks of swell vie as fate calls past a brain block, and their rank was dim. Yu Zhao, Yutong Wang, and Shengyuan Wang rank them in a 2026 set of near three thousand such sick, read for a year. Death and new block are the two ends.

One mark, the swell salt, held its tie to both ends past tuned sums, though a hair's odds gain per step. Its tie to death ran far more firm than to new block. The white cell rate stood at death's edge and no more. The third mark tied to naught. The team cast the salt as a long fate mark, best read with ward marks at its side.
pmc-13534147:
Patrick Hedfeld examines large language models as a problem for business ethics in a twenty twenty-six article. These models now sit at the core of digital markets, yet they raise hard issues: language inequality, opaque workings, data governance, and power held by few firms. Standard AI ethics lists principles, but outcomes stay poor.

Hedfeld applies the institutional ethics of Karl Homann, which blames market incentives, not just bad actors. Speed, scale, secrecy, and control are rewarded, so ethical deficits persist. He argues the open versus closed split is too crude. His answer is partially open governance: access, disclosure, and oversight set layer by layer, to fit both innovation and public aims.
pmc-13534747:
Georgios Zontos and co-authors replace a rule of thumb in hair transplant surgery with geometry. Their 2026 paper tackles follicular unit excision, where surgeons harvest hair follicles from a donor area and must judge how many can go before the area looks thin.

Density alone misleads, they show. Their model folds in shaft thickness, hair length, exit angle, and density to compute the scalp coverage each hair actually provides, and from that the safe harvest ceiling for each patient. Patients with identical densities received very different limits once geometry entered. Thicker, longer hair covered far more; steeper exit angles cut the yield. The authors offer the framework for planning harvests patient by patient and curbing overharvesting.
pmc-13534847:
Liu and seven co-authors compare gene mutation patterns in bowel cancer across age groups, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Bowel cancer is rising in adults under fifty, and early cases may differ at the molecular level. The team pooled clinic and genome data for nearly seven thousand patients from two large collections.

Twenty-two genes varied significantly in mutation rate across four age bands. One gatekeeper gene's mutations climbed steadily with age, from about half of the youngest patients to three quarters of the oldest. Another gene ran the other way, twice as common in the youngest group as in patients over forty. A repair gene peaked in the thirties. The authors argue testing and drug plans should weigh a patient's age band.
pmc-13534947:
Marcello Seligardi and colleagues report in 2026 a rare case of vehicle-assisted suicidal strangulation, with a review of similar cases. A 48-year-old man fastened a rope round his neck to a parked tractor, then drove his car to pull it tight. Police found the body near the still-running car and a snapped rope.

Autopsy showed a bruised ring mark, deep neck injuries, and fractures of the hyoid bone and second neck vertebra. Seventeen prior cases shared high-force wounds that can mimic homicide or accidents. Scene and autopsy correlation is vital to classify such deaths correctly.
pmc-13535247:
Outbreak hunters type bacteria by a shared gene scheme, but the standard distance between two samples counts every gene difference as one step, hiding how big each step really is. De Ruvo and co-authors present cgDist, an algorithm that reads the actual letter differences inside those gene variants, giving finer distances straight from the typing profiles. A cache stores alignment facts so repeat runs skip the heavy math.

The finer measure never falls below the standard count, which keeps results easy to read in context. The authors pitch the tool as a zoom lens for clusters that screening has already found, sharpening follow-up work without the cost of full genome comparisons. Outbreak testing comes next.
pmc-13536547:
Esra Denler and Gizem Kubat Bakir examine in 2026 what shapes the link between daily living ability and recovery after coronary bypass surgery. Recovery varies by person, and single averages can hide who needs extra support. The study held 200 patients from two Istanbul hospitals treated between December 2024 and April 2025.

Daily living scores linked negatively with recovery scores overall, with physical activity the strongest tie. Body mass, schooling, income, smoking, alcohol use, and prior surgery each changed the strength of the link. Tailored nursing plans should weigh these traits when they set recovery support.
pmc-13536647:
Jeong Hyeon Lee and colleagues show in 2026 that hepatocyte growth factor, long suspected of driving skin pigment, in fact suppresses melanin production. The factor is made by skin support cells while its receptor sits on pigment cells. Tests used mouse and human pigment cells plus treated mouse and human skin samples.

The factor cut pigment enzyme levels and melanin output, yet helped pigment cells survive and grow. It worked by keeping a master switch protein out of the cell nucleus through a growth signal path. A topical role against sun-driven dark patches is proposed.
pmc-13536747: Andrew M Waters and co-authors issued a correction notice in 2026 for an earlier study of pancreatic cancer drug response. The notice is a correction only, with no new results or analysis. Two figures contained image errors involving duplicated or swapped panels. Corrected figures are supplied for the record, and the authors state that the errors did not change the findings or conclusions of the original work, with an apology for any confusion.
pmc-13537147:
Brittney Sweetser and co-authors report a 2026 test of a new blood assay for tuberculosis. Finding TB without sputum is a key goal, since many patients cannot give a good sample. The assay reads nine gene signals in blood after the blood meets TB antigens. The team ran the first check of this research-only test in clinics in Uganda and Vietnam.

The study enrolled 214 people aged twelve and up with suspected TB. Each person got sputum tests, the new blood test, and a standard blood test. The new assay spotted active TB with high accuracy, clearing the World Health Organization's minimum bar for a screening test. A two-step use of the test was weaker at telling active disease from quiet infection. The authors say the test needs more refinement.
pmc-13537247:
Zhang and a large team show in twenty twenty-six that magnetism induced in a thin semiconductor can be switched by an electric gate. The material is a layered crystal lightly doped with iron, and it stays stable in air, a rare plus. In bulk form it orders magnetically near room temperature, and the order survives in flakes many layers thick.

As flakes thin and charge drops, the order flips from one aligned type to an opposed type. A gate can tune the flip point, reaching high values in five-layer devices. Calculations trace the flip to a change in how spins couple as charge density varies. The authors see a path to spin devices with electric control.
pmc-13537547:
Tushna Vandrevala and co-authors explore how Black and South Asian communities in the United Kingdom judge health advice. Their 2026 study asks whom people trust, how they seek facts, and how culture shapes those choices. The team used interviews and community observation with sixty-eight people in total.

People often trusted personal contacts and social media, and they wanted advice that felt personal and close to their own lives. When official material lacked that fit, they looked elsewhere. Some habits matched the wider public, but past experience and culture gave them a distinct shape. The authors say health services should work through trusted local voices, use the right channels, and act to curb false claims online.
pmc-13537847:
Marcia Pescador Jimenez and nine co-authors linked street level greenery to dementia risk in a 2026 study. Past work used satellite views, which cannot tell a tree from a lawn. Their team read street photos with deep learning to split the green near each home into trees, grass, and other plants, then followed older adults for years.

The cohort held more than six thousand people tracked from 2000 to 2018. About nine percent fell to dementia in that span. Homes ringed by more grass went with a lower dementia risk in their main model, by about four and a half points over nineteen years. Trees and other green showed no such link. The authors weigh death as a rival end point with care.
pmc-13538047:
Blood tests for Alzheimer's promise diagnosis without brain scans or spinal taps, but nearly all validation comes from Western cohorts. Tolulope Akinyemi and co-authors test the markers in nine hundred and sixty-seven older Nigerians in this 2026 study, part of a local aging cohort. They ran the blood samples through two different high-sensitivity platforms and compared the readings.

Three markers climbed step by step from healthy minds to mild impairment to dementia, on both machines, giving the same story twice. Men carried higher levels than women across groups. A gene variant known to raise Alzheimer's risk also lifted the lead marker after age and sex were accounted for. The findings support using the tests in African clinical settings, where dementia's burden is growing and biomarker research has been scarce.
pmc-13538347:
A correction notice restores two missing names to the author list of a psychology study. The study compared health anxiety felt on behalf of others: parents worrying for children, and dog owners worrying for their pets. It found the worry takes different shapes in the two groups. The paper appeared in Scientific Reports in two thousand twenty-five.

Milena Weigel and Eva Zenz had been left off the original author list by error. The notice prints the full corrected list with each author's workplace. It also rewrites the section that credits who did what on the project. A supplement file was updated with the added names. The notice closes by confirming that the article and its files now stand corrected.
pmc-13538447:
Maria Iryaningrum and co-authors offer a 2026 review on obesity and a kidney damage marker in Asian people. The marker, albuminuria, means protein leaks into urine. Obesity can harm kidneys through blood flow shifts and insulin problems. The team searched four sources for studies that link obesity to the marker in Asian groups, and pooled the results by set rules.

Obesity tied to clearly higher odds of the marker in the full pool. The link held for men and for women apart, with a stronger effect in men. Study results varied a lot in the full pool, less so among women. Quality checks used a standard scale for cohort studies. The authors say weight care may help guard kidney health in these groups.
pmc-13538547:
Hyun Jun Lee and colleagues link pandemic role disruption to alcohol disorder risk among South Korean adults in a 2026 survey study. Lockdown-era shifts broke work, social, and family routines nationwide. Data came from 936 adults aged 20 to 69 years in a 2022 provincial mental health survey. Disruption across three life roles was graded low, moderate, or high, and alcohol risk was screened with a standard test while adjusting for background traits and depression.

About one in seven adults screened at alcohol risk. The share climbed steadily from the least to the most disrupted group, reaching about one in five at the top. After full adjustment, high disruption nearly doubled the odds of alcohol risk versus low disruption, while moderate disruption showed no clear link. The authors caution that one-time data cannot prove cause, yet flag heavy disruption as a warning sign.
pmc-13538947:
Toby Paterson, Roy Sanders, and Vivetha Pooranachandran report a case where a hid heart-mark of a birth rhythm ill was found in plain scans. Their report, from two thousand twenty-six, tells of a young woman.

The ill, a long-wave heart state, is sorted for risk most by gene and wave length, yet those tell the worst risks poorly. A known risk mark — the gap twixt the heart's squeeze and its charge — can sit in plain heart films. The woman had faint spells at sharp sounds, and a worn gauge caught wild heart runs. Her scans looked sound. A fresh read of old films bared a strong mark, read straight off the plain loops.
pmc-13539347:
Jun-ichi Hori and seven co-authors report a hidden cancer behind a common scrotal swelling in this 2026 case report. A sixty-five year old man had surgery for a recurrent hydrocele, a fluid sac around the testicle. Tissue from the operation unexpectedly showed mesothelioma of the tunica vaginalis, a rare cancer of the testicle's covering.

Surgeons then removed the affected half of the scrotum. The tumor was the epithelioid type and had invaded the testicle and the spermatic cord. Marker stains fit the diagnosis. With no further treatment, the man stayed disease free for twelve months after surgery. The authors warn that long standing or returning hydroceles deserve a second look, and that wide excision is the key to local control.
pmc-13540447:
Michal Stark and Yehuda G Assaraf published this 2026 review on folate receptors as targets for finding and treating cancer. These receptors, in alpha and beta forms, are scarce on most healthy tissue but plentiful on certain tumour cells and on immune cells that shield tumours. That pattern makes them ideal docking sites: imaging agents can light tumours up for surgeons, and drug carriers can deliver payloads mainly where the receptors sit.

The review covers guided surgery using receptor-targeted imaging, antibody-drug conjugates, and strategies that reprogramme the suppressive immune surroundings of tumours. One conjugate, AZD5335, carrying a topoisomerase-blocking payload, outperformed earlier entrants and worked even against tumours with low receptor levels, in the clinical results surveyed. The authors report minimal side effects on healthy tissue across the approaches reviewed. They frame folate receptors as a maturing platform for precision oncology, including against cancers that resist standard chemotherapy.
pmc-13540647:
Si-jia Hou and co-authors test whether melatonin, the sleep hormone, can protect the brain in rats with vascular dementia. The team narrowed both neck arteries in 18 rats to cut blood flow to the brain, then gave one group daily melatonin for two weeks. They measured learning in a water maze, blood flow in the brain, and markers of mitophagy, the process that clears worn-out cell power plants.

The untreated rats learned poorly, kept low brain blood flow, and showed too much of that clearance in the memory center, together with signs of cell death. Melatonin eased these changes: blood flow recovered by day 14, maze performance improved, and the clearance markers moved back toward normal. The team reads this as evidence that calming excess clearance is one way the hormone helps.
pmc-13540747:
Monique Murray and six co-authors reviewed story based studies on how gambling turns normal for the young. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, covers work from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-five. It deals with youth and adults up to age thirty-five. Ads, social habits, and digital platforms all shape how gambling looks and feels. Twenty-two studies fed a theme build done in a reflexive way.

Four themes came out. Kin and peers made gambling a norm from an early age, and that pull could cut both ways. Sport linked ads spread the norm wide. Readers in youth health get a map of how a risky act comes to feel like plain life.
pmc-13540947:
Laura Caci and colleagues offer guidance for research teams in a 2026 paper. The readers are implementation researchers. Their problem is choosing a small set of factors. The factors feed configurational comparative methods. Those methods hunt combinations of conditions behind an outcome. Dozens of candidate factors crowd real projects.

The approach runs in four stages. Teams identify factors, then prioritise them. They decide the final set next. Last, they turn each factor into something measurable. Interest-holders join at every stage. An infection prevention trial illustrates the path. It moved from a systematic review to ranking meetings and workshops.
pmc-13541047:
Daniel Faraj, Emily Melissa Drennan, and Michael Galgano present a 2026 case report on fixing a stiff, badly bent neck-and-chest spine. Such bends block level gaze and cut quality of life. In this patient, an earlier neck surgery had sunk its cages, and the spine fused in a crooked pose. Back-only surgery often can not free a bend this severe in two planes at once.

The surgeons worked in two stages. First, from the front, they freed the neck, removed the sunk cages, and rebuilt the column. Then, from the back, they fused a long span and cut bone at several points to set the final line. The staged plan reached a fix that a single approach could not. The case gives spine teams a route for the worst rigid bends.
pmc-13542247:
Mohamed Houta and an international team trace in 2026 how the GI-23 strain of avian infectious bronchitis virus, a coronavirus of chickens, has spread around the world and changed along the way. The strain causes heavy losses in egg and meat production and often escapes vaccines.

The group analyzed two hundred sixty full spike gene sequences from a public bank. About eighteen percent carried signs of recombination, where viruses swap gene chunks. After removing those, family-tree mapping pointed to Central and Eastern Europe, especially Poland and Romania, as likely sources of the American outbreaks. Five positions in the spike gene showed signs of positive selection, meaning changes there were favored. The authors warn that spread plus fast evolution could raise the strain's harm.
pmc-13542447:
Annalisa Amato and colleagues tested gut-guarded grape extract as a heat shield for dairy cow blood cells. Published in 2026, the study fed 30 Fleckvieh cows either plain feed or feed with 470 mg of grape extract per cow daily for 35 days. Heat stress upsets cow redox balance and immune fire, cutting output and breeding success.

Blood draws on days 0, 17, and 35 showed the extract lifting two rust-fighting genes, GPX1 and GSR, most clearly at day 17. During a heat wave at day 35, fed cows showed higher IL1B and IL10 gene activity, hinting at steadier immune control. The authors read the pattern as grape extract backing white-cell tuning to heat stress. Readers get a feed-based lever for cow toughness in hotter summers.
pmc-13543347:
Trang Thu Do's team asked in a 2026 interview study what makes everyday doctors use genetic counsellors placed inside their clinics. In several Australian genomic care models, counsellors act as change agents, bringing genetic expertise to specialists who lack it. Sixteen non-genetic health staff answered questions, and their answers were mapped against diffusion-of-innovation theory and a framework of what shapes behaviour.

Belief in good payoffs drove uptake: clinicians used the counsellors when they saw better patient results and growth in their own genomic skills. Time pressure and the hassle of bringing in another person were the main barriers. How complex the know-how felt, and whether its benefits were visible, also shaped choices. The authors argue that future in-house expert programmes should protect doctors' time, make access simple, and make gains easy to observe.
pmc-13543447:
Emre Uzun and colleagues published a 2026 study of variant histology in bladder urothelial cancer. These are cases where the tumour contains cell patterns beyond the usual type, and the patients studied had their bladders removed surgically. Records covered 317 patients operated between 2019 and 2025, all receiving an ileal conduit for urine drainage. The team compared patients with and without variant patterns, searched for traits predicting them, and tracked overall and cancer-specific survival.

Variant histology appeared in about forty-four percent of patients, most often squamous differentiation. Kidney swelling, clinically positive lymph nodes, and a high white-cell count predicted its presence. Survival was clearly worse with variants, and adjusted models kept variant histology as an independent marker of poorer overall and cancer-specific survival. Spotting the warning traits before surgery, the authors argue, could sharpen prognosis discussions and push treatment planning toward the individual.
pmc-13543547:
Ting Xu and colleagues published a 2026 analysis of whether the amount of high-risk human papillomavirus in a sample predicts the severity of cervical cell changes. Nearly four thousand women who had HPV testing were followed to tissue diagnoses made within three months, ranging from normal through early changes to cancer. The test's cycle threshold, a value that falls as virus amount rises, served as the viral-load measure for HPV16, HPV18, and a pooled group of other types.

Only HPV16 behaved as hoped: its threshold values dropped steadily as lesions worsened, in both single and mixed infections. Carrying several types at once did not raise high-grade risk beyond HPV16 alone. A threshold near 32.25 separated high-grade disease with about eighty percent sensitivity but modest specificity. Viral load for HPV16, the authors argue, could refine risk sorting, while for other types it adds little.
pmc-13543647:
Wenyu Huang and colleagues published a 2026 study predicting which liver cancers will respond to yttrium-90 radioembolization, a treatment that lodges radioactive microspheres in the tumour's blood supply. Records covered fifty-seven patients with confirmed hepatocellular carcinoma who had contrast MRI scans before treatment and a PET scan within a day after it to measure the radiation dose actually absorbed. Response was judged at three months by standard tumour criteria.

Thirty-two patients responded, all partially. The average absorbed dose at twenty-four hours independently predicted response, with each dose increment nudging the odds upward. A combined model mixing clinical features with MRI radiomics, the measurable texture of the scan, reached seventy-nine percent accuracy and caught most responders. Dose delivered plus tumour appearance, the authors argue, can flag early who needs a different plan.
pmc-13544147:
Mohanty and coauthors review the fight against a drug-proof bacterial enzyme. The enzyme breaks near all beta-lactam drugs, even last-line ones. It has spread worldwide since it was first found. New variants bind zinc more tightly and work faster.

Resistance also grows through pore loss and pump action. Films and shed sacs help the enzyme spread as well. No approved drug blocks this enzyme in clinic care yet. The review maps enzyme form, spread, and variant growth. It sums up blocker designs in the pipeline now. Next-step platforms pair blockers with new drug forms.
pmc-13546047:
Yuting Wang and a team of co-authors traced cell death signs in mouse spinal cord after alcohol at a young age. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with the dorsal horn, the cord's sense gate. Alcohol in early life can harm brain growth, but the cord side was dim. Pups got two alcohol shots on day seven of life. The team then read cord harm and shifts in the calm signal cells of the horn.

Stains, live cell reads, and protein tests tracked a named set of paths: calcium flux, two switch proteins, and death marks from the cell's power plants. Stress marks and cell life were read too. Readers in nerve growth get a path that may join early alcohol to pain circuit harm.
pmc-13546547:
Minghui Zhang and colleagues examined in 2026 how tissue subtype affects survival in ampullary carcinoma, a cancer arising where the bile and pancreatic ducts meet the intestine. Standard staging ignores subtype, so the team pulled 726 cases from a national registry covering 2004 to 2021. Just over half were the intestinal subtype, and the rest were pancreatobiliary or mixed.

The pancreatobiliary and mixed group fared far worse, with median cancer-specific survival of 39 months against 168 months for intestinal tumors, and they showed more advanced local growth and nodal spread. A prediction chart that adds subtype to age, stage, surgery, and chemotherapy outperformed staging alone. The authors argue that subtype belongs in routine risk estimates for this cancer.
pmc-13547147:
Tomoko Otsuki and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare inherited disorder of fat metabolism traced to a gene change never described before. A 47-year-old woman with familial chylomicronemia syndrome, a condition that leaves fat particles uncleared from the blood, arrived with pancreas inflammation driven by extremely high triglycerides. She had suffered similar attacks in pregnancy, when levels once passed 6,000 milligrams per deciliter.

Blood tests found almost none of the enzyme that clears these particles and none of its anchor protein, GPIHBP1. Genetic testing revealed a new frameshift mutation in both copies of the GPIHBP1 gene. Fasting and fluids settled the attack, and a strict low-fat diet plus the drug pemafibrate later held triglycerides under the safer threshold during follow-up.
pmc-13547347:
Joshua Zonca and co-authors test how people use advice in this 2026 study. Good choices often depend on weighing outside advice well, yet people gain less from it than they could. Eighty-nine volunteers made perception judgments while consulting seven artificial advisers, each with its own skill and self-knowledge profile, across two experiments.

People did adapt: they leaned more on advisers who proved sharper or better calibrated. Still, a math benchmark showed their use of advice stayed well short of ideal, costing real accuracy. Two errors drove the loss: people trusted their own view too much, and they failed to apply what they knew about an adviser to single trials. Telling them the facts outright did not fix either error, which the authors call a processing limit.
pmc-13547447:
Thokozile Ingrid Metsing and Sanele Buthelezi asked patients to grade the professional skills of final-year eye-care students at a university clinic in Johannesburg. Patient views offer a real-world check that exams cannot give, yet many schools never gather them in an orderly way. Eighty patients aged eighteen to seventy filled in a structured questionnaire. It covered the students' technical skill, how clearly they explained things, their conduct, and overall satisfaction.

Ratings ran high across the board. Nearly every patient rated technical skill good to excellent, and most called the explanations extremely clear. Almost all described the students as respectful and courteous, and 98 percent left satisfied and willing to recommend the clinic. Scores did not differ by age or gender. The authors say patient feedback is a workable extra lens on student professionalism.
pmc-13547847:
Masoumeh Moshaei and co-authors enrich a green microalga with selenium and iron to build a better dietary supplement, in this 2026 paper. The alga Chlorella vulgaris soaks up these trace minerals readily. Both are essential in small doses, and enriched algae could deliver them in food or feed.

The team grew the alga across a range of mineral doses and measured growth and uptake. One iron dose gave the fastest growth and richest harvest. Peak mineral loads in the cells were high for both elements. Some doses also raised the alga's green pigment, flavonoids, and antioxidant power, while other pigments held steady. The profile supports a fortified supplement.
pmc-13548547:
Jin Zhao, Chenyang Xu, and Yuan Peng examine a ratio drawn from two routine blood values as a survival marker, in a 2026 study of two patient cohorts. The patients all lay on heart-lung support machines. The ratio divides lactate, a sign of poor circulation, by albumin, a marker of nutrition and illness severity. Data came from an American intensive care database and a hospital in Kunshan, China, covering 154 patients on veno-arterial ECMO for heart causes.

Higher ratios tracked with higher death rates within twenty-eight days in both cohorts, whether treated as a sliding scale or split into groups. The relationship rose in a straight line rather than jumping at one threshold. As a predictor on its own, though, the ratio was modest, and adding it to established severity scores helped little. The authors present it as a useful prognostic signal, not a replacement for fuller assessment.
pmc-13548647:
Sazzli Kasim and colleagues build a machine learning model to predict death in hospital for heart attack patients who also have high blood pressure, in a 2026 study using a Malaysian registry. Standard risk scores were built mostly on Western patients and ignore the hypertension angle. The team mined registry records from 2006 to 2019, pruning variables with a backward selection method before training several algorithms and calibrating the winner.

A random forest using twenty-eight features reached an accuracy score of zero point nine five, well above the conventional TIMI score in head-to-head checks and reclassification tests. Heart failure severity class and peak heart enzyme levels drove predictions most, while a class of blood pressure medicines leaned toward survival. Explanation tools made the model's reasoning visible case by case. The authors propose the calibrated model for Asian hospital practice.
pmc-13548747:
Konsta Koivunen, Mikhail Saltychev, and Juhani Juhola sorted 962 patients with persistent neck pain into groups by how disability actually patterns in their lives. Clinicians usually sum a disability questionnaire into one score, which can hide different shapes of limitation. The team instead ran a latent class analysis on the ten items of the Neck Disability Index.

Three profiles appeared. Nearly half had little or no disability. A smaller group, fifteen percent, struggled with reading, driving, and lifting while managing self-care and concentration well. Over a third were severely limited across the board. Lower education, obesity, inactivity, and worse pain all raised the odds of landing in the severe group. The authors suggest care and research should treat these profiles as distinct kinds of patients rather than points on one scale.
pmc-13549147:
Ziling Hao and co-authors compare in a 2026 study three pig groups — a local Chinese breed, Yorkshire, and their cross — asking whether gut microbes track meat quality. The crossbred pigs gained better carcass traits than the local breed while keeping its prized meat quality. Their gut mix stayed close to the local parent's.

Four microbe groups marked the hybrids. Several microbes tied to body length, dressing rate, and meat color in the cross. A network map linked nine core microbes to production traits and metabolic pathways. The work is exploratory, offering hypotheses on how gut tenants shape pork.
pmc-13549347:
Yaowu Zhang and seven co-authors design a shorter X-ray focusing lens with a large opening and two focal points. Their paper came out in 2026. At synchrotron facilities, intense X-ray beams need lenses, but the lens material itself absorbs X-rays, and stepped kinoform designs that reduce absorption tend to be long.

Their design shapes the steps of the lens along an oval curve, packing the focusing power into a shorter body. Using a beam propagation simulation, they evaluate how the new lens performs. The goal is a single lens that focuses well without the length penalty of earlier kinoform lenses. Shorter, wider lenses would ease the design of beamlines where space and beam quality both matter.
pmc-13549947:
Jadebeck and colleagues present a statistical framework for metabolic flux analysis that admits it may have the wrong map in this 2026 paper. Flux analysis estimates how fast reactions run inside cells. It uses carbon-13 labeling. But labeling data often cannot single out one correct network structure. So estimates depend on the assumed map. Their method, Bayesian model set averaging, averages results across many possible network structures weighted by how well each explains the data.

The framework explores alternative structures with a dimension-jumping sampling method and scores them with nested sampling, scaling to billions of model variants. On synthetic test cases it produced robust flux estimates, showed when several structures were statistically indistinguishable, and recovered the correct pathway layout as data became more informative. Structural uncertainty is thus carried through into the final flux numbers instead of being hidden.
pmc-13550347:
Yinbo Wang and colleagues follow the mouth microbes of young children through six months of tooth decay treatment, in a 2026 prospective study. Early childhood caries is common and the oral community helps drive it, yet most work stops watching at three months. Children under treatment were sampled at the start, right after care, and at one, three, and six months, alongside saliva acidity and hygiene checks.

Hygiene improved markedly after comprehensive care. Saliva acidity rose right after treatment, then drifted back to its starting level. Microbial richness, meanwhile, climbed at the later visits, and community composition clustered distinctly before versus after treatment. One bacterial genus, Corynebacterium, rebounded by months three and six, while another group tracked with worse decay scores and lower acidity. The authors read treatment as a genuine ecological disturbance and call for randomized confirmation.
pmc-13550447:
Firas Bayram and Annalisa Barla mine roughly 198,000 professional men's tennis matches from 1968 to 2025 to quantify how the sport has changed, in a 2026 sports analytics study. Network analysis and drift-detection machine learning traced competitiveness, match length, and serve and return patterns across eras and surfaces.

The modern field is more even: upsets are commoner and one-sided wins rarer as dominance spreads beyond a few champions. Matches have lengthened by about sixteen and a half minutes on average since 1991. Serving has grown stronger, with more aces per match and higher win rates behind serve, while returning has declined. Surfaces have converged, grass playing more like the rest than it once did. The authors read a sport remade by racket technology and conditioning into a powerful, endurance-based game.
pmc-13550647:
Hu Tianxiang, with five colleagues, published a 2026 method for forecasting solar power output a short time ahead. Clouds make photovoltaic generation swing sharply, which threatens grid stability. The approach first groups past days into sunny, cloudy, and rainy patterns using a time-warping cluster method, then splits the power signal into trend and residual parts with two decomposition techniques.

A hybrid network reads the cleaned components along with weather variables, using convolutional layers for local patterns and a bidirectional state-space model for longer links. On two years of five-minute data from three Australian stations, forecasts were highly accurate and beat eleven rival models, especially in cloudy and rainy weather. Removing parts of the design weakened results, supporting each piece.
pmc-13551347:
Emmanuel Jojo Aryee and co-authors report a rare case of pernicious anemia in a 2026 paper. Vitamin B12 deficiency can mimic other diseases, which delays its recognition. Their patient was a thirty two year old man with darkening skin, fatigue, weakness, and nerve symptoms. Exam showed severe pallor around the eyes and dark patches in the mouth, hands, and feet.

Tests found low counts across all blood cell types and critically low vitamin B12. Antibodies against intrinsic factor confirmed pernicious anemia, where the stomach cannot absorb the vitamin. Injected B12 brought rapid blood improvement and cleared the skin darkening. Readers learn that dark skin patches plus low blood counts should prompt a B12 check.
pmc-13551847:
Wenxiu Luo and twelve colleagues mapped suicide risk in teens with depression in a 2026 study. The patients were aged 10 to 18 and had never had treatment. The sample held 518 teens, most of them girls. The team measured suicidal behavior, childhood trauma, and depression. They also measured hopelessness, social support, and sleep. A network method then mapped how all the factors link.

In the map, emotional abuse linked most strongly to suicide risk. Hopelessness, sleep length, and depression also linked to risk. The team says trauma in childhood sits close to risk in these teens. Emotional abuse stands out above other trauma types. They urge care teams to ask about abuse early and to act on sleep and hopelessness too.
pmc-13551947:
Yuxin Lu, with seven colleagues, published a 2026 method for mapping where proteins touch. Protein contacts drive most cell work. Weak, brief contacts are easy to miss. The team built a library of variants of one proteasome protein, PSMD10. Each variant carried a light-triggered crosslinker at a new spot. Shining light froze partners in place at that spot. Mass spectrometry then named the caught partners.

Scanning many spots in one run mapped several contact zones. It also surfaced three partners not reported before. Their names are T2FA, TBA1C, and ATRIP. The team presents the library method as a broad platform. It can chart contact surfaces without prior knowledge of a protein's shape. Drug makers could use such maps to block chosen protein pairs.
pmc-13552047:
Parth Patel and co-authors evaluate a hardware-free arthroscopic repair for a broken knee anchor point in adults, in a study published in 2026. In tibial spine avulsion, the ligament's bony attachment tears away, most often in the young. Twenty-six skeletally mature patients with displaced fractures had the fragment pulled down and tied through two tunnels drilled in the shin bone, leaving no metal inside the joint.

Every patient healed on imaging by three months. Scores for knee function and activity, stability checks, complications, and return to previous activity were tracked, though follow-up was short and there was no comparison group. The early results support the suture technique as a stable, implant-free option, with longer studies still owed.
pmc-13552147:
Kiana Zanganeh and Jennifer Madden report a forearm fracture that refused to heal until donor bone was added, in a 2026 case report. Monteggia fractures, a broken ulna with a dislocated radial head, are rare, and nonunion strikes in a small share. Their patient, a healthy 42-year-old woman hurt in a car crash, had a type IIC pattern fixed with plates and screws.

The bone failed to unite on schedule. A combined rescue followed: bone allograft, an implantable bone stimulator, and platelet-rich plasma injection. With the graft in place, the fracture healed. The authors argue that considering donor bone early in this fracture type can spare patients a return to the operating room, and they offer the case to guide treatment choices.
pmc-13552647:
Feeding apps guide new mothers daily, yet few mothers read the fine print that governs their data. Diana Arabiat, Harrison See, and Lisa Whitehead asked Australian mothers how they weigh that trade, in work from twenty twenty-six. First-time mothers who fed by breast and used such apps were talked with twice, six months apart, plus a group talk.
