Most mothers knew the apps carried privacy risks, in broad terms. Few had read or grasped the terms they agreed to. Many took small steps to shield data, like sharing less. Still, use went on. The study frames privacy as a right that app design should guard, not a chore dumped on tired parents.
pmc-13553147:
Runbiao Luo and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-six on a ribosome part that may drive the clear cell kind of kidney cancer. That kind is the most common and most fierce form of kidney cancer. The part, RPL28, had been tied to other cancers. The team reads its levels in tumor data banks and in fresh tissue from patients.

Levels ran high in tumors and tracked with worse survival and worse tumor traits. Gene maps tie the part to the immune scene in the tumor and to drug response hints. In lab cells, cutting the part slowed growth and spread. Set tests link it to the shift that lets cancer cells roam. The team flags it as a mark and a target.
pmc-13553347:
Junsong Chang and Yueqi Jing published a 2026 blind-listening experiment on who listeners think wrote a piece of music. A composer's personal style was turned into sampling rules through natural language, yielding 18 short melodic excerpts: AI-made, human-AI joint work, and human-made. Seventy-one musically trained listeners judged each excerpt's creator, rated their confidence, and scored its beauty, without knowing the truth.

Listeners could barely tell the sources apart: guesses in the AI and joint groups sat near chance, and even human pieces were misattributed over half the time. Judged creator still shaped beauty scores, even within the all-AI group where nothing actually differed. The authors call this an inborn bias in how AI music is received. Believe a human wrote it, and the same notes may sound better.
pmc-13553647:
Zhehua Mao leads a seven-author team presenting a 2026 tool that measures blood flow in newborn gut surgery. Surgeons use a glowing dye to judge whether bowel tissue gets enough blood. Shop systems track only a few hand-picked spots and lose them when tissue moves. The new system uses a deep-learning tracker to follow both chosen spots and the whole visible surface.

For each spot it works out peak glow, timing, inflow speed, and washout rate. Spread across the surface, those values become live maps of flow. Early tests on newborn bowel videos showed steady tracking through motion and partial cover. Results matched a shop system while adding the full-surface maps it lacks. More clinic testing is still needed.
pmc-13554447:
Tae Woo Kwon leads a nine-author team testing a two-herb extract as emergency help after ischemic stroke in a 2026 mouse study. Most stroke patients miss the short window for reopening blocked vessels. Backup blood routes, called collaterals, keep borderline tissue alive, yet no approved drug boosts them. The extract blends red sage and notoginseng, plants with vessel and calming actions.

Given before stroke, the extract shrank damaged brain areas and kept backup artery flow strong in the first minutes. It calmed immune cells near the injury and lowered inflammatory signals in dish tests. Barrier proteins between blood and brain were restored, sealing the vessel wall. The authors pitch the blend as added therapy for patients who cannot get vessel reopening.
pmc-13554747:
Sumit Bhatnagar and Ankit Shah wrote a 2026 piece on clearing hard calcium from leg arteries. The work deals with the artery that runs through the thigh and behind the knee. Thick calcium makes the vessel stiff, blocks balloons from opening it fully, and stops drug-coated balloons from working well.

The authors weigh a method that grinds away calcium before the drug step, using a tool that also sucks out debris. They ask when that extra step truly helps, when it just adds cost and risk, and when it may harm. Their point is that firm proof, not gut feel, should guide when doctors choose to clear calcium first.
pmc-13554947:
Linlin Wang, Yong Feng, and Qiang Liu review unstable genomes in lung cancer in a 2026 paper. Their subject is non-small cell lung cancer that can be removed by surgery, yet often comes back afterward. Stage and tumor type alone do not explain which patients relapse.

The review weighs several forms of genomic instability, from scrambled chromosomes to extra loops of DNA outside them. Each form is judged on what it does in the body, what use it might have in care, and how strong the proof is. The authors find that clonal diversity and copy-number complexity look most ready for use in judging risk. Other forms may point to weak spots that drugs could attack.
pmc-13555547:
Li Wan leads an eight-author team making a coronavirus protein messier on purpose to strengthen vaccine responses in a 2026 study. The virus's copying enzyme is highly ordered, which hides its fragments from killer T cells. Splitting it into two loose, complementary pieces kept nearly all the fragments the immune system can recognise. The disordered version was tested in mouse tumour cells and in an mRNA vaccine.

Cells carrying the split protein drew far more killer T cells and slowed tumour growth. Vaccinated animals mounted stronger killer T responses than those given the natural protein. Yet vaccination did not clearly block early infection in a hamster challenge with a newer variant. The authors propose disorder as a hidden viral evasion trick and a design lever for vaccines.
pmc-13555947:
Majid Sadoughi and Fatemeh Hajian Foroushani study how self-compassion builds resilience in medical students through savouring in a 2026 survey. Medical training piles on academic and clinical pressure. Three hundred ten students at Kashan University of Medical Sciences completed standard scales for resilience, self-compassion, and savouring beliefs. Savouring means holding onto and enjoying good moments rather than letting them slip past.

Kinder self-talk tied to both stronger savouring and stronger resilience. Savouring in turn tied to resilience as well. Part of the self-compassion effect ran through savouring, confirming it as a working mechanism. The authors suggest training that builds both traits together, so students gain a double shield against the strain of medical school life.
pmc-13556447:
Tramadol is a painkiller with a side reputation: in rats, it calms panic-like behavior. Kirsten and Mazuco set out to find which brain chemical carries that effect. Male Wistar rats got the drug or a control injection, then faced an elevated T-maze, a standard test that separates fearful avoidance from panic-like escape. Afterward, the team measured two chemicals, serotonin and norepinephrine, in the hypothalamus.

The drug left avoidance untouched but stretched escape latency, the mark of a panic-calming effect. Serotonin levels did not move; the other chemical rose sharply. Body weight was unaffected. The authors conclude the calming runs through norepinephrine in the hypothalamus, not through the serotonin path that panic research usually blames. That split could matter when hunting for better panic treatments.
pmc-13556547:
Suh and Lee compare brain wave patterns in two anxiety disorders in a 2026 study. Panic disorder and generalized anxiety share worry and body signs, and they often occur together. A clear brain marker could help doctors tell them apart and choose care.

The team used quantitative EEG, which turns brain waves into numbers, in a group of patients. They looked for features that split the two disorders in a reliable way. Such markers might also hint at how each disorder works in the brain. The study is small, so its value is as a step toward tests that support, not replace, clinical judgment.
pmc-13556647:
Hillesheim Horst and co-authors test a long-running immune challenge model of schizophrenia in mice in a 2026 study. Two injections of a bacterial toxin switch on the kynurenine pathway and raise a compound also found high in patients. The mice also show memory problems, echoing the illness. What happens past five days was unknown.

The team asked whether the pathway stays switched on at seven days and whether the toxin shifts proteins tied to schizophrenia in brain areas used for thinking. Those proteins matter because current drugs ease the loud symptoms but not the lasting thinking deficits. The study aims to firm up the model for hunting disease-changing treatments.
pmc-13556747:
Lho and four co-authors validate a Korean version of a side-effect scale built for the antipsychotic clozapine. Clozapine works best for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, but effects like excess saliva, constipation, and heart symptoms drive patients to stop it. Existing clinician scales are long and may miss the patient's own burden.

The team translated the Glasgow scale and tested it in one hundred three patients at two Korean hospitals. Scores were consistent, stable over retesting weeks later, and matched two established scales well. Higher burden also tracked with worse quality of life and functioning. Clinicians gain a brief patient-reported tool in Korean.
pmc-13556847:
N Widatalla and co-authors test whether machine learning can predict how much opioid pain relief a patient will need after surgery, in a 2026 conference paper. People vary widely in their response to these drugs, partly due to their genes. An earlier study used plain regression on gene variants and body measures, with modest success that faded on new data. The team reworked that same data with a support vector machine method.

The data covered 354 jaw surgery patients for training and 145 abdominal surgery patients for testing. Five gene variants joined age, sex, and body weight as inputs to the model. Checks within the training set gave a modest fit, much like the older regression. The paper's stated aim is better carry-over to new patients and a clearer view of which inputs matter most, judged with an explanation tool.
pmc-13556947:
He Cao and eight co-authors survey what moves older adults in Shenzhen, China to take the shingles vaccine, in a study from 2026. Shingles burdens older people heavily, yet uptake in mainland China stays low. Beliefs about the disease, family values, and sheer vaccine fatigue all compete.

Over fifteen hundred residents aged sixty and above with health records answered in late 2024. Only eight percent had been vaccinated. Feeling they truly understood the illness raised the odds of uptake. Being tired of repeated vaccinations lowered them. The authors flag understanding and fatigue as changeable levers for future campaigns.
pmc-13557447:
De los Reyes and six co-authors profile the molecules that guide dog egg cells as they mature in a dish, in this two thousand twenty-six study. Breeding and conservation work depends on maturing eggs outside the body, and small regulatory RNAs help control that process.

The team sequenced both messenger RNAs and microRNAs in eggs before and after lab maturation. Matured eggs shifted toward programs for reshaping their interior and ramping up metabolism, while immature eggs looked set for preparation and structural organization. MicroRNAs tied to cell cycle control rose selectively, and pathways for adhesion and cell scaffolding changed, including the Hippo pathway. The map may help labs reproduce in the dish what the oviduct does naturally.
pmc-13557847:
Samantha Costa Amorim Muniz and seven co-authors study enriched early life in mice in a 2026 paper. Experiences around birth shape the hormone systems that govern emotion and social life. Two brain systems, built around oxytocin and vasopressin, are especially open to early influence.

Mice raised with enrichment were compared with standard-housed peers in adulthood. Standard maze and light-box tests measured anxiety, and social tests checked interest in strangers. Brain measures tracked cell size and hormone signals in a key hypothalamic nucleus. Enriched mice showed less anxiety as adults. Brain changes differed between males and females, which underlines sex as a factor in early-life programming of emotion.
pmc-13557947:
Qing, Huang, and Gao ask whether what elderly bladder cancer survivors know, feel, or actually do about diet tracks their quality of life, in a 2026 study. They surveyed 106 patients, all over sixty and cancer-free a year after surgery, scoring dietary knowledge, attitude, and practice alongside a standard quality-of-life measure.

Patients with high overall diet scores reported far better quality of life. Each extra point added a small but steady gain. When the three parts were separated, only actual practice held up: knowing and believing made no independent difference. The authors recommend hands-on, culturally fitted dietary support that changes behavior, while noting the design cannot prove cause.
pmc-13558347:
Osama Samawi and twenty-one colleagues report the Later Stone Age site of Chessungalane in south-central Mozambique. Mozambique sits between East and Southern Africa, a region key to human adaptation. Their 2026 study combines lithic analysis, refitting, and luminescence dating. Dates place occupation from about 23,000 to 7,000 years ago, spanning early Later Stone Age through Wilton times.

Chert arrived only in the last occupation phase for systematic bladelet making through complex steps, likely prized for scarcity and knapping quality. Quartz and quartzite served all phases for simple flake making via shorter, simpler steps, reflecting local abundance and fracture limits. Bladelet making thus appeared much later here than in nearby sequences. Raw material supply and quality strongly shaped technological investment.
pmc-13558447:
Lilian van Tuyl and seven colleagues examined in 2026 whether shifting tasks to other professionals could ease the shortage of forensic physicians in the Netherlands. Frontline forensic medicine faces rising demand, from domestic violence and sexual offence examinations to care of detainees, while training intake lags and departures loom. A national research institute worked with the field to build three task-reallocation scenarios and tested how far each could help.

The Dutch-language article explains how the scenarios were developed with practitioners and what capacity each might free. Moving selected tasks to nurses or other trained staff could release scarce physician time for work only they can do. The authors judge which shifts are realistic and which safeguards they require. Their aim is a forensic service that stays sustainable rather than one patched by overtime.
pmc-13558647:
Long Zhang and seven colleagues present DMC-China, a dataset on dust from major Chinese source regions. Dust from arid and semi-arid China shapes weather and climate from regional to global scales. Particle shape and makeup govern light traits, reactivity, and transport. Their 2026 paper builds the dataset from 55 surface soils via wind-blown sand.

The dataset holds 541,074 particles, analyzed by electron microscopy with X-ray spectroscopy. Samples span gobi, sand dune, saline, grassland, and sediment surfaces. Strict checks kept samples steady and reliable. The dataset offers source profiles of particle size, shape, and makeup for emission, transport, and climate studies.
pmc-13558747:
Daniil Batov and four colleagues measured in 2026 the electric field direction of ultrafast pulses from a thulium fibre laser working at a wavelength near two micrometres. Such sub-picosecond pulses serve in material cutting and in seeding broader light sources, and their usefulness depends on polarisation, not just power and timing. Cheap, easy fibre designs that skip polarisation control can emit pulses with tangled polarisation states, yet measuring the full field vector is rare because it is difficult.

The team applied a tomographic reconstruction method to recover the pulse's transverse electric field across settings of the internal polarisation controllers and across power levels. Their measurements show how the vector pattern shifts with each adjustment. The authors argue that vector characterisation should become routine in laser development, since application efficiency hinges on a property most builders never inspect.
pmc-13559447:
Justyna Danel, Joanna Zając, and Szymon Białka wrote a 2026 editorial of wary hope on a chest tube that drains and dulls pain in one device. Keyhole lung surgery cut wound harm and sped recovery, yet pain stays a hard block. The chest drain is a chief source: it rubs the chest lining and rib nerves, curbs cough, and slows the first steps.

Care guides urge opioid-sparing plans with nerve blocks by the spine or back muscles as the core. They do not back flooding the chest space with numbing drug, for want of surgery-specific proof. The new tube revives that old path in built form. The team weighs its early promise against the guide stance and asks for fit trials before wide use.
pmc-13560347:
Watcharapon Promsut and colleagues ask whether the time of day a calf is castrated changes its inflammatory and stress responses. Their 2026 study sorted twelve four-month-old male Wagyu calves by lot into morning or afternoon surgery, six per group. Blood taken before surgery and at three points over seventy-two hours tracked cytokines, oxidative markers, T cell subsets, and cortisol.

Morning surgery set off a much larger cytokine surge, with IL-6 peaking at one hundred forty-three times its starting level six hours later, plus a rise in the calming IL-10. Afternoon calves showed minimal cytokine movement but carried higher oxidative damage and, paradoxically, higher antioxidant capacity in the reported assays. T cell shares flipped between groups across the follow-up points. Cortisol never differed. The authors suggest surgical timing shapes recovery biology in cattle, with welfare lessons worth heeding.
pmc-13560947:
Cheryl Weiqi Tan and co-authors investigated in 2026 the genetics of a rare lymph node disease across three generations of one family. The disorder brings fever, swollen nodes, and low white cell counts, and its cause is unknown. A two-year-old girl was diagnosed after prolonged fever and rash. Her mother and grandmother had similar histories.

The three affected relatives shared fourteen immune-system gene variants absent in the healthy father. Five of those variants are already tied to autoimmune inflammation. Two matched a pair of affected twins reported in Australia. The family also shared rare variants in three other immune genes and in a complement gene. The authors say combined immune gene sequencing and tissue typing may unravel this disease.
pmc-13561447:
Helena M Swinkels, Mary A Georgilas, and Steven Keeler argue, in French, that closing community swimming pools harms public health across Canada. Pools are often the first targets of budget cuts, and many see them as optional extras. Their 2026 commentary casts them instead as essential health infrastructure. Aquatic activity offers health and social benefits for the well and the unwell alike, and swimming is a basic safety skill. A new federal community fund, announced in March 2026, is framed as a rare chance to repair the damage.

The piece is advocacy grounded in public health reasoning, addressed to Canadian decision makers. It treats a local amenity as preventive medicine at population scale. The authors write in French for a Canadian health audience. Their argument connects drowning prevention, exercise access, and social cohesion to one building with a roof and lanes. Pool closures, they warn, are health policy by stealth.
pmc-13561547:
Shinya Fujita, a lone author, wrote a letter in 2025 that rethinks a case of sudden low platelets tied to a cancer drug. The drug, obinutuzumab, treats blood cancers, and the case team had read the drop as a self-attack on platelets. Fujita notes that no bone marrow test was done to prove platelet making was sound at the low point.

Such a test is key, he says, since low counts can stem from poor making, not just fast loss. Guide lines urge it for patients over 60 or with odd features, both met here. He also questions the care path: first-line steroids or immune globulin were skipped for a growth drug kept for chronic cases. He urges early marrow checks to match care to the true cause.
pmc-13561747:
Christian Gilfrich and co-authors wrote a 2026 editorial on risk calls after bladder removal for cancer. The surgery can cure, but it brings heavy strain and a clouded long view. Once the final tissue report lands, doctors juggle stage, node spread, vessel spread, cut edges, past drug care, frailty, and body reserve, most often by feel.

They discuss a pooled review of 77 studies that summed models for survival and for cancer-free spans. Its worth lies in sums that adjust for the other traits at play. Stage and nodes stay strong, but the pooled work shows how each trait weighs against the rest. No ready score falls out of it, they note. Its gift is a map of which risk layers the next tools must hold.
pmc-13562647:
Kenji Yoshiki and eight colleagues tag brain activity with a fast flicker to watch spatial attention unfold in time. Judging the centre of a line sounds simple, yet it recruits a chain of visual and attention regions within a blink. Their 2026 method flashes line stimuli at rates between 70 and 90 cycles per second while a magnetoencephalography scanner records the brain's magnetic fields. Volunteers explored each line with eye movements only, keeping their hands still. The steady flicker lets the signal of interest stand out at its own frequency.

Activity began in visual areas at the back of both hemispheres around 100 milliseconds. It then spread to right-side junction, frontal, and upper parietal regions between roughly 130 and 220 milliseconds. pmc-13563147:

pmc-13563547:
Tafenzi HA and Belbaraka R present an article dated 2026 on making journal rejection useful for authors in low-resource settings. Peer review guards scientific quality, but its cracks are showing. pmc-13563747:
Damilare Akintunde and co-authors warn that drug resistance has been ignored in the fight against noma, a gangrene of the face that strikes malnourished young children in extreme poverty. Community conditions and weak lab capacity in the regions hit hardest drive the risk. The authors propose steps to bring resistance into noma research and policy.
pmc-13563847:
Yuichi Oba, Noriomi Fujimori, and Hidehiko Hirata present evidence that a common Japanese firefly may really be two species hiding under one name. pmc-13564147:
Abderrahman Atifi offers, in a 2026 perspective piece, a critical look at making rare earth metals with electricity at room temperature instead of in hot, chemical-heavy plants. pmc-13564247:
Lagunas and co-authors present a 2026 genetics study of brown trout across Iceland. Sea-running trout colonized the island as the ice melted about ten thousand years ago. pmc-13564347:
Min Hoan Moon and co-authors published this 2026 study on reading kidney damage early with ultrasound in mice. pmc-13564747:
Ferrante, Ali, Hobbs, and Leiva published in twenty twenty-six a review of high lung blood pressure in patients with certain blood cancers. These cancers, called myeloproliferative neoplasms, drive excess blood cell growth. High pressure in lung vessels is now seen more often in such patients. They call for forward-looking studies to settle screening rules and care choices.
pmc-13565047:
Kristin Sheffield and five co-authors charted real world care for a gene marked lung cancer in a 2026 study. About one lung cancer in eight carries the KRAS G12C mark, and new drugs aim right at it. pmc-13565447:
Benjamin Wolozin and six co-authors trace how a helpful stress response in brain cells turns harmful with age, feeding Alzheimer's-type damage, in a review from twenty twenty-six. When stressed, cells park RNA and proteins in droplets called stress granules. Brief parking is healthy and normal in development and hibernation.

Under chronic stress, though, the droplets persist and harden into seeds for the protein clumps seen in nerve diseases. The tau protein sits at the center of the paradox: stress marks tau, tau then steers granule behavior, and granules in turn brew toxic tau clusters. Aging weakens the cell's cleanup systems, the authors argue, tipping a balanced cycle into disease.
pmc-13565647:
After an earthquake, crowded container settlements raise the risk of infections spreading, and knowledge alone may not change habits. pmc-13565747:
Li Gong and colleagues tested nutrient bag recipes for morel mushrooms in 2026. Morels need added nutrient bags for yield. Standard bags cost growers too much. Local recipes are rarely available either. Ten formulations were compared in fields. One control used the conventional recipe.

Nutrient availability increased for the crop. Costs fell compared with standard bags. Farm waste gained a recycling route. Qinghai Plateau growers are the audience.
pmc-13566247:
Moon-Kyun Cho and six co-authors review plant compounds called polyphenols as skin care leads in a 2026 paper. Most drugs hit one path, while these plant compounds act on many linked paths at once.

pmc-13566547:

pmc-13567047:
Łukasz Kogut, Czesław Puchalski, Julia Jastrzębska, and Grzegorz Zaguła review plastic particles in the human diet in this 2026 paper. Tiny plastic bits now contaminate food and water worldwide. Most swallowed particles pass out again, but lab studies link the tiniest ones to cell stress, inflammation, and hormone disruption across many organs. Human evidence, though, stays thin and mostly observational. The authors weigh biological plausibility against that gap and urge better human studies.
pmc-13567347:
Melo and co-authors test whether a soil additive and a helpful bacterium together shield cowpea from drought. Their 2026 greenhouse study pairs potassium humate with Bacillus aryabhattai on a named cowpea cultivar. Each input alone is a known stimulant; the joint use is new.

pmc-13567647:
Oktawian Bialas offers a 2026 review of silicon nitride coatings on titanium for cardiovascular devices. Titanium implants still invite protein fouling, clotting, bacterial growth, and slow surface decay. A ceramic skin might block all four problems at once.

Surface chemistry and how water spreads on them are tied to protein adsorption, platelet response, blood damage, and cell response. Still and flowing test setups are set side by side. Hurdles on the path to real use, from making each batch the same to long-term body data, close a fair review of a hopeful implant surface.
pmc-13569847:
Alireza Hanifehnezhad and a large team test vaccines against Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus in mice. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. They build four vaccines on a tamed adenovirus carrier. One holds two virus antigens in a single chain, and the rest hold one antigen each.

pmc-13570047:

pmc-13570347:
Zhen Huo, Zhengkui Zhou, and Shuisheng Hou chart how duck muscle grows before hatching, in a 2026 study. Pekin ducks are bred for meat, and the breast and leg muscles follow different clocks. Breast weight rose in an S curve while leg weight climbed steadily. Mature fibers showed in legs by day nineteen but not in breast until day twenty-three. Gene screens named five candidate drivers for breast, twelve for leg, and eleven for the gap between them. Breeders gain targets for shaping the bird's most valuable cuts.
pmc-13570847:

pmc-13571147:
Jinjin Wu and co-authors chart cell changes in hearts with a fast, irregular rhythm tied to valve disease, in this 2026 study. pmc-13571547:

pmc-13571747:

pmc-13571947:

Older patients were those aged seventy or more at the start of care, about a fourth of the full group. Three year rates of freedom from return of the cancer and of overall survival were high for the whole group. The authors check how age, tumor traits, and care traits shaped those outcomes.
pmc-13572347:

pmc-13572447:

pmc-13572547:

pmc-13572647:

pmc-13572847:

pmc-13574647:

pmc-13574847:

pmc-13574947:

pmc-13575147:

pmc-13575247:

pmc-13575847:

pmc-13576447:

pmc-13576747:

pmc-13577147:

pmc-13577347:

pmc-13577547:

pmc-13577647:

pmc-13578247:

pmc-13578447:

pmc-13578947:

Raman spectroscopy identifies substances by those vibrations, but a dull background often buries the signal. Their setup detects broadband squeezed light and compares the twin beams the process emits. Quantum links between the beams cancel much of the background and beat the standard noise floor.

The gain does not come from counting statistics alone. It grows out of paired molecules trading a virtual photon, a channel with no classical counterpart. Simulations show the method resolving a fine bond split in DNA damage products after ultraviolet exposure. The authors point to uses in fast photochemistry and in label-free medical imaging and sensing.
pmc-13579047:
Hameeda Fatima and co-authors present a case from 2026 of a man whose adrenal glands failed after he quit a tainted supplement. A 52-year-old man came in with repeat nausea and vomiting, a fast heart rate, and low salt and potassium in his blood. First tests found no cause.

Deeper tests showed low cortisol and a weak reply to a gland prompt, proof that his glands had been switched off. Steroid care eased his signs. His history then showed he had just quit a daily supplement called Force Forever. The United States drug agency had warned that the product hides two drugs, one of them a strong steroid. Stopping it cold left his body with no steroid cover. The team urges full supplement histories in such cases.
pmc-13579147:
Xianhong Liu and co-authors trace an immune signal chain in chronic prostatitis in this 2026 paper. The condition brings lasting prostate inflammation and pelvic pain to millions of men. What keeps the inflammation alive is poorly understood. The team combined mouse experiments with human tissue and single-cell data.

They found a class of macrophages in diseased tissue that burn sugar fast and drive inflammation. A signal from T cells, called CCL5, switches these cells into that state through a chain of proteins. Removing the signal in mice eased tissue damage and pain sensitivity. Blocking links in the chain also calmed the program. The chain offers several drug targets for a hard-to-treat condition.
pmc-13580447:
Michael Lüscher and seven co-authors chart two decades of ear tube surgery in Danish children. Their 2026 register study covers every child aged zero to twelve from 2003 to 2023. Tube insertion is among the commonest childhood operations. Rates swing widely between places and years, though.

Over seven hundred thousand procedures were logged in about three hundred seventy-two thousand children. Nearly all took place in ear, nose, and throat practices. Yearly counts peaked in 2010, then slid until 2019. The pandemic years dipped sharply before a strong rebound. More children overall received at least one tube across the period. Regional gaps in treatment habits persisted through it all.
pmc-13580547:
Wenhao Yuan, Zhilong Wang, and Fengqi You read the life story of dying metal catalysts from still photos, in a 2026 study. Catalyst particles lose power as they wander and merge, a process called sintering. Watching that happen live is costly, so most labs see only the end state under a microscope.

Their trick, called pseudotime, orders snapshots of gold particles at many ages as if they were frames of one film. The ordering shows that the gap between particles rules their fate: below a clear threshold distance, particles drift and merge, while beyond it they stay put. Live tracking in a gas cell confirmed the threshold within a hair and let them predict sintering with 92 percent accuracy. Spacing particles out thus becomes a design rule for longer-lived catalysts.
pmc-13581147:
Mohsen Malekinejad and co-authors ask what should become of the exposure notification apps built for COVID-19. More than one hundred countries used these phone systems to warn people, quietly and at scale, that they had been near an infected person. The team gathered twenty-two experts from six countries, polled them in a structured consensus process, and followed up with group discussions.

The experts agreed on upgrades: letting users report a home test result themselves, adding public health guidance inside the app, and warning about venues tied to big spread events. They also backed wider uses, such as covering other airborne diseases and feeding the data into outbreak tracking and forecasting. The authors argue these pandemic tools could become standing public health assets for the next emergency, if protocols are revised now.
pmc-13581547:
Xiang Ji and co-authors review whether stimulating a nerve in the neck, timed with training, can restore shoulder movement after stroke, in a paper from 2026. Shoulder weakness limits reaching, self-care, and the use of walking aids. The method pairs brief pulses to the vagus nerve with task practice.

Trials show the pairing improves overall arm function in some people with lasting stroke effects, and it has gained approval for arm impairment. Its effect on the shoulder alone is less clear. The review reads the method through a network that links brain movement areas to a neck spinal segment and then to shoulder muscles. Animal work shows timed pulses reshape movement maps in the brain. The authors set out how shoulder-specific trials should be run.
pmc-13581747:
Huige Ren, Weihao Ou, and eight co-authors feed a helpful bacterium to young channel catfish. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, runs an eight-week feeding trial. One group ate plain feed, and the other got feed with live Bacillus coagulans. Each diet went to three tanks of fish.

The fed group turned feed into growth more cheaply. Gut enzymes that break down food rose in activity. Signs of cell strain in the gut fell. Genes that seal the gut wall also switched on more strongly. The results suggest the bacterium guards the gut barrier while aiding growth, a plus for fish farming.
pmc-13581947:
Hui Shi and co-authors predict a growth marker in thyroid cancer from ultrasound image patterns before surgery, in this 2026 paper. The marker, Ki-67, flags how fast tumor cells divide. Knowing its level early helps plan treatment, but tissue tests come late.

Six hundred twenty-seven patients with confirmed papillary thyroid cancer were split into training and test sets. Models blended image features, standard scan signs, and two gene mutation results. The full blend beat every partial model, reaching the best accuracy and the lowest error score. The authors read this as a practical pre-surgery aid for judging tumor pace.
pmc-13582147:
A mouth cancer's signal markers can differ from place to place inside the same patient, and that patchiness can mislead treatment choices. Cornelius Busse and eight co-authors study two markers in oral squamous cell carcinoma in this 2026 paper. One marker, PD-L1, forecasts response to immune drugs, while the second, c-MET, is a growth signal also under study.

The team stained tumor samples from fifty-nine patients and, for twenty-four of them, matched samples from lymph node spread. Both markers appeared often in the main tumors but at clearly lower levels in the matched node deposits. The authors also checked links with standard clinical traits. Their results warn that a biopsy from the main tumor alone may overstate the markers where the cancer has spread, which matters when immune therapy is chosen.
pmc-13582247:
Jinghua Jiao and five co-authors scan drug harm reports from three lands for cases of delirium caused by drugs. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Delirium is a sudden clouded state of mind that can often be stopped if risks are caught in time. Older adults face the most risk.

They search large report banks from the United States, Japan, and Canada, each with years of data. Reports were most common in women and in those past sixty years of age. Drugs for the mind and for pain gave the strongest and most shared signals. Some single drugs stood out in all three banks. Most cases began soon after drug use, which points to a swift effect.
pmc-13582447:
Mi-Young Park and four co-authors test a mental trick for cutting alcohol craving in this two thousand twenty-six study. Craving is a core force that keeps problem drinking going. It often rides on vivid inner images of drinking. If a task loads the mind's visual workspace, those images may lose their grip. The team recruited fifty problem drinkers, screened with a standard test.

Half the group did a block-tapping task that loads visual memory. The other half did a matched task with no load. The team measured craving by self-report and tracked eye movements to gauge attention to alcohol cues. They took readings before and after the task. The design tests whether a brief visual chore can blunt both urge and attention. Such a tool could aid therapy for alcohol use disorder.
pmc-13583047: Angus Lane and Alexandra Stewart report a teen case where two grave ills struck at once. Lemierre's syndrome, a throat illness with clots, came with bone rot at the skull base. Both came from the germ Arcanobacterium haemolyticum in a teen with a sound body guard. Long, high-dose ceftriaxone then brought gallbladder swelling as a side harm. Their report from twenty twenty-six warns doctors to think of this germ in deep head and neck ills, even in sound hosts.
pmc-13583147:
Some bacteria live on rare earth metals, and they pick favorites among them with striking consistency. Linda Gorniak and co-authors study one such strain in this 2026 paper, feeding it different minerals, an alloy, and pure compounds. Whatever the source, the microbe enriched the light lanthanides, the metals it needs to burn methanol.

Gene activity shifted with the source type, showing the discrimination works at several layers at once: freeing the metals, taking them up, and storing them around the cell core. Such microbes could turn locked mineral stores into shared food for whole communities. The authors link the talent to greener mining of metals the energy transition needs. Sorting at the door, they show, is only part of the story.
pmc-13583247:
Haitao Yu and co-authors report a rare case of poisoning by the pesticide pyridaben, in a 2026 case report. A woman in her early fifties was found unconscious, in a coma with fixed, wide pupils. That picture first suggested a severe brain event, but brain scans were normal.

Blood tests showed very severe acid build-up, a key clue. Family reports and a container found at home pointed to the pesticide, taken after a family dispute. Her state worsened with low blood pressure and seizures. Care included a breathing tube, drugs, and blood cleaning by two methods. Her acid levels cleared within hours, she woke within a day, and she left hospital after a full recovery. The authors warn that this poisoning can mimic brain herniation.
pmc-13583747:
Systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE, is an autoimmune disease that attacks many organs, and its link to stroke has been debated. Jingya Zhang and co-authors pooled the evidence in a 2026 meta-analysis of twenty-five cohort studies covering more than five million people. They compared rates of overall stroke, blocked-artery stroke, and bleeding stroke in people with and without the disease.

Patients with SLE had about two and a half times the risk of stroke overall. Both stroke types were also raised, each more than doubling. Studies differed a lot from each other, but checks showed the finding was robust and not clearly skewed by publication bias. The authors call for stroke prevention attention in lupus care.
pmc-13584247:
Yan and co-authors trace a three-part RNA circuit in severe childhood pneumonia, in this 2026 study. The lung infection's molecular drivers remain undefined. Blood samples from young patients and healthy controls were compared for a long non-coding RNA called EMX2OS, a microRNA named miR-34c-5p, and a protein-coding gene, TBL1XR1, thought to be chained together.

The circuit ran hot in patients: EMX2OS and TBL1XR1 were upregulated while the microRNA was suppressed, and EMX2OS levels carried diagnostic value. In lung cells provoked with bacterial toxin, the same pattern accompanied cell death. It also brought inflammatory cytokine release, oxidative stress, and signs of ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. Silencing EMX2OS reversed the damage, and binding assays confirmed the chain: EMX2OS sponges up the microRNA, freeing TBL1XR1 to rise. The authors propose the axis as a biomarker and drug target.
pmc-13584447:
Black soldier flies are farmed worldwide as protein for animal feed, and breeders now want to improve them the way farmers improved cattle. Donkpegan and co-authors run a pilot breeding program under industrial conditions and measure how heritable the useful traits are.

Over seven generations they tracked 15,179 flies from 266 families, weighing larvae, pupae, and adults and counting eggs. Heritability varied wildly by trait: larval weight under restricted feeding scored 0.58, egg number 0.43, thorax size 0.40, while female weight at emergence was nearly zero. Larval weight gains dragged thorax size and egg number along favorably. Selection on larval weight gave early genetic improvement, though inbreeding crept in. The authors judge pedigree selection workable on the farm scale, with care.
pmc-13584547:
Jie Mei and co-authors publish a correction to their earlier study on a gene mark that may flag hot tumors for immune care in lung cancer, in a notice from 2026. The original study linked the mark, HLA-DRA, to reply to a class of immune drugs.

One panel in a key figure had been pasted twice by mistake during layout work. The notice prints the fixed figure with the right panel in place. The authors state plainly that the fix does not change the study findings. The original article has been updated to match.
pmc-13584847:
Megha Kokane and colleagues build a set of new pyrazole-based compounds and test them against inflammation and tuberculosis. Pyrazoles are ring-shaped building blocks common in drug design. Using microwave heating, a greener and faster way to run reactions, the team made a family of related compounds and confirmed each structure with several standard lab readings.

Two compounds stood out for calming inflammation, cutting levels of the COX-2 protein, a key driver of pain and swelling, at every dose tried. Two others stopped tuberculosis germs at the lowest dose tested, matching the standard drug pyrazinamide. Computer docking, which fits each compound into the COX-2 pocket on screen, backed the lab results. The authors see the family as a starting point for dual-purpose drug work.
pmc-13584947:
Li and co-authors examine how chemotherapy might alter the course of bipolar disorder through the gut. Bipolar disorder and cancer share traits such as immune faults, gut microbe shifts, and chronic inflammation. Chemotherapy, a main cancer treatment, can strongly reshape gut microbes and weaken the gut barrier.

Those gut changes can feed body-wide inflammation. Yet little work asks if such shifts change how bipolar disorder develops in a patient with cancer. The authors trace this gut, microbe, and inflammation axis and weigh what it may mean for mood care during and after chemotherapy.
pmc-13585247:
Harrington and nine co-authors describe how they designed a phone app with young women and pharmacy staff in Kenya. The app, called the Mara Divas App, helps girls and young women aged 15 to 24 choose birth control at community pharmacies. The team ran four full-day design workshops with 33 young women and 10 pharmacy providers.

Journey mapping in the workshops showed that fear of stigma shadowed the whole pharmacy visit, and that many young women knew little about their options. Friendly, private service mattered most to them. The group added video and visual content in three languages, easier navigation, and a confident tone. Women seeking emergency contraception needed a strong reason to engage at all.
pmc-13585647:
Maria Nowak-Ciołek and six co-authors follow girls with ovarian hormone disorder into adulthood in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Polycystic ovary syndrome often starts in the teen years. Its forms differ: some combine high male hormones with irregular cycles, others are milder. The team asked whether the fuller teen forms predict worse adult mental health. They traced women once treated in pediatric hormone wards.

Records gave teen diagnoses, hormone profiles, and other conditions. Adult surveys measured mental health and quality of life. The full-form group was set against milder forms and an at-risk group. Long follow-up of teen endocrine patients is rare. The results can shape counseling at first diagnosis. Pediatric and adult endocrinologists share the audience.
pmc-13585747:
Sheng Li and five co-authors surveyed healthcare workers in private hospitals in Lanzhou, China, about resilience, job satisfaction, and anxiety, in this 2026 study. Private hospital staff face heavy demands, and how these three factors connect was poorly mapped. The survey covered 1,263 workers across ten hospitals.

Workers with stronger resilience reported higher job satisfaction and lower anxiety scores. Job satisfaction also tracked with lower anxiety, and it carried part of the link between resilience and anxiety. Because the survey took one snapshot in time, the authors cannot say which factor drives which. They call for studies that follow workers over time, and they suggest that supporting both personal resilience and day-to-day job experience may ease anxiety in this workforce.
pmc-13585947:
Three authors compare dog elbow scan poses in a 2026 study of dead stock. Pose and beam strength shape scan grade, yet set checks were thin. Twenty dogs gave 40 elbows, each scanned on back and on side at one beam grade, with a sub-set at twice that grade.

Side pose won on all four sharp marks at the base grade in the reads. Twice beam strength gave no firm lift in each pose. Side pose at base grade still beat back pose at twice grade, and eyes near all picked side pose.
pmc-13586047:
Susan J. Keam profiles icotrokinra, the first approved drug in its class for plaque psoriasis. Icotrokinra is a targeted oral peptide that blocks the interleukin-23 receptor, made by Johnson and Johnson with Protagonist for immune-linked diseases. US regulators approved it in March 2026 for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. Eligible patients are adults and children aged 12 and older, weighing at least 40 kg, who qualify for body-wide treatment or light therapy.

It is also under review in Europe and Canada. This 2026 report recaps the development steps behind the first approval, from early studies to the March 17, 2026 US decision. The author presents the oral peptide as a new option next to shots, offering targeted blockade without injections for psoriasis patients who qualify.
pmc-13586447:
Mahyra da Paixão e Silva and co-authors count in 2026 a decade of work on ultraviolet light to clean apples and apple juice. Apples are rich in fiber and vitamins but spoil fast and brown with ease. UV-C light can kill germs with no heat, which may guard taste and food value.

The count found 52 papers in ten years. Spain led with 11, then the United States with 9 and China with 7, and one journal ran the most work. Light care kept apples safer and fresher for longer, most of all when paired with other steps. Blocks stay: the light sinks in poorly, no shared dose rules exist, and few tests run at true factory scale. The team calls for plant-scale work.
pmc-13586547:
Yu Wang and fifteen co-authors published a 2026 study of a blood-vesicle marker for the hardest-to-catch form of liver cancer. The usual marker, AFP, misses a subgroup of these liver cancer patients entirely. The team profiled fat-derived molecules called oxylipins inside vesicles shed by tumor tissue, finding signals invisible in bulk tissue. One molecule, 13(S)-HODE, stood out and was confirmed in blood vesicles with a single-molecule platform.

The marker performed better in AFP-negative patients than in positive ones, exactly where help is needed. A machine learning model joining the marker with routine clinical data reached excellent accuracy, with an area score of 0.962. The authors present the vesicle marker as a consistent signal across tissue and blood, ready for diagnostic development.
pmc-13586647:
Jaewoon Jung and co-authors speed up bond constraints in molecular dynamics on graphics chips, in a 2026 paper. Fixing stiff bond lengths lets simulations take bigger time steps, but the solver's math was long done in double precision. Single and mixed precision are in demand now, yet naive cuts raise drift.

For groups with one hydrogen, an exact analytic fix is given. For heavier groups, two tricks help: mix precisions so updates happen in double, or carry values as pairs of singles to cancel rounding. Energy drift stayed at double precision levels. On chips weak at double math, runtimes fell hard. The work balances speed and trust for GPU based dynamics.
pmc-13586847:
Wen-Qi He and co-authors describe a new hydrangea species from Tibet in a 2026 taxonomy paper. The plant was found in Medog County in the Xizang Autonomous Region of China. Field surveys, herbarium specimens, and molecular family trees all support it as a species new to science, named Hydrangea medogensis.

DNA analysis placed it as a distinct lineage within its clade, sister to the rest. It looks most like Hydrangea stylosa but differs in fertile flower traits the authors list. New species from Medog add to the known richness of one of China's most diverse valleys.
pmc-13587047:
Shigetaka Kageyama writes an editorial on chest pain that lingers after opening blocked heart arteries, published in 2026. A Gulf registry had found bypass surgery linked to the least pain at follow-up, a signal the editorial seeks to explain.

Earlier studies found pain in about 40 percent of patients after stent treatment, but the rate split sharply by disease pattern: 52 percent with diffuse disease, 27 percent with focal. Bypass grafts deliver blood beyond many diseased stretches at once, while stents treat single tight spots. Registry bypass patients mostly had three-vessel disease and nearly always had the blocked vessel grafted. Tiny vessel dysfunction can still cause pain after either route. Kageyama asks future studies to record disease pattern and pain at both ends.
pmc-13587247:
Fredric Blavin, Avani Pugazhendhi, Stephen Zuckerman, and John Holahan replace the yes-or-no label for safety net hospitals with a graded index. These hospitals carry the care of uninsured and low-income patients, yet rival definitions pick out different hospitals, confusing research and policy. Using Medicare cost reports, the team blended three burdens into one score: the Medicaid share of revenue, the weight of unpaid care, and the share of low-income Medicare patients.

Hospitals in the top quarter of the index ran negative margins while the bottom quarter stayed in profit. They also held far fewer days of cash and fell into financial distress more often. The index tracked financial health better than five binary definitions and a federal proxy. Hospitals inside large systems fared better than independents at every level. The authors urge policy to protect by measured burden, not by label.
pmc-13587447:
Cate Bailey and colleagues test a new nine-question quality-of-life form in adults with poor mental health. The form, EQ-HWB-9, aims to capture wellbeing across health and social care, not just symptoms. Their 2026 study sat inside a trial of a free meditation app. In it, 865 people were assigned by chance to fill in either the original wording or a revised version. The revised version carried four small changes, including a swapped order for the first two questions.

Every check supported the form's validity in this group. One change did matter: when the activities question came before the mobility question, people read it more broadly, as its makers intended, with answers spread more widely. The other tweaks changed little. The authors back the new order and say country scoring sets are the next need.
pmc-13587547:
Chloé Magnan and co-authors profile a little-known staph bacterium across Europe, in a 2026 study. Staphylococcus pettenkoferi is turning up more often as a human pathogen, but its variety and drug resistance were poorly charted. Working through a European study group, the team sequenced 61 clinical samples from 17 hospitals in five countries, plus two reference strains, and tested drug response by standard methods.

The samples fell into two main family lines. Fewer than seventy percent stayed sensitive to some common drugs, and nearly all resisted one antibiotic, fosfomycin. Eight samples resisted daptomycin and carried changes in genes tied to that drug's action. The authors say the species deserves more clinical respect than it gets.
pmc-13587647:
Sophie Michelis and colleagues built soft, cell-like microparticles that report eating-sac souring in real time. Eater cells swallow germs into sacs, whose steady souring kills germs and shapes immune signals, but current probes vary with the swallowed object and dock used. Their 2026 platform uses beads with set makeup and soft skins, plus one-to-one uptake and two-colour glow pH sensing.

The design links set surface matching to measured inside-cell pH readouts, letting teams follow the onset and course of souring cleanly. The authors present the modular sensors as a direct way to unravel sac workings, splitting what the bead brings from what the cell does, with uses in germ and defence research.
pmc-13588247:
Li Zhou and co-authors built machine learning models to predict leg vein clots in patients with a lung disease flare, for a 2026 paper. People whose chronic lung disease suddenly worsens face higher clot risk from inflammation, bed rest, and clotting changes. The team used records from fifteen hundred such patients at one center. Ultrasound scans split them into those with a deep vein clot and those without.

A feature picking method found fourteen key predictors from the clinical and lab data. Three model types were trained and compared on held out patients. A boosting model did best, though its discrimination was moderate rather than strong. Patients with clots had higher levels of inflammation and clotting markers. A further analysis named the factors that drove the best model's choices, which may help staff watch the highest risk patients more closely.
pmc-13588347:
Pierre-Yves Robillard and co-authors ask why only some cases of poor fetal growth tied to the placenta come with a dangerous blood pressure disorder, in a study from 2026. The disorder, preeclampsia, threatens both mother and baby. The team looked at a huge birth cohort from one maternity center, built over about twenty-four years. More than ninety thousand births went into the record.

About two thousand cases showed growth restriction with abnormal blood flow signs. Only about a quarter of them came with the pressure disorder. Mothers in that group were older and heavier, with more long-term health risks. Past cases of the disorder and kidney disease raised the risk a lot. Smoking and low weight, by contrast, were linked to lower risk of the combined form. The authors say the split points to how some mothers tolerate the strain.
pmc-13588547:
McCallion and co-authors present a 2026 study on how rest around practice changes brain-to-muscle excitability. Twenty-one healthy adults took part in one session of rest, play, then rest again. The play was thirty minutes on a guitar-style game controller, a fine finger task. Magnetic pulses to the brain, paired with muscle recordings, probed two hand muscles before and after each block.

Playing skill improved within the block, as expected. Excitability in one finger muscle rose most clearly after the second rest, beating both earlier readings. Inner brain circuits that brake or boost signals stayed unchanged. The authors suggest quiet rest after practice helps lock in early motor gains.
pmc-13588847:
Ayan Ali, Liann Abu Salman, and Jordana B Cohen wrote a 2026 review of how blood pressure gets measured unequally, and how the errors feed wider health gaps. A wrong reading can misdiagnose hypertension or leave it uncontrolled, and the mistakes are not random. Office technique varies, cuffs come in the wrong sizes, and home or day-long monitors are unevenly available.

The review covers office, ambulatory, home, and new cuffless devices. Hidden forms of hypertension, masked by day and active at night, go unrecognized most in high-risk groups. Cuffless gadgets could widen access but still lack solid validation across skin tones and body types. Fixes range from standard technique to fairer device testing.
pmc-13588947:
Benedikt Fischer and co-authors ask, in a 2026 note, if Canada's 2018 move to free cannabis shifted drink and smoke use as well. Gains so far are mixed: crime and black trade fell, while many health marks rose. Use of cannabis has climbed in a clear way. Hints of small shifts in drink and smoke marks ride with it, yet no proof ties the two in a cause chain. Two pulls could act: swap, where cannabis takes the place of the old pair, or mate, where all rise as one. Past reads back both in spots.

The health load of drink and smoke in Canada is vast. The team calls for a set, hard-math read of the link as part of the full score of the law.
pmc-13589147:
Jean Paul ten Klooster and four colleagues find a recipe that lets chicken gut organoids grow for the long haul. Miniature intestines in a dish let researchers study gut health without live birds, but chicken versions died out after a few weeks and never grew the branching shapes seen in mammals. Their 2026 study rebuilt the growth cocktail from chicken versions of two signal proteins, then added two more growth factors.

The new mix kept embryonic chicken organoids alive for over forty weeks and produced the branching form at last. Blocking a protein called FoxO1 sped growth further. The cultures proved to hold the full cast of gut cell types, stem cells, mucus-making goblet cells, hormone cells, Paneth cells, and absorptive cells, and flat cultures duly secreted mucus. The authors offer the system for screening feed additives and drugs in place of animal trials.
pmc-13589747:
Bingshun Shi and co-authors review unconventional routes by which mammalian cells release proteins, as a design source for fast secretion switches, published in 2026. Gene switches in mammalian cells usually act by making new RNA and protein, which is slow. Secreted output adds folding and transport steps, delaying any response outside the cell even more.

Faster switches act on proteins that are already made, by controlling their holding, storage, or release. Most current designs use the classical route through the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi. That route brings limits in host range, cargo fit, and leakage. The review argues that unconventional secretion paths place control closer to final export. That shift could widen the designs available for mammalian secretion control.
pmc-13590047:
Bacary Djilocalisse Sadio and co-authors look for hepatitis E virus in pigs in Senegal, in a 2026 study. Little was known about the virus there, even after a human outbreak in 2014. The team took blood from 1,600 pigs at slaughter between late 2018 and the end of 2019 and tested it for viral RNA and for antibodies.

Virus RNA turned up in 69 samples, and every strain they could read belonged to genotype 3, a type known to pass from pigs to people. Among the RNA-negative pigs they checked, over three quarters carried antibodies, showing wide past exposure. The authors call pigs a key reservoir and urge joint human and animal surveillance.
pmc-13590247:
Bryan Salvador Sol and colleagues report the case of a 50 year old woman whose nails were slowly ruined on 16 fingers and toes. The harm caused pain and made walking hard. Fungus tests came back clear more than once, which pointed the team toward nail lichen planus, a rare swelling disorder of the nail. A biopsy of the nail root confirmed that call.

Care began with prednisone by mouth, yet her nails did not improve. The team then used hydroxychloroquine each day plus a strong steroid cream. Over 12 months her pain eased, swelling around the nails fell, and new nail plates grew in less damaged. Sol and colleagues urge early biopsy when many nails fail and fungus tests stay clear, since delay can scar the nail for good.
pmc-13591047:
Vlad Dincă leads a large team presenting, in 2026, the full genome of the Argent and Sable moth. The moth lives in bogs and damp mountain woods across northern lands, and its caterpillars feed inside spun leaf bags on blueberry kin and other shrubs. The team sequenced one male moth caught in North Karelia, Finland. Part of a wider project on European butterflies and moths, the work resolves both copies of the genome.

Each copy runs to roughly 590 million bases, and nearly all of the first copy sits in 31 chromosome sized pieces, including the Z sex chromosome. The small mitochondrial genome was also completed. Dincă and the team offer the assembly as a base for studies of moth evolution and survival as bog habitats shrink.
pmc-13591147:
Chunxiao Zhao and co-authors review calcium mishandling in the failing heart in a 2026 paper. Each heartbeat is a calcium story: ions flood in to trigger contraction, then are pumped away for relaxation. In heart failure that cycle breaks down, and overload poisons the cell.

The review walks the machinery in three layers: release channels, the storehouse pump that refills the cell's calcium vault, and helper exchangers and gates. Two nerve receptors that tune the whole loop get their due. Drugs and gene therapies aimed at single parts are weighed, along with why single targets stall in translation. Restoring balance, not just boosting force, is the authors' thesis.
pmc-13591547:
Ji Heun Lee and four co-authors test a long course of a stress kinase blocker in mice with a muscle wasting illness. The illness breaks muscle over time, and that kinase was found switched on in sick muscle. They gave the blocker for about half a year to sick and healthy mice.

Sick muscle stayed weak and stiff with no gain from the drug. Scar area dipped a bit, but scar proteins and signals did not fall. The kinase stayed on despite the drug. The dose was too weak to change the course, they conclude.
pmc-13591747:
Zewen Wang leads a team building an AI framework that hunts new drugs inside traditional Chinese medicine by starting from whole body effects. Target first drug hunting often misses, so the team worked backward from the traits and uses that Chinese herbal practice records. Their system fuses data on herbs, compounds, targets, pathways, and effects, holding over 800,000 links across thousands of herbs. Two learning engines sit at its core.

One network predicts which targets a compound will hit, beating the best prior method clearly on recall tests. A second engine sifts 168 algorithms to predict herb traits from their effects. As a proof, the system flagged a fat lowering effect for a classic herb, and lab tests on fatty liver cells bore it out, Wang and the team report.
pmc-13592847:
Tatjana Đorđević and three co-authors review plant by-products as sources of blood sugar lowering compounds in this 2026 paper. Farms and food plants throw away peels, husks, and bran in huge amounts. Those scraps carry polyphenols, active proteins, and fibers that can blunt blood sugar rises. The review weighs them as raw material for diabetes care and functional foods. It also weighs the economics of collecting and processing them.

pmc-13593147:

pmc-13593847:

pmc-13594447:
Ulrika Birgersdotter-Green and colleagues wrote back to a letter that probed their test of an AI tool for heart-rhythm fault spotting with the Assert-IQ heart monitor. pmc-13594547:

pmc-13594647:

pmc-13594847:

pmc-13594947:

pmc-13595147:

pmc-13597547:
Mary P Choules and co-authors built a computer model of how the antifungal drug isavuconazole behaves in the body. They used it to ask a question. pmc-13598347:

pmc-13598447:
Ayrton Bangolo and co-authors follow every myeloma patient who started the CAR T-cell path at one center, not just those who reached treatment, in this 2026 study. Disease outside the bone marrow marked three quarters of the non-infused group, far above the infused share, and a leukemia-like form was also commoner there. pmc-13598547:
Eight authors present a study dated two thousand twenty-six on late-life work patterns and brain health. Many Americans face job insecurity near retirement, while staying at work may protect thinking skills. The authors ask how combined paths of work and insecurity relate to later cognition.

Six path groups emerged for each sex. Among women, several paths, including self-employment and early retirement, came with lower memory and executive scores than a secure path to retirement.
pmc-13598647:

A test reaction that opens ring compounds ran faster on the flawed sponges, thanks to open active sites. The dial gives builders finer control of sponge traits.
pmc-13599047:
Maria Eduarda Soares Arcaro and co-authors established Brazilian reference values for the TOMASS test, a standardized bedside measure of how efficiently a person chews and swallows a solid cracker. Ninety-nine healthy adults across three age groups were filmed performing the test, which counts bites, chewing cycles, and swallows and times the whole task.

Older adults differed measurably from younger ones. Chewing cycles separated the youngest group from those over sixty. Total time separated the oldest group from both younger groups. pmc-13599647:
Meng Feng and co-authors link, in a 2026 study, frequent power outages in Maryland to higher hospital rates for mental health crises. Short failures of one to three hours, when frequent, drove much of the link. Grid reliability, the authors argue, is a health issue, not just an engineering one.
pmc-13599747:

He had lost one kidney and part of the other, so his reserve was thin. During care his kidney values worsened and a blood test turned strongly positive for a vessel-attack marker.

pmc-13600047:
Rosa Angela Fabio, Miriam Ricciardello, and Giulia Picciotto dig into why university students put off their work, in this 2026 study. Delaying study harms grades and well-being, and many traits have been blamed. pmc-13601247:
Sisi Cao and a large team target a gene that drives lung cancer spread. Their study from twenty twenty-six examines FOXC1 in metastatic disease. Spread, not the primary tumour, causes most lung cancer deaths. FOXC1 was known to promote cancer growth generally.

pmc-13602047:

A general segmentation model then outlined thirteen organs and targets on both scan types. Outlines from cleaned scans scored closer to clinician drawn ones on standard overlap and distance measures. Gains were clear in organs such as the prostate, bladder, and rectum. The authors argue image quality work pays off in AI accuracy.
pmc-13602147:
Narin Carmel-Neiderman and co-authors test a heat treatment for noses hooked on decongestant sprays in a 2026 study. Overuse of the sprays causes its own chronic blockage, a condition tied to swollen lower turbinates. Radiofrequency ablation shrinks that tissue in an office visit.

pmc-13603147:
Massimo Rossi and co-authors published a review paper in 2026 on the health of the spinal muscles in people with chronic low back pain. Scans of the spine alone do not explain why pain and limits vary so much between patients. The muscles that brace the spine may carry much of the missing story.

pmc-13603247:

Two whole classes took part with no random split: one class of 26 teens got the forest care, and one of 28 kept normal school acts. Anxiety was scored on a known child scale at the start and four checks after. The pilot tests ease of running the care and first hints of gain.
pmc-13603347:

Greenness fell significantly in both new and old districts, while surface temperature rose in both, rising faster in new areas. Plant loss in expanding districts eased as cities developed, and one mature stage even reversed the trend outside the largest city. The study links cooling policy to each city's stage.
pmc-13603547:
Jing Huang, Teng Zhang, and their co-authors compared gut microbes and gene activity in wild and farmed pearl oysters. Their 2026 study uses the species Pinctada maxima, prized for pearls. pmc-13603747:

pmc-13603847:

Eating any of these with the spinach raised uptake by about half or more. More eggs did not help more, and egg whites or oil worked as well as whole eggs. Eggs eaten three hours later did nothing. Timing, not dose or food type, proved to be the key.
pmc-13604247:
Hong Xu, Lijie Jiang, Yuanjun Zhang, and Jingqing Hu test a plant compound in diabetic mice. Their study is from two thousand twenty-six. pmc-13605147:

pmc-13605247:

pmc-13605347:

pmc-13605547:

pmc-13605847:

pmc-13605947:

pmc-13606147:

pmc-13606347:

pmc-13606847:

pmc-13607547:

pmc-13608047:

pmc-13608147:

pmc-13608247:

pmc-13610147:

pmc-13610347:

pmc-13610547:

pmc-13611047:

pmc-13612347:

pmc-13612847:

pmc-13613347:

pmc-13614147:

pmc-13614747:

pmc-13614947:

pmc-13615547:

pmc-13616247:

pmc-13616447:

pmc-13616547:

pmc-13616647:

pmc-13616747:

pmc-13616847:

pmc-13616947:

pmc-13617247:

pmc-13617347:

pmc-13618347:

pmc-13618947:

pmc-13619347:

pmc-13619647:

pmc-13619947:

pmc-13620847:

pmc-13621347:

pmc-13621547:

pmc-13623147:

pmc-13624047:

pmc-13624547:

pmc-13625947:

pmc-13626147:

pmc-13626247:

pmc-13626547:

pmc-13627247:

pmc-13627347:

pmc-13628547:

pmc-13629947:

pmc-13630347:

pmc-13630647:

pmc-13630847:

pmc-13631247:

pmc-13631347:

pmc-13631847:

pmc-13631947:

pmc-13632847:

The team used a nationally representative survey of 3,385 adults aged sixty and older. They scored five hardships before age fifteen: emotional abuse, domestic violence, food scarcity, poor childhood health, and forced migration from armed conflict.

Among women, emotional abuse, domestic violence, food scarcity, and poor childhood health each raised the odds of cardiovascular disease. Among men, forced childhood migration raised risks of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and hypertension. Forced migration also tracked with faster biological aging, more strongly in women, and cumulative hardship showed dose-response patterns.
pmc-13633147:
Luca Guerra and eight colleagues published this 2026 expert consensus on using PET scans to find lymphoma patients who should get cell therapy early. The lymphoma type, diffuse large B-cell, often returns after first treatment or never fully responds. CAR-T therapy, which retools a patient's own immune cells, can cure some of these patients, yet referral often comes late. The panel of imaging specialists and blood cancer doctors reviewed evidence on scan timing and measures.

Scans at diagnosis give tumor volume measures that sharpen risk estimates beyond standard scores. Scans during treatment can flag high-risk patients early through standard rating scales and changes in tumor uptake. A final scan after treatment remains essential for judging response. The panel calls the scan a central marker for this disease. They also demand shared standards for scanning and reporting so results match between hospitals.
pmc-13635047:
Marcus Varanis and three colleagues published this 2026 modeling study refining a classic math description of the circulation. Simple lumped models treat the heart and vessels as an electrical-style circuit, which keeps them fast and readable. Most versions assume artery stretchiness stays fixed, yet real arteries stiffen as pressure climbs. The team made aortic stretchiness vary with pressure in their closed-loop model of the heart, body, and lung circuits.

Under normal settings, the new model matched the classic one almost exactly, producing sensible pressures and flows. Away from that point, the rule changed mainly the pulse near the heart, while average pressure, stroke volume, and output stayed steady. Adjusting single parts reproduced the waveform fingerprints of a leaking aortic valve and stiffened arteries. The authors offer the compact model as a test bench for scenarios that would be impractical or unethical to stage in people.
pmc-13635447:
Jie Zheng, Shanhong Tang, and Juan Zhou report a case of stomach vein bleeding caused by pressure backup on the body's left side, in a 2026 case report. The condition, sinistral portal hypertension, followed repeated pancreas inflammation and made stomach varices bleed again and again. Glue injection through a scope is the usual rescue for such bleeding but often fails to hold.

Reasoning from the blood flow pattern, the team chose to remove the spleen, which removes the pathological circuit feeding the varices. The report weighs that option against scope therapy and partial spleen artery blocking. The authors offer the hemodynamic view as a guide for choosing treatment in similar patients.
pmc-13638047:
Lijuan Zheng and nineteen colleagues build a non-invasive test for alveolar echinococcosis, a dangerous parasitic disease caused by a tapeworm's larval stage in animal hosts. Diagnosis usually leans on blood antibody tests, which miss some patients and cannot separate active infection from old exposure. The team targeted a protein the parasite secretes abundantly. They raised monoclonal antibodies and pinpointed two short stretches of the protein that sit exposed on its surface.

Those two target stretches are strictly conserved across the parasite genus yet differ sharply from the matching host protein, promising clean recognition. Two test formats followed. The standout was a sandwich test that detects the protein directly in feces, catching most infections in mouse samples at an early stage with precise, repeatable readings. The authors present the proof of concept as a path toward screening animal hosts without blood draws.
pmc-13639047:
Zexuan Wu and eleven colleagues published a 2026 mouse study identifying the protein SORBS2 as a guardian of the heart's relaxation phase. Failure of the heart to relax properly underlies a common form of heart failure, yet the cell-level causes remain unclear.

Mice lacking SORBS2 in heart muscle cells developed worsening relaxation problems while pumping strength stayed normal, and many died early. Restoring the protein reversed the relaxation defects and extended life. The protein links cell adhesion, the internal skeleton, and calcium handling; without it, fibers scar and stiffen. A drug blocking one part of that chain partly rescued relaxation.
pmc-13639647:
Naoyuki Iwahashi and one colleague present a 2026 perspective arguing that mutant p53, the protein altered in nearly half of human cancers, can behave like an amyloid disease protein. Many cancer-linked mutants lose their shape, expose sticky segments, and clump into fibers that may seed further misfolding.

Such clumps have been found in ovarian, breast, and lung tumors and track with aggressive disease and poor outcomes. The authors propose treatments that block clumping, restore folding, clear misfolded protein, or stop spread between cells. Their framing borrows from brain disease research to open a new front in precision oncology.
pmc-13640647:
Rochel Hecht and a large team reported in 2026 on a new flu vaccine design that targets a part of the virus called neuraminidase. Most work on a broad flu vaccine has focused on a different surface part. Their aim was to steer the immune response toward a spot on neuraminidase that stays much the same across strains.

They added extra sugar chains to hide other spots and leave the shared spot open. In mice, the new design drew responses as strong as the normal form, but broader across old and new strains. One antibody they found bound a hidden shared spot and partly shielded mice from a harsh flu challenge.
pmc-13642247:
Leihong Wu and two colleagues present GANomics, a 2026 tool that turns gene data from old lab chips into the form made by modern gene reading, and back again. Labs hold decades of chip data that cannot be mixed with new data as they stand.

The system learns from a few samples run on both kinds of gear. It can then swap data either way. In one cancer group of 498 samples and about ten thousand genes, swapped data matched real data well with as few as ten shared samples. Five more data sets gave the same result. Old data can thus join new studies.
pmc-13642947:
Junyuan Wang and twelve colleagues present a 2026 study of RDP3, a food-derived peptide that speeds healing of oral ulcers. Mouth ulcers are common and painful, and current products mostly soothe symptoms rather than repair tissue in several ways at once.

At very low concentration the peptide accelerated mucosal repair in animals and cells and steadied the mouth's microbe balance. It works by blocking part of the interleukin-2 receptor, which quiets a harmful signaling route and stops an inflammatory cell-death process called pyroptosis. Less tissue burned away, inflammation eased, and the lining regrew. The authors position RDP3 as a multifunction ulcer therapy candidate.
pmc-13643547:
Noman, Jain, and Bin Abdulhak comment on a case in which two heart valve implants, placed years apart, ended up harming the heart. An 82-year-old woman had first received a tissue valve for one heart valve. Later, a new valve was placed through a leg artery for a second valve nearby.

The balloon used to open the second valve pressed against the first implant. The gap between the two valves was very small, only a few finger widths of space at the heart's scale. The push tore tissue between the valves and formed a contained leak in the heart wall. The writers draw three lessons from the case. The first is about anatomy: teams should check the space between old and new valves with great care before the procedure.
pmc-13644447:
Gianna Mastrofini and co-authors ran a controlled trial of a two-part supplement plan, reported in 2026. Stress and poor sleep are common, and each can make the other worse. One part of the plan uses plant extracts taken in the morning for stress. The other part, taken at night, uses compounds sold for sleep.

Just over one hundred healthy, active adults took part for four weeks. They were split into four groups, from both parts active to both parts dummy pills. The team tracked daily stress, mood, and sleep by survey and by a wearable device. The design lets readers see what each part adds on its own and what the pair does together.
pmc-13646147:
Rawan Abdul Mahdi Neyef Al-Saliti and five colleagues test a stress inoculation program for performance anxiety among physical education students at Ajloun National University in Jordan. Thirty students took part in a quasi-experimental study with a comparison group and a later follow-up check. The program taught coping in three stages: learning about stress, practicing mental and behavioral skills, and applying those skills to real performance situations. A purpose-built scale measured anxiety before and after.

Students who received the training reported clearly lower performance anxiety than the comparison group after the program. The gain was still present at follow-up, with no meaningful drift back. The authors conclude that stress inoculation works for this group and may help students face exams, demonstrations, and teaching practice with steadier nerves. They offer the staged program as a model other university courses could adapt.
pmc-13646847:
